title: 🌅 WOW, MAINE! 😍 The Best Sunrise in America Can Be Found Right Here in Our State!
text:
Maine Is the Best Place in the U.S. to Watch the Sunrise
There are plenty of reasons to love living in Maine, from our rocky coastline and beautiful beaches to the spectacular fall foliage, which is peaking right now. But did you know Maine is also home to one of America's most famous places to watch the sunrise?
If you're willing to get up before the crack of dawn, Cadillac Mountain in Acadia National Park offers a sunrise experience that's tough to beat!
Read More: 15 Fast Food Restaurants We Wish Would Come To Bangor, Maine
Standing 1,530 feet above sea level, Cadillac Mountain is the tallest mountain on the U.S. Atlantic coast north of Brazil. And the views from the summit? Mind-blowing!
Watching the sky turn shades of pink, orange, and gold as the sun rises over the Atlantic Ocean is a memory you won't soon forget. Below you, you'll see islands, bays, and miles of Maine's stunning coastline. It's the kind of view that makes crawling out of bed that early totally worth it!
And there's so much more to explore at Acadia, no matter the season. From spring through fall, visitors can enjoy scenic drives along the park's paved loop road, hiking, bicycling, and horseback riding on carriage roads. You can also try rock climbing, kayaking, canoeing, swimming at Sand Beach or Echo Lake, and guided boat tours along the coast.
When winter rolls around, the fun doesn't stop. Cross-country skiing, snowshoeing, snowmobiling, and ice fishing are just some of the activities to enjoy.
Ready to plan a family adventure? Check out the official Acadia National Park website for more information.
Keep in mind that depending on the season, you may need a vehicle reservation to drive Cadillac Summit Road, so it's worth checking ahead before you go.
Whether you're a lifelong Mainer or just visiting, watching the sunrise from Cadillac Mountain is an unforgettable way to experience the natural beauty of the 207.
Sure, getting out of bed that early isn't easy. But when you're standing above the Atlantic Ocean, watching the world wake up, you'll probably agree it's worth every minute!

title: Democrats sue to block Trump administration from usurping states' authority to administer elections
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Two weeks from the midterm elections, Democratic Party leaders are suing in federal court to block President Donald Trump’s administration from usurping states’ authority to administer elections or trying to intimidate state and local election officials into complying with illegal demands.
The lawsuit, filed Tuesday in Washington, seeks a court order barring the administration from purging legally registered voters from statewide voter registration lists or denying ballots to legally registered voters.
The plaintiffs, including Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, also ask for a ruling that the administration has illegally threatened state election officials with prosecution before the Nov. 3 election.
The lawsuit cites the Justice Department’s recent actions in California, where it sued to block state election officials from counting mail-in ballots cast by people whom the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
“For over a decade now, President Donald J. Trump has bombarded the American people with lies and misinformation about American elections and voter fraud,” the suit says. “While these lies have been debunked at every turn, that has never deterred the President from employing them as a pretext to seize control over elections, even as courts overwhelmingly reject that effort.”
The Justice Department said in a statement that election integrity is a top priority for the administration and the department’s actions on that front are grounded in law and under court litigation.
The Democratic leaders’ lawsuit was assigned to Chief Judge James Boasberg, who has been vilified by the White House for rulings against the Trump administration since the start of the Republican president’s second term.
The suit’s other plaintiffs are the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Governors Association. Its named defendants are Trump, the Justice Department, Attorney General Todd Blanche, the Department of Homeland Security and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

title: Original copy of Declaration of Independence on display in Augusta
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - An original copy of the Declaration of Independence is in Augusta for the next couple of days as part of a statewide tour.
The copy, known as a Dunlap broadside, is one of 26 surviving first printings circulated on July 4, 1776, within hours of ratification.
The copy was left to the Maine Historical Society in 1905 by Dr. John S. H. Fogg and his wife Mary, of Eliot, as part of his historical document collection.
The Maine Historical Society says Dunlaps can be identified by printing mistakes like uneven spacing and irregular inking, reflecting the urgency to share news of America’s independence.
Printing reflected urgency of the moment
Steve Bromage, the executive director of the Maine Historical Society, said the printing reflected the speed of communication at the time.
“It really had the immediacy and the relative speed of an email or tweet in its own time. Approximately 200 copies were printed that night and sent out to the colonies the next day, where they were posted, read out loud, and reprinted in subsequent editions,” Bromage said.
The display also includes other early printings of the Declaration from Hallowell and Salem, Massachusetts, as well as court documents from Lincoln and York County during the Revolution.
The documents will be on display at the Maine State Archives Building through Oct. 23 before making their final tour stop at Bowdoin College.

title: Judge sides with state regulators on Juniper Ridge Landfill expansion
text:
OLD TOWN, Maine (WABI) - Penobscot County Superior Court ruling clears the way for Juniper Ridge Landfill’s expansion to move forward, siding with state regulators.
The decision leaves the Department of Environmental Protection’s approval in place.
Expansion details
The proposed expansion would add roughly 11.9 million cubic yards of capacity to Juniper Ridge, enough to hold the equivalent of 8.6 Empire State Buildings worth of trash.
The state-owned landfill, operated by Casella Waste Systems, has long drawn concerns over PFAS contamination.
Casella has confirmed plans to move that treatment system to another landfill, located 20 miles away, and seek approval through a separate permitting process. That change raises further questions about how and when PFAS-contaminated wastewater will be treated.
“This ruling is a setback, but it can’t bury the truth that the Penobscot Nation and local residents have brought into the open – that this landfill is part of a broken system that puts polluters’ wallets over people’s health,” said Alex St. Pierre, vice president for environmental justice at CLF. “The knowledge, persistence, and power of these communities have already shifted the conversation – and that momentum will carry forward until justice is served.”
“We have fought pollution, injustice, and decades of harm to heal the Penobscot River, a relative that has sustained our people since time immemorial and continues to sustain communities across Maine,” said Kirk E. Francis, Penobscot Nation Tribal Chief. “We are not asking the state to undo generations of harm overnight. We are asking it not to take us backward. Our cultural survival is tied to the health of the Penobscot River, and there is too much at stake to keep adding to the harms it already carries.”
CLF and Penobscot Nation say they are reviewing the ruling and evaluating next steps.

title: LETTERS: Takes exception about “founding fathers”
text:
To the editor:
Every month I have reason to cross from the coast to the Augusta area via Route 3. I enjoy making a stop at Tobey’s for a donut and a cuppa, but especially to read a copy of The Town Line.
I might live in Northport, but I am always interested to learn how other towns organize themselves and operate. Really, all government is local!
Your October 15, 2026, issue had a commentary by Sheldon Goodine, of China: Election Day: November 2026, with some of the history of why we vote on the day and the date that we do – I always learn something new every day!
But I do take exception with Mr. Goodine about this: “With early voting and mail in votes, our founding fathers would be appalled at what is happening today.”
Actually, I think they would be very happy that citizens did not have to take up to two days to travel to vote, and two days back to home, away from their farm. We have harnessed modern technology to make voting available to everyone eligible, and our vote should reflect the range of opinions. He goes on to make unsubstantiated claims about “opportunity to cheat” in voting. And “Boxes of votes unloaded from a personal vehicle two or three days after election day…”
I take exception, because of my own experience as an election clerk in my town, is that every single ballot must be accounted for (as ironically, in the very same issue, another article by Roland Hallee points out “Ballots: Their Journey“).
The Town Clerk and Deputy Clerk must answer to the Secretary of State’s office, as well as our Select Board. The diverse crew of the warden and the many “Ladies” and (the few) of us gentlemen, all are there to “watch each other,” by being enrolled in a balance of parties. Though we are all friendly to each other, we all recognize we are there to perform a sacred duty. We even must swear an oath to that effect.
Perhaps Mr. Goodine would want to try a stint as an Election Clerk, and learn the ins and outs of the process? He might have a late night or two each year emptying the tabulating machine, triple counting stacks of ballots, checking tally tapes, and sometimes counting again, if something does not add up. That is how I got into this work. I complained about the process and was invited to help out. The rest is history.
Paul Sheridan
Northport

title: Man sentenced to 30 years for role in smuggling tragedy that killed 53 people in Texas
text:
(AP) - A federal judge on Tuesday sentenced a Guatemalan man extradited to the U.S. over his role in a 2022 human smuggling attempt that ended in the deaths of 53 migrants who had been transported in a sweltering tractor-trailer in Texas.
U.S. and Guatemalan prosecutors called Rigoberto Ramon Miranda Orozco’s sentencing another step toward justice in one of the deadliest smuggling attempts along the U.S.-Mexico border. Miranda Orozco, 50, was sentenced to 30 years in prison after admitting to arranging travel and accommodations for two people who died and another who was seriously injured.
Nearly 20 people in the U.S. and Guatemala have been convicted since the discovery of the abandoned trailer full of bodies horrified communities accustomed to seeing their young people leave, trying to flee poverty or violence in Central America and Mexico.
“It was clear that they suffered tremendously in their last few hours on this earth,” U.S. Attorney Justin Simmons told reporters at a news conference following the sentencing.
People tried to ‘claw their way out’ of a trailer with no air conditioning
The trailer’s air conditioning malfunctioned and would not blow cool air to the people trapped inside during the sweltering, three-hour ride in June 2022 from the border city of Laredo to San Antonio, authorities said. Prosecutors have said migrants paid up to $15,000 each to be taken across the U.S. border.
When the abandoned trailer was opened on a remote San Antonio back road, 48 migrants were dead. Another 16 were taken to hospitals, where five more died.
Simmons said investigators found clothing passengers had shed to cool off and claw marks on the trailer’s walls.
“They were literally trying to claw their way out,” he said.
Twenty-one of those who died were from Guatemala, Simmons said.
Miranda Orozco’s attorney, Alfonso Cabanas Jr., called the sentence “very tough.” He said his client was in Guatemala at the time and had no control over the type of transportation the migrants would take to San Antonio nor did he know the air conditioning was malfunctioning.
Cabanas said he doesn’t think harsh punishments will “make a dent” in such operations.
“What we do need is comprehensive immigration reform,” Cabanas said.
Other defendants still await sentencing
U.S. District Judge Orlando Garcia sentenced Miranda Orozco, who was arrested in Guatemala in 2024 and extradited to the U.S. the following year.
He pleaded guilty in July to conspiracy to bring a migrant into the U.S. resulting in death, aiding and abetting bringing a migrant into the U.S. resulting in death, as well as aiding and abetting bringing a migrant into the U.S. resulting in serious bodily injury, prosecutors said.
Simmons said prosecutors in Guatemala were integral in securing convictions for Miranda Orozco and others. Simmons was joined by Guatemalan Attorney General Gabriel García Luna, who reflected on the suffering the migrants inside the tractor-trailer endured.
“They paid for a promise, and those who cashed in on that promise abandoned them to their fate,” García Luna said.
Last year, Felipe Orduna-Torres, described by prosecutors as the leader of the smuggling operations inside the U.S., was sentenced to life in prison in the U.S. Armando Gonzales-Ortega, his top assistant, was sentenced to 83 years.
Sentencing dates have been set for more people, including the truck’s driver.
The tragedy is the deadliest among those that have claimed thousands of lives in recent decades as people attempt to cross the U.S. border from Mexico. Ten migrants died in 2017 after they were trapped inside a truck parked at a Walmart in San Antonio.
In 2003, the bodies of 19 migrants were found in a sweltering truck southeast of San Antonio.
___ This story has been updated to correct the name and age of the man sentenced Tuesday. He is Rigoberto Ramon Miranda Orozco, not Rigoberto Román Miranda-Orozco. And he is 50, not 39.
___
Associated Press writer Laura Turbay contributed to this story.

title: Fake passport websites are charging travelers for free services
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Travelers rushing to renew a passport before an international trip may be vulnerable to scam websites designed to take advantage of that urgency, according to the Better Business Bureau.
Josh Planos, a spokesperson for the Better Business Bureau, said the pressure to receive a passport quickly often drives people toward risky shortcuts.
“In nearly every case, somebody is under the gun and needs to turn around a passport within a matter of weeks and wants to look for every alternative to ensure that it gets to the front doorstep in an adequate amount of time,” Planos said.
Planos said fraudulent websites promise fast turnaround times, then take travelers’ money without ever delivering a passport.
“A lot of folks are turning to websites that really have nothing to do with the government URL, travel.state.gov,” Planos said. “They are looking for third-party sites that charge those expedition fees, and those are really major red flags.”
The official passport application is free to download and file. Copycat sites charge travelers anyway, often disguising the charge as an “expediting” or “processing” fee.
The BBB has collected complaints from consumers who say they were deceived by these sites. One consumer wrote: “I went into the site assuming it was the State.gov site because it resembled it completely, including the URL. I did not notice that it ended as state.com, not state.gov. By the time I had submitted the application for my passport renewal and payment, I noticed that it was a fraud by the language on the confirmation page.”
Planos also cautioned against taking passport photos at home.
“Walgreens offers this service, post office offers this service for free,” Planos said. “I’d encourage you to not try to assemble your own passport. Stick with the professionals and have a real conversation in person with a human being about it.”
The U.S. State Department never charges a fee to download or fill out passport forms. Travelers checking processing times or applying for a passport should start at travel.state.gov or visit a local post office in person.

title: Penobscot County might use old YMCA lot in Bangor as paid parking
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
An undeveloped lot on the corner of Court and Hammond Street in Bangor may be turned into a parking lot.
A proposal brought before Penobscot County Commissioners Wednesday explores potentially developing the lot of the former Bangor YMCA, which the county bought in 2017, into a parking lot. The lot is currently undeveloped, with part of it being gravel and dirt while other portions are used for parking.
The lot has sat empty since Penobscot County paid $2 million to demolish the then 133-year-old building. This isn’t the first idea for how the lot could be used, with previous proposals to use the building or land for apartments or a new county jail having never been realized, but this is the first proposal since 2024.
County Commissioner Chair David Marshall asked County Administrator Blair Tinkham to put together the parking proposal, Marshall said, in an effort to find additional revenue for the county. The plan was drafted Tuesday, Tinkham said, so projections for paving costs or possible revenue have not yet been worked out.
“It’s in the exploratory investigative phase right now, and when we get more information, we will bring it back for further consideration,” Marshall said.
Revenue would come from drivers paying to park in the lot.
Penobscot County officials have been searching for ways to cut costs and bring in more revenue due to a multi-million dollar budget shortfall. A hiring freeze and spike in income from the registry of deeds has helped alleviate the county’s budget deficit, but officials are still searching for more ways to bring in more funds.
Paving could not take place on the portion of the lot made up of gravel and dirt without additional work being done. The Maine National Guard may be able to level the gravel portion for free as part of its annual two-week innovative readiness training, Tinkham said.
The portion of the lot farthest from Hammond Street would need to be repaved, Tinkham said. Repaving could happen quickly and bring revenue to the county before the rest of the lot is paved, Tinkham said.
While the proposal is meant to bring in revenue because of parking demands, Commissioner Dan Tremble said there may not be high demand in that area of the city.
“When I used to be on the [Bangor Downtown Parking Advisory Committee], this part of town had the least demand of any part of town for parking, so I think we should look at what they get for parking around here,” said Tremble, who previously served on the Bangor City Councilor for 15 years.
Even if there isn’t a need for parking on that lot, the county should still grade the lot to make it “more presentable,” Tremble said.
While the lot has been sitting vacant for more than two years, it has been listed for sale. The listing was recently taken down, but commissioners approved on Wednesday it to be relisted by Epstein Properties. The 1.63-acre parcel was most recently listed for $600,000. Penobscot County paid $825,000 for the lot and YMCA building in 2017.
Although the lot is going to be relisted, county officials still will work through the concept proposal, Tinkham said.
“We’ve had several discussions with the staff, and we think that this is potentially an opportunity for us to generate revenue and make it probably more marketable in the future to future buyers of that land,” he said.

title: Vassalboro local ballot has money requests
text:
The Nov. 3 local Vassalboro ballot includes three appropriations requests, totaling a maximum of $58,000; a question that voters should have answered in June, but it was accidentally omitted from the June town meeting warrant; and a request to approve a new Budget Committee Ordinance.
The fund requests ask voters to appropriate up to $20,000 for expenses of finding and hiring a new town manager; up to $8,000 to finish the 2024-25 audit; and up to $30,000 to hire or contract with necessary people to manage finances. The town has been advertising for a finance director. All money needed is to come from Vassalboro’s unassigned fund balance.
Art. 5, the one that should have been on the June ballot, asks voters to authorize select board members to transfer money between accounts when necessary to avoid overdrafts.
The budget committee ordinance partly changes and partly formalizes the present structure. Major provisions say:
   — The budget committee will consist of between seven and 10 members, elected for two-year terms at the annual June town meeting and referendum.  All members must be registered Vassalboro voters.
— Like the present committee, this committee will be advisory only, with its recommendations on proposed expenditures, by the school board and the select board, printed on town meeting warrants and when allowed on relevant local ballots.
The ordinance talks at length about meetings and records being public, as they are now. It calls for cooperation between the committee and the select board, town manager and other elected officials.
A copy of the proposed ordinance is on the town website, vassalboro.net. Clicking on Departments and Hours brings up a box called More Links, including Elections. Clicking on Elections opens a page that includes General Election Information, with sample state and municipal ballots and the Budget Committee Ordinance.
Vassalboro’s Nov. 3 voting will be at Vassalboro Community School. Polls will be open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. There will be no school on Nov. 3.
In-person early voting at the Vassalboro town office will be available through Oct. 29.

title: Trump heads to Iowa Thursday with new farm aid package
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump is rolling out a new $8 billion farming package to provide one-time relief payments to farmers facing rising fertilizer and diesel costs.
The announcement comes ahead of another $26 billion bailout. $12 billion was distributed earlier this year in one-time payments, followed by a $14 billion injection two weeks ago.
The announcement comes ahead of Trump’s visit to Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday. Iowa, an agriculture-heavy state, has felt the effects of Trump’s economic and foreign policies, including the recent importation of millions of tons of foreign beef.
New New York Times polling shows Trump’s approval rating has dropped to an all-time low of 36% with fewer than two weeks until the election.
The White House and the Republican Party is not changing its strategy heading into the midterms.
“The midterms. Historically, it’s all about turnout. So it’s turnout, turnout, turnout. And how do you do that? Well, yet you put President Trump on the ballot. You bring them front and center and you let him do what he does best,” Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters said.
Data from ad-tracking firm AdImpact shows less than 1 out of every 100 dollars spent on Republican ads went toward a commercial that mentioned Trump.
National polling shows the Senate race in Iowa is in a dead heat. The race for governor has raised more than $33 million in the last three months.
Trump will rally at Sioux Gateway Airport. Doors open at 2:30 p.m. Central Time.

title: Russia agrees to resume three-way talks on Ukraine war with Kyiv and Washington, Kremlin says
text:
(AP) - Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations next month with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, a Kremlin official said, potentially setting up the first such talks since February.
Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed “in principle” to restart the talks after Nov. 10, Putin’s foreign affairs adviser, Yuri Ushakov, told reporters following a meeting in St. Petersburg between the Russian leader and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff.
The talks will focus on “building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends,” Ushakov said.
Witkoff’s talks with Putin about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine took place as U.S. President Donald Trump presses Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he supported the push from Washington to restart talks swiftly.
“The agenda is clear: to end the war, bring peace closer, and, as I understand it, prepare everything for a meeting at the leaders’ level,” Zelenskyy said in an audio message issued late Wednesday.
Russia, he added, “has said many times already that it is ready to meet in one format or another. Then something changed. Things were canceled. We’ll see what happens this time.”
Shortly after his message, a missile alert sounded over Kyiv, and loud explosions were heard in the capital.
Representatives of the three countries held three rounds of negotiations early this year, meeting twice in Abu Dhabi in January and February, followed by further talks in Geneva in February.
However, little progress was reported beyond exchanges of prisoners of war as Moscow and Kyiv stuck to their longstanding basic demands.
Latest proposals to end the war have little of value, Kremlin says
The discussion in St. Petersburg lasted about three hours, the Kremlin said, and came a day after Witkoff met with Zelenskyy and some European leaders in Norway’s capital, Oslo.
The proposals that emerged from the Oslo meeting “contained little of real value in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis,” Ushakov said.
However, he later told Russian state TV that while Moscow isn’t “fully satisfied” with the Oslo proposals, they are a step in the right direction.
Witkoff’s meetings suggested leaders are keen to bring new momentum to U.S.-led peace efforts, more than 4½ years after the war began. Efforts by the Trump administration since early last year to end the war have made no significant progress.
Witkoff and Putin met at St. Petersburg’s Constantine Palace, with Ushakov and Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev also at the table. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the discussion by video, Ushakov said.
During the meeting, Witkoff and Kushner proposed a three-way meeting with the U.S., Russia and Ukraine at the technical level and shared progress on their talks with Zelenskyy a day earlier, according to a U.S. official familiar with the talks who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the private meeting.
Witkoff and Kushner also discussed a postwar economic plan, European security and plans for the upcoming meeting, the official said.
Putin says he’s ready to consider restoring economic ties with US
In televised opening remarks, Putin said he was ready to consider prospects for the restoration of U.S.-Russia economic ties and that he was prepared to discuss the U.S.-led conflict with Iran. Moscow stands ready to use its relationship with Tehran to help bring peace, he said.
Ushakov said “large-scale joint economic projects that offer significant prospects for cooperation” between Russia and the U.S. were discussed in detail with Witkoff.
“Some of these are, in fact, nearing the implementation stage,” he said.
In other developments Wednesday, Russia released a retired American teacher who had been imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. Witkoff said it appeared to be a goodwill gesture by the Kremlin after Trump asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard.
Putin also met with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, who was in St. Petersburg for talks with other Russian officials, the Kremlin said.
Russia has cultivated its ties with China, and the two countries last month vetoed a U.S. proposal for U.N. experts to keep monitoring sanctions on Iran.
Putin and Witkoff also discussed a possible meeting next month between the Russian, Chinese and U.S. leaders at an economic summit in China, Ushakov said, adding that Beijing is already preparing for it.
Norway’s prime minister sees a possible ‘new phase’ in talks
After his trip to Russia, Witkoff returned for more consultations in Oslo, where he met with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre at the airport before flying back to the U.S. The meeting lasted just over an hour, Norwegian broadcaster NRK reported.
“I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy,” Støre told the broadcaster. He said the new talks were likely to happen in mid-November.
Asked whether Zelenskyy could accept a border running along the current front line, Støre said: “I don’t think Ukraine will ever formally accept it and say that this is the new border. But whether they can live with it is another matter.”
Trump presses Zelenskyy to compromise
At the White House on Tuesday, Trump increased the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two leaders have soured again.
“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”
If that doesn’t happen, “I think it’s going to be a very bad thing,” Trump said.
Amid fears that Washington was turning its back on Ukraine, Zelenskyy said Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles, after recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice from allies.
Russian attacks kill 5 people and wound at least 23 others, Ukraine says
Overnight Russian attacks in Kyiv left three people dead and 12 wounded, while 10 residential buildings were damaged, the city’s military administration said.
Energy facilities were targeted in Kyiv and three other cities in Russian attacks early Wednesday, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. Outside the eastern city of Kharkiv, two people died and 11 others were wounded when drones exploded in a residential area, he said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces struck a warehouse, an electrical substation and a bulk carrier at sea that was headed to the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
The Russian Defense Ministry reported Wednesday that its air defenses intercepted 373 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula and the Black Sea.

title: Aging Untold: Lupus looks invisible, but the fight inside isn’t
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we break down the daily realities of living with lupus, shedding light on the unpredictable fatigue, pain and invisible burdens of this autoimmune condition.
We explore the complex choices surrounding feeding tubes, helping families understand when they are recommended and what questions to ask.
Then, an in-depth report highlights a breakthrough FDA-cleared blood test that could revolutionize early Alzheimer’s diagnosis.
Lupus is an autoimmune condition that others often can’t see.
“Sam” Cradduck is sharing her personal experience living with lupus.
“The weekend before I went in my first flare, I played eight softball games back-to-back in a tournament — never sat down,” Cradduck said. “And on Wednesday morning, I couldn’t walk to the bathroom. I could not get myself to the bathroom unaided.”
She said the year that followed was difficult, including time spent in a wheelchair and significant weight gain, but it led her to a turning point.
If you have a loved one who loses the ability to eat normally, your family can be thrust into difficult decisions about feeding tubes, comfort and what comes next.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the real decision isn’t just whether to place a feeding tube — it’s understanding what the family is hoping it will accomplish. Is it temporary until somebody gets healthy, or do they have a disease that’s progressing and they’re not going to get back to a baseline level?
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, shared how watching her own family changed her perspective on feeding tubes.
“I had my whole view of feeding tubes change, watching my father-in-law. He had a feeding tube for seven years. My mother-in-law cooked three meals a day, pureed the food and fed him,” O’Rourke said. “They went on cruises. They danced. He became a special cook. We went out to fabulous restaurants. You forgot he had a feeding tube.”
The first blood test the FDA approved to help diagnose Alzheimer’s disease is a significant step forward in treating a condition that affects millions of Americans.
Traditional diagnosis often involves referrals to specialists, expensive PET scans of the brain and lumbar punctures, also known as spinal taps.
However, the blood test, Lumipulse, is a “less invasive option” that “reduces reliance on PET scans and increases diagnosis accessibility,” according to the FDA.
True Friends Hall in Louisiana is a historic hall that once provided refuge for Black families and performers during segregation.
The benevolent society that operated the hall helped families in need and provided a gathering place during an era when Black Americans faced widespread discrimination.
“These organizations supported families. If you had a baby, the house burned down, they would come to the aid. These are men who were carpenters, brickmasons,” Darryl Hambrick, founder of the River Road African American Museum, said.
The hall, built in the late 1800s, is undergoing a major restoration project.

title: Healthy Living with Northern Light Health: Breast cancer
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month.
But experts want women to stay educated about their health year-round.
Bre Bisset, AGNP with Northern Light Primary Care in Ellsworth, spoke about tips to keep in mind for breast health.
Healthy habits that help
Bisset says things women do to take care of their breast health can also benefit their overall health, including:
- Maintaining a healthy weight
- Getting 150 to 300 minutes of exercise each week
- Not smoking
- Limiting or avoiding alcohol
Know your body, talk to your doctor
Experts remind women that they know their body best, so if you notice any changes, it’s important to reach out to your doctor for further evaluation.
“If there’s 10 cancers that we find, four of them are typically discovered first by the woman herself. While that’s a great statistic it doesn’t replace regular mammograms, regular screenings, all that sort of stuff. So to personalize that you should talk to your provider,” Bisset said.
When to get your first mammogram
While family and personal history is different for everyone, Bisset said she advises her patients to get their first mammogram no later than age 40.
She also encourages people to learn more about breast cancer.

title: Israeli forces detain then release US congressional candidate at West Bank olive harvest
text:
Israeli forces detain then release US congressional candidate at West Bank olive harvest
Israeli forces detained U.S. Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander on Wednesday as he helped Palestinian farmers harvest olives in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, releasing him hours later while dozens of other volunteers, including a group of American rabbis, remained in custody.
The incident was the latest in an annual olive harvest that has been marked by violence between Israeli settlers and Palestinian villagers attempting to gather their crops.
The Israeli military said the farmers and volunteers had failed to seek prior approval for the harvest and were detained "due to the security risk posed by conducting an uncoordinated harvest near an Israeli community." It later added that it viewed "the arrival of dozens of activists as an act intended solely to provoke, which undermines the harvesting process."
Lander is running in the U.S. elections on Nov. 3 to represent a heavily Democratic New York district in the U.S. House of Representatives.
"The occupation is a crime under international law," Lander wrote on social media after he was detained. "Harvesting olives isn't a crime under any law I know."
"These detentions by the IDF are one more attempt to undermine Palestinians' right to harvest their olive groves, travel on their roads, and live in their homes," he added in a post after his release.
This year, Palestinians have been required to coordinate with the Israeli military to access more of their privately owned farmland than in previous years. The anti-settlement group Peace Now said last week that the army had expanded by nearly 30% the area of farmland that Palestinians cannot enter without prior approval, to 34 square miles. The Israeli military declined to comment on the exact figures but said Palestinian farmers must coordinate access to areas under Israeli security control.
The detained volunteers were taken to a police facility. Lander was among them but "released after it became known that he was a congressional candidate," the Israeli police said in a statement.
Israeli rights group Yesh Din and the Palestinian Farmers' Union have said the 2026 harvest has been the most violent in recent history, with hundreds of reported thefts, clashes and arson attacks.
Much of the violence has unfolded on land outside Palestinian villages, where Palestinians have historically harvested olives and Israeli settlers have increasingly erected outposts without authorization from Israel's government.
But there were no clashes before Israeli forces arrived Wednesday, according to Beck Strober, a spokesperson for Protect the Harvest, the advocacy group that organized the volunteers at the grove.
Jill Jacobs, one of a dozen American rabbis detained, condemned the Israeli government's restricting the ability of Palestinians to harvest freely.
"The Israeli government is actively advancing the forced displacement of Palestinian communities across the West Bank, using its military to deny Palestinians access to their land and intimidate those who stand alongside them," Jacobs, chief executive of T'ruah: The Rabbinic Call for Human Rights, said in a statement.
Lander, who was endorsed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, defeated U.S. Rep. Dan Goldman in a primary for New York's 10th congressional district. The race was viewed as a referendum on the Democratic Party's support for Israel. Both candidates are Jewish and have criticized Israel, but only Lander called the war in Gaza a genocide.
Lander was not the first U.S. politician detained in the West Bank this year. U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, a California Democrat, said Israeli forces detained him during a visit in July.

title: UMaine presents plan to close $16M of $19M budget shortfall
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Consolidation, eliminating vacant positions and reducing external contracts are parts of a plan to close the University of Maine’s budget shortfall from $19 million to roughly $3 million, according to an email sent to staff by the university’s cabinet members Wednesday afternoon.
UMaine administrators are still working to find additional revenue or potential cuts to cover the remaining $3 million, according to the email.
More than $1 billion in deferred maintenance costs, uncertainty in federal funding and declining enrollment have been cited as causes for UMaine’s shortfall, which will require layoffs and faculty retrenchment. UMaine’s announcement comes at a time when universities across the country are navigating budget shortfalls and staff and faculty layoffs.
Additional revenue gains and expense cuts have been found in several departments — athletic, student life, research, president’s office, finance and administration and facilities management, and strategic partnerships, resources, innovation and engagement — according to the email. The revenue and expense adjustments to these units equate to roughly $6 million, according to the email.
In addition, academic affairs is reducing its expenses by $10 million, which the university announced last month, bringing the budget shortfall to $3 million.
“Assuming these targets are met, the remaining $3M gap will present a challenge and closing this will be the Cabinet’s main focus over the coming weeks,” the email reads.
Specific funds from cuts were not shared in the email, but $1 million in additional revenue will be budgeted, according to the email. The $1 million comes from a 1% revenue increase from the six units and additional events and conferences being held, according to the email.
Reserve funds, which were used in the current year’s budget to reduce a budget shortfall, will also be used, according to the email.
“While striving to decrease the size of the deficit through ongoing reductions to the base budget such as those noted above, the use of one-time funds is inevitable again in FY28. As always, we are exploring ways to generate new reliable revenue,” the email reads.
Layoffs, funding positions with outside funds, not filling vacant positions, and “automation of tasks to streamline essential, time-consuming, manual functions” were all examples given in the email of how expenses will be reduced.
While the email does not lay out specifics, other options were given as possible examples of what could be done under collective bargaining agreements.
Vacant positions in athletics, student life, the president’s office, and strategic partnerships, resources, innovation and engagement could be left unfilled, according to the email. The length of annual appointments in athletics, student life and the president’s office would also be modified, according to the email.
Research centers and institutes could also be consolidated, according to the email.
The email, which was attributed to cabinet members — UMaine President Joan Ferrini-Mundy, Provost Gabriel Paquette, Chief Business Officer Jenny Boyden, Dean of Students Andrea Gifford, Vice President for Research Giovanna Guidoboni, Director of Athletics Jude Killy, Vice President for Human Resources Nicole Lawrence and Vice President of Strategic Partnerships, Resources, Innovation and Engagement Jake Ward — was sent to UMaine and UMaine at Machias staff members Wednesday.
In a letter last month, Ferrini-Mundy announced the university’s $19 million shortfall, but said that cuts and revenue increases, mostly from academic affairs, had decreased the gap to $5.7 million. Staff layoffs and retrenchment would be needed to fill the remaining costs, according to the letter.
UMaine system unions have asked administrators to review their spending before proposing cuts.
UMaine’s budget will be presented to the University of Maine System Board of Trustees in January.

title: A new future for pre-K in RSU 5
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Amanda Edwards lives in Freeport.
As a Freeport resident, working parent and an RSU 5 educator, I have been following the “Save Pownal Elementary” petition and the conversation surrounding the proposed changes to our schools.
I understand why so many people feel strongly about keeping Pownal Elementary as it is. It is a wonderful school that serves as a valuable meeting place for Pownal families. But I also believe we need to ask ourselves what it means to truly serve the children and families of RSU 5, not just today, but for years to come. For my family and many others, converting Pownal Elementary into an early learning school with full-day preschool would be life-changing.
As working parents with two young children, half-day preschool is incredibly difficult to navigate both logistically and financially. My husband and I both work early, long before the school day begins at the current pre-K program at Morse Street Elementary. We have no way to provide midday transportation and no family nearby who can help. Our childcare is outside of Freeport and is not serviced by Freeport school buses.
For us, accessing half-day public preschool means paying for additional care simply to bridge the gaps around the school day. Even with the childcare options offered by RSU 5, which are among the least expensive in the area, the cost of sending our oldest to preschool next year will be more than the already exceptionally high cost of daycare. Full-day preschool would save our family more than $10,000 a year, and I expect that gap will only grow as childcare costs continue to rise.
And our family is far from unique. For many working families, the challenge isn’t simply finding a way to rearrange a schedule or absorb another expense. Childcare is already extraordinarily expensive, and full-day preschool options in the area can cost $15,000, $20,000 or more per child. Even then, families may face waitlists or simply be unable to find a spot. Having one parent leave the workforce to provide childcare is not financially realistic for many families.
This is why I believe the conversation about Pownal Elementary needs to be bigger than whether we are “saving” the school exactly as it exists today. We should also be asking what we could create there.
An early learning school with full-day public preschool would allow RSU 5 to use a beloved community school to provide something our working families desperately need. It would make high-quality early education more accessible, while also helping address one of the biggest challenges facing families with young children: the gap between the school day and the workday.
And for some children, this isn’t simply a financial conundrum. Access to public preschool can be the difference between having a preschool experience and not having one at all. That matters deeply to me because public education changed my life. I grew up in a situation that included food stamps and community programs like Santa’s Giving Tree. Today, I am raising my own children in Freeport and have a career I love in public education. I know firsthand what it can mean when a community invests in giving children opportunities regardless of their family’s financial circumstances.
I understand why people want to save Pownal Elementary. But maybe saving Pownal doesn’t have to mean preserving it exactly as it is. Maybe we can honor what the school has meant to generations of children by giving it a new purpose that meets the needs of the next generation. I hope our community will consider not only what we might lose, but also what we have the opportunity to build: a place where every child in RSU 5 can have access to a high-quality early education, and where working families have a real opportunity to make that education work.
I hope RSU 5 leadership and community members will consider both the significant financial benefit this would provide to individual families and our community as a whole, and the opportunity to give every child in RSU 5 an equitable start to an incredible education.
Correction (Oct. 21, 12:58 p.m.): A previous subhead misstated the location of Pownal Elementary School.

title: My family has been dragged into the US Senate campaign. I want to speak for myself.
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Lana Pelletier is a licensed clinical social worker from Allagash and the longtime partner of U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson. They have two adult sons.
When Troy first talked to me about running for the U.S. Senate, we started with what it would mean for our family. We knew it wouldn’t be easy. We knew the race could get ugly.
But I never imagined U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and her allies would stoop this low.
As a social worker and therapist, I’ve mostly stayed out of the public eye. My work is private, and I want the people I work with to know the focus is on them — not my politics or my partner’s career.
But over the last few months, people who do not know me have increasingly tried to tell the public who I am, what my relationship has been and what kind of family Troy and I have built together.
Collins has brought our family into this campaign herself. She has ridiculed us publicly, invoked my children in debates and treated deeply personal parts of our lives as fair game for political attack.
I know Troy. We’ve been together for nearly 40 years. He is my partner, the father of our children and now a grandfather to our beautiful newborn granddaughter.
I also know myself. I am not the person Collins and her allies seem determined to turn me into.
I am not a helpless woman who needs politicians to tell the world what happened in my own life. And I am not a punchline or a caricature of where I come from.
I’ve spent my career helping people navigate some of the hardest moments of their lives. That work has taught me to take allegations involving violence and abuse seriously — and how much care is required when we talk about it.
That is part of what makes what is happening now so upsetting.
Earlier this year, a police report from nearly four decades ago became part of this campaign. There was a fight between Troy and another young man when Troy was 19 years old. He took accountability for that and has never hidden it. The report included statements attributed to me that I’ve already said I don’t remember making and that are not accurate.
I’m now forced to say it again because Susan Collins and her allies are using my family to tell a story that simply isn’t true.
I’ve spent nearly four decades with Troy since then. I know the life we have actually lived, the family we have raised and the person Troy has been through the years as a caring partner and father.
Our children have been dragged into this campaign. Our relationship has been mocked. Our family has been talked about as though there is something shameful about who we are or where we come from.
There isn’t.
I’m proud of our children. I’m proud of the life Troy and I have built together. I’m proud of how Troy continues to evolve and grow as a leader and advocate.
And I deeply resent watching Collins and her allies treat our lives as something beneath them — especially when serious issues involving women are manipulated into political weapons by people who show so little care for the women involved.
If Collins truly cared about my voice, she could have listened to it. Instead, they’ve decided they know my life better than I do.
They do not.
This is not the first time Collins has asked women to trust her while ignoring what they were telling her. She voted to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme, who helped overturn Roe v. Wade, and still says she does not regret it. Women warned her what was at stake. She did not listen to them either.
I was not pushing Troy to run. But I understood that if people were hurting and he could help, it was bigger than any one of us.
When Troy sees somebody without much power being treated unfairly, he feels it deeply. And he has spent much of his life trying to do something about it.
There are families across Maine struggling to afford healthcare, heating oil and groceries. Their lives matter more than the ugliness of a political campaign.
Those are the people Troy is running for.
I don’t expect everyone in Maine to agree with Troy. Ask him hard questions. Challenge his record. Disagree with him.
But there should still be a line.
Collins has been quick to demand respect and decency for herself. My family deserved the same.
I stayed quiet because I never wanted this election to be about me. Collins and her allies made a different choice.
So if my name, my relationship and my family are going to be used to tell a story that isn’t true, Mainers deserve to hear from the person who actually lived that story.
I know my own life. I know my family.
And after nearly 40 years with Troy, I know who he is, too.

title: Richard Earl Glidden
text:
Richard Earl Glidden, 59, became an angel in heaven on Oct. 17, 2026 at Crawford Commons after a two month battle of pancreatic cancer.
Richard was born March 24, 1967, a son of Eva V. Glidden (Winchenbach) and Ralph F. Glidden Jr. Despite his intellectual disability and cerebral palsy, Richard was the shining light of his family.
Richard was a car enthusiast and enjoyed listening to church gospel music. He appreciated the simple pleasures in life: his coffee, good food, Coca-Cola, and spending time with his family. He loved looking good and always said “Richard’s a handsome boy.” Richard especially looked forward to his weekly date at his sister Corena’s house where watching “The Andy Griffith Show” and discussing old cars with his brother-in-law always put a smile on his face.
Richard will be remembered for his loving disposition and happy personality and that spread joy to all.
He was predeceased by his father; and his siblings, Serena, Sherry, and Ralph “Ricky” Glidden III.
Richard is survived by his mother, Eva Glidden; his devoted sister, Corena Bartlett and her husband, Wade Bartlett; his nephew, Tony Bartlett and his sons; and his nieces; Felichia Glidden, Tonya Kenefick and her husband, Eric, and their children.
A private burial will take place at the family cemetery at Fairview in Jefferson.

title: 13-year-old accused of shooting teacher outside middle school, police say
text:
HOBBS, New Mexico. (KCBD/Gray News) - A 13-year-old in New Mexico is accused of shooting a teacher outside a middle school, according to authorities.
Ryker Teel is facing charges of aggravated assault and tampering with evidence, among others.
Just before 11:40 a.m. on Sept 25, officers say coworkers found teacher Kelly Matthews seriously hurt outside the school.
A caller told 911, “I need the police and I need an ambulance to Highland Middle School immediately. We have a staff member either stabbed or shot out behind the school.”
Police released body camera footage to KCBD, which shows Officer Mann jumping a fence and running to help school nurse Sylvia Pena, who was tending to Matthews’ wounds.
His body camera footage shows Mann asked Matthews who did this to him.
“I don’t know, I don’t know. They were standing and facing that corner right there and I came out and they turned around and they just started firing and took off running,” Matthews said.
In the video, Matthews told investigators the suspect was wearing glasses and a mask of some kind. Mann relayed the description over his police radio.
Police later broadcast a description of a white male with a black hoodie, black pants and a long white shirt underneath the hoodie.
The footage shows officers used that description to find Teel in an alley nearby. When asked his name, he said, “Ryker Teel, sir.”
In handcuffs, Teel apologized and asked, “Is he dead? I’m sorry. I’m sorry. Is he dead?” Officers took Teel into custody.
Detectives later interviewed Teel with his mother and father present. According to the report, after detectives left the interview room, Teel was allegedly overheard telling his father he got the gun from the safe in their home.
The report states he admitted to shooting a man at the school and that he took the gun to school with the intention to shoot “anyone” and not specifically the man he shot.
Matthews’ wife says he’s currently working to recover at a rehab center.
She says they are praying for a full recovery, but each day is a challenge and they aren’t sure what the long-term effects will be. She said she wants to thank everyone for their thoughts and prayers during this difficult time.

title: Deputies find 2 malnourished dogs in cages during Knox County investigation
text:
KNOX COUNTY, Maine (WMTW) - Two severely malnourished dogs were discovered inside a Knox County residence during a probation check that led to a Camden man’s arrest on a felony firearm charge, according to court documents.
Seth M. Young, 28, was arrested on Oct. 15 and charged with possession of a firearm by a prohibited person, a Class B felony.
According to a narrative filed by the Knox County Sheriff’s Deputy, the investigation began when deputies observed suspicious activity involving two vehicles at Andes Variety in Warren.
Deputies later followed a blue Subaru and conducted a traffic stop after noticing the registration had expired.
During the stop, deputies learned that Young, who was a passenger in the car, was on probation with search conditions related to drugs.
Court documents say that deputies accompanied Young to a residence in Spruce Head to conduct a probation check.
During the check, deputies reported encountering an overwhelming smell of feces and discovered two dogs confined in separate cages, according to the deputy’s narrative.
Both dogs were described as malnourished, with their bones visible. Deputies also reported finding a large accumulation of dog feces inside one of the cages.
Pope Memorial Humane Society confirmed on Tuesday that both dogs are now in its care.
Deputies also reported finding a double-barrel shotgun and ammunition inside the residence.
The deputy’s report indicated that additional charges related to the dogs’ welfare could be considered. Court documents do not show any animal cruelty charges filed against Young.
Young was transported to Knox County Jail following his arrest, according to court documents. His bail was set at $2,500 cash, with conditions prohibiting him from possessing firearms or other dangerous weapons.
Young is scheduled to appear in person for a dispositional conference Nov. 13 at 8:30 a.m. at the Knox County Courthouse in Rockland.

title: 30 Years Later: Remembering Maine's historic flood of 1996
text:
30 Years Later: Remembering Maine's historic flood of 1996
Thirty years ago, Maine experienced one of its most devastating flooding events.
30 Years Later: Remembering Maine's historic flood of 1996
Thirty years ago, Maine experienced one of its most devastating flooding events.
Thirty years ago, Maine experienced one of its most devastating flooding events when the remnants of Hurricane Lili brought torrential rainfall to southern Maine and New Hampshire in October 1996.
The storm, which became known as the Great October Washout or the Great Flood of '96, dumped more than a foot of rain across several communities, with some areas receiving more than 19 inches.
In Portland, 2.78 inches of rain fell on Oct. 20, followed by a record-breaking 11.74 inches on Oct. 21. That brought the city’s two-day rainfall total to 14.52 inches.
The Oct. 21 rainfall shattered Portland’s previous single-day record of 7.75 inches, set during Hurricane Bob on August 19, 1991.
Despite the scale of the disaster, the Great October Washout has received relatively little attention over the years compared to other historic Maine storms. The event also serves as another example of the significant impacts tropical weather systems can have on New England, even during the fall.
Archived National Weather Service reports from Oct. 20-22, 1996, show how quickly conditions deteriorated as heavy rain, strong winds and dangerous flooding swept across the region.
At 11:14 p.m. on Oct. 20, the National Weather Service in Gray issued a flood warning for York County, Maine, and several counties in New Hampshire. Flood watches were also in effect for Oxford, Androscoggin and Sagadahoc counties.
At the time, more than 5 inches of rain had already fallen in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, and forecasters warned that another 1 to 3 inches could fall through Monday.
Flooding was already causing problems across southern New Hampshire, where several roads had been closed. The Taylor River in Hampton had risen to the guardrail along Interstate 95, threatening to shut down the highway.
By 6:45 a.m. on Oct. 21, rainfall totals were climbing rapidly. Portland had recorded 3.91 inches, while Hollis, Maine, had received nearly 5 inches. Across the border, Fremont, New Hampshire, had already recorded 8 inches.
The storm also brought powerful winds, with a peak gust of 115 mph reported on Mount Washington and 43 mph in Portland. Offshore, seas reached 23 feet at the Portland Large Navigational Buoy.
As the rain continued, the flooding became increasingly destructive.
By the morning of Oct. 22, the National Weather Service released a report detailing the staggering storm totals across southern Maine.
Initial reports showed Gorham had received 18.89 inches of rain, while Camp Ellis recorded 18.50 inches, Westbrook measured 17.66 inches and Sanford received 17.21 inches.
Other communities also experienced extraordinary rainfall. South Windham received 15.83 inches, Scarborough recorded 15.52 inches and Portland’s Deering area measured 13.55 inches.
However, those totals would soon be updated.
At 2:50 p.m. on Oct. 22, the National Weather Service issued another statement with revised rainfall amounts, showing Camp Ellis had received 19.19 inches of rain, followed by Gorham with 19 inches.
Further analysis after the storm determined that Camp Ellis had actually received 19.21 inches of rain, establishing a Maine state rainfall record.
That total came within just over half an inch of the New England record of 19.76 inches, set in Westfield, Massachusetts, during Hurricane Diane in August 1955.
Westbrook’s updated total was 17.62 inches, while the Portland International Jetport recorded 12.55 inches.
Across New Hampshire, Mount Washington recorded 12.60 inches, while Portsmouth received 12.23 inches.
The tremendous amount of rainfall overwhelmed rivers, streams and drainage systems, washing out roads, flooding neighborhoods and shutting down portions of the Maine Turnpike.
Watch below: Footage from the Great October Washout of 1996
In Old Orchard Beach, flooding devastated areas including Ocean Park, where rising water inundated streets and properties.
The storm also claimed a life in Scarborough when a man drove his pickup truck into floodwaters covering a washed-out section of Old Blue Point Road. His vehicle was swept into a marsh. His wife survived, but he did not.
The flooding also damaged sections of the Portland water system, leaving more than 100,000 people without water service for approximately 24 hours.
The destruction prompted federal disaster declarations for York and Cumberland counties.
According to historical storm records, reported costs totaled approximately $9.43 million in 1996 dollars. Cumberland County accounted for nearly $4.93 million, while York County reported approximately $3.43 million in costs. Oxford County recorded more than $161,000.
The total also included $460,000 through an individual assistance program and more than $456,000 in costs associated with state agencies.
Throughout the storm, the National Weather Service urged residents living near rivers and streams to remain alert for rising water and warned drivers not to attempt to cross flooded roadways.
Three decades later, the Great October Washout remains a powerful reminder of how quickly excessive rainfall can turn into a life-threatening disaster, even after a hurricane has weakened and moved inland.
The archived National Weather Service statements provide a remarkable look back at the historic storm, documenting the warnings, rising rainfall totals and dangerous conditions as one of Maine’s most significant flooding events unfolded.

title: Houlton nurses say CEO has significantly damaged hospital
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This story will be updated.
Registered nurses at Houlton Regional Hospital announced Wednesday that they signed a petition of no confidence in the CEO because the board of trustees failed to respond to concerns, according to the nurses union.
The 55 Houlton nurses, members of the Maine State Nurses Association/National Nurses Organizing Committee, sent a letter of no confidence in CEO Jeff Zewe to the board of trustees in July and invited the board to a meeting to hear their concerns.
“They didn’t show up. All we’ve heard is silence,” several members of the bargaining committee said in a Wednesday statement.
Wednesday’s action comes on the heels of a letter of no confidence sent to Zewe earlier this month by the registered nurses at Northern Maine Medical Center in Fort Kent, also under his leadership. The northern Maine nurses issued the letter after half of the emergency department nurses resigned because Zewe created a toxic environment that put their licenses and patients at risk.
In June 2025, Zewe, who had already been at the helm of the Fort Kent hospital, took on the Houlton hospital leadership in a management agreement.
The Houlton nurses said Wednesday that Zewe has only been leading the Houlton hospital for a little over a year, but has already caused “significant damage to the hospital and community.”
The nurses’ July letter followed a four-day strike in May, the second strike in six months.
In their petition of no confidence the nurses said they must take action “while there is still time to preserve and protect our community hospital,” and called on the board of trustees to immediately terminate his employment.
“We are greatly saddened that the Houlton Regional Hospital Board of Trustees didn’t keep its word to listen to employees,” the bargaining committee said Wednesday.
The committee includes registered nurses Tori Quint, operating room; Mary Howland, acute care department; Erin Mitchell, emergency department; Cassidy Hardy, acute care; Brooke Howland, acute care; Christina Schimdt, operating room; and Kelli Lawlor, operating room.

title: Maine proposes change to moose hunting near Moosehead Lake
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA — The Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife will seek to expand moose hunting in September near Jackman, but not near Greenville.
The proposal is an attempt to balance the interests of hunters with the growth of fall tourism near Moosehead Lake.
Sporting camps and hunting guides said expanded hunting in that region would be good for their businesses, spread out their clients in the woods and reduce impacts for private landowners. Hospitality businesses and guides who lead moose watching tours said an added week of hunting in September would curtail their businesses during peak foliage.
On Wednesday, after officials announced the proposed rule at a meeting of the department’s advisory council, stakeholders described it as a compromise.
“I think the department has brought something forward I feel everyone should be able to look at and say, that’s a reasonable outcome,” Christopher Richards, of Hermon, a board member of the Maine Professional Guides Association, said. “Hopefully it’s something that can move forward without too much heartburn.”
The next step is a rulemaking process with opportunity for public comment.
There are two possible weeks in which a hunter can harvest a bull moose in Maine — one in September and one in October — although the state historically restricted some wildlife management districts to one week only.
Last winter, the department proposed opening both September and October hunts in all 20 of Maine’s 29 districts where moose hunting is allowed. Because of a swell of opposition from Greenville, which has especially marketed itself as a place to see rich colors and wildlife, the state ultimately allowed two weeks of bull hunting in 2026 in every district except four near Moosehead Lake. This year, those four districts only got permits for October.
The state convened a working group to discuss the issue and has been considering the issue internally for months. Nate Webb, the state’s wildlife division director, announced a proposed solution on Wednesday at the advisory council meeting.
Under that proposal, the state would open bull hunting in September in most of Wildlife Management District 8, which stretches from the western edge of Moosehead Lake to the Canadian border and includes Jackman. The southeast corner of the district would still be closed to hunting that week, with the Kennebec River serving as the boundary.
Webb said that district seemed to have the most interest for hunters and the least potential for conflict with other users.
“In order for us to feel comfortable with opening some portion of this area, it would need to be a meaningful addition that would provide a reasonable opportunity for hunters to disperse themselves and take advantage of what for many is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity,” Webb said.
The department would not increase the total number of moose hunting permits allocated for the district if a September hunt is added, Webb said. Instead, the tags would be divided between two weeks instead of one.
Wildlife Management Districts 9, 14 and 17 would remain closed to moose hunting in September. Greenville is located in the southwestern corner of District 9.
People who have been involved in the debate said the proposal won’t make everyone happy but generally agreed that the department tried to balance a wide range of opinions across a large geographic area.
“I’m happy as I can be with the decision,” said Jeremy Hargreaves, who owns Northeast Whitewater and takes thousands of people on moose watching tours throughout the region. “I think we had to concede something to make this work.”
Jennifer Whitlow, owner of Blair Hill Inn in Greenville, has been a vocal opponent of a September hunt near Greenville because moose watching tours are the top activity for her guests.
“The decision reflects a thoughtful, balanced approach that recognizes both wildlife management objectives and the significant economic concerns raised by local businesses and visitors who support our region’s tourism economy,” Whitlow wrote in an email.
Joe Kruse, who owns Lake Parlin Lodge in Jackman, said, if the rule is implemented, he would finally be able to use his property during the moose hunting week in September. This year, he said, his lodge sat empty while he guided clients in another district that week.
“We would like to see it all open. … But if we do have to have a compromise, then I think this is a good one,” Kruse said.
The department will advertise the proposed rule and open public comment on Oct. 28. Written feedback will be accepted through Nov. 28. A public hearing will take place at 5 p.m. on Nov. 18 at Northern Outdoors in The Forks. The advisory council will meet next on Dec. 8.

title: Lupus looks invisible; the fight inside isn’t
text:
(Aging Untold) — Lupus can bring pain, exhaustion and unpredictability that aren’t always visible from the outside.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck shared her personal experience living with lupus after a viewer wrote in asking about the disease, offering a rare, candid look at what it’s really like to live with an autoimmune condition that others often can’t see.
‘Living with uncertainty is tough’
Cradduck said the hardest part of lupus isn’t just physical — it’s not knowing what each day will bring.
“I think I wish people understood that living with uncertainty is tough. You don’t know when what your days are always going to be like,” Cradduck said. “And people have a tendency to really be judgmental and really be ugly.”
Cradduck explained that many lupus patients take steroids like prednisone, which can change their appearance and invite unfair judgment.
“A lot of people on lupus, unfortunately, have to take a lot of steroids. Prednisone is one of the main treatments, which then you get that nice round face, you gain weight,” Cradduck said.
From eight softball games to a wheelchair
Cradduck described how quickly her life changed when she went into her first flare.
“The weekend before I went in my first flare, I played eight softball games back-to-back in a tournament — never sat down,” Cradduck said. “And on Wednesday morning, I couldn’t walk to the bathroom. I could not get myself to the bathroom unaided.”
She said the year that followed was difficult, including time spent in a wheelchair and significant weight gain, but it led her to a turning point.
“I have a disease that I will die with, but I’m not going to let it take my life. I’m going to live every day,” Cradduck said. “But that was a tough decision, and it was a tough place to come to.”
‘A case of mistaken identity’
Cradduck said people often assume she’s healthy simply because of how she looks, even after losing the ability to walk unaided.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said she calls lupus “a case of mistaken identity.”
“You look perfectly healthy on the outside, but you have a war going on on the inside,” Rogers said. “We call that the disease of a thousand faces, because you never know which organ in your body is going to hit.”
She said that unpredictability extends beyond physical symptoms.
“The sad thing for people is you never know which version of you is going to show up tomorrow,” Rogers said.
How to be a good friend to someone with lupus
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared specific ways loved ones can offer support without making the disease the center of every interaction.
“Not every conversation you and I are going to have is going to be about lupus. We’re going to have non-lupus conversations. I’m not going to be the lupus police,” O’Rourke said. “I’m not going to be looking at what you’re eating and saying, ‘Do you think that you should eat that?’ I’m not going to look at you and say, ‘Oh, you look really good today,’ meaning how did you look yesterday.”
She also emphasized the importance of consistency, even when flare-ups get in the way of plans.
“I am not going to let your flare-ups stop me from being a consistent, steadfast friend,” O’Rourke said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said lupus can appear invisible, so give people grace.
“Just because you can’t see their diagnosis, doesn’t mean they’re not dealing with something really hard,” she said.
Finding the right diagnosis — and options beyond traditional medicine
Cradduck said she was diagnosed after experiencing a reaction to sun exposure, following a long period of uncertainty before a lupus diagnosis.
“How it finally got diagnosed was I actually had a sun flare,” Cradduck said. “It was between lupus and the MS for a long time. My rheumatologist was amazing.”
She said managing stress and illness carefully has become essential since her immune system is compromised.
“If I get sick, I don’t just get sick. I don’t just get the flu and then I recover in three or four days like everyone else. It takes me down,” Cradduck said. “COVID was really, really hard on me.”
Rogers encouraged others to stay open to options beyond conventional treatment.
“We have options outside of traditional medicine that we are now starting to see from an integrative standpoint — things that you can do to not necessarily resolve it all the way,” Rogers said. “Sometimes you can, or dumb it down. People just need to be open and understand there are options out there.”
Key takeaways
- Lupus is often invisible. Patients can look healthy on the outside while fighting constant internal pain and uncertainty.
- Fatigue is relentless. Give yourself grace, and avoid comparing your journey to someone else’s.
- Judgment can be hurtful. Comments about appearance or assumptions based on how someone looks can add to the burden of an invisible illness.
- Support means consistency. Keep inviting, keep including — don’t let flare-ups end the relationship.
- Diagnosis can take time. Autoimmune conditions like lupus can be mistaken for other diseases, such as MS, before being correctly identified.
- A diagnosis changes capacity, not identity. Adapting with resilience can prevent a chronic illness from defining a person’s life.

title: Sanford mayoral candidate was charged with OUI in September
text:
A Sanford mayoral candidate was arrested and charged with operating under the influence late last month, records show.
Matthew Dupuis, 37, was taken into custody around 10 p.m. on Sept. 30, according to arrest logs from the Sanford Police Department.
Dupuis did not respond to several calls and emails this week seeking comment. It wasn’t clear Wednesday whether he has an attorney representing him in the case.
The arrest log indicates that Dupuis was pulled over near Bridge and Main streets in Sanford. Police Chief Eric Small declined to release reports about the case, citing the investigation’s ongoing status.
Dupuis posted bail, according to staff at the York County Courthouse.
He is scheduled to be arraigned on the morning of Nov. 12, according to court staff, though the York County District Attorney’s Office had not filed a complaint in the case by midday Wednesday.
Dupuis pleaded guilty to a Class D assault charge in 2021, according to a state criminal background check.
A Republican, Dupuis is one of four candidates seeking the mayor’s role this fall, facing Deputy Mayor Maura Herlihy, City Councilor Pete Tranchemontagne and Daniel White. Dupuis unsuccessfully ran for mayor in 2024, receiving about 31% of the votes to Becky Brink’s 55%.
Dupuis said in his responses to the Press Herald Voter Guide that his priorities if elected mayor would be stopping the proposed data center and sludge plant, and bringing a veterans home to the city.
