title: Sharon Kennedy Bukulmez
text:
Sharon Kennedy Bukulmez is the strongest woman I know. Born May 27, 1965, in Olean, N.Y., to Colleen Kennedy (Irish) and Salih Bukulmez (Turkish). My mother’s life was guided by caregiving, humanitarian travel, community building, and creating. She attended Purdue University and UNC Wilmington and proceeded to work as a medical technologist at John Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, Md. She served as a medical worker in the U.S. Peace Corps in Liberia, and in Zambia through St. Joseph’s Hospital. She married Steve Grubb in 1991, and they travelled together to Mandeville, Jamaica, where she worked in a school for pregnant students and young mothers. She gave birth to her first son, Peter, while teaching and living in Jamaica. As a young mother, Sharon achieved a master’s degree in Community Health from Towson University and lived in Carney, Md., where they welcomed their other two children, Maureen and Joseph. In 2000, the family moved to a new community in Bass Harbor, Maine.
Mom was an active teacher in the local homeschool community and believed deeply in the independence and autonomy of her children, helping each of us find our own path with education. She would take the homeschool kids (and anyone else who wanted to join) on daily outings between our structured lessons. We rollerbladed on closed campground roads, ice skated on Chris’s pond, rode bikes on carriage trails, and paddled the many beautiful waters across MDI. We explored every season and all weather.

title: Stranger brings 6-year-old home after being dropped off early and found walking near busy road
text:
CLEVELAND, Ohio. (WOIO/Gray News) - A stranger in Ohio brought a 6-year-old home after the girl was dropped off early and found walking near a busy road.
Mari Richardson was getting ready to pick up her daughter at the bus stop when the girl arrived home in a stranger’s car more than 20 minutes before she was supposed to arrive.
“My daughter could have never made it home. If it wasn’t for this lady. And I’m just so thankful for her,” Richardson said.
Tiyonna Betts saw the girl crying and walking by herself on busy road.
“I asked her does she know where she was going? She said no, she was lost. The bus driver just dropped her off,” Betts said.
Richardson said she is grateful a kind woman brought her daughter home.
“My daughter was scared. She was scared. She’s only 6 years old. And I’m just so thankful that she does know landmarks that she was able to direct her home,” Richardson said.
“God led me to that baby, and I’m just overjoyed that I was used to be a blessing,” Betts said.
Rightway Transportation told 19 News that the driver dropped the girl off nearly 40 minutes early with no parent waiting, which violates company policy.
Richardson said she could no longer trust the school bus to transport her daughter and is looking for other ways to get her daughter to school.
“I don’t feel like enough has been done. I did not, I don’t feel like this matter is taken, is being taken as serious as it should. Because my daughter could have never made it home. My last time seeing her literally could have been Friday morning,” Richardson said.
Richardson filed a police report and wants to press charges.
Rightway Transportation told 19 News that the driver had been disciplined and taken off the route.

title: FAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing's long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing's long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service
Nearly a decade after Boeing unveiled its largest 737 Max jet, the company has cleared a major hurdle in its effort to bring the plane to airlines. The Federal Aviation Administration approved the Max 10 for passenger service Tuesday, ending years of delays.
The 737 Max 10’s certification represents another milestone in Boeing’s efforts to restore its reputation and financial footing after years of safety, quality and production challenges. With production approved, the aircraft can now be sold to domestic and foreign carriers.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the certification followed “extensive safety reviews,” including thousands of hours of test flights, and called it a major win for American manufacturing.
“To think that it took us almost 10 years to get here. We all probably had a little less gray hair 10 years ago," Duffy said during a visit to Boeing's manufacturing plant Tuesday in Everett, Washington.
The Max 10 is an important piece of the company's effort to regain ground in the narrow-body market. For airlines, the larger plane offers a way to carry more passengers on a single flight, potentially lowering costs per seat. For travelers, it could eventually mean more seats on popular routes, though the impact on fares will depend on how airlines deploy the planes and how much competition they face.
Stephanie Pope, president and CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said during Duffy's visit that the certification "clears the path to deliver an airplane that will set a new standard in commercial aviation." The Max 10 will typically seat 185-210 passengers, according to Boeing, compared with 175-195 on the Max 9 and 160-180 on the Max 8.
“Today is a very, very special day. It caps years of hard work and dedication by many," Pope said. "It marks another major milestone in our recovery, and it unlocks a key to our future growth.”
The company expects to begin deliveries in 2027.
The single-aisle jet was introduced at the Paris air show in 2017 to help Boeing compete with rival Airbus. But technical and regulatory hurdles repeatedly delayed certification.
Boeing’s struggles have been particularly acute since two deadly crashes involving the smaller Max 8 killed 346 people in 2018 and 2019 off the coast of Indonesia and in Ethiopia. In 2024, a panel flew off of an Alaska Airlines Max 9 in midair, renewing scrutiny of Boeing’s manufacturing and safety practices.
The delays have held up a key part of Boeing's business. More than 30 customers worldwide have ordered 1,555 Max 10s that Boeing has yet to deliver, accounting for more than 30% of its total 737 Max backlog.
Major customers include United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, American Airlines and Ryanair. Alaska Airlines joined that list in January, ordering 105 Max 10s, with options for 35 more.
The Max 10 is intended to compete with Airbus’s A321neo model family, which entered service in 2017. The largest A321neo can carry more passengers and fly farther without refueling than the Max 10.
Still, Boeing designed the Max 10 to carry more passengers while burning less fuel than older aircraft — a potentially attractive combination for airlines facing soaring jet fuel costs amid the U.S. war with Iran. Those rising costs have put added pressure on airlines to control expenses.
Certification means the FAA has determined that the Max 10’s design meets safety standards, following engineering reviews and flight testing. But Boeing must continue to show it can consistently build the aircraft to the approved design, and each plane must be cleared before it can fly passengers.
The Max 10’s certification completes the lineup of four 737 Max models. The FAA cleared the Max 7 for airline operations in August.
Pope on Tuesday described the certification of both the Max 7 and Max 10 in the same year as a sign of the company’s resilience.
In the wake of the fatal Max 8 crashes, the FAA overhauled how it certifies Boeing aircraft. But over the past 18 months, the agency has gradually eased some of its restrictions on the company, increasing the limit on how many planes Boeing can produce. In July, the FAA also said Boeing could once again issue airworthiness certificates for its 737 Max and 787 planes at the end of production, allowing the company to take back some responsibility for determining whether finished aircraft are ready to fly.

title: In final Michigan Senate debate, El-Sayed and Rogers question each other's loyalties
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers clashed in their final Senate debate Wednesday, with El-Sayed trying to tie his opponent to President Donald Trump and Rogers saying his rival’s progressive policies would be too extreme for Michigan.
The debate kicked off a breakneck final stretch in one of the nation’s most closely watched and competitive Senate races. Former President Barack Obama will rally in Detroit on Saturday, followed by Trump on Sunday.
Wednesday’s hourlong debate followed one on Oct. 8 that devolved into personal insults and attacks, with the candidates continuing to argue even during a commercial break. This time, the exchanges were slightly less contentious and focused on policy, though both candidates repeatedly returned to their central attacks.
“Those playing MAGA bingo at home, you just heard like three of the buzzwords,” El-Sayed said after Rogers criticized his policies. Rogers later shot back: “The bingo game ought to be how many times can he put the word Trump in any answer.”
The most contentious exchange came when Rogers again tried to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, repeating an allegation he and Trump have raised in recent weeks. El-Sayed has denied any affiliation with the group.
“If you are going to go to the United States Senate, we need to know: Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” Rogers said.
El-Sayed, who would be the country’s first Muslim senator, called Rogers’ questioning of his commitment to the Constitution “shameful.”
“I’m proud to be an American,” El-Sayed said. “I’m proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray.”
Rogers offered qualified criticism of Trump’s tariffs, calling them a “mixed bag” and questioning those imposed on Canada because of the close ties between the two countries’ auto industries. But he also praised Trump’s immigration enforcement and defended the threat posed by Iran, while El-Sayed blamed the president’s war there for higher gas and grocery prices.

title: Will Maine college students, motivated by crucial Senate race, choose to vote here?
text:
BRUNSWICK — On a crisp October morning, a group of Bowdoin College students grabbed free lattes and hot chocolate from a campus coffee shop and took a brief walk into town.
The Sip and Stroll, one of many events run by the nonpartisan election engagement group Bowdoin Votes, was designed to lead students on the short walk down to Brunswick Town Hall to cast their ballots.
As Nov. 3 approaches, college students have to choose not just for whom they want to vote but also where they should cast their ballot. Like most Bowdoin students, none of those strolling Tuesday morning grew up in Maine — they hailed from Colorado, Alabama, Connecticut and Massachusetts — but they’re all choosing to vote here this fall.
“I felt like my vote would have more of an impact here than it would in Alabama,” said 19-year-old Isa Alvidrez.
“It’s a much more challenging race,” Caden Christopher, 18, from Connecticut said. “I’m generally not a ‘vote blue no matter who’ person, but I think in the immediate, it’s important that Democrats get control of the Senate.”
They were referring, of course, to the high-profile matchup between Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson, where candidates are fighting for the small number of undecided voters who will determine whether Collins gets a sixth term.
Caroline Pippert, a visiting professor of political science at Bowdoin who studies young voter behavior, said how competitive a race is can be a major factor in where students choose to vote, especially in one with as much national recognition and campaign spending as Maine’s senate contest.
“All of these first-year students that didn’t live in Maine yet had likely heard about this race before they even moved here,” Pippert said.
While young voters, especially men, turned toward Trump in the 2024 presidential election, polls show them likely swinging back to the left in these midterms. Amid the closely watched tossup Senate races around the country, including those in Ohio, Michigan and Kansas, young voter turnout could make a big difference.
That could be especially true in Maine, which has one of the most active youth voting populations in the country. During the 2022 midterms, 35.7% of 18 to 29-year-olds in the state voted, well above the national average of 23% and behind only Michigan, according to data from the Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement at Tufts.
Pippert said in times where young people increasingly feel pessimistic about the efficacy of politics, it’s hard to tell how young voters will act. Will the dissatisfaction result in a boost in turnout? Will it mean young people stay home? Could it cause a shift in which party they support?
“The common thread is frustration, and it will be interesting to see how that frustration manifests,” she said.
WHAT DO POLLS SAY?
Political polls offer a little insight into how the youth voting bloc might turn out.
A New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll from late September showed 19 to 24-year-olds leaning slightly toward Jackson — but it didn’t survey enough respondents to be statistically significant. The same was true of an early October Washington Post poll and a more recent survey by Suffolk University, both of which showed Jackson performing well among young voters.
A national poll of 18 to 29-year-olds from the spring showed them favoring Democrats, and found economic pressures to be the biggest issue for young voters. Nearly 60% said the country seems to be on the wrong track. A New York Times analysis released Thursday showed young voters moving 15 points to the left since the 2024 election.
Representatives of both major parties in Maine declined interviews about their young voter outreach, but shared statements. Kristina Parker, communications director for the Maine Republican Party and a Gen-Z voter herself, said that the biggest thing motivating young people in the state to vote is the cost of their electricity bills.
“Maine Democrats have controlled the state legislature for 48 out of the last 50 years, and the invoices for their outrageous policies are landing in young people’s hands,” Parker said. “Young voters can’t afford a house in Maine, let alone bankroll leftist wasteful spending from Augusta Democrats.”
The Maine Democratic Party’s deputy organizing director, Reese Remington, said in a statement that the party has reached young voters through its campus organizing program.
“Young Mainers have a critical voice in this election and they know better than anyone that to have an affordable future in Maine, Susan Collins must go,” Remington said.
Pippert said young voters are generally issues-focused, and the most concerning issue currently is affordability. Young voter turnout is always lower than older groups, especially in midterms, and peaked in 2018 at 28%, she said.
ON CAMPUS
Like Bowdoin, the state’s public flagship University of Maine has a nonpartisan elections group called UMaine UVote.
UVote student ambassadors Cecilia Pike and Justine Ordinario help students deal with the logistics of voting and show them that it’s easy to register and cast a ballot.
“On our campus, I’d definitely say that I’ve seen a lot of people be extremely passionate about this election,” said Pike, 19, from Jay. “And the people that we talk to that are registered to vote, they are passionate about other people registering, because they understand the weight of their vote in these elections.”
The Senate race has sparked a lot of discussion and controversy at UMaine, said Ordinario, a 21-year-old from Nevada. As a nonpartisan group, UVote doesn’t lead those conversations. “But we are able to facilitate where they can get their information and lead those discussions to a healthy place, that can ultimately lead to: ‘Vote in the election, and get your voice out there,'” she said.
On the UMaine campus in early September, students said they were generally aware of and planning to vote in the election. At the time, about two months out from the midterms, many said they would need to do more research and get informed before casting their ballots — it was not long after the Democratic party had switched its nominee from Graham Platner to Jackson.
“There’s a lot of information that’s come out recently, and I feel like by the time it actually gets to November, I may not feel the way I feel now,” said Aden Barnes, an 18-year-old environmental science student from Brunswick. Barnes said the biggest issues for her are reproductive rights, women’ s healthcare and LGBTQ healthcare.
Quinn Chessa, 21, a food science major originally from Oregon, said he’d been planning to cast a ballot for Platner, and that Jackson would likely now get his vote.
Although enrolled as a Democrat, Chessa said he prefers to think of himself as unaligned with either party. And he’s increasingly concerned about a lack of productivity in politics, and the value of voting.
“As a voter, I do feel really quite disconnected,” he said. “Does my vote actually make any change?”
HERE OR THERE?
Unlike UMaine, where 64% of students are from in-state, some of Maine’s smaller liberal arts colleges attract a politically engaged but mostly out-of-state population. Just 11% of Bowdoin students, 10% of Bates students and 8% of Colby students are from Maine.
College students have the right to vote where they go to school, and thanks to Maine’s same-day voter registration, it’s an easy option. But students are divided on the ethics.
Dueling op-eds from Colby students recently ran in the Press Herald’s opinion pages, debating the merits of voting in a hometown or in Waterville.
Junior Cleo Rehkopf, arguing that her peers should vote at home, said casting her ballot in the city she’ll soon leave would effectively be “diluting the vote” of locals who will live with the election’s consequences. Senior Anthony Simescu, writing in opposition, said treating student participation in local elections as a distortion assumes that a town “belongs only to those who never leave” even though many Americans are mobile throughout their lives.
Some towns have embraced student participation. In Orono, where UMaine is located, voters decided in 2024 to move municipal elections from March to November so that more students could participate (the previous date often fell during the university’s spring break.)
The Bowdoin Votes coordinators, Amelia Kane and Caroline Clinton, both 21 and seniors from Massachusetts, are agnostic. “Our headline is vote,” Clinton said. “And wherever you want to vote, we’re happy to support you,” Kane added.
Their organization leads the walks to the polls, but also helps students get their absentee ballots for their hometowns. This year, they’ve registered 287 students and provided more than 65 with absentee ballot support.
It’s a little quieter this year than the 2024 presidential election, they said, but students are pretty informed on the names and issues. The challenge is getting students to prioritize making time to do it.
According to early voting data, in the Waterville ward that covers Colby College, about 7.4% of voters have submitted their ballot already. The UMaine-specific precinct in Orono saw just four early votes returned by Oct. 16. The town of Brunswick splits Bowdoin into three different voting districts, so it’s difficult to determine early voting numbers there.
Pippert said the biggest factors country-wide that influence where a college student votes are institutional ones — like same-day registration, whether a student ID counts as identification or how challenging it is to get an absentee ballot. (In Maine, identification is not required at the polls.)
It also matters to students that they feel politically informed.
“College students think really heavily about this,” Pippert said. “And it’s not just something they’re doing on a whim.”
When the Bowdoin students strolled to Town Hall on Tuesday, they were greeted warmly by poll workers, excited to see young people voting, and voting early. At the booths, Kane carried a list of all of the student dorm street addresses: Bowdoin students get their mail to a box in the student center, but need their physical address to vote, which many don’t know offhand.
Kane said she has a close relationship with the town clerk’s office, which is a big supporter of Bowdoin Votes and their initiatives. But the question of where to vote still belongs within each individual.
“Am I voting in Maine because the race is more interesting or because I feel more connected to Maine?” Kane said. “For me, it’s definitely a mix of both.”
Staff Writer Ethan Horton contributed to this report.

title: Maine brewers can make hemp drinks the right way. Congress is about to stop us.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Kai Adams is co-founder of Sebago Brewing Company and founder of Mystic Cove THC Drinks in Gorham.
Sebago Brewing Company was founded in 1998. Today, we operate four brewpubs and a production brewery. We have a robust distribution business and our pubs service more than 12,000 guests a week. We employ 225 Mainers with a payroll of nearly $5 million a year.
Sebago Brewing is a trusted Maine company that gives back to our communities and has done so for nearly three decades. Our business is built on our core values of quality and value.
A couple of years ago, a guest asked me over the bar when we were going to make a THC
drink. Around the same time, our sales team started seeing hemp beverages popping up in retail coolers across the state.
Several cannabis companies began calling to ask if we could produce drinks for them. We had just installed a new high-speed canning line and had a team of brewers who understood ingredients, recipes and quality control. We listened to our customers and launched Mystic Cove in February 2025.
I grew up on Sebago Lake, where there’s a special place called Mystic Cove. The name has
always meant “lake life” to me, and it felt like the right fit for a drink meant to be enjoyed slowly with friends. We launched with four 5mg flavors, including a blueberry lemon that could only come from Maine.
Committed to responsible service, we worked with our service staff to implement a THC service policy where a guest who is drinking alcohol could have one Mystic Cove, two for a guest who is not. Every batch is full-spectrum lab tested, each packaging run is tested for potency during the run and nothing ships until the results are in.
We track every ingredient from the moment it arrives, so what the label says is exactly what is in the can. We train our distributors and educate our customers; a new product only works when people understand it.
The people who chose these drinks surprised me. The first guest to order one at our brewpub was almost 70 years old. One of our servers, who no longer drinks, told me it was the first time in years she felt like she was having an experience at a bar instead of just ordering an iced tea. These are adults looking for another option alongside beer, wine and spirits, and they deserve that choice.
Hemp beverages are not the largest part of our business, but they matter a great deal. For an industry facing flat beer sales, two new products gave our distributors and customers something to be excited about.
The work also taught us contract production, which has since brought in new brewing contracts. That is real value for a company that has more than 200 families depending on it.
Under current federal law, these drinks will be banned on Dec. 11, 2026. The new limit
of 0.4 milligrams of THC per container is a ban in all but name, and most of our customers have no idea it is coming. Many of them believe this issue was settled months ago. When the shelves go empty, Maine retailers and distributors will lose sales, customers will take their business elsewhere and the state will lose tax revenue it could be collecting.
There is a better path forward, and it starts with treating hemp beverages like beer. That means requiring age verification, labeling products clearly, taxing them fairly and selling them through the same distributors and retailers that already handle alcohol responsibly.
The Hemp Beverage Alliance, a national trade group I’m a proud member of, is urging Congress toward exactly this kind of framework. Moving these drinks into the cannabis dispensary system would shut out the brewers who have the equipment and experience to make them safely.
To Sen. Collins, Sen. King and Rep. Pingree: craft beer has been one of this state’s great economic success stories, and hemp beverages can be its next chapter. Maine brewers
are ready to make these products the right way, and I urge you to regulate this category instead of banning it.
To every reader who enjoys these drinks or simply believes adults deserve the choice, you can help. Tell Congress, even in a single sentence, why these drinks matter to you and that you support safe, regulated sales. Dec. 11 is getting close, and your voice matters now.

title: Former NFL ﻿﻿defensive end Allen Bailey dies at 37
text:
'One of my favorites': Former NFL player dead at 37, Andy Reid confirms
Former NFL defensive end Allen Bailey has died at 37, the Kansas City Chiefs confirmed during a news conference Wednesday.
Bailey was drafted by the Chiefs in the third round, 86th overall, of the 2011 NFL Draft. He played for the team from 2011 through 2018. In 2019, he signed with the Atlanta Falcons and remained on the team until he was released in February 2021.
"Sad news, the passing of Allen Bailey. Our hearts go out to his family. Prayers are with them. Way too young, obviously," Chiefs head coach Andy Reid said. "One of my favorite players. Great kid, and just sorry to see that happen to him."
His cause of death has not been released; however, Bailey's brother told TMZ that the family believes he died of natural causes.

title: Light-colored Pickup Sought In I-95 Hit-and-run That Injured Maine DOT Worker

Maine State Police released a photo of a truck and trailer they believe were involved in an I-95 incident that sent a Maine DOT worker to the hospital.
Maine State Police are Looking for the Driver in an I-95 Hit-and-Run Crash
Witnesses told police the vehicle involved in the crash was a light-colored pickup truck, towing a black dump trailer.
State Police say they believe the photo released this week is the vehicle that caused the crash and then drove away without stopping.

The incident happened on I-95 in Pittsfield on Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at 8:17 am.
Maine DOT Worker Was Seriously Injured When Hit By a Construction Barrel
Maine Department of Transportation workers were unloading construction barrels from a truck as traffic passed by, on the other side of a row of concrete Jersey barriers.
A vehicle, believed to be the one in the photo released by the police, struck a Jersey barrier on the right, causing a construction barrel to strike a worker in the construction zone.
The pickup truck continued northbound without stopping.
Witnesses say the driver allegedly turned around as the crash happened and then drove away.
The injured worker, 56-year-old Richard Smart of Westfield, was transported to Northern Light Sebasticook Valley Hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries.
He has since been released from the hospital.
Maine Police Seek Info About the Driver of Pickup in a Hit-and-Run Crash
Anyone who recognizes the vehicle in the photo or has information about the driver is asked to contact the Bangor Regional Communications Center at 207-973-3700, extension 9, and ask to speak with Trooper Klayton Peckham.
Maine State Police remind drivers to slow down, remain alert, and use extra caution when traveling through construction zones.
Roadside workers are often just a few feet away from moving traffic, and a moment of inattention can have devastating consequences.

title: 'That's all on bodycam, baby!': Video shows deputies wrangling escapedcaiman in an Oklahoma creek
text:
'That was crazy!': Bodycam shows Oklahoma law enforcement wrangling escaped pet caiman in a creek
"Yeah, baby!" An escaped caiman that sparked a months-long search in rural Oklahoma was finally caught on camera in a creek near homes.
'That was crazy!': Bodycam shows Oklahoma law enforcement wrangling escaped pet caiman in a creek
"Yeah, baby!" An escaped caiman that sparked a months-long search in rural Oklahoma was finally caught on camera in a creek near homes.
A caiman that escaped into rural Oklahoma in August was captured months later, and the wild moment was caught on camera.
The reptile, which belongs to the alligator family, was found in a Cleveland County creek. The animal's disappearance prompted a search that lasted months, and a warning was issued to pet owners in the area to be on the lookout for the caiman.
Body camera video provided by the Cleveland County Sheriff's Office showed the moments the caiman was captured by the Adam Night Shift crew. The crew searched the area after residents reported seeing the animal close to homes.
Members of Adam Night Shift, dressed in waders, spotted the caiman and sprang into action.
"Yeah, baby!" a deputy yelled after the reptile was caught. "Let me get a picture of this!"
As the deputy held the caiman up for a picture, he seemed equally as excited.
"That's all on bodycam, baby!" the deputy said while laughing.
The animal was safely returned to its owner.
What is a caiman?
A caiman is a small-to-medium-sized predatory reptile that belongs to the alligator family. There are several distinctive species native to Central and South America.
Caimans look very much like alligators and crocodiles, and they mostly live along the edges of rivers and other bodies of water. They are not native to Oklahoma

title: Here are 3 Maine high school football games to watch in Week 8
text:
This season, Varsity Maine reporters will offer up suggestions each week for three games that are worth a drive to watch in person, with a brief explanation of why we think these games are worth a fan’s time.
It’s Week 8 of the Maine high school football season — the final week for most of the state, but the penultimate week for Class A and C teams.
Some teams are still fighting for postseason spots, while others have clinched berths but are seeking a higher seed.
Here are three games to keep on your radar:
Kennebunk (6-1) at Marshwood (6-1), 6 p.m. Friday
Friday’s clash between the Rams and the Hawks could be a preview of the Class B South final. It no doubt will determine the top seed in the region.
After starting the season 1-1, Kennebunk has won five games in a row. The Rams are coming off a hard-fought 20-14 victory over Westbrook. Ethan White scored two touchdowns for Kennebunk, which has a deep group of running backs and a productive passing game led by Giovanni D’Elia.
Marshwood was undefeated until last weekend, when it lost to Biddeford, 37-14. The Hawks have shredded most of their opponents with a relentless rushing attack, but their top two running backs are questionable because of injuries.
Lisbon (5-2) at Freeport (5-2), 6 p.m. Friday
Despite these teams having the same record, Lisbon is currently fourth in the Class D South Crabtree standings, while Freeport is in first place.
The Greyhounds lost to second-place Winthrop/Monmouth/Hall-Dale 34-3 in the season opener but are 5-1 since then and bring a three-game winning streak to Freeport.
Freeport has two close losses, against Class D North leader Winslow (14-6) and Class C contender Wells (28-24). Even with starting quarterback Andrew Thomas injured, the Falcons defeated Morse and Dirigo the past two weeks, and they can clinch the No. 1 seed by defeating Lisbon.
Bonny Eagle (7-0) at Thornton Academy (7-0), 1 p.m. Saturday
Saturday’s matinee is not only a potential Class A South final preview, but also features the top-two teams in the Varsity Maine poll.
Thornton has the recent upper-hand. The Trojans were victorious in both of last season’s matchups — 42-21 in the regular season and 40-28 in the regional final.
Thornton’s multifaceted offense is tough to stop. Five players have rushed for 160 yards or more, led by Brennan Tabor with 634 yards. Noah Fullerton helms a prolific passing attack, completing 42 of 60 passes for 772 yards and 16 scores. His top targets are Logan LeBlanc (18 catches, 454 yards, nine TDs) and Logan O’Keefe (11 catches, 110 yards, four TDs), but eight players have caught passes. Tabor, also one of the state’s top defensive players, has scored a team-best 14 touchdowns.
Bonny Eagle quarterback Lucas Klehn is a touchdown machine and the player the Golden Trojans will have to watch for most. Klehn has contributed nine touchdowns in the Scots’ last two games — a passing touchdown and four rushing touchdowns against Oxford Hills on Oct. 9 and four rushing TDs against Exeter (New Hampshire) on Oct. 15. But Klehn isn’t the Scots’ only weapon. Drew Gervais, the state’s fastest sprinter, is the top receiving target, while Ben Noe and Ben Havu have both rushed for more than 300 yards.

title: AARP Maine poll finds affordability top issue for older voters
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - A new AARP Maine poll finds affordability is the top issue for likely voters age 50 and older heading into the November election.
Rising costs cited as top concern
Nearly half of respondents age 50 and older said rising electricity costs have forced them to cut back on other essentials.
Noël Bonam, AARP Maine State Director, said the cost of everyday essentials is driving voter concerns.
“When an older adult wants to go get groceries from the grocery store, the gas is costing them a whole lot more to get there. The groceries are costing a whole lot more, right? And when they come back home, they try to turn on electricity just for lights or to turn up the heat. Everything is costing a lot more. So that’s a huge motivation for older adults,” Bonam said.
Health care and rural access
Health care is another concern among respondents, both the cost of care and the ability to access it. Bonam said transportation and internet access create additional hurdles in rural communities.
“We don’t have good, reliable internet everywhere for older adults to be able to access telehealth. And that when you’re living in a rural area, that also plays out if you don’t have access to at least telehealth,” Bonam said.
Social Security a key issue
The poll found 81 percent of voters age 50 and older consider Social Security an important issue when deciding their vote. Bonam said conversations with residents in Aroostook County underscored how much that income matters.
“I was in Caribou and Presque Isle as well, and where I’ve spoken to older adults, and many of them said that is what they depend on. It’s something that they paid into. They were expecting it, that it would be available when they needed it, and they need it now,” Bonam said.
Voter motivation high
Eighty-seven percent of likely voters age 50 and older rated their motivation to vote a ten on a ten-point scale. Bonam encouraged voters to ask candidates for specific plans.
“We’re hearing a lot about, we’re going to fix this, we’re going to fix that. But we’re not hearing enough about how those fixes will take place. And I think any voter should hold them accountable and say, please tell me how you’re going to do it,” Bonam said.
The survey of 982 likely Maine voters was conducted September 20-22.

title: Collins and Jackson condemn use of attack ads in Senate race
text:
Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson condemn use of attack ads in Maine's Senate race
Both candidates running for the U.S. Senate in Maine condemned attack ads against each other on Wednesday.
Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins spent Wednesday morning campaigning with former Sen. Joe Manchin, a longtime Democrat from West Virginia who became an independent just months before departing the Senate in January 2025.
"This is a United States senator who basically is a Maine senator," Manchin said. "She's not a Trump senator. She's not a Republican senator or a Democrat senator. She's an American senator."
Collins was asked about a recent radio advertisement that was paid for by the Senate Leadership Fund PAC.
The ad was to the tune of a song and included lyrics such as: "If he screws his own family, he'll screw yours too."
"Well, first of all, I had nothing to do with that ad, and I said that it should be taken down," Collins said.
Collins said that she cannot legally contact the PAC. She added that she had nothing to do with the advertisement.
Collins was first elected to the Senate in 1996. She said this race has not been like one she's ever been involved with before.
"This campaign has been unique in Maine's history, in the number of personal attacks," Collins said. "I've been accused of all sorts of things."
In Augusta, several women, many of whom worked with Jackson in the Maine Legislature, gathered to host a "Women for Troy" event.
The speakers pointed toward the radio ad along with a separate anti-Jackson television ad. They said that ad portrayed the former lawmakers as "victims and villains."
According to the group, this wasn't their experience with Jackson in Augusta.
"He lifted up the voices of women," said former Democratic state lawmaker Rebecca Millett. "He appointed them into leadership positions. He trusted us with the important work of leading powerful committees and our colleagues."
Many members of the group also spoke on the unique style of attack ads in the Senate race. Some also said the level of the advertisements was at a level they've never seen before.
"They can't defend Susan Collins' record, so they are resorting to personal attacks," Millett said. "This TV ad and the disgusting radio ad that goes along with it reek of desperation. And it says a lot more about Sen. Collins and her backers than it says about Troy."
Jackson wasn't in attendance for Wednesday's event. His campaign spokesperson Dan Gottlieb provided a statement in response to the radio advertisement.
In part, Gottlieb said in his statement: "If Collins believes these attacks are wrong, she owes Troy’s family an apology for spreading them herself and must take responsibility for her allies pushing the same personal attack on his family on TV right now."
Maine Women's Lobby also spoke at the event, publicly endorsing Jackson. Members of the lobby mentioned Jackson's voting record and their approval of his work in childcare and the state's paid family and medical leave program.

title: Here’s why Alabama’s governor commuted the death sentence of a man convicted of killing a sheriff’s deputy
text:
MONTGOMERY, Ala. (WSFA/Gray News) - Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey commuted the death sentence of a man convicted of killing a sheriff’s deputy.
Toforest Johnson’s sentence was commuted to life in prison with no chance of parole.
“We are grateful to Governor Ivey for diligently reviewing Toforest’s case and taking action to spare an innocent man from execution,” said Ty Alper, one of Johnson’s attorneys. “This significant milestone was made possible by Alabamians from all sectors of society united in their belief that Toforest does not belong on death row. That list now includes Governor Ivey.”
Johnson was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1995 capital murder of Jefferson County Deputy Sheriff William Hardy.
Johnson was sentenced in 1998 and has spent more than half of his life on death row. He is currently housed at Holman Prison in Atmore, Alabama.
In a statement, Ivey raised concerns about the amount of evidence against Johnson, questioning whether it was sufficient to carry out his sentence. However, she did not say she thought Johnson was innocent.
Johnson’s attorney said his client is innocent.
“Now it is up to the courts to overturn his conviction and grant him a new trial. We will keep fighting until he is home with his family,” he said.
In 2024, Jefferson County District Attorney Danny Carr pushed for a new trial. In 2025, former Alabama Attorney General Bill Baxley, along with a group of former Alabama state and federal prosecutors, asked a judge to grant Johnson a new trial.
There are currently 154 people on Alabama’s death row. Johnson was still listed on the Alabama Department of Corrections’ website as on death row at the time of Ivey’s announcement.

title: Meta ordered to pay New Mexico $25 billion over Cambridge Analytica breach
text:
A judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy and content moderation policies on Facebook.
Judge Francis Mathew handed down the amount, which state Attorney General Raúl Torrez described as “one of the largest, if not the single largest state verdict against a company in American history.”
Torrez said the verdict should be a warning for tech companies and that New Mexico would continue to hold them accountable.
“This judgement should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” Torrez said at a news conference.
The state had sought $35 billion to $40 billion.
Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws when a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, harvested Facebook user data to generate targeted political ads for the 2016 election.
Forty-eight other states settled with Facebook in a nationwide case, but New Mexico chose to take the social media company to court on its own.
Attorneys for New Mexico sought what could have been the largest judgement in U.S. history, arguing the company would only change its ways with a sum that affected its stock price.
Lawyers for Meta argued for paying no more than $3.4 billion. An award 10 times that or even more would violate due process, was unconstitutional and would not hold up under appeal, they said.
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez has said they money will go into a state fund for education.
Meta argued the state failed to prove misleading statements about privacy and that content moderation actually harmed New Mexicans. Interest on the penalty would accrue during an appeal, but the number of violations Meta is charged with could be reduced.
Meta attorney Matt Nicholson argued in court that a sum as high as $40 billion would be “shocking to the conscience” while an attorney for New Mexico, Randi McGinn, urged standing up to “tech titans who think they are bulletproof and can do whatever they want.”
Company argues state failed to prove harm
The state’s case focused on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads. The now-defunct firm’s clients included the 2016 campaign for President Donald Trump.
Attorneys for New Mexico argued that the state’s entire population, not just Facebook users, were deceived by the company’s public statements about privacy on the platform. Facebook’s lawyers argued that the state failed to prove whether people were actually harmed by these deceiving statements.
“The jury didn’t make findings that any New Mexican heard or saw these statements, or was harmed by them,” said Nicholson during a hearing Oct. 1.
New Mexico prosecutors also argued that Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate on the platform. Defense attorneys vehemently denied the allegations, saying the company’s content moderation policies are robust and freedom of speech has to be considered.
Jury found over 43 million violations of state law
New Mexico was the only state to pursue a trial around the Cambridge Analytica scandal after 48 other states signed a settlement for $18 billion in August.
Besides New Mexico, Florida was the only other state that did not sign the settlement, which included an agreement to release Meta from future liability related to the Cambridge Analytica privacy breach.
During the trial, jurors assessed whether Facebook misled users about privacy and content moderation 34 separate times. State prosecutors, though, argued Facebook’s statements deceived the entire population of New Mexico and extended beyond social media users.
In the end, jurors agreed with this premise and found Facebook liable for 2.1 million violations on certain counts, bringing the total number of violations to over 43 million.
Facebook’s attorneys have argued in subsequent court filings that the state’s consumer protection laws don’t apply to people in New Mexico who weren’t using the platform at the time.
Torrez told reporters following the verdict that all money awarded will go into a fund for the state’s education system. The state is also seeking an injunction to stop similar practices.
Meta questions evidence and tally of violations
Meta plans to appeal the jury’s verdict, potentially reducing the number of violations and therefor the total financial penalty. Lawyers for the company said it was unprecedented for the state to count the number of violations based on how many individuals may have heard or seen the misleading statements from the company, arguing there was no evidence these statements ever harmed anyone.
During closing arguments, lawyers for Facebook said the state’s evidence was outdated and that despite having five years to gather material, New Mexico found only one other instance of a data breach.
In one of the few wins for the defense, jurors found the state didn’t prove that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.
The state said the company favored certain accounts and allowed for violent or inaccurate content to proliferate. Attorney Randi McGinn said in her closing argument for the state that Facebook profited off harmful content, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg denied during his video deposition. Zuckerberg said the company has to carefully balance freedom of speech with content moderation.
Attorneys for Facebook said the company has adapted its policies since the state’s lawsuit was filed in 2021 and that it removes 99% of content that violates standards.
___
Schuettler reported from Phoenix. Schuettler is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

Federal government to release barrels of heating oil from South Portland to bring down costs
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Federal government to release barrels of heating oil from South Portland to bring down costs
For the first time, the Trump administration is releasing thousands of barrels of heating oil from a reserve in South Portland in an effort to bring down fuel costs ahead of winter in New England.
Federal government to release barrels of heating oil from South Portland to bring down costs
For the first time, the Trump administration is releasing thousands of barrels of heating oil from a reserve in South Portland in an effort to bring down fuel costs ahead of winter in New England.
The U.S. Department of Energy will make up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil available from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve as Maine faces higher fuel costs heading into the winter months.
The move follows a Sept. 22 request from Maine Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King, who urged the administration to tap the reserve to help increase supply and put downward pressure on prices.
The reserve contains about 1 million barrels of ultra-low sulfur diesel designated for heating oil, including about 200,000 barrels stored in South Portland, according to the Department of Energy.
The reserve also has barrels located near Boston, Massachusetts; New Haven, Connecticut; and the New York harbor area. 
According to the department, the oil will made available through an exchange; fuel retailers must request a minimum of 25,000 barrels and return the same volume of fuel oil plus a premium, in order to ensure that the reserve is refilled for next year.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright authorized the exchange and described it as a temporary response to a temporary supply disruption.
“After receiving Senators Collins’ and King’s letter and extensive discussions with Senator Collins, I have directed the Department to exchange barrels from our Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to mitigate heightened home heating oil costs during the upcoming winter,” Wright said.
The department said the 315,000 barrels represent a 13% increase in the regional supply.
Collins said about half of Maine households rely on fuel oil for heat and said she has repeatedly pressed the administration to increase supply.
“I am pleased that the Administration has acted upon our request to release heating oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve,” Collins said.
King said Maine has been particularly impacted by rising fuel costs.
“Maine has been hit especially hard by the run up in fuel prices since the beginning of the Iran War and the most obvious example is home heating oil,” King said. “This release of stored oil in New England will hopefully be some help.”
The department also notes because the majority of people in the Northeast rely on heating oil to stay warm, the region is "especially vulnerable to fuel oil disruptions."
Some families in Maine have been worried about being able to afford their home heating bills, with one mother in Limington estimating that it will cost her $5,000 to heat her home this winter.
“For our fellow Mainers, I'm worried," said Brittney Worden, a resident of Limington in an interview with ABC news. "This is such a high increase and the overall effect that it's going to have on our community. This is scary."
Maine's heating oil prices have risen dramatically this year. The state Department of Energy Resources reported a statewide average of $6.02 per gallon on Sept. 21, an 81% increase from the same time last year.
“As President Trump's war abroad drives up the price of gas, kerosene, and heating oil here at home, I welcome this move to release home heating oil from the national reserve, which I hope will provide Maine people with some meaningful financial relief as the seasons change and the cold quickly sets in," Gov. Janet Mills said in a statement. "I thank the Congressional Delegation for their advocacy, and I continue to urge them to appropriate additional LIHEAP funding to supplement this move."
The Northeast reserve was established to protect the region from disruptions in heating oil supplies. Federal officials say it has historically been held as a one-million-barrel emergency supply and has only been released twice in its 26-year-history.
This release marks the first time the reserve will be used to lower home heating oil prices.
Fuel transfers or deliveries are expected to be completed by November 13, 2026.

title: 🌅 WOW, MAINE! 😍 The Best Sunrise in America Can Be Found Right Here in Our State!
text:
Maine Is the Best Place in the U.S. to Watch the Sunrise
There are plenty of reasons to love living in Maine, from our rocky coastline and beautiful beaches to the spectacular fall foliage, which is peaking right now. But did you know Maine is also home to one of America's most famous places to watch the sunrise?
If you're willing to get up before the crack of dawn, Cadillac Mountain in Acadia National Park offers a sunrise experience that's tough to beat!
Read More: 15 Fast Food Restaurants We Wish Would Come To Bangor, Maine
Standing 1,530 feet above sea level, Cadillac Mountain is the tallest mountain on the U.S. Atlantic coast north of Brazil. And the views from the summit? Mind-blowing!
Watching the sky turn shades of pink, orange, and gold as the sun rises over the Atlantic Ocean is a memory you won't soon forget. Below you, you'll see islands, bays, and miles of Maine's stunning coastline. It's the kind of view that makes crawling out of bed that early totally worth it!
And there's so much more to explore at Acadia, no matter the season. From spring through fall, visitors can enjoy scenic drives along the park's paved loop road, hiking, bicycling, and horseback riding on carriage roads. You can also try rock climbing, kayaking, canoeing, swimming at Sand Beach or Echo Lake, and guided boat tours along the coast.
When winter rolls around, the fun doesn't stop. Cross-country skiing, snowshoeing, snowmobiling, and ice fishing are just some of the activities to enjoy.
Ready to plan a family adventure? Check out the official Acadia National Park website for more information.
Keep in mind that depending on the season, you may need a vehicle reservation to drive Cadillac Summit Road, so it's worth checking ahead before you go.
Whether you're a lifelong Mainer or just visiting, watching the sunrise from Cadillac Mountain is an unforgettable way to experience the natural beauty of the 207.
Sure, getting out of bed that early isn't easy. But when you're standing above the Atlantic Ocean, watching the world wake up, you'll probably agree it's worth every minute!

title: New Mexico attorney general accuses Epstein attorney, accountant of abuse cover-up at ranch
text:
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — New Mexico’s attorney general filed a lawsuit Wednesday against Jeffrey Epstein’s attorney and accountant, accusing them of concealing his sex trafficking operation at a sprawling Santa Fe-area ranch where the disgraced financier entertained guests.
The lawsuit seeks to stop attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn from accepting any payments from Epstein’s estate, estimated at more than $100 million.
Indyke worked as Epstein’s attorney for roughly two decades. Both he and Kahn have testified in Congress that they did not know about Epstein’s abuse, though New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez has a different view.
“None of this could be done by just one man,” Torrez said. “This was something that was facilitated, that was made possible by handlers, by lawyers, by accountants, by others who have yet to face real consequences.”
He said Indyke and Kahn “stand to benefit substantially” from Epstein’s estate unless a court intervenes.
“Those resources rightfully belong in the hands of survivors,” Torrez said, referring to victims of Epstein’s abuse.
Phone and email messages seeking comment from attorneys for Indyke and Kahn were not immediately returned Wednesday. The U.S. Justice Department did not immediately return an email seeking comment on any federal investigation of the pair in New Mexico.
___
EDITOR’S NOTE — This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org
___
Epstein killed himself in August 2019 in a federal jail in New York City, where he was awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.
His former girlfriend and close associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, is serving a 20-year prison sentence after her 2021 conviction on sex trafficking charges in New York. Witness testimony at Maxwell’s trial alleged she and Epstein had sexually abused women at the New Mexico ranch.
Epstein purchased the Zorro Ranch in Stanley, a sparsely populated ranching community about 30 miles (48 kilometers) south of Santa Fe, in 1993. He built a 26,700-square-foot mansion with a sprawling courtyard, a living room roughly the size of the average American home, and a private airstrip and helipad.
Epstein never faced charges in New Mexico, though the state attorney general’s office in 2019 confirmed that it was investigating and planned to forward its findings to federal authorities in New York. Hector Balderas, who was attorney general at the time, said the state’s outdated laws failed to protect children from abuse.
Torrez reopened the state’s investigation this year. In August, he sued the Justice Department, accusing it of blocking the state from investigating alleged sex crimes at the ranch. The government said it was not releasing some information to the state to avoid disclosing victim-identifying information.
Also in August, a commission established by state lawmakers to investigate whether local authorities looked the other way, released a 119-page report that found that authorities repeatedly deferred to investigations in New York, Palm Beach, Florida, and the Virgin Islands, while leaving Epstein’s offenses in New Mexico unexamined and unpunished.
The ranch was sold by Epstein’s estate in 2023 to the family of Don Huffines, a Republican who is the Texas state comptroller. The money was set aside for creditors.
Probate proceedings related to Epstein’s will and assets are being handled in the U.S. Virgin Islands.
___
White contributed from Detroit.

title: Trump administration asks US Supreme Court to lift halt on Big Bend border wall
text:
Trump administration asks US Supreme Court to lift halt on Big Bend border wall
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Wednesday to let it resume building a border wall project through the Big Bend region of Texas.
The government filed an emergency appeal asking the justices to lift a lower court decision halting construction. That ruling marked a setback to one of President Donald Trump's signature projects.
Related video above: Protesters urge Texas Parks and Wildlife to oppose any border construction at Big Bend State Park
The administration has been racing forward with construction on a border wall and other infrastructure from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.
But in the Big Bend region, the administration has run into opposition from ranchers, residents, business owners and environmentalists who argue the projects are a waste of money in an area of historically low illegal immigration and that construction could harm the region's scenic landscapes.
Opponents have filed numerous lawsuits seeking to stop the project, which in the Big Bend consists of a mixture of walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology.
Ruling in one of those cases, Judge Kathleen Cardone on Oct. 2 ordered the government to stop construction across the roughly 500-mile project area while the case plays out in the courts. It was a major victory for the bipartisan opposition.
The case hinges on sweeping waivers signed by the Secretary of Homeland Security that allow U.S. Customs and Border Protection to bypass environmental and other regulations that would otherwise slow down construction of such a major project.
The government argued that the Big Bend sector is an area of high illegal entry, and said legislation dating back to 1996 explicitly gives the secretary these far-reaching powers as necessary to build physical barriers or roads near the border to stop people from crossing illegally.
Opponents disagreed, arguing that Congress gave that power to waive regulations specifically in areas of “high illegal entry.” They said Big Bend, a remote and rugged region, doesn’t fit that description.
Cardone sided with the opponents.
“The Court finds that Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of their major questions doctrine claim that the Big Bend Waivers were issued in excess of the Secretary’s authority,” she wrote.
Trump has long vowed to build a border wall along the roughly 2,000-mile length of the southwest border. Last summer, Republicans in Congress allocated Homeland Security $46 billion to finish the project, which will be a mixture of 30-foot-tall steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology.
The opposition in Texas’s Big Bend region had been brewing for months, but it escalated in August when bulldozers were spotted clearing land in Big Bend National Park.
The preliminary injunction filed by Cardone stops construction there as well as land up and downriver from the park that is owned by private landowners or the state.
The government has argued that if this region is one of the only areas left without a wall or other border infrastructure, illegal immigration could end up funneling to the Big Bend. But opponents have argued that other forms of infrastructure such as drones or surveillance towers are just as effective and a lot less expensive than the wall plans.

title: Current credit card interest rates
text:
Current credit card interest rates
The average credit card interest rate is 19.70%, down from a record-high 20.79% set on Aug. 14, 2024.
Current credit card interest rates
Bankrate Data Center
Since 1976, Bankrate has been the go-to source for personal finance data, publishing average rates on the most popular financial products and tracking the experience of consumers nationwide.
See more
Credit card rates are creeping up again
How are credit card rates set?
Your credit card APR has two parts: the Prime Rate, plus a markup your card issuer chooses.
The Prime Rate is the benchmark that banks use for their most creditworthy customers and the basis for many financial products. It’s typically 3 percentage points higher than the top end of the federal funds rate, which is set by the Federal Reserve’s Federal Open Market Committee. Currently, the Prime Rate is 7%.
The issuer’s markup is where the rest of your rate comes from, and it’s set at the issuer’s discretion. On average, this margin often runs between 12 and 13 percentage points.
Credit cards carry a higher markup than other loans, such as mortgages and auto loans, because credit card debt is unsecured — it isn’t backed by a physical asset such as a home or car that the issuer can seize if you don’t repay the debt.
When the Fed moves, your rate moves
Your credit card rate changes along with the Fed rate, but these changes are typically incremental. For example, the Fed raised the benchmark rate by 25 basis points on Sept. 16, 2026, bringing the target range to 3.75% to 4.00%. In the following month, the average credit card interest rate rose by 0.12%, according to Bankrate’s data.
Because most cards carry a variable APR with the Prime Rate baked in, a Fed rate change passes straight through to your rate — either up or down — and your issuer isn’t required to give you notice. Most people see it within one to two billing cycles. The exact timing is up to the issuer: some use the Prime Rate as of your statement date, while others use the first or last day of the month.
When your issuer changes your rate because the Prime Rate changes, it applies to your existing balance and all new purchases.
Your rights when your credit card interest rate changes
Whether your issuer is required to let you know about a rate change depends on the reason for the change. If the rate moved because the Prime Rate moved, the issuer isn’t required to alert you. The change is automatic and is built into your card agreement.
But if your issuer changes your interest rate for another reason, such as applying a penalty APR for a late payment, you have the right to know. The issuer is required to give you a 45-day notice before any such changes. You have the right to opt out of the new terms, but if you do, your card company will likely close your account. You won’t have to pay off the entire balance immediately, but your minimum payment may increase.
If you agree to the new terms, the new APR can only apply to new balances, except in certain circumstances.

How do credit card rates affect you?
When you carry a balance, your issuer divides your APR by 365 to get the daily rate, then applies it to your average daily balance, or the average of what you owed on each day of the billing cycle. That’s the part that matters: If you carry a balance, interest builds every single day. Paying it down is the only thing that stops it.
Let’s say you have $5,000 of credit card debt and your interest rate is 20% APR. If you only make minimum payments, you’ll be in debt for about 23 years and pay roughly $7,723 in interest, according to Bankrate’s minimum payment calculator.
But if you pay your credit card purchases in full each month, you aren’t charged interest and you typically receive an interest-free grace period of at least 21 days. For example, if your billing statement is generated on the 1st of the month, you usually have until at least the 22nd to pay without interest accruing. And because the clock doesn’t start until your statement closes, something you bought on the first day of the cycle gets the whole cycle plus the grace period — close to seven weeks interest-free.
Keep in mind: An interest-free grace period applies only to purchases. If you’ve made a balance transfer or taken a cash advance, a different APR applies and there’s usually no grace period. Cash advances typically start accruing interest the day you take them out. Likewise, if you transfer a balance to a card, interest will begin to accrue immediately unless you have an intro 0% APR balance transfer promotion.
-  Our methodology When we refer to the average credit card rate, we mean the average midpoint of the APR ranges assessed by 111 popular credit cards offered by the 50 largest U.S.-based credit card issuers. Most credit cards charge different interest rates to different customers based upon their creditworthiness. A consumer with an excellent credit score, for example, might be charged 14.99%. That same card might charge as high as, say, 24.99% to someone with a lower credit score. In that example, we would use 19.99% (the midpoint between 14.99% and 24.99%) in our average credit card rate calculations.

title: Australian lawmaker has both legs amputated after alleged deliberate attack by car rammer
text:
Australian lawmaker has both legs amputated after alleged deliberate attack by car rammer
The Australian lawmaker hit by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack has now had both legs amputated, her husband announced Wednesday.
Helen Haines, an independent federal MP, remains in critical condition in the hospital after being hit on a main road outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, northeastern Victoria, mid-afternoon Monday.
“Helen’s left leg was amputated on Monday. We had been hoping that her right leg would be saved, but… the surgeons had to also remove her right leg,” Phil Haines, the MP’s husband of nearly 40 years, told a press conference at The Alfred hospital in Melbourne.
“But the good news in all this is Helen is alive and she’s stable,” he added.
On Monday, Haines, 65, was standing at the rear of her parked car, unpacking items from the trunk, when a man driving a Toyota Land Cruiser drove past her before allegedly turning around and ramming her into her vehicle. It’s not clear why.
As bystanders rushed to her aid, a local barber pulled the driver from the car, detaining him until police arrived. Haines was immediately airlifted to Melbourne for surgery.
Haines, a popular and respected politician in Canberra, has represented her community as an independent MP since 2019.
The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, appeared in court on Wednesday and has since been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.
Speaking after Phil Haines at the same news conference, Governor-General Sam Mostyn said she was keeping King Charles III updated on developments.
The governor-general is appointed by the king as Australia’s formal head of state, though the country is led by a prime minister under a parliamentary system.
“Australia is still reeling with the shock and distress of this terrible attack,” Mostyn said. “I know that here in Victoria, in particular, people are simply dumbfounded and finding it very hard to fathom the scale of this tragedy.”
As a pile of bouquets grew outside Haines’ electorate office, her husband urged people to consider donating instead.
“She loves flowers, but it’s a bit difficult to look after many bunches of flowers,” Phil Haines said. “We will ask people if they would like to support Helen financially to make a donation to Save the Children Fund.”
Security briefings
Though police are still to determine if the incident was politically motivated, the alleged attack shocked the country and has shone a spotlight on the safety of its political leaders.
Members of parliament received in-depth security briefings in Canberra on Wednesday as the Australian Federal Police (AFP) commissioner pointed to rising reports of harassment and threats against federal parliamentarians.
Authorities were seeing “increasing political polarization and anti-government sentiment, conspiracy-driven and grievance-based behaviors,” Commissioner Krissy Barrett told a news conference.
“Lone actors motivated by a convergence of personal grievance, mental health vulnerabilities, and ideological concerns,” were contributing to the rising trend, she added.
Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush said police had no intelligence on Haines’ alleged attacker that pointed to an imminent risk.
In a very short court hearing Wednesday morning, Nugent’s lawyer said Nugent had a rare neurological condition – and was currently unmedicated.
No application for bail was made, and the next hearing is scheduled for Feb. 4, 2027.

title: Before Maine looks for an economic ‘secret sauce,’ it should look inward
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
John Surdyk lives in Waterville.
In the winter of 1882, the Kennebec River was one of the busiest industrial sites in New England. Crews sawed ice from the river, hauled it to wooden icehouses along the banks and shipped it to Boston, New York and Washington.
Economic developers would call it a textbook cluster: specialized labor, local capital and shared infrastructure all organized around one product. It lasted barely a generation. Mechanical ice plants and home refrigeration gutted the trade by about 1920.
I learned this story after moving to the Kennebec Valley this summer, and it stayed with me at Maine Blue Economy Week in Portland three weeks ago.
The gathering of founders, researchers, lenders and investors was a valuable opportunity for me to see Maine’s social and economic capital at work. Maine has world-class research institutions, strong educational institutions and tenacious founders who pursue profit and, often, public benefit. I met people building electric outboard motors and sustainable seafood brands. The work coming out of the state’s labs and institutes impressed me.
Much of the conversation at the event revolved around one idea: an “ocean cluster” informed by the experiences of others in Massachusetts, Alaska and elsewhere. I understand the pull, but borrowing a model is harder than it looks.
Harvard’s Michael Porter helped popularize clusters, and the idea is intuitively attractive since it implies a recipe or “secret sauce.”
The evidence that governments can build one on purpose is thinner than the idea’s popularity suggests. Some economic geographers argue the concept deserves a public-policy health warning. Florida spent more than $1 billion over two decades luring research institutes to seed a biotech cluster, and by most public accounts, the results have disappointed.
Part of the trouble is how we learn from one another.
I have participated in research into how universities and governments borrow startup policies from each other, and the pattern is humbling. We hear the success stories, but failed clusters rarely keynote a conference. We also copy what we can see, such as the structure of a public-private partnership, an incentive package, even a brand (Silicon Alley, Silicon Prairie). What we miss is the local history, tacit knowledge and relationships that make a place work. A region can learn and easily learn the wrong lesson.
The story of New Bedford, shared at the conference, made the point very well. Whaling. Textile mills. Commercial fishing.
Academics call this progression of pivots regional branching where new industries grow by putting a workforce’s existing skills to new uses. The lesson is not “build a cluster.” It’s that improvisation matters as much as planning. Entrepreneurs already know this.
So what might Maine do instead?
Treat its blue economy strategy the way a Bigelow scientist or a startup founder treats a promising hypothesis. Run small experiments. Measure the results. Take the data seriously (even when it’s unwelcome), and adjust. Hard-won local knowledge will likely serve the state better than imitating somewhere else’s pathway.
One keynote at the conference was titled “Our Heritage Is Innovation.” Maybe so. The ice kings were innovators, too.

title: A new drug offers hope for children with rare Hunter syndrome
text:
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. (InvestigateTV) — Nearly 10% of Americans live with a rare disease, and most of these conditions have no approved treatment options.
One of those conditions, Hunter syndrome, mostly affects boys and has had only one approved treatment since 2006. A new drug approved this year is offering families a different outlook.
Rare diseases are referred to by patients and doctors as “orphan diseases” because they receive little attention in research and health care, according to the National Institute for Children’s Health Quality.
Most rare diseases, about 72%, are genetic, and of those, about 70% start in childhood. Children living with rare disorders often face long delays for an accurate diagnosis, a process often called “a diagnostic odyssey,” along with chronic physical and mental health issues and complex care needs.
Hunter syndrome, also known as mucopolysaccharidosis type two, or MPS II, is one such genetic disease. Since 2006, enzyme replacement therapy has been the only approved treatment, but that medication addressed only some physical symptoms of the disease, such as joint stiffness.
Diagnosis after months of questions
Atlas Neuerburg is almost 4 years old. He likes to spin vinyl records on his father’s turntable, is a fan of John Candy, Michael J. Fox and “Back to the Future,” and practices swinging a bat in his yard.
Before Atlas’ parents, Nick and Jenny Neuerburg, had a name for their son’s condition, they were in and out of doctors’ offices for what seemed like typical early childhood issues.
“He was just a little bit slow with gross motor stuff. He was slow to crawl. Slow to walk,” Jenny Neuerburg said.
During Atlas’ regular 18-month checkup, a doctor examined his stomach.
“The doctor touched his stomach and asked if it always felt hard like that,” Jenny Neuerburg said. “Then she called us the next morning and said, ‘I’ve been thinking of his stomach all night and it’s bothering me.’”
A hard or distended stomach is a common sign of MPS II, according to the Cleveland Clinic. Other early indicators include a wider than normal head, chest and short neck; stiffness in the joints; persistent ear infections or hearing loss; and distinctive facial features.
Symptoms generally appear between 18 months and 4 years of age, and the most severe cases can be life-threatening.
“That led to blood tests and eventually genetic testing and that’s how we found out,” Jenny Neuerburg said. “The day after Christmas, so we’ll always remember that.”
Relocating for clinical trial
At the time, the Neuerburgs lived in Kansas. A specialist at Children’s Mercy Hospital in Kansas City pointed them toward North Carolina.
“We actually packed up our entire house in Kansas City and started driving across country,” Nick Neuerburg said.
The couple’s research led them to Dr. Joseph Muenzer, a pediatric geneticist with UNC Health in Chapel Hill and an expert in Hunter syndrome and other forms of MPS. His clinic is one of a handful of sites in the country running a clinical trial for a drug that targets neurological aspects of the disease.
“There’s probably four or five sites around the country,” Muenzer said.
Children with Hunter syndrome are unable to produce the enzyme that typically clears a buildup of cellular waste material, known medically as glycosaminoglycans, or GAGs. Without the enzyme, the material builds up and leads to progressive damage in the body and brain.
The trial Atlas joined tested a weekly intravenous infusion that replaces the missing enzyme. Unlike other treatments, it crosses the blood-brain barrier — the tightly locked layer of cells that defend the brain from harmful substances — allowing it to reach both body and brain.
“I preach both the physical disease and the brain disease, something we didn’t have before. So it’s a life changer for the MPS II community,” Muenzer said. “For the first time, for a lot of these families, they were given hope.”
Atlas joined the trial as a toddler, celebrating his third birthday during one of his weekly infusions.
More than two years later, he shows no further signs of decline. Muenzer said other trial participants are seeing similar results.
“I have a few patients in the clinical trial who were started when they were around two years of age,” Muenzer said. “And now at six and seven, you almost don’t know they have Hunter’s syndrome anymore because their physical disease basically has not developed, and they’re developmentally appeared to be normal.”
A mother’s hope
In March 2026, the Food and Drug Administration granted accelerated approval for the drug, called Avlayah, for patients through age 16.
Kim Stephens, executive director of the Muenzer MPS Research and Treatment Center, believes the approval is what patients’ families have been waiting for.
“We’re going to have some kids that won’t develop like a typical Hunter syndrome child. And that’s going to be really amazing for our community,” Stephens said.
Stephens’ son, Cole, was diagnosed with Hunter syndrome at age 2. As the disorder progressed, Cole lost most language skills except for two words: “help” and “mommy.”
Today, Cole is 15, and it’s unlikely he’ll say the word “mommy” again.
Stephens knows Avlayah is not a cure and won’t reverse what Cole has lost. But she hopes the drug can slow what comes next.
“[I] want him to be able to laugh and run and enjoy his favorite things and do puzzles and just continue to be the happy child he is,” Stephens said.
In May 2026, Cole received his first infusion. After the initial doses, Stephens said she sees a difference in Cole’s ability to focus. While she can’t say for sure whether the change is the direct result of the drug, she feels strongly it is.
Cost and access
A spokesperson for Denali Therapeutics, the manufacturer of Avlayah, said the U.S. list price for the drug is $5,200 per vial, but individual costs vary based on a patient’s body weight and insurance plan.
So far, the Neuerburgs have not paid anything out of pocket because Atlas is involved in the ongoing clinical trial. The hope is that one day Atlas will be able to receive his treatment at home instead of traveling to Muenzer’s clinic once a week.
Jenny Neuerburg said she sees something special in her son’s future.
“I feel like there’s something about him,” she said. “He’s going to change the world.”
