title: New UN initiative will aim to tackle the military uses of AI
text:
New UN initiative will aim to tackle the military uses of AI
The United Nations is launching a new initiative on the military uses of artificial intelligence, aimed at addressing some dire concerns about the threat the rapidly developing technology could pose to humanity.
Related video: Trump waives new sanctions on Russia under law named for late Sen. Graham
The initiative by the U.N. Institute for Disarmament Research plans to launch Thursday, establishing the first international forum for key players to try to tackle the issue.
Robin Geiss, head of the Geneva-based institute known as UNIDIR, warned at a U.N. press conference Tuesday that “the margin for human judgment is increasingly narrow, including in the nuclear domain.”
It’s difficult to assess how close the world is to machines possibly acting outside of human control, Geiss said, and that uncertainty “is the issue we’re trying to resolve here.”
One problem is that AI is increasingly creeping into so many areas — early warning systems, information gathering and reconnaissance, to name a few — “and it’s quite difficult to say at which point we’re actually really losing control,” he said.
For a long time, he said, there was widespread reluctance to deal with AI guardrails, but the proliferation of its capabilities and the potential impact have led to “a growing realization that we stand at a crossroad — that now is the time to act, including on military AI.”
Geiss said the U.N. recognizes that global competition to lead on AI poses serious obstacles.
“But concerns about AI’s impact are already transcending geopolitical blocs, and they’re prompting action from major powers,” he said, pointing to a proposal last month for the U.S. and China to set up an AI safety alert system for issues that could threaten national security.
The risks posed by AI were a major topic in speeches by leaders of many of the U.N.’s 193 member nations at their annual high-level meeting last month.
UNIDIR this summer established a Center of Excellence on AI, Peace and Security, the first permanent platform by the world body focused on those issues. Geiss said it received funding from all five major nuclear powers — the U.S., Russia, China, Britain and France.
On Thursday, UNIDIR will launch a new forum as part of the center to bring together “actors from every relevant sector and all over the world” to work on AI in military uses.
Geiss was vague on exactly what the initiative will do, but he said it will be part of other AI efforts being launched by the center this week. Another will focus on the role of industry and aims to develop “a framework for responsible industry behavior,” he said.
Decisions by companies on design and development “determine whether AI-enabled military capabilities are ultimately reliable, predictable and whether they can operate in line with international law,” Geiss said.
For that reason, he said, UNIDIR is developing a framework of responsible industry behavior that will “provide practical, voluntary guidelines" that follow international law and ensure human rights.
The U.N. agency will hold consultations this week with defense technology companies, software developers, subcontractors, investors and others that will work alongside governments, civil society, academia and experts, Geiss said.
UNIDIR also is launching an initiative focused on the risks of AI misuse by armed groups, he said, warning that such actors are already using the technology to support operational planning, execution and logistics.
“The urgent issue of AI in the military domain will certainly no longer be allowed to linger in the shadows,” Geiss said. “The time has come to pull our strengths and confront AI in the military head-on.”

title: Vance says Republicans shouldn't complain about Ramaswamy ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother
text:
Vance says Republicans shouldn't complain about Ramaswamy ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother
Vice President JD Vance said during a campaign visit to Ohio on Wednesday that he is "disgusted" by the Republican pushback against an ad by Vivek Ramaswamy that features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent in the governor's race, Dr. Amy Acton, and raises questions about her traumatic childhood.
Video above: Video gives new insight into security incident at Amy Acton campaign event
"Politics is a tough business," Vance said to reporters.
In Cincinnati, the vice president said it was "not really my concern" whether the controversial 60-second spot was appropriate, and said he was focused on supporting Republican candidates in their midterm races.
"I'm a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America," Vance said in his first public comments on the ad, which has roiled one of the most contentious and expensive governor's races in the country.
The advertisement features Acton's birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her "a liar" and insinuating she has mental health issues. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather was indicted for raping Acton, who was 12 at the time.
The video was criticized by both Democrats and Republicans when it exploded into public view Tuesday, just two weeks before Election Day. On Wednesday, one of the candidates Vance was supporting at the rally offered a different view.
"I would not have run that ad," Republican Sen. Jon Husted said in a statement to The Associated Press. He did not raise the issue during his joint appearance at the rally with Vance and Ramaswamy. Husted is in a tough fight with former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who on Tuesday called the spot "disgusting."
Nikki Haley, who sparred with Ramaswamy during the 2024 Republican presidential primary over the personal nature of his attacks, called him "a bad guy" in a social media post Tuesday. "It's a shame he continues to get away with it," she wrote.
Ramaswamy, a billionaire tech entrepreneur, claimed credit for the ad and said he will spend $4 million to promote it despite the backlash from some members of his own party. He didn't address it in remarks before Vance spoke at a rally outside Cincinnati.
Acton, Ohio's former health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child.
Police and court records show Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter Amy, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton's biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur, who has since died, failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive.
Acton said she has not seen her mother since she appeared in a courtroom in the late 1970s. Her campaign on Tuesday posted a video of her brother who supported her backstory about living in a tent and being abused.
In his remarks to reporters ahead of the rally, Vance said Acton "lies about every single one of her positions."
Acton's campaign declined to respond to Vance's comments, saying that her painful history was not the centerpiece of her run for governor.
Michael Wedding, 20, came to Vance's rally Wednesday — but not to support Ohio's Republican ticket. He said he would part with his large Republican family and vote for Acton for governor, adding that he attended the rally in large part to see Ramaswamy in person.
He said he had seen the ad and found it "very, very gross."
"She was sexually abused as a child," he said of Acton, "and I thought it was kind of scummy that they would use that in an advertisement. I don't think it's right to use her sexual abuse as a kid, or give any sort of platform to that."
Binkley reported from Washington. Associated Press video journalist Patrick Aftoora-Orsagos contributed to this story from Sharonville, Ohio.

title: QUINN QUESTIONS: My return to fashion
text:
All my life, I’ve found it hard to resist a good bargain. So, the pandemic a few years ago briefly curtailed my excellent purchasing decisions.
I was always out in the stores, shopping for the latest in exercise equipment, self-help videos, or ideas to impress my supervisors.
I really liked clothes. At work, I usually wore nice khakis and a golf shirt that made me look semi-cool.
I shopped both in-store and online. Truth is, I wanted to look better than I actually am. I believe in that old saying, “If you don’t have a good act, you better wear a good costume.”
But my shopping stopped when in-office activities got cancelled temporarily. Instead, my company scheduled a series of daily video conferences.
So, I had to adjust to just looking great above the waist. I positioned my home office in a small storage space. I put a bookcase behind my chair, so viewers would think I had actually read those books.
But each day at home my physical appearance descended closer to Hades. First, I quit shaving my scraggly beard. I looked like a guy who fell face-first onto grass clippings.
I started to wear sweatshirts with the sleeves cut off. I bought two pair of gray sweatpants, which I alternated every other week.
One day a cousin came for a visit, and he suddenly appeared at my storage room desk. He said he found me by the smell.
But eventually we returned to the office. I’m showering every other day now, and my wife says I look almost normal again.
Truthfully, my socks don’t match every day. But that’s a style choice.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: Readers Theater to feature 4 children’s books in Bath performance
text:
The characters from four children’s picture books are coming to the Morse High School stage this weekend. Local nonprofit Midcoast Literacy will present a live Readers Theater performance from 2 to 3 p.m. Saturday in the school auditorium.
Before the show there will be activities for kids inspired by the stories starting at 1 p.m. For families with children ages 4-10, the one-hour performance by local, professional actors will feature “Mercy Watson to the Rescue” by Kate DiCamillo, “Bears Don’t Share!” by Lorna Scobie, “Lilly’s Purple Plastic Purse” by Kevin Henkes and “It’s Raining Bats & Frogs” by Rebecca Colby.
Tickets are $10 each or $35 for a family (four to eight people) and can be purchased at midcoastliteracy.org or by calling 207-443-6384.
“Putting together this active and visual take on children’s books is one of our favorite ways to encourage reading at home,” Daniel Burson, Midcoast Literacy’s executive director, said in a prepared release. “Seeing the kids getting into the pre-show activities and then watching the show, with faces painted, intent on the stories, is always a thrill. And it’s all about sharing the love of reading with families.”
Readers Theater is a style of live performance that blends the reading aloud of a book with theatrical elements. The cast of actors simultaneously narrates the story and brings added life to the characters through voice, expression and movement. In “Mercy Watson to the Rescue,” porcine wonder Mercy Watson creates havoc in the neighborhood when her decision to snuggle in the Watsons’ bed causes trouble and the fire department is called. In “Bears Don’t Share!”, with winter on the way, Squirrel and his friend Bear are on the hunt for some food. There’s just one problem: Bears don’t share! In “Lilly’s Purple Plastic Purse,” Lilly loves school and her favorite teacher, Mr. Slinger, until her new favorite musical purse distracts the class and has to be taken away. And in “It’s Raining Bats & Frogs,” what’s Delia the witch to do when a rainstorm threatens the annual Halloween parade? Grab her magic wand and make it fun!
Midcoast Literacy’s Oct. 24 Readers Theater event is sponsored by Bowdoin College and Fiction: A Novel Bookshop. All proceeds will support Midcoast Literacy’s Read Together tutoring program for children ages 6-14.

title: Maine women’s basketball schedules game in Portland
text:
The University of Maine women’s basketball team will play in Portland for the first time in three years when it takes on Fairfield at 6 p.m. on Dec. 9 at the Expo.
It will be the first Portland appearance for the Black Bears since taking on Indiana, then led by Gorham native Mackenzie Holmes, on Nov. 30, 2023, at the Cross Insurance Arena. Their last game at the Expo was against Navy on Nov. 24, 2019.
Maine, which will open its season at home Nov. 5 against Siena, went 19-13 a year ago, losing to Vermont in the America East tournament final.
Five in-state players are on Maine’s roster: Emmie Streams-Stevens of Bangor High, Izzy Allen of Central, Lizzy Gruber of Gardiner, Maddie Fitzpatrick of Cheverus and Bailey Breen of Oceanside.

title: Inmate convicted of murder dies in prison
text:
CHARLESTON, Maine (WABI) - An inmate serving a 37-year murder sentence at Mountain View Correctional Facility in Charleston has died.
According to the Maine Department of Corrections, Andrew St. George, 64, died Tuesday morning.
St. George was sentenced just last year for the murder of his estranged wife.
Prosecutors said he stabbed her before running her over with a truck and then confessed to his son.
No cause of death was given.
The Maine Attorney General’s Office and Medical Examiner have been notified of the death as consistent with DOC policy.

title: Feds release emergency heating oil to lower Maine prices; Collins, King claim win
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The federal government will release up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil into the Northeast, the Department of Energy announced Wednesday, using a rare measure to lower prices that continue to hover near record-highs.
The 1 million-barrel Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve has only been tapped twice before, most recently in the aftermath of Hurricane Sandy in 2012. Maine Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King wrote to President Donald Trump last month to ask for the release, saying heating costs were high enough to warrant emergency action.
Since this new heating oil supply won’t hit the Maine market until next month, it’s unclear how much it will impact prices, which currently sit at $5.97 per gallon in Maine on average. But Collins and King said it should offer some relief.
U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said that he had directed staff to begin the process of releasing the reserves, but added that it was a “temporary measure to solve a temporary supply disruption,” according to a joint news release from Collins and King on Wednesday.
Trump and his administration officials have long told the public that the U.S. and Israel’s war in Iran, which has constricted the crucial oil passageway of the Strait of Hormuz, would be quickly resolved.
Since February, when the conflict began, heating oil costs have gone up by 56% in Maine. Costs are up 77% over this time last year.
“Maine has been hit especially hard by the run up in fuel prices since the beginning of the Iran War and the most obvious example is home heating oil,” King said in the release. “Maine is one of the most dependent states in the country on home heating oil and the cost is absolutely through the roof. This release of stored oil in New England will hopefully be some help.”
Heating oil has become a campaign issue for Collins with just weeks until Election Day. Collins and her Democratic challenger, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, have blamed each other for high energy costs. Gubernatorial candidates have also called for more heating assistance.
The Department of Energy is using an “exchange” to release this heating oil — a process where oil companies bid on and receive at least 25,000 barrels of the strategic reserves, and then must return the entire portion they took, plus at least 5% extra, at a later date.
Companies must return heating oil to the federal government by April 2027 or face an additional premium that increases by 2.5% monthly, according to the Department of Energy’s request for bids. Those companies will pick up oil from one of three locations in New England next month; one of the locations is Sunoco’s tank site in South Portland.
This is the first time the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve has been utilized to lower heating oil prices, rather than to respond to a sudden supply-line disruption or natural disaster.
“The department anticipates this release will put downward pressure on home heating oil costs and make a real difference for Maine homeowners as they prepare for winter,” Collins said in the release.
Collins’ office said the 315,000 barrels would increase heating oil supply in New England by 13%, using Oct. 9 statistics from the U.S. Energy Information Agency. But heating oil reserve also covers New York, where about 1.7 million residents use heating oil, kerosene or propane during cold months.
With costs still near their record high, Maine’s federally supported heating assistance fund, the Home Energy Assistance Program, will likely not go as far as in past winters — even with an early release of those funds and a carryover from last year.
Maine, as the state most reliant on heating oil, stands to gain most from the early release of these heating assistance funds. About 45,000 people received the assistance last year, MaineHousing said.
Applications for heating assistance are open now. Maine residents hoping to apply for HEAP funding or looking for other assistance can contact their local community action program or call 211. The state also releases an annual Winter Heating Guide with cost-saving resources for households of all incomes.

title: Up and Down the Kennebec Valley: Medical history in central Kennebec Valley (China)
text:
China
As past stories in this subseries have shown, identifying a 19th century doctor with a single town isn’t always easy. They tended to move around, and even when settled, to ignore town lines as they treated people.
The following article will share information your writer was able to find about doctors who spent at least part of their careers in China, the town north of Windsor, last week’s setting.
Henry Kingsbury’s Kennebec County history and the China bicentennial history name a couple dozen (at least) doctors who practiced in China. Your writer started with four identified by last names only, doctors Bennett, Goodspeed, Leach and Tebbets.
The China history says an unnamed source called Dr. Bennett, who lived on Neck Road in the northwestern part of town, the first physician in China, “but he apparently did not stay long”; the first permanent physician, according to the same source, was Dr. Daniel Stevens (see below).
AI provided a Dr. Gilman Lougee Bennett (1805-1872), who allegedly lived on (non-existent) Middle Road, in China Village. More reliable sources say Dr. Bennet was a prominent physician in Parsonsfield (close to the New Hampshire border, more than 100 miles from China). He appears again below.
Dr. Isaac R. Goodspeed was born in China on May 30, 1831. He graduated from Bowdoin Medical School in 1854, and the same year married Elizabeth P. Woodcock, of Gardiner. They promptly headed west to Wisconsin and then to California. A 2008 article found on line calls him “one of the foremost citizens of San Mateo County” for 56 years.
Dr. Leach is mentioned in the China history as owner of one of the earliest automobiles in China, one he bought after 1912. Your writer found no other information.
Dr. Tebbetts appears in the China history as a South China resident whose house was saved when an April 1872 fire burned most of the village, including Tebbetts’ stable. However, if “Dr. Tebbetts” was actually Dr. Benjamin L. Tibbetts, see below.
This article will share random information about the lives of 11 more China doctors, described more or less in chronological order.
* * * * * *
At least two sources say Dr. Daniel Stevens was the first doctor to open a practice in China, settling on Neck Road around 1807 or 1808. Kingsbury said he arrived in 1808 and practiced until he died in 1841, age 59.
An on-line genealogy says Stevens was born Aug. 11, 1782, in Worcester, Massachusetts. He married Almina Almira Stevens on June 23, 1811, in China, (or Dec. 10, 1811, in Albion, FamilySearch says; this source gives him a different wife named Sarah on the same page as Almina).
Almina, born in Paris (Maine) on June 7, 1791, bore either four sons and two daughters or two sons and one daughter. She died Dec. 15, 1822, age 31; her widower died Aug. 10, 1841. Both are buried in the China Village Cemetery.
* * * * * *
Dr. John Hall appears in the China history as a Revolutionary War veteran and early settler on the east side of China Lake. A descendant still lived in town in 1976.
Find a Grave says Dr. Hall was born May 17, 1754, in Tewksbury, Massachusetts. WikiTree says on Dec. 13, 1782, in Pembroke, New Hampshire, he married Hannah Foster, who was born in Pembroke on July 11, 1762.
Find a Grave says the first of their three daughters was born March 7, 1787, in Warner, New Hampshire, and the third in Merrimack County, New Hampshire, in 1793; WikiTree says a son named Moses was born in 1791. The suggestion is that a family of six moved to the Maine wilderness in the early 1800s.
Hannah Hall died May 21, 1818, age 55; Find a Grave lists her place of death as “USA.” Dr. Hall died April 18, 1836, aged 81, in China. Both are buried in China’s Lakeshore Cemetery, with other early settlers.
* * * * * *
Find a Grave says Dr. James Hazelton Brainerd was born Oct. 8, 1789, in South Hadley, Massachusetts. He came to China from Berry (Barre?), Massachusetts, after practicing medicine in Westminster, Massachusetts.
This source says China was “then a prominent stage route town,” and Brainerd “had a large practice….He was called in consultation for miles around.”
Dr. Brainerd appears in the China history as a prominent, but impoverished, resident of China Village in the early 1830s.
The China history says in 1831, his (unnamed) wife died, “leaving him with several small children, and he fell upon hard times and was unable to pay his debts.” The history has copies of court orders assigning parts of his land and his Main Street house – “the easterly half of the westerly foreroom,” for example – to his creditors.
Find a Grave says on Nov. 2, 1820, Brainerd and Susan Richardson (born Nov. 1, 1801) were married in Princeton, Massachusetts. Find a Grave lists five children born between 1821 and 1829; the first two sons died in infancy. Susan died Nov. 17, 1830.
Dr. Brainerd’s second wife was Priscilla Hamblin Chadwick (1806 -1890); Find a Grave says they married May 11, 1831, in China. They had at least eight children; another source says their first son, Fredus Oldridge, was born Dec. 15, 1831.
Priscilla died in Fitchburg, Massachusetts, on July 22, 1890, and is buried there, Find a Grave says.
In 1849, Dr. Brainerd was one of seven men who successfully revived the Masons’ Central Lodge, after it had been inactive for 20 years; he was named the lodge master. Find a Grave says, “He held various town offices and was in the State Legislature.” Your writer failed to find reliable confirmation of the last statement.
Dr. Brainerd died April 6, 1857, age 67. He and Susan are buried in the China Village Cemetery.
* * * * * *
Dr. Alexander Hatch was born in Augusta Sept. 15, 1792, FamilySearch says. He married Elizabeth H. Hatch (born Jan. 27, 1794) in 1815, in Wells. They were the parents of one son and three daughters born between 1816 and 1823. The last daughter, born July 9, 1823, lived only a week, and her mother died Sept. 23, 1823.
On Dec. 27, 1837, Find a Grave says, Dr. Hatch married Eliza Ann Fairbanks (born in 1809) in Augusta. They had at least one son, George, born in 1843. Another Find a Grave site lists six children, including three sons who apparently died at birth or soon thereafter; this page has a photo of a gravestone listing Alex II, Alex III and Horace, “sons of Dr. Alex R. Hatch.”
Eliza died in 1858. On Aug. 16, 1859, Find a Grave says, Dr. Hatch married Mrs. Nancy M. Young in China.
Dr. Hatch died on December 31, 1863, in China, at the age of 71, and is buried in China Village Cemetery.
* * * * * *
Dr. Timothy Fernald Hanscom, FamilySearch says, was born in Eliot, on Aug. 6, 1795, third of eight children. On December 2, 1819, in Palermo, he married Asenath Greeley, born Feb. 13, 1801, in Palermo. By 1820 they were living in China Village.
The couple had a daughter and two sons between 1820 and 1830. Asenath died Feb. 21, 1864; her widower died Aug. 6, 1884. Both are buried in China Village Cemetery.
* * * * * *
Dr. Frank P. Fletcher, according to Kingsbury, was a China native, one of the children of Colonel Robert Fletcher (who earned his title in the War of 1812). Kingsbury says Frank graduated from Brunswick Medical School, practiced in Hope (about 35 miles south and east of China) and “at Weeks Mills the last years of his life.” He is not listed among Fletchers in the index to the China bicentennial history.
Find a Grave identifies him as Dr. Franklin Parker Fletcher, born in China May 15, 1808; married Maria S. Arnold (1812 – March 4, 1860) and had by her a son and four daughters between 1834 and 1845; and died in China Oct. 5, 1896. The doctor and his wife are buried in China’s Weeks Mills Cemetery.
* * * * * *
Dr. George Edward Brickett was born Nov. 24, 1824, in Hartford, Vermont. Kingsbury said he attended the Lancaster, New Hampshire, academy; studied medicine in Limerick, Maine, with Doctor Swasey; and in 1846 “graduated in medicine at Hanover, N.H.” (presumably from Dartmouth College).
He apparently opened his practice in China (evidence suggests in the South China area) in 1849 – Kingsbury said he had been there 12 years before becoming the 21st Maine’s surgeon in 1861. He might have been highly regarded as a doctor; Kingsbury mentioned one man who studied medicine with him (but did not settle in the area).
The China history says Brickett was “first assistant surgeon and later surgeon in the 3rd infantry regiment, created in the spring of 1861.” That position lasted until August, when he “either resigned or was discharged.” In the summer of 1862, “when the 21st infantry regiment was raised,” he again became surgeon, “with David P. Bolster of China as his assistant.”
Meanwhile, the China history says, China voters at a Sept. 9, 1861, town meeting had elected a new supervisor of schools because Brickett had joined the army.
After serving through the war, Brickett settled in Augusta.
Brickett’s wife, the former Melinda Chadwick Freeman, was born in China Feb. 24, 1832. She died May 30, 1905, and Brickett died Jan. 28, 1910, both in Augusta.
Their son, and apparently only child, was George Hartwell Brickett, born Sept. 6, 1860, in China. He followed his father’s profession, graduating in 1885 from Bellevue Medical College in New York and opening an Augusta practice. Find a Grave says he died in Pittsfield on Jan. 31, 1935.
All three are buried in the South China Village Cemetery.
* * * * * *
Dr. Benjamin Lamprey Tibbetts, born in 1836 in Parsonsfield, “prepared for college” and began studying medicine either with Dr. G. L. Bennett (Gilman Lougee Bennett, according to the Parsonsfield history found on line; mentioned above) or with Dr. Samuel Bradbury in Limington (according to Kingsbury; the two western Maine towns are about 20 miles apart).
Tibbetts “took a medical course” in 1860 at Dartmouth and another the next year at Bowdoin; graduated from Dartmouth in 1861; and in 1862 “began a practice course in the Boston Hospital,” Kingsbury wrote.
In 1863, Kingsbury said, Tibbetts succeeded Dr. Brickett in China – he was the Dr. Tebbetts mentioned above, in South China, specifically. In 1876, he moved to North Vassalboro.
The Parsonsfield history writer called Tibbetts “of Vassalboro.” He commented that Tibbetts “has been very successful in his professional career, and has accumulated quite a fortune.”
Kingsbury said Dr. Tibbetts died in September, 1892.
* * * * * *
Dr. David Bolster, according to Kingsbury, was born in 1827 in Paris, Maine. He attended Hebron Academy, “studied medicine with Doctors Brickett and Millett, and graduated in 1852 from Bowdoin Medical College.”
He practiced for three years in Leeds and Washington before moving to China, “where he practiced until 1877.” His practice was interrupted by the Civil War; Kingsbury wrote that he began as assistant surgeon in the 21st Maine Infantry Regiment in September, 1862, and later was commissioned in the 16th Maine, “in which he served until the close of the war” in the spring of 1865.
Dr. Bolster’s is the seventh name on Kingsbury’s undated list of the first 14 masters of South China’s Dirigo Masonic Lodge, founded in 1860.
In 1877, Kingsbury said, Bolster moved to Augusta, where he was still in practice in 1892. That year he was serving as “secretary of the County Medical Society.”
* * * * * *
Dr. Gustavus Judson Nelson was born in 1846 in Guilford, attended China Academy, Lincoln Academy and Waterville Classical Institute, and entered Colby in 1871, Kingsbury said.
After two years as China Academy’s principal and one term heading Freedom Academy, he studied medicine with “Doctors Crosby and Wilson” and “in 1877 graduated from Bowdoin Medical College.”
Kingsbury says Nelson started his practice in Weeks Mills, and in February 1892 moved to China Village.
When the three-man China Board of Health was created in 1887 (to comply with a new state law), Dr. Nelson was appointed to the three-year term and became the board’s head. By 1895, he was secretary as the board dealt with two cases of diphtheria and one each of typhoid fever, smallpox and scarlet fever. In each case, quarantine and disinfection prevented an epidemic.
In 1878, the China history says, he was the town’s school supervisor; when the supervisor was replaced by an elected five-person committee in 1879, he was on it. In 1903 and 1904 he was active in creating a high school in China Village.
In 1911 and for four years following he served on the China Village Cemetery Association board.
Find a Grave identifies his wife as Ella F. Nelson, born in 1852. They had one daughter, born in 1882. Dr. Nelson died Feb. 17, 1915; his widow died in 1924. Both are buried in the China Village Cemetery.
* * * * * *
Dr. Louis Cook, Kingsbury said, was born in Dixmont in 1872, “graduated in medicine from the University of New York, in 1889,” and opened a practice in China Village. He is not listed in the bicentennial history index, and your writer found no on-line information.
Main sources
Grow, Mary M., China Maine Bicentennial History including 1984 revisions (1984)
Kingsbury, Henry D., ed., Illustrated History of Kennebec County Maine 1625-1892 (1892)
Websites, miscellaneous.

title: Stranger brings 6-year-old home after being dropped off early and found walking near busy road
text:
CLEVELAND, Ohio. (WOIO/Gray News) - A stranger in Ohio brought a 6-year-old home after the girl was dropped off early and found walking near a busy road.
Mari Richardson was getting ready to pick up her daughter at the bus stop when the girl arrived home in a stranger’s car more than 20 minutes before she was supposed to arrive.
“My daughter could have never made it home. If it wasn’t for this lady. And I’m just so thankful for her,” Richardson said.
Tiyonna Betts saw the girl crying and walking by herself on busy road.
“I asked her does she know where she was going? She said no, she was lost. The bus driver just dropped her off,” Betts said.
Richardson said she is grateful a kind woman brought her daughter home.
“My daughter was scared. She was scared. She’s only 6 years old. And I’m just so thankful that she does know landmarks that she was able to direct her home,” Richardson said.
“God led me to that baby, and I’m just overjoyed that I was used to be a blessing,” Betts said.
Rightway Transportation told 19 News that the driver dropped the girl off nearly 40 minutes early with no parent waiting, which violates company policy.
Richardson said she could no longer trust the school bus to transport her daughter and is looking for other ways to get her daughter to school.
“I don’t feel like enough has been done. I did not, I don’t feel like this matter is taken, is being taken as serious as it should. Because my daughter could have never made it home. My last time seeing her literally could have been Friday morning,” Richardson said.
Richardson filed a police report and wants to press charges.
Rightway Transportation told 19 News that the driver had been disciplined and taken off the route.

title: Russia releases American man imprisoned on charges of fighting as mercenary in Ukraine
text:
(AP) - Russia on Wednesday freed an American who had been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, a deal completed during a visit by a top U.S. envoy and at a time when President Donald Trump has taken a series of actions meant to benefit Moscow.
Trump told reporters at the White House that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin during a recent call to free Stephen Hubbard and that, unlike previous releases, the U.S. did not have to give up anyone in return.
“He is the happiest man around,” Trump said of Hubbard, describing the 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan as a “very high-quality, innocent man.” Hubbard’s legal team denied the Russian accusations, saying he was not involved in any military activity.
The release occurred during a visit to St. Petersburg by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who in a face-to-face interaction with Putin praised the Russian leader as a “humanitarian” as the men held talks about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and as Trump simultaneously pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Hubbard, who before his arrest had lived in Ukraine for years, was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison during closed court proceedings. Prosecutors said he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Russia’s invasion in 2022, and that he fought alongside Kyiv’s forces until being captured two months later.
The U.S. government under President Joe Biden’s administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained. His family also disputed the Russian allegations.
“He was just for bait. It was all about bait. And that’s why they kidnap Americans,” his sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, said in an interview with The Associated Press. She said she expected Hubbard to stay with her in Colorado.
“Steven James Hubbard is the face of America,” she said. “They could do that to anybody. They just happened to see him. ‘Oh, that’s an American, let’s go get him.’”
US envoy calls Putin a ‘humanitarian’
Witkoff, a key Trump administration figure who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end a war that will hit the five-year mark in February 2027, thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, telling him, “Because of you, he’s going home to his family.”
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir,” Witkoff said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media Wednesday that Hubbard’s release was “raised by the American side for a certain time,” and Putin decided to free the man out of “humanitarian considerations.”
Speaking to reporters after the talks, Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said the Kremlin leader had pardoned Hubbard, who upon his release was taken to St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo airport for Witkoff to bring him home to the United States.
Video showed Witkoff and Hubbard shaking hands, with the newly released American thanking the envoy. Witkoff introduced Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev to Hubbard and described him as someone “who had a lot to do with this happening.”
“We just met President Putin, he sends you blessings and wishes you good things,” Witkoff added.
Hubbard, a U.S. Air Force veteran, taught English overseas and had by 2012 retired to Cyprus, where one of his sons is a priest. He later moved to Ukraine to be with a woman he had met, his lawyers said, remaining in the country after the relationship ended and living there at the time of Russia’s 2022 invasion. He was detained in April of that year after Russian forces took control of the area where he was living.
His case was taken up by lawyers at the U.S.-based law firm of Boies Schiller Flexner and the Russian firm of EPAM Law, which together had represented Marc Fogel, the American teacher freed from Russian custody last year, and worked for his release.
“They thought they weren’t going to see him again alive, and Stephen didn’t think he was going to come out of there alive,” one of Hubbard’s lawyers at Boies Schiller, Martin De Luca, said in an interview of Hubbard’s family. “Obviously, they’re overjoyed, but they feel very much like it’s a miracle.”
His sister said she had spoken with Hubbard soon after his release. “That was awesome. He was just laughing. He said, ‘I can’t believe this is happening,’” Hubbard Fox said of her brother.
Trump told reporters Wednesday night that Hubbard is expected to visit the White House some time in the coming days.
Other Americans remain jailed in Russia
The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship being roiled by fresh tensions at the same time that the Trump administration has advanced policies that aid Putin.
Those include Trump’s move last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine. Named after the late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Moscow’s war.
That decision followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections.
Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday. He was expected to exchange ideas from that meeting, as well as proposals from European and American colleagues, in his talks with Russian leaders in St. Petersburg.
Hubbard is the second American freed by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of Marine veteran Robert Gilman, who had been gravely ill and was imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer.
Other Americans, including some with serious illnesses, remain jailed in Russia. Hubbard was the last remaining American designated as wrongfully detained, although advocates say that label should be applied to other prisoners.
When asked Wednesday night if he thinks more Americans will be released, Trump told reporters, “Yeah, I think so. That’ll come.”
Russia reported more arrests of foreigners in recent days. The FSB security service said Wednesday it detained a German national suspected of mercenary activities and last week announced arrests of a Swedish national suspected of sabotage and a Japanese journalist accused of espionage.

title: Entire police department resigns; chief accuses mayor of placing tracker on his truck
text:
MILNER, Ga. (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — A Georgia city’s entire police force has resigned, the city manager announced during a Monday council meeting.
Milner City Manager Tausha Grose said the entire full-time police department has stepped down, along with most of the reserve officers.
The department’s last day is Oct. 28.
Grose also said she filed her own resignation and will work until Oct. 30.
Small department, small city
Milner, located about 45 miles southeast of Atlanta, has a population of less than 1,000 people.
The police department consisted of five people, including Chief Lamar Bunn.
The Lamar County Sheriff’s Office is expected to serve in the department’s absence.
Chief cites lack of trust
During Monday’s meeting, Bunn indicated he stepped down partially due to a lack of trust in the city council and mayor. He accused Mayor Craig Timmons of placing a tracker on his personal truck.
“I didn’t ask them to do it,” he said about the rest of the force deciding to resign. “It’s not like I said, ‘Hey guys, let’s quit.’ No, I didn’t do that. So, I don’t know what needs to happen from here.”
Push to unincorporate
Former city council member Skip Seda said if the city loses its police force and city manager, he would push to unincorporate Milner.
“Because we already paying taxes for Milner, and about the only darn thing the difference between us and the county is that police force. That’s it. So, why would we continue to pay Milner taxes?” he said.

title: October 23rd Trunk Or Treat At Mid Mall Benefits Sarah's House In Holden
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Don't get me wrong, there are lots of awesome things about a local Trunk-or-treat; the fun decorations, the candy, the safe and enclosed space kids can venture about in as they show off their outfits and collect their treats.
Read More: Free Halloween Activities Coming To Glenburn This Fall
But when you incorporate all of that goodness with helping a good cause, that's a real 'level up' as the kids say.
For the third year in a row, you'll be able to level up your trunk-or-treat game at the Mid Mall Trunk-or-Treat in Bangor.
On Friday October 23rd, you can dress up with your kiddos and visit the dozens of local businesses and individuals who have sponsored a trunk and get goodies in the process.
The event will take place in Mid Mall area off the Bangor Mall Blvd, and promises plenty of candy, food trucks, decorated trunks, music and entertainment.
It's a free event appropriate for all ages. Over 24 local businesses have worked together to make the event come to life and keep the event free.
Benjamin Smith, Director of HR & Marketing for FYZICAL Therapy & Balance Centers and event organizer, says they expect about a thousand folks to make their way through the parking lot this year.
That's not only great exposure for the local businesses, but also a fair amount publicity for this year's charity benefactors, Sarah's House in Holden, Maine.
Read More: Trick-or-Treating in Bangor, Maine: Maple Street Is a Must-Visit
"What started as an opportunity for neighboring businesses to come together and do something fun for local families has really grown into something special. One of my favorite things about this event is seeing businesses that might otherwise never cross paths come together for a common purpose. Everyone puts their own creative spin on their trunk, the kids have an absolute blast, and we get to create a fun, safe,
and memorable evening for families in our community. We're expecting our biggest turnout yet, and I couldn't be more excited!"
Smith says not only will people from Sarah's House will be on hand collecting things from their wishlist, if people with to donate, but there's also another way to help the organization, too.
"We're also proud to feature Sarah's House as this year's nonprofit beneficiary. Sarah's House provides a home away from home for individuals traveling to the Bangor area for cancer treatment. Representatives will be on-site collecting much-needed wish list items, and Darling's Ice Cream Truck for a Cause will be helping raise funds for the organization."

The 3rd Annual Mid Mall Trunk-Or-Treat will run from 5 PM to 7 PM. Families are encouraged to dress up and bring a treat bag to collect all the candy.

title: 45 places to volunteer in Maine
text:
There are so many places to volunteer in Maine. The challenge for those who want to give back to their communities is finding and picking an organization to join.
So, I put out a call on social media asking Mainers where they volunteer and what organizations are in need of more help. Here’s what they said.
This is not a comprehensive list; there were more responses than could be included in one story. If some organizations are missing here, put them in the comments!
GREATER PORTLAND
Maine Needs is a nonprofit in Portland that provides necessities like clothing, hygiene products and household items. (maineneeds.org/volunteer)
The Trauma Intervention Program of Greater Portland provides immediate assistance to those who are emotionally traumatized in emergency situations. Volunteers need to go through an intense 55-hour training over two weeks. (tipgreaterportland.org/volunteer)
Ruth’s Reusable Resources in Portland transfers surplus business supplies to children and teachers in need. (ruths.org/support-3rs)
Friends of Casco Bay, based in Portland, is looking for volunteers to serve as water reporters, do coastal cleanups or help with events and things in the office. (cascobay.org/how-to-help/volunteer)
Hope Squad is a mobile outreach group providing resources to the homeless population in Portland. (hopesquadmaine.org/get-involved)
Portland Adult Education needs volunteers to assist in classrooms and to work as tutors with students who are learning English. (portlandadulted.org/about-us/join-our-team)
The West End Neighborhood Association in Portland addresses issues that concern the quality of life of those who live and work in the neighborhood. (wenamaine.org/get-involved/volunteer)
The Bayside Neighborhood Association in Portland advocates for those who live in the Bayside neighborhood. (baysideportland.org)
Partners For World Health in Portland collects surplus medical supplies and distributes them locally and globally. (partnersforworldhealth.org/volunteering)
Based in Portland, Preble Street provides housing, food, and critical services to people across Maine. (preblestreet.org/you-can-help/volunteer)
Portland History Docents is a collaborative effort by local historic sites to provide a training program for new prospective volunteer guides. (portlandhistorydocents.org/)
Hope Acts in Portland offers asylum seekers access to basic needs, assistance with the immigration process and English learning resources. (hopeacts.org/volunteer)
The Independent Seniors Network helps older adults maintain active, social, safe and independent lives in their own homes. (portlandareavillages.helpfulvillage.com/pages/10010-volunteer-with-us!)
Friends of the Eastern Prom is a nonprofit community organization committed to preserving the park’s historic public landscape, protecting its environmental integrity, and enhancing its recreational use. (easternpromenade.org/volunteer)
The Altrusa International Portland, Maine Club is a nonprofit club devoted to delivering books and literacy, scholarships, and serving its communities. (altrusaportland.org/volunteer)
South Portland Food Cupboard is a food pantry distributing food to hungry people in South Portland and neighboring communities. (southportlandfoodcupboard.org/volunteer)
The Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland in Westbrook is looking for people to assist with daily shelter operations. (arlgp.org/volunteer/volunteer-at-arlgp)
Based in Westbrook, Furniture Friends collects and distributes gently used furniture to people in need in southern Maine. (furniturefriends.org/volunteer)
Discover Downtown Westbrook creates a positive downtown environment by supporting businesses, hosting events and making downtown a livable and walkable destination. (downtownwestbrook.com/volunteer)
The St. Vincent De Paul Soup Kitchen serves meals to Portland’s needy Monday through Friday, from 11 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.(portlandcatholic.org/st-vincent-de-paul-soup-kitchen)
Scarborough Adult Education is in need of instructors, commenters said. (scarboroughschools.org/adult-learning-center)
ITN Portland provides personalized, reliable transportation to help people get to medical appointments, the grocery store, or to visit friends and family when they stop driving. (itnportland.org/get-involved/volunteer-to-drive)
MAINE AND BEYOND
The Rocky Coast Rabbit Rescue and Sanctuary — a nonprofit based in Portland and Norway that provides rescue, homes and care for rabbits across New England — is looking for people to foster or volunteer. (rockycoastrabbitrescue.org/how-to-help)
You can join the Newry-based Maine Adaptive as a volunteer instructor for its winter and summer programs or to help out with equipment and in the office to promote education and training for people with disabilities. (maineadaptive.org/volunteer)
People in Portland and Lewiston can volunteer to mentor kids or help with English learning at the Root Cellar, a faith-based nonprofit. (therootcellar.org/volunteer)
Pittie Posse Rescue and Sanctuary, which rescues and trains dogs in Maine, is looking for people to volunteer or foster. (pittieposserescue.com/help)
The nonprofit AgeMaine serves older adults and their caregivers with locations in Biddeford, Portland and Springvale. (agemaine.org/getinvolved/volunteer)
Community Doulas provides professional doula support with equitable pricing to Maine families. (communitydoulas.org/volunteer)
Ronald McDonald House in Bangor and Portland provides a home to keep families together while children are receiving medical treatment. (ronaldmcdonaldhousemaine.org)
Age Friendly Saco promotes active aging with opportunities for health, engagement, and safety. (agefriendlysaco.org/volunteer-opportunities)
United Way of Southern Maine tackles needs like childcare, food insecurity, housing instability, and substance use. (uwsme.org/get-involved/volunteer)
The Maine Association for New Americans empowers immigrants through peer support, mental health education and mentorship programs. (mana-maine.org/welcoming-the-stranger-join)
The Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition improves the legal, social, and economic conditions for immigrants in Maine. (maineimmigrantrights.org/ways-to-help)
Maine Medical Center is looking for volunteers in Portland, Sanford and Biddeford to provide a helping hand to patients. (mainehealth.org/locations/mainehealth-maine-medical-center/giving/volunteer)
The Center for Grieving Children in Portland and Sanford provides a safe space, peer support, outreach and education to grieving children, teens, young adults, families and the community. (cgcmaine.org/get-involved/#volunteer)
WindowDressers produces low-cost insulating window inserts to help lower heating costs and improve warmth. (windowdressers.org/volunteer)
The Locker Project fights child hunger through food rescue, fresh food distributions and community partnerships. (mainelockerproject.org/volunteer-signup)
The Restorative Justice Project Maine promotes a justice that is community based, repairs harm, and creates safety and well-being for all. (rjpmaine.org/get-involved/volunteer-roles)
Friends of Feral Felines is committed to helping feral cats in southern Maine by neutering and releasing, providing food and medical care, and fostering cats. (feralfelines.net/volunteer)
Lasagna Love is a global nonprofit that connects volunteer lasagna chefs with people in need to provide homemade meals. (lasagnalove.org/volunteer)
Volunteers for the American Red Cross can help out with many things, from disaster relief to blood drives. (redcross.org/volunteer/become-a-volunteer)
For Make-A-Wish Maine, you can volunteer as a wish granter, translator, family ambassador and more. It is based in South Portland. (wish.org/maine/volunteer)
College Guild offers free correspondence courses that connect incarcerated people with a community beyond prison walls. (collegeguild.org/being-a-reader)
The Yuls Foundation for Foster Youth provides mentoring and support services to young adults transitioning out of the foster care system.(yulsfoundation.org/volunteer-application)
AARP Maine advocated for the health, financial security and overall well-being of Maine residents 50 years and older. (aarp.org/states/maine)

title: Supporters, opponents make their case ahead of Penobscot County jail vote
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Penobscot County has long hoped for a new jail, while some local groups have spent years opposing it. Now, voters will decide the first step.
Question 1 on Penobscot County ballots asks voters to allow commissioners to scout locations outside Bangor for a new jail.
“Our jail here in Penobscot County was built in 1869, four years after the end of the Civil War and 21 years before electricity even came to Bangor,” explained David Marshall, Chair of the Penobscot County Commissioners.
Marshall says annual jail costs include $815,000 for maintenance and $2.1 million for transportation.
Those urging a no vote arguing transportation funds could be cut and reallocated if the county can keep people from entering jail in the first place.
“Vote no. Send a message to the county commissioners: We don’t want a new jail. We want fewer people in the jail and we want money to be used instead for diversion,” said Larry Dansinger, an organizer with the No Penobscot County Jail Expansion.
Dansinger was joined Wednesday afternoon in front of the jail by others in the organization, which has opposed a new jail since 2019.
“We don’t do enough to move people out of this building and into the treatment that will actually make a difference in their lives and make a difference in terms of public safety,” said organizer Doug Dunbar, who spent about 10 weeks at Penobscot County Jail nine years ago.
He said being selected for a court-ordered rehabilitation program was the catalyst he needed to achieve sobriety.
The No Jail Expansion group says its plan would have judges consider criminal history and personal circumstances, such as being a caregiver or a youthful offender, when ordering diversion over jail time.
Marshall says Penobscot County already does that to an extent.
“All the people currently in the jail are people who are facing felony charges. We have nobody in there facing misdemeanor charges, all of those people are diverted,” Marshall detailed. “We divert some felons who are facing felony charges if they qualify for bail or if there is monitoring, so they qualify for a monitoring program. We have a MAT program, medically assisted treatment program, to deal with chemical dependency and that is a very successful program for us. Once they leave the confines of the jail, or the correctional facility, it’s no longer our responsibility. It is the responsibility of either the municipality or the state.”
For Dunbar and others, passing the referendum would kill momentum for investing in alternatives like diversion programs.
“Do we simply want a nicer building or do we want a safer community? And do we want people to get so they don’t go back into this building over and over and over again?” Dunbar asked.
Marshall says the jail’s condition is the biggest barrier to expanding services.
“We are trying to do the best we can do given the circumstances, and the biggest impediment there to providing better service is the jail itself and that facility, 157 years old, doesn’t cut it today,” Marshall said.
Penobscot County will vote on Question 1 on Election Day.
The referendum only seeks to authorize the county to look outside Bangor. Any other plans involving the jail will require a separate vote.

title: Joe Manchin says Donald Trump ‘owns this economy’ on Maine stop with Susan Collins
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
LEWISTON, Maine — During a diner stop with U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, former U.S. Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia said Wednesday that President Donald Trump “owns this economy” in a nod to the headwinds facing Maine’s five-term incumbent.
Collins, a Republican in a close race with Democrat Troy Jackson, brought Manchin to Simones’ Hot Dog Stand to argue she is no rubber stamp for the unpopular president. Manchin is a former Democrat who became an independent before leaving the Senate in 2025.
When a reporter asked whether she blames Trump for the state of the economy, Collins mentioned former President Joe Biden and pivoted to the nearly $37 million in heating aid she pressed the administration to release this month. She handed the question to Manchin, who said Democrats “paid the price” for Biden’s policies and that Collins would serve as a check.
“They own this economy,” Manchin said of the Trump administration. “This is their economy, and they have to face up to that.”
The exchange showed how Collins has run against Trump’s policies in a Democratic-leaning state without running expressly against him, confining her critiques to specific issues. Jackson, who holds a narrow lead in most public polls less than two weeks before Election Day, argues her breaks aren’t meaningfully checking the president.
Collins and Manchin arrived on her campaign bus and walked into Simones’, a longtime stop for Maine candidates, trailed by dozens of reporters. They sat at a table in a back room with a group of local Republican officials and talked about energy and the economy.
After the roundtable, reporters were moved outside for a news conference. Democratic protesters who had set up well before the event, carrying signs depicting Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, traded shouts with Collins staffers and supporters.
Asked whether Trump should reverse his decision to buy Russian diesel despite a sanctions law passed last month, Collins said yes. She said the deal won’t increase U.S. supply “in any measurable way” but will give Russia more money “to attack Ukraine.” She was one of six senators, four of them Republicans, who called on Trump this month to reverse course.
Last month, she called Trump’s cancellation of nearly $1 billion in spending illegal while aiming her criticism at the White House budget office. In August, she voted against Todd Blanche for attorney general, saying the Justice Department had “become increasingly political.” On tariffs, she has said “Canada is not China” while lobbying for item-by-item exemptions for pulp, concrete and road salt.
Manchin has crossed party lines for Collins before. In 2019, while still a Democratic senator, he endorsed her reelection and said he would “go up and campaign for Susan Collins,” but he did not. National Democrats were targeting her that cycle over her vote for Kavanaugh, a vote Manchin also cast in 2018.
In 2022, the two led the bipartisan overhaul of the Electoral Count Act, the law that Trump and his allies tried to exploit after the 2020 election. On Wednesday, Collins named it among the laws they passed together. Manchin also criticized Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-New York, who has led the last two campaigns against Collins.
“I told him he was crazy in 2020 from working against her so hard, and he’s crazy now to work against her,” Manchin said.

title: Susan Collins, Joe Manchin take breakfast at Lewiston’s Simones’ Hot Dog Stand
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Key Takeaways Key Takeaways are written by Maine Trust staff and highlight the most important points of this article so you can get the gist at a glance.
- Susan Collins received campaign support from independent Joe Manchin, a consultant and former conservative Democratic senator from West Virginia who joined her in Lewiston for breakfast.
- Manchin described Collins as the “soul of the Senate” and urged Mainers to return her to Washington, D.C., on Nov. 3.
- Critics of Collins and Manchin noted their support for Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was instrumental in overturning Roe v. Wade.
- Manchin was also criticized for his role as adviser to a private equity firm critics say caused the closure of paper mills in Jay and Bucksport that led to the loss of more than 1,000 jobs.
LEWISTON — Simones’ Hot Dog Stand was bustling with politics once again Wednesday morning as U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and former Democratic U.S. Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia stepped off a coach bus with an entourage, briefly stopped for news photos, and ducked into the establishment for a midmorning breakfast.
Like the old friends they are, Collins and Manchin, a former conservative Democrat who left the party in 2024, sat down for breakfast at Simones’ on Chestnut Street, both opting for the sausage, egg and cheese sandwich.
“We’ve always welcomed all the politicians during the election season,” owner Jim Simones said, as his staff dodged the media and Collins’ supporters while preparing breakfasts. “We don’t care what party affiliation. We’ve been like a soap box for all of them. We’re happy, we’re all excited that we get to see all these people and it’s just a good time. The democratic process, this is how it works. The candidates come out, say what they want to say and we make a decision.”
Lewiston mayoral candidate Rick LaChapelle and House District 96 candidate Lee Clement, both Republicans, and former Auburn Mayor Jason Levesque joined the two at their table for chitchat as swarms of reporters and Collins supporters surrounded them.
“It’s obvious that Lewiston and Auburn are really the hub of Maine’s future,” Levesque said to the Sun Journal. “This is where the potential lies, and for her to come here and visit … it’s a message that we all need to understand that Lewiston can be better, we can do better, and Maine needs it to do better. She’s done so much for Lewiston and Auburn, it’s just unbelievable.”
Later, addressing the media, Manchin said he was happy to be in Maine supporting Collins’ reelection campaign and reminding folks that Collins is not a “Trump senator” or a Republican senator or a Democratic senator, but is a Maine senator and “the most independent-minded person” he has ever met.
“We bonded the first day we met … and we’ve still been very close. We worked on every bipartisan legislation … in Congress for the last 14 years. This is a true blue-blooded Maine person. … You’ve heard me say that she’s the soul of the Senate. You lose Susan Collins, you lose the soul of the Senate.”
Manchin served in the Senate under three presidential administrations; Collins has served under five. Manchin said he and Collins approached every president the same way.
“You want your president to succeed, you want to work with him, but you want to speak truth to power when it’s not right,” Manchin said. “She has done that and treated all three the same, and she has not changed.”
Collins said she and Manchin were part of every bipartisan initiative that passed in the Senate in the years they worked together, naming a bipartisan infrastructure bill that brought in funds for roads and bridges, bills expanding access to broadband and work on COVID-19 response funds.
“I am delighted to have him here, and I just so enjoy our partnership in getting things done for Maine, for West Virginia, and for America,” Collins said.
Collins answered a host of questions addressing her wishes for continued sanctions on Russia and her support for Ukraine, success in requesting early release of low-income heating assistance funds, wishes to minimize tariffs on Canadian goods and feelings about the state of attack advertisements in Maine and across the country.
Collins said by cutting a deal with Russia on diesel, the accomplishment is not increasing supply in any measurable way, but is funding Russia to continue attacking Ukraine. “There’s no doubt that Russia is the aggressor and that that was an unprovoked conflict, and so I do not support his decision.”
After successfully pushing the Trump administration to release LiHEAP funding — the earliest release in history, she said — Collins said what America needs now is to increase its energy supply.
“ We want to send West Virginia gas to Maine,” Manchin said. “We need a pipeline. We need infrastructure. We need permitting reform. We need all these things to provide the energy this country needs. The Northeast should not be paying these high prices.”
On tariffs, Collins said she very much considers the relationships we have with other countries when deciding what to support and what to oppose.
“Canada is our friend, our neighbor, our biggest trading partner, our ally. That’s very different from tariffs on China,” Collins said. “So, I think there’s a distinction there. You are hearing more and more members of the Republican side of the aisle speak out against the Canadian tariffs because of the impact on fertilizer, for example, that our farmers are so dependent on. … So I’m hearing a growing realization of how harmful these tariffs are, and, as you know, I’ve voted repeatedly against them. Again, I’m negotiating with the administration to try to get further waivers.”
The Maine Democratic Party on Wednesday criticized the duo for their support of Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh and for “betraying Maine women and selling out Maine workers.” Kavanaugh was one of five justices who voted to overturn abortion protections afforded by Roe v. Wade.
“Today, Susan Collins is campaigning with fellow Brett Kavanaugh supporter Joe Manchin, just down the river from the paper mill his private equity firm put out of business,” said party spokesperson Misha Linnehan. “Manchin and Collins may have caucused with different parties … (but) Mainers know they’re one and the same.”
The statement criticized Manchin’s role as an adviser to Apollo Global Management, a private equity firm that bought the Jay and Bucksport paper mills and who Democrats say was responsible for their closures and the loss of over 1,000 jobs.
Democrats also criticized Collins for accepting more private equity funds, some $700,000, than any other 2026 candidate in the country, according to the Wall Street Journal. Manchin is involved with several private equity and global investment firms.
Outside Simones’, a group of protesters carried a variety of signs Wednesday, including large images of Kavanaugh.
“It’s just time for her to go. She does not listen to people in her district, she does not support women’s health,” one women’s advocate said. “As an advocate, I can say that she has cost lives.”
“Our democracy is crumbling and she’s doing nothing to stop it as the rich get richer,” another protester said.
“Congress is meant to be a check and balance for the executive branch and she’s just been a rubber stamp for Trump this whole time,” said another.

title: This business turns vinyl records into mixtapes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (InvestigateTV) — Vinyl record sales in the U.S. increased in 2025 for the 19th consecutive year, according to the RIAA. Sales remain below 1970s levels, when more than 300 million LPs and EPs were sold each year.
Since April 2008, music fans have marked Record Store Day, which highlights independent record stores and vinyl culture. A Portland business is combining the vinyl resurgence with another personal music keepsake: the mixtape.
Mixtape Vinyl, based in Portland, has created vinyl record mixtapes for 10 years. Jennifer Dawson and the late Portland-based singer-songwriter David Freel, of the band Swell, founded it in 2016.
“We get people who are quite often trying to woo somebody,” Dawson said. “It’s obviously a crush, and they’re putting their favorite songs onto a vinyl instead of a cassette.”
Dawson and her team use a lathe, a rotating cutting machine, to create albums for occasions including weddings, graduations and gender reveals.
“And I think the most meaningful records that we’ve done are the memorial records,” Dawson said. “So someone has passed and there’s either an interview or they recorded some songs at some point. And we, yeah, and we make that record for the family or for the friends.”
The albums are fully customizable, including the jacket and the color or picture that appears on the disc.
“We make them as if those songs belong together,” Dawson said.
Mixtape Vinyl was among the first businesses in the market when it started, and an industry has since developed around the concept. There are no laws preventing the practice since the albums are not for commercial use.
Dawson said Taylor Swift songs are frequently requested.
“Sitting on the dock of the bay is on a lot of records by Otis Redding,” Dawson said.
A pressing of 10 records costs at least $350, or $10 a record. For more information, customers can email Mixtape Vinyl at orders@vinylondemand.com.

title: Bates Hosts Talk on Importance of Ukrainian Literary Voices
text:
The German and Russian Studies Departments, the European Studies Program and the Harward Center for Community Partnerships hosted a talk featuring Oleh Kotsyuba, an expert on Ukrainian literature and culture, on Monday.
During his talk, Kotsyuba, director of print and digital publications at the Harvard Ukrainian Research Institute (HURI), underscored the dualism of culture as a force for erasure and empowerment.
Russia, Kotsyuba said, “invokes its own cultural greatness in order to project influence and deny Ukrainians their own history.”
Kotsyuba’s work at HURI uses culture as a counterweight to this cultural erasure.
Kotsyuba translates and publishes Ukrainian authors in America, bringing their lives into the zeitgeist of the American political consciousness.
This year, HURI published 17 books, from poetry—like Alex Averbuch’s “Furious Harvests”— to novels—such as Valerian Pidmohylnyi’s “The City.”
Kotsyuba charted his somewhat ironic journey to becoming a Ukrainian researcher and advocate, saying that he initially wanted to be a teacher for German literature. In fact, he largely dismissed the possibility of Ukrainian studies.
After earning a Master of Arts at Ludwig Maximilians University in Munich, Germany, he realized that “Ukrainian studies are so underemployed and there are so many gaps.”
This awareness, coupled with an acute understanding of the lack of American understanding of Ukrainian culture, led him into Ukrainian cultural and literary studies.
He spoke at length about the current war on Ukrainian culture, detailing the scale of Russian destruction of Ukrainian learning and history.
Russia’s erasure of Ukrainian culture, Kotsyuba argued, is on a larger scale than many understand; he cited the Mariupol theatre bombing in 1991, as well as the 13,000,000 Ukrainian books destroyed.
He added that 563 cultural sites have been harmed, including 43 museums and 24 libraries.
The paradox, Kotsyuba said, is that while Russia continues to destroy Ukrainian culture, it claims that the West aims to silence it, referring to it as Nazi-era suppression.
Kotsyuba pointed to Russia’s claims of victimhood in its 2023 Foreign Policy Concept. Paragraph 43 lists the goal of “counteracting the Russophobia campaign led by the unfriendly foreign states and their associations.”
Ukrainian voices, he added, directly contest Russian President Vladimir Putin’s claims to rewrite the narrative, saying “Ukrainian voices can defeat false binaries.”
Lewiston Mayor Carl Sheline, who introduced Kotsyuba, had a similar message, that this talk “reminds us that the elevation of Ukrainian voices and literature is critical to increasing public knowledge and support for Ukraine.”
On the importance of making Ukrainian voices accessible to American audiences, Kotsyuba said, “If something doesn’t exist, people can not see it they cannot debate it… [if] they cannot find it in any language they know.”
“It can also save real lives,” Kotsyuba explained. American voters who gain knowledge can make informed decisions at the polls. Publishing Ukrainian literature is an important part of that education, “a successful book can outlast quite a few news cycles, it can enter the syllabus, and into the archives.”
During a post-talk conversation with Professor Cheryl Stephenson in the Department of German and Russian Studies, Kotsyuba responded to audience questions.
When asked if the HURI protects culture for its own sake, Kotsyuba emphasized the humans behind Ukrainian works, saying, “it’s not about protecting a culture for culture’s sake, its a people, there is no culture if there are no people.”
The HURI’s work is not about creating a monolithic image of what Ukrainian culture is or should be, “that’s what propaganda is,” he said.
In a comment via text to The Bates Student, Sheline said, “the attacks on Ukrainian culture are real and tangible,” and that Russia aggression “serves as a call to action to support Ukrainian cultural advocacy and makes the work that HURI is doing more relevant than ever.”
Kotsyuba concluded the talk with a Czech proverb: “you live a new life for every new language you speak. If you know only one language, you only live once.”
The same, Kotsyuba argued, can be said about culture. “Culture is important.”
