title: In struggling LA, Mayor Karen Bass fights for 2nd term against democratic socialist-backed Raman
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — To voter Roy Lyons, Los Angeles has been losing luster for years. A homeless crisis endures despite billions of dollars of spending. City Hall’s budget keeps swelling — as do the taxes needed to support it.
As the retired insurance broker from the Sherman Oaks neighborhood ponders his pick in the upcoming mayoral election, he’s leaning toward the unpopular incumbent, Mayor Karen Bass, over her fellow progressive Democrat Nithya Raman, a little-known city council member who is backed by the Democratic Socialists of America. She endorsed Bass before changing her mind and entering the race.
Neither choice gives him confidence about the future.
“Is this the best we can do?” asked Lyons, a Democrat, who attended a recent candidate forum. “I don’t think either one shines.”
If Bass wins the Nov. 3 election, it will be because she was able to persuade voters like Lyons to give her a second chance after a rough first term that included the deadly Palisades Fire, which ignited when she was out of the country and caught the fire department unprepared.
Nearly three weeks into mail voting, only 5% of ballots have been returned, according to ballot tracking firm Political Data Inc.
On a recent sunny afternoon as he dropped off his ballot in the Studio City neighborhood, Kim Hansen said his vote for Raman represented what he considered the “least worst” option.
“I don’t like either of them,” said Hansen, a piano player who isn’t registered with a party. “I still wish there was somebody really good to vote for.”
City Hall struggles with the basics
The campaign is unfolding as the city contends with myriad urban ailments. In the latest data released in July, homelessness increased in the city, dealing a setback to Bass. Residents are dealing with climbing rent and housing costs, rising utility bills and buckled streets and sidewalks.
Hollywood jobs have been fleeing for years for cheaper filming locales, and the restaurant industry has been shaken by mounting closures. In August, the candidates sparred over their support for street food vendors versus brick-and-mortar restaurants. Meanwhile, the 2028 Olympics are on the horizon, raising questions about the public face the city will present to the world.
At issue is whether voters want to stick with the mayor or pivot to the political left with Raman and follow New York’s lead, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor.
Bass represents the Democratic establishment as she’s backed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, along with nearly every member of the city council, including several aligned with the democratic socialists. She served in the state legislature and Congress before becoming mayor in 2022 and was under consideration to be former President Joe Biden’s running mate in 2020.
Raman has picked up notable support from advocacy and political groups, including Our Revolution, which was founded by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, and the Sierra Club. She’s thin on endorsements from prominent local politicians. She landed a widely publicized private meeting with former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, who is not involved in the race, that hinted at her efforts to broaden her circle.
One of the unknowns is where supporters of Republican Spencer Pratt — a former reality personality who lost his home in the Palisades Fire and was defeated in the primary — might turn on Election Day.
A rough term, a mayor imperiled
Bass won a meager 34% of the vote in the June primary — meaning two out of three voters picked someone else. Raman is in her first run for citywide office. While she represents change and a generational shift — she is 45, Bass, 73 — she has struggled at times to define what that would mean.
At a recent debate, the two traded scathing criticism, with Raman pressing her case for change and Bass arguing the city would be at risk with Raman’s “extreme” views, referring to her positions on police hiring and homelessness.
“We cannot afford another four years of decline, of mismanagement, of excuses,” Raman said. Bass told her rival: “You are not ready for prime time.”
A sense of foreboding has even crept into City Hall. Council member Traci Park said recently that she was voting for — but not endorsing — Bass. She warned that Raman would take the city backward.
“I have deep concerns about the leadership and effectiveness of both candidates,” said Park, a Democrat whose district includes the Palisades burn area.
In a city known to shrug at local politics — the media tend to showcase crime, sports and Hollywood rather than City Hall — the race has been overshadowed by the national fight for Congress, two wars and anxiety over inflation and grocery prices. The LA mayor — a position that shares power with the city council — has never had the clout of counterparts in New York or Chicago. And the office has a history of being a political graveyard for its former occupants who have been frustrated in efforts to reach higher office.
“This is a hard time to be an incumbent anything, because people are so disillusioned with how government is responding to their needs,” said LA-based Democratic consultant Bill Burton. “I think this race is a coin flip, but I also think that there is a palpable lack of enthusiasm.”
A clash of ideas over police and public safety
Four years ago, Bass defeated billionaire Republican-turned-Democrat Rick Caruso, who had promised to expand the police department and place a stronger emphasis on public safety. In the primary, crime was a major plank for Pratt.
Now it’s Bass who is stressing public safety with backing from the police union.
Bass has pushed to hire more police, while Raman said she intends to replace the police chief because of broken trust with citizens stemming from federal immigration raids. Raman once posted “defund the police” on social media in 2020, but more recently said staffing at the Los Angeles Police Department should remain at its current level.
The race also has historical markers: two women of color facing off for the city’s top job. Bass is the first Black woman to hold the post, and Raman could be the first South Asian woman in the job.
In Studio City, college student Beatrix Davis described herself as an “anti-capitalist” who supports Sanders, but was uninspired by either choice for mayor. She went with Raman, but said she pales in comparison to Mamdani who is willing to “take a stand and speak his mind.”
“I wasn’t all in for her,” she said of Raman, but added, “Bass is incompetent.”

title: Before Maine looks for an economic ‘secret sauce,’ it should look inward
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
John Surdyk lives in Waterville.
In the winter of 1882, the Kennebec River was one of the busiest industrial sites in New England. Crews sawed ice from the river, hauled it to wooden icehouses along the banks and shipped it to Boston, New York and Washington.
Economic developers would call it a textbook cluster: specialized labor, local capital and shared infrastructure all organized around one product. It lasted barely a generation. Mechanical ice plants and home refrigeration gutted the trade by about 1920.
I learned this story after moving to the Kennebec Valley this summer, and it stayed with me at Maine Blue Economy Week in Portland three weeks ago.
The gathering of founders, researchers, lenders and investors was a valuable opportunity for me to see Maine’s social and economic capital at work. Maine has world-class research institutions, strong educational institutions and tenacious founders who pursue profit and, often, public benefit. I met people building electric outboard motors and sustainable seafood brands. The work coming out of the state’s labs and institutes impressed me.
Much of the conversation at the event revolved around one idea: an “ocean cluster” informed by the experiences of others in Massachusetts, Alaska and elsewhere. I understand the pull, but borrowing a model is harder than it looks.
Harvard’s Michael Porter helped popularize clusters, and the idea is intuitively attractive since it implies a recipe or “secret sauce.”
The evidence that governments can build one on purpose is thinner than the idea’s popularity suggests. Some economic geographers argue the concept deserves a public-policy health warning. Florida spent more than $1 billion over two decades luring research institutes to seed a biotech cluster, and by most public accounts, the results have disappointed.
Part of the trouble is how we learn from one another.
I have participated in research into how universities and governments borrow startup policies from each other, and the pattern is humbling. We hear the success stories, but failed clusters rarely keynote a conference. We also copy what we can see, such as the structure of a public-private partnership, an incentive package, even a brand (Silicon Alley, Silicon Prairie). What we miss is the local history, tacit knowledge and relationships that make a place work. A region can learn and easily learn the wrong lesson.
The story of New Bedford, shared at the conference, made the point very well. Whaling. Textile mills. Commercial fishing.
Academics call this progression of pivots regional branching where new industries grow by putting a workforce’s existing skills to new uses. The lesson is not “build a cluster.” It’s that improvisation matters as much as planning. Entrepreneurs already know this.
So what might Maine do instead?
Treat its blue economy strategy the way a Bigelow scientist or a startup founder treats a promising hypothesis. Run small experiments. Measure the results. Take the data seriously (even when it’s unwelcome), and adjust. Hard-won local knowledge will likely serve the state better than imitating somewhere else’s pathway.
One keynote at the conference was titled “Our Heritage Is Innovation.” Maybe so. The ice kings were innovators, too.

title: Obituary: Winston Sidney Higgins
text:
ALBION – Winston Sidney Higgins, born February 2, 1942, to Clarence and Laura (Rowe) Higgins of Benton, Maine, passed away on Oct. 12, 2026 to be with his Lord and Savior.
Winston grew up in Albion where he attended McDonald School. He shared a special bond with his identical twin brother Clifton, a connection that was such a meaningful part of his life, along with seven other siblings, Ronald, Clyde, Clayton, Wayne, Freeman, Mike and Jeff.
Winston spent most of his career as a dairy farmer in Albion. Some of his proudest moments were spent with his children, especially his grandchildren allowing them a wonderful playground of curiosity and the love of animals. Winston was also employed by Lee Brothers of Albion and was well respected. After many decades of farming Winston decided to retire, but not for long. He joined Nitram and maintained the winter plowing for the town of Albion, always stopping along the way to chat to a friend or two. He also served the town of Albion as Road Commissioner. And did he stop there? No, Winston went full-time at Johnny’s Selected Seeds where he worked in the warehouse alongside his daughter Sarah.
He had love for all children and was known as Papa to all, including any little friends that crossed his path. He took this role in his life very serious.
Winston is survived by the love of his life Rebecca (Creasey) Higgins of 64 years of marriage, Mark and Judy Higgins of Sidney, Sarah (Higgins) and Mark Squire of Albion, Danny Higgins ad Sean Weber of Orrington, Laurie (Higgins) and Joseph Ball of Albion, two brothers, Ronald and Linda Higgins of Portland and Jeff Higgins of Oakland.
Grandchildren, Nicholas Higgins (passed), Jake Higgins and Kori Ellis, Lyndsey Weiss and Mike Chasteen, Ashley Ball and Micah Orenstein, Robert Weiss and Kendall Valesquez, Jesse Ball and Chelsea Whitmore, Lucas and Katy Higgins, Emily Higgins, Nicholas Weber, and Jeb Higgins.
Great Grandchildren, Deven Young, Bella Chasteen, Natalie Weiss-Maheu, Avery Ball, Jonah Orenstein, McKenzie Ball, Easton Higgins, Marley Weiss, Juniper Orenstein, Aubrey Weiss, and Peter Higgins.
Services will be held at the Albion Christian Church on Oct. 24, 2026 at 1 pm.

title: Evacuations and shelter-in-place orders issued after chemical release in Toledo, Ohio
text:
TOLEDO, Ohio (AP) — A ruptured chemical tank billowed a white plume into the air for hours Wednesday, forcing hundreds of residents out of their homes due to the potentially toxic leak and the possibility of an explosion.
More than 50,000 people in Toledo, Ohio, were advised to stay indoors for much of the day until the city lifted a shelter-in-place order in the evening.
City leaders were allowing the chemical to vent instead of trying to stop the leak, saying that would be more dangerous. Videos show a plume still swirling from the tank early Wednesday afternoon, more than 14 hours after the tank began leaking Tuesday night in an industrial area.
Some residents felt irritation in their eyes and throats and sought treatment, and city officials said one sheriff’s deputy who responded to the blast later drove himself to a hospital because he felt unwell.
Mark White Jr., who lives within the affected area, was sleeping with his windows open and woke to what he described as a burning plastic smell. He decided to evacuate to a shelter at an elementary school because he has asthma.
“I don’t know what this chemical can do to my lungs, long term or anything,” White said.
MC Tank Transport said the tank contained glycidyl methacrylate, which it described as “an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.”
The Ohio Environmental Protection Agency said without elaborating that the leak happened because of an error while the material was being transferred.
Mayor says the chemical leak has slowed
Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz said Wednesday afternoon there was no reason to panic and that the city was working with state and federal environmental officials.
He said they decided to allow the tank to continue releasing the chemical because there was little threat to the public and that it would be more dangerous to ask first responders to go near the chemical trucking company’s facility where more tanks were stored.
“There’s no question the situation is improving,” said Kapszukiewicz, who added that drones monitoring the leaking tank show its temperature is dropping and that the plume is diminishing.
Still, it could take hours before the tank is safe to approach, he said.
Nearly 1,000 residents were told to evacuate overnight within a 1-mile (1.6-kilometer) radius of the leak. A shelter-in-place order for more than 50,000 people covering a 3-mile (4.8-kilometer) radius included neighborhoods along the Lake Erie shoreline and stretched just across the state line into Michigan. By Wednesday evening, the shelter-in-place had been lifted and the evacuation order was cut down to half a mile (0.8 kilometers).
Schools across the city were closed Wednesday, and automaker Stellantis shut down production at its nearby Jeep assembly plant.
Residents worry about chemical’s risks
Health officials said the symptoms reported so far were primarily eye and throat irritation. Testing was ongoing to determine the chemical’s concentration in the air and whether it posed additional health risks.
ProMedica, which operates hospitals and urgent care centers in the Toledo area, said it evaluated about 30 people who reported symptoms that might have been related to the leak. Most were treated and released, the health care provider said.
Residents well beyond the shelter-in-place zone described smelling paint or burning chemicals. City officials tried to assure them that the odors did not indicate there was anything harmful in the air.
Kristine Kowalinski, who lives just outside the affected area, said she was staying inside because she’s sensitive even to smoke from wood burning. She said she’s worried about what’s in the air and on the ground.
“My main concern is how did that affect everything overnight when it was raining down on cars, houses, my garden,” she said.
Kapszukiewicz said the chemical is liquid inside the tank but becomes a gas when released. Officials began worrying early on that the tank, which can hold 5,500 gallons of the chemical, could explode, he said.
Chemical can irritate eyes and cause headaches
People who come into contact with glycidyl methacrylate may feel as if their eyes, nose, mouth and skin are burning, the city fire department said. Overexposure can cause headaches, dizziness, tiredness, nausea and vomiting.
“It’s really toxic if you touch it, if you ingest it,” said Karim Baroudi, director of the Toledo-Lucas County Health Department. “Now we’re trying to kind of determine how much of a toxicity is in the air that the people are breathing so we can give better guidance.”
Baroudi advised residents to close their windows and that those who “feel irritation in the eyes, heavily breathing, just take a shower for now.” The fire department said those who experience symptoms should contact a medical professional.
Emergency and hazardous material crews were not approaching the tank because of the risk of an explosion, Kapszukiewicz said.
Arkansas-based MC Tank Transport said in a statement the company is working with the fire department and other emergency authorities. Company representatives were on their way to Toledo, Kapszukiewicz said.
“Our immediate and overriding concern is the safety of area residents, emergency responders and our employees,” the company said.
___
McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire. Associated Press journalists Beatrice Dupuy in New York and Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

title: Pope Leo’s doctors confirm he needs no further treatment for lung cancer
text:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV will need no further treatment for lung cancer after tests confirmed the disease was localized, the Vatican said Wednesday.
Leo, 71, had part of one lung removed last week in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Leo was discharged from Rome’s Gemelli Polyclinic on Saturday, four days after surgery, and said he would gradually resume his activities.
The pope’s personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and his surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said the final tests on tissue removed during the surgery confirmed the diagnosis and that the cancer had not spread.
“A subsequent oncology assessment confirmed that no further treatment is necessary,” the doctors said in a statement.
The pope had the lower section, or lobe, of his right lung removed to try to ensure that all the cancer was removed.
Additional treatment is offered for patients whose cancer has spread, such as into the lymph nodes, or who have certain other signs that their cancer might be particularly aggressive. Surgery often can be enough when tumors are caught very early, such as when someone has an X-ray or other scan that shows a spot long before it’s large or causing symptoms.
The pope appears to have had one of those “incidental findings,” a nodule in his lung spotted during another exam.
In an interview with Vatican News on Saturday, Margaritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, confirmed that the nodule was found by chance during routine abdominal examinations, and that the pope had not been experiencing any symptoms.
“The statements suggest that this is a stage I lung cancer for which surgery is highly effective and expected to be curative,” said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. He said the lack of further treatment suggests a relatively small cancer, and that it had not spread to lymph nodes.
The pope carried on business while in the hospital, including a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and has appeared strong in two public appearances at the Vatican since his surgery: the traditional Sunday blessing from a window overlooking St. Peter’s Square and Wednesday’s longer audience in the square, greeting the faithful from around the world.
“Thank you! Thank you for the support of your prayers,” Leo said during the audience.
His next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
Margaritora told Vatican News that there was “no clinical reason” to prevent the trip, which includes a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and high altitude stops.
The pope had revealed that a nodule would be surgically removed during the traditional Sunday blessing on Oct. 11, in an unusually transparent disclosure broadcast on live television that broke the tradition of secrecy surrounding papal health issues.
____

title: Paris to hold public hearing on data center moratorium
text:
Paris is holding a public hearing Oct. 26 for comment on two ordinances: to establish a moratorium on data centers and to codify residency requirements for convicted sex offenders.
The hearing is at 6 p.m. Monday, preceding the regular Select Board meeting at Paris Town Office at 33 Market Square.
A special town meeting will be Nov. 17 at 6 p.m. at the Paris Fire Department at 137 Western Ave.
The topic of data centers was raised during the Select Board’s Oct. 13 business meeting. The board voted unanimously to place a 180-day moratorium on accepting applications for data center development and directed the Planning Board to draft an ordinance.
If approved by voters Nov. 17, the data center moratorium will be retractive to Oct. 13, the date selectmen approved it. The board will be authorized to extend the moratorium after 180 if an ordinance has not been adopted at that time.
The Select Board may also cancel it if and when an ordinance is enacted.
Regarding an ordinance restricting residencies of sex offenders, Town Manager Natalie Andrews said the Select Board moved to adopt one at the request of Police Chief Michael Ward. If approved by voters Nov. 17, it would codify state law on sex offender definitions and also where convicted sex offenders are allowed to live.
State law defines the term as Class A, B or C crimes against minors under the age of 14 and the requirement to be listed in the state registry.
Sex offenders will not be allowed to reside within 750 feet of any private or public schools; or any public parks, athletic fields or recreational facilities where children are the primary users.
Exempted from the ordinance are sex offenders whose residency in a restricted area preceded the ordinance.

title: Mortgage rate history: 1972 to 2026
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mortgage rate history: 1972 to 2026
Key takeaways
- As of October 21, 2026, the average rate for a 30-year, fixed loan was 7.39% — up from the beginning of the year, and higher than the 2025 average of 6.66%.
- Over the past four decades, the 30-year fixed rate ranged from a 2021 low of 2.65% to a 1981 high above 18%.
- The average 30-year fixed rate bottomed in 2021 at just under 3%.
- 87% of all borrowers in 2025 paid more than the most competitive rate available to them, according to Bankrate’s Hidden Homeownership Tax research — meaning rate history matters less to your bill than whether you actually shopped your own rate.
The residential mortgage as we know it today is less than a century old. In fact, until the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) was established in 1934, only one in 10 Americans owned a home. That all changed with the introduction of the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage during the Great Depression, which made homeownership possible for millions.
Recent changes in mortgage rates have put a strain on the housing market. Historically low rates at the start of the 2020s led to a surge in home prices, and rates have stayed consistently between 6% and 7% since the Federal Reserve raised rates in 2022. However, home prices remain high. This combination of climbing prices with higher-than-recent rates has made housing affordability a major problem.
Mortgage rates over time
-  Average 30-year fixed mortgage rate by year Here is a timeline of the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate by year. Bankrate first began aggregating rate data in 1982; all data prior was sourced from Freddie Mac. The 2026 average is through October 14. * Freddie Mac rate data
Current mortgage rates
As of October 21, 2026, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate is 7.39%, per Bankrate’s lender survey. Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey, a separate weekly benchmark based on conforming purchase loans with 20% down and strong credit, put the 30-year fixed average at 7.40% as of October 15, 2026 — unchanged from the week before and up from 6.27% a year earlier.
Rates fell through most of the first two months of 2026, bottoming at a 2026 low of 6.01% on Feb. 19 — the lowest weekly average since September 2022. They’ve climbed back into the mid-6% range since, as persistent inflation and Treasury yields have kept upward pressure on mortgage pricing.
You don't have to accept the first rate you're quoted.
In 2025, the typical borrower overpaid by $278 a month — $3,343 a year — simply by not comparing enough lenders, according to Bankrate’s Hidden Homeownership Tax research. You can’t control the Fed, oil prices or Treasury yields, but you can control how many lenders you compare — and that’s the part most borrowers skip.
2020s mortgage rate trends
Entering 2020, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was already below 4%. Then the COVID-19 pandemic pushed it to a weekly low of 2.65% in January 2021 — the lowest rate on record.
In 2022, the Federal Reserve began raising its benchmark interest rate to fight inflation, and mortgage rates rose sharply alongside it. By October 2023, the 30-year mortgage rate broke through 8% for the first time since 2000.
Rates stayed in the 6s and 7s through most of 2024. The Fed cut its benchmark rate three times in late 2024 and three more times in 2025, but mortgage rates didn’t fall in lockstep — they drifted down over the course of 2025, closing the year averaging 6.66%.
Rates kept falling into early 2026 until the conflict with Iran disrupted oil markets in February, which analysts tied to a jump in 10-year Treasury yields — and mortgage rates followed that upward trajectory.
2010s mortgage rate trends
In the 2010s, the 30-year mortgage rate trended downward, beginning in the 4% range, dipping below 4%, and ending the decade back in that range. These low rates were brought on in part by the Federal Reserve’s Great Recession-era policies.
2000s mortgage rate trends
Driven by the subprime mortgage crisis of the late 2000s, the 30-year mortgage rate tumbled from about 8% at the start of the decade down to 5.4% by 2009. At the time, the Federal Reserve implemented quantitative easing, buying mortgage-backed securities in bulk to drive down interest rates and usher in an economic recovery.
1990s mortgage rate trends
The 1990s saw a significant shift in the 30-year mortgage rate, which plunged to an average of 6.91% in 1998. This drop was brought on by the dot-com bubble, an era when investors rushed to buy stocks from overvalued technology companies. When these stocks plummeted, investors turned their focus to fixed-income investments, such as bonds. As bond prices rose and yields fell, mortgage rates, which follow the 10-year Treasury yield, also declined.
1980s mortgage rate trends
The median U.S. home price rose from $63,700 in 1980 to $123,900 by 1990, according to the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Mortgage rates peaked at 18.4% in October 1981 alone as the Federal Reserve fought runaway inflation — though the full 1981 annual average came in lower, at 16.64%, since rates were lower for the rest of the year. Once inflation cooled, rates eased into the 9% range, closing the decade at 9.78%.
1970s mortgage rate trends
The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage started the decade at about 7.5% in 1971 (the earliest year with available data), according to Freddie Mac. By 1979, the rate had risen to an average of 11.2%. During this decade, the Federal Reserve’s expansionary policy and other factors helped drive inflation and borrowing costs way up.
Mortgage rate predictions
While we can try to guess based on historical data, no one knows for certain what will happen to future mortgage rates over time — whether they’ll change at all, or when. Still, we regularly ask economists and other experts to weigh in. For week-to-week predictions, check out our mortgage rate poll.
Is buying right for you at today’s rates?
If your monthly payment at today’s average rate fits your budget with room for property tax and insurance increases, buy now — home prices have historically risen faster than rates have fallen, so waiting rarely pays off. If the payment only works at a rate meaningfully below where the market sits today, hold off and spend that time raising your credit score above 740 and building a 20% down payment — both will do more for your rate than guessing when the Fed moves next. Estimate your monthly payment with Bankrate’s mortgage calculator.
Learn more: How mortgage rates are determined
Is refinancing right for you at today’s rates?
If you can cut your rate by at least 0.75 to 1.0 percentage points and you plan to stay in the home for five or more years, refinancing is usually worth the cost. If you’re planning to sell within the next two to three years, run the break-even math first — it may not pay off.
Here’s the math: Closing costs on a refinance typically run 2% to 5% of the loan amount. On a $300,000 balance, that’s $6,000 to $15,000 upfront. If cutting your rate saves you $300 a month, a $11,000 closing cost takes about 37 months — just over three years — to break even. Stay past that point and you come out ahead; sell or refinance again before it, and you lose money on the deal.
78.7% of refinance borrowers overpaid on their new rate in 2025, according to Bankrate’s Hidden Homeownership Tax research. Compare current refinance rates from at least three lenders to find the best offer for you.
Next steps
Mortgage rates are affected by two things: world events and your personal finances. As we’ve seen recently, the COVID-19 pandemic led to bottomed-out mortgage rates — the lowest our country has ever seen. On a smaller, more recent scale, the conflict with Iran has caused upward pressure on mortgage rates as oil prices and inflation rise.
You can’t control major global events, but you can control your finances. Saving for a down payment, paying down debt and growing your income will all land you with a better mortgage offer. You also need to shop around lenders because not every lender will give you a great deal. Bankrate consistently has mortgage offers below the market average. Use our tool to compare mortgage rates with top lenders and weigh the pros and cons of each.

title: Tennessee Titans release defensive lineman after gun incident at team facility
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) — Defensive lineman Jordan Elliott was released by the Tennessee Titans after retrieving a gun from his car following a practice altercation, head coach Robert Saleh confirmed Wednesday.
The altercation was with offensive tackle JC Latham, according to a report from NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo.
The incident occurred in the parking lot last week.
Saleh confirmed the details of the incident to reporters on Wednesday, while defending Elliott’s character.
“This is a man who is a father, a great husband,” Saleh said. “He’s never committed a crime in his entire life, and he pulled a gun in the parking lot. The first question that everyone forgets to ask is, ‘Why?’”
Saleh went on to vouch for Elliott as a man and a player, and invited teams who are in need of a defensive lineman to give him a call because Elliott “should be on an NFL roster.”
Team’s initial statement
When the Titans initially announced his removal on Tuesday, the statement only acknowledged that there had been an incident involving Elliott at the team facility. After reviewing the incident, the team decided to release Elliott and did not have further comment.
“On Thursday, October 15, there was an incident at our team facility involving Jordan Elliott,” the Titans said in a statement. “Following our review of the incident, we have made the decision to release Elliott from our roster.”
Coach addresses incident
Saleh was first to speak during Wednesday’s press conference and addressed the incident, the team and the league’s response directly.
Elliott was inactive for the Titans’ game on Sunday against the Indianapolis Colts before he was released.

title: Time is on Troy Jackson’s side

title: ‘This is what I remember’: Teacher speaks after surviving Oregon elementary school shooting
text:
BEND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - Becky Drury, a teacher who was shot at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend last week, shared a message Wednesday about what she remembers from that day.
“I’d like to share my memories of what happened at Silver Rail Elementary because I want to make sure the events of that day and my actions in particular are reported accurately.
“Here is what I remember: Once I realized something was happening outside, I ran to see what was going on. I then saw the shooter and immediately ran back into the classroom. I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there. Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground.
“Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured. I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else. So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again.
“This is what I remember. I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act.
“What happened in that classroom was unimaginable, and like so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy. My thoughts are with those who were hurt, those we lost, their families, our school, and the Bend community. I am truly grateful for the kindness and support we have received as we face the difficult days ahead together.
“We also ask for continued privacy and space as we continue down the long road of recovery.
“Finally, to the media, please utilize trusted voices in our community. Accurate, respectful reporting is a truly important service that will help heal the wounds inflicted by that awful day.”
The shooting occurred last Thursday when police say a 16-year-old former student went into Silver Rail Elementary and fired inside a special needs classroom.
Teacher Megan Lambert, 25, was killed along with students Rhoam Summer, 5, and two other children, ages 8 and 11.
Drury needed surgery on her left arm and right hand, her husband Will Drury said.
A student, 7-year-old Saylor, was also hurt in the shooting. She was given life-saving care at the school and taken to Oregon Health & Science University, police said last week.
Previously, Bend police said Drury had shielded Saylor during the shooting, but Drury’s statement contradicts that information.
A motive for the school shooting currently remains unclear.

title: Susan Collins calls for removal of radio ad calling Troy Jackson a 'creep'
text:
LEWISTON, Maine (AP) — Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins distanced herself from a new radio ad attacking Democratic opponent Troy Jackson as a “freak” and a “creep” because “he has two kids with his cousin,” saying Wednesday that it should be taken down.
The spot, airing on Maine radio in the form of a country song, is from the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate Republicans. Among the lyrics in the jingle: “If he’ll screw his own family, he’ll screw yours too.”
Collins told reporters during a campaign appearance in Lewiston that she “had nothing to do with that ad.” She added that federal law bans her from coordinating with the super PAC, but she has publicly called for it to be removed.
Previously, in a Politico story in September, Collins referenced Jackson’s relationship with a second cousin.
“I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin,” Collins said. “I don’t know whether people know that or not.”
In an op-ed published Wednesday, Lana Pelletier, Jackson’s partner, criticized the radio ad and other attacks on her family by Collins and her supporters, saying she never thought they “would stoop this low.”
“Sen. Collins has been quick to demand respect and decency for herself. My family deserved the same,” Pelletier said.
“I am not a helpless woman who needs politicians to tell the world what happened in my own life. And I am not a punchline or a caricature of where I come from,” she added.
Jackson, a former state lawmaker and lumberjack, and Pelletier are longtime partners who have two sons together.
Jackson’s campaign manager, Dan Gottlieb, said Wednesday that Collins owes Jackson’s family an apology.
“Susan Collins herself spread these disgusting personal attacks on Troy’s family,” he said. “Now she wants Mainers to believe she’s above the very attacks she helped spread.”
Democrats are hoping for a win by Jackson over the incumbent Collins as the party tries to retake the Senate.
Also Wednesday, Collins lamented how negative much campaign advertising has been during this election cycle.
“This race is unique in Maine history in the number of personal attacks,” Collins said.
Story by Kimberlee Kruesi and Patrick Whittle, Associated Press

title: Maine's First Bee City Uses Fallen Foliage To Help Thousands Of Native Bee Species Survive
text:
While most people think that once the leaves fall in the autumn, the best thing to do is clean them up and dispose of them, there are also those who follow the school of thought that you should just leave the leaves where they land.
Read More: What Not To Include In Leaf Collection, Bangor And Brewer
While you might assume this way of thinking is rooted in laziness, science actually backs it up!
In fact, the City of Bangor is also getting behind the effort. While they will have crews hitting the city roads and sidewalks with giant vacuums that will such up the fallen foliage, they're also encouraging those who don't want to rake, to just let things be.
They posted on their Facebook page, that leaving the leaves right where they are, or moving them around trees and garden beds could actually help the little ecosystem in your yard.
"Fallen leaves serve as overwintering habitat for many butterfly and moth species, and as insulation for plant roots and the soil, where other pollinators like bumblebees tend to overwinter. If leaving them where they are isn't an option, you can also rake them into garden beds or around tree bases. Leaving dead plants in the garden standing over the winter is also helpful since various native bees hibernate in hollow stems."
This is in keeping with Bangor becoming the first "Bee City" affiliate in the state of Maine, which was made official in 2024.
According to the folks over at Bangor Beautiful, along with practice like reducing harmful chemicals and emphasising programs like No Mow May, the goal of a Bee City is to ultimately help the nation's bee population.
"Bee City USA® and Bee Campus USA work to galvanize communities to sustain pollinators, in particular the more than 3,600 species of native bees in this country, by increasing the abundance of native plants, providing nest sites, and reducing the use of pesticides.
The Xerces Society of Invertebrate Conservation says that you can gently move the leaves to areas like tree beds or gardens, if you're worried about the grass dying. But overall, the less you disturb the leaves, the better.
"Too many leaves can kill grass, but in soil they can suppress weeds, retain moisture, and boost nutrition. Avoid shredding leaves with a mower. Raking or blowing (electric) are alternatives that will keep leaves whole for the best cover and protect the insects and eggs already living there. If you decide you need to clean up the leaves and debris in spring, make sure you wait until late in the season so as not to destroy all the life you’ve worked to protect."
So, if you were looking for an excuse to take it easy on the yard work this fall, this might just bee a good one to use, as it's a win-win for everyone; you and the bugs!

title: Vance says GOP shouldn’t complain about Ramaswamy ad with Amy Acton’s estranged mother
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Vice President JD Vance defended an ad Wednesday by Vivek Ramaswamy that features the estranged mother of Dr. Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent for Ohio governor, and spotlights the abuse she experienced as a child, even as the Republican in a tight race to retain Vance’s former seat in the Senate distanced himself from the ad.
During a campaign visit to Ohio, Vance told reporters he was “disgusted” by fellow Republicans who were pushing back against the ad, then later drew cheers at a political rally when he defended Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and 2024 presidential candidate.
Vance said he has watched Democrats “throw every dirty trick in the political book at Vivek,” who he considers a close personal friend -- including calling him a ‘murderer’ — while “the whole time Vivek has stood tall and talked about what he wants to accomplish.”
“And now the media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because, guess what, Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out as it is and calls Amy Acton a liar,” he said.
During the same rally, U.S. Sen. Jon Husted shared the stage with Vance and Ramaswamy, but steered clear of discussing the ad, in which Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, calls her daughter “a liar” and insinuates that she has mental health issues. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather was indicted for raping Acton, and the candidate has not seen her since 1978.
“I would not have run that ad,” Husted said in a statement to The Associated Press. A day earlier, his Democratic opponent, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, called the spot “disgusting” and said everybody — including Husted — should denounce it.
President Donald Trump also weighed in Wednesday, telling reporters he knew nothing about the ad but had heard that “the mother went very rogue on the daughter.”
“It’s a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much, but I don’t think that has anything to do with Vivek,” the president said.
‘Let’s heal,’ Acton implores voters
Acton, Ohio’s former state health director, spent the day traveling to a previously scheduled campaign appearance in rural Wyandot County, in the northwestern part of the state. Her campaign also released a new positive ad, which — somewhat ironically — featured her appealing to voters to “find more breathing room, and let’s heal what has divided us.” She has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child.
In Cincinnati, the vice president said “politics is a tough business” and that the contents of Ramaswamy’s ad were “not really my concern.” He said he was focused on supporting Republican candidates in the midterm elections.
“I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” Vance said in his first public comments on the ad, which has roiled one of the most contentious and expensive governor’s races in the country.
Some Republicans denounce ad, Ramaswamy. Haley calls him ‘a bad guy’
The video was criticized by both Democrats and Republicans when it exploded into public view Tuesday, just two weeks before Election Day.
Nikki Haley, who sparred with Ramaswamy during the 2024 Republican presidential primary over the personal nature of his attacks, called him “a bad guy” in a social media post Tuesday. “It’s a shame he continues to get away with it,” she wrote. Meghan McCain called it “dastardly” and Dan Hauser, a long-time aide to Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, said he deleted his post sharing the video once he realized “the very serious accusations that caused their issues.”
The Ramaswamy campaign’s initial statement on the ad did not claim responsibility for its production, but the candidate eventually did so when he spoke to reporters at an evening campaign event. His campaign will spend $4 million to air it on TV and online in the closing weeks of the race, despite the backlash. He didn’t address the ad in remarks at the rally where Vance spoke outside Cincinnati.
Police and court records show Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton’s biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur, who has since died, failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive.
Acton said she has not seen her mother since she appeared in a courtroom in the late 1970s. Her campaign on Tuesday posted a video of her brother who supported her backstory about living in a tent and being abused.
Vance told reporters before the rally that Acton “lies about every single one of her positions.”
Acton’s campaign declined to respond to Vance’s comments, saying that her painful backstory was not the centerpiece of her run for governor.
Voter: ‘I don’t think it’s right’
Michael Wedding, 20, came to Vance’s rally Wednesday — but not to support Ohio’s Republican ticket. He said he would be parting with his large Republican family and vote for Acton for governor, adding that he attended the rally in large part to see Ramaswamy in person.
He said he had seen the ad and found it “very, very gross.”
“She was sexually abused as a child,” he said of Acton, ”and I thought it was kind of scummy that they would use that in an advertisement. I don’t think it’s right to use her sexual abuse as a kid, or give any sort of platform to that.”
___
Binkley reported from Washington. Associated Press video journalist Patrick Aftoora-Orsagos contributed to this story from Sharonville, Ohio.

title: Top returning scorer for UMaine women’s basketball is a ‘real threat in America East’
text:
ORONO, Maine — Lala Woods’ University of Maine women’s basketball career got off to an impressive start a year ago.
She was a freshman guard and hadn’t played in the team’s first 11 games after missing her senior season at Wheeling Park High School in Wheeling, West Virginia, due to knee surgery.
Needing some supplemental scoring to complement America East Player of the Year Adrianna Smith, UMaine head coach Amy Vachon sent Woods into the Quinnipiac game, and she responded with eight points in 14 minutes of a 63-55 road victory, including a pair of crucial 3-pointers.
She would go on to hit three 3-pointers in a 59-57 victory at Harvard and would finish the season as the team’s fourth-leading scorer, averaging 8.4 points per game over 21 games along with 2.4 rebounds, an assist and a steal. She averaged 32.7 minutes of playing time per game.
She averaged 11.2 points per game over her last six games and 4.7 rebounds over her last eight and was chosen to the America East All-Rookie Team.
Woods is the top returning scorer for this year’s Black Bears team after the departure of Smith, Asta Blauenfeldt and Sarah Talon.
That could certainly put added pressure on her, but she doesn’t see it that way.
“I’m excited. This is why I play basketball. I like the pressure,” said the 5-foot-8 Woods. “I’m confident in what I can do, and my coaches and teammates have confidence in me.”
Woods was second on the team a year ago in 3-pointers made (34) and attempted (112). She shot 42.2 percent on her two-pointers (27-for-64).
This year, she is looking to add an inside game to her range.
“Last year, I shot a lot of threes. I’ve been working on getting to the rim and finishing strong. I want to be able to score at all three levels,” Woods said.
“And I want to be able to play really well at both ends of the floor,” she added.
Vachon said she is looking for Woods to “take another step forward.”
“She was number three on the (opponents’) scouting reports last year, but now she will be number one on the scouting report,” Vachon said.
Teams began keying on Woods more at the end of last season, so it was tough for her to get shots off, according to Vachon.
“But she has had a really great offseason and has really worked on different aspects of her game,” Vachon said. “Hopefully, she will continue where she left off.”
“She has really proven herself to be a real threat in America East,” said UMaine senior center Lizzy Gruber. “And I think a lot of teams know that and will be coming for her, but she has that in her.”
Senior forward Kaliyah Sain never got to play with Woods a year ago because she tore the posterior cruciate ligament in her knee during the eighth game of the season and missed the rest of the campaign.
“I’m really excited to be on the court with her,” Sain said. “I didn’t have a chance last year. Playing with her in practice is fun. She brings a lot of energy, and she is a confident shooter. We trust her with the ball to do anything with it. She’s good to be around.”
Despite primarily being a 3-point shooter and perimeter player, Woods showed that she wasn’t afraid to mix it up in the paint, battling for rebounds.
“She does it all,” Sain said.
“Coach wants us all to rebound as much as we can,” said Woods. “Rebounds win games. You have to do that, too. I love to play and put on a show when I’m out there. I play with passion. It’s a game I love, and I go out there and give it everything I have.”
The Black Bears were picked to finish fourth in the America East coaches’ preseason poll due to the loss of their top three scorers, but Woods feels this team has a lot of potential.
“We lost three key scorers, but we have a lot of scorers people don’t know about,” said the former three-time all-state selection who scored 1,213 career points.
“Everyone is fighting for playing time. It’s going to be exciting to see what we can do this year,” Woods said.
The Black Bears, 19-13 overall last season and 61-43 losers to Vermont in the America East championship game, will open the season at 6 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 5 when they entertain Siena University on the Skip Chappelle Court in the Memorial Gymnasium.

text:

This year, voting Democrat is a matter of survival. If we want to heat our house, live in a clean environment free of data centers, be able to have a steak dinner once in a while and not worry that our kids will be facing a dystopian future, vote Democrat.

title: Troy Jackson’s partner responds to Republican attack ads
text:
Troy Jackson’s longtime romantic partner is criticizing Republican efforts to exploit their relationship and family in the closing days of Maine’s hotly contested U.S. Senate race.
Lana Pelletier, Jackson’s partner for 40 years and his second cousin, wrote in an op-ed published Wednesday in the Bangor Daily News that national Republicans and Jackson’s opponent, Republican Sen. Susan Collins, have crossed a line by focusing on their personal lives.
“Our children have been dragged into this campaign. Our relationship has been mocked. Our family has been talked about as though there is something shameful about who we are or where we come from,” Pelletier wrote. “There isn’t.”
She added, “I deeply resent watching Collins and her allies treat our lives as something beneath them — especially when serious issues involving women are manipulated into political weapons by people who show so little care for the women involved.”
The final stretch of Maine’s Senate campaign has gotten nasty, with national Republicans mounting an all-out attack on Jackson and his family.
On Tuesday, the SLF PAC, a super PAC tied to Republican Senate leader John Thune, R-S.D., began airing a radio ad about Jackson’s family. It’s a country song whose chorus includes the refrain, “If he’ll screw his own family, he’ll screw yours, too.”
The brass-knuckle tactics highlight the lengths to which powerful D.C. figures will go to win Maine’s Senate seat, which could determine control of the upper chamber during President Donald Trump’s final two years in office.
Since Jackson became the Democratic nominee on July 25, roughly three-quarters of the $101.8 million in ad spending has backed negative ads, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. Republican-aligned groups have spent about $47 million attacking Jackson, while Democratic-aligned groups have spent some $31 million attacking Collins.
Collins has asked the PAC to take down the ad about Jackson’s relationship to his partner. During a campaign stop Wednesday at Simones’ Hot Dog Stand in Lewiston, Collins said she had “nothing to do with” the spot and reiterated her desire for it to be removed from the airwaves.
But it wasn’t the only one that attacked Jackson’s family.
One TV commercial from SLF PAC, which is largely funded by out-of-state billionaires, said Jackson “keeps it in the family,” while another claimed that taxpayer money was used for “a sleazy deal with Jackson’s cousins, who are also his in-laws.” Yet another from an SLF-affiliated group, The Maine Standard, calls him “a creep.”
Republicans have also attacked Jackson’s son Chace, who was a state lobbyist during his father’s final term as state Senate president.
Collins has not remained above the fray. She brought up Jackson’s son’s lobbying during their first televised debate, accusing Jackson of flip-flopping on issues tied to his son’s lobbying efforts.
And in a September video interview with Politico, she coyly noted Jackson’s relationship with Pelletier.
“Well, I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin,” Collins said. “I don’t know whether people know that or not. … It’s not something I’m going to be emphasizing.”
Jackson, meanwhile, has accused Collins of personal corruption. At a debate earlier this month, he implied that she supported Trump’s war in Iran because it would benefit her family’s stock portfolio. Collins demanded that Jackson apologize for the remark. (Collins initially supported Trump’s right to conduct war under the War Powers Act, but voted repeatedly in favor of ending the conflict once the 60-day deadline for congressional approval had passed.)
At her campaign stop Wednesday, Collins noted that she too has been the victim of personal attacks by Jackson and his Democratic allies, who have tied her to disgraced financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein in ads.
Collins voted to table a provision calling for the release of the so-called Epstein files in a defense spending bill, but supported adding such a provision to an appropriations bill. She also joined a unanimous Senate vote in support of the Epstein Files Transparency Act.
An ad by Win Senate, a super PAC linked with Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., accused Collins of voting to cover up the Epstein files. It also claimed Collins received $3 million from a former Epstein business partner — a claim rated false by PolitiFact.
“This campaign has been unique in Maine’s history in the number of personal attacks,” Collins said. “It’s interesting because in comparing with my colleagues who are in tough races across the country, every single one of them has had an ad run against them trying to link us to Jeffrey Epstein. That is so absurd.”
Pelletier said in her op-ed that she expects people to challenge Jackson on his views and his record, “but there should be a line.”
“Collins has been quick to demand respect and decency for herself,” she wrote. “My family deserved the same.”
Jackson’s partner wasn’t the only one pushing back against Republican attacks Wednesday.
His former colleagues from the Maine Legislature gathered at the Maine Women’s Lobby in Augusta to speak out against recent attack ads, at least one of which features some of their faces.
Rebecca Millett, a former state lawmaker from Cape Elizabeth, appears in the “creep” ad crafted by the SLF PAC-affiliated The Maine Standard.
The spot highlights media reports that Jackson would lose his temper as Senate president, including one instance when he allegedly threw a water bottle.
Millett said the spot “reeks of desperation.”
“They put a black bar across my eyes, and the eyes of many other people here today, to suggest that we were somehow victims or villains,” she said, adding that she believes Jackson was a respectful and thoughtful leader and colleague.
The Maine Women’s Lobby also made a formal endorsement of Jackson at the event, a practice Destie Hohman Sprague, its executive director, said the organization usually doesn’t do.
When asked about Jackson’s alleged temper toward female colleagues while leading the state Senate, former Maine Sen. Cathy Breen said his behavior was not gendered in any way.
“When you’re in the thick of it, and the budget is coming down to the final hours, all of us are emotional. All of us are stressed out,” Breen said. “So, yeah, has Troy lost his temper now and then? Sure. So have I. I don’t hold that against him.”
Staff Writer Joe Charpentier contributed to this story.

title: Feds issue warning for nearly 400,000 pressure cookers that could seriously burn you
text:
(CNN) - Federal safety officials are warning customers to stop using nearly 400,000 pressure cookers linked to serious burn injuries.
The Consumer Product Safety Commission says people should stop using Power Quick Pot 6-quart pressure cookers immediately and dispose of them.
Officials say the lids can open while the cookers are still pressurized, causing hot contents to shoot out. The agency has received 24 reports of the malfunction, resulting in serious burns.
The affected cookers were sold online on such sites as Walmart.com and Amazon.com and at retailers nationwide between 2018 and 2023.
The model number, which can be found on the back of the cookers, is Y6D-36.
Officials say the importer, Tristar Products, has refused to issue a recall or offer a remedy to customers.

title: Free rides on Election Day offered by Greater Portland Metro to aid voters
Fake passport websites are charging travelers for free services
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Travelers rushing to renew a passport before an international trip may be vulnerable to scam websites designed to take advantage of that urgency, according to the Better Business Bureau.
Josh Planos, a spokesperson for the Better Business Bureau, said the pressure to receive a passport quickly often drives people toward risky shortcuts.
“In nearly every case, somebody is under the gun and needs to turn around a passport within a matter of weeks and wants to look for every alternative to ensure that it gets to the front doorstep in an adequate amount of time,” Planos said.
Planos said fraudulent websites promise fast turnaround times, then take travelers’ money without ever delivering a passport.
“A lot of folks are turning to websites that really have nothing to do with the government URL, travel.state.gov,” Planos said. “They are looking for third-party sites that charge those expedition fees, and those are really major red flags.”
The official passport application is free to download and file. Copycat sites charge travelers anyway, often disguising the charge as an “expediting” or “processing” fee.
The BBB has collected complaints from consumers who say they were deceived by these sites. One consumer wrote: “I went into the site assuming it was the State.gov site because it resembled it completely, including the URL. I did not notice that it ended as state.com, not state.gov. By the time I had submitted the application for my passport renewal and payment, I noticed that it was a fraud by the language on the confirmation page.”
Planos also cautioned against taking passport photos at home.
“Walgreens offers this service, post office offers this service for free,” Planos said. “I’d encourage you to not try to assemble your own passport. Stick with the professionals and have a real conversation in person with a human being about it.”
The U.S. State Department never charges a fee to download or fill out passport forms. Travelers checking processing times or applying for a passport should start at travel.state.gov or visit a local post office in person.

title: ‘Glee’ Reboot Coming to Streaming
text:
‘Glee’ Reboot Coming to Disney+ and Hulu
Congratulations Gleeks. You favorite show is coming back.
Glee will return in reboot form on Disney+ and Hulu. According to Deadline, the Disney streamers have ordered a new Glee series.
“The move has been on the cards for some time,” they added, “with co-creator Ryan Murphy regularly discussing its potential return over the last few months as he promotes FX series The Shards.”
READ MORE: The Worst Final Seasons of Otherwise Great TV Shows
Murphy created the original iteration of Glee with Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan. The show followed the members of a choir (one might even call it a glee club, perhaps) from a high school in Ohio, combining typical teen coming-of-age drama with high-energy musical numbers, mostly covers of beloved pop songs.
After a premiere in the spring of 2009, the series lasted for six seasons and 121 episodes, and also inspired a highly lucrative side business inspired by the show’s music. There were best-selling Glee soundtrack albums and digital singles, and the series also spawned live concerts and even a live concert movie in 2011. The original Glee series finale aired on Fox on March 20, 2015. Over its first run on the air, the show won a total of six Primetime Emmy Awards.
It’s not clear year whether the new Glee will be a strict reboot — a totally new version of the premise of a show about a high school glee club — or some sort of soft reboot that’s also a legacyquel featuring a new group of students along with some of the members of the previous cast. (Several original Glee stars have passed away, including Cory Monteith who starred as quarterback turned singing star Finn Hudson on the show.) It’s easy to envision a version of the show where one of the original stars plays the new director of the glee club, for example.

title: Hundreds of Mainers lost their health insurance due to Medicaid eligibility changes
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - Hundreds of Mainers have lost health coverage after changes to Medicaid eligibility took effect Oct. 1.
Before the change, some noncitizens who were in the U.S. lawfully, including asylum-seekers and refugees, could access Medicaid.
Medicaid is funded by a mix of state and federal money. Changes included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act mean the federal government will no longer reimburse states for Medicaid coverage provided to noncitizens.
“Providers are in a tough position because they now, as of October 1st, have clients on their caseload who now have no way to pay for the services that the provider would otherwise be offering,” said Katie Collins, a paralegal at Maine Equal Justice.
Green card holders and lawful permanent residents will retain access. According to the Maine Department of Health and Human Services, 980 Mainers have lost full MaineCare coverage.
“It puts a lot of strain also on the rest of the health system because that is money that’s not going to the hospitals or going to the providers from Medicaid,” Collins said.
In an April statement notifying states about the change, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz wrote: “The Trump Administration has a public mandate, a statutory obligation, and a moral duty to safeguard our federal healthcare programs.”
“What is frustrating is that individuals who are undocumented have never been eligible for Medicaid,” Collins said. “It really seems like the only point is stripping health care from people who otherwise were eligible but are not citizens or do not have permanent status.”
Pregnant women and people younger than 21 are exempt from the change and will remain covered. Some noncitizens may be able to enroll in free care programs offered by hospitals. Otherwise, they will be limited to emergency care coverage.
“When people are going without health care, the effect of that really ripples throughout an entire community, both the families, the individuals and, like I was saying before, the health care systems generally,” Collins said.
8 Investigates reached out to a number of hospital systems to see what impacts this eligibility change is having. A spokesperson for MaineHealth wrote that while it’s too soon to say what the impact will be, the system is anticipating a rise in emergency room usage and unpaid medical bills.

title: Pope Leo XIV needs no further cancer treatment, Vatican says
text:
Pope Leo XIV needs no further cancer treatment, Vatican says
Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer surgery last week was a success, and no further treatment is required, the Vatican press office said in a bulletin Wednesday.
“The final histological reports and molecular biology analyses of the tissue removed during the Holy Father’s surgery have been completed today,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, who treated the pope.
Related video above: What to know about lung cancer and when to get screened
“The results have confirmed that the condition was a pulmonary adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized. A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the bulletin added.
Pulmonary adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer, accounting for roughly 40% of all cases. It’s slow-moving and often affects non-smokers.
Leo’s announcement on Oct. 11 that he required surgery for a “nodule” on his lung came as a shock both within and outside the Vatican, given the pope’s penchant for clean living. After a short stay at a hospital in Rome, where doctors removed the lobe of his left lung, Leo returned home on Oct. 17.
The next day, he made his first public appearance since his diagnosis, leading the Sunday Angelus from the balcony of the Apostolic Palace.
“This experience has given me a profound sense of closeness to all those who are going through illness or a state of infirmity,” he told crowds of worshipers.
The all-clear arrives ahead of the pontiff’s planned South America trip next month. The news that the pope had cancer complicated plans for the journey, scheduled to include stops in Peru, Uruguay and Argentina and require at least 14 flights.
Though the Vatican has not officially confirmed the pope’s plans for travel, Margaritora told Vatican News that he saw “no clinical reasons” for canceling the trip.

title: Deputy jumps into deep water to rescue nonverbal 8-year-old
text:
LAFAYETTE PARISH, La. (Gray News) - A sheriff’s deputy is being credited with rescuing a nonverbal child who had wandered into a Louisiana pond.
On the evening of Sept. 6, Lafayette Parish sheriff’s deputies responded to the 200 block of Blushing Groom Drive in unincorporated Carencro after an 8-year-old non-speaking child with autism had been reported missing. While en route, deputies were told the child had been found but was seen entering a nearby pond.
When deputies arrived, bystanders were gathered around the bank as the child went underwater.
Recognizing immediate danger to the child, Cpl. Jared Havard entered the neck-deep water while wearing full duty attire. Havard reached the child and brought her safely to the bank, where she was reunited with her family.
