title: Will Maine college students, motivated by crucial Senate race, choose to vote here?
text:
BRUNSWICK — On a crisp October morning, a group of Bowdoin College students grabbed free lattes and hot chocolate from a campus coffee shop and took a brief walk into town.
The Sip and Stroll, one of many events run by the nonpartisan election engagement group Bowdoin Votes, was designed to lead students on the short walk down to Brunswick Town Hall to cast their ballots.
As Nov. 3 approaches, college students have to choose not just for whom they want to vote but also where they should cast their ballot. Like most Bowdoin students, none of those strolling Tuesday morning grew up in Maine — they hailed from Colorado, Alabama, Connecticut and Massachusetts — but they’re all choosing to vote here this fall.
“I felt like my vote would have more of an impact here than it would in Alabama,” said 19-year-old Isa Alvidrez.
“It’s a much more challenging race,” Caden Christopher, 18, from Connecticut said. “I’m generally not a ‘vote blue no matter who’ person, but I think in the immediate, it’s important that Democrats get control of the Senate.”
They were referring, of course, to the high-profile matchup between Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson, where candidates are fighting for the small number of undecided voters who will determine whether Collins gets a sixth term.
Caroline Pippert, a visiting professor of political science at Bowdoin who studies young voter behavior, said how competitive a race is can be a major factor in where students choose to vote, especially in one with as much national recognition and campaign spending as Maine’s senate contest.
“All of these first-year students that didn’t live in Maine yet had likely heard about this race before they even moved here,” Pippert said.
While young voters, especially men, turned toward Trump in the 2024 presidential election, polls show them likely swinging back to the left in these midterms. Amid the closely watched tossup Senate races around the country, including those in Ohio, Michigan and Kansas, young voter turnout could make a big difference.
That could be especially true in Maine, which has one of the most active youth voting populations in the country. During the 2022 midterms, 35.7% of 18 to 29-year-olds in the state voted, well above the national average of 23% and behind only Michigan, according to data from the Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement at Tufts.
Pippert said in times where young people increasingly feel pessimistic about the efficacy of politics, it’s hard to tell how young voters will act. Will the dissatisfaction result in a boost in turnout? Will it mean young people stay home? Could it cause a shift in which party they support?
“The common thread is frustration, and it will be interesting to see how that frustration manifests,” she said.
WHAT DO POLLS SAY?
Political polls offer a little insight into how the youth voting bloc might turn out.
A New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll from late September showed 19 to 24-year-olds leaning slightly toward Jackson — but it didn’t survey enough respondents to be statistically significant. The same was true of an early October Washington Post poll and a more recent survey by Suffolk University, both of which showed Jackson performing well among young voters.
A national poll of 18 to 29-year-olds from the spring showed them favoring Democrats, and found economic pressures to be the biggest issue for young voters. Nearly 60% said the country seems to be on the wrong track. A New York Times analysis released Thursday showed young voters moving 15 points to the left since the 2024 election.
Representatives of both major parties in Maine declined interviews about their young voter outreach, but shared statements. Kristina Parker, communications director for the Maine Republican Party and a Gen-Z voter herself, said that the biggest thing motivating young people in the state to vote is the cost of their electricity bills.
“Maine Democrats have controlled the state legislature for 48 out of the last 50 years, and the invoices for their outrageous policies are landing in young people’s hands,” Parker said. “Young voters can’t afford a house in Maine, let alone bankroll leftist wasteful spending from Augusta Democrats.”
The Maine Democratic Party’s deputy organizing director, Reese Remington, said in a statement that the party has reached young voters through its campus organizing program.
“Young Mainers have a critical voice in this election and they know better than anyone that to have an affordable future in Maine, Susan Collins must go,” Remington said.
Pippert said young voters are generally issues-focused, and the most concerning issue currently is affordability. Young voter turnout is always lower than older groups, especially in midterms, and peaked in 2018 at 28%, she said.
ON CAMPUS
Like Bowdoin, the state’s public flagship University of Maine has a nonpartisan elections group called UMaine UVote.
UVote student ambassadors Cecilia Pike and Justine Ordinario help students deal with the logistics of voting and show them that it’s easy to register and cast a ballot.
“On our campus, I’d definitely say that I’ve seen a lot of people be extremely passionate about this election,” said Pike, 19, from Jay. “And the people that we talk to that are registered to vote, they are passionate about other people registering, because they understand the weight of their vote in these elections.”
The Senate race has sparked a lot of discussion and controversy at UMaine, said Ordinario, a 21-year-old from Nevada. As a nonpartisan group, UVote doesn’t lead those conversations. “But we are able to facilitate where they can get their information and lead those discussions to a healthy place, that can ultimately lead to: ‘Vote in the election, and get your voice out there,'” she said.
On the UMaine campus in early September, students said they were generally aware of and planning to vote in the election. At the time, about two months out from the midterms, many said they would need to do more research and get informed before casting their ballots — it was not long after the Democratic party had switched its nominee from Graham Platner to Jackson.
“There’s a lot of information that’s come out recently, and I feel like by the time it actually gets to November, I may not feel the way I feel now,” said Aden Barnes, an 18-year-old environmental science student from Brunswick. Barnes said the biggest issues for her are reproductive rights, women’ s healthcare and LGBTQ healthcare.
Quinn Chessa, 21, a food science major originally from Oregon, said he’d been planning to cast a ballot for Platner, and that Jackson would likely now get his vote.
Although enrolled as a Democrat, Chessa said he prefers to think of himself as unaligned with either party. And he’s increasingly concerned about a lack of productivity in politics, and the value of voting.
“As a voter, I do feel really quite disconnected,” he said. “Does my vote actually make any change?”
HERE OR THERE?
Unlike UMaine, where 64% of students are from in-state, some of Maine’s smaller liberal arts colleges attract a politically engaged but mostly out-of-state population. Just 11% of Bowdoin students, 10% of Bates students and 8% of Colby students are from Maine.
College students have the right to vote where they go to school, and thanks to Maine’s same-day voter registration, it’s an easy option. But students are divided on the ethics.
Dueling op-eds from Colby students recently ran in the Press Herald’s opinion pages, debating the merits of voting in a hometown or in Waterville.
Junior Cleo Rehkopf, arguing that her peers should vote at home, said casting her ballot in the city she’ll soon leave would effectively be “diluting the vote” of locals who will live with the election’s consequences. Senior Anthony Simescu, writing in opposition, said treating student participation in local elections as a distortion assumes that a town “belongs only to those who never leave” even though many Americans are mobile throughout their lives.
Some towns have embraced student participation. In Orono, where UMaine is located, voters decided in 2024 to move municipal elections from March to November so that more students could participate (the previous date often fell during the university’s spring break.)
The Bowdoin Votes coordinators, Amelia Kane and Caroline Clinton, both 21 and seniors from Massachusetts, are agnostic. “Our headline is vote,” Clinton said. “And wherever you want to vote, we’re happy to support you,” Kane added.
Their organization leads the walks to the polls, but also helps students get their absentee ballots for their hometowns. This year, they’ve registered 287 students and provided more than 65 with absentee ballot support.
It’s a little quieter this year than the 2024 presidential election, they said, but students are pretty informed on the names and issues. The challenge is getting students to prioritize making time to do it.
According to early voting data, in the Waterville ward that covers Colby College, about 7.4% of voters have submitted their ballot already. The UMaine-specific precinct in Orono saw just four early votes returned by Oct. 16. The town of Brunswick splits Bowdoin into three different voting districts, so it’s difficult to determine early voting numbers there.
Pippert said the biggest factors country-wide that influence where a college student votes are institutional ones — like same-day registration, whether a student ID counts as identification or how challenging it is to get an absentee ballot. (In Maine, identification is not required at the polls.)
It also matters to students that they feel politically informed.
“College students think really heavily about this,” Pippert said. “And it’s not just something they’re doing on a whim.”
When the Bowdoin students strolled to Town Hall on Tuesday, they were greeted warmly by poll workers, excited to see young people voting, and voting early. At the booths, Kane carried a list of all of the student dorm street addresses: Bowdoin students get their mail to a box in the student center, but need their physical address to vote, which many don’t know offhand.
Kane said she has a close relationship with the town clerk’s office, which is a big supporter of Bowdoin Votes and their initiatives. But the question of where to vote still belongs within each individual.
“Am I voting in Maine because the race is more interesting or because I feel more connected to Maine?” Kane said. “For me, it’s definitely a mix of both.”
Staff Writer Ethan Horton contributed to this report.

title: VCS short staffed especially educational technicians
text:
Vassalboro Community School is short of staff, especially educational technicians.
And so are many other Maine schools, Superintendent Ray Grogan told school board and audience members at their half-hour-long Oct. 13 board meeting.
Administrators described problems created and attempts to resolve them as they try to hire more people to fill vacancies.
Board members approved some appointments, including an in-house social worker and a school nurse; they accepted a larger number of resignations, including at least three educational technicians.
Meanwhile, Principal Tabitha Brewer said, despite the problems, “really great things are happening” as the new school year continues. She reported on class trips, awards and other events, like Custodian Appreciation Day, when student-made “cards, signs and posters” were delivered to the custodians’ office.
The Oct. 13 agenda included the usual updated policies presented for board approval (a long list of policies is on the vcsvikings website under School Board).
Basketball coach needed
Unless the Vassalboro Community School finds a junior varsity basketball coach soon, there will be no JV team this year, Principal Tabitha Brewer says.
The coach need not be affiliated with the school; he or she need not even live in Vassalboro. School personnel will do their best to adjust practice times to fit a new coach’s schedule, though they cannot change the game schedule.
Applicants for the post will be interviewed and screened, and must pass the state Department of Education’s CHRC (Criminal History Record Check). Brewer will help any applicant who has not already passed CHRC learn about it.
VCS is at 1116 Webber Pond Road, in Vassalboro. Anyone interested in the coaching position there is invited to call the school at 207-923-3100, or email tbrewer@vcsvikings.org.
Unfinished business included plans to enlarge the driveway, to allow for more off-road parking as parents wait to pick up students in the afternoon. Grogan plans to meet with Vassalboro Codes Officer Eric Currie to find out what can be done and what town permits are needed.
The next Vassalboro School Board meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m., Tuesday, Nov. 10, in the school library.
There will be no school Tuesday, Nov. 3, because town voting will be in the school gymnasium. Polls are open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.

title: 3rd gas leak in a year at Gorham elementary school prompts investigation
text:
After resolving gas leaks in Narragansett Elementary School on Sunday, Gorham School District facilities staff and mechanics are investigating the root cause of the repeated issue. The leak is the third the school has experienced in the past year.
Superintendent Heather Perry said this week’s leak was identified when someone on the athletic field beside the school smelled gas on Sunday and reported it to the Gorham Fire Department at about 12:30 p.m. Maine Natural Gas found one large leak in a roof ventilator and two small leaks in exterior ventilators in modular classrooms.
Maine Natural Gas staff shut the gas valves off Sunday and worked with mechanics from Johnson & Jordan to repair them Monday. Families were notified of the leak Sunday and school operated normally this week after staff determined the building was safe.
Two separate leaks within a month at Narragansett Elementary School late last year prompted evacuations and school to close for two days while staff dealt with the issues, which Perry said at the time were unrelated. One prior leak about two and a half years ago also prompted an evacuation.
Perry said the repetitious leaks have led staff to launch in-depth investigations to determine the root of the problem and identify how to fix it, and that the school department responds to all incidents quickly.
“We’re as concerned as anybody else might be that this … continues to repeat itself a little bit,” Perry said. “That’s why we’re focused a lot on the preventative maintenance side of things right now and trying to get to the bottom of it.”

title: The Cony-Gardiner football rivalry still means something in modern era
text:
GARDINER — For years, there was a kind of finality that the Cony-Gardiner football rivalry game provided. That’s not the case this year — just ask the Tigers.
With Class C teams playing nine regular season games this year, Friday’s battle with the Rams at Hoch Field will not be the finale for Gardiner. Instead, the Tigers will host Greely for senior night Oct. 30 before the playoffs begin the following week.
It’s a peculiar place for Gardiner to be in this rivalry. The Tigers have clinched a playoff berth, but at 3-4, there’s only so far they can move up in the standings. They’re also banged up, and further injuries could seriously threaten their depth. So, how much does Gardiner want to stake Friday against Cony?
“There was zero hesitation from our kids — they’re all-in for this,” said Gardiner Pat Munzing. “It’s still the game; that’s where we start our schedule. There’s this buildup to it, and we’ve kind of had our eye on it the entire season. It’s still that important to both schools and both communities.”
That’s a sentiment that largely prevails with Gardiner and Cony as they prepare for the 148th installment of the state’s oldest rivalry at Hoch Field. The realities of the modern rivalry might be different, but this is still Tigers vs. Rams — and no matter the context, it’s still means everything.
A year ago, there was nothing standings-wise on the line for Cony as it entered this game. The dominant team in Class B North by a wide margin, the Rams had long clinched the No. 1 seed by the time Gardiner came to town. In the NFL, coach B.L. Lippert noted, a team might rest its starters in such a scenario.
Cony’s players, though, thought that was sacrilege. The Rams gave everything they had, beating a good Gardiner 54-10. Lippert recalled how receiver Ethan Demmons, one of his star players, insisted that he return from an injury to play the Tigers.
“He said, ‘Coach, I want to play to get a game under my belt, and I want to play against Gardiner,’” Lippert said. “From a Crabtree standpoint, we didn’t need to win that game, and we might have rested some (healthier) guys if it was a different team, but in Cony-Gardiner, you’re not going to rest guys if you can play them at all.”
Cony senior Anderson Noyes has a similar feeling this year. On Aug. 24, Noyes, the Rams’ star running back, broke his fibula in the team’s preseason scrimmage against Leavitt. All along, Noyes has been targeting a late-season return — a return sweetened by this game’s historic significance.
“Absolutely (that’s a factor); we love playing Gardiner — we love ‘em, but we hate ‘em,” said Noyes, who returned last week against Brunswick. “The doctor put me at eight weeks, which was just in time for this week. My recovery went (well), and I drank my milk and ate my vitamins, and I was ready a week early.”
In some ways, Lippert said, this era’s Cony-Gardiner matchups do feel different. At Cony, he points out, the bonfires and pep rallies of Gardiner week are now vestiges of the past. The Rams, in the midst of one of their most successful eras historically, are also playing well beyond this game into the playoffs year after year.
Lippert acknowledged Cony’s staff doesn’t spend much time discussing the the rivalry’s history with players, he knows many of them are reminded of it this week through their parents and grandparents. Munzing said Gardiner does talk about the history, and his players seem to understand it.
“It feels like you’re a part of something,” the Tigers’ Dominic Webber, a senior wide receiver and defensive back, said of the game’s significance. “Everyone wants to play in this game. … All that matters is beating them.”
The rivalry, like most others, has ebbed and flowed over the years. The 1920s, 1930s and 1940s belonged to Cony, while Gardiner dominated the ’80s and ’90s under John Wolfgram and Rob Munzing, Pat’s father. These days, the Rams are back on top, having won seven straight games and 12 of the past 13 against the Tigers.

title: Woman accused of intentionally crashing into oncoming semi, killing 73-year-old passenger
text:
PIKE COUNTY, Ill. (WGEM/Gray News) — An Illinois woman has been arrested on first-degree murder charges following a July crash that investigators allege was intentional.
Pike County Sheriff David Greenwood said deputies responded July 24 at 7:54 p.m. to a head-on collision between a passenger car and a semitruck pulling a trailer on U.S. 54 near the top of Atlas Hill.
Three occupants in the passenger vehicle were injured and taken to a hospital, Greenwood said.
One of those passengers, 73-year-old Cherie Wells of Pittsfield, later died from her injuries in St. Louis County, Missouri.
Deputies determined during the investigation that the driver, identified as Jaime Rhode of Griggsville, purposely steered in front of the oncoming semi with the intent to kill all occupants in her vehicle, Greenwood said.
An arrest warrant was signed Friday charging Rhode with two counts of first-degree murder and one count of attempted first-degree murder.
Rhode was arrested Tuesday and booked in the Pike County Jail.

title: Sen. Susan Collins visits young entrepreneurs in Farmington
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FARMINGTON — U.S. Sen. Susan Collins visited the Center for Entrepreneurial Studies on Main Street where young entrepreneurs eagerly showed off their creations, shared their business ideas and received encouragement from the senator.
Collins toured the nonprofit’s makerspace and retail shop on Tuesday, stopping to speak with children about their projects and the skills they had learned. She admired their handmade products and purchased jewelry created by Elucia Seaberg, 15, a high school junior who hopes to participate in the U.S. Senate Page Program. Seaberg showed Collins her jewelry collection, explaining her creations as the senator examined the pieces before making her purchase.
Gracie Guay, 16, who has participated in CES for approximately two years, assisted Collins behind the counter. Guay has been developing retail, customer service and business skills through the program.
The visit was an exciting occasion for the children and volunteers, who welcomed Collins and accompanied her through the facility.
Collins encouraged the young entrepreneurs to never give up on their dreams, pointing to her own journey from Caribou High School to the U.S. Senate as an example of what determination and perseverance can accomplish.
Other young entrepreneurs who met with Collins included Ian House, Aero Keim and Kaylynn Greenman. The students gathered around a table with the senator to discuss their projects and experiences at CES.
Founded in 2018 by former Mt. Blue High School business teacher Bonita Tompkins, the Center for Entrepreneurial Studies provides hands-on entrepreneurship and workforce training for young people ages 10 to 24. According to the organization, CES has served 193 young people since opening, offering its programs at no cost to participants and their families. Its Main Street location features a retail shop where participants sell their creations and a makerspace where they develop products and learn practical skills.
The makerspace received support from a $25,000 Maine Community Foundation grant, helping the organization expand opportunities for participants to create and market their own products.
Collins also helped secure $250,000 in federal funding in fiscal year 2023 that supported a year of planning, completed in spring 2025, for a proposed six-acre youth entrepreneurship campus on Whittier Road in Farmington. Plans include a marketplace, teaching kitchen, community and coworking center, and outdoor learning space.
Collins’ visit gave young entrepreneurs a chance to showcase their creations, share their ambitions and receive encouragement as they continue developing their businesses.

title: Hannaford, Maine community colleges partner to expand food access for students
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hannaford, Maine community colleges partner to expand food access for students
An estimated 41% of college students experience food insecurity
Hannaford, Maine community colleges partner to expand food access for students
An estimated 41% of college students experience food insecurity
Hannaford Supermarkets and the Foundation for Maine’s Community Colleges are partnering to expand access to food resources for college students across Maine.
The organizations announced plans Wednesday to invest in efforts to provide fresh, nutritious food and reduce barriers to accessing food assistance at the state’s seven community college campuses and beyond.
The announcement came during an event at Southern Maine Community College, where students, staff and volunteers stocked the campus’s Captain’s Cupboard pantry with staple foods.
An estimated 41% of college students experience food insecurity, according to information provided by the organizations.
Organizers said the effort aims to make food resources more accessible and help students feel comfortable seeking assistance.
“We all face different barriers, and it’s really important that everybody feels comfortable accessing all the resources,” SMCC President Kristen Miller said. “So just making it really just part of us is part of who we are is really important.”
The partnership is intended to expand food access across Maine’s community college system and beyond.

title: 68-year-old woman killed by stray bullet while sitting on her back porch, family says
text:
GASTONIA, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A 68-year-old woman was shot and killed while sitting on the back porch of her North Carolina home on Monday, according to her family.
The deadly shooting happened late in the afternoon on Oct. 19, at the Dwell Townhomes on Hillgate Avenue in Gastonia.
The family of Pamela Shanks told WBTV that Shanks was sitting on her porch, which backs up to Laurel Lane, when the fatal shots were fired. The family said the shooting may have involved a dispute between others in the neighborhood.
Neighbors told WBTV they heard several shots late Monday afternoon, then saw multiple young people run away in black clothing.
Gastonia police confirmed Shanks was not the intended target of the shooting on Laurel Lane and died after being hit by a stray bullet.
Investigators remained at the townhomes for hours Monday, roping off a large portion of the complex, including a playground. Police are working to determine how many people fired guns and who the intended target was.
As of Tuesday afternoon, no arrests had been made.
“Half of my heart was just like, it was folded and I don’t know which way to go and it hurts so bad,” Shanks’ niece, who asked to to remain, said in a phone call with WBTV Tuesday.
The shooting has left Shanks’ family heartbroken and pleading for justice.
“She was the light. She made everybody laugh. She made jokes. It’s just like now we won’t see that part of her no more, because someone took her life over some dummy stuff. So it’s just like, I’m still in shock,” the niece said.
Shanks’ niece also had a message Tuesday for anyone who fires a gun recklessly.
“I just want them to think, it’s consequences behind what you do. Anything you do dealing with killing somebody, shooting a gun. I don’t care if you’re just shooting in the air, it’s consequences behind that,” she said.

title: Waterville man arrested after throwing knives at police during standoff
text:
WATERVILLE — An hourslong standoff Tuesday night ended when Waterville police officers negotiated with a suspect who threatened to harm them.
When officers located the Waterville man around 6 p.m. on Autumn Street, he refused to open the door to his apartment and threatened to kill officers with a firearm, Maj. Jason Longley wrote in a news release.
Members of the police department’s crisis negotiating and critical response teams set up a perimeter around the apartment and negotiated with him for several hours.
The suspect still refused to leave his apartment, and threw knives at officers around the perimeter, Longely wrote. At around 11 p.m., the Maine State Police Tactical Team arrived to assist the Waterville officers and spent another hour negotiating with the man.
The state police troopers took him into custody without incident around midnight.
Officers took the man to MaineGeneral Medical Center in Augusta with minor injuries from a prior accident, and then to Kennebec County jail.
He is charged with aggravated reckless conduct and criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon, and misdemeanors of terrorizing, refusing to submit to arrest or detention and creating a police standoff.
He is scheduled to appear in court Dec. 28 at the Capital Judicial Center in Augusta.

Ashland woman arrested on arson charges
text:
ASHLAND, Maine (WAGM) - The Maine Fire Marshal’s Office announced the arrest of an Ashland woman following an investigation into two intentionally set fires involving neighboring residential properties on Frenchville Road in Ashland.
On Oct. 10, 2026, the Ashland Police Department responded to 1158 Frenchville Road for a reported ongoing criminal mischief complaint. Officers located 26-year-old Brooke Robinson of Ashland at the property. Robinson was arrested and given a summons for criminal mischief.
On Oct. 13, 2026, the Ashland Police Department contacted the Fire Marshal’s Office requesting assistance after additional information was developed during the initial investigation.
Fire damage found at both properties
Investigators identified fire damage to the exterior of the residence at 1158 Frenchville Road. Following an examination of the damage, Fire Marshal investigators determined the fire was incendiary in nature, having been intentionally set by holding an open flame against the exterior siding of the residence.
Investigators determined Robinson was also responsible for setting fires at 1164 Frenchville Road, a neighboring property, before proceeding to 1158 Frenchville Road.
Investigators identified two separate areas of fire damage at 1164 Frenchville Road. Both areas were also determined to be incendiary in nature, with the damage caused by an open flame being held against the exterior siding and insulation materials.
Arrest warrant issued
Following the investigation, the case was submitted to the Aroostook County District Attorney’s Office, and an arrest warrant was issued charging Robinson with two counts of arson.
On Oct. 20, 2026, Fire Marshal investigators, with assistance from the Presque Isle Police Department, arrested Robinson. Robinson was transported to the Aroostook County Jail.
The Fire Marshal’s Office acknowledged the assistance of the Ashland Police Department and Presque Isle Police Department throughout the investigation and arrest.

title: Biddeford City Council unanimously blocks city workers from cooperating with ICE
text:
The Biddeford City Council unanimously voted Tuesday night to approve an ordinance prohibiting city employees from cooperating with federal immigration officers.
The ordinance was proposed last month, and all nine councilors showed support for it at a first reading on Oct. 6.
The council’s approval of the ordinance comes about three months after Biddeford resident Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was shot and killed by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer at the intersection of Hill and Pool streets. City, state and federal leaders, as well as Durán Guerrero’s family, have called for a transparent investigation into his killing.
“I think for us to be reviewing this forces us to face an unpleasant truth,” Councilor Jake Pierson said on Oct. 6. “Someone was killed in our streets, unjustly.”
Biddeford’s ordinance is modeled after bylaws set by cities like Portland and Lewiston, which both passed similar ordinances limiting city employees and resources from cooperating with ICE. The state also has its own protections in place, including a law that went into effect in July limiting police coordination with federal immigration agencies.
At the Oct. 6 council meeting, City Attorney Harry Center said Biddeford police already don’t cooperate with ICE, but an ordinance strictly prohibiting all city employees from interacting with federal immigration agencies would strengthen the city’s approach.
The ordinance also prohibits city employees from requesting information about residents’ citizenship or immigration status.
“Ordinances are not for today’s people. We know (police) Chief (Jo-Ann) Fisk is at the top of her game. We know that we went through a horrific event in this city,” Pierson said on Oct. 6. “But 10 years from now, there may be no one on this council who lived here today.”
The ordinance will go into effect on Nov. 19, 30 days after its approval.

title: ‘Wonderland of Rocks' is officially the nation's newest national park
text:
‘Wonderland of Rocks' is officially the nation's newest national park
Chiricahua National Monument is now officially Chiricahua National Park, after President Donald Trump signed the Chiricahua National Park Act into law on Oct. 20.
The change follows a yearslong effort to redesignate the protected rugged mountain landscape in southeastern Arizona.
The Senate passed the bipartisan Chiricahua National Park Act on Sept. 30.
“Chiricahua’s towering rock spires, rich Apache heritage and remarkable biodiversity make it one of America’s most extraordinary landscapes,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum following the announcement. “This new designation will shine a national spotlight on one of Arizona’s hidden gems, creating opportunities to welcome more visitors, strengthen local economies and share this incredible landscape with more Americans.”
Chiricahua joins the Grand Canyon, the Petrified Forest and Saguaro as Arizona’s fourth national park.
Chiricahua is best known for its "Wonderland of Rocks," a maze of tall pinnacles, columns and balanced boulders.
"The area supports remarkable biodiversity and provides opportunities for hiking, wildlife viewing, birding and stargazing," the National Park Service said.
The formations began as volcanic ash and debris from a massive eruption about 27 million years ago, then took shape as the rock fractured and eroded.
The Chiricahua Mountains rise above surrounding desert grasslands and support a varied mix of plants and wildlife.
First established as a national monument by President Calvin Coolidge in 1924, Chiricahua was the homeland of the Chiricahua Apache and was later settled by early homesteading families at Faraway Ranch.
“While its name is changing, our commitment remains the same: protecting this remarkable landscape and its cultural heritage while providing opportunities for visitors to experience and enjoy it for generations to come," said Jessica Bowron, comptroller at the National Park Service.
A national park is generally established by Congress to protect a broad landscape, while a national monument is designated to protect a nationally significant resource. A national park label typically brings more visitors and economic opportunities.
The last new national park was designated in 2020, as West Virginia's New River Gorge National River was renamed New River Gorge National Park and Preserve.

title: 78-year-old priest unable to walk carried out of ICE facility by fellow detainees
text:
78-year-old priest unable to walk carried out of ICE facility by fellow detainees
A 78-year-old Ugandan priest who spent more than a year in immigration detention was released from a Colorado facility Tuesday, but he was unable to walk out on his own.
Cameras captured two fellow detainees carrying Edward Nalwamba from an ICE detention facility operated by private prison corporation GEO to his ride after staff reportedly refused to allow him to use a wheelchair beyond the facility's gate.
Nalwamba, who has lived in Colorado for more than two decades, was released after a federal judge granted his petition challenging his continued detention and ordered immigration officials to free him by Tuesday.
His release comes after 13 months in ICE custody, during which his attorney says his health deteriorated dramatically.
"I was walking. I was exercising. I was playing ping pong," Nalwamba said shortly after his release, describing his physical condition before he was detained in September 2025.
Now, he says he cannot walk without assistance. Nalwamba told CBS Colorado that staff initially brought him toward the facility's exit in a wheelchair, but would not allow him to take it the rest of the way to his transportation.
"They get me outside and say we can't go beyond this," Nalwamba explained. "And I'm asking, 'Can't the car come here?' They say, 'No.' I say, 'So how am I going to get the car?'"
Nalwamba said two other detainees stepped in and offered to carry him. He knew one of the men from his housing unit but said he did not know the other.
"Those friends offered to carry me, and, I mean, I'm so grateful to them," he said.
The circumstances of his release have drawn criticism from Colorado U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper.
In a social media post Tuesday, Hickenlooper said members of his staff visited the detention center earlier in the day and specifically requested that GEO staff allow Nalwamba to call his caretakers before his release and provide a wheelchair to take him to his ride home.
The senator said GEO staff assured his office that both requests would be honored.
"They failed to deliver on either," Hickenlooper wrote. "No phone call. No wheelchair. No human decency."
Hickenlooper called the incident an act of cruelty and pledged to continue holding those responsible accountable.
CBS Colorado reached out to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security seeking an explanation for the wheelchair restrictions, the circumstances surrounding Nalwamba's release and allegations concerning his medical treatment.
DHS responded to CBS Colorado with this statement: "On September 18, 2025, ICE arrested Edward Nkugwa Kironde Nalwamba, an illegal alien from Uganda, in Lakewood, Colorado. Nalwamba legally entered the country on January 1, 2002, but chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws. He was granted voluntary departure by an immigration judge on March 2, 2007, and still refused to depart. On June 2, 2009, the Board Immigration Appeals dismissed his appeal and on April 8, 2010, following a dismissal of his appeal in the 10th Circuit, he was issued a final order of removal. On October 20, ICE was forced to release Nalwamba after an activist judge ordered his release. He remains in the country illegally."
Nalwamba's attorney, Joy Athanasiou, says her client entered into ICE custody in good health but has experienced serious medical problems while detained.
"When he came to the detention center a year ago, he was extremely healthy. He was very fit. He exercised regularly. He could do 15 to 20 push-ups. Now, he is wheelchair-bound. He is extremely weak," Athanasiou said.
Athanasiou said Nalwamba was diagnosed with pneumonia in January, lost more than 30 pounds and collapsed while detained. She also says he has suffered from an ongoing respiratory illness since June, and accuses ICE of failing to provide adequate testing and treatment.
Nalwamba described experiencing chest pain, coughing, dizziness and weakness in his legs.
His attorney says his supporters are working to arrange a medical appointment and hope he can begin physical therapy and rehabilitation.
In a statement provided to CBS Colorado in June, the Department of Homeland Security defended the medical care available to people in ICE custody.
"It is a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody," a DHS spokesperson said. According to the agency, that includes access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care.
Nalwamba previously served as a priest at Resurrection Anglican Fellowship in Greenwood Village for approximately 15 years. He arrived in the United States from Uganda in 2002 and remained in the country after his tourist visa expired.
Nalwamba and his supporters have said he fears returning to Uganda because of persecution connected to his pro-democracy political activities.
In its June statement, DHS said Nalwamba had overstayed his visa, was granted voluntary departure in 2007 and received a final order of removal in 2010. ICE detained him on Sept. 18, 2025.
Before that arrest, Nalwamba says he had been living under an immigration order of supervision.
His attorneys challenged his prolonged detention through a federal habeas corpus petition, arguing the government could not continue holding him indefinitely.
Athanasiou says she is concerned that ICE could attempt to detain Nalwamba again.
On Monday, a judge granted the petition and ordered Nalwamba released no later than Oct. 20. Despite that ruling, his underlying immigration case remains unresolved.
"I am back to where I was when they first arrested me," Nalwamba said. "So I was asking myself, 'Why did they arrest me in the first place?'"

title: Maine needs Susan Collins to stay in the Senate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Timothy S. Hodgdon of East Boothbay is president and CEO of Hodgdon Group LLC. He is the fifth generation to run the Hodgdon shipbuilding business which began in 1816, four years before Maine became a state. The company has delivered a long line of notable boats over the years and to date has built over 475 vessels of all types.
As a business owner in Maine, I want to express my strong support for Sen. Susan Collins in the upcoming election. I am increasingly concerned that backlash from the current political landscape could result in what should otherwise be a strong race for Collins into a much more difficult contest in November.
Collins has served Maine for decades, and during that time she has consistently worked to bring federal resources and opportunities back to our state. Her seniority and experience in Washington, and particularly her position as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, give Maine an important voice and critical influence when decisions are made regarding federal funding and priorities. The Appropriations Committee plays a central role in determining discretionary federal spending, making this position particularly consequential for a state the size of Maine.
That influence has produced significant, tangible results for Maine, which cannot be delivered by an inexperienced U.S. Senate replacement. Her work has supported Bath Iron Works, the University of Maine, transportation and infrastructure projects, and hundreds of other initiatives throughout all 16 Maine counties. According to Collins’ office, she has helped secure nearly $1.5 billion in Congressionally Directed Spending for 672 projects since 2021.
I believe Maine voters need to look carefully at what Collins’ position in the Senate means for our state and what will be lost if she is no longer representing Maine in Washington.
The televised debates between Collins and Troy Jackson raise a fundamental question for me: How many times must Collins correct the record before those corrections are given their due?
Throughout these debates, she has repeatedly addressed Jackson’s claims, which I believe are disingenuous, about her position on the Iran war, her voting record on the One Big Beautiful Bill, and her relationship with Donald Trump (among other questionable statements). She has explained that she voted nine times to end the Iran war, defended her decision to oppose the Big Beautiful Bill at final passage, and challenged what she considers misleading characterizations of her relationship with the president. Yet Jackson frequently returns to the same accusations, seemingly disregarding the explanations and responses she has already provided.
Vigorous debate and legitimate criticism are essential to our political process. But voters deserve more than repeated allegations and selective interpretations of a candidate’s record. They deserve a fair opportunity to hear the answers, consider the context, and judge the facts for themselves. When a candidate responds directly to an accusation, that response should be part of the discussion — not simply brushed aside as the same accusation is repeated.
The real issue is not whether Collins’s record should be scrutinized; it absolutely should be. It is whether that scrutiny is being conducted fairly, accurately, and with due regard for the facts. Maine voters deserve a debate that informs rather than misleads, and that evaluates candidates on their complete records rather than on accusations repeated often enough to create an impression.
It is also significant that Collins is the only Republican in either the U.S. House of Representatives or the U.S. Senate from New England, which I believe results in an unhealthy partisan position, regardless of your party affiliation. Replacing her with a first-term senator would represent a substantial loss of seniority, institutional knowledge, leadership, and demonstrated ability to secure federal resources, an outcome that we cannot afford.
To say it frankly, I believe there is no opponent who can fill Collins’ shoes as our senator from Maine. Her record, experience, and performance all speak for themselves; Maine needs her to stay in the Senate.

title: Art center presents film series with latest exhibition in Rockland
text:
The Center for Maine Contemporary Art and Rockland’s Strand Theatre will present a three-part film series in conjunction with “Because the Sky is Blue,” on view at CMCA through Jan. 17, 2027. Bringing together three distinct approaches to filmmaking, the series extends the exhibition’s exploration of painting and its boundaries into the medium of film.
The first screening is at 5 p.m. Sunday. The featured film will be Derek Jarman’s “Blue” (1993), his final film. It’s a deeply personal and formally daring meditation on memory, love, mortality and the expressive possibilities of color. Created during the final years of Jarman’s life, as he confronted AIDS-related illness and deteriorating vision, the film challenges conventional ideas of what cinema can communicate through images.
The screening will be introduced by and followed by a Q&A with Tom Sapsford, associate professor in classical studies at Boston College, whose research includes Jarman’s engagement with classical antiquity and gay counterculture.
The second in the series, “Double Tide” (2009) by Sharon Lockhart, will be shown at 5 p.m. on Nov. 1. The film documents the work of a female clam digger on the mudflats of Midcoast Maine. Filmed during the rare occurrence of two daylight low tides, the film offers a portrait of a singular form of labor defined by the elemental forces of nature. Lockhart’s work is also featured in “Because the Sky is Blue.”
The event will include an introduction by CMCA Curator and Interim Director Grant Wahlquist.
The third and final screening is at 12:30 p.m. on Nov. 8. This is a special family-friendly screening of Albert Lamorisse’s short film “The Red Balloon” (1956), following a young boy and a spirited red balloon through the streets of Paris. After the screening, attendees are invited to CMCA’s ArtLab to create and decorate their own hanging paper balloon sculptures.
All film screenings are at Strand Theatre, 345 Main St., Rockland. Visit rocklandstrand.com for tickets.

title: Obituary: James Stearns Gates
text:
AUBURN – James Stearns Gates, Jim to friends and family, 75, of Waterville, passed away on Oct. 13, 2026, after a dignified 10-year journey with Alzheimer’s.
At ease at his place of serenity, Lake Pennesseewassee in Norway, Maine, he was a passionate and avid water skier and kayaker in earlier times. Yet, in life, he was not the sort to create a wake. Rather, his quiet manner, kindness, thoughtfulness and grace rippled wherever he went – and he indelibly touched peoples’ hearts. He gave freely and, more than most, expressed heartfelt appreciation for the kindness of others. He was genuinely grateful for the many family, friends and care givers that helped him manage the tragedies of his illness since diagnosis in 2017, especially those at his final station, Schooner Memory Care in Auburn.
Born in Weston, Mass. to Lloyd Stearns Gates of West Paris, Maine and Loretta Hassall Gates of Queens, NY, Jim graduated from Weston High School and then went on to earn degrees in architecture and education from Vermont Technical College and University of Southern Maine. His career passion was serving and educating young adults. He modeled the way for them to lead kind, courteous, impacting lives.
Jim taught architecture and drafting at Lawrence High School, Fairfield, Maine for 30 years and left his mark as a regular class advisor, inveterate cheerleader, co-chair of accreditation and the founder of Project Graduation – establishing a safe and fun environment for celebration on graduation night. Over the years, many of his students noted the extra care, mentoring, and guidance he provided, beyond the daily lesson plans, to help them navigate the challenges of adolescence. He also served as counselor and water-skiing instructor for many summers at Camp Chickawah in Harrison, Maine.
Leaning in on his training and a keen eye for architectural detail, he completed hundreds of designs for building and home construction projects during his lifetime. His most visible work included expansions to the Christ Episcopal and Second Congregational churches in Norway, Maine. Also, inspired by the work of Gustav Stickley, he acquired a 1910 craftsman design bungalow needing restoration and turned it into a showpiece of the style, including curated finishes, fixtures, furniture, and appointments.
An enduring interest in antique cars started in high school when he acquired a 1955 Chevy sedan for restoration. Later, he restored a 1930 Packard pickup truck. But his ultimate pride and joy was the restoration of a rare model 1960 Corvette convertible – an attention grabber wherever he went. Oh, how he loved to take family and friends for a ride!
Jim was a beloved son, brother, cousin, uncle and friend. He is survived by his brothers, Richard and his wife Elizabeth (ne. Morton) of Bergen, NY, John and his wife Cherilyn (ne. Frost) of Towson, Md., and Steve of Lovell, Maine; a sister, Barbara Tinder and her husband James of Stoneham, Maine, sister-in-law Sharon (ne. McPhee) Gates of Peru, Maine; nephews Andy, Chris, Jeremy, Tyler and Nicholas Gates and Matt Tinder, and nieces Zoe Gates, Emily (Gates) Margolis, Lizz and Lisa Tinder, and Tara Oldham. He was preceded in death by his youngest brother Bill. All will miss Jim’s quick wit and dry, understated humor.
A celebration of Jim’s life and interment, yet to be scheduled, will be held in the Summer of 2027.
Jim leaves behind a legacy of gentlemanly kindness and caring for others. We live in the hope that the ripples he made during his life will endure.
Arrangements are under the care of Chandler Funeral Homes & Cremation Service, 45 Main Street, South Paris. Online condolences may be shared with his family at http://www.chandlerfunerals.com

title: Sen. Susan Collins visits young entrepreneurs in Farmington
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FARMINGTON — U.S. Sen. Susan Collins visited the Center for Entrepreneurial Studies on Main Street where young entrepreneurs eagerly showed off their creations, shared their business ideas and received encouragement from the senator.
Collins toured the nonprofit’s makerspace and retail shop on Tuesday, stopping to speak with children about their projects and the skills they had learned. She admired their handmade products and purchased jewelry created by Elucia Seaberg, 15, a high school junior who hopes to participate in the U.S. Senate Page Program. Seaberg showed Collins her jewelry collection, explaining her creations as the senator examined the pieces before making her purchase.
Gracie Guay, 16, who has participated in CES for approximately two years, assisted Collins behind the counter. Guay has been developing retail, customer service and business skills through the program.
The visit was an exciting occasion for the children and volunteers, who welcomed Collins and accompanied her through the facility.
Collins encouraged the young entrepreneurs to never give up on their dreams, pointing to her own journey from Caribou High School to the U.S. Senate as an example of what determination and perseverance can accomplish.
Other young entrepreneurs who met with Collins included Ian House, Aero Keim and Kaylynn Greenman. The students gathered around a table with the senator to discuss their projects and experiences at CES.
Founded in 2018 by former Mt. Blue High School business teacher Bonita Tompkins, the Center for Entrepreneurial Studies provides hands-on entrepreneurship and workforce training for young people ages 10 to 24. According to the organization, CES has served 193 young people since opening, offering its programs at no cost to participants and their families. Its Main Street location features a retail shop where participants sell their creations and a makerspace where they develop products and learn practical skills.
The makerspace received support from a $25,000 Maine Community Foundation grant, helping the organization expand opportunities for participants to create and market their own products.
Collins also helped secure $250,000 in federal funding in fiscal year 2023 that supported a year of planning, completed in spring 2025, for a proposed six-acre youth entrepreneurship campus on Whittier Road in Farmington. Plans include a marketplace, teaching kitchen, community and coworking center, and outdoor learning space.
Collins’ visit gave young entrepreneurs a chance to showcase their creations, share their ambitions and receive encouragement as they continue developing their businesses.

title: Russia releases imprisoned American man, US envoy Witkoff says on visit to St. Petersburg
text:
Russia releases imprisoned American man during visit by US envoy
Russia on Wednesday released an American who had been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, in a deal reached during a visit by a top U.S. envoy and at a time when President Donald Trump has taken a series of actions meant to benefit Moscow.
The White House said Trump had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin during a phone call last week to free Stephen Hubbard, and that, unlike previous releases, his had not required the U.S. to give up anyone in return.
“Welcome home, Stephen, it’s great to have you back,” Trump said in a Truth Social post that said Hubbard, a former teacher from Michigan, was on his way home following a visit to St. Petersburg by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff.
Hubbard was sentenced after a closed trial in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison. Prosecutors said he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, and that he fought alongside Kyiv's forces until being captured two months later. The U.S. government under the Biden administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained.
Witkoff, a key Trump administration envoy who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end a war that will hit the five-year mark in February 2027, thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, telling him, “Because of you, he's going home to his family.”
The Russian leader responded that Hubbard was at Pulkovo airport in St. Petersburg following the release.
The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship being roiled by fresh tensions at the same time that the Trump administration has advanced policies that aid Putin.
Those include Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine. Named after the late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Moscow’s war. That reversal followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections.
Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday. He was expected to exchange ideas from that meeting, as well as proposals from European and American colleagues, in his talks Wednesday with Russian leaders in St. Petersburg.
Hubbard is the second American freed by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of Marine veteran Robert Gilman, who had been gravely ill and was imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer.
Other Americans, including some with serious illnesses, remain jailed in Russia. Hubbard was the only one designated as wrongfully detained, although advocates say that label should be applied to other prisoners.
Global Reach, a group that works to free Americans detained abroad and currently represents five American held in Russia, praised the release but called for the other prisoners to come home as well.
“We are grateful to the Trump Administration for reuniting Stephen Hubbard with his family, but at the same time, we know that there are five other families of Americans held in Russia who are going to have a hard time understanding why their loved one was not included in the deal,” Eric Lebson, the group's chief strategy officer, said in a statement.
Hubbard had been imprisoned since 2022 on charges that Hostage Aid Worldwide, a hostage advocacy group, has called bogus.
The organization in August posted an open letter to Trump that it said was written by Patricia Hubbard Fox, Hubbard’s sister, in which she offered praise for Trump but also said her brother had been subjected to “constant beatings, torture and starvation” while in custody.
“Even so, everything that you’re doing isn’t going to matter to my kidnapped, American Veteran brother, Stephen James Hubbard (soon to be 74) if Putin won’t cave and let him come home and he dies up there in a Nazi prison (crying),” the letter said.
___
Tucker reported from Washington; Litvinova reported from Tallinn, Estonia.

title: Crews respond to house fire in Scarborough
text:
Five people safely escape Scarborough house fire on Spurwink Road
One firefighter was taken to a hospital to be treated for dehydration
Five people safely escape Scarborough house fire on Spurwink Road
One firefighter was taken to a hospital to be treated for dehydration
The Scarborough Fire Department says five people were able to safely escape a burning home Wednesday morning.
Officials said the homeowner of 100 Spurwink Road called 911 at about 6 a.m. to report that smoke was coming from a second-floor bedroom.
Crews arrived at the scene within 5 minutes of the call being placed and saw heavy smoke and flames coming from the second floor of the two-story house.
Scarborough firefighters called for mutual aid and members of the Cape Elizabeth Fire Department responded to the scene.
Firefighters were able to keep the fire contained to the second-floor bedroom. Officials said the fire was under control less than 30 minutes after crews arrived at the home.
The five people who were in the home when the fire started were able to safely evacuate before firefighters arrived. Officials said one of those people was evaluated by Scarborough Emergency Medical Services for possible smoke inhalation, but that person declined transport to a hospital.
One Scarborough firefighter was taken to an area hospital to be treated for dehydration and has since been released, officials said.
Investigators from the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office responded to the scene to help Scarborough firefighters with the fire investigation, and the investigators determined the fire was caused by an electrical issue.
Scarborough Code Enforcement said the home cannot be occupied until electrical repairs can be completed, according to officials.
Officials closed the section Spurwink Road between Ocean Avenue and Pleasant Hill Road for hours. The road was back open by 8:15 a.m.
The Scarborough Police Department and Central Maine Power also assisted firefighters at the scene. Firefighters from Saco, Biddeford, Old Orchard Beach and Gorham responded to Scarborough to help cover empty firehouses.

title: Feds issue warning for nearly 400,000 pressure cookers that could seriously burn you
text:
(CNN) - Federal safety officials are warning customers to stop using nearly 400,000 pressure cookers linked to serious burn injuries.
The Consumer Product Safety Commission says people should stop using Power Quick Pot 6-quart pressure cookers immediately and dispose of them.
Officials say the lids can open while the cookers are still pressurized, causing hot contents to shoot out. The agency has received 24 reports of the malfunction, resulting in serious burns.
The affected cookers were sold online on such sites as Walmart.com and Amazon.com and at retailers nationwide between 2018 and 2023.
The model number, which can be found on the back of the cookers, is Y6D-36.
Officials say the importer, Tristar Products, has refused to issue a recall or offer a remedy to customers.

title: Australian politician had both legs amputated after being repeatedly hit by a car
text:
MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — Doctors have amputated both of Australian federal lawmaker Helen Haines’ legs as she remains in critical condition after being repeatedly hit by a car in an apparent act of political violence, her husband said Wednesday.
The 65-year-old independent politician is receiving treatment in a Melbourne hospital where she was flown by helicopter.
Phil Haines, her husband, gave the family’s first public comments on her condition since she was hit by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV in her hometown of Wangaratta on Monday, speaking hours after a man accused of running her over made an initial appearance in court.
Husband says Haines has lost both her legs
Haines’ husband said her left leg was amputated on Monday and her right leg was amputated on Wednesday after doctors abandoned hope of saving it.
“The good news in all this is that Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family,” the husband told reporters in Melbourne.
“We are grateful and thankful that at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape,” he said.
He added that their 40th wedding anniversary will be in November.
Man accused of attack makes first appearance in court
Earlier Wednesday, Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old man from nearby Tarrawingee, appeared in the Wangaratta Magistrates’ Court charged with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.
Nugent didn’t apply for bail or enter a plea. He will remain in custody until his next court appearance in February. Police have yet to determine a motive.
Nugent’s lawyer Chirag Patel told Magistrate Allison Vaughan that his client was suffering from potential mental health issues but had never been diagnosed with any mental health problem.
Patel said Nugent suffered from a neurological condition, idiopathic transverse myelitis, and a concussion. The lawyer did not explain how Nugent had been concussed.
The rare condition damages the spinal cord’s protective myelin sheath and disrupts nerve signals between the brain and body. This leads to rapid muscle weakness, sensory loss, pain, and bladder and bowel dysfunction, according to the Cleveland Clinic medical center.
Witnesses say the driver rammed his victim, pinning her against her own car before reversing and ramming her a second time.
Australia worries about balancing security with keeping politicians accessible
The well-regarded lawmaker’s plight has shocked Australians, as political violence is uncommon in the country and politicians are highly accessible to the public. Most lawmakers are not accompanied by security details and go about their work and personal lives on their own.
Senior opposition lawmaker James Paterson on Wednesday called for a review of lawmakers’ personal security in response to the alleged crime.
“The reality is that Australian parliamentarians by global standards are uniquely accessible to the public and that’s a good thing,” Paterson told Australian Broadcasting Corp.
“But we … can’t have a situation where shocking attacks like this take place because that will fundamentally change our democracy forever if it becomes a serious risk to your life to be a member of parliament,” Paterson added.
But Prime Minister Anthony Albanese urged lawmakers to continue to engage openly with the public despite worsening animosity within the community.
“We want to make sure that people can feel as much comfort as possible that everything’s being done to maximize security,” Albanese told News24.
“I think parliamentarians across the board are determined to make sure that we can continue to engage as we need to in this great democracy of ours,” Albanese added. “That interaction is really important in our democracy.”
Security agencies brief lawmakers on personal security
Lawmakers began online meetings with Australia’s security agencies on Wednesday to discuss their safety. Such briefings are a regular occurrence.
Albanese described the briefings as an “opportunity for people who feel anxious to be able to ask questions” of security agencies.
Australian Federal Police provide personal security only to those lawmakers who are assessed as higher risk, usually because they have attracted the attention of dangerous people. Prime ministers always have personal protection and immigration ministers often do because they anger people with visa decisions.
Paterson said providing police protection to all 226 federal lawmakers would not be practical. But he suggested increased security at electorate offices, such as Haines’ office where she was hit. Paterson said lawmakers were “most identifiable” at their offices. Coming and going could be a “risky moment.”
Federal Police Commissioner Kissy Barrett told reporters providing police protection to all parliamentarians would take an “incredible amount of resourcing.”
Police received 1,067 reports of threatening, harassing, nuisance and offensive communications against high officeholders including federal lawmakers and their office staff in the last fiscal year — a 12% increase on the previous year. Barrett said almost one suspect a week was charged over such threats.
Australia hasn’t recorded the political violence seen in other countries
Elsewhere in the world, authorities have warned of growing threats to lawmakers. The United States has seen a rise in political violence over the past decade.
That includes the 2022 hammer assault on the husband of then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi; the 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump during his presidential campaign, as well as another on the president at the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner in April; and the assassinations in 2025 of a Democratic Minnesota state lawmaker and her husband, and of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk.
In Britain, killings of politicians have also led to tighter security. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, while Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the militant Islamic State group.
In July, the former British politician and reality TV contestant Ann Widdecombe was found beaten to death with a hammer at her home. A man has been charged with murder and terrorism-related offenses.
___
Graham-McLay reported from Wellington, New Zealand.

title: Patriots, Bears quarterbacks are no strangers to each other
text:
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — Caleb Williams and Drake Maye have known each other for years. They were part of the same draft class and grew up going to the same football camps.
Maye’s mobility, Williams said, always has been a weapon for him.
“We’ve got to be able to bottle him up,” he said.
Maye leads the New England Patriots into Soldier Field on Thursday night to take on Williams and the Chicago Bears in a matchup of two of the NFL’s top young quarterbacks. Both Maye and Williams have a big right arm and are also dangerous with their legs.
“I think Drake Maye’s one of those guys that does an outstanding job with his feet,” Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said. “There’s been times where you watch it and there’s pressure on the quarterback, and he makes people miss and creates some plays down the field.”
The 24-year-old Maye seems to have settled down after a rough start to the season. He has completed 64.1% of his passes for 878 yards and 10 touchdowns during New England’s three-game winning streak, throwing just one interception during the impressive stretch.
He could become the first Patriots quarterback since Tom Brady in 2014 to throw for at least three TDs in four consecutive games.
“It’s a dangerous combination of a guy that’s an elite deep-ball thrower along with he can crush you with his legs,” Bears coach Ben Johnson said. “I think that combination is deadly. It’s really picked up steam over these last three games.”
Maye was selected by New England with the No. 3 pick in 2024, two spots after Williams went No. 1 overall to Chicago.
Williams, who turns 25 on Nov. 18, missed three games because of a right hamstring injury before returning Sunday at Atlanta. He showed no signs of any rust, going 30 of 36 for 305 yards and a touchdown in a 31-23 victory over the Falcons.
“He’s special in the way he can move and kind of escape and evade pressure, and throwing on the run is pretty cool to watch,” Maye said. “So I don’t know if I’m that shifty in the pocket. He can do some cool things and he’s got crazy arm talent, and it’s fun to watch.”
Patriots safety Kevin Byard went up against Williams in practice during the previous two seasons with the Bears. He said Williams is an elite athlete who is tough to bring down in the pocket.
“I’ve been in this league long enough. I kind of know what the whole deal is gonna be,” Byard said. “Caleb versus Drake, obviously same draft class, two phenomenal quarterbacks. Drake’s been playing phenomenal, Caleb’s been playing phenomenal. So I think for us, it’s gonna be a 60-minute mental fight on both sides of the ball.”

Patriots WR A.J. Brown vs. Bears CB Jaylon Johnson. Brown is looking to bounce back after he had a rough game in his return from a high ankle sprain. He was targeted 10 times in Sunday’s win over the Jets, but dropped three balls and finished with just three catches for 27 yards. The Patriots are looking for more from Brown after acquiring him in a June 1 trade with the Eagles. Johnson and the Bears held the Falcons to 257 yards.

title: Rapper convicted of murdering woman, unborn child writes letter to judge asking for death penalty
text:
(Gray News) – A rapper from Tampa sent a letter to the judge presiding over his case asking for the death penalty.
Billy Adams, known as “Ace NH,” was convicted in September of the murder of 22-year-old Alana Sims and her unborn child, WTSP reported.
At the time, a jury recommended Adams be executed, but the official sentencing hearing is scheduled for Dec. 1.
Adams mailed a handwritten letter to Judge Mark Wolfe asking him to honor the jury’s decision.
“I want to waive mitigation at this hearing, and I want to be sentenced to what the jury voted to give me,” Adams wrote. “My lawyers explained mitigation to me and they explained the consequences of waiving mitigation.”
Adams went on to write that he understood what he was giving up and he doesn’t have an issue with the death penalty.
“I’m writing to put this on the record,” he said.
The letter concludes with Adams writing, “I have asked my lawyers to respect my wishes when we go to court.”
Just because Adams is requesting the death penalty doesn’t mean he will automatically be sentenced to death. A judge will decide that during the hearing in December.
Family members told WTSP Sims was five months pregnant when she was killed. She was found lying dead on the street in February 2023.
According to WTSP, the woman’s 1-year-old son was found unharmed, sleeping in an SUV next to her body.

title: New burger restaurant coming into former Taste of India in downtown Bangor
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new burger joint is set to open next month in downtown Bangor, in the Main Street storefront that formerly housed Taste of India.
The restaurant, called Burgers & Bad Decisions, will be open from early in the morning through late at night, catering to first responders and families and filling a gap for a downtown area with few food options at those hours.
Owner Shianne Levesque said she wants to create a relaxed, family-friendly atmosphere where people can grab something to eat before or after work, “Or if you’re with your kids and don’t feel like cooking, come on in and have something to eat as well.”
Levesque has managed other restaurants in the area and hopes to start welcoming customers into her own business in early November. She plans to open at 5 a.m. and close around midnight.
“It’s been something I’ve wanted to do for a while,” she said.
Levesque used to work at the Penobscot County Jail and said she remembers how difficult it was to finish up a long shift and look for a convenient place to eat a meal.
She envisions people bringing their kids to the restaurant for breakfast before school and also plans to offer a discount to first responders, law enforcement and veterans.
Besides staples like burgers and chicken tenders, Levesque’s menu will have breakfast foods like waffles and breakfast sandwiches all day, and everything on the menu will have a vegetarian option, she said. The restaurant will also offer signature drinks, and a non-alcoholic version of each.
“The bad decisions [name] is because it’s not a completely healthy menu, and we are a bar as well,” Levesque said. “A lot of our signature drinks are sweet and sugary, and a lot of our signature burgers are very loaded with stuff.”
Burgers & Bad Decisions will quickly fill a storefront that’s been empty for just a few weeks after Taste of India closed in the last week of September after its longtime owners announced their retirement.
Levesque said she chose the space at 68 Main St. because she liked that its relatively small size makes it feel comfortable and homey. She’s installed new kitchen equipment and done some painting, but otherwise, the space didn’t need a lot of renovation.
She plans to add about a half dozen arcade games to the front of the restaurant for customers to enjoy.
Anyone under 18 will also eat free from the kids menu on Mondays, Levesque said.
“It hits personally, because I am a single mother,” she said, adding that she wants the restaurant to be a safe place for families or anyone in the community who’s struggling.
She considered keeping the restaurant open 24 hours a day but said she decided to start out by closing at midnight for now, although she plans to stay open a bit later on weekend nights. The storefront’s proximity to several local bars makes it a convenient stop for people looking to eat after a late night out, she said.
“This is a safe place for families and friends to hang out and just anybody, to be honest, whether you’re 2 years old or you’re 90 years old,” Levesque said. “I want you to feel at home.”

Maine's First Bee City Uses Fallen Foliage To Help Thousands Of Native Bee Species Survive
text:
While most people think that once the leaves fall in the autumn, the best thing to do is clean them up and dispose of them, there are also those who follow the school of thought that you should just leave the leaves where they land.
Read More: What Not To Include In Leaf Collection, Bangor And Brewer
While you might assume this way of thinking is rooted in laziness, science actually backs it up!
In fact, the City of Bangor is also getting behind the effort. While they will have crews hitting the city roads and sidewalks with giant vacuums that will such up the fallen foliage, they're also encouraging those who don't want to rake, to just let things be.
They posted on their Facebook page, that leaving the leaves right where they are, or moving them around trees and garden beds could actually help the little ecosystem in your yard.
"Fallen leaves serve as overwintering habitat for many butterfly and moth species, and as insulation for plant roots and the soil, where other pollinators like bumblebees tend to overwinter. If leaving them where they are isn't an option, you can also rake them into garden beds or around tree bases. Leaving dead plants in the garden standing over the winter is also helpful since various native bees hibernate in hollow stems."
This is in keeping with Bangor becoming the first "Bee City" affiliate in the state of Maine, which was made official in 2024.
According to the folks over at Bangor Beautiful, along with practice like reducing harmful chemicals and emphasising programs like No Mow May, the goal of a Bee City is to ultimately help the nation's bee population.
"Bee City USA® and Bee Campus USA work to galvanize communities to sustain pollinators, in particular the more than 3,600 species of native bees in this country, by increasing the abundance of native plants, providing nest sites, and reducing the use of pesticides.
The Xerces Society of Invertebrate Conservation says that you can gently move the leaves to areas like tree beds or gardens, if you're worried about the grass dying. But overall, the less you disturb the leaves, the better.
"Too many leaves can kill grass, but in soil they can suppress weeds, retain moisture, and boost nutrition. Avoid shredding leaves with a mower. Raking or blowing (electric) are alternatives that will keep leaves whole for the best cover and protect the insects and eggs already living there. If you decide you need to clean up the leaves and debris in spring, make sure you wait until late in the season so as not to destroy all the life you’ve worked to protect."
So, if you were looking for an excuse to take it easy on the yard work this fall, this might just bee a good one to use, as it's a win-win for everyone; you and the bugs!
