title: Here’s what’s on the ballot in Winslow
text:
WINSLOW — On Election Day, voters will choose who represents them in three town council races and decide a myriad of proposed charter amendments. Here’s what to know.
In addition to council candidates, residents will vote for school committee members, at-large library trustees and a Kennebec Water District representative on Nov. 3. They’ll also weigh in on Kennebec County races for treasurer and register of deeds and elect their representatives to the Legislature.
TOWN COUNCIL
In District 1, voters will choose among three candidates to fill one seat.
Scott Holst is a retired career firefighter who worked in Winslow and Waterville for almost 45 years. He regularly attends council and school budget meetings and said he thinks he could work out ways for Winslow to balance municipal and school interests in its budget.
Holst ran for the councilor at-large seat last year and came in third out of five.
“I work well with people,” Holst said. “We sit back, we compromise and we come up with a plan, and that’s what I want to be part of.”
Incumbent District 1 Councilor Michael Joseph was elected to the council in 2023, when he described himself as a conservative Christian businessman looking to cut unnecessary spending. Joseph did not respond to the Maine Trust’s voter guide survey or to requests for comment.
Political newcomer Erin McCullough grew up in Hancock County and moved to Winslow 10 years ago when her son started kindergarten. As a school councilor for 17 years, McCullough said she has hard conversations every day. She’s used to collaborating with people and she’s focused on solutions.
McCullough said Winslow’s biggest challenge is that its services are outgrowing its tax base. She wants to stimulate economic growth to support those services, and better balance its municipal and education budgets so schools don’t take so many heavy hits. She also said she wants to cut down on unplanned spending.
“Voters can expect transparency from me, and can expect just a basic level of respect if we don’t agree on something,” McCullough said. “We all want our town to be a sustainable place where families want to come and move and bring their kids. We just need to figure out how to get there together rather than against each other.”
In District 3, another incumbent and newcomer will vie for votes for the seat up for election.
Frances Hudson holds the current District 3 seat and has been chair of the council for two years. Hudson said she has proven her leadership skills and delivered on her promises, having passed a motion to dissolve the town’s Department of Public Safety and kept meetings efficient. Last year, the council voted to limit the length of public comment.
If reelected, Hudson said she’d like to get a post office back in Winslow. She also said she, the council and the town manager work well together, and she’s proud to have kept taxes flat for two of her three years on the council.
The council voted Tuesday to request a review of its tax assessment after Hudson said she was “blindsided” by residents’ complaints of high bills this year. Before the tax assessment, the mill rate dropped from last year, officials increased the municipal budget by 16% and had a statistical revaluation.
Daniel Potelle, who is challenging Hudson, is a first-time candidate. He was raised in Fairfield and has been in the printing business for about 40 years.
Potelle said he decided to run after town officials asked for steep cuts to the proposed school budget this year. Potelle is married to a teacher and wants to stand behind Winslow’s school systems, especially after he felt residents who spoke in support of the schools weren’t heard.
“My son is a special needs adult and he went through the Winslow public schools and he received a really good, solid education,” Potelle said. Now, he said, a lack of resources means teachers are “managing their classes rather than teaching their classes.”
Potelle said he’d like to encourage better communication to Winslow residents and wants to promote the town as a great place to live and raise a family.
Charles Lambert is running unopposed for the council’s District 5 seat.
Lambert wrote in the Maine Trust for Local News voter guide that he does not agree with the current council’s priorities. He said he wants to keep taxes in check while still funding education and encouraging positive discourse.
OTHER LOCAL RACES
Voters in Districts 1 and 3 will also vote for their school committee board members, Joel Selwood and Karen Andrus, respectively, both of whom are running unopposed.
No candidate is running for the District 5 open school committee seat.
Voters will also elect two at-large library trustees from a pool of three candidates. Candidates Gwen Hawes and Charles Morrill are already on the board, and candidate Joseph Slater is a newcomer.
Amy Stabins, who is currently a trustee for the Kennebec Water District, is running for reelection unopposed.
REFERENDUMS
Voters will consider seven ballot questions designed to amend Winslow’s charter.
Before these questions landed on the ballot, the town’s charter committee recommended the changes, which the council reviewed and sent to town lawyers.
Answering yes to Question 1 would mean that a councilor who is absent from more than three consecutive regular meetings would forfeit the seat.
In 2024, Hudson and Joseph questioned another councilor’s ability to govern after a medical issue, and tried to vacate his seat following his absence from council duties for more than a month.
As Winslow council meetings take place monthly, the charter amendment would apply to any absence of at least three months.
A yes vote to Questions 2 and 3 would standardize language used to describe where meetings are held and to refer to the town manager.
A yes vote to Question 4 would create staggered terms for the Zoning Board of Appeals.
A yes to Question 5 would remove some outdated language that created staggered terms for the school committee. It would also define an “excessive absence,” warranting removal, as one from more than three consecutive regular monthly meetings.
A yes to Question 6 would allow town officials to operate under the existing budget if the council does not adopt a budget on time. Currently, if the council doesn’t adopt a budget on time, the town temporarily maintains its existing budget.
Finally, a yes to Question 7 would make the charter consistent with state laws about the administration of municipal elections when it comes to undeclared and write-in candidates.
COUNTY RACES
Kennebec County residents can choose between Democrat Joanne Mason and Republican Monte Sylvester for county treasurer. They will also elect a register of deeds, with incumbent Republican Matthew Boucher and Democrat Kevin Lamoreau running.
Maeghan Maloney, a Democrat, is running unopposed to retain her role as district attorney.
STATE RACES
House District 63 voters will choose between incumbent Republican Paul R. Flynn and Democrat Taylor Marie West, who is a member of the Winslow School Board. Flynn did not respond to the Maine Trust’s voter guide survey.
Voters in House District 64 will choose between incumbent Flavia DeBrito, who is a Democrat, and Republican challenger Shawn Packard.
In the Senate District 16 race, residents will choose between incumbent Republican Scott Cyrway and Democrat Patric Moore. Cyrway did not respond to the Maine Trust’s voter guide survey.
To find your House district and build your ballot, type your address into the voter guide’s search tool.
Editor’s note: This story was updated to correct what Question 6 would change in the town charter if approved.

title: Supreme Court rebuffs Trump administration restrictions on medical care for transgender inmates
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to allow the Trump administration to immediately enforce new medical restrictions for transgender people in prison.
The decision leaves in place a lower-court block on the policy. It was adopted after an executive order from President Donald Trump, who has taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term.
Justice Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas would have allowed the policy to be enforced.
The Supreme Court has previously allowed other policies for transgender people to move ahead for now, including restrictions on military service and passport sex markers.
Trump’s order called on the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care policies so that federal funds aren’t spent “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.”
The new policy would halt surgeries, taper off hormones and end social accommodations like makeup and wigs. Prisons would continue to offer mental health services.
Attorneys for transgender inmates challenged the policy in court and U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth ordered treatments to continue. Lamberth, who was nominated to the bench by President Ronald Reagan, pointed out that untreated gender dysphoria can cause severe side effects like depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts.
The Trump administration appealed, arguing that treatments raised security concerns and “could no longer be justified.” A divided appeals court panel left the order in place.
About 600 inmates were receiving hormone therapy in 2025, the agency said in court records. Withdrawing care would have significant effects on their bodies and mental health, their lawyers said. The government has not detailed evidence of security problems linked to hormone therapy for transgender inmates over the 30 years it has been provided, they wrote.
The conservative-majority Supreme Court has previously upheld state laws banning certain medical treatments for transgender youth, and restricting sports participation by transgender athletes in women’s sports.

title: Youth planning boards get behind-the-scenes tour of Bangor amphitheater
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The Substance Affected Youth Program brought its youth planning boards together for a behind-the-scenes tour of the Maine Savings Amphitheater in Bangor.
The group, made up of high school and middle school students, is responsible for planning the annual Penquis Youth Summits.
This marks the fourth year of the summit, and the second-year organizers have split planning between high schoolers and middle schoolers.
Both groups united to get a firsthand look at what goes into planning and executing a major event at the venue, from logistics to staging to hospitality, lessons they can carry into planning this year’s summits.
“I’m fortunate enough to be employed part-time through Waterfront Concerts and we’ve built a partnership with the SAY program. They’ve done tours for us in the past. And it just occurred to us that these kids are charged with throwing a large format event for 200 or 250 of their peers. So, bringing them to a venue like this and letting them get a behind-the-scenes look at how a show is put on and the things that the concert staff go through that will be similar to what they go through in planning seemed like a good place to start,” said Joe Costello, SAY Program youth resource navigator.
Group leaders say everything the students learned will translate when it comes time to plan the event in May.
The skills the students are acquiring on the planning boards are ones they will be able to use for life.

title: Down East district attorney candidates disagree on how to address case backlog
text:
Two attorneys competing to become the top elected prosecutor in Hancock and Washington counties have opposing positions on how to use limited resources to handle a backlog that has kept some cases in limbo for years.
District Attorney Robert Granger of Blue Hill seeks a second four-year term. His challenger, Steven Juskewitch, is a trial attorney from Dedham who has run unsuccessfully for the seat multiple times and has a disciplinary history with the Board of Overseers of the Bar.
Both are running as independents.
The race’s central issues broadly result from understaffing and underfunding throughout Maine’s criminal justice system, and the candidates’ approaches show how local offices are trying to manage the effects of these larger structural problems. The incumbent wants to continue prioritizing prosecuting serious crimes in response, while his challenger wants to try every possible case.
District 7 currently has about 1,600 cases backlogged on its trial docket, according to Granger, and gets up to 300 more each month. Numbers are estimates of cases being worked on, he said.
They peaked around 1,800 in 2023, went down to about 1,400 last year with a full-time justice in Ellsworth, then rose between that justice’s retirement and a new appointment, he said.
Granger attended George Stevens Academy in Blue Hill and previously worked as a wildland firefighter, aircraft captain and instructor, and a law enforcement officer for Vermont’s Fish and Wildlife Department.
After graduating from law school in 1991, he served a one-year appointment as a federal law clerk and then worked as a trial attorney in state and federal courts in Bangor in Ellsworth for 32 years.
To address the backlog in his first term, he prioritized prosecuting the most serious crimes — such as attempted murder, aggravated assault, manslaughter, gross sexual assault, domestic violence, child abuse, child pornography and fraud — and handling lesser offenses through deferred dispositions. Defendants plead guilty but sentencing is delayed for them to meet conditions like community service or paying restitution, and original charges are then typically reduced or dismissed.
Granger’s office is still prosecuting cases from before his tenure because the area didn’t have a full-time judge until April 2024, he said, noting that the courts set the order of trials — not the DA.
Among his accomplishments, Granger listed getting a new prosecutor assigned to the district to focus on drug trafficking cases, reinstating a detective position and leading a transition from paper to online work for some files. He also touts his staff of experienced prosecutors, with a combined 155 years of trial experience.
He would continue his approach to prioritizing cases if reelected. Granger is also open to discussing restorative justice programs, though he said his office questions its efficacy.
He would also keep advocating for adding another prosecutor in the district.
Granger has made progress towards his goals, but four years isn’t enough, he said. He’s also worried about the state’s Speedy Trial Act, which has aimed to reduce backlogs.
The outcome of a case awaiting a decision from Maine’s highest court could mean that people in jail without a lawyer amid the state’s public defender shortage will be released or have their cases dismissed.
“If major criminal cases such as sexual assault cases, aggravated assault and child abuse cases are dismissed because we lack court time to try them all the public will understandably become extremely upset and community safety will most certainly be compromised,” he said. “The public needs to appreciate this problem.”
Juskewitch’s Ellsworth practice focuses on criminal defense and personal injury. He represented municipalities in southern Maine and prosecuted major felonies in Cumberland County before coming to Hancock County. He was previously an assistant district attorney here and has practiced law since 1976.
He also spent 28 years in the Army, serving with the 82nd Airborne Division.
Juskewitch said his primary reasons for running include staff turnover since Granger’s election, “resulting in an unbelievable number of dismissals, delayed trials, and not guilty verdicts.” The key to his campaign is providing timely and fair justice, he said.
Juskewitch wants to try every possible case, he said at an Oct. 14 candidate forum, and believes the district dismisses too many while not adequately presenting cases to the grand jury. A grand jury reviews evidence from a prosecutor and decides whether someone should be charged with a crime.
He said he would approach the backlog by prioritizing people already in jail and work backwards chronologically, then do the same for the unincarcerated.
He’d review cases with defense attorneys and investigating police officers to resolve them, he said. If unsuccessful, he’d hold judicial settlement conferences with active retired justices and set trial dates.
Granger has said trying every case is not possible.
Some Washington County residents feel underrepresented in the combined district and have pushed for their own DA. The district has offices in Ellsworth, Machias and Calais.
Around 1,000 cases are pending in Hancock County among four prosecutors and 600 in Washington County for two prosecutors, according to Granger.
The courts have also recently set more annual trial terms in Hancock County, he said, reducing Washington County’s from six to three. Those are also shared with the Attorney General’s homicide prosecutions and civil cases Down East, he said.
Granger went to Washington County weekly until that county’s budget crisis led officials to limit travel spending, he said.
His deputy handles most day-to-day business there, and Granger takes on complex, high-profile cases in both counties and also assists with grand juries, deferred disposition conferences and arraignments in both.
Juskewitch expects to spend 40% of his time in Washington County and have a deputy there if elected, he said, promising to spend nights away from home and dedicate significant time to training staff and police, without providing specific examples of trainings.
He also highlighted experience allocating time and resources in his Army service and in Cumberland County.
Juskewitch said he has more experience in management and prosecution than past DAs, highlighting work delegating, training and allocating resources in the military. His campaign website says he has successfully prosecuted more felony trials than all current prosecutors combined.
“The primary change in the DA offices will be the training and guidance based on my experience which I will provide to prosecutors and staff in order for them to accept and succeed with the responsibilities and duties I will delegate to them,” he said.
Five complaints have been filed against Juskewitch with the Board of Overseers of the Bar, and he’s been warned or sanctioned at least three times over his conduct with clients.
Juskewitch said his “extensive” legal practice has included “a number of difficult individuals” who weren’t happy with results.
“I can not say more except, with possible exception of one, I still maintain a good relationship with each of them,” he said. “I am satisfied with the status of the relationship with the exception.”
Granger has had four bar complaints filed against him, he said at the Oct. 14 forum, but none resulted in disciplinary action.

title: Family of passenger in Greg Biffle plane crash alleges NASCAR driver hired unqualified pilot
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - The personal assistant and longtime friend of NASCAR driver Greg Biffle has filed a wrongful-death lawsuit alleging Biffle hired an unqualified flight crew to save costs.
Greg Biffle’s estate is facing four major wrongful death lawsuits, totaling $40 million in claims.
Biffle and his longtime friend Craig Wadsworth were two of seven people killed in the tragic plane crash in Statesville in late December 2025.
Wadsworth’s estate filed the lawsuit last Friday in Iredell County against the estates of Greg Biffle, pilot Dennis Dutton, Dutton’s 20-year-old son Jack Dutton, and GB Aviation Leasing, a company owned by Biffle.
The suit claims Biffle and pilot Dennis Dutton knew a qualified second co-pilot was required to fly the plane, but allowed the pilot’s 20-year-old son, Jack Dutton, to fly without proper qualifications.
The lawsuit continued, stating Biffle was motivated “at least in part, by the desire to avoid the expense” of a professional co-pilot, citing a conversation in which Dennis Dutton told Biffle he had found someone to act as co-pilot and it would be “cheap.”
The estate alleges Biffle was willfully negligent, choosing personal convenience, cost savings and an opportunity to give “an inexperienced airman” cockpit experience over stopping the flight or hiring someone more experienced — leading to Wadsworth’s death.
The suit also names GB Aviation Leasing LLC, a private aviation company owned by Biffle, which operated the aircraft and leased the hangar space.
The company allegedly held no air carrier certificate — an FAA authorization required to operate as a commercial charter airline.
Additionally, Wadsworth’s estate claims Biffle was negligent both as Dutton’s boss and as owner and manager of the company that authorized the crew.
Dennis Dutton and Jack Dutton were also named for negligence as pilot in command and as acting crewman.
Wadsworth’s family is seeking at least $25,000, plus court costs and interest, from the Dutton estates, Biffle estate and GB Aviation.

title: 7-year-old girl’s body exhumed months after death from alleged abuse
text:
SUFFOLK COUNTY, N.Y. (WABC) — The body of a 7-year-old New York girl has been exhumed months after her death, according to her mother’s attorney.
Prosecutors said Jor’Dynn Duncan suffered months of abuse before dying from an untreated infection.
Attorney Heather Palmore said her client, Portia Duncan, gave authorization to the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office for Jor’Dynn’s body to be exhumed.
“We don’t know why they asked for the exhumation of Jor’Dynn’s body,” Palmore said. “What I will say is, in my experience as a former prosecutor, there may be things or evidence that they’re looking to corroborate or uncover.”
Mother described as devastated
Palmore said the 7-year-old’s mother is emotional over the exhumation but understands it is a necessary part of getting to the truth and getting justice for Jor’Dynn.
“She’s devastated,” Palmore said. “It is a nightmare for her. It’s a nightmare for her family and those who love Jor’Dynn.”
Details of the case
According to prosecutors, the girl endured months of alleged systematic cruelty and sadistic abuse, much of which was recorded on a cellphone, before dying from a massive untreated infection from her injuries.
The 7-year-old had about 90 injuries on her body at the time of her death, according to the Suffolk County Medical Examiner’s Office.
Jor’Dynn’s legal guardian, Emily Kelly, her mother, Barbara Renner, and Kelly’s daughter, Elyssa Seymore, are all facing charges in connection with the child’s death and previously pleaded not guilty.
“Any reasonable person would have been able to conclude that something was wrong here,” Palmore said.
The second grader was taken out of her mother’s custody after an alleged failed drug test.
Notice of claim filed
In July, Portia Duncan’s attorneys filed a notice of claim alleging the county, Bayport-Blue Point School District and others were negligent in monitoring her health and safety and failed to intervene.
Palmore said they will be filing a lawsuit shortly.
“It’ll be very clear that the institutions that were set in place and that we rely on to take care of children when their parents can’t, that they failed her,” Palmore said.
The Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office declined to comment. The three women charged in the case are awaiting trial.

title: Russia releases American man imprisoned on charges of fighting as mercenary in Ukraine
text:
(AP) - Russia on Wednesday freed an American who had been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, a deal completed during a visit by a top U.S. envoy and at a time when President Donald Trump has taken a series of actions meant to benefit Moscow.
Trump told reporters at the White House that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin during a recent call to free Stephen Hubbard and that, unlike previous releases, the U.S. did not have to give up anyone in return.
“He is the happiest man around,” Trump said of Hubbard, describing the 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan as a “very high-quality, innocent man.” Hubbard’s legal team denied the Russian accusations, saying he was not involved in any military activity.
The release occurred during a visit to St. Petersburg by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who in a face-to-face interaction with Putin praised the Russian leader as a “humanitarian” as the men held talks about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and as Trump simultaneously pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Hubbard, who before his arrest had lived in Ukraine for years, was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison during closed court proceedings. Prosecutors said he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Russia’s invasion in 2022, and that he fought alongside Kyiv’s forces until being captured two months later.
The U.S. government under President Joe Biden’s administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained. His family also disputed the Russian allegations.
“He was just for bait. It was all about bait. And that’s why they kidnap Americans,” his sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, said in an interview with The Associated Press. She said she expected Hubbard to stay with her in Colorado.
“Steven James Hubbard is the face of America,” she said. “They could do that to anybody. They just happened to see him. ‘Oh, that’s an American, let’s go get him.’”
US envoy calls Putin a ‘humanitarian’
Witkoff, a key Trump administration figure who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end a war that will hit the five-year mark in February 2027, thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, telling him, “Because of you, he’s going home to his family.”
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir,” Witkoff said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media Wednesday that Hubbard’s release was “raised by the American side for a certain time,” and Putin decided to free the man out of “humanitarian considerations.”
Speaking to reporters after the talks, Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said the Kremlin leader had pardoned Hubbard, who upon his release was taken to St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo airport for Witkoff to bring him home to the United States.
Video showed Witkoff and Hubbard shaking hands, with the newly released American thanking the envoy. Witkoff introduced Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev to Hubbard and described him as someone “who had a lot to do with this happening.”
“We just met President Putin, he sends you blessings and wishes you good things,” Witkoff added.
Hubbard, a U.S. Air Force veteran, taught English overseas and had by 2012 retired to Cyprus, where one of his sons is a priest. He later moved to Ukraine to be with a woman he had met, his lawyers said, remaining in the country after the relationship ended and living there at the time of Russia’s 2022 invasion. He was detained in April of that year after Russian forces took control of the area where he was living.
His case was taken up by lawyers at the U.S.-based law firm of Boies Schiller Flexner and the Russian firm of EPAM Law, which together had represented Marc Fogel, the American teacher freed from Russian custody last year, and worked for his release.
“They thought they weren’t going to see him again alive, and Stephen didn’t think he was going to come out of there alive,” one of Hubbard’s lawyers at Boies Schiller, Martin De Luca, said in an interview of Hubbard’s family. “Obviously, they’re overjoyed, but they feel very much like it’s a miracle.”
His sister said she had spoken with Hubbard soon after his release. “That was awesome. He was just laughing. He said, ‘I can’t believe this is happening,’” Hubbard Fox said of her brother.
Trump told reporters Wednesday night that Hubbard is expected to visit the White House some time in the coming days.
Other Americans remain jailed in Russia
The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship being roiled by fresh tensions at the same time that the Trump administration has advanced policies that aid Putin.
Those include Trump’s move last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine. Named after the late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Moscow’s war.
That decision followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections.
Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday. He was expected to exchange ideas from that meeting, as well as proposals from European and American colleagues, in his talks with Russian leaders in St. Petersburg.
Hubbard is the second American freed by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of Marine veteran Robert Gilman, who had been gravely ill and was imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer.
Other Americans, including some with serious illnesses, remain jailed in Russia. Hubbard was the last remaining American designated as wrongfully detained, although advocates say that label should be applied to other prisoners.
When asked Wednesday night if he thinks more Americans will be released, Trump told reporters, “Yeah, I think so. That’ll come.”
Russia reported more arrests of foreigners in recent days. The FSB security service said Wednesday it detained a German national suspected of mercenary activities and last week announced arrests of a Swedish national suspected of sabotage and a Japanese journalist accused of espionage.
___
Associated Press writers Thomas Peipert and Michelle L. Price contributed to this report.

title: Video shows moments leading up to deadly police shooting at Walmart that killed 1-year-old child
text:
SENATOBIA, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - Video has been obtained showing the moments leading up to a shooting involving Senatobia police that killed a 1-year-old child in June.
Darkhorse Press released the video days after Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s office determined the officers’ actions that day were justified.
The footage included five videos: three body-camera videos from Senatobia officers and two surveillance videos from Walmart.
On June 14, Senatobia police responded to an alleged shoplifting involving diapers at an area Walmart involving two women.
One-year-old Kohen Wiley was inside a car with his mother, who was holding him, and his great-aunt, who was driving when the shooting occurred.
One of the released videos from that day shows the store’s security guard talking to the child’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, and his great-aunt.
Moments later, video showed the child, identified as Kohen Wiley, being held by his mother while they were running to the car.
Kohen’s mother gets in the passenger seat of the vehicle with him, while the other woman jumps into the driver’s seat.
Another video showed law enforcement officers in the store’s loss prevention office being interrupted by a store employee saying, “Two women are running.”
Moments later, video showed law enforcement officers running after Vellesiya Wiley and the other woman as both got into the car.
Officers were then seen in front of the car as the driver backed out of the parking spot, telling the driver to stop with guns drawn.
However, the driver appears to then drive toward officers, hitting one and crossing into the next parking lot aisle, striking a parked vehicle, prompting police to shoot.
It was unclear from the videos provided which officers fired their weapons. One-year-old Kohen Wiley did not survive the shooting.
Body-camera video from the officer who was hit by the vehicle was not part of the videos released.
In the final body-camera video that was released, officers were outside of an emergency medical center, where one can be heard saying, “I didn’t even see a f—ing baby in her lap.”
“Nobody knew the baby was there,” another officer said. “All I saw was two females in the car.”
The footage appears to contradict parts of Vellesiya Wiley’s previous account.
In a June 17 video statement released through attorneys Ben Crump and Van Turner, Vellesiya Wiley said she continued walking “because it had nothing to do with me” after officers stopped her friend, and said her friend drove toward the other side of the lot, away from officers.
Vellesiya Wiley also previously said she had lifted Kohen up “trying to show them that he was in the car” after seeing officers draw their guns.
According to the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, it has assigned five agents to the case, with investigators reviewing witness statements, body- and dash-camera video and Walmart surveillance video.
The officer who fired was placed on administrative leave, which city leaders said was standard practice after deadly police shootings.
In July, Kohen Wiley’s cause of death was ruled a homicide, according to an independent autopsy report requested by the family.
Van Turner, along with civil rights attorney Ben Crump, is representing the Wiley family. They have renewed calls for MBI and Walmart to release all surveillance video from the incident.
WMC has reached out to the Mississippi Department of Public Safety about the released videos through Darkhorse Press and whether there were plans to release the videos independently.
DPS said it still plans to sit down with the Wiley family this week and then release it.
Family attorneys were aware of the video and plan to meet with the family Thursday to review the video themselves.
Copyright 2026 WMC via Gray Local Media, Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Gay couple harassed while working for solar panel company in Maine, lawsuit says
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A gay couple is suing a solar panel company, alleging they were sexually harassed and retaliated against while working in Maine.
Wilmer Muchacho, 46, and Jose Cordero, 30, a married couple from New York City, started working in Holden as solar panel installers for Centre Electric around May 2023. The federal lawsuit says the Minnesota company discriminated against the couple before ultimately firing them.
The lawsuit, filed Oct. 14, in U.S. District Court of Maine in Bangor, alleges Centre Electric violated the Maine Human Rights Act, the federal Civil Rights Act and the Maine Whistleblowers’ Protection Act, as well as retaliated against the couple for reporting illegal conduct.
Muchacho and Cordero want a judge to order Centre Electric to provide civil rights training to employees, as well as award back pay for lost wages and unspecified compensatory damages. The couple wants the case to go to a jury trial.
Centre Electric did not respond to a request for comment.
“In the United States, everyone deserves to be treated with dignity at work, no matter who we love,” Muchacho told the Bangor Daily News. “We are putting our trust in a jury of Maine people to hear our story and to help us find justice.”
About four months after the couple started working in Holden, their coworkers started harassing them for being married, the lawsuit said. The coworkers called them slurs for gay men and referred to them as sexually transmitted diseases.
Muchacho and Cordero reported the harassment to their supervisor and they were transferred to another work site in Mattawamkeag. Coworkers at the new location also harassed the couple about their relationship, the lawsuit said. Coworkers allegedly threw food at the couple.
Centre Electric took no additional action to stop the harassment, according to the lawsuit. The company started retaliating against the men.
Other employees were allowed to go to their car to warm up on breaks, allowed meal and bathroom breaks and were given weekend work, the lawsuit said. It said the couple were denied all of those opportunities.
Muchacho and Cordero were terminated from Centre Electric in February 2024, for what the company said was tardiness and disrespectful behavior. But, they were not given any warnings for the supposed issues before they were fired, the lawsuit said.
Both men repeatedly complained to the company about the harassment and discrimination, but no action was taken, the lawsuit said.
The couple filed complaints with the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity, which found there was reasonable cause to believe there was retaliation on the basis of sex, and issued them right to sue letters, the lawsuit said.

title: Houlton Regional Hospital nurses publish letter of no confidence in CEO
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HOULTON, Maine (WABI) - Nurses from Houlton Regional Hospital have published a letter of no confidence in the hospital’s CEO, claiming their concerns have been ignored by the board of trustees.
Nurses from the hospital have gone on strike twice in the past year saying they needed to protect language in their contracts that limits the amount of patients a nurse can be assigned and requires a minimum number of available nurses for the emergency department.
Union members said the nurses submitted the letter and petition of no confidence to the board in July urging them to remove CEO Jeff Zewe from his position.
In a statement, the nurses said, “We presented the Board of Trustees with a letter of no confidence and invited the Board to a meeting to hear from nurses. They didn’t show up. All we’ve heard is silence.”
In a letter to the community shared with WABI in response to the letter, the board says it has been working since May of 2025 to improve the hospital’s financial outlook, saying at the time they were on the brink of filing for bankruptcy. The board says they enlisted the help of leadership from Northern Maine Medical Center in Fort Kent, namely Zewe and their CFO Aaron Teachout, adding the turnaround under their leadership has restored stability and allowed them to invest in technology and employees. The nurses’ union claims more than half of the ER nurses at NMCC have resigned due to poor conditions caused by management.
The board’s reads says in part, “Transformation of this scale can be challenging and requires ongoing engagement with staff at all levels. We remain committed to listening to employee concerns and working collaboratively with clinical teams to ensure both staff satisfaction and high-quality patient outcomes.”
You can read the full letters from the nurses union and the hospital below:
Letter of no confidence from HRH nurses
Dear Board of Trustees,
The nurses of Houlton Regional Hospital have NO CONFIDENCE in CEO Jeff Zewe for the following reasons:
Failure to Provide Continuity of Care
• The Hospital has announced that long-time Emergency Department physicians and the physicians who care for hospitalized patients are being replaced. The Hospital now also relies on virtual physicians overnight for admitted patients. These changes remove respected physicians who know our community and our patients.
• The Hospital has promised expanded services, yet physicians and surgeons continue to leave almost as quickly as they are recruited. Cardiology, orthopedic and hospitalist providers and a general surgeon have all come and gone, disrupting continuity of care and raising serious concerns about the Hospital’s ability to retain the providers our community deserves.
Failure to Retain Staff and Local Expertise
• While the Hospital has struggled with ongoing nursing turnover and relies heavily on traveling nurses, it has also lost its Chief Nursing Officer, Acute Care Manager, and OR Manager within the last year. All were long-time nurses of our Hospital and trusted members of our community.
Diminishing Security Capacity
• The highly respected Director of Security has left, and security staffing has been reduced after years of efforts to achieve appropriate staffing levels to meet the needs of patients and staff.
Failure to Staff Appropriately
• The Hospital continues to overflow the Acute Care Unit and is not consistently following its own policies regarding higher staffing levels for the sickest patients. Many of these patients would be cared for in an Intensive Care Unit at other hospitals, where one nurse typically cares for only two patients because of the severity of their illnesses. At Houlton Regional Hospital, those same patients are often included in full assignments of five patients, reducing the level of care each patient can receive.
• The Hospital staffs only two nurses in the Emergency Department from 11:00 p.m. to 9:00 a.m., leaving the department inadequately staffed and limiting its ability to provide timely care when critical patients, including laboring mothers, require the attention of all available staff.
Failure to Reach a Fair Contract
• The Hospital has failed to reach a fair settlement with the nurses. It continues to insist on removing staffing language from the contract – the very language that has protected patients and nurses and contributed to the positive patient outcomes the Hospital frequently cites.
Reliance on Outside Consultants
• The Hospital increasingly relies on out-of-state consultants from Mississippi, Texas, and
elsewhere, placing greater value on their recommendations than on the knowledge and
experience of local staff when making decisions that impact our patients and our Hospital.
Creating an Unhealthy Culture
• The Hospital has fostered an unhealthy culture characterized by a corporate mentality and a
top-down approach that devalues local staff and erodes the community-focused, nonprofit spirit
of our Hospital. Patients want to remain in Houlton and receive care close to family and friends,
whose support is vital to recovery. The Hospital is rapidly moving away from the community centered environment that makes Houlton special.
Jeff Zewe has been CEO for just over a year and has already caused significant damage to our Hospital and community. One of the hospitals where Mr. Zewe previously served as CEO, located in Bradford, Pennsylvania, has since closed following major changes that began during his tenure. We must take action while there is still time to preserve and protect our community hospital.
For all of these reasons, we, the undersigned, have NO CONFIDENCE in Jeff Zewe’s continued employment as CEO of Houlton Regional Hospital. We respectfully call upon the Board of Trustees to terminate his employment immediately.
Sincerely,
The Undersigned Nurses of Houlton Regional Hospital
Response from HRH board of trustees
To our valued community members of Houlton and throughout Aroostook County:
As the Board of Trustees of Houlton Regional Hospital, we are entrusted with the responsibility of ensuring that our hospital continues to provide safe, high-quality care to our patients while operating in a fiscally responsible and sustainable manner. We have been provided with comprehensive information regarding the hospital’s operational and financial position and have remained actively engaged in evaluating the challenges, opportunities, and decisions necessary to strengthen HRH for the future.
The Board has been involved in every major decision impacting the hospital’s direction and has worked diligently to ensure that Houlton Regional Hospital remains a trusted healthcare resource for our community—today, tomorrow, and for generations to come.
In May 2025, HRH faced significant financial and operational challenges. The hospital had approximately one day cash on hand and was on the brink of filing for bankruptcy. Unpaid obligations threatened disruptions in critical supplies and services, placing the stability of care at risk.
At that time, the Board of Trustees took decisive action by entering into a Management Services Agreement with Northern Maine Medical Center (NMMC). Under the leadership of NMMC President and CEO Jeff Zewe and CFO Aaron Teachout, a comprehensive stabilization and recovery effort was initiated.
Over the past 13 months, HRH has undergone a substantial turnaround. The organization has restored operational stability, strengthened financial footing, and expanded access to care across the region. Building on previously announced initiatives and service enhancements, HRH has successfully introduced and grown key service lines, including pain management, behavioral health, cardiology, and urology. Additional services, including gynecology, orthopedics, oncology and wound care, are in development, and therapy services have been expanded to meet increasing patient demand.
As part of this transformation, HRH has made significant investments in technology to enhance patient care. Over the past 13 months, the hospital has invested over $2 million in advanced imaging equipment. Recent upgrades include the installation of a new Canon Aquilion 160-slice CT scanner, replacing an older 32-slice unit and significantly improving diagnostic capabilities. The addition of Canon Aplio i700 and Aplio i900 ultrasound systems will expand capacity for both general ultrasound and echocardiography, allowing for increased access to exams. A new Canon SOLTUS portable X-ray system has also been introduced, improving efficiency and responsiveness for bedside imaging. In addition, we have also made significant upgrades to our Operating Room and sterilization equipment. Lastly, we are adding jobs at HRH from growth, while many hospitals are reducing jobs.
These advancements reflect a continued commitment to high-quality care, patient access, and long-term sustainability. The hospital remains focused on ensuring that patients in the greater Houlton area have reliable, local access to essential healthcare services.
While we have made significant improvements in our equipment, we have also invested in our number one asset, our employees, by making well overdue market wage adjustments and enhanced benefits. As we continue to negotiate in good faith with our nurses, we can assure the community our hospital is very well staffed providing very good quality outcomes.
As the Board of Trustees, we believe in the importance of maintaining a strong, local hospital in our community. If our hospital closes, we could face significant economic and public health consequences, including job loss, reduced access to emergency and specialty care, increased travel distances for care, and challenges in attracting and retaining businesses. Our hospital serves as vital economic anchors to the health of our community
The progress achieved at HRH in such a short time represents an almost unheard-of turnaround in a time when our nation is seeing hospital closures and elimination of services on a daily basis.
The challenges facing rural hospitals are not unique to just Houlton. Across Maine and throughout the country, healthcare organizations continue to face significant financial pressures, including rising operational costs, workforce shortages, declining reimbursement, and increasing demands for services. These challenges have led some communities to experience reductions in healthcare access or the loss of local hospital services altogether. In Maine alone, there are reported to be up to ten hospitals at risk of closing with two considered at immediate risk. This reality underscores the importance of preserving and strengthening rural hospitals like Houlton Regional Hospital, which serve as essential healthcare providers, employers, and community anchors.
Through focused leadership and strategic partnership, the hospital has not only remained open, but has strengthened services, expanded care offerings and has become financially viable.
Transformation of this scale can be challenging and requires ongoing engagement with staff at all levels. We remain committed to listening to employee concerns and working collaboratively with clinical teams to ensure both staff satisfaction and high-quality patient outcomes.
“Our priority remains clear: to increase access, provide high quality, accessible healthcare to the people of this region while building a sustainable future for Houlton Regional Hospital,” said Lynette McLaughlin, Board Chair.
Copyright 2026 WABI. All rights reserved.

title: Death Notice: Carl W. Butler
How accurate are Democrats’ attacks on GOP opponents about opposing Iran war’s end?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How accurate are Democrats’ attacks on GOP opponents about opposing Iran war’s end, including Jackson's claims about Collins?
Democrats in competitive U.S. Senate races are capitalizing on public anger about the Iran war. Republicans, they say, keep voting against resolutions that could stop it.
Polls show that voters disapprove of President Donald Trump’s handling of the war and overwhelmingly believe he lacks an exit strategy. Trump initially predicted it would last four to six weeks. It has now stretched on for more than seven months.
For voters, the economy and cost of living are still the dominant issues by a wide margin, said Rina Shah, a strategist and former senior GOP congressional aide. “But a large majority of voters” correctly link the war to energy prices and inflation.
The U.S. and Israel launched the war Feb. 28, causing gas prices to rise as Iran countered military attacks by squeezing oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Gas prices are averaging above $4 a gallon nationally under a president who campaigned on a promise of reducing the cost to below $2.
The Democratic attacks in ads and debates zero in on Congressional War Powers Resolution votes. A tally by The New York Times found that, since March, the House held six such votes and the Senate held 14.
Since May, some of the resolutions passed. But to take effect, the chambers would have to pass identical resolutions, and then Trump would have to sign the measure. If the president vetoed it, which is likely, Congress could override only with two-thirds votes in each chamber. No war powers resolution has ever overcome a veto.
Democrat Troy Jackson: Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, “voted against it nine times before she voted for it five times.” (said in Oct. 8 debate)
Jackson reversed the votes.
He was responding to Collins’s statement that she had “voted nine times to bring the war in Iran to an end.”
Collins has said the War Powers Act gives permission for the president to wage war for 60 days, and she opposes the president’s decision to extend the war beyond that threshold without getting congressional approval.
Since the 60-day deadline on April 30, Collins has voted with Democrats nine times in support of ending the war. Before that deadline hit, Collins voted five times against such resolutions: March 4, March 18, March 24, April 15 and April 22.
During an earlier debate, Jackson said Collins voted for the Iran war “five times.”
Iowa Democrat Josh Turek: Republican Sen. Ashley Hinson “has voted in favor of (the Iran war) seven times.” (said in Oct. 7 debate)
This is mostly accurate.
Hinson has voted against six resolutions calling for the Iran war’s end. In a Sept. 15 vote, seven Republicans joined Democrats to pass the resolution through the House. It failed in the Senate.
One of the votes Turek pointed to was not a direct call to end the Iran war. In June, Hinson voted against Michigan Democratic Rep. Rashida Tlaib’s resolution to withdraw U.S. forces from hostilities in Lebanon. There were no U.S. forces engaged in conflict in Lebanon. However, the fighting between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon is connected to the Iran war and has threatened a potential U.S.-Iran peace deal.
Hinson said during the Oct. 7 debate she wanted an “immediate and successful end” to the war but doesn’t want Congress to limit Trump’s authority.
Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown: Republican Sen. Jon Husted “voted 14 times for the war in Iran pushing gas, diesel prices to record highs.” (Ad)
This needs context.
Only one of Husted’s votes was on a resolution to end the war itself; the other 13 times he cast votes on procedural motions, keeping resolutions from coming to the floor. One was in 2025 after the U.S. struck nuclear sites in Iran and the other 12 were in 2026.
Days before the most recent vote in September, Husted told Politico, “The war needs to come to an end as quickly as possible so that we can lower gas prices.”
During an Oct. 15 debate with Brown, Husted said he wanted the war’s end to “happen on America’s terms and not Iran’s terms.”
In an email to PolitiFact, Husted’s spokesperson Amy Natoce said, “As you well know, a vote against a War Powers Resolution is not a vote ‘to continue the Iran War.’”
An expert said the resolution votes allow lawmakers to take a stance on continuing the war.
“Voting against such a resolution, in effect, allows the president to continue his chosen policies,” said Mark F. Cancian, a retired Marine Corps colonel and senior adviser with the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “The Republicans argue that the president is trying to negotiate a favorable end to the conflict. On the other hand, those efforts have been unsuccessful, so the conflict has continued at various levels of intensity.”
Aaron Pickrell, who has worked on past campaigns for Democrats in Ohio, including Barack Obama, said the economy, inflation and affordability are dominating this cycle.
“It’s not hard for people to tie high prices with the war in Iran and having the option to vote to end the war can be seen by some as a vote to lower gas prices,” Pickrell said.
Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff: Republican Rep. Mike Collins “voted seven times for the war in Iran.” (said in Oct. 8 debate)
That’s mostly accurate.
Ossoff’s campaign pointed to six war powers resolution votes and a vote in favor of a national security appropriations resolution. The funding vote was not entirely about Iran but said money could be used for preventing a nuclear Iran.
Collins replied by echoing Trump’s justification for the war.
“The President had every right to go in there and make sure that Iran does not get a nuclear weapon,” Collins said, adding “they were this close to getting a nuclear weapon and they would have used it.”
When Trump launched the war he exaggerated Iran’s nuclear capabilities and has since inflated the impact of U.S. military strikes. The 2025 U.S. military strikes likely set back Iran’s nuclear program but did not eliminate it, and the attacks in this year’s war have not further weakened Iran’s nuclear capabilities, military and nuclear experts said.
Brian Darling, a Republican strategist and former staffer for Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul, said when GOP candidates point to any votes or statements that the war needs to end soon, it shows they understand the widespread opposition to the war.
“An issue that is on the top of minds for voters may prove to be a tie breaker in these Senate elections,” Darling said.
PolitiFact Researcher Caryn Baird and Staff Writer Caleb McCullough contributed to this article.

title: A new drug offers hope for children with rare Hunter syndrome
text:
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. (InvestigateTV) — Nearly 10% of Americans live with a rare disease, and most of these conditions have no approved treatment options.
One of those conditions, Hunter syndrome, mostly affects boys and has had only one approved treatment since 2006. A new drug approved this year is offering families a different outlook.
Rare diseases are referred to by patients and doctors as “orphan diseases” because they receive little attention in research and health care, according to the National Institute for Children’s Health Quality.
Most rare diseases, about 72%, are genetic, and of those, about 70% start in childhood. Children living with rare disorders often face long delays for an accurate diagnosis, a process often called “a diagnostic odyssey,” along with chronic physical and mental health issues and complex care needs.
Hunter syndrome, also known as mucopolysaccharidosis type two, or MPS II, is one such genetic disease. Since 2006, enzyme replacement therapy has been the only approved treatment, but that medication addressed only some physical symptoms of the disease, such as joint stiffness.
Diagnosis after months of questions
Atlas Neuerburg is almost 4 years old. He likes to spin vinyl records on his father’s turntable, is a fan of John Candy, Michael J. Fox and “Back to the Future,” and practices swinging a bat in his yard.
Before Atlas’ parents, Nick and Jenny Neuerburg, had a name for their son’s condition, they were in and out of doctors’ offices for what seemed like typical early childhood issues.
“He was just a little bit slow with gross motor stuff. He was slow to crawl. Slow to walk,” Jenny Neuerburg said.
During Atlas’ regular 18-month checkup, a doctor examined his stomach.
“The doctor touched his stomach and asked if it always felt hard like that,” Jenny Neuerburg said. “Then she called us the next morning and said, ‘I’ve been thinking of his stomach all night and it’s bothering me.’”
A hard or distended stomach is a common sign of MPS II, according to the Cleveland Clinic. Other early indicators include a wider than normal head, chest and short neck; stiffness in the joints; persistent ear infections or hearing loss; and distinctive facial features.
Symptoms generally appear between 18 months and 4 years of age, and the most severe cases can be life-threatening.
“That led to blood tests and eventually genetic testing and that’s how we found out,” Jenny Neuerburg said. “The day after Christmas, so we’ll always remember that.”
Relocating for clinical trial
At the time, the Neuerburgs lived in Kansas. A specialist at Children’s Mercy Hospital in Kansas City pointed them toward North Carolina.
“We actually packed up our entire house in Kansas City and started driving across country,” Nick Neuerburg said.
The couple’s research led them to Dr. Joseph Muenzer, a pediatric geneticist with UNC Health in Chapel Hill and an expert in Hunter syndrome and other forms of MPS. His clinic is one of a handful of sites in the country running a clinical trial for a drug that targets neurological aspects of the disease.
“There’s probably four or five sites around the country,” Muenzer said.
Children with Hunter syndrome are unable to produce the enzyme that typically clears a buildup of cellular waste material, known medically as glycosaminoglycans, or GAGs. Without the enzyme, the material builds up and leads to progressive damage in the body and brain.
The trial Atlas joined tested a weekly intravenous infusion that replaces the missing enzyme. Unlike other treatments, it crosses the blood-brain barrier — the tightly locked layer of cells that defend the brain from harmful substances — allowing it to reach both body and brain.
“I preach both the physical disease and the brain disease, something we didn’t have before. So it’s a life changer for the MPS II community,” Muenzer said. “For the first time, for a lot of these families, they were given hope.”
Atlas joined the trial as a toddler, celebrating his third birthday during one of his weekly infusions.
More than two years later, he shows no further signs of decline. Muenzer said other trial participants are seeing similar results.
“I have a few patients in the clinical trial who were started when they were around two years of age,” Muenzer said. “And now at six and seven, you almost don’t know they have Hunter’s syndrome anymore because their physical disease basically has not developed, and they’re developmentally appeared to be normal.”
A mother’s hope
In March 2026, the Food and Drug Administration granted accelerated approval for the drug, called Avlayah, for patients through age 16.
Kim Stephens, executive director of the Muenzer MPS Research and Treatment Center, believes the approval is what patients’ families have been waiting for.
“We’re going to have some kids that won’t develop like a typical Hunter syndrome child. And that’s going to be really amazing for our community,” Stephens said.
Stephens’ son, Cole, was diagnosed with Hunter syndrome at age 2. As the disorder progressed, Cole lost most language skills except for two words: “help” and “mommy.”
Today, Cole is 15, and it’s unlikely he’ll say the word “mommy” again.
Stephens knows Avlayah is not a cure and won’t reverse what Cole has lost. But she hopes the drug can slow what comes next.
“[I] want him to be able to laugh and run and enjoy his favorite things and do puzzles and just continue to be the happy child he is,” Stephens said.
In May 2026, Cole received his first infusion. After the initial doses, Stephens said she sees a difference in Cole’s ability to focus. While she can’t say for sure whether the change is the direct result of the drug, she feels strongly it is.
Cost and access
A spokesperson for Denali Therapeutics, the manufacturer of Avlayah, said the U.S. list price for the drug is $5,200 per vial, but individual costs vary based on a patient’s body weight and insurance plan.
So far, the Neuerburgs have not paid anything out of pocket because Atlas is involved in the ongoing clinical trial. The hope is that one day Atlas will be able to receive his treatment at home instead of traveling to Muenzer’s clinic once a week.
Jenny Neuerburg said she sees something special in her son’s future.
“I feel like there’s something about him,” she said. “He’s going to change the world.”

title: Obituary: Louis Eugene Carlow
text:
PFLUGERVILLE, Texas – Louis Eugene Carlow passed away Oct. 3, 2026, at BSW Hospital in Round Rock, Texas, following a long battle with cancer, surrounded by his loving family.
Born August 25, 1948, in Waterville, Maine, he was the son of the late Louis Adams Carlow and Lois Miriam Carlow (Seekins). He graduated from Waterville High School, enlisted in the U.S. Air Force, and earned a B.S. in Business Administration from the University of Maine at Augusta. He spent most of his career as a truck driver and owner-operator. No matter where life took him, Maine always held a special place in his heart, and he treasured spending summers there at the lake.
He is survived by his beloved wife, Martha Carlow (Bujold); children Jesse Carlow and his wife Carla, Ryan Carlow, and Erin (Carlow) Mason; grandchildren Tyler, Ryan, and Astrid; sister Laura Guite (Carlow); and several nieces and nephews.
A memorial service will be held Oct. 24, 2026, at 11 a.m. at Tree of Life Church in Pflugerville, Texas.
Louis will be remembered for his service, ingenuity, love for his family, and the lasting friendships he built throughout his life.

title: Are Maine’s votes for sale?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Millions of dollars have been pouring into Maine lately, and not because outsiders think we Mainers are swell folks. No.
They could have sent large checks to the state treasurer for that. Instead, that money has been sent for specialists to pummel us with skewed political assertions. But a lie repeated is still a lie. Repetition does not make something true.
PAC dollars are an investment in Sen. Collins’ votes because that’s where the donors’ gravy is. The only hope they have to get Collins’ votes is to buy ours. Is our vote for sale?
Thankfully, Sen. Collins does have some successes to show. However, increasingly her votes have sent a lot more money elsewhere, including the president’s whims. Really, 30 years of influence buys us road salt, cement and concrete?
Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me six times, shame on me.
M-A Barker
Scarborough

title: 3 takeaways from Waterville’s mayoral forum
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WATERVILLE — Mayoral candidates Michael Morris and Matthew Boulerice vied for votes Wednesday night for the first time since Morris defeated Boulerice three years ago.
In a Morning Sentinel forum hosted at Thomas College, both candidates answered questions about affordability, public safety and economic growth and fielded several questions from the audience.
While Morris made it clear his work as mayor is still in progress, Boulerice pushed for efficiency and proactivity.
Around 45 people attended the forum in Ayotte Auditorium. Here’s what they heard from the candidates.
LEADERSHIP
In his closing statement, Boulerice asked residents to consider whether Waterville is more affordable, safer or more efficient than it was three years ago.
“The mayor sets the tone and brings people together,” Boulerice said. “I firmly believe this election comes down to leadership, setting political differences aside, and deciding what form of leadership we want to move our city forward.”
While Boulerice criticized the incumbent, saying the city is not moving forward, Morris said change was in progress, referencing economic growth, the council’s early start on next year’s budget process and his hope of making Waterville an arts destination.
Boulerice, who focused on process, said that as mayor, he would have made sure the council did not pass a budget that he would need to veto and been more proactive about attracting developers. Morris vetoed the city budget after it passed in July because he felt it relied too heavily on the city’s undesignated fund balance, which he had warned councilors against in his first budget memo.
Morris said Waterville is recovering from frequent city manager turnover in recent years and impacts from the state and federal governments. With a new city manager already working on next year’s budget, Morris focused on plans in place to fight homelessness and improve recreation in Waterville.
“Effective leadership is not about simply moving quickly,” Morris said. “This role requires patience, humility and attention to voices that are beyond the most vocal participants. I understand to folks out there that leadership may look slow … but we’re really making sure that we protect the public resources, and that takes time.”
Asked to choose one topic he would focus on in his first 90 days in office, neither candidate had a concrete answer.
Boulerice said he wanted to see less leniency and more accountability in the city’s approach to addiction and homelessness, building on services like the homeless shelter and Operation HOPE, which the city already offers.
Morris said in the office he deals with these issues every day, and that they take time. When Boulerice criticized Morris for introducing an ordinance Tuesday, just weeks before the election, that calls for banning people from sleeping on sidewalks and keeping their belongings there to protect pedestrians, Morris said he began work on that ordinance in July.
“This is tough work and it’s not fast work,” Morris said. “We’re not playing with private money; we’re playing with public money … people are paying for this.”
WORKING WITH THE COUNCIL
Morris said he approaches working with the City Council by understanding all seven personalities involved. He said he knows what each councilor is passionate about and works with that knowledge to build consensus.
Boulerice said councilors are not aligned enough when they enter meetings, and said the mayor should have an idea of how discussions will go.
“We’ve seen multiple examples of this play out in a public forum, and it looks terrible to the public,” Boulerice said. “It looks like nobody’s on the same page, it looks like some people are hearing about these ideas and topics for the first time.”
Morris pointed out that to comply with public meeting laws and ensure city decision making is a public process, councilors can’t make decisions and have discussions ahead of meetings.
HOT TOPICS
Asked how they would increase city revenues, Boulerice mentioned code enforcement fees and charging for parking.
Morris said the city looked into charging for parking, and because the businesses in The Concourse lease parking spaces, it wouldn’t be a viable option. Instead, he said he’d like to see the city improve on traffic and parking enforcement.
Both candidates said they saw Amazon’s plans to open a facility on the Waterville-Sidney line as a positive development, and Boulerice said he’d talk to more developers to encourage them to come to Waterville. He’d like to see more messaging in the southern parts of the state to make it clear that Waterville is a good destination. Morris said Amazon would be the first of many developments to pick the city and that investments made in infrastructure there would benefit other developments.
Asked whether they would support the use of Flock cameras — one brand of artificial intelligence-enabled license plate readers used by police departments to collect data on virtually anyone who passes those recording devices — both candidates said they would need more information.
Asked about how they would help taxpayers with the rising cost of living, both said they would be stricter on city spending; the source of most of the city’s revenues is property taxes.
While Boulerice remained focused on efficiency on all fronts, Morris said he continues to learn and grow as mayor.
Boulerice asked voters for “the opportunity to show you what the next three years could look like.”
Morris said, “We have the right team, we have the right plans in place, and I am running to see this vision through.”

title: Acadia expanding disability access to a busy oceanfront walking path
text:
Part of one of Acadia National Park’s most popular trails will now be accessible to people with disabilities.
In the last month and a half, trail crews repaired and improved a 500 foot stretch of Ocean Path, which hugs the eastern edge of Mount Desert Island from Sand Beach to Otter Point and is known for its sweeping coastal vistas.
It’s the latest investment centered around improving accessibility in Acadia. In March, the park began construction on a pedestrian path at the top of Cadillac Mountain between the east and west parking lots along Summit Road. Prior to then, the park built the new Hemlock Path boardwalk in the Great Meadow.
Acadia is already renowned for its 45-mile network of accessible carriage roads, but park officials and partners have been working to expand visitor accessibility in other parts of the park.
The 2.2 mile Ocean Path, which is sandwiched between the coast and Park Loop Road, was already accessible from Sand Beach to Thunder Hole — roughly .7 miles — where the trail already has been rehabbed with a mix of concrete and packed gravel, according to the park service.
Past Thunder Hole, one of Acadia’s top year-round destinations, the trail is uneven with rocky gravel, impassable by wheelchairs and mobility scooters.
Now, after six weeks of trail work in collaboration with the Appalachian Mountain Club, park crews have improved a 500 foot stretch at the southern end of Ocean Path, west of Otter Point Overlook. The latest repairs make much of the trail accessible to all, except for the granite staircases that extend the path past Otter Cliffs.
Crews applied compacted rock material to ensure the trail would survive for years to come, according to Friends of Acadia, a local conservation nonprofit.
Friends of Acadia, through its Acadia Trails Forever endowment, funded much of the work, according to the group.
“We’re grateful for the skilled work of the Appalachian Mountain Club trail crew in rehabilitating this section of the Ocean Path,” said Stephanie Clement, the group’s vice president of conservation. “The trail is popular at all times of year, and these improvements help keep it in good shape while making Otter Point’s beautiful coastal views more accessible.”

title: Vote Mary Shannon Lindstrom for Scarborough

title: Sheriff’s deputy killed, another officer hurt in shootout while trying to serve warrant
text:
VAN ZANDT COUNTY, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) - A sheriff’s deputy was killed and a police officer was injured late Tuesday during a warrant service that ended in a shootout, authorities said.
County Court at Law Judge Joshua Wintters confirmed the deputy killed was Adam Sherifi.
According to Van Zandt County Sheriff Kevin Bridger, deputies were assisting the Canton Police Department with serving felony warrants in the 4300 block of State Highway 198. Bridger said the suspect had outstanding warrants for aggravated assault and aggravated assault on a peace officer.
Around 10:22 p.m., shots were reportedly fired from inside the home toward deputies and officers outside. Bridger said law enforcement returned fire and struck the suspect.
During the exchange, a Canton police officer and a Van Zandt County sheriff’s deputy were shot. The officer was taken to a hospital for treatment, and the deputy died from his injuries. The suspect was found dead inside the home from a gunshot wound.
Wintters said the Canton officer who was injured is Christopher Watson. Wintters said Watson is in danger of losing an arm.
“I sure hope that he has the doctors and the surgeons with the ability to make sure that he doesn’t lose the use of that arm,” Wintters said.
Texas Rangers are investigating the shooting.
A vigil was held at the Van Zandt County Courthouse. Nancy White, who was related by marriage to Sherifi, said emotions are running high.
“It’s very quick and very sudden and there’s so many emotions and none of them are good. We shouldn’t be doing this today. He’s a great father. He loves his wife and his children,” White said. “He was the provider. He was the protector. He was who a father and man should be.”
White said the community always shows up in moments like this.
“Whenever somebody is hurting, we always show up. We might bicker like family, but we always show up like family. So the fact that this happened, and you have as many people show up as you did, shows you that we are the community that we love,” White said. “It really shows how much we show up for people and hardships, whether it be tornado, power outage or a loss of a loved one. We need to remember that our first responders are protectors and that we have to protect them and their families, and that we need to provide for them and make sure that they have the things that they need in that process, too.”
