title: Dry stretch continues, blustery days ahead
text:
Dry stretch continues, blustery days ahead
Dry stretch continues, blustery days ahead
A long stretch of dry weather is underway in Maine with plentiful sunshine and seasonable temperatures. More and more cirrus clouds stream in Wednesday afternoon as temperatures peak mainly in the 50s.
Clouds increase in southern Maine Wednesday night as an offshore storm approaches New England. Rain reaches Cape Cod and the Gulf of Maine but is not expected to reach Maine's coastline. Clouds Thursday morning give way to another sunny afternoon.
Winds pick up Thursday morning and gust to 30 to 35 mph. It stays breezy overnight Thursday night, and winds gust to around 30 mph on Friday. Sunshine continues for Friday and the weekend, with no meaningful rain in sight next week.
Highs are in the 50s and low 60s over the weekend, followed by a milder day on Monday. Temperatures in the 60s to around 70 degrees are likely Monday afternoon, followed by a cooler stretch.

title: Suspected gunman in National Guard shooting in DC is charged with multiple firearms offenses
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A Washington man accused of wounding a Georgia National Guard member who tried to help break up a fight has been charged with multiple gun crimes.
Jarrell Lamont Jackson, 41, is charged with unlawful possession of a firearm and ammunition by a felon, assault with a dangerous weapon and possession of a firearm during a crime of violence.
He is accused of shooting Georgia National Guard member Karon Jones, 20, in the leg when guard members sought to intervene in the fight Sunday. Three members of the unit returned fire, wounding Jackson. Neither man sustained life-threatening injuries.
The shooting happened at about 11:10 p.m. as seven or eight guard members in a parked van were monitoring the fight on a sidewalk in southeast Washington in the Eastern Market neighborhood, said Jeffery Carroll, interim chief of the Metropolitan Police Department.
“This brazen attack on the National Guard by a repeat violent offender firing into a crowded corridor is exactly the kind of lawlessness our city refuses to tolerate,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro in announcing the charges.
President Donald Trump deployed the guard to Washington in August 2025 as part of what he said was a crime-fighting mission. The force, which rose to a peak of about 5,000 troops over the summer, has supported arrest operations, patrolled city streets and neighborhoods and participated in cleanup efforts.
Trump’s Republican administration says the deployment has contributed to a decrease in crime in the city, where crime was already on the decline before the National Guard arrived. Officials and activists in the overwhelmingly Democratic city say the deployment is a waste of taxpayer money and has normalized the militarization of a major American city.
The city, which filed a lawsuit in September 2025, has argued that the mobilization is an illegal use of the military for domestic law enforcement. A federal appeals court panel heard arguments Oct. 14 in that lawsuit. A lower court sided with D.C.
Over 2,900 Guard members remain in the district, including more than 500 from Georgia, the second largest contingent behind the District of Columbia, which had 656 members involved in the Joint Task Force-District of Columbia as of Tuesday.

title: True Friends Hall restoration aims to save Louisiana music landmark
text:
DONALDSONVILLE, La. (Aging Untold)— A historic hall that once provided refuge for Black families and performers during segregation is getting new life through a major restoration project.
True Friends Hall, built in the late 1800s in Donaldsonville, served as a cornerstone of the local Black community for decades. The benevolent society that operated the hall helped families in need and provided a gathering place during an era when Black Americans faced widespread discrimination.
“These organizations supported families. If you had a baby, the house burned down, they would come to the aid. These are men who were carpenters, brickmasons,” Darryl Hambrick, founder of the River Road African American Museum, said.
Musical heritage and the Chitlin’ Circuit
During segregation, True Friends Hall was part of the Chitlin’ Circuit, a network of performance venues across the United States for Black musicians, comedians and other entertainers. The circuit helped shape American music by creating new genres such as blues, jazz and rock and roll, producing artists such as Aretha Franklin, B.B. King and Little Richard.
The hall welcomed major performers including New Orleans legends Fats Domino and Irma Thomas, as well as megastars like James Brown. Because African Americans were not allowed at certain venues, True Friends Hall served as a welcoming refuge for Black performers.
“Making their way into New Orleans, you couldn’t stay in hotels, restaurants. Here at True Friends, you got a meal, you got a place to stay, and you had a great time,” Hambrick said.
Community gathering place
Beyond music, True Friends Hall was where Black families and friends could gather and celebrate.
“This was the pulse of the community. You could come here and get help, you could come here and have a great time,” Hambrick said.
Restoration plans
The hall closed in the 1980s and deteriorated over the years. After receiving $1.3 million from the state of Louisiana, Hambrick and the River Road African American Museum are working on a major restoration project.
Plans call for a performance stage, offices and space for a music academy.
The project needs additional funding beyond the state allocation.
Hambrick expects the restoration timeline to be much shorter than the 26 years it took to establish the museum, which involved moving and restoring a Rosenwald school.
“I hope it doesn’t take 26 years to do this building because I don’t have 26 years,” he said.
True Friends Hall is believed to be the largest and oldest existing benevolent hall still standing in Louisiana.

title: Deputy jumps into deep water to rescue nonverbal 8-year-old
text:
LAFAYETTE PARISH, La. (Gray News) - A sheriff’s deputy is being credited with rescuing a nonverbal child who had wandered into a Louisiana pond.
On the evening of Sept. 6, Lafayette Parish sheriff’s deputies responded to the 200 block of Blushing Groom Drive in unincorporated Carencro after an 8-year-old non-speaking child with autism had been reported missing. While en route, deputies were told the child had been found but was seen entering a nearby pond.
When deputies arrived, bystanders were gathered around the bank as the child went underwater.
Recognizing immediate danger to the child, Cpl. Jared Havard entered the neck-deep water while wearing full duty attire. Havard reached the child and brought her safely to the bank, where she was reunited with her family.

title: Nationwide recall hits certain pet meds over potency concerns
text:
Some veterinary drugs recalled nationwide over potency concerns
A company that makes medicine for pets is voluntarily recalling certain compounded veterinary medications that could be too weak to treat animals or possibly be strong enough to cause toxicity or an overdose.
Wedgewood Pharmacy and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Wednesday said the medications are still within their expiration dates, but they're being recalled due to "inconsistencies in the reliability of certain analytical testing data" generated by the company's laboratory.
Related video above: How to stay ahead of recalls
"Through our own quality processes, we identified inconsistencies in certain analytical testing data that affect our confidence in that testing data," a statement on the company's website says.
"When we don't have the level of confidence we require, we believe the responsible thing to do is to act. That is why Wedgewood has initiated a voluntary recall of certain affected products," the company added.
Thus far, Wedgewood has received 98 complaints. Of those, 7 are "serious," according to the FDA, which advises consumers to contact their veterinarians if they have medical concerns.
What products are affected?
The recall covers certain products shipped nationwide from Feb. 18 through Oct. 6 to veterinary practices, pharmacies and other customers.
The medications in question include powders, pastes, suspensions, injections, eye and ear treatments, sprays and gels. They were made for companion, equine, exotic, zoo, wildlife and aquatic animals, and are not intended for animals raised for food, according to the FDA.
The impacted products are not intended for use in food-producing animals, the notice states.
A complete list of affected products — as well as their lot numbers and expiration dates — can be found by clicking here or viewing the table we built below.
What to do if you have an affected product
The FDA says Wedgewood is working with Sedgwick to notify affected customers via email and mail, and it is arranging a refund or, where possible, replacement of recalled products.
Pet owners should stop using an affected medication, keep it, and contact Wedgewood’s recall service at 866-562-5931.
The company's hours are Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. ET, and Saturday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET.
Veterinary practices, pharmacies, and other customers are asked to "immediately" check their inventory and quarantine affected products and contact Wedgewood’s recall services; practices or pharmacies that have dispensed affected products should identify and notify their customers.
The FDA says adverse reactions or quality problems experienced with use of the products may be reported to the FDA at 1888-FDA-VETS or online at http://www.FDA.gov/reportanimalae.

title: Injuries reported after 4 school buses crash on interstate during field trip in Alabama
text:
CHILTON COUNTY, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - Authorities in Alabama are investigating a crash involving four school buses in Chilton County on Wednesday.

title: Rockland library to host discussion on historical fiction book based on witch trials
text:
Rockland Public Library will host a discussion of “Daughters of the Witching Hill” by Mary Sharratt from 6 to 7:30 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 29, in the Community Room. This event is free.
“Daughters of the Witching Hill” is a historical fiction book based on the English witch trials. title: Maine brewers can make hemp drinks the right way. Congress is about to stop us.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Kai Adams is co-founder of Sebago Brewing Company and founder of Mystic Cove THC Drinks in Gorham.
Sebago Brewing Company was founded in 1998. Today, we operate four brewpubs and a production brewery. We have a robust distribution business and our pubs service more than 12,000 guests a week. We employ 225 Mainers with a payroll of nearly $5 million a year.
Sebago Brewing is a trusted Maine company that gives back to our communities and has done so for nearly three decades. Our business is built on our core values of quality and value.
A couple of years ago, a guest asked me over the bar when we were going to make a THC
drink. Around the same time, our sales team started seeing hemp beverages popping up in retail coolers across the state.
Several cannabis companies began calling to ask if we could produce drinks for them. We had just installed a new high-speed canning line and had a team of brewers who understood ingredients, recipes and quality control. We listened to our customers and launched Mystic Cove in February 2025.
I grew up on Sebago Lake, where there’s a special place called Mystic Cove. The name has
always meant “lake life” to me, and it felt like the right fit for a drink meant to be enjoyed slowly with friends. We launched with four 5mg flavors, including a blueberry lemon that could only come from Maine.
Committed to responsible service, we worked with our service staff to implement a THC service policy where a guest who is drinking alcohol could have one Mystic Cove, two for a guest who is not. Every batch is full-spectrum lab tested, each packaging run is tested for potency during the run and nothing ships until the results are in.
We track every ingredient from the moment it arrives, so what the label says is exactly what is in the can. We train our distributors and educate our customers; a new product only works when people understand it.
The people who chose these drinks surprised me. The first guest to order one at our brewpub was almost 70 years old. One of our servers, who no longer drinks, told me it was the first time in years she felt like she was having an experience at a bar instead of just ordering an iced tea. These are adults looking for another option alongside beer, wine and spirits, and they deserve that choice.
Hemp beverages are not the largest part of our business, but they matter a great deal. For an industry facing flat beer sales, two new products gave our distributors and customers something to be excited about.
The work also taught us contract production, which has since brought in new brewing contracts. That is real value for a company that has more than 200 families depending on it.
Under current federal law, these drinks will be banned on Dec. 11, 2026. The new limit
of 0.4 milligrams of THC per container is a ban in all but name, and most of our customers have no idea it is coming. Many of them believe this issue was settled months ago. When the shelves go empty, Maine retailers and distributors will lose sales, customers will take their business elsewhere and the state will lose tax revenue it could be collecting.
There is a better path forward, and it starts with treating hemp beverages like beer. That means requiring age verification, labeling products clearly, taxing them fairly and selling them through the same distributors and retailers that already handle alcohol responsibly.
The Hemp Beverage Alliance, a national trade group I’m a proud member of, is urging Congress toward exactly this kind of framework. Moving these drinks into the cannabis dispensary system would shut out the brewers who have the equipment and experience to make them safely.
To Sen. Collins, Sen. King and Rep. Pingree: craft beer has been one of this state’s great economic success stories, and hemp beverages can be its next chapter. Maine brewers
are ready to make these products the right way, and I urge you to regulate this category instead of banning it.
To every reader who enjoys these drinks or simply believes adults deserve the choice, you can help. Tell Congress, even in a single sentence, why these drinks matter to you and that you support safe, regulated sales. Dec. 11 is getting close, and your voice matters now.

title: Scarborough fire displaces 5 people
text:
An electrical fire in a Scarborough home displaced five people Wednesday morning and sent a firefighter to the hospital to be evaluated for dehydration.
The Scarborough Fire Department responded to a report of a fire in a room on the second floor of a two-story colonial style home at 100 Spurwink Road around 6 a.m. Firefighters had the fire under control in 30 minutes and kept the damage contained to the room where the fire originated.
The five occupants of the home safely evacuated before the firefighters arrived, and one was evaluated for possible smoke inhalation. The firefighter who was transported to the hospital has been released.
The fire was caused by an electrical issue, so Central Maine Power helped cut power to the building. The occupants cannot return until electrical repairs are completed.
The American Red Cross was called to assist the occupants.

title: Music at the Mill returns with Ying Quartet in Brunswick
text:
The acclaimed Ying Quartet will return to Brunswick on Monday as part of the Bowdoin International Music Festival’s Music at the Mill series. Doors open at 6 p.m., the concert is at 7 p.m. and there will be a post-concert reception at 8:15 p.m. at Dutchman’s at Fort Andross Mill, 14 Maine St.
The Ying Quartet — Robin Scott and Janet Ying, violin; Phillip Ying, viola; and David Ying, cello — will play Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s String Quartet No. 19 in C Major, K. 465, “Dissonance,” and Johannes Brahms’ String Quartet No. 1 in C Minor, Op. 51, No. 1.
Mozart and Brahms approached these string quartets with both reverence and ambition. Mozart’s “Dissonance,” dedicated to Joseph Haydn, opens with famously enigmatic harmonies before unfolding into music of extraordinary warmth and vitality. Nearly a century later, Brahms wrestled with the legacy of Ludwig van Beethoven as he composed his first string quartet, revising and refining it over many years. The result is a work of remarkable intensity and craftsmanship, balancing dramatic energy with moments of charm and wit.

title: Extreme adventurer Ash Dykes goes missing for nearly a day during Congo expedition
text:
(Gray News) - Extreme adventurer and TikTok star Ash Dykes went missing for more than 16 hours during an expedition in the Congo Basin.
Dykes has embarked on a six-part mission called “Project 6,” in which he will go on an expedition in six of “the most extreme environments on Earth” over a year.
The first part of the mission was an expedition in the Congo Basin, in which Dykes is attempting a world first by traveling 700 km down the Sangha River in an inflatable kayak.
Dykes has been on the river for more than two weeks and reported that he had passed the halfway mark of his journey on Monday. According to People, he is also accompanied by a local guide and a videographer.
Wednesday morning, the crew gave followers a scare after it was reported that they hadn’t been heard from for more than 16 hours.
“Please bear with us, It’s been more than 16 hours since we last heard from Ash and the team which is concerning,” a post on Dykes’s Facebook page said.
A few hours later, it was reported that Dykes had finally made contact and everyone was safe. According to a Facebook post, the team’s Starlink was out and their power bank had died, so the only way they could make contact was through Dykes’s Garmin.
“There’s no way for them to send videos or updates, they can only send short messages whenever they get signal on the Garmin,” the post said.
This is not the first obstacle Dykes has encountered on this trip.
The first happened as soon as he and his team touched down in Cameroon. He told his followers on TikTok that they discovered the bag containing the pumps for the kayaks was missing and most likely was stuck in Paris. They were able to get the bag, but it did set them back a day or two.
Dykes also reported that their visas had been denied and they needed to find “different way round to enter overland from Cameroon to the Central African Republic.”
While on the trip, Dykes has encountered several risks, including a near run-in with a swarm of Africanized honey bees (also known as killer bees) and a “nasty little sting” from a mysterious insect. Dykes said that he felt something moving inside his shirt on his back and was stung while going to grab it. Although he suspected it was a bee, he wasn’t sure what kind of insect stung him.
Dykes holds five world records, including four world firsts, and has more than 15 million followers on TikTok.
The remaining five expeditions in his Project 6 mission have not been disclosed.

title: Chris Lewey will look out for District 82 and our environment
text:
Most small business owners don’t have the time or energy to add running for office to an already crowded “to-do” list, but Chris Lewey of Fryeburg is doing it with grace and style.
In addition to managing his own business, Lewey wants to go to bat for our threatened natural resources while building a tax structure that’s fair and just. We need both!
Lewey’s running in Maine House District 82 to “protect the natural resources and wildlife Trump loves to threaten” and for which, as a long-standing resident, I have only gratitude. I’ve lived in western Maine since 1977 and seen firsthand how our magnificent environment has been affected, minus the protection it needs.
Lewey also knows rural residents don’t always have access to the affordable healthcare every person needs and he’s ready to fight for that on their behalf as well.
An educator, biologist and small business owner, Lewey wants to represent Brownfield, Fryeburg, Hiram, Lovell and Porter because he deeply loves this district and with a master’s degree in environmental studies (which couldn’t be more appropriate), wants very much to protect it.
Let’s give him a chance to do that.
Toni Seger
Lovell

title: Poll: 1 in 3 Americans support second execution attempt for Christa Pike after failed first try
text:
Poll: 1 in 3 Americans support second execution attempt for Christa Pike after failed first try
Video above: How could a lethal injection go wrong?
A segment of Americans is in favor of a second attempt to execute an inmate who survived an initial execution attempt.
According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Tuesday, Oct. 20, one-third of respondents in the four-day poll thought the government should try again to kill a death row inmate after a first execution attempt failed.
The poll noted that 39% of respondents thought the government should instead allow the inmate who survived an execution attempt to serve a sentence of life in prison.
Twenty-six percent of respondents were not sure what the better choice was.
The poll comes weeks after Christa Gail Pike, 50, survived an execution attempt that was overseen by the Tennessee Department of Correction on Sept. 30.
During the execution attempt, Tennessee Department of Correction officials gave Pike two doses of execution drugs.
Pike survived the execution attempt.
After the execution attempt, Pike was taken to a hospital and was on a ventilator.
It was not clear that Pike would survive, but during her hospital stay, Pike’s attorneys said she woke up and began talking and walking with assistance.
She has since been released from the hospital and returned to the custody of the Tennessee Department of Correction at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, which is a women’s prison in Nashville.
On Sept. 30, the Tennessee Department of Correction released the following statement after the attempted execution of Pike:
“The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office.
"The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.”
Following the failed execution, Gov. Bill Lee announced that Frank Strada, the Commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Correction, would resign in October.
The state also failed to execute inmate Tony Carruthers in May.
Pike was sentenced to death following the 1995 beating and stabbing death of fellow Job Corps worker Colleen Slemmer, who was 19.
Pike was 18 years old at the time of the murder and has been on death row since March 30, 1996.

title: Federal fuel relief offered to Maine farmers and fishermen
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture is launching an $8 billion fuel relief program that offers a one-time cash payment to help food producers manage the strain of high diesel prices and rising operating expenses.
The Harvest Relief program breaks ground as the first federal bailout to extend emergency fuel aid to fishermen as well as farmers, according to USDA. It comes at a time when the dock price of lobster remains static, said Ben Martens, director of the Maine Coast Fisherman’s Association.
“Getting some support in fuel relief would be a big help for many on our working waterfronts,” Martens said. “Many have put off important maintenance work due to the lack of available cash or the increased cost of getting that work done.”
Others, like Christian LaMontagne, are fishing less to cut fuel costs. The Long Island lobsterman is also slowing his boat down to conserve fuel, which doubles the time it takes to get out to where he has set his traps.
In a video he posted to YouTube, LaMontagne broke the problem down into a simple metric: how many lobsters must he catch to fill his fuel tank? In September 2025, that number was 40. This year, he’d have to catch 104.
“Our lobster revenue is going down and our expenses are going up, ” LaMontagne said in the video. “That little gap in between is where we used to live and it just got squashed. It absolutely did. There’s nothing there left.”
The average cost of diesel hit record highs nationally ($6.53 per gallon) and in Maine ($6.55 per gallon) in September, according to AAA. A gallon of diesel currently costs about $6.32 in Maine, up almost $3 from a year ago.
Gaining a seat at the federal table is a victory for Maine’s seafood industry and its specialty crop growers, like wild blueberry, potato and apple farmers, but the program appears to create a two-tiered system that favors growers of row crops such as corn, soy and wheat.
Heartland grain farmers get fixed payout rates, automated, prefilled applications, and a hard-and-fast November payout date. Fishermen and specialty crop growers don’t have a defined share of the $8 billion fund. Instead, they get a “submit receipts and wait” relief model.
Following the establishment of the USDA’s Office of Seafood in April, federal agriculture leaders have worked to integrate seafood producers into standard safety net programs that have historically been reserved for land-based farmers.
The creation of the Harvest Fuel Relief Program follows visits by federal agricultural officials, including USDA Undersecretary Richard Fordyce, to coastal communities like Stonington and Prospect Harbor to talk with fishermen about that exclusion.
While land-based farmers benefit from rapid federal crop insurance payouts, fishermen have traditionally had to rely on federal fishery disaster declarations, which don’t happen often and have three- to five-year waits before relief is distributed.
The financial lifeline comes at a challenging time for Maine’s working waterfronts and farms.
State harvest data shows that last year’s lobster catch was valued at $461.4 million: a 20% drop from 2024 after adjusting for inflation. Meanwhile, Maine’s specialty farmers face identical diesel price surges without access to standard commodity price floors.
The explicit inclusion of fisheries provides the sector hope, but it is impossible to say how much this helps Maine fishermen until final criteria are set, said Carl Wilson, commissioner of the Maine Department of Marine Resources.
Maine funded a fuel rebate program to help fishermen survive pandemic-era economic shocks.
Patrice McCarron, executive director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, welcomed the federal recognition of compounding fuel expenses across working waterfronts, but also said it was too early to say how helpful it will be. Fishermen need it, she said.
“Higher diesel prices affect far more than the cost of running the boat,” McCarron said. “They drive up the cost of bait, traps, equipment and nearly everything else needed to operate a lobster business, squeezing already-thin profit margins.”
It’s unclear how much of the $8 billion relief fund will be left for them to divvy up. The USDA told specialty farmers and fishermen to gather fuel cost records and email them to [email protected] for agency consideration when setting rates.
The Maine Coast Fisherman’s Association is working to provide data to USDA to justify fishermen’s inclusion, Martens said. He asks that as many fishermen as possible write to USDA to help shape the developing structure and make sure some of that fund is set aside just for them.
The organization also has created an online form that will help fishermen generate an individualized letter to submit to USDA to justify their inclusion in the bailout. It will anonymize and aggregate the form responses to develop a fleet-wide case for eligibility, Martens said.
“While $8 billion sounds like a lot of money, it will quickly get absorbed into the agriculture community,” he said. “We need to act fast.”

title: He built an M&M museum and keeps adding to the collection
text:
WAGGONER, Ill. (InvestigateTV) - It may not look very big on the outside, but once you step inside Beal’s M&M Museum in Waggoner you’ll be treated to different flavors of iconic memorabilia.
The museum houses more than 5,000 M&M items displayed from wall to wall and floor to ceiling.
Steve and Patricia Beale started the collection with California Raisins. When Steve Beale could not find them anymore, he switched to M&Ms.
The collection was kept in a bedroom in their house. When they could not open the door anymore, they decided to build a space to display it.
The couple built a 20-by-30-foot shed and kept adding to the collection. None of the items are for sale.
“Once you start selling, then you’re not a collector,” Steve told us, “you’re in it for the money.”
The museum is free to visit. Steve Beale said he likes to share what he has and what he knows.
The museum has had visitors from around the world. The Beales give visitors a fun-size bag of M&Ms, and the museum has become a stop on historic Route 66.
Steve Beale said his favorite kind of M&Ms is peanut. Patricia Beale said her favorite is peanut butter.

title: 'Put your paws together': Smithsonian Zoo names red panda after nationwide vote
text:
'Put your paws together': Smithsonian Zoo names red panda after nationwide vote
The votes are in — the Smithsonian Zoo has officially named its new red panda cub.
Related video: New pandas arrive at Zoo Atlanta
The zoo said in June, red pandas Keahi and Rocket welcomed a female cub at its conservation campus in Front Royal, Virginia. The cub, according to a previous social media post, has so far "distinguished herself with bold and feisty behavior."
Earlier this month, the zoo provided three possible names for the cub, opening up a nationwide poll in an effort to choose her official name.
A voting form previously listed her three possible names: Dolly, inspired by country music legend Dolly Parton; Pyra, meaning "heat" in Greek; and Dolpa, a region of Nepal home to wild red pandas.
On Oct. 20, the zoo posted the final results.
"With flaming locks of auburn fur and a cuteness that extends beyond the hours of 9 to 5, this little firecracker officially has a name: Dolly," the zoo said in an updated post on Facebook.
Officials said more than 20,000 votes were cast, with 65% of the vote in favor of the name Dolly.

title: A chemical tank explodes in Ohio, forcing evacuations and prompting fears of another blast
text:
TOLEDO, Ohio (AP) — A chemical tank explosion in Toledo, Ohio, forced hundreds of residents to evacuate their homes or shelter in place Wednesday due to fears of a toxic release and the possibility of another explosion.
Video showed a plume billowing from the tank Wednesday morning, hours after the leak first erupted Tuesday night.
Some residents felt irritation in their eyes and throats, and one sheriff’s deputy who responded to the blast drove himself to a hospital because he felt unwell, city officials said.
MC Tank Transport said the tank contained glycidyl methacrylate, which it described as “an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.”
The leaking tank was in a largely industrial area. Nearly 1,000 residents were told to evacuate overnight within a 1-mile (1.6-kilometer) radius of the explosion, Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz said at a news conference Wednesday morning.
A shelter-in-place zone order covering a 3-mile (4.8-kilometer) radius included neighborhoods along the Lake Erie shoreline and stretched just across the state line into Michigan.
Health officials said the chemical was mostly an irritant so far, causing watery eyes, and that tests were ongoing to determine how much toxicity was in the air.
Kristine Kowalinski, who lives just outside the impacted area, said she was staying inside because she’s sensitive to even wood burning outside. She said she’s worried about what’s in the air and on the ground.
“My main concern is how did that affect everything overnight when it was raining down on cars, houses, my garden,” she said.
Kapszukiewicz said the chemical is liquid inside the tank but becomes a gas when released.
“There is still concern that the tank is emitting this chemical and it has the potential within 12 hours of the incident to be explosive,” the mayor said, adding that it can hold 5,500 gallons of the chemical in liquid form. He said officials don’t know what caused the explosion.
People who come into contact with glycidyl methacrylate may feel as if their eyes, nose, mouth and skin are burning, the city fire department said. Overexposure can lead to headache, dizziness, tiredness, nausea and vomiting.
“It’s really toxic if you touch it, if you ingest it,” said Karim Baroudi, director of the Toledo-Lucas County Health Department. “Now we’re trying to kind of determine how much of a toxicity is in the air that the people are breathing so we can give better guidance.”
Baroudi advised residents to close their windows and that those who “feel irritation in the eyes, heavily breathing, just take a shower for now.” The fire department said those who experience symptoms should contact a medical professional.
First responders, hazmat and safety teams are not approaching the tank because of the risk of more explosions, and will reassess conditions later Wednesday morning, Kapszukiewicz said.
Arkansas-based MC Tank Transport said in a statement the company is working with the fire department and other emergency authorities. Company representatives were on their way to Toledo, Kapszukiewicz said.
“Our immediate and overriding concern is the safety of area residents, emergency responders and our employees,” the company said.
___
McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire. Associated Press writer Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

title: Polymarket removes contract allowing wagers on fate of Cornell students accused of sexual assault
text:
Polymarket removes contract allowing wagers on fate of Cornell students accused of sexual assault
Polymarket has removed a contract from its prediction market platform that allowed users to wager on whether any of the seven men accused of sexually assaulting or exploiting a Cornell student in 2024 will be charged with a felony sex crime.
The market was made available on Sept. 30 and was slated to close on Jan. 31. It had more than $450,000 in volume before it was taken off Polymarket's international platform. The company's U.S. exchange is regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which bans trading related to “activity that is unlawful under Federal or State law.”
“Our primary goal at Polymarket is to bring objective, data-driven insight to the most important questions of our time,” a Polymarket spokesperson said Tuesday. “This market addressed whether the government would take action — a process that deserves scrutiny, particularly in a case of such serious concern. That said, we believe in the wisdom of crowds, have heard them loud and clear, and removed the market.”
Front Office Sports was the first to report on the contract.
Some outcry over the Polymarket contract has been aimed at its celebrity promoters. Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has an endorsement deal with Polymarket, and he recently appeared in a star-studded commercial that also included cameos by Derek Jeter, Eli Manning, Sue Bird and several celebrities.
Messages were left by the AP on Tuesday with representatives for James, Jeter, Manning and Bird.
Polymarket also has partnership agreements with the NHL, Major League Baseball, Major League Soccer, the UFC and ATP Tour. Messages were left by the AP seeking comment from each organization.
A spokesman for Spike Lee, who also appeared in the Polymarket commercial with James, said the director had no comment. Messages also were left with representatives for actors Craig Robinson, John Leguizamo and Alexandra Daddario — who were also part of the commercial with James.
A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All of those men have denied her allegations, saying either that their interactions were consensual or that they weren’t involved.
Online critics characterized the Polymarket contract as degrading and questioned why celebrity ambassadors would associate themselves with the company. An online petition launched by UltraViolet, a women-led national advocacy organization, singled out James, Manning, Daddario and model Emily Ratajkowski while calling on other famous endorsers to cut ties with the company.
A message was left seeking comment from a representative for Ratajkowski, who also appears in the celebrity-filled commercial with James.
Prediction markets provide an opportunity to trade on the result of future events. Sports account for a major portion of the volume generated by the array of typically yes-or-no question, depending on the platform.
When a U.S. Army sergeant was indicted earlier this year over bets on the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, he was trading on Polymarket’s international platform. The Associated Press reported in April that 50 brand new accounts on Polymarket’s international platform placed substantial bets on a U.S.-Iran ceasefire in the hours, even minutes, before President Donald Trump announced a ceasefire on social media, raising concerns of insider trading.
Polymarket had an active market on its international platform on Tuesday that allowed customers to trade on whether Cornell president Michael Kotlikoff will be out by Oct. 31. It had more than $10,700 in volume.

title: Meet Salem, our Adoptable Pet of the Week
text:
Meet Salem, our Adoptable Pet of the Week in Greater Portland
This week's featured adoptable pet from the Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland is Salem, a spunky and smart 6-month-old puppy who is looking for a home just in time for Halloween.
Matt Blanchard of the Animal Refuge League said Salem has lived with children and cats in the past and enjoys playing with other dogs.
Salem likes making friends wherever she goes, but Blanchard also noted that the pup is still learning some manners.
"She kind of goes between bouts of being a very polite, sweet girl — she is well-trained, she is very intelligent — but also has those puppy tendencies that come out. She likes to get a little jumpy sometimes," Blanchard said. "She's definitely looking for a family that is going to kind of help her manage those puppy tendencies and grow up into being a great adult dog."
More information about Salem is available on the Animal Refuge League's website, as long as she is still looking for her forever home.
Anyone who is interested in meeting Salem or other adoptable pets can visit the Animal Refuge League's shelter at 217 Landing Road in Westbrook between 11 a.m. and 4 p.m., except on Wednesdays, when the shelter is closed for adoptions.
The Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland does adoptions on a first-come, first-served basis. On the days the shelter is open, sign-in sheets will be placed on the front door at 9 a.m. to track the order of arrival of adopters who show up early. People who arrive early are asked to remain on the campus once they sign in.
Dog owners who are interested in adopting dogs that are older than 6 months are required to have their dogs meet the adoptable pet before a new pet can be brought home.

title: Sheriff’s deputy killed, another officer hurt in shootout while trying to serve warrant
text:
VAN ZANDT COUNTY, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) - A sheriff’s deputy was killed and a police officer was injured late Tuesday during a warrant service that ended in a shootout, authorities said.
County Court at Law Judge Joshua Wintters confirmed the deputy killed was Adam Sherifi.
According to Van Zandt County Sheriff Kevin Bridger, deputies were assisting the Canton Police Department with serving felony warrants in the 4300 block of State Highway 198. Bridger said the suspect had outstanding warrants for aggravated assault and aggravated assault on a peace officer.
Around 10:22 p.m., shots were reportedly fired from inside the home toward deputies and officers outside. Bridger said law enforcement returned fire and struck the suspect.
During the exchange, a Canton police officer and a Van Zandt County sheriff’s deputy were shot. The officer was taken to a hospital for treatment, and the deputy died from his injuries. The suspect was found dead inside the home from a gunshot wound.
Wintters said the Canton officer who was injured is Christopher Watson. Wintters said Watson is in danger of losing an arm.
“I sure hope that he has the doctors and the surgeons with the ability to make sure that he doesn’t lose the use of that arm,” Wintters said.
Texas Rangers are investigating the shooting.
A vigil was held at the Van Zandt County Courthouse. Nancy White, who was related by marriage to Sherifi, said emotions are running high.
“It’s very quick and very sudden and there’s so many emotions and none of them are good. We shouldn’t be doing this today. He’s a great father. He loves his wife and his children,” White said. “He was the provider. He was the protector. He was who a father and man should be.”
White said the community always shows up in moments like this.
“Whenever somebody is hurting, we always show up. We might bicker like family, but we always show up like family. So the fact that this happened, and you have as many people show up as you did, shows you that we are the community that we love,” White said. “It really shows how much we show up for people and hardships, whether it be tornado, power outage or a loss of a loved one. We need to remember that our first responders are protectors and that we have to protect them and their families, and that we need to provide for them and make sure that they have the things that they need in that process, too.”

Lawsuit filed against 'Princess Diaries' actor: Couple alleges elder abuse, fraud
text:
Lawsuit filed against 'Princess Diaries' actor: Couple alleges elder abuse, fraud
A couple has filed a lawsuit against a former "Princess Diaries" actor, alleging fraud and elder abuse against him.
Related video: Reese’s pumpkins come with a new disclaimer after lawsuit
In court documents obtained by USA Today and People Magazine, Erik von Detten and Rosland Capital LLC— a precious metals company he worked for as a broker— are facing a lawsuit filed by Sheila, 85, and 97-year-old Norman Greenberg.
The Greenbergs are a married couple living in La Jolla, California, court documents said.
According to court papers, the couple claims that the precious-metal asset management firm and von Detten exploited "the fears and vulnerability of seniors" by claiming that "the ancient stability" of gold and other precious metals would help them avoid forthcoming "complete financial ruin."
The couple says they paid more than $2.1 million for gold coins worth only $1.3 million, saying they later found they had paid more than what the coins were worth due to "substantial markups."
Their lawsuit also accuses Rosland of capitalizing on older customers' concerns about their finances by promoting gold and other precious metals as stable investments, USA Today reported.
In addition, the couple claimed that von Detten, 44, persuaded them to invest an additional $114,000 in gold through their family trust after they depleted their retirement funds.
According to the filing, von Detten—who played superficial heartthrob Josh Bryant in the Anne Hathaway-led 2001 film "Princess Diaries"—was assigned to work with Sheila and Norman Greenberg after they asked to speak with the top advisor.
Rosland Capital later filed for bankruptcy after the Greenbergs filed their lawsuit.
Court documents said the couple had been drawn to the company after seeing a TV commercial that they said created concern about the safety of their wealth.
The actor stepped away from the spotlight after reprising his role as Sid in "Toy Story 3." He did, however, star in the Lifetime movie "My Acting Coach Nightmare" in 2024.
He joined Rosland Capital in 2018.
Officials said the couple are seeking at least $900,000 in damages and want to recover their losses.
In addition to claims of fraud and elder abuse, von Detten and the company are accused of breach of fiduciary duty and conversion.
A case management conference is scheduled for Nov. 9, 2026.

title: Trump announces $8B plan to provide relief for farmers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH/Gray News) - President Donald Trump announced a new $8 billion program intended to provide temporary relief to farmers heavily impacted by rising fuel and production costs.
Trump made the announcement while speaking in Park City, Kansas, Monday. He was appearing at a rally in support of Sen. Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent who’s in a tight race with Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton.
During his speech, Trump said the program, called the Harvest Fuel Relief program, is “in support to offset diesel costs during this harvest season.” In a news release, the U.S. Department of Agriculture said it will make $8 billion available for one-time payments to farmers.
“This $8 billion investment will help bring certainty to our farmers during this harvest so they can continue to feed our nation,” U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brook Rollins said in the department’s news release.
It would be the second such relief package for farmers in 11 months after a $12 billion aid package was announced last December.
Kansas farmers said it was a mix of welcome news, but frustrations remain and expectations are measured.
While the president said that the $8 billion relief package is coming, Matt Splitter, a Rice County farmer, said he’s more concerned with fair markets and trade policy.
“When an administration does some retaliatory actions to places or other countries where we do source a lot of our inputs, you know, fertilizer being one of them, then it does put some, for agriculturalists, for farmers, it puts some unfair tariffs on the products that we rely on to raise a crop,” Splitter said.
Splitter said the timing of another relief package for farmers fits, as fall harvest and planting is well underway.
“This is our peak season. This is where a lot of our diesel is burned in our machines,” Splitter said.
The timing of the announcement is also not lost when it comes to the midterm election, which is two weeks away.
The relief program for farmers is among the latest financial promises from President Trump. Last month, he pledged to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and the Senate in the midterm elections.
The president repeated the promise during Monday’s speech in Park City.
President Trump also pushed for year-round E15, which is a big desire for corn farmers.
“With Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E-15 permanent. But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it. That’s it. I’m only doing it for him,” Trump said on Monday.
Splitter said his farm is just six miles from an ethanol plant and doesn’t believe the issue should be dependent on who wins the Kansas Senate race.
“The people are voting for who they want, whether it be Marshall or Hamilton, whoever it may be. But then the administration would be retaliatory to what the people have voted for. So I just, I’m not a big fan of that kind of retaliatory actions,” Splitter said.
The Kansas Corn Growers Association said it appreciates the Trump administration’s efforts to address the challenges facing Kansas farmers.
It added that the Harvest Fuel Relief program will help ease the burden, which it says includes signing year-round E15 into law.

title: Federal fuel relief offered to Maine farmers and fishermen
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture is launching an $8 billion fuel relief program that offers a one-time cash payment to help food producers manage the strain of high diesel prices and rising operating expenses.
The Harvest Relief program breaks ground as the first federal bailout to extend emergency fuel aid to fishermen as well as farmers, according to USDA. It comes at a time when the dock price of lobster remains static, said Ben Martens, director of the Maine Coast Fisherman’s Association.
“Getting some support in fuel relief would be a big help for many on our working waterfronts,” Martens said. “Many have put off important maintenance work due to the lack of available cash or the increased cost of getting that work done.”
Others, like Christian LaMontagne, are fishing less to cut fuel costs. The Long Island lobsterman is also slowing his boat down to conserve fuel, which doubles the time it takes to get out to where he has set his traps.
In a video he posted to YouTube, LaMontagne broke the problem down into a simple metric: how many lobsters must he catch to fill his fuel tank? In September 2025, that number was 40. This year, he’d have to catch 104.
“Our lobster revenue is going down and our expenses are going up, ” LaMontagne said in the video. “That little gap in between is where we used to live and it just got squashed. It absolutely did. There’s nothing there left.”
The average cost of diesel hit record highs nationally ($6.53 per gallon) and in Maine ($6.55 per gallon) in September, according to AAA. A gallon of diesel currently costs about $6.32 in Maine, up almost $3 from a year ago.
Gaining a seat at the federal table is a victory for Maine’s seafood industry and its specialty crop growers, like wild blueberry, potato and apple farmers, but the program appears to create a two-tiered system that favors growers of row crops such as corn, soy and wheat.
Heartland grain farmers get fixed payout rates, automated, prefilled applications, and a hard-and-fast November payout date. Fishermen and specialty crop growers don’t have a defined share of the $8 billion fund. Instead, they get a “submit receipts and wait” relief model.
Following the establishment of the USDA’s Office of Seafood in April, federal agriculture leaders have worked to integrate seafood producers into standard safety net programs that have historically been reserved for land-based farmers.
The creation of the Harvest Fuel Relief Program follows visits by federal agricultural officials, including USDA Undersecretary Richard Fordyce, to coastal communities like Stonington and Prospect Harbor to talk with fishermen about that exclusion.
While land-based farmers benefit from rapid federal crop insurance payouts, fishermen have traditionally had to rely on federal fishery disaster declarations, which don’t happen often and have three- to five-year waits before relief is distributed.
The financial lifeline comes at a challenging time for Maine’s working waterfronts and farms.
State harvest data shows that last year’s lobster catch was valued at $461.4 million: a 20% drop from 2024 after adjusting for inflation. Meanwhile, Maine’s specialty farmers face identical diesel price surges without access to standard commodity price floors.
The explicit inclusion of fisheries provides the sector hope, but it is impossible to say how much this helps Maine fishermen until final criteria are set, said Carl Wilson, commissioner of the Maine Department of Marine Resources.
Maine funded a fuel rebate program to help fishermen survive pandemic-era economic shocks.
Patrice McCarron, executive director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, welcomed the federal recognition of compounding fuel expenses across working waterfronts, but also said it was too early to say how helpful it will be. Fishermen need it, she said.
“Higher diesel prices affect far more than the cost of running the boat,” McCarron said. “They drive up the cost of bait, traps, equipment and nearly everything else needed to operate a lobster business, squeezing already-thin profit margins.”
It’s unclear how much of the $8 billion relief fund will be left for them to divvy up. The USDA told specialty farmers and fishermen to gather fuel cost records and email them to [email protected] for agency consideration when setting rates.
The Maine Coast Fisherman’s Association is working to provide data to USDA to justify fishermen’s inclusion, Martens said. He asks that as many fishermen as possible write to USDA to help shape the developing structure and make sure some of that fund is set aside just for them.
The organization also has created an online form that will help fishermen generate an individualized letter to submit to USDA to justify their inclusion in the bailout. It will anonymize and aggregate the form responses to develop a fleet-wide case for eligibility, Martens said.
“While $8 billion sounds like a lot of money, it will quickly get absorbed into the agriculture community,” he said. “We need to act fast.”

title: Mel Brooks, 100, asked ‘Spaceballs’ team to film his scenes first due to his age
text:
Mel Brooks, 100, asked ‘Spaceballs’ team to film his scenes first due to his age
Mel Brooks is making sure he'll be in the new "Spaceballs" movie.
The legendary actor and filmmaker apparently asked to film his scenes for “Spaceballs: The New One” before the rest of the cast because he was 100, co-star Daphne Zuniga, who plays Princess Vespa, said.
“It was his idea,” Zuniga said Sunday during a panel in Hartford, Connecticut. “You better film me now because I’m 100.”
Related video above | Mel Brooks reveals secrets of "Young Frankenstein"
Brooks, who turned 100 in June, worked with the film’s writers and remains a “big influence” on the sequel, Zuniga said.
The movie reunites Brooks with Zuniga, Rick Moranis and Bill Pullman, who starred in the 1987 original.
“Spaceballs: The New One” is scheduled to open April 23, 2027.
Brooks, known for his films “The Producers,” “Blazing Saddles” and “Young Frankenstein,” is among a small group of entertainers to have won an Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony.
As he celebrated his 100th birthday earlier this year, Brooks reflected on his legacy and career. He said he doesn't think much about his mortality, saying laughingly, “I gave up after 60 thinking about it because if I did, I’d be thinking about it all the time. So I don’t think about it much. When and if it happens it’s going to be a sad day — for everybody but me."
“I enjoy living,” he added. “I’d like to do it as long as I can.”

title: ‘This is what I remember’: Teacher speaks after surviving Oregon elementary school shooting
text:
BEND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - Becky Drury, a teacher who was shot at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend last week, shared a message Wednesday about what she remembers from that day.
“I’d like to share my memories of what happened at Silver Rail Elementary because I want to make sure the events of that day and my actions in particular are reported accurately.
“Here is what I remember: Once I realized something was happening outside, I ran to see what was going on. I then saw the shooter and immediately ran back into the classroom. I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there. Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground.
“Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured. I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else. So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again.
“This is what I remember. I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act.
“What happened in that classroom was unimaginable, and like so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy. My thoughts are with those who were hurt, those we lost, their families, our school, and the Bend community. I am truly grateful for the kindness and support we have received as we face the difficult days ahead together.
“We also ask for continued privacy and space as we continue down the long road of recovery.
“Finally, to the media, please utilize trusted voices in our community. Accurate, respectful reporting is a truly important service that will help heal the wounds inflicted by that awful day.”
The shooting occurred last Thursday when police say a 16-year-old former student went into Silver Rail Elementary and fired inside a special needs classroom.
Teacher Megan Lambert, 25, was killed along with students Rhoam Summer, 5, and two other children, ages 8 and 11.
Drury needed surgery on her left arm and right hand, her husband Will Drury said.
A student, 7-year-old Saylor, was also hurt in the shooting. She was given life-saving care at the school and taken to Oregon Health & Science University, police said last week.
Previously, Bend police said Drury had shielded Saylor during the shooting, but Drury’s statement contradicts that information.
A motive for the school shooting currently remains unclear.

title: Mortgage rate history: 1972 to 2026
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mortgage rate history: 1972 to 2026
Key takeaways
- As of October 21, 2026, the average rate for a 30-year, fixed loan was 7.39% — up from the beginning of the year, and higher than the 2025 average of 6.66%.
- Over the past four decades, the 30-year fixed rate ranged from a 2021 low of 2.65% to a 1981 high above 18%.
- The average 30-year fixed rate bottomed in 2021 at just under 3%.
- 87% of all borrowers in 2025 paid more than the most competitive rate available to them, according to Bankrate’s Hidden Homeownership Tax research — meaning rate history matters less to your bill than whether you actually shopped your own rate.
The residential mortgage as we know it today is less than a century old. In fact, until the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) was established in 1934, only one in 10 Americans owned a home. That all changed with the introduction of the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage during the Great Depression, which made homeownership possible for millions.
Recent changes in mortgage rates have put a strain on the housing market. Historically low rates at the start of the 2020s led to a surge in home prices, and rates have stayed consistently between 6% and 7% since the Federal Reserve raised rates in 2022. However, home prices remain high. This combination of climbing prices with higher-than-recent rates has made housing affordability a major problem.
Mortgage rates over time
-  Average 30-year fixed mortgage rate by year Here is a timeline of the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate by year. Bankrate first began aggregating rate data in 1982; all data prior was sourced from Freddie Mac. The 2026 average is through October 14. * Freddie Mac rate data
Current mortgage rates
As of October 21, 2026, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate is 7.39%, per Bankrate’s lender survey. Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey, a separate weekly benchmark based on conforming purchase loans with 20% down and strong credit, put the 30-year fixed average at 7.40% as of October 15, 2026 — unchanged from the week before and up from 6.27% a year earlier.
Rates fell through most of the first two months of 2026, bottoming at a 2026 low of 6.01% on Feb. 19 — the lowest weekly average since September 2022. They’ve climbed back into the mid-6% range since, as persistent inflation and Treasury yields have kept upward pressure on mortgage pricing.
You don't have to accept the first rate you're quoted.
In 2025, the typical borrower overpaid by $278 a month — $3,343 a year — simply by not comparing enough lenders, according to Bankrate’s Hidden Homeownership Tax research. You can’t control the Fed, oil prices or Treasury yields, but you can control how many lenders you compare — and that’s the part most borrowers skip.
2020s mortgage rate trends
Entering 2020, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was already below 4%. Then the COVID-19 pandemic pushed it to a weekly low of 2.65% in January 2021 — the lowest rate on record.
In 2022, the Federal Reserve began raising its benchmark interest rate to fight inflation, and mortgage rates rose sharply alongside it. By October 2023, the 30-year mortgage rate broke through 8% for the first time since 2000.
Rates stayed in the 6s and 7s through most of 2024. The Fed cut its benchmark rate three times in late 2024 and three more times in 2025, but mortgage rates didn’t fall in lockstep — they drifted down over the course of 2025, closing the year averaging 6.66%.
Rates kept falling into early 2026 until the conflict with Iran disrupted oil markets in February, which analysts tied to a jump in 10-year Treasury yields — and mortgage rates followed that upward trajectory.
2010s mortgage rate trends
In the 2010s, the 30-year mortgage rate trended downward, beginning in the 4% range, dipping below 4%, and ending the decade back in that range. These low rates were brought on in part by the Federal Reserve’s Great Recession-era policies.
2000s mortgage rate trends
Driven by the subprime mortgage crisis of the late 2000s, the 30-year mortgage rate tumbled from about 8% at the start of the decade down to 5.4% by 2009. At the time, the Federal Reserve implemented quantitative easing, buying mortgage-backed securities in bulk to drive down interest rates and usher in an economic recovery.
1990s mortgage rate trends
The 1990s saw a significant shift in the 30-year mortgage rate, which plunged to an average of 6.91% in 1998. This drop was brought on by the dot-com bubble, an era when investors rushed to buy stocks from overvalued technology companies. When these stocks plummeted, investors turned their focus to fixed-income investments, such as bonds. As bond prices rose and yields fell, mortgage rates, which follow the 10-year Treasury yield, also declined.
1980s mortgage rate trends
The median U.S. home price rose from $63,700 in 1980 to $123,900 by 1990, according to the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Mortgage rates peaked at 18.4% in October 1981 alone as the Federal Reserve fought runaway inflation — though the full 1981 annual average came in lower, at 16.64%, since rates were lower for the rest of the year. Once inflation cooled, rates eased into the 9% range, closing the decade at 9.78%.
1970s mortgage rate trends
The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage started the decade at about 7.5% in 1971 (the earliest year with available data), according to Freddie Mac. By 1979, the rate had risen to an average of 11.2%. During this decade, the Federal Reserve’s expansionary policy and other factors helped drive inflation and borrowing costs way up.
Mortgage rate predictions
While we can try to guess based on historical data, no one knows for certain what will happen to future mortgage rates over time — whether they’ll change at all, or when. Still, we regularly ask economists and other experts to weigh in. For week-to-week predictions, check out our mortgage rate poll.
Is buying right for you at today’s rates?
If your monthly payment at today’s average rate fits your budget with room for property tax and insurance increases, buy now — home prices have historically risen faster than rates have fallen, so waiting rarely pays off. If the payment only works at a rate meaningfully below where the market sits today, hold off and spend that time raising your credit score above 740 and building a 20% down payment — both will do more for your rate than guessing when the Fed moves next. Estimate your monthly payment with Bankrate’s mortgage calculator.
Learn more: How mortgage rates are determined
Is refinancing right for you at today’s rates?
If you can cut your rate by at least 0.75 to 1.0 percentage points and you plan to stay in the home for five or more years, refinancing is usually worth the cost. If you’re planning to sell within the next two to three years, run the break-even math first — it may not pay off.
Here’s the math: Closing costs on a refinance typically run 2% to 5% of the loan amount. On a $300,000 balance, that’s $6,000 to $15,000 upfront. If cutting your rate saves you $300 a month, a $11,000 closing cost takes about 37 months — just over three years — to break even. Stay past that point and you come out ahead; sell or refinance again before it, and you lose money on the deal.
78.7% of refinance borrowers overpaid on their new rate in 2025, according to Bankrate’s Hidden Homeownership Tax research. Compare current refinance rates from at least three lenders to find the best offer for you.
Next steps
Mortgage rates are affected by two things: world events and your personal finances. As we’ve seen recently, the COVID-19 pandemic led to bottomed-out mortgage rates — the lowest our country has ever seen. On a smaller, more recent scale, the conflict with Iran has caused upward pressure on mortgage rates as oil prices and inflation rise.
You can’t control major global events, but you can control your finances. Saving for a down payment, paying down debt and growing your income will all land you with a better mortgage offer. You also need to shop around lenders because not every lender will give you a great deal. Bankrate consistently has mortgage offers below the market average. Use our tool to compare mortgage rates with top lenders and weigh the pros and cons of each.

title: Orionid meteor shower peaks tonight — Here's how to see it
text:
Orionid meteor shower peaks tonight — Here's how to see it
It's your second chance to see an October meteor shower.
The second annual meteor shower of October, the Orionids, is a fairly dependable meteor shower. The Orionids’ radiant is the constellation Orion, specifically its bright star Betelgeuse. The meteors of the Orionids come from the debris of the comet Halley, which passes near Earth about every 76 years, but delivers two meteor showers to Earth’s atmosphere per year — the Orionids in the fall and the Eta Aquarids in May.
The previous meteor shower in October was the Draconids.
The Orionids are known to be bright and fast, and the fall weather usually makes for ideal conditions to view them. According to NASA, the Orionids can show up to 20 meteors per hour on a good night, though some showers have been known to reach 60-70 meteors per hour.
The evening and early morning of Oct. 21-22 is just the peak — you may be able to see this shower anytime from Oct. 2 to Nov. 7.
As with any meteor shower, you want to find a spot away from light pollution and allow your eyes to adjust to the night sky. This can usually take about 15-20 minutes.
The shower's radiant will appear to be Orion's left arm, in the northeast night sky, just around midnight ET. Best viewing may be between midnight and 2 a.m. ET, or after moonset, which is around 2:30 a.m. ET.
You will want a night of clear weather for the best meteor viewing. Thankfully, conditions this evening look pretty clear. Check your local forecast or check here.

title: Maine proposes change to moose hunting near Moosehead Lake
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA — The Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife will seek to expand moose hunting in September near Jackman, but not near Greenville.
The proposal is an attempt to balance the interests of hunters with the growth of fall tourism near Moosehead Lake.
Sporting camps and hunting guides said expanded hunting in that region would be good for their businesses, spread out their clients in the woods and reduce impacts for private landowners. Hospitality businesses and guides who lead moose watching tours said an added week of hunting in September would curtail their businesses during peak foliage.
On Wednesday, after officials announced the proposed rule at a meeting of the department’s advisory council, stakeholders described it as a compromise.
“I think the department has brought something forward I feel everyone should be able to look at and say, that’s a reasonable outcome,” Christopher Richards, of Hermon, a board member of the Maine Professional Guides Association, said. “Hopefully it’s something that can move forward without too much heartburn.”
The next step is a rulemaking process with opportunity for public comment.
There are two possible weeks in which a hunter can harvest a bull moose in Maine — one in September and one in October — although the state historically restricted some wildlife management districts to one week only.
Last winter, the department proposed opening both September and October hunts in all 20 of Maine’s 29 districts where moose hunting is allowed. Because of a swell of opposition from Greenville, which has especially marketed itself as a place to see rich colors and wildlife, the state ultimately allowed two weeks of bull hunting in 2026 in every district except four near Moosehead Lake. This year, those four districts only got permits for October.
The state convened a working group to discuss the issue and has been considering the issue internally for months. Nate Webb, the state’s wildlife division director, announced a proposed solution on Wednesday at the advisory council meeting.
Under that proposal, the state would open bull hunting in September in most of Wildlife Management District 8, which stretches from the western edge of Moosehead Lake to the Canadian border and includes Jackman. The southeast corner of the district would still be closed to hunting that week, with the Kennebec River serving as the boundary.
Webb said that district seemed to have the most interest for hunters and the least potential for conflict with other users.
“In order for us to feel comfortable with opening some portion of this area, it would need to be a meaningful addition that would provide a reasonable opportunity for hunters to disperse themselves and take advantage of what for many is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity,” Webb said.
The department would not increase the total number of moose hunting permits allocated for the district if a September hunt is added, Webb said. Instead, the tags would be divided between two weeks instead of one.
Wildlife Management Districts 9, 14 and 17 would remain closed to moose hunting in September. Greenville is located in the southwestern corner of District 9.
People who have been involved in the debate said the proposal won’t make everyone happy but generally agreed that the department tried to balance a wide range of opinions across a large geographic area.
“I’m happy as I can be with the decision,” said Jeremy Hargreaves, who owns Northeast Whitewater and takes thousands of people on moose watching tours throughout the region. “I think we had to concede something to make this work.”
Jennifer Whitlow, owner of Blair Hill Inn in Greenville, has been a vocal opponent of a September hunt near Greenville because moose watching tours are the top activity for her guests.
“The decision reflects a thoughtful, balanced approach that recognizes both wildlife management objectives and the significant economic concerns raised by local businesses and visitors who support our region’s tourism economy,” Whitlow wrote in an email.
Joe Kruse, who owns Lake Parlin Lodge in Jackman, said, if the rule is implemented, he would finally be able to use his property during the moose hunting week in September. This year, he said, his lodge sat empty while he guided clients in another district that week.
“We would like to see it all open. … But if we do have to have a compromise, then I think this is a good one,” Kruse said.
The department will advertise the proposed rule and open public comment on Oct. 28. Written feedback will be accepted through Nov. 28. A public hearing will take place at 5 p.m. on Nov. 18 at Northern Outdoors in The Forks. The advisory council will meet next on Dec. 8.

title: Time is on Troy Jackson’s side
