title: Democrat Amy Acton in Ohio pushes back against unattributed ad featuring her estranged mother
text:
Democrat Amy Acton in Ohio pushes back against unattributed ad featuring her estranged mother
Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor who has made no secret of a difficult childhood that included homelessness and sexual abuse, pushed back forcefully Tuesday against an unattributed ad circulating online in which her long-estranged mother calls her "a liar" and insinuates she has mental health issues.
The ad began circulating overnight, just two weeks before Election Day. Acton, Ohio's former public health director, is in a tight race with Republican billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy, a 2024 presidential candidate who has benefited from spending on his behalf that has exceeded $120 million.
The online ad, which first surfaced in a post by an Ohio political blogger, spread quickly across social media platforms. It does not include the "paid for" tag that is legally required to air on TV so viewers can know who produced and paid for it. D.J. Brynes, who blogs as "The Rooster," told CNN he got the video from a voter who viewed it as part of a poll and recorded it.
It was not clear if Acton's mother was paid for the one-minute spot. Her last known telephone number has been disconnected.
Acton suggested Ramaswamy was behind the ad.
"I won't normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is just something I'm complaining about, who today just released an ad using my birth mother, who I was removed from at the age of 12 for severe abuse and neglect, and sexual abuse," she told Spectrum News, a cable news outlet in Ohio.
She said Ramaswamy was accused of similar personal attacks during his run for the GOP presidential nomination: "This is a lifelong pattern with my opponent."
Ramaswamy's campaign issued a statement that did not address if he was responsible for the ad or knew who produced it. In the statement, campaign spokeswoman Connie Luck said Acton "has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of."
In a statement released by Acton's campaign, her brother, Philip Stearns, said the two were removed from their mother Donna Arthur's custody as children after their stepfather, Arthur's husband, was indicted for raping Acton as a child. Acton has not seen Arthur, whose last known address was in Pennsylvania, since they were in a courtroom together in 1978.
Later Tuesday, the Acton campaign released a response ad featuring Stearns, who recalls his older sister taking "the worst" of the abuse they faced as children in order to protect him and disparages Ramaswamy and his allies for exploiting the situation.
According to police and court documents obtained by The Associated Press, Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton's biological father reported his alleged conduct to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978.
Cledith Arthur pleaded not guilty. He was indicted by a grand jury that September, but failed to show at a court hearing and remained a fugitive until at least 1981. He has since died.
High-profile Republicans who back Ramaswamy — including Donald Trump Jr. and influencer Laura Loomer — elevated the video in online posts.
But other Republicans joined Democrats in condemning the ad. Meghan McCain called it "dastardly" and Dan Hauser, a strategist for Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, said he deleted his retweet of the ad once he realized "the very serious accusations that caused their issues."
The Democrat running for U.S. Senate in Ohio, Sherrod Brown, described the spot as "disgusting" and said everyone — including his opponent, Sen. Jon Husted — should be willing to condemn it. A spokesperson for Husted's campaign didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Acton's mother does not mention Ramaswamy's name in the ad, but she suggests that Acton has misrepresented her opponent and the time her family was homeless and living in a tent when she was a child — an experience Stearns corroborates.
___
Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York contributed to this report.

title: Christina Applegate isn't alone. Multiple sclerosis is misdiagnosed in nearly 1 in 5 cases
text:
Christina Applegate isn't alone. Multiple sclerosis is misdiagnosed in nearly 1 in 5 cases
Emmy winner Christina Applegate on Tuesday revealed on her podcast that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis after years of debilitating symptoms. But the "Anchorman" actress isn't alone.
About 15% of people who are initially given a multiple sclerosis diagnosis end up being misdiagnosed and don't have the condition. That's a pooled proportion calculated from six studies that researchers reviewed in 2024.
"Almost one in five of these people who'd been told they had MS, some for decades, didn't actually have it, and a majority of them were on medication to treat their MS," Dr. Marwa Kaisey, a neurologist at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, told ABC News.
Why is multiple sclerosis misdiagnosed so often?
These misdiagnoses happen frequently because there is no singular test that can conclusively identify it, according to experts.
Also, many other illnesses mimic symptoms that are similar to MS. The National Multiple Sclerosis Society lists a variety of other conditions that medical staff may try to rule out on its website when navigating a potential MS diagnosis, including central nervous system infections like Lyme disease, inflammatory disorders of the central nervous system, and certain genetic disorders and deficiencies.
Multiple sclerosis is a disease that causes the breakdown of the protective covering of nerves in the body, according to the Mayo Clinic.
Symptoms can vary widely between people, depending on where there is nervous system damage in the body. It can cause numbness, weakness, trouble walking, vision changes, among other symptoms.
While there is no cure for MS, there are treatments for it.
What Applegate said about her misdiagnosis
Applegate revealed the misdiagnosis on her "MeSsY" podcast, which she co-hosts with Jamie Lynn Sigler, in a two-part episode that went live on Tuesday.
Applegate, 54, said her doctor recently gave her tests after changes in her treatments did not go as expected.
 "This may come as great news, but to me, it comes — as like, I'm back at square one," Applegate said on the podcast, her voice breaking. "It's hard to say that. She came into my room, and she said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS.'"
"What does that moment feel like?" Sigler asked her.
"Well, I was like, not happy at all. You know, not everybody else was so happy," Applegate said. "Because you don't get misdiagnosed, and then all of a sudden, I'm better, right? I haven't gotten better, Jamie. If anything, I've gotten worse in some ways, so I'm back at square one, that I don't know what's going on with me."
She continued: "I'm just in a state of shock right now."
Applegate's health journey
Applegate earlier this year had an extended hospital stay that lasted months.
She began to experience numbness in her toes in 2021, which led to various medical tests, including nerve tests. That led to her MS diagnosis in June 2021, which she revealed publicly later that year.
Applegate and Sigler "get vulnerable" on their podcast, providing their perspectives about both of them having been diagnosed with MS.

title: FDA issues highest-risk warning for cheese recall after more than a dozen sickened
text:
(Gray News) - The FDA issued its highest-risk warning for a California-based company amid concerns over a multistate cheese E. coli outbreak.
The Class I classification applied to all affected Graziers raw milk cheese products manufactured by California-based Sierra Nevada Cheese Company, including Monterey Jack, jalapeño jack, medium cheddar and sharp cheddar varieties, according to a press release.
The affected products were distributed in Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, Texas, Washington and Wisconsin.
Investigators said 13 people in nine states became sick. More than half of those infected were children age 5 and younger.
The company announced the initital recall on Sept. 28.
The company is telling consumers not to eat any of the recalled cheeses. People should either throw the cheeses out or return them to the store where they were purchased for a refund.

title: City of Ellsworth adds trees, fruit orchard in Union River Estates area
text:
ELLSWORTH, Maine (WABI) - Volunteers in the City of Ellsworth began digging holes, planting trees and cleaning up areas around the Friendly City on Tuesday.
The effort is a collaboration between the city’s Arbor Commission, Parks and Recreation Department and community volunteers.
Federal funding for urban forestry
Within the Inflation Reduction Act passed by the federal government in 2022, significant funds were designated for Urban Forestry projects across the country.
Ellsworth applied to boost ecosystem services by removing invasive plants, adding native ones, and improving the environment around the waterfront and low-income housing areas.
The city qualified for an unmatched $174,000 grant spanning three years according to Tabatha White, an Arbor Commission member and Ellsworth city councilor.
The city’s first stop was Union River Estates.
“We’ve been able to actually remove some of the dead and diseased trees that were here and now we’re replacing them and adding even more trees in and probably the best part of it is, we’re adding a fruit orchard in between both low-income housing areas so Union River Estates and Straw,” said White.
“If we look at it, we go back to like you know what is the financial impact over the last four years, we’re looking at $100-120 thousand dollars in tree plantings that have not cost the taxpayers of Ellsworth, the citizens of Ellsworth anything, it’s all come through grant funding which is a pretty cool way to go about doing projects like this,” said Roddy Ehrlenbach, Director of Ellsworth Parks and Recreation.
What’s next
The project continues at Harbor Park starting Wednesday, Oct. 28.
To volunteer, follow the link or call 207-667-2563 ext. 1371. Registering will also keep volunteers updated on weather-related schedule changes.

title: Judge sides with state regulators on Juniper Ridge Landfill expansion
text:
OLD TOWN, Maine (WABI) - Penobscot County Superior Court ruling clears the way for Juniper Ridge Landfill’s expansion to move forward, siding with state regulators.
The decision leaves the Department of Environmental Protection’s approval in place.
Expansion details
The proposed expansion would add roughly 11.9 million cubic yards of capacity to Juniper Ridge, enough to hold the equivalent of 8.6 Empire State Buildings worth of trash.
The state-owned landfill, operated by Casella Waste Systems, has long drawn concerns over PFAS contamination.
Casella has confirmed plans to move that treatment system to another landfill, located 20 miles away, and seek approval through a separate permitting process. That change raises further questions about how and when PFAS-contaminated wastewater will be treated.
“This ruling is a setback, but it can’t bury the truth that the Penobscot Nation and local residents have brought into the open – that this landfill is part of a broken system that puts polluters’ wallets over people’s health,” said Alex St. Pierre, vice president for environmental justice at CLF. “The knowledge, persistence, and power of these communities have already shifted the conversation – and that momentum will carry forward until justice is served.”
“We have fought pollution, injustice, and decades of harm to heal the Penobscot River, a relative that has sustained our people since time immemorial and continues to sustain communities across Maine,” said Kirk E. Francis, Penobscot Nation Tribal Chief. “We are not asking the state to undo generations of harm overnight. We are asking it not to take us backward. Our cultural survival is tied to the health of the Penobscot River, and there is too much at stake to keep adding to the harms it already carries.”
CLF and Penobscot Nation say they are reviewing the ruling and evaluating next steps.

title: Bigger, stronger Cooper Flagg looking forward to NBA season
text:
A bigger and stronger Cooper Flagg will take the court with his Dallas Mavericks for their regular season opener at Houston against the Rockets Wednesday night.
The 19-year-old phenom from Newport gained 23 pounds through his offseason workout regimen, going from 205 pounds to 228 pounds, according to the Dallas Morning News.
Flagg told the newspaper that the added strength and muscle will help him be more well-rounded and create space.
“I don’t think there’s any areas where adding strength can hurt you. I’m so excited,” the 6-foot-10 forward added.
Matt MacKenzie, who owns and operates the Eastern Maine Sports Academy in Veazie and is Flagg’s trainer, told the Dallas Morning News that you are going to see “a more confident, more decisive version of Cooper on the offensive end.”
Flagg is coming off an exceptional rookie season for the Mavs, who drafted him with the first overall pick in 2025.
As the 2025-26 Rookie of the Year, he led the Mavs and all NBA rookies in scoring, averaging 21 points per game. He also led the Mavs in steals (1.2 per game) and minutes played (33.5 per game) and was second in assists (4.5) and fifth in rebounds (6.7).
He shot 46.8% from the floor: 51.3% off two-point shots and 29.5% off threes. He was an 82.7% shooter from the free throw line.
The Mavs finished at 26-56 and missed the playoffs in the Western Conference.
But nine-time NBA All-Star guard Kyrie Irving has returned after missing the entire 2025-26 season due to knee surgery.
The Mavs also have a new president in Masai Ujiri and a head coach in Dusty May, who led the University of Michigan to the NCAA title last season.
In a Bangor Daily News story in August, Flagg said that the upcoming season is a “new beginning for us.”
“It’s a fresh slate and we want to show we’ve improved. We need to stay healthy and having Kyrie is obviously going to help,” said Flagg at the third annual Flagg Brothers Basketball ProCamp at the New Balance Fieldhouse and the Memorial Gym on the University of Maine’s campus in Orono.
His twin brother, Ace, was a freshman at UMaine this past season and was chosen to the America East All-Rookie Team.
Cooper said he was focusing on all aspects of his game in the offseason while working out with MacKenzie and the Dallas staff.
“I’m trying to get better all-around. I’m always in the gym working on everything,” he said.

title: Family of passenger in Greg Biffle plane crash alleges NASCAR driver hired unqualified pilot
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - The personal assistant and longtime friend of NASCAR driver Greg Biffle has filed a wrongful-death lawsuit alleging Biffle hired an unqualified flight crew to save costs.
Greg Biffle’s estate is facing four major wrongful death lawsuits, totaling $40 million in claims.
Biffle and his longtime friend Craig Wadsworth were two of seven people killed in the tragic plane crash in Statesville in late December 2025.
Wadsworth’s estate filed the lawsuit last Friday in Iredell County against the estates of Greg Biffle, pilot Dennis Dutton, Dutton’s 20-year-old son Jack Dutton, and GB Aviation Leasing, a company owned by Biffle.
The suit claims Biffle and pilot Dennis Dutton knew a qualified second co-pilot was required to fly the plane, but allowed the pilot’s 20-year-old son, Jack Dutton, to fly without proper qualifications.
The lawsuit continued, stating Biffle was motivated “at least in part, by the desire to avoid the expense” of a professional co-pilot, citing a conversation in which Dennis Dutton told Biffle he had found someone to act as co-pilot and it would be “cheap.”
The estate alleges Biffle was willfully negligent, choosing personal convenience, cost savings and an opportunity to give “an inexperienced airman” cockpit experience over stopping the flight or hiring someone more experienced — leading to Wadsworth’s death.
The suit also names GB Aviation Leasing LLC, a private aviation company owned by Biffle, which operated the aircraft and leased the hangar space.
The company allegedly held no air carrier certificate — an FAA authorization required to operate as a commercial charter airline.
Additionally, Wadsworth’s estate claims Biffle was negligent both as Dutton’s boss and as owner and manager of the company that authorized the crew.
Dennis Dutton and Jack Dutton were also named for negligence as pilot in command and as acting crewman.
Wadsworth’s family is seeking at least $25,000, plus court costs and interest, from the Dutton estates, Biffle estate and GB Aviation.

title: Lupus looks invisible; the fight inside isn’t
text:
(Aging Untold) — Lupus can bring pain, exhaustion and unpredictability that aren’t always visible from the outside.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck shared her personal experience living with lupus after a viewer wrote in asking about the disease, offering a rare, candid look at what it’s really like to live with an autoimmune condition that others often can’t see.
‘Living with uncertainty is tough’
Cradduck said the hardest part of lupus isn’t just physical — it’s not knowing what each day will bring.
“I think I wish people understood that living with uncertainty is tough. You don’t know when what your days are always going to be like,” Cradduck said. “And people have a tendency to really be judgmental and really be ugly.”
Cradduck explained that many lupus patients take steroids like prednisone, which can change their appearance and invite unfair judgment.
“A lot of people on lupus, unfortunately, have to take a lot of steroids. Prednisone is one of the main treatments, which then you get that nice round face, you gain weight,” Cradduck said.
From eight softball games to a wheelchair
Cradduck described how quickly her life changed when she went into her first flare.
“The weekend before I went in my first flare, I played eight softball games back-to-back in a tournament — never sat down,” Cradduck said. “And on Wednesday morning, I couldn’t walk to the bathroom. I could not get myself to the bathroom unaided.”
She said the year that followed was difficult, including time spent in a wheelchair and significant weight gain, but it led her to a turning point.
“I have a disease that I will die with, but I’m not going to let it take my life. I’m going to live every day,” Cradduck said. “But that was a tough decision, and it was a tough place to come to.”
‘A case of mistaken identity’
Cradduck said people often assume she’s healthy simply because of how she looks, even after losing the ability to walk unaided.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said she calls lupus “a case of mistaken identity.”
“You look perfectly healthy on the outside, but you have a war going on on the inside,” Rogers said. “We call that the disease of a thousand faces, because you never know which organ in your body is going to hit.”
She said that unpredictability extends beyond physical symptoms.
“The sad thing for people is you never know which version of you is going to show up tomorrow,” Rogers said.
How to be a good friend to someone with lupus
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared specific ways loved ones can offer support without making the disease the center of every interaction.
“Not every conversation you and I are going to have is going to be about lupus. We’re going to have non-lupus conversations. I’m not going to be the lupus police,” O’Rourke said. “I’m not going to be looking at what you’re eating and saying, ‘Do you think that you should eat that?’ I’m not going to look at you and say, ‘Oh, you look really good today,’ meaning how did you look yesterday.”
She also emphasized the importance of consistency, even when flare-ups get in the way of plans.
“I am not going to let your flare-ups stop me from being a consistent, steadfast friend,” O’Rourke said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said lupus can appear invisible, so give people grace.
“Just because you can’t see their diagnosis, doesn’t mean they’re not dealing with something really hard,” she said.
Finding the right diagnosis — and options beyond traditional medicine
Cradduck said she was diagnosed after experiencing a reaction to sun exposure, following a long period of uncertainty before a lupus diagnosis.
“How it finally got diagnosed was I actually had a sun flare,” Cradduck said. “It was between lupus and the MS for a long time. My rheumatologist was amazing.”
She said managing stress and illness carefully has become essential since her immune system is compromised.
“If I get sick, I don’t just get sick. I don’t just get the flu and then I recover in three or four days like everyone else. It takes me down,” Cradduck said. “COVID was really, really hard on me.”
Rogers encouraged others to stay open to options beyond conventional treatment.
“We have options outside of traditional medicine that we are now starting to see from an integrative standpoint — things that you can do to not necessarily resolve it all the way,” Rogers said. “Sometimes you can, or dumb it down. People just need to be open and understand there are options out there.”
Key takeaways
- Lupus is often invisible. Patients can look healthy on the outside while fighting constant internal pain and uncertainty.
- Fatigue is relentless. Give yourself grace, and avoid comparing your journey to someone else’s.
- Judgment can be hurtful. Comments about appearance or assumptions based on how someone looks can add to the burden of an invisible illness.
- Support means consistency. Keep inviting, keep including — don’t let flare-ups end the relationship.
- Diagnosis can take time. Autoimmune conditions like lupus can be mistaken for other diseases, such as MS, before being correctly identified.
- A diagnosis changes capacity, not identity. Adapting with resilience can prevent a chronic illness from defining a person’s life.

title: Entire police department resigns; chief accuses mayor of placing tracker on his truck
text:
MILNER, Ga. (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — A Georgia city’s entire police force has resigned, the city manager announced during a Monday council meeting.
Milner City Manager Tausha Grose said the entire full-time police department has stepped down, along with most of the reserve officers.
The department’s last day is Oct. 28.
Grose also said she filed her own resignation and will work until Oct. 30.
Small department, small city
Milner, located about 45 miles southeast of Atlanta, has a population of less than 1,000 people.
The police department consisted of five people, including Chief Lamar Bunn.
The Lamar County Sheriff’s Office is expected to serve in the department’s absence.
Chief cites lack of trust
During Monday’s meeting, Bunn indicated he stepped down partially due to a lack of trust in the city council and mayor. He accused Mayor Craig Timmons of placing a tracker on his personal truck.
“I didn’t ask them to do it,” he said about the rest of the force deciding to resign. “It’s not like I said, ‘Hey guys, let’s quit.’ No, I didn’t do that. So, I don’t know what needs to happen from here.”
Push to unincorporate
Former city council member Skip Seda said if the city loses its police force and city manager, he would push to unincorporate Milner.
“Because we already paying taxes for Milner, and about the only darn thing the difference between us and the county is that police force. That’s it. So, why would we continue to pay Milner taxes?” he said.

title: Legislative response to AI is already overdue
text:
Jake Plante is a resident of Brunswick and author of the book “Uncle Sam and Mother Earth: Reflections on the Environmental Movement and the Role of Governance.”
Although I really can’t fathom how AI could destroy human civilization in a matter of years, the dire warnings from AI developers are enough to get me to sit up and pay attention.
But there’s something Silicon Valley isn’t saying. It’s something that offers a ray of hope for our collective management of AI risk.
As best as I can tell, the AI threat to humanity centers around its ability to percolate through and take over the internet. The internet is AI’s breathable atmosphere.
So wouldn’t it make sense to reexamine our reliance on the internet?
Much of our critical infrastructure, including financial services, energy management, government records and communication systems, is now inextricably woven to the internet. And it just keeps on progressing in this direction. Banks, stores, medical services and the business world at large are constantly pushing us to conduct our transactions online.
Relying on the internet as our economic backbone is great — until it isn’t. The internet offers major efficiencies but the downside is that it leaves us vulnerable. I’m reminded of this every year when I receive a written letter apologizing for the seizure of my personal data by hackers.
A similar trade-off exists with the electric grid. Power interruptions are happening more frequently due to rough storms. The result is a growing lack of user confidence in reliable service and the considerable cost to families if they lose heat or have to replace spoiled foods. The answer for many has been to acquire back-up generators.
Having back-up systems to the internet is one option to protect us against an internet takeover or collapse. This would require government and businesses to create redundant local networks with independent servers, which would kick in when the internet goes down. These back-ups would maintain vital services and help thwart worst-case scenarios involving diabolical takeovers by AI.
Another option is to unplug from the internet altogether. This seems extreme given the times we live in but that approach has security benefits, as demonstrated in the way we uphold our democracy. Our voting machines and tabulations are separated from the internet and the system is backed up by paper ballots in virtually every state. Likewise, our nuclear weapon systems are isolated from the public internet.
Imagine if internet connectivity was a business option and not an accepted fact. It’s something to think about at all levels, including individual transactions. Would it be too retro to incentivize renewed use of cash and checks?
Disentangling our nation’s vital services from internet failures provides some peace of
mind. Certainly, it wouldn’t be the whole answer. AI might attack us with drones, robots and viruses so they say. To meet the challenges, in addition to reducing our dependency on the internet, the time has come to legislate guardrails on AI development.
Humans don’t heed warnings very well unless something collapses in a visible way and people get hurt. Our lackadaisical mindset hurts our response to problems like climate change. It permeates the financial sector with risky acceptance of cryptocurrency.
We’re slow to react in many other ways, including the new existential threat from AI. We’ve let the genie out of the bottle and now we have to figure out what to do.
It’s hard to slow technological wheels from turning. The AI race is being fueled by the inertia of greed and competition, including fears about China winning the race. It’s hard to urge caution when it comes to human exploration. In the 19th century, the British military crushed the Luddite rebellion over textile workers’ resistance to job-changing automation. The Luddites, who wanted fair labor practices, have been wrongly characterized as anti-technology ever since.
Today, our equivalent of the Luddite rebellion isn’t destroying AI models or the internet, it’s having the foresight and courage to manage them safely and wisely.

title: More online dating app users are relying on AI as a tool for their profiles
text:
More online dating app users are relying on AI as a tool for their profiles
Jack is on the search for the love of his life. He’s tried Hinge, invite-only apps, even paid for Bumble premium.
He’s now experimenting with AI.
“Give me a fun short write-up of who I am for a dating app,” Jack, a 38-year-old data science professional from San Francisco, typed into ChatGPT. Jack asked that he be referred to using a pseudonym for this article, citing his concerns about his upcoming visa renewal.
After all, the chatbot has served as Jack’s right-hand man for nearly a year, choosing his outfits, teaching him to play guitar. “The Alfred to my Batman,” he calls the tool.
Related video above: They're Perfect. They're Consistent. They're... AI. | How AI Romance Scams Work
Then Jack pasted ChatGPT’s answer into Hinge: “Life’s not a checklist — it’s about shared moments and growth. I’m practical, open-minded, love rock, long drives, trivia, sports, and a good laugh along the way.”
It wasn’t any help. Jack admits to a single-digit batting average on Hinge, and his AI wingman didn’t improve his stats.
Jack is among many dating app users now outsourcing at least part of the online dating process to AI. More than half of U.S. adults younger than 30 have used a dating app, according to Pew Research Center, and now AI is an easily accessible tool to cut through the chaos of endless swiping and online chatter.
Dating apps are simultaneously trying to fill the gaps between online interaction and in-person meetups. Bumble is ditching the swipe for AI-driven matchmaking. Grindr is currently piloting bot-to-bot conversations to vet human dates. And Hinge is integrating AI into existing platforms, offering users personalized help with profile creation and conversation starters.
“If your end goal is to get offline and meet the love of your life, you probably want any tool that’s going to help you do that,” said Jui Ramaprasad, a professor of information systems at the University of Maryland, College Park.
Others say it’s just adding another layer of technology. Dating apps have relied on algorithms for decades, and on AI since 2023, including facial recognition and improved matchmaking calculations.
“From my vantage point, all I’m seeing is, okay, it’s still algorithms matching, but humans have less agency over that process,” said Douglas Zytko, a computer science professor at the University of Michigan-Flint.
The romantic Turing Test
When Franky Vergara’s cousin asked him how to respond to a flirtatious Hinge message, Vergara, a 23-year-old living in San Diego, didn’t know how to help.
“Honestly, ask ChatGPT to give you a couple ideas of what to say,” he recalled telling her.
She took his advice and sent an AI-generated message. “The message she sent didn’t have an ‘AI-vibe,’” Vergara recalled. “I think it felt more like a human-like text.”
It’s becoming increasingly common for people to use ChatGPT to open a conversation on a dating app, said Kathryn Coduto, an assistant professor of media science at Boston University. “That’s because people put a lot of pressure on the opening lines of a conversation.”
Kylee Baxa, a 23-year-old in New York, has received a few AI-generated dating app messages. Her Hinge profile has a reference to “The 100,” a science fiction show released in 2014, which led to conversations about the show and, in turn, dates.
But multiple times a date has admitted using AI to learn details about the show without having seen it, just to connect. The ploy didn’t work.
Baxa considers herself a proponent of AI but draws the line at the dating space.
“Here’s the deal: We are already losing the art of human connection in ways, like, I can’t even go up to a guy and flirt with them, and a guy can’t really feel comfortable coming up to a girl and flirting with them,” Baxa said.
“I do worry for people who have a great interaction, but it ends up being with an AI,” Coduto said. “And then when they meet the person, it’s not who they thought it was.”
Tricking others to go on a date
Jack uploaded a bunch of his photos to ChatGPT and asked which of them would fare best on his dating profile, asking for options to portray his “fun and whimsy.”
ChatGPT suggested a few images, including one of him with a dog. The photo makes him seem “vulnerable” and “gentle,” ChatGPT said.
Overall, Jack’s experience with AI assistance in his love life hasn’t worked. He thinks friends are more useful allies in this area of life.
“Having a friend write your profile may actually elicit more of who you are and what you’re looking for than you writing it yourself,” Ramaprasad said.
Baxa has also been disappointed with AI-assisted dating, but the stakes feel higher. One Hinge date referred to himself as “funemployed,” which she assumed meant he was taking time to travel because the photos in his profile were in Mykonos.
“Why are all your photos in the same place?” Baxa asked her date who then admitted he’d never been to Mykonos.
“He was just like, ‘Yeah, I just used Chat to update my Hinge since I didn’t have many photos of me that weren’t selfies. Like, they’re still me. It’s still my face,” Baxa recalled him saying. She quickly ended the date.
AI may even raise a legal question of consent. If AI-generated content gives someone a misleading impression about a potential partner, what kinds of misrepresentations are significant enough to impact consent?
There isn’t a universal definition of what qualifies as informed consent to sex or intimacy, Zytko said. His concern is whether AI-generated content risks misinforming a partner’s decision to pursue intimacy if that content is misleading.
Can AI dating apps solve the loneliness epidemic?
Mihir Manohar, a 32-year-old and living in New York, spent about an hour answering a long questionnaire about his dating preferences on the AI-driven dating app Amata.
In exchange, Amata’s chatbot pitched Manohar a date match: his now-girlfriend, Casey.
Amata arranged for the couple to meet at a wine bar and they hit it off. They’ve been together now for 10 months.
Before using Amata, Manohar was “completely against the traditional dating apps.” He didn’t want to swipe or submit to a dating app algorithm. He’d heard too many stories about ghosting and endless generic messages. He just wanted to go on a date.
This new wave of dating apps is a way for people to navigate choice overload and fatigue, Ramaprasad said.
“There’s less room for error when it comes to two people meeting,” Manohar said about Amata. “And less room for disappointment.”
New dating apps, including Amata, Sitch and Ditto, ask users dozens of questions about their values, interests, and preferences. In exchange, users are given a smaller pool of options in place of endless swiping.
Amata’s goal is to get people offline and into the real world as soon as possible, founder Ludovic Huraux said. He suggests AI could end the loneliness epidemic, a growing public health concern fueled by rising levels of social isolation and lack of meaningful connection.
“If AI can help reconnect people in real life, it is very positive,” Huraux said. “If AI increases the time spent online and increases this loneliness crisis, it will be bad, and we would have failed.”
Critics also worry AI will remove agency for users.
“I find it kind of terrifying,” Zytko said. “There seems to be this dominant view at big tech companies that people want the online dating experience to be automated and expedited.”
Protecting yourself in the age of AI-enhanced online dating
To show your identity is legitimate, Coduto recommends verifying your account, which involves taking a selfie in real-time to confirm identity.
Depending on what you’re comfortable disclosing, personal details in your profile also differentiate the real from the AI. But dating apps are largely not transparent about how personal information is stored, analyzed, and shared and require you to legally consent to sharing data.
“The mix in photos is also important,” Coduto said. “Besides an occasional filter, look for photos with friends and family or doing an activity, so things that show that you aren’t just sitting there taking a bunch of selfies.”
Looking for these details in others’ profiles can help delineate between users who are using AI to fabricate their profiles and presenting authentic personas. In messages and profiles, keep an eye out for “repetitive phrases,” she said, another current sign of AI communication.
Coduto cautions against using AI in any form. As soon as online interactions move offline, your date will know, she said.
And as with any dating app, safety is always a risk.
“Using AI is by no means a reason to ignore or not perform manual safety checks and taking deliberate measures to protect yourself when you meet a stranger for the first time face-to-face, where there’s always that risk of physical sexual harm,” Zytko said.
And maybe AI-infused dating will have an unintended consequence. Coduto suspects an AI backlash could potentially fuel the growth of in-person dating events, such as run clubs and speed dating hours.
“I think that if these apps really push AI, people will say, ‘Well, I do have other options, and maybe I will go back to meeting people in person,’” Coduto said.

title: Bonny Eagle-Thornton game highlights this week’s football storylines
text:
The two best high school football teams in Maine go head-to-head this week with identical 7-0 records.
That’s right, it’s time for the annual regular-season showdown that so often gives fans a preview of the Class A South final.
Thornton Academy hosts Bonny Eagle at 1 p.m. Saturday at Hill Stadium in Saco. Both teams have been dominant. Both have star players producing at high levels.
The big question is: Can Bonny Eagle get its first win against Thornton since the Class A championship game in 2019? Thornton has won six straight in the series, including twice last season when the Connor Ayoob-powered Golden Trojans won the regular-season game in Standish and then the regional final in Saco, wearing down the Scots in the second half in both games.
Thornton’s unparalleled depth is again an advantage, but this year’s Bonny Eagle team seems to be built just a bit differently. Also, first-year starting quarterback Lucas Klehn is playing at such a high level that he has emerged as the front-runner for player of the year honors.
Playing behind a big offensive line, Klehn has rushed for 870 yards and 23 touchdowns on 110 carries while completing 68% of his passes (46 of 67, 789 yards), with seven TD passes and zero interceptions. He has real playmakers to help him out in running backs Ben Noe (58 carries, 466 yards) and Ben Havu (31 carries, 291 yards) and receiver Drew Gervais (25 receptions, 428 yards, 3 TDs). Havu is Bonny Eagle’s top tackler, and Klehn is a hard hitter from the secondary.
For Thornton, the big change this season is a dynamic passing game. Second-year starter Noah Fullerton isn’t throwing a lot, but he’s completing 70% of his attempts (42 of 60, 772 yards), with 16 touchdowns and three interceptions. Logan LeBlanc (18 receptions, 454 yards) is the big-play target, with nine touchdown catches. In recent weeks, Brennan Tabor (69 carries, 634 yards, 13 TDs) has emerged as the top rusher, with help from Josiah Blain (57 carries, 371 yards). Tabor and Blain are the defensive leaders at inside linebacker, with 42 and 43 solo tackles, respectively.
JUST HOW GOOD IS LEAVITT?
That question was posed to Hornets coach Mike Hathaway when he was watching host Greely (6-1) beat Hermon (6-1) last week. Those are the two teams closest to Leavitt (7-0) in the Class C standings. Leavitt has beaten Greely and is at Hermon on Friday.
Hathaway said his squad isn’t at the level of the historic 2023 team that went 11-0 and beat Class A contender Oxford Hills, eventual Class A champion Thornton (on the road), and Class B runner-up Lawrence.
But he did put this year’s squad in the very good category, citing the high number of returners and a very deep and talented skill group as key strengths. The defense has also been quite good, allowing only 39 points.
BIDDEFORD IS BACK
Class A and Class C teams have one more game after this week before the playoffs. For the rest of Maine’s teams, this weekend will determine playoff seeding.
Biddeford is trying to follow up on the season’s biggest upset to date, a 37-14 win at previously unbeaten Marshwood in which the Tigers recovered from a 14-0 deficit.
Biddeford (5-2) can secure a bye to the regional semifinals if it beats Cheverus (2-5) on Friday at Waterhouse Field. That result would also end the Stags’ season.
“Our team is maturing, and as they’re maturing, they’re understanding the game better and getting better,” said Steve Allosso, now in his fifth season as Biddeford’s head coach.
Estevao Lembissa, a junior slot back who lines up all over the field, has emerged as a big-time playmaker. He had a 71-yard touchdown reception and a 49-yard rushing TD in the second half against Marshwood.
“He’s fast. He’s quick. He’s tough. And he has super character,” Allosso said. “One of the best I’ve ever coached, and this team is overflowing with character.”
Quarterback Ernest Dore and left guard Caiden Howe are top seniors. Juniors Stanley Richerson (RB/DE) and Alex Gosselin (WR/OLB) give the offense added options. Junior linebacker Marcus Perkins is becoming a force.
Despite their record, the much-improved Tigers have struggled to put together consecutive strong efforts, something Allosso said is a point of emphasis this week. The Marshwood win followed a 37-6 loss at Skowhegan.
KENNEBUNK AT MARSHWOOD
Kennebunk vs. Marshwood is Class B South’s version of Bonny Eagle-Thornton. Both teams are 6-1 and tied for first place in the Crabtree standings. The winner gets the No. 1 playoff seed. The loser would slip to No. 3 and miss out on a first-round bye if Biddeford wins.
Marshwood is dinged up. Fullback Greg Castoras was hurt late in the Biddeford game and is “day-to-day,” said Marshwood coach Andrew Elwell. The Hawks have been without their top halfback, Noah Goodwin, for the past two games. Goodwin is questionable for Friday’s game.

title: Biddeford City Council unanimously approves federal immigration enforcement ordinance
text:
BIDDEFORD, Maine (WMTW) — The Biddeford City Council unanimously approved an ordinance Tuesday night establishing restrictions on the city’s involvement in federal immigration enforcement.
Councilors approved the measure during its second reading without amendments.
The ordinance is set to take effect on Nov. 19, 30 days after its approval.
The ordinance adds a new section to the city’s municipal code outlining limits on how city employees and resources may be used to assist federal immigration authorities.
The ordinance applies to city employees and municipal resources, not federal immigration agents themselves. It does not prevent U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement from carrying out operations within city limits.
The vote follows months of discussions surrounding immigration enforcement in Biddeford, including a September meeting in which the city’s solicitor outlined the municipality’s legal options.

US is a big reason for the world losing ground in the fight against climate change, UN report says
text:
US is a big reason for the world losing ground in the fight against climate change, UN report says
Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says.
If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit above current temperatures, according to Wednesday's update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That's about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit more than last year's projections by the same science team.
“This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions,” the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas.
Related video above: Explaining why glaciers in the U.S. are melting
“In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation,” the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased their emissions like most European nations — added 189 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 70% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report.
The United States is going “hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it,” said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics. He wasn't part of the U.N. report but, like several other outside scientists, said it was scientifically sound.
Shooting far past Paris climate goal
The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate- fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 4.7 degrees Fahrenheit hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 5 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year's projection.
Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit and preferably 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact. The world is now at about 2.5 degrees Fahrenheit above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 3.2 degrees Fahrenheit and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees.
The world is falling “dangerously short” of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, “but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink.”
Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — “is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen.
“The report's message is clear,” said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts. She wasn't part of this study. “We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all.”
An added tenth of a degree of danger
Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century.
“This report shows that America’s retreat isn’t just a political embarrassment. It has real consequences for the planet and for millions of people around the world,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate organization. “An extra tenth of a degree might sound insignificant, but in climate terms it is enormous. It means more dangerous heat waves, more destructive floods, more failed harvests and more lives lost. For vulnerable communities in Africa, already living on the front lines of the climate crisis, every fraction of a degree matters. These are not abstract numbers. They are human lives.”
Hare said that extra one-tenth of a degree pushes an additional 140 million people “into dangerously hot conditions” and increases the odds of the collapse of the Amazon rain forest or ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. It also would cost the world and shave about $1.2 trillion from the global economy, said University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann.
And the U.S. effect is probably even bigger than what the United Nations calculates because if the world's largest historical climate polluter doesn't do much to fight global warming other nations ease off in their efforts too, said Johan Rockstrom, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany.
“The rest of the world is exhausted when it comes to counting the damage that the U.S. is willingly doing to allies, multilateral structures, economic cooperation, disaster relief,” Australian climate scientist Malte Meinshausen said. “The rest of the world should probably continue to focus even less on the U.S.”

title: UMaine shares plan to bring budget deficit down to $3M
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The University of Maine on Wednesday shared a pathway to bring next year’s budget deficit down to roughly $3 million, taking the step about a month after it announced plans to cut the original $19 million gap in half.
The university announced in September a plan to cut about $10 million off its shortfall, including layoffs to faculty and staff, consolidating some courses and decreasing instructional budgets.
A letter shared Wednesday, signed by UMaine administrators, comes with a plan to make up for another $6 million, which would reduce the shortfall to about $3 million.
The letter says the university plans to cut spending and increase revenue through non-academic means. Among other cuts, it states that “workforce reductions will unfortunately be necessary to more closely align the university’s expenses with revenue on an ongoing and permanent basis.”
The plan also includes relying less on external vendors, utilizing reserve funds, and centralizing some functions, such as research centers and institutes.
It also calls for the elimination of vacant positions from athletics, student life and the president’s office. The plan includes an expected $1 million increase in base revenue beginning in fiscal year 2028.
“Assuming these targets are met, the remaining $3M gap will present a challenge and closing this will be the Cabinet’s main focus over the coming weeks,” the letter states.
Last month, university administrators said UMaine’s operating costs have risen faster than state funding or tuition revenue and that federal changes have impacted research funding and financial aid.
The university will present its budget proposal for the next fiscal year to the board of trustees in January.

title: Trump envoy Witkoff meets Putin in St. Petersburg for Ukraine war talks
text:
(AP) - Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations next month with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, a Kremlin official said, potentially setting up the first such talks since February.
Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed “in principle” to restart the talks after Nov. 10, Putin’s foreign affairs adviser, Yuri Ushakov, told reporters following a meeting in St. Petersburg between the Russian leader and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff.
The talks will focus on “building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends,” Ushakov said.
Witkoff’s talks with Putin about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine took place as U.S. President Donald Trump presses Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he supported the push from Washington to restart talks swiftly.
“The agenda is clear: to end the war, bring peace closer, and, as I understand it, prepare everything for a meeting at the leaders’ level,” Zelenskyy said in an audio message issued late Wednesday.
Russia, he added, “has said many times already that it is ready to meet in one format or another. Then something changed. Things were canceled. We’ll see what happens this time.”
Shortly after his message, a missile alert sounded over Kyiv, and loud explosions were heard in the capital.
Representatives of the three countries held three rounds of negotiations early this year, meeting twice in Abu Dhabi in January and February, followed by further talks in Geneva in February.
However, little progress was reported beyond exchanges of prisoners of war as Moscow and Kyiv stuck to their longstanding basic demands.
Latest proposals to end the war have little of value, Kremlin says
The discussion in St. Petersburg lasted about three hours, the Kremlin said, and came a day after Witkoff met with Zelenskyy and some European leaders in Norway’s capital, Oslo.
The proposals that emerged from the Oslo meeting “contained little of real value in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis,” Ushakov said.
However, he later told Russian state TV that while Moscow isn’t “fully satisfied” with the Oslo proposals, they are a step in the right direction.
Witkoff’s meetings suggested leaders are keen to bring new momentum to U.S.-led peace efforts, more than 4½ years after the war began. Efforts by the Trump administration since early last year to end the war have made no significant progress.
Witkoff and Putin met at St. Petersburg’s Constantine Palace, with Ushakov and Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev also at the table. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the discussion by video, Ushakov said.
During the meeting, Witkoff and Kushner proposed a three-way meeting with the U.S., Russia and Ukraine at the technical level and shared progress on their talks with Zelenskyy a day earlier, according to a U.S. official familiar with the talks who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the private meeting.
Witkoff and Kushner also discussed a postwar economic plan, European security and plans for the upcoming meeting, the official said.
Putin says he’s ready to consider restoring economic ties with US
In televised opening remarks, Putin said he was ready to consider prospects for the restoration of U.S.-Russia economic ties and that he was prepared to discuss the U.S.-led conflict with Iran. Moscow stands ready to use its relationship with Tehran to help bring peace, he said.
Ushakov said “large-scale joint economic projects that offer significant prospects for cooperation” between Russia and the U.S. were discussed in detail with Witkoff.
“Some of these are, in fact, nearing the implementation stage,” he said.
In other developments Wednesday, Russia released a retired American teacher who had been imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. Witkoff said it appeared to be a goodwill gesture by the Kremlin after Trump asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard.
Putin also met with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, who was in St. Petersburg for talks with other Russian officials, the Kremlin said.
Russia has cultivated its ties with China, and the two countries last month vetoed a U.S. proposal for U.N. experts to keep monitoring sanctions on Iran.
Putin and Witkoff also discussed a possible meeting next month between the Russian, Chinese and U.S. leaders at an economic summit in China, Ushakov said, adding that Beijing is already preparing for it.
Norway’s prime minister sees a possible ‘new phase’ in talks
After his trip to Russia, Witkoff returned for more consultations in Oslo, where he met with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre at the airport before flying back to the U.S. The meeting lasted just over an hour, Norwegian broadcaster NRK reported.
“I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy,” Støre told the broadcaster. He said the new talks were likely to happen in mid-November.
Asked whether Zelenskyy could accept a border running along the current front line, Støre said: “I don’t think Ukraine will ever formally accept it and say that this is the new border. But whether they can live with it is another matter.”
Trump presses Zelenskyy to compromise
At the White House on Tuesday, Trump increased the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two leaders have soured again.
“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”
If that doesn’t happen, “I think it’s going to be a very bad thing,” Trump said.
Amid fears that Washington was turning its back on Ukraine, Zelenskyy said Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles, after recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice from allies.
Russian attacks kill 5 people and wound at least 23 others, Ukraine says
Overnight Russian attacks in Kyiv left three people dead and 12 wounded, while 10 residential buildings were damaged, the city’s military administration said.
Energy facilities were targeted in Kyiv and three other cities in Russian attacks early Wednesday, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. Outside the eastern city of Kharkiv, two people died and 11 others were wounded when drones exploded in a residential area, he said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces struck a warehouse, an electrical substation and a bulk carrier at sea that was headed to the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
The Russian Defense Ministry reported Wednesday that its air defenses intercepted 373 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula and the Black Sea.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Ellsworth High School music director to appear on ‘Jeopardy!’
text:
Ellsworth High School music director Jamie Calandro is scheduled to appear on “Jeopardy!” next Monday, Oct. 26, the school announced.
Calandro’s appearance on the long-running TV quiz show comes on the heels of former Bangor Daily News reporter Emily Burnham winning one ‘Jeopardy!’ game in September before coming up short in her bid to hold the championship.
Appearances on the show by Maine residents aren’t frequent, but they aren’t rare either.

title: DOE to release 315,000 barrels from Northeast heating oil reserve
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MAINE (WABI) - The Department of Energy will release up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, a third of the reserve.
Senators Susan Collins and Angus King announced the move in a press release Wednesday. In September, the senators urged the administration to take the step to help protect Mainers from high heating oil costs ahead of winter.
The oil will be available through an exchange in which companies submit bids to receive barrels from the reserve, according to the release.
The release of 315,000 barrels brings a 13% supply increase in New England, which will help bring down prices.
NEHHOR reserves have only been released twice in the reserve’s 26-year history and have never been used to lower home heating oil prices.

title: Whether `stringing' or `looping,' tobacco is the tie that binds many North Carolina farm families
text:
RALEIGH, N.C. (AP) — When Sophie Sunday told her schoolmates she was taking off halfway through the school day, they couldn’t wait to find out why.
“`I’m going to loop tobacco at the fair,’” the seventh grader told them. “And they’re, like, `What?’ They don’t have a clue.”
To be fair, most people don’t.
At 12, Sophie was the youngest contestant in the North Carolina State Fair’s annual tobacco stringing contest, which pays homage to a way of life that was already largely past when her parents were kids.
Traditionally, tobacco was harvested by hand, hung in a log barn and cured to a golden-brown with a wood fire that had to be stoked day and night. But before it could go into the barn, the green tobacco had to be strung on long wooden sticks.
What you called this practice depended on what part of the state you lived in. Because the fairgrounds are in the capital, Raleigh, they call it a stringing contest.
“Where I grew up, in the middle of the state, we call it stringing,” said Pat Short, superintendent of the fair’s Heritage Circle. “But down east, in the eastern part of the state, they call it looping tobacco.”
Today, North Carolina’s flue-cured tobacco crop is harvested mostly by machine and packed tightly into natural gas-heated metal bulk barns that look more like shipping containers.
It’s a different world from when 97-year-old Ruth Coats, the oldest contestant, worked her family’s tobacco near the Virginia border. Once the state’s largest cash crop, tobacco was the beating heart of many family farms. Tobacco “allotments” — the rights to grow it — were hereditary.
“It was good, hard work, but it made you much stronger,” she said with a giggle. “A lot of memories of my family and friends.”
Teams like The Tie Masters and Mule Stringers compete
Although North Carolina remains the nation’s No. 1 tobacco producer, the leaf has fallen to the state’s third most valuable cash crop, behind corn and soybeans. Growers produced more than 248 million pounds (112,490,907 kilograms) last year, valued at nearly $546 million, according to the U.S Department of Agriculture. Most tobacco ends up in smoking products.
“When we were growing up, if people had anywhere from 6 to 10 acres of tobacco, they could actually raise enough money to raise their family,” said Ken Jones, Sophie’s grandfather. “But now, most of the guys contract (with tobacco companies) 400 to 600 acres (162 to 243 hectares) of tobacco at one time.”
On Friday, teams with names like The Tie Masters, the Mule Stringers and 89 & Twine battled it out in a white tent as temperatures reached 90 degrees Fahrenheit (32 Celsius).
With a “ready set and go” from Short, a pair of “handers” gathered clumps of yellow-green leaves from a table and passed them to the stringer, who wrapped twine around the stems of the leaves, then the stick.
When they’d strung at least 36 bundles, they wrapped the twine around the stick’s end and tore it off.
The fastest teams can tie a stick in under a minute.
Three generations of one family vied for first place
Peggy Medlin remembers being so fast as a teenager that her boss let the other two loopers go.
“And I made $6 for looping 600 sticks,” the 89-year-old recalled with a grin.
But it’s not just about speed. Before presenting a stick to the judges, a worker gave each a couple of good shakes to make sure no leaves fell out.
“Because in the curing process, that would be a bad thing if it caused it to catch on fire,” explained Andrea Ashby, director of public affairs for the state Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services.
A dozen teams competed this year. Sophie was one of three generations of her family vying for the $250 first prize.
Sandy Jones grew up on a southeastern North Carolina farm and learned to loop from her mother. She taught her own daughter, Annie, when she was about 5, and her granddaughter when she was about the same age.
Jones’ squad, the defending champion Maple Hill Loopers, included her husband, Ken, and son-in-law Mike Sunday. Sophie, mom Annie and her great-aunt comprised The 3 Suckers — a play on the small side shoots that can stunt the growth of healthy leaves.
The Maple Hill Loopers were edged out by The Benson Nites, which finished with a time of just under one minute and four seconds.
The Suckers didn’t place, but that didn’t matter to Sophie.
“I think of it as tradition,” she said.
Short said the tobacco strung at the fair — which was grown at the nearby Oxford Tobacco Research Station — will be sold to a contractor and likely go into cigarettes. Sophie confessed to being a bit conflicted about tobacco, a plant that has killed untold humans, but is also showing promise in vaccine production and other pharmaceutical research.
“Every single year I go, I’m like, `Why do we do this? It’s, like, bad for people,’” she said. “But the leaves can also get used for, like, different things, not just smoking.”
And when she has kids of her own, she’s going to teach them how to loop.
“It makes my heart smile,” her grandmother said.

title: Roger Goodell says the NFL welcomes a review of how Eagles handled Jalen Hurts' blood clots
text:
Roger Goodell says the NFL welcomes a review of how Eagles handled Jalen Hurts' blood clots
The NFL welcomes an investigation into the Philadelphia Eagles’ handling of Jalen Hurts’ blood clots after the players’ union asked for one, Commissioner Roger Goodell said Wednesday.
Goodell said in his news conference at the end of the NFL’s annual fall meeting that Dr. Allen Sills, the league's chief medical officer, has gone through the steps that were followed and added that the union had a right to call for a review.
“Obviously, there was a medical evaluation, and I think our protocols were incredibly good there,” Goodell said. “The protocols were followed. Our process is to make sure that’s the case, and our chief medical officer has gone through that, so we’re comfortable that what we’ve seen in the protocols have happened.”
Related video above: Tufts doctor explains Jalen Hurts’ diagnosis and recovery outlook
Sills on Tuesday offered a passionate defense of the Eagles medical staff. The NFL said officials were in touch with team doctors and trainers, as well as the Cleveland Clinic in London.
League executive vice president Jeff Miller said officials had a good sense of the course of events. He disputed a report that Hurts was awake for more than 30 hours before playing against Jacksonville on Oct. 11, saying that the QB returned to the hotel and slept for roughly seven or eight hours.
Hurts is on injured reserve and expected to miss the rest of the season after a blood clot in his left calf traveled to his lungs. The Eagles and agent Nicole Lynn said Monday that Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary embolisms. Hurts’ treatment involves blood thinners, and he will not be allowed to participate in any football activities until he is off them.
Goodell downplayed the role that international travel may have had in the situation.
“The most important thing here is Jalen’s health, ultimately, and the future of him,” Goodell said. “He’s a wonderful young man: not just a great player, but he’s someone we all care deeply about. I’m more worried about his health, ultimately, but the protocols were followed.”
Sills said Tuesday the decision to allow someone with a blood clot to fly depends on several variables, including the location, a patient's history and more.
“What I can tell you is expert people getting a lot of opinions,” Sills said. "This isn’t just one doctor saying yay or nay. You’re going to poll a panel of experts both within the team and outside the team to get the best judgment and experience with a particular condition.”

title: 6 arrested for allegedly running marriage fraud ring, feds say
text:
Federal prosecutors announce bust of decade-long marriage fraud scheme
Federal prosecutors announced charges resulting from an investigation of a group that allegedly arranged "hundreds of sham marriages" with the goal of helping individuals obtain immigration benefits.
Massachusetts U.S. Attorney Leah Foley said six people were charged in connection with the case, including five who were arrested on Wednesday morning. She spoke at the Moakley Federal Courthouse in Boston alongside John Soars, Assistant Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England, and Shawn Saucier, Northeast Regional Chief of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.
Foley said the alleged marriage fraud ring lasted more than a decade and generated more than $6 million in profits for the perpetrators.
According to the U.S. Attorney, the alleged mastermind of the scheme is Jennifer Gonzalez, a U.S. citizen. Other suspects were identified as:
- Erica Daniels, 29
- Chreise Alejandro, 39
- Amara Pugh, 31
- Jessica Tavares, 31
- Jaylin Hill, 26
Hill was already in state custody, serving a prison sentence for a firearms offense. The others were arrested and are expected to make their first appearances in federal court on Wednesday afternoon.
Video below: Prosecutors announce marriage scheme
"Gonzalez allegedly charged between $38,000 and $40,000 per marriage and arranged 18 to 20 sham marriages per year for over 10 years, on the low end," Foley said.
A recording provided by a cooperating witness captured Gonzalez bragging about investing the proceeds in businesses and property in the Dominican Republic, Foley said.
Daniels, Alejandro, Tavares and Hill, who are all U.S. citizens, were each allegedly paid to enter into one or more marriages to help immigrants obtain legal status. After staying married for a short time, the couples would get divorced, and Foley said new marriages followed soon after.
"And this was all done to circumvent our immigration laws," Foley said.
Pugh, also a citizen, allegedly worked as the secretary for the business.
The prosecutors allege that multiple defendants also lied on Massachusetts SNAP benefit applications by falsely claiming to have never been married.

title: Community folk dance with Pourparler in Saco
text:
SACO – Need a dose of exuberance in your life? Join us for a lively evening of music, movement and cultural discovery! Learn a variety of fun, easy-to-follow folk dances inspired by traditions from around the world, led by talented community dance leaders from across the U.S. and Canada, at Ferry Beach from 7:30 to 9:30 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 24.
These dance leaders are visiting Maine for Pourparler, an annual gathering supported by the National Folk Organization and the Country Dance & Song Society. Come experience the joy of folk dance, discover new rhythms, and connect with others through the universal language of dance, all accompanied by live music!
Everyone is welcome. Great for families and singles of all ages and experience levels; whether you’re a seasoned dancer or stepping onto the dance floor for the very first time. No experience or partner is needed.
Free-will admission donations will help cover costs, $5 suggested. Pre-registration is appreciated to help us plan, but walk-ins are welcome! Register on the event page on the Ferry Beach website: https://www.ferrybeach.org/community-folk-dance.html. Ferry Beach is at 5 Boardwalk Drive, Saco, ME 04072.
The annual Pourparler gathering convenes dance and music educators who teach folk, ethnic, world and traditional dance in schools and other community settings. The conference is in a different state each year, and this is the first time in Maine (the way dance should be!).

title: Maine Sen. Collins enlists ex-Democratic colleague Manchin in effort to highlight her independence
text:
LEWISTON, Maine (AP) — Maine Republican Susan Collins has promoted her reputation as one of the most independent U.S. senators and she is using the waning days of the election season to sell that message to voters by campaigning with a former Democratic colleague who has endorsed her.
Collins is trying to fend off a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson, a onetime state Senate president, and on Wednesday she made appearances with Joe Manchin, a West Virginian who became an independent late in his career before retiring.
After stopping for breakfast at Simones’ Hot Dog Stand in Lewiston, Collins spoke of how she and Manchin were “part of every piece of bipartisan legislation that passed and became law” during their time together in office.
Manchin said to lose Collins would be “to lose the soul of the Senate.” He praised her independent streak, her willingness to buck Republican President Donald Trump and her record of fighting for Maine’s interests.
“This is a true blue-blooded Maine person who knows exactly where she came from,” Manchin said.
They stopped later a New Balance shoe facility in Norway. Jackson, 58, is scheduled to campaign Thursday in Portland with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the progressive congresswoman from New York.
Collins, 73, is in what may be her toughest reelection fight as she seeks her sixth term.
It’s only the second time that she’s sought reelection in a midterm with a sitting Republican president, and the national trends are much less favorable to the GOP than they were the last time she did so, in 2002. Trump’s approval has fallen well below where it was when he took office last year, and a recent poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that a strong majority of voters want change in Washington.
‘We need more people like Susan Collins’
Collins has been working to persuade voters that she is independent of Trump and willing to break with him. In Manchin, she enlisted a politician who was one of the most moderate voices in the Senate. Manchin said in 2023 that Trump would “ destroy democracy in America” if he was elected to a second term.
Among the few dozen Collins supporters at the Lewiston event was Mike Marcotte.
“I may not have always been a fan of her complete package of votes, but when I look at the vitriol that’s in the U.S. Senate right now, we need more people like Susan Collins,” he said.
Jackson got a late start on campaigning after the party’s initial nominee existed the race, but trails Collins in the money race by less than $3 million after an aggressive quarter in which he raised more than $20 million. Jackson has campaigned relentlessly and his events have drawn hundreds. Collins has largely stuck to smaller appearances.
Some of Jackson’s backers demonstrated across the street from the hot dog stand. A few held signs bearing the face of Brett Kavanaugh, the U.S. Supreme Court justice whom Collins voted to confirm and whose vote eventually helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion.
“Someone needs to stand up and be a check on Donald Trump and his harmful policies,” said David Sysko.
Collins’ loyalty to Trump has been a central focus of the race
Collins has broken with Trump and Republicans over the years. She voted to convict him at his impeachment trial in 2021. Increasingly during the campaign, she has worked to distance herself from the president as Democrats argue that she is too close to him.
Collins said in early October that she is “not exactly his favorite senator,” and that she did not expect Trump to campaign in Maine. He has steered clear of the state with the Nov. 3 election nearing.
Pinning Collins to Trump is central to the Democrats’ strategy. In one ad, a nurse says the state is in a healthcare crisis “because of Susan Collins and Donald Trump,” citing Collins’ vote for Trump’s push for Medicaid cuts. Collins did vote to advance the bill, but ultimately voted against it.
Trump also was a major focus of four contentious debates between the candidates this month, where Collins sought to distance herself from the president and Jackson repeatedly accused her of doing Trump’s bidding.
Asked at the final debate to name a time in which she bucked her own party and succeeded, Collins gave the example of rallying support against Trump’s nomination of Pete Hegseth, who was confirmed as defense secretary.
Democrats seized on the moment and released a statement that said the exchange “underscores a central question in the Maine Senate race: Does Collins, a Republican in a state that disapproves of President Donald Trump and has grown bluer in recent years, stand up to her party enough to earn the independent streak she has staked her career on?”
Jackson has characterized Collins as out of touch with the struggles of working-class people in Maine. He has described Collins as a “rubber stamp” for the president and criticized her votes on Kavanaugh and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Trump’s second-term health secretary. Collins has said she does not regret either vote.
Republicans have cast Jackson as a bully
Republican ads against Jackson, a logger from northern Maine, have focused more on accusations of his having a volatile personality and behaving like a bully with female colleagues. Jackson has denied those accusations.
Collins distanced herself on Wednesday from a Republican super PAC attack ad that she said “should be taken down.”
The senator was a top target of Democrats in 2020 when she defeated challenger Sara Gideon by nearly 9 percentage points. Collins is the only Republican senator from New England, a distinction she has had since January 2013.

title: Breast Cancer Awareness Month: How to lower your risk year-round
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month.
But experts want women to stay educated about their health year-round.
Bre Bisset, AGNP with Northern Light Primary Care in Ellsworth, spoke about tips to keep in mind for breast health.
Healthy habits that help
Bisset says things women do to take care of their breast health can also benefit their overall health, including:
- Maintaining a healthy weight
- Getting 150 to 300 minutes of exercise each week
- Not smoking
- Limiting or avoiding alcohol
Know your body, talk to your doctor
Experts remind women that they know their body best, so if you notice any changes, it’s important to reach out to your doctor for further evaluation.
“If there’s 10 cancers that we find, four of them are typically discovered first by the woman herself. While that’s a great statistic it doesn’t replace regular mammograms, regular screenings, all that sort of stuff. So to personalize that you should talk to your provider,” Bisset said.
When to get your first mammogram
While family and personal history is different for everyone, Bisset said she advises her patients to get their first mammogram no later than age 40.
She also encourages people to learn more about breast cancer.
For more information and resources, check the link.
