title: 6 people have been arrested for allegedly running a marriage fraud ring, federal authorities say
text:
Wedding rings were exchanged, and photos of a smiling bride and well-dressed groom made it look like these were legitimate marriages.
But federal authorities argued Wednesday that the ceremonies were part of an elaborate, decade-long marriage fraud ring that netted a half-dozen people in Massachusetts millions of dollars. Prosecutors charged six people, including the alleged ringleader Jennifer Gonzalez, with conducting as many as 20 marriages to help immigrants obtain legal status.
The other five were allegedly paid by Gonzalez to take part in the marriages — several of them taking part in multiple nuptials. Each marriage cost an immigrant from $38,000 to $40,000. All face charges including harboring illegal aliens, conspiracy to harbor illegal aliens, conspiracy to commit marriage fraud and marriage fraud.
“What an affront the alleged conduct revealed here today must be to those who play by the rules,” U.S. Attorney Leah Foley told reporters. “To see a for-profit business whose sole purpose is helping people cheat and skip the line by simply paying for it must be so offensive and disheartening to those who follow our country’s laws.”
Five of the six were arrested Wednesday morning and are expected to appear in federal court later in the day. A sixth defendant is currently in state prison serving a sentence for a firearms crime.
“Ms. Gonzalez got rich off selling the American Dream all the while investing her money in another country,” Foley said, detailing how Gonzalez allegedly used profits from the marriage ring to buy businesses and real estate in the Dominican Republic. She is an American citizen.
An attorney for Gonzalez, 43, of Fall River, Massachusetts, could not be reached for comment.
The arrests are the latest effort to crack down on marriage fraud and come as the Trump administration has increased restrictions on both legal and illegal immigration and reduced the avenues available for people to enter the country or become a citizen.
In August, 11 people were charged with participating in a multimillion-dollar scheme to help hundreds of Chinese nationals fraudulently obtain green cards through sham marriages to U.S. citizens. In that scheme, American citizens were paid as much as $30,000 to enter into bogus marriages with immigrants seeking lawful permanent resident status. The decade-long scheme netted tens of millions of dollars.
Three years ago, a similar scheme was prosecuted in Massachusetts. Marcialito Biol Benitez, a 49-year-old Philippine national living in Los Angeles, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit marriage fraud and immigration document fraud. Benitez admitted operating a large-scale marriage fraud agency in which he arranged marriages between foreign nationals and American citizens.
In the latest case, prosecutors said the investigation was ongoing. They allege in the court documents that some of the defendants lied on applications for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, by falsely claiming they never had been married. Gonzalez is also accused of spending $120,000 she received in SNAP benefits. Prosecutors also accused the defendants of engaging in housing and unemployment fraud.
None of the immigrants who entered into the marriages have been charged.
“Marriage fraud undermines the processes that ensure honest, lawful individuals can marry United States citizens and enjoy everything the United States has to offer to them,” John Soares, assistant special agent in charge, Homeland Security Investigations in New England, told reporters. “Fraudsters, like the individuals arrested today, make that process more difficult.”

title: Lincolnville writer flexes mastery of the uncanny in her latest genre-bending novel
text:
Elizabeth Hand has no formal education as a fiction writer, but nonetheless has written over 30 books, including novels, short story collections and franchise adaptations. Based in Maine for over 40 years, she has won the World Fantasy, Nebula and Shirley Jackson awards for her writing. Her novel “A Haunting on the Hill” is the only follow-up to Shirley Jackson’s novel, “The Haunting of Hill House,” authorized by the author’s estate.
As one might intuit from her accolades, Hand’s work is firmly rooted in genre fiction — science fiction, fantasy, horror, mystery, historical fiction and the gothic, among others, which she blends masterfully and seamlessly into formulations uniquely her own.
“Unspeakable Things,” her latest novel, falls firmly in the latter two, or even three, categories. It follows Olivia, a young artist living in 1920s Cornwall, England. She falls into a volatile and seductive relationship with the enigmatic Tamsyn, another girl living near Olivia’s isolated seaside manor. As the two circle closer to one another, a shocking death occurs, propelling them into realms of art, privilege and peril that they are barely able to understand. But danger doesn’t just come from the outside — it also lurks in the bond between them.
Hand spoke with the Press Herald about her creative process, queer representation, historical research and how Maine has influenced this novel set overseas.
The sheer volume of your work is just astonishing. Looking back to the first novel that you wrote, I’m curious about how your perspective on writing a novel has changed over time.
My first novel, “Winterlong,” came out in 1990. It grew out of a novella that had been published. I’d been playing around with it for a long time. I had no idea what I was doing. It’s been a process of trial and error, but by my fourth novel I started to have a better sense of it. You can see there is a learning curve, and there continues to be one.
I didn’t study creative writing, so I was always making it up as I went along. It’s worked to my advantage that I’ve done things my own way rather than adhere to any one path and any one genre over the years, never saying no to something and trying things out all the time. Not trying to reinvent myself, but because I have a low boredom threshold I’ll be like, “All right, I’ve never done that. What could possibly go wrong?”
This book has subverted genre tropes around queer people in such an interesting way. Where does that stem from?
I’ve written a lot about queer characters from the beginning of my career. It’s something I’ve been writing about since the late 1980s. Not all my characters in my novels are queer. Not all the novels are centered on that, but a lot of them are. These are people I know or have known. That tends to be who and what I write about.
I’ve always been fascinated by the trope of the doomed woman who is trying to find her way alone in the world. She’s orphaned or poor, and needs to marry well. I wanted to play with that And I have this l-time fascination with the 1920s. That whole strain of writing and theater and music and art, which was influenced by queer people. It seemed like a fun cocktail to put all these things in together and add something that might kill you, but only in large doses.
I’m not going to spoil the ending, but I absolutely did not see it coming in a very beautiful, disturbing way. How many different iterations of the ending did you have?
I always knew how it was going to end. The different things leading up to it — that was the part that changed. There was this whole other subplot that involved a London policewoman who was investigating the crimes. I wrote literally hundreds of pages of that. There was a certain point where I was talking with my editor, and I said, “Oh my God, this draft is 850 pages long.” We both reluctantly agreed that we needed to cut it. Arthur Quiller-Cooch said, “Kill your darlings.” — not Faulkner, who gets the credit. This was killing a big darling, but it had to be done.
So you cut 75,000 words, or something like that?
It had to go. It wasn’t working. The book went through multiple revisions. There’s shorter fiction of mine that comes to me fully formed and doesn’t need a lot of revision. But the novels do. I love to write historical novels, and they take a lot of time and energy and effort with research, which I love doing.
I’m curious about what your research process was for this or your other historical fiction novels.
The 1920s are a time I’ve been interested in since I was in high school. I read or reread nonfiction books and novels that are set in that era and then did the kind of research that the internet is great for, which is just falling down rabbit holes. I don’t use AI at all, on principle. I just don’t do it.
I do try as much as possible to find primary sources. I’ll buy old magazines from whatever year the novel’s set. They’re a wealth of information because you get advertisements, you get fiction, you get articles about celebrities of the time, many of whom are totally forgotten. They have information about clothes, what things cost, all of this stuff. Then of course, after the book is done, I have a stack of moldering magazines that no one needs.
I’m always fascinated when I read people’s work about how other art forms influence them. The book has constant references to historical painters.
In most of my books, the central characters are some sort of artists. They’re performers, they’re actors, they’re visual artists, painters. I’m just fascinated by the creative process. To me, it’s like magic. How does it work? I don’t understand it for myself. Writing about painters, photographers, actors, musicians, there’s something tactile there. You can describe the work and what goes into it, unlike with a writer.
Did you bring any influence from Maine as a location, Maine as a culture, into this novel, even though it’s very much set in Britain?
The first time I went to Cornwall, where this novel is set, I thought, “Oh my God, it looks like Maine!” It’s very similar culturally and socially too. Traditional fishing and rural agrarian communities, but living on poor soil. It’s been impacted by the collapse of the fishing industry and by tourism and climate change. And all of the second homes. I’ve been here since the late 1980s. I’m not a Mainer, but I have seen the shifts. Quote unquote “normal people” can’t live here anymore. If I hadn’t moved here when I did, I couldn’t live here. I would never be able to afford it now.
Cornwall has fascinated me since first going there 25 years ago. I obviously don’t live there. I can’t write about it with that kind of knowledge. But the landscape is quite similar. I was walking around in these villages and I said, “I could live here, but what would be the point? Because I already live in a place like this. It’s beautiful.”
Sky Davis is a writer, producer and reporter based in Brooklyn. They’re a former senior editor on the Pocket FM audio fiction platform, and their work has appeared in The Rumpus and The Christian Science Monitor, among other outlets.

title: Offshore storm bringing breezy conditions
text:
Offshore storm bringing breezy conditions
Offshore storm bringing breezy conditions
Wednesday will start off sunny, but cloud cover will start to increase a bit this afternoon. We have a cooler day in store with high temperatures in the mid-50s. Wednesday will also feel cool because conditions will be breezy, with wind gusts reaching 20 to 25 mph.
The reason we have such a windy day is because of an offshore storm that is slowly making its way northeast. On Wednesday, the high pressure overhead will help to keep most of the impacts out in the Atlantic, but the difference between high and low pressure will cause the breezy conditions.
Thursday will also be blustery, with wind gusts reaching 30 to 35 mph. It'll be warmer and cloudier on Thursday, and a cold front will also help to keep the offshore storm away from the coast.
We won't be seeing beneficial rainfall from this storm, and the week ahead is looking dry with no chances for showers.

title: Sprinchorn exhibit at Bates offers a freshly relevant take on the artist’s Maine work
text:
The great gift of a reappraisal of any artist’s work is to see it through new perspectives — derived from research into forgotten or newly discovered aspects of an artist’s work and life — and the retrospective intelligence (dare I say wisdom?) gained from historical distance. Last month, I wrote about the Carl Sprinchorn exhibition at the Ogunquit Museum of American Art, “All the World Is a Painting,” which closes Nov. 1 (clear your calendar if you must, but go see it; you won’t be sorry).
Now comes “Carl Sprinchorn: Points of View” (through Dec. 19) at Bates College Museum of Art, an exhibition curated by Samantha Sigmon and developed in conjunction with the Ogunquit, a relationship that has produced a handsome and thorough volume from University of Maine Press, “Carl Sprinchorn: A Rediscovery.”
“All the World” frankly discussed Sprinchorn’s homosexuality. This was something averted in polite society during his own time, yet so integral to the art that made him most famous: his portrayals of lumberjacks in Patten, Maine. Christopher Reed’s essay for the catalog establishes early on the precariousness of being out in the early 20th century, “when any articulation of homosexuality was risky, as Sprinchorn’s correspondence files document. A chummy letter from the artist John Blomshield — an extravagant figure sometimes cited as the inspiration for the promiscuous American, Clive, in Christpher Isherwood’s “Good-Bye to Berlin” — worried with facetious flair about a patron who was helping him find a studio in New York:
“I do not know her well, at all, so do not quite know which way is north. There are still a number of sophisticated people (you must believe this) who consider homosexuality — a horrid word — an unusual and exciting phenomenon. Ah well…”
Curator Devon Zimmerman also recontextualized Sprinchorn’s art through the lens of the immigrant experience in America, which not only made the artist’s work feel freshly relevant, but illuminated just how radically that immigrant experience has changed since Sprinchorn’s day, implicitly admonishing viewers to consider why this is so.
Whereas the Ogunquit show was rich with paintings, “Points of View” concentrates on Bates College’s holdings of works on paper. To be sure, there are magnificent oils. Among them are “The Great Basin, Katahdin” (1940) and “Early Autumn” (1917), which corroborate Sprinchorn’s considerable skill as a landscape painter. Others, such as the watercolor “Sunrise — 1947,” reveal one of his singular techniques by quoting from Sprinchorn himself: “I used to make 5 or 6 quick, instant strokes and color notes on so many large sheets of water color [sic] paper within a matter of a few minutes…then hold on to the idea and finish them without looking at the sun again.”
What is more interesting to me about this watercolor, however, is the way it cements Sprinchorn’s position at the center of the many crosscurrents of modernism. The first allusion I made upon viewing “Sunrise—1947” was to Arthur Dove. It is impossible that Sprinchorn would not have known Dove’s work. Dove was one of the most highly acclaimed artists in Alfred Stieglitz’s stable at the legendary 291 Fifth Avenue gallery in New York, which also included Marsden Hartley and Georgia O’Keeffe, both of whom had connections (in O’Keeffe’s case, more tangentially) to Maine. Though he traveled widely during his career, the exhibition also confirms how Maine occupied a vital creative center of Sprinchorn’s life. Dove died the year before Sprinchorn painted “Sunrise—1947,” and his depiction of the sunrise seems inconceivable without the many versions of suns painted by Dove, among them: “Morning Sun,” “Sunset,” even “Moon” (all of 1935) and “Sun” of 1943.
This is speculation, of course. And having just seen the superb production of Tom Stoppard’s “Arcadia” at Portland Stage — one subplot of which revolves around the way historians tend to project their own assumptions on the subjects they are researching — I hesitate to put too fine a point on this. But both these exhibitions seem to me to make connections to the precedents and modernist trends Sprinchorn was absorbing into his own oeuvre, from van Gogh to Matisse to Dove to Hartley.
More intriguing still is how the many sketches and studies on view at Bates point up that Sprinchorn’s decision to de-emphasize facial features of his famous lumberjacks as a way of amplifying their homoerotic physicality was a deliberate one. Two self-portraits on hotel stationery from 1924 prove that Sprinchorn was most assuredly capable of rendering facial features and expressions with skill, which means that his choice to depict eyes, nose and mouth as simple slits in his paintings was intentional.
What is more, the drawings forced me to examine my own preferences for other subject matter Sprinchorn depicted outside of his lumber camp paintings (most specifically, the landscapes). This stylistic decision in his drawings certainly contributes to the immediacy of the drawings themselves. They are never meant to be finished works, but to capture an idea, a gesture, a pose (and so on) that can be further explored and refined in a finished work. So, in the drawings, we accept the lack of defined faces and expressions more easily. In finished paintings, however, I expected something more and could not help viewing his slitty features as in some way lacking or crude.
Was Sprinchorn’s judgement to obliterate facial features and expressions an effective move? Marsden Hartley, his friend and obvious influence, had at least made an effort at expressions and features, even though he was after the same beefcake effect of male bodies. Personally, it feels like Sprinchorn’s simplification of faces contributed to a kind of cartoonish effect in his paintings that diminishes them. Yes, we still intuit the eroticism of male bodies, but we might have perceived this more fully if eyes and looks were allowed to enhance that physical attraction by radiating a more smoldering sexuality.
On the other hand, a series of drawings Sprinchorn made in the late 1920s — most prominently “Dormant, Semi-dormant, and Awake” (1922) — display a wit and imagination that made me wish he had more fully explored in his figural paintings. The energy of its zigzag lines communicates tremendous sexual electricity. Bodies are concisely yet sensually articulated, carrying more charge in my mind than his lumberjacks.
Which is why it is worth seeing both shows. Maybe, in the end, it is just a difference between genres — the immediacy of sketching versus the more considered and refined process of painting. Artists have struggled with this for centuries. Eugène Delacroix was perhaps the most successful at bridging this divide. To this day I know artists who still struggle with preserving the urgency and energy of a drawing while making a painting. But without seeing both shows, it is hard to understand that conundrum. Each offers pleasures unique to its exhibition. But taken together, they form a holistic understanding and appreciation of Sprinchorn’s contributions to the modernist canon.
Jorge S. Arango has written about art, design and architecture for over 35 years. He lives in Portland and can be reached at [email protected]. This column is free to access through support by The Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation.
‘Carl Sprinchorn: Points of View,‘ Bates College Museum of Art Olin Art Center, 75 Russell St., Lewiston. 10 a.m.-7:30 p.m. Monday and Wednesday, and 10 a.m.-5 p.m. Tuesday, Thursday and Friday through Dec. 19. For more, 207-786-6158 or bates.edu/museum

title: 68-year-old woman killed by stray bullet while sitting on her back porch, family says
text:
GASTONIA, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A 68-year-old woman was shot and killed while sitting on the back porch of her North Carolina home on Monday, according to her family.
The deadly shooting happened late in the afternoon on Oct. 19, at the Dwell Townhomes on Hillgate Avenue in Gastonia.
The family of Pamela Shanks told WBTV that Shanks was sitting on her porch, which backs up to Laurel Lane, when the fatal shots were fired. The family said the shooting may have involved a dispute between others in the neighborhood.
Neighbors told WBTV they heard several shots late Monday afternoon, then saw multiple young people run away in black clothing.
Gastonia police confirmed Shanks was not the intended target of the shooting on Laurel Lane and died after being hit by a stray bullet.
Investigators remained at the townhomes for hours Monday, roping off a large portion of the complex, including a playground. Police are working to determine how many people fired guns and who the intended target was.
As of Tuesday afternoon, no arrests had been made.
“Half of my heart was just like, it was folded and I don’t know which way to go and it hurts so bad,” Shanks’ niece, who asked to to remain, said in a phone call with WBTV Tuesday.
The shooting has left Shanks’ family heartbroken and pleading for justice.
“She was the light. She made everybody laugh. She made jokes. It’s just like now we won’t see that part of her no more, because someone took her life over some dummy stuff. So it’s just like, I’m still in shock,” the niece said.
Shanks’ niece also had a message Tuesday for anyone who fires a gun recklessly.
“I just want them to think, it’s consequences behind what you do. Anything you do dealing with killing somebody, shooting a gun. I don’t care if you’re just shooting in the air, it’s consequences behind that,” she said.

title: Former DA challenges current DA in Cumberland County
text:
Former DA challenges current DA in Cumberland County
Stephanie Anderson is coming out of retirement to run against Jackie Sartoris in the Cumberland County District Attorney's race.
Former DA challenges current DA in Cumberland County
Stephanie Anderson is coming out of retirement to run against Jackie Sartoris in the Cumberland County District Attorney's race.
When voters in Cumberland County go to the polls in just a few weeks they will be choosing who they want to be district attorney. It's a race between an incumbent and a candidate who used to hold the position.
"This is all about returning power to the folks Who were used to having it for 32 years in," Cumberland County District Attorney Jackie Sartoris said.
"I left a legacy I was proud of and it turns out that legacy is being destroyed," former Cumberland County District Attorney Stephanie Anderson said.
Anderson was DA for 28 years before retiring back in 2018. She's a longtime republican, but is in this race as an independent.
"When I retired from the DA's office, I unenrolled because I am and always have been independent. And frankly, there's a lot about both parties that I do not like," Anderson said.
Anderson was backing Democratic primary candidate Valerie Adams who was defeated by Sartoris back in June.
Adams worked in the DA's office while Anderson was at the helm, as well as when Sartoris was running the office.
Maine's Total Coverage previously reported that Adams claimed she was let go by Sartoris when she learned Adams planned to primary her.
If Adams won the primary, Anderson said she would have withdrawn from the race.
"It was to restore trust and competency in the DA's office. That's what this race is about," Anderson said about her reason to run.
Sartoris is wrapping up her first term as DA. four years ago she defeated on term incumbent, Jonathan Sahrbeck, in a hotly contested race.
Now, she's touting her record.
"Homelessness is down 41% in Cumberland County since I became the district attorney," Sartoris said. "We specifically have a program where we are pushing people towards the Homeless Services Center."
According to MaineHousing, homelessness is down 34.7% since 2024.
Anderson and Sartoris will go head to head on November 3.

title: Ohtani's Dodgers rare jersey sells for $2.05M
text:
Ohtani's Dodgers rare jersey sells for $2.05M
Ohtani's Dodgers rare jersey sells for $2.05M
A Los Angeles Dodgers jersey worn by Shohei Ohtani during the 2025 MLB Tokyo Series opener has broken the record for the most expensive baseball jersey worn by a player in the 21st century, selling for more than $2 million at an auction on "The Realest."
Ohtani wore the jersey during his first official Major League Baseball game in Japan.
The jersey includes his autograph, handwritten inscriptions, and the first gold MLB logoman patch ever worn in an official game.
The previous record for the most expensive baseball jersey worn in this century was held by a New York Yankees jersey worn by Aaron Judge during his MLB debut in 2016, which sold for a reported $1.792 million.

title: Trump heads to Iowa Thursday with new farm aid package
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump is rolling out a new $8 billion farming package to provide one-time relief payments to farmers facing rising fertilizer and diesel costs.
The announcement comes ahead of another $26 billion bailout. $12 billion was distributed earlier this year in one-time payments, followed by a $14 billion injection two weeks ago.
The announcement comes ahead of Trump’s visit to Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday. Iowa, an agriculture-heavy state, has felt the effects of Trump’s economic and foreign policies, including the recent importation of millions of tons of foreign beef.
New New York Times polling shows Trump’s approval rating has dropped to an all-time low of 36% with fewer than two weeks until the election.
The White House and the Republican Party is not changing its strategy heading into the midterms.
“The midterms. Historically, it’s all about turnout. So it’s turnout, turnout, turnout. And how do you do that? Well, yet you put President Trump on the ballot. You bring them front and center and you let him do what he does best,” Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters said.
Data from ad-tracking firm AdImpact shows less than 1 out of every 100 dollars spent on Republican ads went toward a commercial that mentioned Trump.
National polling shows the Senate race in Iowa is in a dead heat. The race for governor has raised more than $33 million in the last three months.
Trump will rally at Sioux Gateway Airport. Doors open at 2:30 p.m. Central Time.

title: DOJ watchdog declines to investigate handling of Reflecting Pool case, lawyers say
text:
Justice Department watchdog declines to investigate handling of Reflecting Pool case, lawyers say
The Department of Justice's inspector general has declined to investigate the handling of the criminal case against an Olympian cleared of accusations that he intentionally damaged the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, according to a letter Wednesday from the man's lawyers.
The internal watchdog told David Hearn's lawyers that the allegations of professional misconduct that they made fall outside its jurisdiction and are instead within the purview of the department's Office of Professional Responsibility, according to the letter, which urges Inspector General Don R. Berthiaume to reconsider the decision.
“Given the substantial public attention devoted to this matter, and the significant questions raised concerning the conduct of federal officials, declining independent review would risk undermining public confidence in the Department’s ability to police its own conduct. Such a result would be inconsistent with the purposes for which Congress established the OIG and would be a betrayal of its mission,” the letter says.
Hearn's lawyers this month had asked for investigations by the inspectors general at the departments of Justice and Interior, citing a broad variety of “incompetence and misconduct” that they said occurred during the criminal investigation and prosecution of their client. They say they believe they have identified potential crimes in the Trump administration's handling of the case, including witness tampering, obstruction of justice and the subornation of false testimony.
The Justice Department moved to dismiss the case last summer, saying newly produced evidence from the Interior Department showed that Hearn, 67, of Bethesda, Maryland, was not responsible for damage to the pool’s lining. A District of Columbia judge later permanently threw out the prosecution.
Hearn’s lawyers said in their initial letter to the watchdogs that the evidence that established their client’s innocence had been in the Justice Department’s possession for weeks and was “simply ignored.” They asked the inspectors general to investigate why prosecutors “rushed to indict” under what they said was pressure from Republican President Donald Trump, who had launched a massive renovation project of the Reflecting Pool for the celebration in Washington of America's 250th anniversary.
In renewing their request for an inspector general investigation, Hearn's team argues that the watchdog is uniquely positioned — both in terms of tools and independence — to dig into allegations of misconduct against the government officials involved in the case.
They note that unlike the inspector general's office, the Office of Professional Responsibility, which also investigates some categories of professional misconduct, reports to the deputy attorney general and attorney general and has no obligation to publicize its work or report its findings to Congress.
Hearn's lawyers also say the inspector general is the right office to investigate the potential criminal misconduct they believe they have identified within the government, asserting that prosecutors elicited false testimony from a witness who testified before the grand jury and violated Hearn's civil rights by proceeding with a flawed criminal case. They say the inspector general should investigate whether U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro, whose office handled the case, violated ethical rules in a news conference when she announced charges against Hearn.
The U.S. attorney's office did not respond to a request seeking comment when Hearn's attorneys raised the allegations earlier this month.
Among Hearn's attorneys is Michael Bromwich, a Justice Department inspector general during the Clinton administration.
“In a case such as this one, when some of the allegations directly involve the United States Attorney for the District of Columbia, there is substantial reason to question whether any meaningful independent review would occur,” the lawyers' letter says. “Your decision not to investigate would be consigning these serious allegations to oblivion despite the enormous public interest in the matter and the absence thus far of any accountability for the individuals involved.”

title: 3 nearly vital things those in the Midcoast should know
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I’m trying to tone down my hyperbole. If I had made a New Year’s resolution, it would have been this.
I want to reserve my absolutes so that they have meaning (for example, this looks like it will be the scariest winter fuel heating season I have experienced as an adult). See that? That’s a proper use of absolutes. However, I can improperly use an absolute by saying the chicken I made last night “was the worst.” That’s too hyperbolic, as I have messed up chicken many times before, usually with bad spice decisions like “How much cumin is too much cumin?” or “Did I even put any chili powder in it?”
I’m fooling around a bit to prove a point, in that, we are living through very intense times, and it is easy to overstate the severity of things. Yet by doing so we are doing ourselves a disservice. Not everything can be unprecedented. Admittedly, certain aspects of our world right now can be viewed 100% legitimately as unprecedented — you will get no argument from me. However, other things are just regular good, or regular bad, but aren’t unprecedented.
I don’t make this point to be pedantic. I make it because, if we are constantly referring to things in absolutes — the best, the worst, the scariest, the lowest, the highest — then we are shocking our nervous systems and our mental health into survival mode, and/or panic mode. Even when we boast about extreme good, we are competing against what good has come before, and also unintentionally flaunting our unsurpassable good in front of those in our circles, who may be struggling. We cannot be healthy if we are constantly assaulting ourselves and those around us with the intense weight of everything being the most extreme it has ever been. We need to remind ourselves that not everything is a crisis on all fronts.
With that, I have three updates that I think are “nearly vital” for you to know about because I think they can help. They can help you connect with your community, or to find resources, or to increase your knowledge, or in any other way, just help. Here they are:
CANDIDATE VIDEO RELEASES FRIDAY
Raise your hand if you are tired of political signs, mailers, videos, text messages, and TV commercials. OK, now literally everyone reading this, please put your hand down.
As is a biannual tradition, we have been bombarded with political messages (and not ironically, very extreme messaging). Still though, do you know your local candidates? Well, I do (most of them, at least) and I want to share them with you.
For much of last week, and wrapping up this week, the chamber has offered recorded Zoom videos for the 23 candidates running for the state House in our 16-community chamber region. These are roughly 12-minute videos where I ask each candidate the same six questions.
We are releasing all of the completed candidate videos this Friday, Oct. 23, so everyone has a week and a half to learn more about the candidates. It should be noted that not all candidates have responded to the offer to be interviewed — please reach out if we haven’t filmed yet (or check your campaign email address). In fairness to the candidates who have filmed, I cannot hold the finished videos beyond Friday — it would not be fair to them.
The videos will be mentioned on the Bath Brunswick Topsham Regional Chamber Facebook page, chamber website, and the videos themselves will live on the chamber’s YouTube page. Feel free to share them.
MERRYMEETING TREE FEST IS 1 MONTH AWAY
The Merrymeeting Tree Fest is four weeks away! This incredible six-day event over two weekends is awesome, and there are tons of ways for you to participate in the fun. We will do a deep dive next week but, things to know right now:
• Half of our tree spaces are still available for tree sponsors (max 55)
• Nonprofits are signing up for wreath sponsors, but more are welcome
• Hammond Lumber Co. is our presenting sponsor this year, but many other sponsorship levels are available
• Volunteering is a great way to connect with your community. We have up to 11 shifts every two hours of the festival. You can also donate your volunteering time this year to the nonprofit of your choice (each two-hour shift is a $30 donation)
• Entertainers, we have five to seven slots still open (email [email protected])
All of this information lives on the Merrymeeting Tree Fest page at MidcoastMaine.com. You can also follow the Merrymeeting Tree Fest Facebook page, on which we will begin posting daily updates on by early next week.
UNITED WAY HEATING RESOURCES, 211 AND OTHERS
As you know, there is a close relationship between our chamber and the United Way of Mid Coast Maine. We work together on many workforce initiatives, including the Connecting to Tomorrow internship program. However, the United Way is also an outstanding collector of resource information for our communities.
With the anxiety about the forthcoming heating season upon us, we have been sharing their 2026-2027 Heating Resource guide in our weekly e-newsletters that outlines the different organizations, based on your community, that can assist with heating needs. To find this, log onto their website, and look for the resources page under the “Get Help” link at the top of their home page at UWMCM.org.
On that page as well, you will see their other phone number lists for their community resource directory (housing, food, clothing, etc.) and their public transportation guide. These are great items for business owners to post in breakrooms.
Finally, you can always call 211.
Twenty-four hours per day your call will be answered by a human, and they can help direct you to the resources in your neighborhood. Please share this essential information far and wide because you never know who could use a little help.
Cory King is executive director of the Bath-Brunswick-Topsham Regional Chamber of Commerce.

title: Sen. Collins enlists ex-Democratic colleague Manchin in effort to highlight her independence
text:
Sen. Susan Collins enlists ex-Democratic colleague Joe Manchin in effort to highlight her independence
The Maine Republican is trying to fend off a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson in a tight reelection campaign.
Sen. Susan Collins enlists ex-Democratic colleague Joe Manchin in effort to highlight her independence
The Maine Republican is trying to fend off a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson in a tight reelection campaign.
Maine Republican Susan Collins has promoted her reputation as one of the most independent U.S. senators, and she is using the waning days of the election season to sell that message to voters by campaigning with a former Democratic colleague who has endorsed her.
Collins is trying to fend off a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson, a onetime state Senate president, and on Wednesday, she made appearances with Joe Manchin, a West Virginian who became an independent late in his career before retiring.
After stopping for breakfast at Simones' Hot Dog Stand in Lewiston, Collins spoke of how she and Manchin were “part of every piece of bipartisan legislation that passed and became law” during their time together in office.
Manchin said to lose Collins would be “to lose the soul of the Senate.” He praised her independent streak, her willingness to buck Republican President Donald Trump and her record of fighting for Maine's interests.
“This is a true blue-blooded Maine person who knows exactly where she came from,” Manchin said.
They stopped later a New Balance shoe facility in Norway.
Jackson, 58, is scheduled to campaign Thursday in Portland with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the progressive congresswoman from New York.
Collins, 73, is in what may be her toughest reelection fight as she seeks her sixth term. It's only the second time that she's sought reelection in a midterm with a sitting Republican president, and the national trends are much less favorable to the GOP than they were the last time she did so in 2002. Trump's approval has fallen well below where it was when he took office last year, and a recent poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that a strong majority of voters want change in Washington.
'We need more people like Susan Collins'
Collins has been working to persuade voters that she is independent of Trump and willing to break with him. In Manchin, she enlisted a politician who was one of the most moderate voices in the Senate. Manchin said in 2023 that Trump would “destroy democracy in America” if he was elected to a second term.
Among the few dozen Collins supporters at the Lewiston event was Mike Marcotte.
“I may not have always been a fan of her complete package of votes, but when I look at the vitriol that's in the U.S. Senate right now, we need more people like Susan Collins,” he said.
Jackson got a late start on campaigning after the party's initial nominee exited the race, but trails Collins in the money race by less than $3 million after an aggressive quarter in which he raised more than $20 million. Jackson has campaigned relentlessly, and his events have drawn hundreds. Collins has largely stuck to smaller appearances.
Some of Jackson's backers demonstrated across the street from the hot dog stand. A few held signs bearing the face of Brett Kavanaugh, the U.S. Supreme Court justice whom Collins voted to confirm and whose vote eventually helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion.
“Someone needs to stand up and be a check on Donald Trump and his harmful policies,” said David Sysko.
Collins' loyalty to Trump has been a central focus of the race
Collins has broken with Trump and Republicans over the years. She voted to convict him at his impeachment trial in 2021. Increasingly during the campaign, she has worked to distance herself from the president as Democrats argue that she is too close to him.
Collins said in early October that she is “not exactly his favorite senator,” and that she did not expect Trump to campaign in Maine. He has steered clear of the state with the Nov. 3 election nearing.
Pinning Collins to Trump is central to the Democrats’ strategy. In one ad, a nurse says the state is in a healthcare crisis “because of Susan Collins and Donald Trump,” citing Collins’ vote for Trump’s push for Medicaid cuts. Collins did vote to advance the bill in a procedural move to open debate, but ultimately voted against it.
Trump also was a major focus of four contentious debates between the candidates this month, where Collins sought to distance herself from the president and Jackson repeatedly accused her of doing Trump's bidding.
Asked at the final debate to name a time in which she bucked her own party and succeeded, Collins gave the example of rallying support against Trump's nomination of Pete Hegseth, who was confirmed as defense secretary.
Democrats seized on the moment and released a statement that said the exchange “underscores a central question in the Maine Senate race: Does Collins, a Republican in a state that disapproves of President Donald Trump and has grown bluer in recent years, stand up to her party enough to earn the independent streak she has staked her career on?”
Jackson has characterized Collins as out of touch with the struggles of working-class people in Maine. He has described Collins as a “rubber stamp” for the president and criticized her votes on Kavanaugh and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Trump's second-term health secretary. Collins has said she does not regret either vote.
Republicans have cast Jackson as a bully
Republican ads against Jackson, a logger from northern Maine, have focused more on accusations of his having a volatile personality and behaving like a bully with female colleagues. Jackson has denied those accusations.
Collins distanced herself on Wednesday from a Republican super PAC attack ad that she said “should be taken down.”
The senator was a top target of Democrats in 2020 when she defeated challenger Sara Gideon by nearly 9 percentage points. Collins is the only Republican senator from New England, a distinction she has had since January 2013.

title: Anson select board chairman resigns for ‘personal reasons’
text:
ANSON — The chairman of the town’s Board of Selectmen has resigned.
James Smith submitted his letter of resignation Friday, according to a copy provided by Town Administrator Angel Aguirre.
Smith wrote in the brief letter he was stepping down for “personal reasons” and did not elaborate further.
“Thank you for the privilege,” Smith wrote.
Two voicemails left with Smith on Tuesday were not returned.
The board held an emergency meeting Friday afternoon. Members accepted Smith’s resignation, Aguirre said via email, and decided to vote to determine the new chair and vice chair at their next regular meeting Oct. 27.
Currently serving as vice chair is Brenda Garland.
The board also held off on discussing whether to fill the vacancy or wait until annual municipal elections in March, said board member Leanne Dickey on Tuesday.
Running unopposed, Smith was most recently elected in March to a three-year term. Anson voters first elected Smith in 2017.
He took over as chairman in the summer of 2025 following the resignation of Arnold Luce, who was an Anson selectman for decades.
Luce stepped down while facing criminal charges stemming from an incident involving a woman at his meat processing business.
Earlier this year, Luce pleaded guilty to one misdemeanor count of unlawful sexual touching, and prosecutors dismissed one misdemeanor count of assault. Per the plea agreement, he was sentenced to 180 days in jail, all of which was suspended, and one year of probation.
The Board of Selectmen meets at the town office at 5 Kennebec St.; meetings start at 6 p.m.

title: 11-foot gator removed from Florida property after 'stalking' couple
text:
11-foot gator removed from Florida property after 'stalking' couple
A cross now sits where 71-year-old Steven Hamilton was killed by an alligator in Winter Garden, Florida, and a memorial for him nearby continues to grow.
Police say Hamilton was taking a photo with a fish he had caught when the alligator pulled him into the water at Dr. Bradford Memorial Park, killing him. The attack happened at a pond next to Lake Apopka, which is home to thousands of alligators.
Randy Forbes, who has lived on a lakefront property along Lake Apopka in Oakland, Florida, for two decades, grew up in Florida, so alligators are nothing new to him. But he worries some of them may be losing their fear of humans, putting people in danger.
An 11-foot alligator was recently removed by nuisance trappers from the shore near Forbes' home because of what he described as unusual behavior.
"He would just follow us up and down the dock, and it got to the point where I was just not comfortable at all," Forbes said.
Last month, Forbes said he and his wife were pressure-washing the dock at his Oakland home when he noticed the alligator getting too close for comfort.
"I tried shooing him off a little bit. He wouldn't move. He just continued stalking us up and down the dock," Forbes said.
Fearing the alligator may attack a child in the neighborhood, he contacted the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission's nuisance alligator hotline, and a group of trappers stopped by and removed two gators.
“The first one they pulled out of the lake was about 8 feet, 10 inches,” Forbes said. “Then they got the one that we think was the culprit. He was 11 feet, 1 inch.”
On a regular summer day, Forbes said he'll see several alligators sunbathing in his backyard. It's a sight he's grown accustomed to in the two decades he's lived on his lakefront property.
"Typically, when I walk down toward the lake, they'll run off," Forbes said. "This one, he did no running."
He suspects the alligator was no longer fearful of humans.
"I have a real strong suspicion that people are feeding these gators, especially from the public docks," Forbes said.
That's why Friday's deadly attack at Dr. Bradford Memorial Park in Winter Garden, which Forbes called "absolutely tragic," has made him more cognizant of his surroundings.
"I do mow all the way down to the water's edge, so I can guarantee you from this point out, I will be a little more cautious and make sure that I know exactly what's in my surroundings," Forbes said.
Forbes said the two alligators that were removed from his property were relocated to Gatorland, unlike the alligator involved in Friday's deadly attack, which police confirm was killed.
"It is Mother Nature," Forbes said. "You have to be aware of your surroundings, pay attention, and know that any body of water in Florida can potentially hold an alligator that can do some damage."

title: Brunswick’s Pejepscot History Center is investing in the future of history
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
History buffs know that two Brunswick residents played pivotal roles in the course of the Civil War. Harriet Beecher Stowe’s “Uncle Tom’s Cabin” conveyed the atrocities of human slavery, emboldening abolitionists to advance their cause. Joshua Chamberlain’s heroic leadership in the battle of Little Round Top at Gettysburg helped turn the tide of the war in favor of the Union.
The rich history of Brunswick and the surrounding areas goes much deeper than Harriet Beecher Stowe and Joshua Chamberlain.
Larissa Picard, executive director of the Pejepscot History Center for the past 11 years, knows the importance of showcasing the region’s history for the community, as well as for visitors from around the world.
“This region has a significant history,” she explains. “The story of Maine is the story of our country. The shipbuilding, the textile mills, the ties to the slave economy. History is about telling stories, and we try to tell those stories. After all, we are humans, not robots. History is not all black and white; there can be darkness underlying the stories.”
The Pejepscot History Center is in the midst of a major $2 million capital campaign designed to “reimagine, revitalize and improve the accessibility” of the two Park Row museums: the Pejepscot Museum and Research Center and the Skolfield-Whittier House Museum.
The campaign, titled “Building Connections: Opening Doors to Our Community,” includes five major goals:
1. Create a fully ADA-complaint entrance on the north side of the Pejepscot History Museum, featuring a gently sloped ramp, automated doors, and a spacious new reception area.
2. Create an enclosed passageway that will connect the Pejepscot History Museum and the Skolfield-Whittier House.
3. Install a permanent orientation exhibit that gives visitors an overview of the center’s history and collections. At the same time, more flexible display spaces will expand rotating exhibits.
4. Create greater capacity for community-building events.
5. Create better spaces for collections and archives.
These changes will greatly expand the history center’s capacity to further enrich and expand its full slate of offerings.
Did you know, for example, that in addition to offering popular summer walking tours, the center enables organizations to get prepared talks on topics ranging from Pejepscot’s Literary Lions or immigration stories to Brunswick to the slave trade and abolition? Customized talks can also be prepared.
On the educational front, the history center offers prepared programs for students at all grade levels.
Upcoming special events include, Thanks-For-Giving Member Party on Nov. 20 and Santa Day on Dec. 5.
The numbers tell the tale. Over 5,000 people visit the history center’s three museums every year and nearly 2,000 people attend the public programs every year.
The capital campaign has already raised $1.4 million toward its $2 million goal. For more information on the campaign or ways to support the center, visit pejepscothistorical.org.
David Treadwell, a Brunswick writer, welcomes commentary and suggestions for future “Just a Little Old” columns at [email protected].

title: Another woman alleges sexual assault at fraternity near University of Chicago
text:
Another woman alleges sexual assault at fraternity near University of Chicago
The University of Chicago is set to hold a public safety meeting Wednesday night, after a woman reported this month that she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house near campus and another woman filed a lawsuit alleging she was sexually assaulted at a different fraternity house in February.
A 19-year-old college student, identified as Jane Doe, claims in a lawsuit she was sexually assaulted Feb. 7 by a fraternity member at an Alpha Delta Phi party. The suit, filed Monday, names Alpha Delta Phi Inc. and the Chicago Society of Alpha Delta Phi as defendants; the University of Chicago is not named as a defendant.
The suit indicates the plaintiff is seeking information from the University of Chicago with an eye toward potentially adding it as a defendant.
Chicago police told CNN a 19-year-old woman reported she was sexually assaulted around 1 a.m. Feb. 8 inside a residence on the 5700 block of South University Avenue and later went to a hospital. Police did not name the fraternity, but Doe told officers she was assaulted at its address on that block, according to the lawsuit.
The incident — now more than eight months old — is still under investigation.
CNN has reached out to the University of Chicago and Alpha Delta Phi for comment and to Doe’s attorneys for further information. Doe does not attend the University of Chicago, her attorney, Georgia Booth, told WLS.
CNN obtained the suit from The Chicago Maroon, the university’s student newspaper, which was first to report on it.
The University of Chicago last week said a person of interest was banned from campus after a 21-year-old woman reported she was sexually assaulted Oct. 11 at another nearby fraternity house. Chicago police are investigating.
Both allegations come as colleges and universities face heightened scrutiny over their handling of sexual assault cases amid an investigation into an alleged gang rape in 2024 at a fraternity house at Cornell University in New York.
In the alleged February incident in Chicago, Doe attended a party at Alpha Delta Phi’s house and accepted a shot of unidentified alcohol from a fraternity brother that quickly made her feel “unsteady and lightheaded,” her lawsuit states. The man then led Doe to a secluded bedroom on another floor, where he allegedly made “unwanted and nonconsensual sexual advances” after she “lost all physical and verbal ability to refuse” him, according to the lawsuit.
“Jane Doe was mentally and physically incapable of providing consent,” the suit alleges.
Doe pleaded with the man to use a condom, but he refused, the complaint says. The fraternity brother then penetrated her “without her consent” and left her “alone and unconscious in the room,” according to the suit.
The suit says Doe’s friend was initially blocked by other fraternity brothers from going upstairs to check on her, until a member who saw Doe unconscious told them to let the friend up. The friend found Doe unconscious and helped her out of the house, the complaint states.
The next morning, Doe found bloodstains in her underwear and reported the incident to the Chicago Police Department, naming the fraternity brother who allegedly sexually assaulted her, according to the lawsuit, prompting police to investigate.
Doe’s suit claims the fraternity failed to abide by its own rules of conduct, which it lays out in detail, including duties to provide sober monitors at events and to protect against sexual assault by its members.

title: Justice Kagan warns Supreme Court rulings are fueling polarization and undermining democracy
text:
Justice Kagan warns Supreme Court rulings are fueling polarization and undermining democracy
Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday said voting and elections decisions from her conservative Supreme Court colleagues have helped make the country more politically polarized and less democratic.
In a speech two weeks before the pivotal midterm elections for control of Congress, the liberal-leaning justice sharply criticized how the majority’s rulings have affected the nation’s political environment.
“The court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effect of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that does not work as well as it should,” she said during a talk before students and professors at Catholic University's law school in Washington, D.C.
She blasted rulings that weakened the Voting Rights Act and campaign finance regulations while opening the door for more partisan gerrymandering. She dissented from those decisions.
“Over the last couple of years especially, both political parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, … making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so,” she said. “The people of America look around and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare, and they're right.”
The court’s majority, for its part, said in a 2019 ruling that courts drawing voting districts for maximum advantage is a political dispute and federal courts can’t step in. Conservatives have separately ruled that key campaign finance regulations violate the freedom of speech. This year, the court further narrowed protections in the Voting Rights Act, which had helped increase minority representation.
That helped feed a redistricting frenzy touched off by President Donald Trump, who is trying to hold on to the Republicans' slim House majorities in the November election.
Still, Kagan said it's unfair to say the majority reflexively supports the president. She pointed to key areas where the court has pushed back against Trump, including tariffs, birthright citizenship and mail ballots.

title: NFL defends Eagles' handling of Jalen Hurts' blood clots while union calls for an investigation
text:
NFL defends Eagles' handling of Jalen Hurts' blood clots while union calls for an investigation
The NFL staunchly defended the Philadelphia Eagles' handling of quarterback Jalen Hurts' blood clots on Tuesday, while hours later the players' union called for an investigation of the situation.
A person with knowledge of the situation confirmed to The Associated Press that the Eagles were not being disciplined for their actions with Hurts. The person spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because conversations between the league and team were to remain private.
Dr. Allen Sills, the NFL's chief medical officer, offered a passionate defense of how the Eagles treated Hurts, following a statement from the league that said officials had been in contact with Philadelphia's medical personnel and the Cleveland Clinic in London throughout the process.
"I have complete confidence in the Eagles' medical staff and their handling of this situation, and I would characterize their work as very conservative, very patient-focused and appropriately guarded at every step," Sills said at the league's annual fall meeting. "I don't think you can take that outcome and say there was something flawed about the process. Sometimes in medicine, we do all the right things and diseases progress and other things develop.
"In this case, everyone was incredibly conservative and incredibly vigilant and was very quick to make diagnoses of these conditions that might not have been diagnosed in a nonathlete."
The NFL Players Association in a statement said it was told by the league that a review was not planned.
"Before conclusions are drawn about how this situation was handled, there must be a full investigation into what occurred," the union said. "Determining the facts is essential to ensuring players receive the highest level of care and protection going forward."
Hurts is on injured reserve and expected to miss the rest of the season after a blood clot in his left calf traveled to his lungs. The Eagles and agent Nicole Lynn said Monday that Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary embolisms.
NFL executive vice president Jeff Miller took issue with "uninformed speculation" in reports Monday that Hurts went more than 30 hours without sleep last weekend before playing.
"Jalen Hurts returned to the hotel, slept for a period of time and went to the stadium," Miller said, estimating that Hurts slept for around seven or eight hours. "Both talking to the Eagles' staff and making sure from people on the ground, tracking the case, talking to the independent hospital and doctors involved that we have, I think, a complete understanding of the course of events."
Sills said the league and the players' union study and track blood clots annually. He declined to go into specifics about Hurts' condition, citing patient privacy, and reiterated multiple times that treating a blood clot involves looking at multiple factors.
Dr. Caron Rockman, a vascular surgeon for roughly 30 years, said based on what she has read, there's no evidence the Eagles acted improperly while dealing with what she called not a textbook issue.
"It's a judgment call," said Rockman, who is currently a chair at Hackensack University Medical Center in New Jersey and did not treat Hurts. "I think it's really a case-by-case basis. In my personal opinion, superficial vein thrombosis is not a (disqualification) to fly."
Hurts' treatment moving forward involves blood thinners, and he will not be allowed to participate in any football activities until he is off them.
Hurts played in London against Jacksonville on Oct. 11, three days after informing medical staff of the injury after practice. He was initially diagnosed by specialists in London with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis.
"I think there was incredible vigilance, there was conservative care, state-of-the-art imaging that was done in London," Sills said. "And, as far as the timing and the decision-making, I have great confidence in that and believe that everyone acted with an abundance of caution."
Sills in his opening statement that lasted more than five minutes said all decisions are made with medicine over football.
"The notion that there are external factors or that any of our physicians would put a player in harm's way — that's nonsense," Sills said.

title: 7 Maine thrillers for Halloween (that weren’t written by Stephen King)
text:
Maine can be a pretty scary place.
There are isolated islands, windswept mountain peaks and foreboding forests all promising some hidden horror or secret. It’s also a place of interminable winters, spooky old houses and storied shipwrecks.
All those things make it fertile ground for horror stories, something Maine native Stephen King has proven over the course of his 50-year career. But Maine has inpired lots of other writers to craft tales of horror or suspense. Every year there are more scary books by Maine writers, or terrible tales set in Maine. Following are some suggestions for recent Maine horror or suspense books, to help you get in the proper mood for the spooky season.
‘Carry Me to My Grave’ by Christopher Golden
Golden, a New York Times best-selling author who lives in Massachusetts, has won the Bram Stoker Award and Shirley Jackson Award for previous works of horror. This one, which came out in August, stems from supernatural happenings in the fictional Maine town of Shediak. The story is set in the 1950s and focuses on Malcom Wise and his mother, Maggie.
As a boy, Malcolm was taunted by other kids calling his mother a witch. Now as she’s dying, Maggie makes Malcom promise to return her body to her Maine birthplace, by train. But she needs to be buried before sunrise on the second morning after her death. But as soon as Maggie dies, there are “things” digging themselve up out of the ground all over the country.
‘The Ghosts of Riddell House’ by Kevin St. Jarre
This gothic ghost story came out in September and focuses on two paranormal investigators hired to get to the bottom of some spooky stuff at a notorious and remote Maine house. One, Tanya Libby, feels cursed by her abilities to hear the dead. The other, Burch Kinney, makes his living pretending he’s something he’s not. St. Jarre lives in Cape Elizabeth and grew up in Madawaska.
‘How to Survive in the Woods’ by Kat Rosenfield
This domestic thriller is set in Maine’s 100-Mile Wilderness, the last stretch of the Appalachian Trail. Emma Sharp, raised by a doomsday prepper, is feeling trapped and controlled in her marriage as she sets out to hike the trail with her husband and his former girlfriend. It’s a story of desire and dread and deadly things happening in the darkness of the woods.
Rosenfield spent childhood summers on Deer Isle, where her grandparents lived, as well as on Sebec Lake. Monson and Cloud Pond are a couple of the Maine locations in the book, which came out in March. She’s also written for Entertainment Weekly and The New York Times.
‘The Siren of Groves Peak’ by Glenn Rolfe
In the small lobstering town of Groves Peak, a violent murder at sea creates chaos and hints at darker secrets. Rolfe, who lives in Gardiner, says the fictional town is on the coast between Portland and Rockland. The book came out in June. One of Rolfe’s previous books, “When Night Falls,” was set in Old Orchard Beach in the ’90s and featured a serial killer and unnatural creatures.
‘Unspeakable Things’ by Elizabeth Hand
In 1920s Cornwall, on the coast of England, two young women go on the run when they’re implicated in the disappearance of a famous author. They seek refuge at a country house filled with “a debauched coterie of London’s Bright Young Things” as well as the estate’s mysterious owner. Sinister intrigue ensues. The book came out in October.
Hand, who lives in Lincolnville, wrote the 2023 novel “A Haunting on the Hill,” a new story about the namesake structure in Shirley Jackson’s 1959 classic “The Haunting of Hill House.”
‘We, the Missing’ by Arwyn Sherman
An anxious teenager tries to protect her mother from a rash of disappearances in their city, loosely based on Portland. The teen discovers a world of darkness, deadly creatures and monstrous angels. It’s the debut novel for Sherman, who lives in West Bath. Sherman will talk about the novel at a book launch at the Portland Public Library at 6:30 p.m. Oct. 29, with fellow horror writers Katherine Silva and Nicole Mann.
‘Where the Soul Goes’ by Katherine Silva
A gay, asexual chef goes on a road trip with Death to save an alternative 1980s human race from a degenerative illness, through gastronomy. Silva, who lives in Waldoboro, says several locales in the book were inspired by small towns and cities across Maine. Her writing often highlights her love of wilderness. The book came out in September 2025.

title: Youth planning boards get behind-the-scenes tour of Bangor amphitheater
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The Substance Affected Youth Program brought its youth planning boards together for a behind-the-scenes tour of the Maine Savings Amphitheater in Bangor.
The group, made up of high school and middle school students, is responsible for planning the annual Penquis Youth Summits.
This marks the fourth year of the summit, and the second-year organizers have split planning between high schoolers and middle schoolers.
Both groups united to get a firsthand look at what goes into planning and executing a major event at the venue, from logistics to staging to hospitality, lessons they can carry into planning this year’s summits.
“I’m fortunate enough to be employed part-time through Waterfront Concerts and we’ve built a partnership with the SAY program. They’ve done tours for us in the past. And it just occurred to us that these kids are charged with throwing a large format event for 200 or 250 of their peers. So, bringing them to a venue like this and letting them get a behind-the-scenes look at how a show is put on and the things that the concert staff go through that will be similar to what they go through in planning seemed like a good place to start,” said Joe Costello, SAY Program youth resource navigator.
Group leaders say everything the students learned will translate when it comes time to plan the event in May.
The skills the students are acquiring on the planning boards are ones they will be able to use for life.

title: Tennessee Titans release defensive lineman after gun incident at team facility
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) — Defensive lineman Jordan Elliott was released by the Tennessee Titans after retrieving a gun from his car following a practice altercation, head coach Robert Saleh confirmed Wednesday.
The altercation was with offensive tackle JC Latham, according to a report from NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo.
The incident occurred in the parking lot last week.
Saleh confirmed the details of the incident to reporters on Wednesday, while defending Elliott’s character.
“This is a man who is a father, a great husband,” Saleh said. “He’s never committed a crime in his entire life, and he pulled a gun in the parking lot. The first question that everyone forgets to ask is, ‘Why?’”
Saleh went on to vouch for Elliott as a man and a player, and invited teams who are in need of a defensive lineman to give him a call because Elliott “should be on an NFL roster.”
Team’s initial statement
When the Titans initially announced his removal on Tuesday, the statement only acknowledged that there had been an incident involving Elliott at the team facility. After reviewing the incident, the team decided to release Elliott and did not have further comment.
“On Thursday, October 15, there was an incident at our team facility involving Jordan Elliott,” the Titans said in a statement. “Following our review of the incident, we have made the decision to release Elliott from our roster.”
Coach addresses incident
Saleh was first to speak during Wednesday’s press conference and addressed the incident, the team and the league’s response directly.
Elliott was inactive for the Titans’ game on Sunday against the Indianapolis Colts before he was released.

title: Founder-director of Portland Community Squash to step down
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Portland Community Squash is searching for its next executive director as founder Barrett Takesian prepares to step away from the full-time role after 15 years.
The full-time position will oversee fundraising, finances, staff and strategic planning. The board expects to interview candidates in late fall, with a new director starting in early 2027.
Takesian will move into a temporary part-time role to help with the transition.
“I am incredibly proud of this community for building an organization that is ready to thrive under its next leader,” Takesian said in a news release. “I’m excited to support this transition while dedicating more time to social entrepreneurship here in Maine. I’ve been working toward this milestone for some time, and I’m looking forward to sharing more about what’s next.
Takesian was a 2025 Mainebiz 40 Under 40 honoree.
About the organization
Portland Community Squash has grown since its founding into a community center serving around 1,800 people through squash, education and wellness programs.
In 2024, the nonprofit completed a $6 million expansion of its facility at 66 Noyes St., funded by philanthropy and a $3 million Maine Community Bank loan.
Portland Community Squash operates on a $1.5 million annual budget, more than half from contributions. It has seven full-time employees and 20 part-timers, plus volunteers.
The board is seeking candidates with leadership and financial management experience and a strong fundraising record.

title: Hundreds of Mainers lost their health insurance due to Medicaid eligibility changes
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - Hundreds of Mainers have lost health coverage after changes to Medicaid eligibility took effect Oct. 1.
Before the change, some noncitizens who were in the U.S. lawfully, including asylum-seekers and refugees, could access Medicaid.
Medicaid is funded by a mix of state and federal money. Changes included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act mean the federal government will no longer reimburse states for Medicaid coverage provided to noncitizens.
“Providers are in a tough position because they now, as of October 1st, have clients on their caseload who now have no way to pay for the services that the provider would otherwise be offering,” said Katie Collins, a paralegal at Maine Equal Justice.
Green card holders and lawful permanent residents will retain access. According to the Maine Department of Health and Human Services, 980 Mainers have lost full MaineCare coverage.
“It puts a lot of strain also on the rest of the health system because that is money that’s not going to the hospitals or going to the providers from Medicaid,” Collins said.
In an April statement notifying states about the change, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz wrote: “The Trump Administration has a public mandate, a statutory obligation, and a moral duty to safeguard our federal healthcare programs.”
“What is frustrating is that individuals who are undocumented have never been eligible for Medicaid,” Collins said. “It really seems like the only point is stripping health care from people who otherwise were eligible but are not citizens or do not have permanent status.”
Pregnant women and people younger than 21 are exempt from the change and will remain covered. Some noncitizens may be able to enroll in free care programs offered by hospitals. Otherwise, they will be limited to emergency care coverage.
“When people are going without health care, the effect of that really ripples throughout an entire community, both the families, the individuals and, like I was saying before, the health care systems generally,” Collins said.
8 Investigates reached out to a number of hospital systems to see what impacts this eligibility change is having. A spokesperson for MaineHealth wrote that while it’s too soon to say what the impact will be, the system is anticipating a rise in emergency room usage and unpaid medical bills.

title: Nearly 100 cases of norovirus reported inside one elementary school, health officials say
text:
OVERLAND PARK, Kan. (KCTV/Gray News) - Health officials have confirmed a norovirus outbreak at Bentwood Elementary School in Kansas after nearly 100 cases were reported over the past week.
Johnson County Department of Health and Environment Director Charlie Hunt said the total case count has grown to 97, with 95 of those cases inside the school among students and staff, plus two more among family members outside the school.
Hunt said that number is likely an undercount because of how contagious norovirus is.
JCDHE said two cases have been confirmed by lab testing.
Health officials noted the remaining cases are considered epidemiologically linked, meaning people experienced similar symptoms at the same time in the same setting.
Norovirus is highly contagious, causing vomiting and diarrhea. It spreads easily in schools where students and staff are in close contact, health experts said.
Hunt said there are about 2,500 norovirus outbreaks reported each year nationally, and that figure is also likely an undercount.
Hunt said norovirus is sometimes referred to as a ‘stomach flu’ but is not related to influenza. He said norovirus primarily causes vomiting and diarrhea, while influenza is primarily a respiratory illness. Hunt said there is no vaccine for norovirus, and antibiotics are not effective because it is a viral infection.
To prevent transmission, officials urge frequent handwashing with soap and water, thorough cleaning and disinfection of contaminated surfaces, and staying home when sick.
Health officials urged anyone who gets norovirus to stay home for at least 48 hours after symptoms stop.

title: Former NFL defensive end Allen Bailey dies at 37
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (KCTV/Gray News) - Former NFL defensive end Allen Bailey has died at the age of 37.
Bailey, 37, played 10 seasons in the league and spent eight of them with the Kansas City Chiefs after being drafted by the team in the 2011 NFL Draft.
Chiefs head coach Andy Reid, who coached Bailey for six of his eight seasons in Kansas City, called Bailey “one of my favorite players” on Wednesday, acknowledging Bailey’s death during his weekly press conference.
“It’s terrible,” Reid said of any time a former player of his passes at a young age. “[Bailey] had a father who passed away young, too. It’s life, but it makes you sick.”
The Chiefs also issued a statement as an organization on Wednesday:
“Allen Bailey was an excellent teammate, generous man, and kind soul. We’re deeply saddened to hear of his passing, and our thoughts and prayers are with his family and friends.”
Patrick Mahomes, who was a teammate of Bailey for two seasons, shared a story Wednesday of the first time he walked into the locker room and saw Bailey.
“I step in the locker room and see Allen Bailey, and I’m like, ‘This isn’t the Big 12 anymore,’” Mahomes recalled of Bailey’s imposing figure. “It was surreal to see him, and I tell that story every single year. Obviously, it’s terrible to hear the news that we heard.
Mahomes added, “A great teammate. He was one of those glue guys on the team. He made plays and was the guy who made everything go. Terrible to hear that news. We’re praying for him and his family.”
In eight seasons with the Chiefs, Bailey started 61 of the 102 games he played in and tallied 207 tackles and 19.5 sacks. Bailey’s best statistical seasons came in 2014 and 2018, with a career-high six 6 sacks coming in his final season with the Chiefs and his lone touchdown, a fumble recovery scoop-and-score in Kansas City’s 54-51 shootout loss to the Los Angeles Rams on Nov. 19, 2018.
Following the 2018 campaign, Bailey signed a two-year contract with the Falcons in free agency. He appeared in 31 games with Atlanta before being released in February 2021.
Bailey was from the small town of Sapelo Island, Georgia, and made his way to the University of Miami, where he starred for the Hurricanes in college.
Bailey’s brother, Alford Bailey Jr., told TMZ that his body was discovered in his Florida home on Tuesday. No immediate cause of death was released.
