title: Polymarket removes wagers on fate of Cornell students accused of rape
text:
(AP) - Polymarket has removed a contract from its prediction market platform that allowed users to wager on whether any of the seven men accused of sexually assaulting or exploiting a Cornell student in 2024 will be charged with a felony sex crime.
The market was made available on Sept. 30 and was slated to close on Jan. 31. It had more than $450,000 in volume before it was taken off Polymarket’s international platform. The company’s U.S. exchange is regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which bans trading related to “activity that is unlawful under Federal or State law.”
“Our primary goal at Polymarket is to bring objective, data-driven insight to the most important questions of our time,” a Polymarket spokesperson said Tuesday. “This market addressed whether the government would take action — a process that deserves scrutiny, particularly in a case of such serious concern. That said, we believe in the wisdom of crowds, have heard them loud and clear, and removed the market.”
Front Office Sports was the first to report on the contract.
Some outcry over the Polymarket contract has been aimed at its celebrity promoters. Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has an endorsement deal with Polymarket, and he recently appeared in a star-studded commercial that also included cameos by Derek Jeter, Eli Manning, Sue Bird and several celebrities.
Messages were left by the AP on Tuesday with representatives for James, Jeter, Manning and Bird.
Polymarket also has partnership agreements with the NHL, Major League Baseball, Major League Soccer, the UFC and ATP Tour. Messages were left by the AP seeking comment from each organization.
A spokesman for Spike Lee, who also appeared in the Polymarket commercial with James, said the director had no comment. Messages also were left with representatives for actors Craig Robinson, John Leguizamo and Alexandra Daddario — who were also part of the commercial with James.
A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All of those men have denied her allegations, saying either that their interactions were consensual or that they weren’t involved.
Online critics characterized the Polymarket contract as degrading and questioned why celebrity ambassadors would associate themselves with the company. An online petition launched by UltraViolet, a women-led national advocacy organization, singled out James, Manning, Daddario and model Emily Ratajkowski while calling on other famous endorsers to cut ties with the company.
A message was left seeking comment from a representative for Ratajkowski, who also appears in the celebrity-filled commercial with James.
Prediction markets provide an opportunity to trade on the result of future events. Sports account for a major portion of the volume generated by the array of typically yes-or-no question, depending on the platform.
When a U.S. Army sergeant was indicted earlier this year over bets on the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, he was trading on Polymarket’s international platform. The Associated Press reported in April that 50 brand new accounts on Polymarket’s international platform placed substantial bets on a U.S.-Iran ceasefire in the hours, even minutes, before President Donald Trump announced a ceasefire on social media, raising concerns of insider trading.
Polymarket had an active market on its international platform on Tuesday that allowed customers to trade on whether Cornell president Michael Kotlikoff will be out by Oct. 31. It had more than $10,700 in volume.

title: Justice Department watchdog declines to investigate handling of Reflecting Pool case, lawyers say
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Justice’s inspector general has declined to investigate the handling of the criminal case against a former Olympian cleared of accusations that he intentionally damaged the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, according to a letter Wednesday from the man’s lawyers.
The internal watchdog told David Hearn’s lawyers that the allegations of professional misconduct that they made fall outside its jurisdiction and are instead within the purview of the department’s Office of Professional Responsibility, according to the letter, which urges Inspector General Don R. Berthiaume to reconsider the decision.
“Given the substantial public attention devoted to this matter, and the significant questions raised concerning the conduct of federal officials, declining independent review would risk undermining public confidence in the Department’s ability to police its own conduct. Such a result would be inconsistent with the purposes for which Congress established the OIG and would be a betrayal of its mission,” the letter says.
Hearn’s lawyers this month had asked for investigations by the inspectors general at the departments of Justice and Interior, citing a broad variety of “incompetence and misconduct” that they said occurred during the criminal investigation and prosecution of their client. They say they believe they have identified potential crimes in the Trump administration’s handling of the case, including witness tampering, obstruction of justice and the subornation of false testimony.
The Justice Department moved to dismiss the case last summer, saying newly produced evidence from the Interior Department showed that Hearn, 67, of Bethesda, Maryland, was not responsible for damage to the pool’s lining. A District of Columbia judge later permanently threw out the prosecution.
Hearn’s lawyers said in their initial letter to the watchdogs that the evidence that established their client’s innocence had been in the Justice Department’s possession for weeks and was “simply ignored.” They asked the inspectors general to investigate why prosecutors “rushed to indict” under what they said was pressure from Republican President Donald Trump, who had launched a massive renovation project of the Reflecting Pool for the celebration in Washington of America’s 250th anniversary.
In renewing their request for an inspector general investigation, Hearn’s team argues that the watchdog is uniquely positioned — both in terms of tools and independence — to dig into allegations of misconduct against the government officials involved in the case.
They note that unlike the inspector general’s office, the Office of Professional Responsibility, which also investigates some categories of professional misconduct, reports to the deputy attorney general and attorney general and has no obligation to publicize its work or report its findings to Congress.
Hearn’s lawyers also say the inspector general is the right office to investigate the potential criminal misconduct they believe they have identified within the government, asserting that prosecutors elicited false testimony from a witness who testified before the grand jury and violated Hearn’s civil rights by proceeding with a flawed criminal case. They say the inspector general should investigate whether U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro, whose office handled the case, violated ethical rules in a news conference when she announced charges against Hearn.
The U.S. attorney’s office did not respond to a request seeking comment when Hearn’s attorneys raised the allegations earlier this month.
Among Hearn’s attorneys is Michael Bromwich, a Justice Department inspector general during the Clinton administration.
“In a case such as this one, when some of the allegations directly involve the United States Attorney for the District of Columbia, there is substantial reason to question whether any meaningful independent review would occur,” the lawyers’ letter says. “Your decision not to investigate would be consigning these serious allegations to oblivion despite the enormous public interest in the matter and the absence thus far of any accountability for the individuals involved.”

title: Wreath Mary calling it quits after 50 years of wreath making
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sometimes you are born into a family business. Other times, you marry into one. “I’ve always been a person who has lots of different jobs,” says Mary Lockhart. Her journey into artisan wreath-making began as the latter.
Mary married her husband, Rodger, on November 1, 1975. That same month, while the men in the family headed out for deer season, Mary’s mother-in-law, Marian Lockhart, and Aunt Betty introduced her to the craft of weaving fresh balsam wreaths. It began as a seasonal tradition for the Lockhart women, turning leftover boughs from the annual Christmas tree harvest into festive decor. In the early days, Mary wrapped wreaths while Rodger’s mother and aunt added flowers. “They were decorated the old-fashioned way,” Mary recalls.
“I loved to do it. I did it for something to do because everyone else in my house was out deer hunting, so I was always here by myself,” Mary says. “I made 25 wreaths that first year. Each year after that, the business grew.”
Balsam wreaths require a precise harvest window. Temperatures must drop below freezing for three consecutive days to properly cure the evergreen needles. Because customers desire fresh wreaths and kissing balls or swags for holiday decorating and gift-giving, mid-November through mid-December becomes a whirlwind season for the wreath-maker. As demand expanded, Mary’s husband and son began harvesting fir boughs from family land near their camp in Palermo.
If you can imagine it in evergreen, Mary Lockhart has likely crafted it. Over the past five decades she’s wrapped virtually every size, spanning six inches to five feet in diameter. Twelve inches is the standard size, though custom requests were always welcome. “People would call and tell me what they wanted. I’ve done 6, 8, 12, 16, 18 inches… all of my wreaths are double-sided; I’ve never made a single-sided wreath.” One year, she tackled a massive order of 450 wreaths for an Inland Hospital fundraiser. Along the way, family and friends lent a hand, and Mary passed the time-honored skill down to her daughter, Sarah.
At her home in China Village, a small greenhouse attached to the garage served as the production shop. “We’d cut the boughs down to size, then I’d hoop them,” Mary explains. “We always laughed and sang while working in the greenhouse!” Christmas carols weren’t on the playlist, however: “We’re country-western people.”
Mary cherished chatting with customers when they stopped by to collect their holiday greens. “People would come and watch me work… I enjoyed the craft and found it both rewarding and challenging.” She made wreaths for many local families, setting a road sign out each Fall. “They always knew where to find me. I even had folks who’d bring their wire hoops back!”
One evening, Mary’s son, Junior, walked into the greenhouse while she was working late. Mary jokingly quipped, “I can probably do this in the dark.” Taking her literally, Junior flipped off the light switch. Mary stood in the pitch-black workshop, momentarily stunned. But her hands didn’t miss a beat. Guided purely by muscle memory, she continued binding a perfect wreath. She chuckles at the memory: “That shut him up!”
During another crunch-time season with a massive order looming, Mary and her high-school-aged daughter, Sarah, turned production into a timed race. Working in tandem, the mother-daughter duo wrapped an incredible 60 wreaths in six hours.
Reflecting on five decades dedicated to the craft, Mary remarks, “I can’t believe it’s been 50 years. I can’t believe we’ve been married 50 years. Wreath-making was a hobby…somehow I managed to keep going for 50 years!”
Last autumn marked Mary’s final season. After half a century of continuous labor, her hardworking hands are asking for some rest. Mary knows her phone will still ring with long-time regulars, but she is standing firm on her retirement: “I can’t say yes to one person, because then I’d have to make wreaths for everyone!”
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: This business turns vinyl records into mixtapes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (InvestigateTV) — Vinyl record sales in the U.S. increased in 2025 for the 19th consecutive year, according to the RIAA. Sales remain below 1970s levels, when more than 300 million LPs and EPs were sold each year.
Since April 2008, music fans have marked Record Store Day, which highlights independent record stores and vinyl culture. A Portland business is combining the vinyl resurgence with another personal music keepsake: the mixtape.
Mixtape Vinyl, based in Portland, has created vinyl record mixtapes for 10 years. Jennifer Dawson and the late Portland-based singer-songwriter David Freel, of the band Swell, founded it in 2016.
“We get people who are quite often trying to woo somebody,” Dawson said. “It’s obviously a crush, and they’re putting their favorite songs onto a vinyl instead of a cassette.”
Dawson and her team use a lathe, a rotating cutting machine, to create albums for occasions including weddings, graduations and gender reveals.
“And I think the most meaningful records that we’ve done are the memorial records,” Dawson said. “So someone has passed and there’s either an interview or they recorded some songs at some point. And we, yeah, and we make that record for the family or for the friends.”
The albums are fully customizable, including the jacket and the color or picture that appears on the disc.
“We make them as if those songs belong together,” Dawson said.
Mixtape Vinyl was among the first businesses in the market when it started, and an industry has since developed around the concept. There are no laws preventing the practice since the albums are not for commercial use.
Dawson said Taylor Swift songs are frequently requested.
“Sitting on the dock of the bay is on a lot of records by Otis Redding,” Dawson said.
A pressing of 10 records costs at least $350, or $10 a record. For more information, customers can email Mixtape Vinyl at orders@vinylondemand.com.

title: Aging Untold: Lupus looks invisible, but the fight inside isn’t
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we break down the daily realities of living with lupus, shedding light on the unpredictable fatigue, pain and invisible burdens of this autoimmune condition.
We explore the complex choices surrounding feeding tubes, helping families understand when they are recommended and what questions to ask.
Then, an in-depth report highlights a breakthrough FDA-cleared blood test that could revolutionize early Alzheimer’s diagnosis.
Lupus is an autoimmune condition that others often can’t see.
“Sam” Cradduck is sharing her personal experience living with lupus.
“The weekend before I went in my first flare, I played eight softball games back-to-back in a tournament — never sat down,” Cradduck said. “And on Wednesday morning, I couldn’t walk to the bathroom. I could not get myself to the bathroom unaided.”
She said the year that followed was difficult, including time spent in a wheelchair and significant weight gain, but it led her to a turning point.
If you have a loved one who loses the ability to eat normally, your family can be thrust into difficult decisions about feeding tubes, comfort and what comes next.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the real decision isn’t just whether to place a feeding tube — it’s understanding what the family is hoping it will accomplish. Is it temporary until somebody gets healthy, or do they have a disease that’s progressing and they’re not going to get back to a baseline level?
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, shared how watching her own family changed her perspective on feeding tubes.
“I had my whole view of feeding tubes change, watching my father-in-law. He had a feeding tube for seven years. My mother-in-law cooked three meals a day, pureed the food and fed him,” O’Rourke said. “They went on cruises. They danced. He became a special cook. We went out to fabulous restaurants. You forgot he had a feeding tube.”
The first blood test the FDA approved to help diagnose Alzheimer’s disease is a significant step forward in treating a condition that affects millions of Americans.
Traditional diagnosis often involves referrals to specialists, expensive PET scans of the brain and lumbar punctures, also known as spinal taps.
However, the blood test, Lumipulse, is a “less invasive option” that “reduces reliance on PET scans and increases diagnosis accessibility,” according to the FDA.
True Friends Hall in Louisiana is a historic hall that once provided refuge for Black families and performers during segregation.
The benevolent society that operated the hall helped families in need and provided a gathering place during an era when Black Americans faced widespread discrimination.
“These organizations supported families. If you had a baby, the house burned down, they would come to the aid. These are men who were carpenters, brickmasons,” Darryl Hambrick, founder of the River Road African American Museum, said.
The hall, built in the late 1800s, is undergoing a major restoration project.

title: New Mexico sues Epstein’s attorney and accountant, accuses them of hiding sex trafficking operation
text:
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — New Mexico’s attorney general filed a lawsuit Wednesday against Jeffrey Epstein’s attorney and accountant, accusing them of concealing his sex trafficking operation at a sprawling Santa Fe-area ranch where the disgraced financier entertained guests.
The lawsuit seeks to stop attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn from accepting any payments from Epstein’s estate, estimated at more than $100 million. They serve as coexecutors, and New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said they “stand to benefit substantially” from the estate unless a federal judge intervenes.
Indyke worked as Epstein’s attorney for roughly two decades. Both he and Kahn have testified in Congress that they did not know about Epstein’s abuse, though Torrez has a different view.
___
EDITOR’S NOTE — This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org
___
“None of this could be done by just one man,” Torrez said at a news conference, where he stood with two of Epstein’s accusers. “This was something that was facilitated, that was made possible by handlers, by lawyers, by accountants, by others who have yet to face real consequences.”
In response to the lawsuit, an attorney for the pair said they “emphatically reject” the allegations and note that New Mexico officials never sought to interview Indyke and Kahn before going to court. Dan Weiner said they would have cooperated.
“Not a single woman has ever accused Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn of committing sexual abuse or witnessing sexual abuse, nor claimed at any time that she or anyone else reported to them any allegation of Mr. Epstein’s abuse,” Weiner said in an email.
The U.S. Justice Department declined to comment on any federal investigation of Indyke or Kahn.
Epstein owned the Zorro Ranch for decades
Earlier this year, Indyke and Kahn agreed as executors of the estate to settle a class-action lawsuit brought against them by Epstein accusers for up to $35 million. They did not admit any wrongdoing as part of the deal.
Torrez’s lawsuit is an effort to possibly recover more money for victims, with New Mexico acting as the plaintiff.
Epstein purchased the Zorro Ranch in Stanley, a sparsely populated ranching community about 30 miles (50 kilometers) south of Santa Fe, in 1993. He built a massive home on the property, which spanned thousands of acres, and constructed several guest homes, a private airstrip and a helipad.
___
EDITOR’S NOTE — This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org
___
Epstein died by suicide in a New York jail cell in August 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges.
His former girlfriend and close associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, is serving a 20-year prison sentence after her 2021 conviction on sex trafficking charges in New York. Witness testimony at Maxwell’s trial alleged she and Epstein had sexually abused women at the ranch.
“We cannot undo what happened or return what was taken from us, but we can demand answers,” said Epstein accuser Anouska De Georgiou. “We can pursue justice and we can insist that wealth, power and influence never place anyone beyond accountability.”
The Associated Press does not name people who say they were sexually abused unless they have come forward publicly.
Indyke and Kahn played key roles, lawsuit says
The lawsuit accuses Indyke and Kahn of conspiracy and racketeering in supporting the “Epstein Enterprise.”
“They arranged payments to survivors to purchase their silence and leave them indebted to Epstein, handled costs for expenses connected to the abuse, monitored survivors’ spending, and prepared tax returns for some survivors,” the lawsuit states.
The lawsuit points to financial records indicating over $3 million in payments were made — with no discernible business purpose — from Epstein-related accounts directly to girls or women from 2003 to 2013.
Between 2013 and 2019, the lawsuit states, Indyke and Kahn authorized and signed off on payments totaling hundreds of thousands of dollars to “the enterprise’s sex trafficking survivors, including those who also acted as recruiters, and other expenses including legal fees, apartment rent and tuition.”
According to the suit, some payments were funneled through a nonprofit that was overseen by Indyke and Kahn. The complaint states that more than $30,000 was paid out by the C.O.U.Q. Foundation in 2012 to girls or women for purposes apparently unrelated to the charity.
The lawsuit also notes a 2017 email from Kahn to Epstein regarding payment of “the latest batch of medical expenses for girls.”
“At the end of the day this is not about the past. It is about the truth. It’s about justice, and it’s about making sure that accountability does not end with Epstein,” said Julia Molchanova, another Epstein accuser.
No crimes were pursued in New Mexico
Epstein never faced charges in New Mexico, though the state attorney general’s office in 2019 confirmed that it was investigating and planned to forward its findings to federal authorities in New York. Hector Balderas, who was attorney general at the time, said New Mexico’s outdated laws failed to protect children from abuse.
Epstein was not required to register as a sex offender in New Mexico, despite a 2008 guilty plea in Florida.
Torrez reopened the state’s investigation this year. In August, he sued the Justice Department, accusing it of blocking the state from investigating alleged sex crimes. The government said it was not releasing some information to the state because disclosing victim-identifying information would violate court orders in New York.
Also in August, a commission established by state lawmakers to investigate whether local authorities looked the other way, released a 119-page report that said authorities repeatedly deferred to investigations in New York, Palm Beach, Florida, and the Virgin Islands, while leaving Epstein’s offenses in New Mexico unexamined and unpunished.
Epstein’s estate sold the ranch in 2023 to the family of Don Huffines, a Republican who is the Texas state comptroller. The money was set aside for creditors.
Probate proceedings related to Epstein’s will and assets are being handled in the U.S. Virgin Islands.
___
White reported from Detroit. AP reporter Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado, contributed to this story.

title: Dunlap, Michaud campaign in Bangor about LePage residency questions
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Democratic candidate for Congress Matt Dunlap held a press conference on Wednesday with former Maine congressman Mike Michaud.
The focus was former governor Paul LePage’s residency in Florida that came up during a debate on WABI on October 15th.
Michaud says LePage voted in a Florida election as a resident eight days before registering to vote in Maine in 2025.
Dunlap says he is committed to holding public meetings even after he is elected, ensuring his constituents see him in Maine.
“The choice is clear for the voters in the Second Congressional District is, do you want a man from Hancock County or a man from Ormond Beach, Florida? That’s a clear choice,” said Michaud.
“While people are bleeding out their radiators and praying that the furnace makes it one more season, Paul LePage will be in Ormond Beach. While you’re splitting wood in the dark, he’ll be at the pool. While you’re wondering if the oil truck comes in before the tank runs dry, he’ll be checking the weather in Maine from somewhere warm.,” said Dunlap.
Lepage campaign senior advisor Brent Littlefield responded, saying, “This is a ridiculous argument and shows failed Auditor Matt Dunlap is grasping at straws, appearing with a candidate Paul LePage defeated... Paul LePage is a Mainer through and through. After admitting in the last debate he would raise gas taxes again, Matt is trying to distract.”

title: 13-year-old accused of shooting teacher outside middle school, police say
text:
HOBBS, New Mexico. (KCBD/Gray News) - A 13-year-old in New Mexico is accused of shooting a teacher outside a middle school, according to authorities.
Ryker Teel is facing charges of aggravated assault and tampering with evidence, among others.
Just before 11:40 a.m. on Sept 25, officers say coworkers found teacher Kelly Matthews seriously hurt outside the school.
A caller told 911, “I need the police and I need an ambulance to Highland Middle School immediately. We have a staff member either stabbed or shot out behind the school.”
Police released body camera footage to KCBD, which shows Officer Mann jumping a fence and running to help school nurse Sylvia Pena, who was tending to Matthews’ wounds.
His body camera footage shows Mann asked Matthews who did this to him.
“I don’t know, I don’t know. They were standing and facing that corner right there and I came out and they turned around and they just started firing and took off running,” Matthews said.
In the video, Matthews told investigators the suspect was wearing glasses and a mask of some kind. Mann relayed the description over his police radio.
Police later broadcast a description of a white male with a black hoodie, black pants and a long white shirt underneath the hoodie.
The footage shows officers used that description to find Teel in an alley nearby. When asked his name, he said, “Ryker Teel, sir.”
In handcuffs, Teel apologized and asked, “Is he dead? I’m sorry. I’m sorry. Is he dead?” Officers took Teel into custody.
Detectives later interviewed Teel with his mother and father present. According to the report, after detectives left the interview room, Teel was allegedly overheard telling his father he got the gun from the safe in their home.
The report states he admitted to shooting a man at the school and that he took the gun to school with the intention to shoot “anyone” and not specifically the man he shot.
Matthews’ wife says he’s currently working to recover at a rehab center.
She says they are praying for a full recovery, but each day is a challenge and they aren’t sure what the long-term effects will be. She said she wants to thank everyone for their thoughts and prayers during this difficult time.

title: Troy Jackson’s partner responds to Republican attack ads
text:
Troy Jackson’s longtime romantic partner is criticizing Republican efforts to exploit their relationship and family in the closing days of Maine’s hotly contested U.S. Senate race.
Lana Pelletier, Jackson’s partner for 40 years and his second cousin, wrote in an op-ed published Wednesday in the Bangor Daily News that national Republicans and Jackson’s opponent, Republican Sen. Susan Collins, have crossed a line by focusing on their personal lives.
“Our children have been dragged into this campaign. Our relationship has been mocked. Our family has been talked about as though there is something shameful about who we are or where we come from,” Pelletier wrote. “There isn’t.”
She added, “I deeply resent watching Collins and her allies treat our lives as something beneath them — especially when serious issues involving women are manipulated into political weapons by people who show so little care for the women involved.”
The final stretch of Maine’s Senate campaign has gotten nasty, with national Republicans mounting an all-out attack on Jackson and his family.
On Tuesday, the SLF PAC, a super PAC tied to Republican Senate leader John Thune, R-S.D., began airing a radio ad about Jackson’s family. It’s a country song whose chorus includes the refrain, “If he’ll screw his own family, he’ll screw yours, too.”
The brass-knuckle tactics highlight the lengths to which powerful D.C. figures will go to win Maine’s Senate seat, which could determine control of the upper chamber during President Donald Trump’s final two years in office.
Since Jackson became the Democratic nominee on July 25, roughly three-quarters of the $101.8 million in ad spending has backed negative ads, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. Republican-aligned groups have spent about $47 million attacking Jackson, while Democratic-aligned groups have spent some $31 million attacking Collins.
Collins has asked the PAC to take down the ad about Jackson’s relationship to his partner. During a campaign stop Wednesday at Simones’ Hot Dog Stand in Lewiston, Collins said she had “nothing to do with” the spot and reiterated her desire for it to be removed from the airwaves.
But it wasn’t the only one that attacked Jackson’s family.
One TV commercial from SLF PAC, which is largely funded by out-of-state billionaires, said Jackson “keeps it in the family,” while another claimed that taxpayer money was used for “a sleazy deal with Jackson’s cousins, who are also his in-laws.” Yet another from an SLF-affiliated group, The Maine Standard, calls him “a creep.”
Republicans have also attacked Jackson’s son Chace, who was a state lobbyist during his father’s final term as state Senate president.
Collins has not remained above the fray. She brought up Jackson’s son’s lobbying during their first televised debate, accusing Jackson of flip-flopping on issues tied to his son’s lobbying efforts.
And in a September video interview with Politico, she coyly noted Jackson’s relationship with Pelletier.
“Well, I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin,” Collins said. “I don’t know whether people know that or not. … It’s not something I’m going to be emphasizing.”
Jackson, meanwhile, has accused Collins of personal corruption. At a debate earlier this month, he implied that she supported Trump’s war in Iran because it would benefit her family’s stock portfolio. Collins demanded that Jackson apologize for the remark. (Collins initially supported Trump’s right to conduct war under the War Powers Act, but voted repeatedly in favor of ending the conflict once the 60-day deadline for congressional approval had passed.)
At her campaign stop Wednesday, Collins noted that she too has been the victim of personal attacks by Jackson and his Democratic allies, who have tied her to disgraced financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein in ads.
Collins voted to table a provision calling for the release of the so-called Epstein files in a defense spending bill, but supported adding such a provision to an appropriations bill. She also joined a unanimous Senate vote in support of the Epstein Files Transparency Act.
An ad by Win Senate, a super PAC linked with Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., accused Collins of voting to cover up the Epstein files. It also claimed Collins received $3 million from a former Epstein business partner — a claim rated false by PolitiFact.
“This campaign has been unique in Maine’s history in the number of personal attacks,” Collins said. “It’s interesting because in comparing with my colleagues who are in tough races across the country, every single one of them has had an ad run against them trying to link us to Jeffrey Epstein. That is so absurd.”
Pelletier said in her op-ed that she expects people to challenge Jackson on his views and his record, “but there should be a line.”
“Collins has been quick to demand respect and decency for herself,” she wrote. “My family deserved the same.”
Jackson’s partner wasn’t the only one pushing back against Republican attacks Wednesday.
His former colleagues from the Maine Legislature gathered at the Maine Women’s Lobby in Augusta to speak out against recent attack ads, at least one of which features some of their faces.
Rebecca Millett, a former state lawmaker from Cape Elizabeth, appears in the “creep” ad crafted by the SLF PAC-affiliated The Maine Standard.
The spot highlights media reports that Jackson would lose his temper as Senate president, including one instance when he allegedly threw a water bottle.
Millett said the spot “reeks of desperation.”
“They put a black bar across my eyes, and the eyes of many other people here today, to suggest that we were somehow victims or villains,” she said, adding that she believes Jackson was a respectful and thoughtful leader and colleague.
The Maine Women’s Lobby also made a formal endorsement of Jackson at the event, a practice Destie Hohman Sprague, its executive director, said the organization usually doesn’t do.
When asked about Jackson’s alleged temper toward female colleagues while leading the state Senate, former Maine Sen. Cathy Breen said his behavior was not gendered in any way.
“When you’re in the thick of it, and the budget is coming down to the final hours, all of us are emotional. All of us are stressed out,” Breen said. “So, yeah, has Troy lost his temper now and then? Sure. So have I. I don’t hold that against him.”
Staff Writer Joe Charpentier contributed to this story.

title: Russia releases detained American Stephen Hubbard during a visit by Trump administration envoy
text:
Russia on Wednesday released a retired American teacher who had been imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said Wednesday at a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
The release of Stephen Hubbard had been foreshadowed a day earlier in Washington, when President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he had talked with Putin “at length” about the issue and had asked him to free the Michigan man.
Hubbard is the second American detainee in just over two months to be freed by Russia, and his exit from custody occurred not only during a visit by Witkoff but also at a time when Trump has taken a series of actions meant to benefit Russia as Washington’s alliance with Ukraine shows signs of fraying.
Hubbard was sentenced after a closed trial in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison. Prosecutors said he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Russia sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022, and that he fought alongside them until being captured two months later. The U.S. government under the Biden administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained.
Witkoff, a key Trump administration envoy who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end a war that will hit the five-year mark in February, thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, telling him, “Because of you, he’s going home to his family.” The Russian leader responded that Hubbard was at the St. Petersburg airport, Pulkovo, after the release.
The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv alliance being stretched by tensions over drone support as the Trump administration advances policies that aid Putin.
Trump decided Friday, for instance, to waive sanctions on Russia in a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine. Named after late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Russia’s war.
That reversal followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections next month.
Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday. He was expected to exchange ideas from that meeting, as well as proposals from European and American colleagues, in his talks with Russian leaders in St. Petersburg on Wednesday.
Hubbard is the second American freed by Russia in about the last two months, following the release in August of Marine veteran Robert Gilman, who had been gravely ill and was imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer.
Some two dozen Americans remain imprisoned in Russia for various reasons, according to the Foley Foundation, a hostage advocacy organization.
Hubbard had been imprisoned since 2022 on charges that Hostage Aid Worldwide, a hostage advocacy group, has called bogus.
The organization in August posted an open letter to Trump that it said was written by Patricia Hubbard Fox, Hubbard’s sister, in which she offered praise for Trump but also said brother had been subjected to “constant beatings, torture and starvation” while in custody.
“Even so, everything that you’re doing isn’t going to matter to my kidnapped, American Veteran brother, Stephen James Hubbard (soon to be 74) if Putin won’t cave and let him come home and he dies up there in a Nazi prison (crying),” the letter said.
_____
Tucker reported from Washington.

text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) - A Waterville man is accused of causing a standoff with police Tuesday night.

Obituary: Marilyn Mae Thurber
text:
BUXTON – Marilyn Mae Thurber passed away peacefully and unexpectedly at her home in Buxton, on Oct. 12, 2026. She was born in Portland, on July 27, 1949, to Phillip Davis and Margaret Winslow.
Marilyn graduated from Windham High School in 1967 with high honors. She loved reading and spending her summers at Highland Lake throughout her teenage years.
Marilyn was a licensed practical nurse. Through the Scarborough medical community, she met Charles “Chuck” Frederick Thurber III, M.D., “the love of her life.” They became a couple in the late 1980s and married in 1994.
In 1993, Marilyn and Chuck moved from Scarborough to Charlottesville, Virginia, where Chuck taught at the University of Virginia School of Medicine and Marilyn worked at several medical clinics. She enjoyed working out at J’s Gym, where she made many new friends. During their years in Virginia, she also developed her talents in quilting and watercolor painting. She especially enjoyed her quilting club, sharing her love of quilting and the friendships she made there.
In 2005, Marilyn and Chuck returned to Maine, purchasing land in Buxton and building their home. They welcomed neighbors, friends, and family for parties and barbecues. Marilyn adored her neighbors, who became like family to her.
Marilyn was a devoted Baptist and attended Little Falls Baptist Church, where Pastor Tony Vafiades served. Her faith was an important part of her life.
Her studio above the garage became a place to explore her endless creativity through printmaking, stamping, handmade cards, acrylic sculpture, and oil painting. She generously shared her creations with family, friends, and online communities.
Marilyn cherished her family, including her stepsons, Christopher and Byron, and her four grandchildren, Danilo, Alicia, Sava, and Isabel. She lovingly made personalized birthday cards and keepsakes for her grandchildren and enjoyed sharing her creativity with them in “Grandma Marilyn’s Studio.”
Marilyn had a deep love for all the dogs she and Chuck welcomed into their lives over the years. They were her babies, and she cherished each one as family.
Marilyn was a true American patriot, proudly reflected in her clothing and throughout her home.
Marilyn was predeceased by her beloved husband, Chuck, and her brother, Phillip “Butch” Davis.
She is survived by her son, Jacob Tabachnick, and his partner, Rhonda Rafuse; her brother David Davis and his partner, Christy-Lynn Barnes; her brother Richard Winslow and his wife, Norma Winslow; and her sister-in-law, Dianne Davis, wife of her late brother, Phillip “Butch” Davis. She is also survived by her stepson Christopher Thurber and his wife, Simonida, of Exeter, New Hampshire; her stepson Byron Thurber and his wife, Ana, of San Francisco, California; and grandchildren Danilo, Alicia, Sava, and Isabel. She is also survived by nieces and nephews.
A service will be held on Monday Oct. 26, 2026, at 2 p.m., at the Chad E. Poitras Cremation and Funeral Service Chapel, 498 Long Plains Road (Rt. 22), Buxton. Online condolence messages can be submitted at the funeral home website, http://www.mainefuneral.com

title: FACT FOCUS: When it comes to Trump's economy, these are the numbers that matter before Nov. 3
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is trying to convince voters before the Nov. 3 midterm elections that the U.S. economy is rocketing upward. But voters say inflation remains a challenge because the Iran war has pushed up gasoline prices, grocery bills have remained expensive and high interest rates have made it harder to afford a home or a new car.
The economy is neither as strong as Trump has claimed nor as weak as consumer sentiment surveys suggest. But with its mix of inflation, inequality and stock market gains, the economy is unsatisfying to most of the public, and its performance has not lived up to Trump’s promises.
Here’s a closer look at the numbers that matter.
Inflation at 3.7% annually has risen under Trump
Voters expected Trump to quash inflation. In his inaugural address last year, the Republican pledged: “I will direct all members of my Cabinet to marshal the vast powers at their disposal to defeat what was record inflation and rapidly bring down costs and prices.”
And at an Oct. 3 campaign appearance in Vandalia, Ohio, he told the crowd: “We have almost no inflation.” But Labor Department reports don’t bear that out.
The consumer price index had been rising at an annual clip of 3% in January 2025, when Trump returned to the White House. Inflation continued to slow until April 2025, when Trump announced a sweeping set of tariffs and prices began to climb again. The inflationary pressures were compounded this year with the start of the Iran war.
Inflation has not returned to peaks seen during President Joe Biden’s term. But the data tells a clear story of inflation on a downward trend that moved jaggedly upward under Trump. The last CPI report before Election Day showed inflation was 3.7% over the past 12 months.
GDP growth has been averaging a little over 2%
A University of Michigan survey of consumer sentiment shows that people are less confident about the U.S. economy now than during the coronavirus pandemic in 2020 or the 2008 financial crisis. Unlike those periods, America is not in a recession. The broadest measure of economic growth, gross domestic product, has been expanding at a bit more than 2% annually under Trump. That is a solid figure but not as fast as economic growth had been under Biden, Trump’s Democratic predecessor.
But Trump keeps telling voters that growth has never been more propulsive. The Republican president claims historic levels of foreign investment that are a mix of exaggerations and wishful thinking. “We have growth the likes of which — and we’re going to have growth the likes of which — we’ve never seen before,” Trump said last week at a rally in Arizona.
The unemployment rate is low, but job growth has slowed
The 4.2% unemployment rate has been a sign of the economy’s health. Trump inherited a low rate that has continued under his presidency in an environment that many economists have described as “low hire, low fire.”
Trump likes to say there have never been so many jobs in U.S. history, but that’s largely because of population growth rather than his policies. Employers are adding on average almost 39,000 jobs a month during Trump’s second term. Monthly hiring gains were three times larger — topping 121,000 on average — in the year before Trump returned to the White House.
One factor in slower job growth is Trump’s crackdown on immigration, which means fewer people are looking for jobs. The unemployment rate for people born in the U.S. has largely held steady, which would suggest that Americans are not taking the jobs formerly held by immigrants.
Borrowing costs have risen
With an increasing national debt, persistently high inflation and the energy price spikes tied to the Iran war, it’s getting more expensive to borrow money for a home, auto or other basic needs. Interest on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note is above 5%, having hit its highest levels since 2002. That makes it costlier for people to borrow and harder for the U.S. government to repay its bonds.
Stocks have kept setting records
Trump likes to brag about how stock markets continue to set record highs under his presidency, although Biden could have made similar claims. The S&P 500 index is up about 12% this year. It rose by about 16.4% last year.
But the increase in 2024 — before Trump became president — was 23.3%. The stock market is a function of more than presidential politics, as growth in tech stocks has sustained the broader market. Trump’s tax cuts may have helped corporate earnings, as federal revenues from business taxes fell 16% last year, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
Inequality is widening
Since Trump returned to the White House, the wealth of the top 0.1% of households has increased by $5.5 trillion in just 18 months, according to Federal Reserve data. The bottom 50% of households have seen their wealth increase by $380 billion.
That means the bottom half of households on average saw their net worth improve by $5,600 under Trump’s presidency. The richest 0.1% saw their net worth increase on average by $40.8 million, a sum more than 7,000 times greater than the average gain for a household in the bottom half.
___
Find AP Fact Checks at https://apnews.com/APFactCheck.

title: Chemical tank leak in Ohio forces evacuations as city allows plume to vent
text:
TOLEDO, Ohio (AP) — A ruptured chemical tank billowed a white plume into the air for hours Wednesday, forcing hundreds of residents out of their homes due to the potentially toxic leak and the possibility of an explosion.
More than 50,000 people in Toledo, Ohio, were advised to stay indoors for much of the day until the city lifted a shelter-in-place order in the evening.
City leaders were allowing the chemical to vent instead of trying to stop the leak, saying that would be more dangerous. Videos show a plume still swirling from the tank early Wednesday afternoon, more than 14 hours after the tank began leaking Tuesday night in an industrial area.
Some residents felt irritation in their eyes and throats and sought treatment, and city officials said one sheriff’s deputy who responded to the blast later drove himself to a hospital because he felt unwell.
Mark White Jr., who lives within the affected area, was sleeping with his windows open and woke to what he described as a burning plastic smell. He decided to evacuate to a shelter at an elementary school because he has asthma.
“I don’t know what this chemical can do to my lungs, long term or anything,” White said.
MC Tank Transport said the tank contained glycidyl methacrylate, which it described as “an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.”
The Ohio Environmental Protection Agency said without elaborating that the leak happened because of an error while the material was being transferred.
Mayor says the chemical leak has slowed
Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz said Wednesday afternoon there was no reason to panic and that the city was working with state and federal environmental officials.
He said they decided to allow the tank to continue releasing the chemical because there was little threat to the public and that it would be more dangerous to ask first responders to go near the chemical trucking company’s facility where more tanks were stored.
“There’s no question the situation is improving,” said Kapszukiewicz, who added that drones monitoring the leaking tank show its temperature is dropping and that the plume is diminishing.
Still, it could take hours before the tank is safe to approach, he said.
Nearly 1,000 residents were told to evacuate overnight within a 1-mile (1.6-kilometer) radius of the leak. A shelter-in-place order for more than 50,000 people covering a 3-mile (4.8-kilometer) radius included neighborhoods along the Lake Erie shoreline and stretched just across the state line into Michigan. By Wednesday evening, the shelter-in-place had been lifted and the evacuation order was cut down to half a mile (0.8 kilometers).
Schools across the city were closed Wednesday, and automaker Stellantis shut down production at its nearby Jeep assembly plant.
Residents worry about chemical’s risks
Health officials said the symptoms reported so far were primarily eye and throat irritation. Testing was ongoing to determine the chemical’s concentration in the air and whether it posed additional health risks.
ProMedica, which operates hospitals and urgent care centers in the Toledo area, said it evaluated about 30 people who reported symptoms that might have been related to the leak. Most were treated and released, the health care provider said.
Residents well beyond the shelter-in-place zone described smelling paint or burning chemicals. City officials tried to assure them that the odors did not indicate there was anything harmful in the air.
Kristine Kowalinski, who lives just outside the affected area, said she was staying inside because she’s sensitive even to smoke from wood burning. She said she’s worried about what’s in the air and on the ground.
“My main concern is how did that affect everything overnight when it was raining down on cars, houses, my garden,” she said.
Kapszukiewicz said the chemical is liquid inside the tank but becomes a gas when released. Officials began worrying early on that the tank, which can hold 5,500 gallons of the chemical, could explode, he said.
Chemical can irritate eyes and cause headaches
People who come into contact with glycidyl methacrylate may feel as if their eyes, nose, mouth and skin are burning, the city fire department said. Overexposure can cause headaches, dizziness, tiredness, nausea and vomiting.
“It’s really toxic if you touch it, if you ingest it,” said Karim Baroudi, director of the Toledo-Lucas County Health Department. “Now we’re trying to kind of determine how much of a toxicity is in the air that the people are breathing so we can give better guidance.”
Baroudi advised residents to close their windows and that those who “feel irritation in the eyes, heavily breathing, just take a shower for now.” The fire department said those who experience symptoms should contact a medical professional.
Emergency and hazardous material crews were not approaching the tank because of the risk of an explosion, Kapszukiewicz said.
“Our immediate and overriding concern is the safety of area residents, emergency responders and our employees,” the company said.
___
McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire. Associated Press journalists Beatrice Dupuy in New York and Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

Pakistani authorities arrest man accused in $126 million US postage fraud scheme
text:
Pakistani authorities arrest man accused in $126 million US postage fraud scheme
Pakistani authorities acting on intelligence arrested a man Tuesday accused of running an online counterfeit postage operation that U.S. prosecutors say caused more than $126 million in losses to the U.S. Postal Service, Pakistan’s cybercrime investigation agency said.
Related video: Trump announces announce $25 million whistleblower program for alleged government fraud
Faheem Akram, 33, was arrested after a weekslong search involving raids across several parts of the country, a senior official at the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency, Atif Ameer, told reporters.
Akram, a resident of Khanewal in eastern Punjab province, was indicted by a federal grand jury in the Southern District of Florida, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the district said in a Sept. 28 statement. The office alleged that Akram operated LabelsBank.com, an unauthorized website that sold more than 5.1 million counterfeit postage labels to more than 5,200 customers. The labels typically cost $2 each, regardless of a package’s weight, size or destination.
The counterfeit labels allowed customers to ship packages at prices far below legitimate postal rates, resulting in lost revenue and shipping costs for the Postal Service, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office. Its estimate of more than $126 million represents alleged losses to the Postal Service rather than proceeds from the website’s sales.
Ameer said Pakistani investigators found that Akram operated the website from August 2023 through September 2026 and used 16 bank accounts for the business. Those included accounts held by Akram, his brother, wife, sister and aunt, he said.
It was unclear whether Akram would be extradited to the United States or face trial in Pakistan.

title: Mortgage rates fall well below 7.5%
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mortgage rates fall well below 7.5%
Current mortgage rates
The 30-year fixed mortgages in this week’s survey had an average total of 0.36 discount and origination points. Discount points are a way to lower your mortgage rate, while origination points are fees lenders charge to create, review and process your loan.
Shop smarter for mortgage rates
Bankrate connects you to the latest lender offers, tailored to you. Find your low rate today.
Explore mortgage rates
Monthly mortgage payment at today’s rates
The national median family income for 2026 is $106,800, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the median price of an existing home sold in August 2026 was $417,500, according to the National Association of Realtors. Based on a 20% down payment and a 7.38% mortgage rate, the monthly principal and interest payment of $2,310 amounts to about 26% of the typical family’s monthly income.
Meanwhile, home prices are still rising — the National Association of Realtors reports the median home price was up 1.3% over the past year, and the median of $417,500 was an all-time high for the month of September. However, values have begun to dip in many formerly hot markets. Still, signs are mixed. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller index released in late September showed national home prices grew 1.9% in the year ending in July, marking an acceleration.
What will happen to mortgage rates in the rest of 2026?
Inflation rose to 3.7% in September, although the Fed’s preferred measure, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index, was 3.0% for September. Oil prices have spiked amid the conflict in Iran, pushing inflation up and lifting mortgage rates from their 2026 low of 6.09%. Rising inflation has been the main driver of higher mortgage rates — the consumer price index has pushed well above the Fed’s 2% target, although 10-year Treasury yields fell to 5.1% this week, down from 5.3% last week.
“There is no single switch that will bring mortgage rates meaningfully lower,” says Jeff DerGurahian, head economist at loanDepot. “We likely need several factors to fall into place including cooler oil prices, softer consumer spending and a steady run of inflation reports showing progress toward the Fed’s 2% target.”
Housing economists no longer expect mortgage rates to fall below 6% in the near future, and even a return below 7% seems a stretch. That reality that’s affecting home sales. Higher mortgage rates, still-record home prices and persistent inflation are likely to put the brakes on home sales. Instead, rates have risen sharply, a situation only exacerbated by the Fed’s Sept. 16 rate hike.

title: Abuse and estrangement: What controversial Ohio governor’s race ad didn’t mention
text:
Abuse and estrangement: What Ramaswamy’s Ohio governor’s race ad with Amy Acton’s mom didn’t mention
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy released a campaign ad in which his Democratic competitor’s mother calls her daughter a “liar” and warns voters not to support her for Ohio governor.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
“Don’t vote for people who lie,” Donna Arthur says in the ad. “Don’t let her become your governor. If you think she’ll make your life better, you’re fooling yourself. It will only get worse.”
Not mentioned in the video: That Democrat Amy Acton, 60, has been estranged from her mother since she was a child in the 1970s, after Acton’s stepfather was charged with sexual abuse.
The ad prompted bipartisan backlash after Acton’s family members and allies pointed to the strained family history.
The video began circulating on social media Oct. 19, with no information about who had produced and paid for it. It was first published by D.J. Byrnes, an Ohio political blogger known as “The Rooster.” Byrnes said a voter who had seen it as part of a poll recorded it and forwarded it to him, CNN reported.
In excerpts from an Oct. 20 interview with WOSU-FM, an Ohio public radio station, Acton said she believed the ad was funded by Ramaswamy. She said she was removed from her mother’s care at age 12 and hadn’t seen her since. “It’s awful to see her this way, and it’s even more incredible to see that my opponent has taken advantage of someone who’s clearly not well, who is older, and this is totally in line with who he is,” Acton said in the radio interview. The full interview was slated to air Oct. 21.
Despite the backlash, Ramaswamy’s campaign took responsibility for the ad Oct. 20 and said it planned to spend $4 million to promote it.
The same day, Acton’s campaign released a statement in which Acton recounts her family history. It also released an ad, titled “Abuse,” in which Acton’s brother Phil Stearns said he and his sister were abused as children.
“I received a lot of abuse, but Amy always got the worst of it,” Stearns said. “She continued to receive that abuse because she knew she had to protect me.”
On Oct. 20, a Ramaswamy town hall attendee interrupted the candidate to criticize the ad and defend Acton. Ramaswamy warned the man that he would be removed if he continued interrupting. A police officer eventually escorted the attendee from the venue.
What is known about Acton’s childhood?
Acton has publicly discussed her difficult childhood for years. In a 2019 interview with The Vindicator, the Youngstown newspaper, Acton described family life in her early years as “out of control” and recounted sexual abuse by her stepfather, as well as neglect and instability.
After Acton’s stepfather was arrested, Acton’s mother lost custody of Acton and her brother, according to Acton’s Oct. 20 press release. Acton went on to earn a medical degree and have a career in public health, including serving as Ohio’s director of health during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Some details of Acton’s adolescence are difficult to verify independently, because it was the late 1970s — nearly five decades ago — and she was a minor at the time. But after the ad surfaced, the Acton campaign shared with the media, including PolitiFact, extensive screenshots of court materials and other documentation.
In 1978, Cledith Arthur was arrested and indicted by a grand jury on charges of raping a 12-year-old girl, according to an Aug. 11, 1978, article in The Vindicator. Acton, who was born in 1966, would have been 12 years old in 1978.
The campaign said Acton has been estranged from her mother since she was 12.
Court records provided by Acton’s campaign show Cledith Arthur pleaded not guilty and later failed to appear in court. By October 1978, a warrant had been issued for his arrest, and he was considered a fugitive. An arrest warrant was reissued in 1981, according to an image of a sheriff’s office document shared by the campaign. The Acton campaign has said he was never arrested and didn’t face trial.
Stearns said Donna Arthur remained married to Cledith Arthur until his death. He reportedly died in 2004.
The Acton campaign also shared records about other legal cases involving Acton’s mother. Pennsylvania court records corroborate that both Donna Arthur and Cledith Arthur were convicted of felony theft by deception in 1996.
Donna Arthur also was convicted of animal neglect in Pennsylvania in 2021 after authorities found cats and kittens in a hot, locked vehicle. The Pennsylvania Superior Court vacated the conviction and sentence in 2023 and remanded the case for further proceedings.
In 2020, while Acton was Ohio’s director of health, Donna Arthur disputed her daughter’s account of childhood abuse in an interview with Operation Rescue, an anti-abortion group.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.
PolitiFact Researcher Caryn Baird contributed to this report.

title: Letter: Rick Bennett advocated for Mainers most in need
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I will be voting for Rick Bennett for governor because I believe he is way ahead in vision, courage, and experience both in business and legislative leadership.
But, let me be specific on one massive injustice. For 61 years, the federal government has followed the Institution for Mental Diseases (IMD) Exclusion law, which bans the use of federal dollars by state hospitals and psychiatric facilities with 16 beds or more for psychiatric services. No other illness has this requirement. I believe it was a terribly unintelligent decision in part because there was also insufficient funds for what was proposed in the community.
In addition, the mislabeling of these various illnesses has resulted in catastrophic widespread injustice, which costs close to $300 billion a year in America.
After years of traumatic neglect by so many at several levels, state Sens. Joe Baldacci and Rick Bennett had the vision to bravely work together in the Legislature for several years to seek a waiver for “mental illness” in the discriminatory federal IMD law for Maine. LD 563 did not pass but their advocacy encouraged the Maine Department of Health and Human Services to include elements of this bill in Maine’s Whole Person Care Waiver so that Maine will have more progressive treatment teams in the community.
We all have expressed concern about the homelessness problem and its continuing tragedy. Thank Heaven Baldacci and Bennett sought treatment for Mainers in most need rather than ignorant abuse at so many levels. That is one major reason why I urge all to vote for Rick Bennett for Maine governor.
Joe Pickering Jr.
Bangor

title: REVIEW POTPOURRI: Tchaikovsky’s concerto and its remarkable history
text:
Tchaikovsky
The most frequently recorded Piano Concerto is the first of three by Peter Ilyich Tchaikovsky (1840-1893) in B flat minor.
After finishing his scoring of the work in early 1875, the composer played parts of it for the arrogant Nicolai Rubinstein who trashed it for its “banality and general ugliness. ”
Being a manic-depressive most of his life and highly self-critical, Tchaikovsky, in a state of shock, then showed it to German pianist/conductor Hans von Bulow (1830 – 1894) who was touring Russia and would soon be sailing to the United States, one of the first of any classical pianists to tour here.
Von Bulow liked the work, Tchaikovsky wanted to give its world premiere thousands of miles away from Moscow – and from himself – in case everyone there hissed it. Von Bulow agreed and that world premiere occurred in Boston on October 25, 1875, with the German at the keyboard and Benjamin Johnson Lang (1837-1909) brought in at the last minute to conduct, as Von Bulow had quarreled constantly with the previous conductor.
(Maestro Lang would be worthy of a biography. He was a major advocate in Boston for first American performances of pieces by Mendelssohn, Liszt, Brahms and of Wagner’s 16-hour Ring cycle – he and his wife witnessed its own world premiere at Bayreuth in 1876 as honored guests of that composer, who in turn was already married to Bulow’s ex-wife Cosima. In 1885, Lang himself played the Concerto with, as of 1881, the recently formed Boston Symphony. When Lang died in 1909, he left an estate of $600,000 in today’s currency. )
The Boston audience responded very favorably to that first performance and demanded that the 3rd movement be encored three times, but the critics were a bit persnickety, being more favorable in their reviews later in New York. However, when the trombones messed up, Bulow yelled, “May the brass go to Hell!”
The pianist later gave his own assessment of the Concerto – “The ideas are so original, so noble, so powerful; the details are so interesting, and though there are many of them, they do not impair the clearness and unity of the work. I should weary you if I were to enumerate all the characteristics which compel me to congratulate equally the composer as well as those who shall enjoy actively or passively the work.”
In 1941, pianist Vladimir Horowitz recorded an RCA Victor Red Seal 78 set of the music with his father-in-law Arturo Toscanini conducting the NBC Symphony, one that was a million seller. In 1958, a Texan, Van Cliburn, became the first American to win the Moscow competition and, also for RCA, recorded the Tchaikovsky, selling well over a million copies. His conductor was Kirill Kondrashin, who later defected to the West.
For me, the Concerto has enough emotional depth to generate a number of different approaches and I own a sizable number of recordings, including both Horowitz, who played with high voltage virtuosity, at times very hyper, with the aiding and abetting of his wife’s Papa and the NBC musicians; and the more elegant Cliburn, who gave enough brilliant virtuosity of his own to impress the Soviet judges and audiences yet bestowed a sense of poetry and delicacy uniquely his own.
Interestingly I own three different broadcast performances of Horowitz playing the Tchaikovsky in which he toned down his hyper aggression and played with considerable poetic sentiment.
As it so happens, today I played one of the most lyrically rapturous recordings I have ever heard of the Concerto, it being so enjoyable I played it twice. The back of the jacket had my notation of the last time I heard it being December 30, 1999, just two days before the Waterville Morning Sentinel announced on its front page the “The sun has set on the 1900s”, to this day one of the most eerie headlines I had ever read.
That record is on an 87-cent label, Coronet-CXS-107, was released during the early 1960s and sold on the racks of the much missed dime store chains that had its branches here in Waterville – McClellan’s, Montgomery Wards, Woolworth, Mammoth Mart, W.T. Grant, Zayre, etc.
The listed pianist is Karl Bernhard with the York Symphony. I googled the record and found out that Bernhard is one of several pseudonyms used by el cheapo LP labels for pianist Sondra Bianca, who is still living at the age of 95 and who withdrew for unknown reasons decades ago from an active recording and concert career to focus on teaching, but who continues to be one of the most underrated, divinely inspired artists whose own records were released in this country, mostly by MGM. This recording and others of Miss Bianca are accessible on YouTube and highly recommended.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: Meta ordered to pay New Mexico $25B for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook
text:
Meta ordered to pay New Mexico $25 billion for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook
Meta is expected to appeal
Meta ordered to pay New Mexico $25 billion for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook
Meta is expected to appeal
A judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy and content moderation policies on Facebook.
Judge Francis Mathew handed down the amount, which state Attorney General Raúl Torrez described as "one of the largest, if not the single largest state verdict against a company in American history."
Related video above: Could Meta's settlement-driven child safety changes become the new industry standard?
Torrez said the verdict should be a warning for tech companies and that New Mexico would continue to hold them accountable.
"This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley," Torrez said at a news conference.
Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws go to state education spending.
"We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," said Torrez, who acknowledged that the money would be tied up if Meta appeals as expected.
Representatives for Meta, which previously said it plans to appeal the September verdict, didn't immediately respond to a message seeking comment about the amount. The Menlo Park, California-based company was scheduled to report its quarterly earnings Wednesday afternoon and its shares were trading 2% higher following the penalty announcement.
New Mexico goes it alone
Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws when a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, harvested Facebook user data to generate targeted political ads for the 2016 election.
Forty-eight other states settled with Facebook in a nationwide case, but New Mexico chose to take the social media company to court on its own.
Attorneys for New Mexico had sought $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum that affected its stock price.
Lawyers for Meta argued for paying no more than $3.4 billion. An award 10 times that or even more would violate due process, was unconstitutional and would not hold up under appeal, they said.
Meta argued the state failed to prove misleading statements about privacy and that content moderation actually harmed New Mexicans. Interest on the penalty would accrue during an appeal, but the number of violations Meta is charged with could be reduced.
Meta attorney Matt Nicholson argued in court that a sum as high as $40 billion would be "shocking to the conscience" while an attorney for New Mexico, Randi McGinn, urged standing up to "tech titans who think they are bulletproof and can do whatever they want."
Company argues that the state failed to prove harm
The state's case focused on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads. The now-defunct firm's clients included the 2016 campaign for President Donald Trump.
Attorneys for New Mexico argued that the state's entire population, not just Facebook users, were deceived by the company's public statements about privacy on the platform. Facebook's lawyers argued that the state failed to prove whether people were actually harmed by these deceptive statements.
"The jury didn't make findings that any New Mexican heard or saw these statements, or was harmed by them," said Nicholson during a hearing Oct. 1.
New Mexico prosecutors also argued that Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate on the platform. Defense attorneys vehemently denied the allegations, saying the company's content moderation policies are robust and freedom of speech has to be considered.
Jury finds more than 43 million violations of state law
New Mexico was the only state to pursue a trial around the Cambridge Analytica scandal after 48 other states signed a settlement for $18 billion in August.
Besides New Mexico, Florida was the only other state that did not sign the settlement, which included an agreement to release Meta from future liability related to the Cambridge Analytica privacy breach.
During the trial, jurors assessed whether Facebook misled users about privacy and content moderation 34 separate times. State prosecutors, though, argued Facebook's statements deceived the entire population of New Mexico and extended beyond social media users.
In the end, jurors agreed with this premise and found Facebook liable for 2.1 million violations on certain counts, bringing the total number of violations to over 43 million.
Facebook's attorneys have argued in subsequent court filings that the state's consumer protection laws don't apply to people in New Mexico who weren't using the platform at the time.
Torrez told reporters following the verdict that all money awarded will go into a fund for the state's education system. The state is also seeking an injunction to stop similar practices.
Meta questions evidence and tally of violations
In appealing the jury's verdict, Meta might reduce the number of violations and therefore the total financial penalty. Lawyers for the company said it was unprecedented for the state to count the number of violations based on how many individuals may have heard or seen the misleading statements from the company, arguing there was no evidence these statements ever harmed anyone.
During closing arguments, lawyers for Facebook said the state's evidence was outdated and that despite having five years to gather material, New Mexico found only one other instance of a data breach.
In one of the few wins for the defense, jurors found the state didn't prove that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.
The state said the company favored certain accounts and allowed for violent or inaccurate content to proliferate. Attorney Randi McGinn said in her closing argument for the state that Facebook profited off harmful content, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg denied during his video deposition. Zuckerberg said the company has to carefully balance freedom of speech with content moderation.
Attorneys for Facebook said the company has adapted its policies since the state's lawsuit was filed in 2021 and that it removes 99% of content that violates standards.
Schuettler reported from Phoenix. Schuettler is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Polymarket removes wagers on fate of Cornell students accused of rape
text:
(AP) - Polymarket has removed a contract from its prediction market platform that allowed users to wager on whether any of the seven men accused of sexually assaulting or exploiting a Cornell student in 2024 will be charged with a felony sex crime.
The market was made available on Sept. 30 and was slated to close on Jan. 31. It had more than $450,000 in volume before it was taken off Polymarket’s international platform. The company’s U.S. exchange is regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which bans trading related to “activity that is unlawful under Federal or State law.”
“Our primary goal at Polymarket is to bring objective, data-driven insight to the most important questions of our time,” a Polymarket spokesperson said Tuesday. “This market addressed whether the government would take action — a process that deserves scrutiny, particularly in a case of such serious concern. That said, we believe in the wisdom of crowds, have heard them loud and clear, and removed the market.”
Front Office Sports was the first to report on the contract.
Some outcry over the Polymarket contract has been aimed at its celebrity promoters. Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has an endorsement deal with Polymarket, and he recently appeared in a star-studded commercial that also included cameos by Derek Jeter, Eli Manning, Sue Bird and several celebrities.
Messages were left by the AP on Tuesday with representatives for James, Jeter, Manning and Bird.
Polymarket also has partnership agreements with the NHL, Major League Baseball, Major League Soccer, the UFC and ATP Tour. Messages were left by the AP seeking comment from each organization.
A spokesman for Spike Lee, who also appeared in the Polymarket commercial with James, said the director had no comment. Messages also were left with representatives for actors Craig Robinson, John Leguizamo and Alexandra Daddario — who were also part of the commercial with James.
A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All of those men have denied her allegations, saying either that their interactions were consensual or that they weren’t involved.
Online critics characterized the Polymarket contract as degrading and questioned why celebrity ambassadors would associate themselves with the company. An online petition launched by UltraViolet, a women-led national advocacy organization, singled out James, Manning, Daddario and model Emily Ratajkowski while calling on other famous endorsers to cut ties with the company.
A message was left seeking comment from a representative for Ratajkowski, who also appears in the celebrity-filled commercial with James.
Prediction markets provide an opportunity to trade on the result of future events. Sports account for a major portion of the volume generated by the array of typically yes-or-no question, depending on the platform.
When a U.S. Army sergeant was indicted earlier this year over bets on the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, he was trading on Polymarket’s international platform. The Associated Press reported in April that 50 brand new accounts on Polymarket’s international platform placed substantial bets on a U.S.-Iran ceasefire in the hours, even minutes, before President Donald Trump announced a ceasefire on social media, raising concerns of insider trading.
Polymarket had an active market on its international platform on Tuesday that allowed customers to trade on whether Cornell president Michael Kotlikoff will be out by Oct. 31. It had more than $10,700 in volume.
