title: Australian politician had both legs amputated after being repeatedly hit by a car
text:
MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — Doctors have amputated both of Australian federal lawmaker Helen Haines’ legs as she remains in critical condition after being repeatedly hit by a car in an apparent act of political violence, her husband said Wednesday.
The 65-year-old independent politician is receiving treatment in a Melbourne hospital where she was flown by helicopter.
Phil Haines, her husband, gave the family’s first public comments on her condition since she was hit by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV in her hometown of Wangaratta on Monday, speaking hours after a man accused of running her over made an initial appearance in court.
Husband says Haines has lost both her legs
Haines’ husband said her left leg was amputated on Monday and her right leg was amputated on Wednesday after doctors abandoned hope of saving it.
“The good news in all this is that Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family,” the husband told reporters in Melbourne.
“We are grateful and thankful that at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape,” he said.
He added that their 40th wedding anniversary will be in November.
Man accused of attack makes first appearance in court
Earlier Wednesday, Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old man from nearby Tarrawingee, appeared in the Wangaratta Magistrates’ Court charged with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.
Nugent didn’t apply for bail or enter a plea. He will remain in custody until his next court appearance in February. Police have yet to determine a motive.
Nugent’s lawyer Chirag Patel told Magistrate Allison Vaughan that his client was suffering from potential mental health issues but had never been diagnosed with any mental health problem.
Patel said Nugent suffered from a neurological condition, idiopathic transverse myelitis, and a concussion. The lawyer did not explain how Nugent had been concussed.
The rare condition damages the spinal cord’s protective myelin sheath and disrupts nerve signals between the brain and body. This leads to rapid muscle weakness, sensory loss, pain, and bladder and bowel dysfunction, according to the Cleveland Clinic medical center.
Witnesses say the driver rammed his victim, pinning her against her own car before reversing and ramming her a second time.
Australia worries about balancing security with keeping politicians accessible
The well-regarded lawmaker’s plight has shocked Australians, as political violence is uncommon in the country and politicians are highly accessible to the public. Most lawmakers are not accompanied by security details and go about their work and personal lives on their own.
Senior opposition lawmaker James Paterson on Wednesday called for a review of lawmakers’ personal security in response to the alleged crime.
“The reality is that Australian parliamentarians by global standards are uniquely accessible to the public and that’s a good thing,” Paterson told Australian Broadcasting Corp.
“But we … can’t have a situation where shocking attacks like this take place because that will fundamentally change our democracy forever if it becomes a serious risk to your life to be a member of parliament,” Paterson added.
But Prime Minister Anthony Albanese urged lawmakers to continue to engage openly with the public despite worsening animosity within the community.
“We want to make sure that people can feel as much comfort as possible that everything’s being done to maximize security,” Albanese told News24.
“I think parliamentarians across the board are determined to make sure that we can continue to engage as we need to in this great democracy of ours,” Albanese added. “That interaction is really important in our democracy.”
Security agencies brief lawmakers on personal security
Lawmakers began online meetings with Australia’s security agencies on Wednesday to discuss their safety. Such briefings are a regular occurrence.
Albanese described the briefings as an “opportunity for people who feel anxious to be able to ask questions” of security agencies.
Australian Federal Police provide personal security only to those lawmakers who are assessed as higher risk, usually because they have attracted the attention of dangerous people. Prime ministers always have personal protection and immigration ministers often do because they anger people with visa decisions.
Paterson said providing police protection to all 226 federal lawmakers would not be practical. But he suggested increased security at electorate offices, such as Haines’ office where she was hit. Paterson said lawmakers were “most identifiable” at their offices. Coming and going could be a “risky moment.”
Federal Police Commissioner Kissy Barrett told reporters providing police protection to all parliamentarians would take an “incredible amount of resourcing.”
Police received 1,067 reports of threatening, harassing, nuisance and offensive communications against high officeholders including federal lawmakers and their office staff in the last fiscal year — a 12% increase on the previous year. Barrett said almost one suspect a week was charged over such threats.
Australia hasn’t recorded the political violence seen in other countries
Elsewhere in the world, authorities have warned of growing threats to lawmakers. The United States has seen a rise in political violence over the past decade.
That includes the 2022 hammer assault on the husband of then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi; the 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump during his presidential campaign, as well as another on the president at the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner in April; and the assassinations in 2025 of a Democratic Minnesota state lawmaker and her husband, and of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk.
In Britain, killings of politicians have also led to tighter security. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, while Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the militant Islamic State group.
In July, the former British politician and reality TV contestant Ann Widdecombe was found beaten to death with a hammer at her home. A man has been charged with murder and terrorism-related offenses.
___
Graham-McLay reported from Wellington, New Zealand.

title: Man wanted on felony charges out of Rumford arrested in Westbrook
text:
Maine man wanted on felony charges out of Rumford arrested in Westbrook
The U.S. Marshals Service says a Maine man who was wanted on multiple felony charges in connection with an incident that happened in Rumford last week has been taken into custody.
Blake Lachance, 21, of Lewiston, was arrested Tuesday at a Westbrook home on Seavey Street. He was charged with one count each of aggravated assault with a dangerous weapon, criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon and reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon following an Oct. 14 incident in Rumford.
The Rumford Police Department said on Oct. 14 that authorities sought to arrest Lachance after an investigation into reports of gunfire and suspected drug trafficking. Watch our reporting on the Oct. 14 incident in the video embedded below.
Rumford police then requested help from the U.S. Marshals Service-led Maine Violent Offender Task Force in finding and apprehending Lachance. Task force investigators then worked with the U.S. Marshals Service, Homeland Security Task Force, Rumford Police Department, Lewiston Police Department and Westbrook Police Department.
Investigators learned that Lachance had fled to a residential neighborhood in Westbrook, so the U.S. Marshals Service requested assistance from the Cumberland County Emergency Services Unit, which is led by the Cumberland County Sheriff's Office, and the Southern Maine Regional SWAT team, which is led by the South Portland Police Department.
Officials said Lachance attempted to run away from the Seavey Street home when law enforcement units arrived on Tuesday, but a perimeter team was able to take him into custody without further incident.
Westbrook resident Michael Spaulding, who lives on Seavey Street, said he noticed a slew of activity outside of his window between 8 and 9 p.m. Tuesday.
"They had the whole house surrounded. They had the whole block surrounded," Spaulding said. "I see the dude they were trying to arrest take off, and then I see three of the marshals run after him."
Lachance was turned over to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service and taken to a local jail, where he remains held pending his initial court appearance.
Details of Rumford incident
Rumford police said that over the weekend of Oct. 10-11, they received information concerning suspected drug trafficking involving locals and people from out of town at a Waldo Street apartment. Police said they also received reports from concerned residents, who told police that people associated with the apartment at 209 Waldo St. were armed and had been periodically firing guns in the surrounding neighborhood.
Before sunrise on the morning of Oct. 14, Rumford police responded to a report of gunfire in the Waldo Street area. Responding officers determined that the people believed to be involved had been inside the apartment and were potentially still there.
Given the possibility of encountering armed suspects, officers from the Rumford Police Department and Oxford County Sheriff's Office established a perimeter around 209 Waldo St. while investigators prepared applications for search and arrest warrants.
The Maine State Police Tactical Team was called in to help secure the area and execute the search warrant, which was authorized by a court later that morning.
Police said that as officers prepared to search the apartment, Rumford Public Works crews established temporary road closures and traffic detours in the surrounding neighborhood. MedCare Ambulance paramedics were also staged nearby as a precaution.
In a Facebook post shared shortly before 12:15 p.m. on Oct. 14, Rumford police said people near the intersection of Waldo Street and Maine Avenue were advised to shelter in place and stay inside.
Rumford police said the Maine State Police Tactical Team entered the apartment shortly before 1 p.m. and determined the suspects were no longer inside. Investigators believe the suspects had fled the apartment several hours earlier, around the time police initially responded to the report of gunfire in the morning.
At 1:20 p.m. on Oct. 14, Rumford police announced that the shelter-in-place advisory had been lifted and that roads that were closed were being reopened.
According to officials, a subsequent search of the apartment, coupled with information developed during the ongoing investigation, yielded additional evidence supporting the reports that police received from members of the public.
While announcing the charges brought against Lachance, Rumford police said they expected to bring criminal charges against more people as investigators continued to develop evidence and identify those involved.

title: Supreme Court rebuffs Trump administration restrictions on medical care for transgender inmates
text:
Supreme Court rebuffs Trump administration restrictions on medical care for transgender inmates
The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to allow the Trump administration to immediately enforce new medical restrictions for transgender people in prison.
The decision leaves in place a lower-court block on the policy. It was adopted after an executive order from President Donald Trump, a Republican who has taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term.
The brief order did not detail its legal reasoning. Justice Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas would have allowed the policy to be enforced as the lawsuit played out in lower courts.
The Supreme Court has previously allowed other policies for transgender people to move ahead for now, including restrictions on military service and passport sex markers.
Related video above: Supreme Court rule states can ban transgender girls from female school sports
Trump's order called on the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care policies so that federal funds aren’t spent “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.”
The new policy would halt surgeries, taper off hormones and end social accommodations like makeup and wigs. Prisons would continue to offer mental health services.
Attorneys for transgender inmates challenged the policy in court and U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth ordered treatments to continue. Lamberth, who was nominated to the bench by Republican President Ronald Reagan, pointed out that untreated gender dysphoria can cause severe side effects like depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts.
The Trump administration appealed, arguing that treatments raised security concerns and “could no longer be justified.” A divided appeals court panel left the order in place.
About 600 inmates were receiving hormone therapy in 2025, the agency said in court records. Withdrawing care would have significant effects on their bodies and mental health, their lawyers said. The government has not detailed evidence of security problems linked to hormone therapy for transgender inmates over the 30 years it has been provided, they wrote.
The conservative-majority Supreme Court has previously upheld state laws banning certain medical treatments for transgender youth, and restricting sports participation by transgender athletes in women’s sports.

title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to lift halt on Big Bend border wall
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Wednesday to let it resume building a border wall project through the Big Bend region of Texas.
The government filed an emergency appeal asking the justices to lift a lower court decision halting construction. That ruling marked a setback to one of President Donald Trump’s signature projects.
The administration has been racing forward with construction on a border wall and other infrastructure from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.
But in the Big Bend region, the administration has run into opposition from ranchers, residents, business owners and environmentalists who argue the projects are a waste of money in an area of historically low illegal immigration and that construction could harm the region’s scenic landscapes.
Opponents have filed numerous lawsuits seeking to stop the project, which in the Big Bend consists of a mixture of walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology.
Ruling in one of those cases, Judge Kathleen Cardone on Oct. 2 ordered the government to stop construction across the roughly 500-mile project area while the case plays out in the courts. It was a major victory for the bipartisan opposition.
The case hinges on sweeping waivers signed by the secretary of Homeland Security that allow U.S. Customs and Border Protection to bypass environmental and other regulations that would otherwise slow down construction of such a major project.
The government argued that the Big Bend sector is an area of high illegal entry, and said legislation dating back to 1996 explicitly gives the secretary these far-reaching powers as necessary to build physical barriers or roads near the border to stop people from crossing illegally.
Opponents disagreed, arguing that Congress gave that power to waive regulations specifically in areas of “high illegal entry.” They said Big Bend, a remote and rugged region, doesn’t fit that description.
Cardone sided with the opponents.
“The Court finds that Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of their major questions doctrine claim that the Big Bend Waivers were issued in excess of the Secretary’s authority,” she wrote.
Trump has long vowed to build a border wall along the roughly 2,000-mile length of the southwest border. Last summer, Republicans in Congress allocated Homeland Security $46 billion to finish the project, which will be a mixture of 30-foot-tall steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology.
The opposition in Texas’s Big Bend region had been brewing for months, but it escalated in August when bulldozers were spotted clearing land in Big Bend National Park.
The preliminary injunction filed by Cardone stops construction there as well as land up and downriver from the park that is owned by private landowners or the state.
The government has argued that if this region is one of the only areas left without a wall or other border infrastructure, illegal immigration could end up funneling to the Big Bend. But opponents have argued that other forms of infrastructure such as drones or surveillance towers are just as effective and a lot less expensive than the wall plans.

title: Democrats' faith in election results is falling but still exceeds Republicans', AP-NORC poll finds
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Daemien Williams used to trust U.S. election results, but not anymore.
The 50-year-old Democrat in Centreville, Illinois, worries that President Donald Trump and other Republicans will try anything from intimidating voters to seizing ballots to hold onto power in November’s midterm elections — and, in the process, jeopardize the outcome.
“I don’t put anything past these people,” he said. “My trust level is at its all-time low.”
Registered voters who identify as Democrats have lost faith in America’s election results since the midterm elections four years ago, according to a new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. Their confidence that votes will be counted accurately has dropped from 75% in 2022 to 55% this year.
The overwhelming majority of Democratic voters also say the president attempting to influence U.S. elections is a “major problem,” a view that’s shared by independents but not most Republicans.
Meanwhile, Republican voters’ confidence in the results has risen slightly since 2022 — but they’re still less likely to say they have faith in the electoral process than Democrats.
The survey, conducted less than a month before Election Day, signals how opinion has changed since Trump returned to the White House last year and began a wide-ranging effort to expand federal authority over elections. Even though the Constitution gives states and Congress control over voting processes, Trump has tried to overhaul them through executive action and lawsuits, so far without success.
With the Nov. 3 elections approaching, the Republican president has signaled he wants federal prosecutors to be on the lookout for fraud, suggesting he may try legal challenges if the votes don’t go his way.
Williams said that, despite his concerns, he still plans to vote in the midterms because it’s the only power he has in choosing his representation.
“If you take that away from America, you pretty much take away the foundation of this country,” he said.
Republicans have gained more faith in the process since Trump’s return
Democratic voters, who had largely trusted U.S. elections even after Trump falsely claimed he won the 2020 race and his supporters violently stormed the U.S. Capitol to champion that cause, have recently begun to doubt the upcoming results. But they still have more confidence than Republican and independent voters.
Slightly fewer than half of all U.S. voters have “a great deal” or “quite a bit” of confidence in the accuracy of the vote, down to 45% this year from 50% in 2022. Independents have remained steady with a lower level of trust, with 34% saying they have a “great deal” or “quite a bit” of confidence in both years.
Republicans, meanwhile, are growing more confident since Trump returned to power, even as they remain less confident than Democrats. About 38% of GOP voters have a “great deal” or “quite a bit” of confidence in the results this year, compared with 26% in 2022.
Some voters said their confidence levels related to escalating threats from Trump that he could get involved in the elections. Earlier this month, his administration filed a lawsuit against California officials claiming they didn’t adequately address alleged noncitizen voters on their rolls, and it warned that election workers who process ballots from noncitizens could face criminal investigation and prosecution.
His administration has said it has no plans to send the military or immigration agents to patrol polling places, although the head of the Department of Homeland Security said immigration officers could be sent there for targeted operations, such as making an arrest with a warrant. Trump critics have expressed fears over potential voter intimidation, with some pointing to a Department of Justice plan to deploy 1,000 monitors to voting locations.
Alan Curtis in Grove, Oklahoma, is among the Republican voters feeling better this year. The 67-year-old, who was suspicious of election fraud before the presidential election in 2024, sees Trump’s bully pulpit as a strong deterrent.
“I think the election officials will be running scared,” he said. “The people in other political parties are afraid of what Donald Trump might do.”
Curtis said he still believes that Democrats could try to cheat — an accusation made often by the president without providing evidence — but he expects Trump will step in with lawsuits or other interventions if he sees anything suspicious.
“He’s going to challenge anything where he sees things that look out of the ordinary,” Curtis said of Trump.
If there are legal challenges, few Americans have faith in the U.S. Supreme Court to decide them fairly. Just 17% of registered voters were “extremely” or “very” confident the court would handle a case related to the midterm elections in a fair and nonpartisan manner.
Democrats see presidential election interference as a big problem
While some Republicans view Trump getting involved as a positive, the poll shows the vast majority of Democrats feel the opposite.
About 9 in 10 Democratic voters believe that the president attempting to influence election outcomes is “a major problem,” compared with only about 2 in 10 Republican voters.
Brooklyn Johnson, a 26-year-old Democrat in Davis, California, said she dislikes Trump’s dubious promise of $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans retain control of the House and the Senate in the midterms.
“The fact that he’s been trying to bribe people, that’s a little weird,” she said. “It doesn’t seem legal.”
Eugenio Mendez, an independent voter in Columbia, South Carolina, who leans toward Democrats, is so concerned about Trump interfering that it’s affecting his voting plan.
“I don’t trust that mailing my ballot will be counted,” said the 49-year-old Mendez.
He said he’ll vote in person this year because he worries Trump could use his influence over the U.S. Postal Service to meddle with mail-in ballots. Trump signed an executive order this year directing changes at the Postal Service designed to restrict mail voting, but the Supreme Court did not allow the plan to move forward for the midterms.
Voters of different parties see distinct election problems
While Democrats worry about presidential interference, Republicans are more concerned about people voting when they are ineligible. About 7 in 10 Republican voters say this is a “major problem” in U.S. elections compared with just 25% of Democratic voters.
Majorities of voters from both parties also say foreign governments trying to influence election outcomes, artificial intelligence-generated election misinformation and states redrawing legislative districts to intentionally favor one party are “major problems.”
Approaches to voting laws, which differ by state, are also a major dividing line between the parties. Republican voters overwhelmingly favor requiring voters to show ID when casting a ballot and providing proof of citizenship when registering to vote, changes Trump tried unsuccessfully to pass through Congress.
Democrats are more likely than Republicans to favor allowing voters to register and cast a ballot the same day, as well as to support mailing a ballot to all registered voters, a practice Trump and other Republicans have criticized.
But while their support was not as strong as Republicans’, a majority of Democratic voters also favor a voter ID requirement.
___
Swenson reported from New York.
___
The AP-NORC poll of 1,119 adults, including 925 registered voters, was conducted Oct. 8-12 using a sample drawn from NORC’s probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel, which is designed to be representative of the U.S. population. The margin of sampling error for adults overall is plus or minus 3.9 percentage points, and the margin of error for registered voters is plus or minus 4.2 percentage points.

title: Trump envoy Witkoff to meet Putin in St. Petersburg for Ukraine war talks
text:
Trump envoy Witkoff to meet Putin in St. Petersburg for Ukraine war talks
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff arrived in St. Petersburg on Wednesday for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as U.S. President Donald Trump pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
The visit came a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and some European leaders in the Norwegian capital, Oslo.
Related video: High diesel prices adding pressure to GOP, but Trump remains confident his party will defeat Democrats
Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations after his trip to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.
“I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy,” Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning.
Zelenskyy was still in Oslo on Wednesday, where he was visiting the country’s Parliament and meeting lawmakers.
Witkoff’s meetings suggested leaders are keen to bring momentum to U.S.-led peace efforts, more than 4 1/2 years after Russia’s army invaded. Efforts by the Trump administration since early last year to end the war have made no significant progress, and there was no suggestion of an imminent breakthrough.
Russia and Ukraine are still far apart in their terms for a settlement, as their armies remain locked on the battlefield and they pummel each other with daily long-range strikes.
Putin’s aide Yuri Ushakov said the Russian president will host Witkoff at the Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg in the first half of the day on Wednesday. Presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev will take part in the meeting, he said.
“Negotiations on a settlement in Ukraine are, naturally, an integral part of today’s agenda,” Ushakov told reporters.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Tuesday that Moscow is willing to listen to new U.S. proposals about Ukraine but he doesn’t expect any “miracle” from Washington.
At the White House on Tuesday, Trump increased the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two men have soured again.
If that doesn’t happen, “I think it’s going to be a very bad thing,” Trump said.
The change happened after Zelenskyy spoke with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

title: More Clouds & Breezy Conditions Thursday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - High pressure parked over the Northeast has kept us dry and sunny for the first half of the week. That changes some Wednesday night into Thursday as a strong low to our south slides farther north.
Clouds continue to spread from south to north Wednesday night. How fast they arrive will decide how cool it gets. Lows range from the low 40s along the coast, where clouds move in first, to the low 30s in the north, where skies stay clear longer.
Thursday: More Clouds, Gusty Winds
The low slides well offshore Thursday. For us, that means more clouds, gusty NNE winds, and some rough seas. Winds pick up through the day, with gusts to 30 mph possible. Highs in the 50s and 60s. A cold front later in the day Thursday will help clear the clouds and push the low farther out to sea.
Friday: Sunshine Returns, Breezy and Cooler
High pressure builds in behind the front. Expect lots of sunshine, but cooler and breezy. Highs in the 40s and low to mid 50s. Northerly winds gust to 30 mph.
Weekend: Beautiful Fall Weekend
The high stays in control Saturday and Sunday. Expect sunny skies both days with MUCH lighter winds. Saturday will be the cooler of the two, with highs in the 50s. Sunday warms up, with highs from the upper 50s to the mid 60s.

title: Teacher who survived Oregon school attack says she had no chance to protect children
text:
A teacher wounded in last week’s attack on a special education classroom at an Oregon elementary school says she never had a chance to try to shelter any of the children inside.
In a statement issued by a family friend, Becky Drury said Wednesday that she ran to see what was going on when she realized something was happening — but immediately saw the shooter and rushed back to the classroom.
“I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there,” Drury said. “Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground.”
Her left hand was nearly severed by a gunshot, and her right arm was struck as well. Unable to get up or defend herself or others, she said, “I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again.”
Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, last Thursday when a former student there, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, blasted his way through locked doors with a shotgun and attacked the classroom. Another student was critically injured.
Authorities said another teacher threw her phone at the gunman and then tackled him and wrestled with him for control of the weapon, likely saving lives before the gunman was shot by a father who followed him into the building.
Some news reports had suggested that Drury threw herself on top of one student to protect her. Drury, who remains hospitalized, said she wanted to correct the record.
“Accurate, respectful reporting is a truly important service that will help heal the wounds inflicted by that awful day,” she said.
School reopened in the district Wednesday for the first time since the shooting. Dozens of officers were on hand at each school to welcome children back, the Bend Police Department said.
In a social media post, the department said it continues investigating the attack, including serving search warrants at the attacker’s home, as well as on his electronic devices and his social media accounts on a variety of platforms.
The statement said police have confirmed that the pump-action shotgun used in the attack had been legally purchased. The Associated Press previously reported it had been purchased by the suspect’s mother, according to a law enforcement source who was not authorized to discuss the investigation. But investigators said they were still looking into how the boy obtained it.

title: Jackson Laboratory celebrates 10 years of the Maine Cancer Genomics Initiative
text:
Maine (WABI) - For rural Mainers with cancer, advanced care once meant driving to Boston or traveling to an academic center. A decade in, the Jackson Laboratory’s Maine Cancer Genomics Initiative says it has flipped that model.
The Jackson Laboratory’s Maine Cancer Genomics Initiative is celebrating 10 years of making advanced tumor testing available where rural patients live.
Dr. Jens Reuter, the Chief Medical Officer at Jackson Laboratory, says MCGI was founded in 2016 because genomic testing was costly and scarce outside cities.
“The gap was really the largest in rural areas outside of academic centers,” said Dr.Reuter.
“We wanted more patients in rural areas to access these targeted therapies, to access clinical trials. And we were quite successful with that,” Dr.Reuter said.
Dr. Reuter notes that about 80% of the cancer patients in the country are seen in the community and not at an academic center.
He says MCGI has now impacted the lives of more than 4,000 cancer patients in Maine and their families.
Patient advisory board member Chadwick Rhodes, diagnosed in 2019, described the burden of having to travel for care.
“A lot of people, when they’re going through cancer, they don’t like to have to travel to Boston or travel a long ways from their home,” said Rhodes.
“A patient can be in Fort Kent and go to the nearest medical center and get their tumor tested... and then go right back home and wait for the testing to go to an oncologist. It doesn’t necessarily require an overnight stay depending on where the tumor is. I think that’s the biggest deal for a patient,” Rhodes said.
And now, its impact is going well beyond Maine.
“The good news is that now it’s been so successful after 10 years, which we’re celebrating now, that it’s being modeled in, I think, 16 other rural locations across the United States,” said Rhodes.

title: New Mexico sues Epstein’s attorney and accountant, accuses them of hiding sex trafficking operation
text:
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — New Mexico’s attorney general filed a lawsuit Wednesday against Jeffrey Epstein’s attorney and accountant, accusing them of concealing his sex trafficking operation at a sprawling Santa Fe-area ranch where the disgraced financier entertained guests.
The lawsuit seeks to stop attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn from accepting any payments from Epstein’s estate, estimated at more than $100 million. They serve as coexecutors, and New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said they “stand to benefit substantially” from the estate unless a federal judge intervenes.
Indyke worked as Epstein’s attorney for roughly two decades. Both he and Kahn have testified in Congress that they did not know about Epstein’s abuse, though Torrez has a different view.
___
___
“None of this could be done by just one man,” Torrez said at a news conference, where he stood with two of Epstein’s accusers. “This was something that was facilitated, that was made possible by handlers, by lawyers, by accountants, by others who have yet to face real consequences.”
In response to the lawsuit, an attorney for the pair said they “emphatically reject” the allegations and note that New Mexico officials never sought to interview Indyke and Kahn before going to court. Dan Weiner said they would have cooperated.
“Not a single woman has ever accused Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn of committing sexual abuse or witnessing sexual abuse, nor claimed at any time that she or anyone else reported to them any allegation of Mr. Epstein’s abuse,” Weiner said in an email.
The U.S. Justice Department declined to comment on any federal investigation of Indyke or Kahn.
Epstein owned the Zorro Ranch for decades
Earlier this year, Indyke and Kahn agreed as executors of the estate to settle a class-action lawsuit brought against them by Epstein accusers for up to $35 million. They did not admit any wrongdoing as part of the deal.
Torrez’s lawsuit is an effort to possibly recover more money for victims, with New Mexico acting as the plaintiff.
Epstein purchased the Zorro Ranch in Stanley, a sparsely populated ranching community about 30 miles (50 kilometers) south of Santa Fe, in 1993. He built a massive home on the property, which spanned thousands of acres, and constructed several guest homes, a private airstrip and a helipad.
___
___
Epstein died by suicide in a New York jail cell in August 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges.
His former girlfriend and close associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, is serving a 20-year prison sentence after her 2021 conviction on sex trafficking charges in New York. Witness testimony at Maxwell’s trial alleged she and Epstein had sexually abused women at the ranch.
“We cannot undo what happened or return what was taken from us, but we can demand answers,” said Epstein accuser Anouska De Georgiou. “We can pursue justice and we can insist that wealth, power and influence never place anyone beyond accountability.”
The Associated Press does not name people who say they were sexually abused unless they have come forward publicly.
Indyke and Kahn played key roles, lawsuit says
The lawsuit accuses Indyke and Kahn of conspiracy and racketeering in supporting the “Epstein Enterprise.”
“They arranged payments to survivors to purchase their silence and leave them indebted to Epstein, handled costs for expenses connected to the abuse, monitored survivors’ spending, and prepared tax returns for some survivors,” the lawsuit states.
The lawsuit points to financial records indicating over $3 million in payments were made — with no discernible business purpose — from Epstein-related accounts directly to girls or women from 2003 to 2013.
Between 2013 and 2019, the lawsuit states, Indyke and Kahn authorized and signed off on payments totaling hundreds of thousands of dollars to “the enterprise’s sex trafficking survivors, including those who also acted as recruiters, and other expenses including legal fees, apartment rent and tuition.”
According to the suit, some payments were funneled through a nonprofit that was overseen by Indyke and Kahn. The complaint states that more than $30,000 was paid out by the C.O.U.Q. Foundation in 2012 to girls or women for purposes apparently unrelated to the charity.
The lawsuit also notes a 2017 email from Kahn to Epstein regarding payment of “the latest batch of medical expenses for girls.”
“At the end of the day this is not about the past. It is about the truth. It’s about justice, and it’s about making sure that accountability does not end with Epstein,” said Julia Molchanova, another Epstein accuser.
No crimes were pursued in New Mexico
Epstein never faced charges in New Mexico, though the state attorney general’s office in 2019 confirmed that it was investigating and planned to forward its findings to federal authorities in New York. Hector Balderas, who was attorney general at the time, said New Mexico’s outdated laws failed to protect children from abuse.
Epstein was not required to register as a sex offender in New Mexico, despite a 2008 guilty plea in Florida.
Torrez reopened the state’s investigation this year. In August, he sued the Justice Department, accusing it of blocking the state from investigating alleged sex crimes. The government said it was not releasing some information to the state because disclosing victim-identifying information would violate court orders in New York.
Also in August, a commission established by state lawmakers to investigate whether local authorities looked the other way, released a 119-page report that said authorities repeatedly deferred to investigations in New York, Palm Beach, Florida, and the Virgin Islands, while leaving Epstein’s offenses in New Mexico unexamined and unpunished.
Epstein’s estate sold the ranch in 2023 to the family of Don Huffines, a Republican who is the Texas state comptroller. The money was set aside for creditors.
Probate proceedings related to Epstein’s will and assets are being handled in the U.S. Virgin Islands.
___
White reported from Detroit. AP reporter Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado, contributed to this story.

title: 7 Maine thrillers for Halloween (that weren’t written by Stephen King)
text:
Maine can be a pretty scary place.
There are isolated islands, windswept mountain peaks and foreboding forests all promising some hidden horror or secret. It’s also a place of interminable winters, spooky old houses and storied shipwrecks.
All those things make it fertile ground for horror stories, something Maine native Stephen King has proven over the course of his 50-year career. But Maine has inpired lots of other writers to craft tales of horror or suspense. Every year there are more scary books by Maine writers, or terrible tales set in Maine. Following are some suggestions for recent Maine horror or suspense books, to help you get in the proper mood for the spooky season.
‘Carry Me to My Grave’ by Christopher Golden
Golden, a New York Times best-selling author who lives in Massachusetts, has won the Bram Stoker Award and Shirley Jackson Award for previous works of horror. This one, which came out in August, stems from supernatural happenings in the fictional Maine town of Shediak. The story is set in the 1950s and focuses on Malcom Wise and his mother, Maggie.
As a boy, Malcolm was taunted by other kids calling his mother a witch. Now as she’s dying, Maggie makes Malcom promise to return her body to her Maine birthplace, by train. But she needs to be buried before sunrise on the second morning after her death. But as soon as Maggie dies, there are “things” digging themselve up out of the ground all over the country.
‘The Ghosts of Riddell House’ by Kevin St. Jarre
This gothic ghost story came out in September and focuses on two paranormal investigators hired to get to the bottom of some spooky stuff at a notorious and remote Maine house. One, Tanya Libby, feels cursed by her abilities to hear the dead. The other, Burch Kinney, makes his living pretending he’s something he’s not. St. Jarre lives in Cape Elizabeth and grew up in Madawaska.
‘How to Survive in the Woods’ by Kat Rosenfield
This domestic thriller is set in Maine’s 100-Mile Wilderness, the last stretch of the Appalachian Trail. Emma Sharp, raised by a doomsday prepper, is feeling trapped and controlled in her marriage as she sets out to hike the trail with her husband and his former girlfriend. It’s a story of desire and dread and deadly things happening in the darkness of the woods.
Rosenfield spent childhood summers on Deer Isle, where her grandparents lived, as well as on Sebec Lake. Monson and Cloud Pond are a couple of the Maine locations in the book, which came out in March. She’s also written for Entertainment Weekly and The New York Times.
‘The Siren of Groves Peak’ by Glenn Rolfe
In the small lobstering town of Groves Peak, a violent murder at sea creates chaos and hints at darker secrets. Rolfe, who lives in Gardiner, says the fictional town is on the coast between Portland and Rockland. The book came out in June. One of Rolfe’s previous books, “When Night Falls,” was set in Old Orchard Beach in the ’90s and featured a serial killer and unnatural creatures.
‘Unspeakable Things’ by Elizabeth Hand
In 1920s Cornwall, on the coast of England, two young women go on the run when they’re implicated in the disappearance of a famous author. They seek refuge at a country house filled with “a debauched coterie of London’s Bright Young Things” as well as the estate’s mysterious owner. Sinister intrigue ensues. The book came out in October.
Hand, who lives in Lincolnville, wrote the 2023 novel “A Haunting on the Hill,” a new story about the namesake structure in Shirley Jackson’s 1959 classic “The Haunting of Hill House.”
‘We, the Missing’ by Arwyn Sherman
An anxious teenager tries to protect her mother from a rash of disappearances in their city, loosely based on Portland. The teen discovers a world of darkness, deadly creatures and monstrous angels. It’s the debut novel for Sherman, who lives in West Bath. Sherman will talk about the novel at a book launch at the Portland Public Library at 6:30 p.m. Oct. 29, with fellow horror writers Katherine Silva and Nicole Mann.
‘Where the Soul Goes’ by Katherine Silva
A gay, asexual chef goes on a road trip with Death to save an alternative 1980s human race from a degenerative illness, through gastronomy. Silva, who lives in Waldoboro, says several locales in the book were inspired by small towns and cities across Maine. Her writing often highlights her love of wilderness. The book came out in September 2025.

title: Current credit card interest rates
text:
Current credit card interest rates
The average credit card interest rate is 19.70%, down from a record-high 20.79% set on Aug. 14, 2024.
Current credit card interest rates
Bankrate Data Center
Since 1976, Bankrate has been the go-to source for personal finance data, publishing average rates on the most popular financial products and tracking the experience of consumers nationwide.
See more
Credit card rates are creeping up again
How are credit card rates set?
Your credit card APR has two parts: the Prime Rate, plus a markup your card issuer chooses.
The Prime Rate is the benchmark that banks use for their most creditworthy customers and the basis for many financial products. It’s typically 3 percentage points higher than the top end of the federal funds rate, which is set by the Federal Reserve’s Federal Open Market Committee. Currently, the Prime Rate is 7%.
The issuer’s markup is where the rest of your rate comes from, and it’s set at the issuer’s discretion. On average, this margin often runs between 12 and 13 percentage points.
Credit cards carry a higher markup than other loans, such as mortgages and auto loans, because credit card debt is unsecured — it isn’t backed by a physical asset such as a home or car that the issuer can seize if you don’t repay the debt.
When the Fed moves, your rate moves
Your credit card rate changes along with the Fed rate, but these changes are typically incremental. For example, the Fed raised the benchmark rate by 25 basis points on Sept. 16, 2026, bringing the target range to 3.75% to 4.00%. In the following month, the average credit card interest rate rose by 0.12%, according to Bankrate’s data.
Because most cards carry a variable APR with the Prime Rate baked in, a Fed rate change passes straight through to your rate — either up or down — and your issuer isn’t required to give you notice. Most people see it within one to two billing cycles. The exact timing is up to the issuer: some use the Prime Rate as of your statement date, while others use the first or last day of the month.
When your issuer changes your rate because the Prime Rate changes, it applies to your existing balance and all new purchases.
Your rights when your credit card interest rate changes
Whether your issuer is required to let you know about a rate change depends on the reason for the change. If the rate moved because the Prime Rate moved, the issuer isn’t required to alert you. The change is automatic and is built into your card agreement.
But if your issuer changes your interest rate for another reason, such as applying a penalty APR for a late payment, you have the right to know. The issuer is required to give you a 45-day notice before any such changes. You have the right to opt out of the new terms, but if you do, your card company will likely close your account. You won’t have to pay off the entire balance immediately, but your minimum payment may increase.
If you agree to the new terms, the new APR can only apply to new balances, except in certain circumstances.

How do credit card rates affect you?
When you carry a balance, your issuer divides your APR by 365 to get the daily rate, then applies it to your average daily balance, or the average of what you owed on each day of the billing cycle. That’s the part that matters: If you carry a balance, interest builds every single day. Paying it down is the only thing that stops it.
Let’s say you have $5,000 of credit card debt and your interest rate is 20% APR. If you only make minimum payments, you’ll be in debt for about 23 years and pay roughly $7,723 in interest, according to Bankrate’s minimum payment calculator.
But if you pay your credit card purchases in full each month, you aren’t charged interest and you typically receive an interest-free grace period of at least 21 days. For example, if your billing statement is generated on the 1st of the month, you usually have until at least the 22nd to pay without interest accruing. And because the clock doesn’t start until your statement closes, something you bought on the first day of the cycle gets the whole cycle plus the grace period — close to seven weeks interest-free.
Keep in mind: An interest-free grace period applies only to purchases. If you’ve made a balance transfer or taken a cash advance, a different APR applies and there’s usually no grace period. Cash advances typically start accruing interest the day you take them out. Likewise, if you transfer a balance to a card, interest will begin to accrue immediately unless you have an intro 0% APR balance transfer promotion.
-  Our methodology When we refer to the average credit card rate, we mean the average midpoint of the APR ranges assessed by 111 popular credit cards offered by the 50 largest U.S.-based credit card issuers. Most credit cards charge different interest rates to different customers based upon their creditworthiness. A consumer with an excellent credit score, for example, might be charged 14.99%. That same card might charge as high as, say, 24.99% to someone with a lower credit score. In that example, we would use 19.99% (the midpoint between 14.99% and 24.99%) in our average credit card rate calculations.

title: ‘I thought I lost my baby’: Mother speaks out after toddler found alive in morgue
text:
GILBERT, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - New details are emerging in the case of an 18-month-old boy who was pronounced dead at an Arizona hospital, only to be found alive in the morgue hours later.
Vincent Fiordilino, 18 months, was taken to Mercy Gilbert Medical Center on Feb. 8 after nearly drowning in a swimming pool. He was pronounced dead — but five hours later, he was found alive in the hospital morgue.
Now, nearly eight months after the incident, Vincent’s mother, Alexus Fiordilino, is speaking publicly for the first time. She said she still relives that day.
“I didn’t even think stuff like that happened. I thought I lost my baby, and he was back,” she said. “There isn’t a day I don’t think about that day.”
The incident began when the family found Vincent floating face down in a pool at a Super Bowl party. Police arrived and performed CPR before paramedics took the toddler to Mercy Gilbert.
Fiordilino said she begged first responders to save her son.
“I remember just begging the police officers and the fire department to just save him,” she said. “I’m saying goodbye. And I’m begging him. I’m just begging Vincent to come back.”
Hours later, she got the call that he was alive.
“I remember feeling really grateful. And I remember just wanting to rush to him. I needed to get back to him. I felt so bad that he was alone,” she said.
Attorney questions canceled test, delayed labs
The family’s attorney says new documents reveal a potential lapse in care, stating the doctor ordered then canceled a test that would have shown how much oxygen was in Vincent’s blood.
The toddler arrived at the hospital around 6:04 p.m. on Feb. 8. At 6:08 p.m., a doctor ordered an arterial blood gas test to check oxygen in the blood. That test was canceled, according to documents shared by the family’s attorney. At 6:11 p.m., labs were collected. At 6:20 p.m. — nine minutes later — Vincent was pronounced dead.
Body camera footage shows officers asking at 6:13 p.m., “Do we have results on the gas yet?” Staff responded they did not. Those results did not come in until 6:38 p.m., 18 minutes after the toddler was declared dead.
The documents also show the doctor did not sign his report until the day after Vincent was found alive.
“I think that man failed to do his job properly... He failed my son in every step of the way,” Fiordilino said.
Gilbert Police are asking the Arizona Attorney General’s Office to review the case for possible felony child abuse charges against the doctor. The family’s attorney said they will be filing a complaint against the hospital and doctor next week.
Fiordilino said she believes if doctors had waited for the lab results, Vincent would be in a very different place. The toddler has significant medical issues that will require lifelong care, the family’s attorney said.
“We trusted the professionals that took an oath, made a promise, that they would do everything they could. And they looked at my son for whatever reason and decided he wasn’t worth it,” she said.
The attorney general’s office said it has not decided whether to review the case at this time.

Mortgage rates fall well below 7.5%
Current mortgage rates

Explore mortgage rates
Monthly mortgage payment at today’s rates
The national median family income for 2026 is $106,800, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the median price of an existing home sold in August 2026 was $417,500, according to the National Association of Realtors. Based on a 20% down payment and a 7.38% mortgage rate, the monthly principal and interest payment of $2,310 amounts to about 26% of the typical family’s monthly income.
Meanwhile, home prices are still rising — the National Association of Realtors reports the median home price was up 1.3% over the past year, and the median of $417,500 was an all-time high for the month of September. However, values have begun to dip in many formerly hot markets. Still, signs are mixed. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller index released in late September showed national home prices grew 1.9% in the year ending in July, marking an acceleration.
What will happen to mortgage rates in the rest of 2026?
Inflation rose to 3.7% in September, although the Fed’s preferred measure, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index, was 3.0% for September. Oil prices have spiked amid the conflict in Iran, pushing inflation up and lifting mortgage rates from their 2026 low of 6.09%. Rising inflation has been the main driver of higher mortgage rates — the consumer price index has pushed well above the Fed’s 2% target, although 10-year Treasury yields fell to 5.1% this week, down from 5.3% last week.
“There is no single switch that will bring mortgage rates meaningfully lower,” says Jeff DerGurahian, head economist at loanDepot. “We likely need several factors to fall into place including cooler oil prices, softer consumer spending and a steady run of inflation reports showing progress toward the Fed’s 2% target.”
Housing economists no longer expect mortgage rates to fall below 6% in the near future, and even a return below 7% seems a stretch. That reality that’s affecting home sales. Higher mortgage rates, still-record home prices and persistent inflation are likely to put the brakes on home sales. Instead, rates have risen sharply, a situation only exacerbated by the Fed’s Sept. 16 rate hike.

title: Patriots, Bears quarterbacks are no strangers to each other
text:
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — Caleb Williams and Drake Maye have known each other for years. They were part of the same draft class and grew up going to the same football camps.
Maye’s mobility, Williams said, always has been a weapon for him.
“We’ve got to be able to bottle him up,” he said.
Maye leads the New England Patriots into Soldier Field on Thursday night to take on Williams and the Chicago Bears in a matchup of two of the NFL’s top young quarterbacks. Both Maye and Williams have a big right arm and are also dangerous with their legs.
“I think Drake Maye’s one of those guys that does an outstanding job with his feet,” Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said. “There’s been times where you watch it and there’s pressure on the quarterback, and he makes people miss and creates some plays down the field.”
The 24-year-old Maye seems to have settled down after a rough start to the season. He has completed 64.1% of his passes for 878 yards and 10 touchdowns during New England’s three-game winning streak, throwing just one interception during the impressive stretch.
He could become the first Patriots quarterback since Tom Brady in 2014 to throw for at least three TDs in four consecutive games.
“It’s a dangerous combination of a guy that’s an elite deep-ball thrower along with he can crush you with his legs,” Bears coach Ben Johnson said. “I think that combination is deadly. It’s really picked up steam over these last three games.”
Maye was selected by New England with the No. 3 pick in 2024, two spots after Williams went No. 1 overall to Chicago.
Williams, who turns 25 on Nov. 18, missed three games because of a right hamstring injury before returning Sunday at Atlanta. He showed no signs of any rust, going 30 of 36 for 305 yards and a touchdown in a 31-23 victory over the Falcons.
“He’s special in the way he can move and kind of escape and evade pressure, and throwing on the run is pretty cool to watch,” Maye said. “So I don’t know if I’m that shifty in the pocket. He can do some cool things and he’s got crazy arm talent, and it’s fun to watch.”
Patriots safety Kevin Byard went up against Williams in practice during the previous two seasons with the Bears. He said Williams is an elite athlete who is tough to bring down in the pocket.
“I’ve been in this league long enough. I kind of know what the whole deal is gonna be,” Byard said. “Caleb versus Drake, obviously same draft class, two phenomenal quarterbacks. Drake’s been playing phenomenal, Caleb’s been playing phenomenal. So I think for us, it’s gonna be a 60-minute mental fight on both sides of the ball.”

title: ‘Poison Ivy’ Is the Next Batman Villain Getting a TV Show
text:
‘Poison Ivy’ TV Show In Development at HBO
It’s a great time to be a Batman villain.
Two years after The Penguin became an Emmy-winning HBO Max series, and the same week that Clayface gets to take center stage in his own big-screen movie, comes word that longtime DC villain Poison Ivy will now get her own TV series as well.
According to Variety, the series “is in the works at HBO with The Penguin showrunner Lauren LeFranc as a producer.”
READ MORE: DC Comics That Can Never Become DC Movies
Created by Carmine Infantino, Robert Kanigher, and Sheldon Moldoff in the 1960s, Poison Ivy (real name Pamela Isley) has used her ability to control and manipulate plants to serve as a perpetual thorn in the side of Batman for decades. (Thorn, ha.) While typically portrayed as an antagonist to Batman, she has evolved in recent years into more of an antihero, and has headlined her own monthly DC comic — something that can’t be said for characters like Penguin or Clayface.
On screen, Ivy has previously been played by Uma Thurman, who brought a decidedly over-the-top flavor to her performance in Joel Schumacher’s Batman & Robin opposite George Clooney and Chris O’Donnell.
One assumes the TV version of Poison Ivy will ... take a different approach to the material.
The character previously popped up on the live-action series Gotham and Batwoman, and in numerous Batman cartoons. In the ongoing Harley Quinn animated series on HBO Max, Ivy (voiced by Lake Bell) is the title character’s partner and best friend.
It’s not clear from Variety’s report whether this Poison Ivy series would be set within the primary DC Universe that houses films like Superman and Clayface, or whether, like The Penguin, it would be connected to Matt Reeves’ The Batman movie. The sequel to that film, The Batman Part II is currently in production and due in theaters in 2028. After Penguin, Clayface, and now Poison Ivy, who’s next? My money’s on Condiment King.

title: Feds release emergency heating oil to lower Maine prices; Collins, King claim win
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The federal government will release up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil into the Northeast, the Department of Energy announced Wednesday, using a rare measure to lower prices that continue to hover near record-highs.
The 1 million-barrel Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve has only been tapped twice before, most recently in the aftermath of Hurricane Sandy in 2012. Maine Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King wrote to President Donald Trump last month to ask for the release, saying heating costs were high enough to warrant emergency action.
Since this new heating oil supply won’t hit the Maine market until next month, it’s unclear how much it will impact prices, which currently sit at $5.97 per gallon in Maine on average. But Collins and King said it should offer some relief.
U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said that he had directed staff to begin the process of releasing the reserves, but added that it was a “temporary measure to solve a temporary supply disruption,” according to a joint news release from Collins and King on Wednesday.
Trump and his administration officials have long told the public that the U.S. and Israel’s war in Iran, which has constricted the crucial oil passageway of the Strait of Hormuz, would be quickly resolved.
Since February, when the conflict began, heating oil costs have gone up by 56% in Maine. Costs are up 77% over this time last year.
“Maine has been hit especially hard by the run up in fuel prices since the beginning of the Iran War and the most obvious example is home heating oil,” King said in the release. “Maine is one of the most dependent states in the country on home heating oil and the cost is absolutely through the roof. This release of stored oil in New England will hopefully be some help.”
Heating oil has become a campaign issue for Collins with just weeks until Election Day. Collins and her Democratic challenger, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, have blamed each other for high energy costs. Gubernatorial candidates have also called for more heating assistance.
The Department of Energy is using an “exchange” to release this heating oil — a process where oil companies bid on and receive at least 25,000 barrels of the strategic reserves, and then must return the entire portion they took, plus at least 5% extra, at a later date.
Companies must return heating oil to the federal government by April 2027 or face an additional premium that increases by 2.5% monthly, according to the Department of Energy’s request for bids. Those companies will pick up oil from one of three locations in New England next month; one of the locations is Sunoco’s tank site in South Portland.
This is the first time the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve has been utilized to lower heating oil prices, rather than to respond to a sudden supply-line disruption or natural disaster.
“The department anticipates this release will put downward pressure on home heating oil costs and make a real difference for Maine homeowners as they prepare for winter,” Collins said in the release.
Collins’ office said the 315,000 barrels would increase heating oil supply in New England by 13%, using Oct. 9 statistics from the U.S. Energy Information Agency. But heating oil reserve also covers New York, where about 1.7 million residents use heating oil, kerosene or propane during cold months.
With costs still near their record high, Maine’s federally supported heating assistance fund, the Home Energy Assistance Program, will likely not go as far as in past winters — even with an early release of those funds and a carryover from last year.
Maine, as the state most reliant on heating oil, stands to gain most from the early release of these heating assistance funds. About 45,000 people received the assistance last year, MaineHousing said.
Applications for heating assistance are open now. Maine residents hoping to apply for HEAP funding or looking for other assistance can contact their local community action program or call 211. The state also releases an annual Winter Heating Guide with cost-saving resources for households of all incomes.

title: InvestigateTV+: In-depth look at Hunter syndrome
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A rare genetic disorder is stealing time and basic skills from hundreds of boys nationwide. InvestigateTV+ takes an in-depth look at the disease and a groundbreaking treatment.
Plus, with obesity still surrounded by stigma, we examine the changing landscape of weight loss care and how access and insurance can impact outcomes.
Then we take a candy-coated detour on Route 66 to a Midwest shed packed wall to wall with M&M memorabilia.
A groundbreaking treatment
Nearly 10% of Americans live with a rare disease, and most of these conditions have no approved treatment options.
One of those conditions, Hunter syndrome, mostly affects boys and has had only one approved treatment since 2006. A new drug approved this year is offering families a different outlook.
The weight loss journey
Weight is a daily struggle for millions of Americans and for a lot of them it’s not just the health risks, it’s shame and setbacks.
More Americans are choosing weight loss injections over bariatric surgery, according to a new study. But some patients face a different reality when it comes to treatment options due to their insurance coverage.
Turning records into mixtapes
Since April 2008, music fans have marked Record Store Day, which highlights independent record stores and vinyl culture.
A Portland business is combining the vinyl resurgence with another personal music keepsake: the mixtape.
He built an M&M museum
It may not look very big on the outside, but once you step inside Beal’s M&M Museum in Waggoner you’ll be treated to different flavors of iconic memorabilia.
The museum houses more than 5,000 M&M items displayed from wall to wall and floor to ceiling.

title: Letter to the Editor: Why Franklin County is considering an appointed treasurer
Rockland strangling suspect violated bail 1 day after release from jail, police say
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — A Thomaston man was arrested a second time within 48 hours after police said he contacted the victim he had earlier been accused of strangling during a domestic assault.
Samuel N. Atwood, 58, of Thomaston, was arrested by Rockland police on Oct. 20 and charged with violating a condition of release. He is being held without bail until at least his initial appearance scheduled for Oct. 22.
He had been released on $750 bail after appearing in court via Zoom on charges of felony domestic violence aggravated assault, and a misdemeanor charge of domestic violence criminal threatening.
An affidavit filed with the court by Rockland Police for the original charges stated it responded Oct. 18 to a reported domestic dispute on Chestnut Street in Rockland. The woman said Atwood pushed her down on a bed, put one of his hands around her neck and the other over her mouth and nose. She struck her head on the bottom of the window sill when she was forced down, according to the affidavit.
The woman said while she was struggling to breathe, he told her he was going to kill her.
A witness reported hearing their arguments but this time it was more intense and the witness heard the woman saying “Sam no, Sam don’t, and Sam stop.” The witness said he also heard a loud thud shortly before police were called to the scene.
Atwood denied the dispute was ever physical.
