title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Glenn Chadbourne’s cartoon this week likely sums up all of our feelings regarding the upcoming election. Regardless of where you fall on the political spectrum, you’re likely sick of the ads about the mid-term elections, especially if you already cast your ballot.
Thankfully, there are only two weeks left until Election Day, and you best believe we’re counting down the days.
This cycle has been a bit of a mixed bag, admittedly. Unfortunately, we were unable to organize local forums this year due to staffing and internal scheduling challenges. We plan to bring them back for the 2028 election, however, we’re going to give ourselves a few months before we start thinking about that.
With the exception of only a few truly negative interactions, letter writers stayed within the bounds of our guidelines. Only a few letters without an implicitly stated local connection didn’t make it into the paper, an outcome we mention is possible in the guidelines.
This is the final edition for the general public to submit letters about candidates or ballot measures under consideration on Nov. 3.
Candidates for office will have the opportunity in the Oct. 29 edition to respond to a letter or article in the LCN in order to clarify or correct information about their candidacy. They may also respond to attack ads such as mailers or ads or information transmitted through online platforms, in order to clarify or correct information about their candidacy.
This week also marks the final candidate profiles of the year, with all of our uncontested county candidates featured on either page 1 or page 1A. All of our previous interviews are available at lcnme.com to read.
Next week, our reporters will have articles previewing local ballot measures, such as the Twin Villages’ consideration of an interlocal public works agreement, Edgecomb’s proposal to allow the sale of liquor for off-premise consumption, and Wiscasset, which has half a dozen items for residents to weigh in on, including a data center moratorium.
As elections come to a close and decisions are made final, remember that even if it doesn’t go your way, voting plays a positive role in a participatory democracy. Whoever or whatever you feel passionate about, remember the only way to ensure your voice is heard is by casting your ballot.

title: Maine farmers and fishermen can get federal assistance to offset high fuel prices
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine farmers and fishermen can now get federal assistance to offset rising diesel prices.
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins said Tuesday that farmers and fishermen are eligible for assistance under the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s $8 billion “Harvest Fuel Relief” program.
Under that new program, farmers and fishermen can get a one-time payment to offset those higher production costs. Rates will be announced in November.
“The rising cost of fuel and other inputs has placed significant financial strain on hardworking farmers, fishermen, lobstermen, and their families. After speaking with both the White House and Secretary Rollins, I am pleased to have been assured that Maine fishermen and lobstermen will benefit from the Administration’s new agricultural relief package,” Collins said in a statement. “I will continue advocating for Maine’s fishermen, lobstermen, and specialty crop growers, who are integral to our state’s heritage, economy, and way of life, to ensure they receive the support they need to overcome these challenges.”
Energy costs have spiked since President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began a war against Iran, which effectively choked off shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas flow.
As of Wednesday, the price for a gallon of diesel in Maine is $6.43, up 66% from a year ago, when it cost $3.86, according to AAA. Farmers and fishermen rely on diesel to power tractors, boats and other equipment, which can drive up the cost of food at the grocery store.
Lobstermen have already been battered by tough economic conditions. Inflation, trade uncertainty and a late molt chipped away at the value of last year’s catch, which was in reality closer to the value of 2008’s, the Maine Department of Marine Resources said in March.
This is just the latest move from the Trump administration to tamp down on growing unease about rising energy costs ahead of the midterm elections.
On Wednesday, the Trump administration said it would release about 315,000 barrels, or 13.2 million gallons, of heating oil from the Northeast reserves as costs stand near record highs. Maine is very vulnerable to price spikes because more than half of households here — more than 300,000 — rely on heating oil to stay warm during the winter. But with daily consumption during the winter averaging between 2 to 7 gallons a day, that supply injection would equal only about nine days of consumption for Maine alone.
Earlier this month, the Trump administration released about $37 million in low-income heating assistance for Maine. An additional $1.4 million was awarded to the state’s four federally recognized tribes.
Other developments across the globe could further strain energy supply chains. The ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine also has strained global fuel supplies as both sides trade blows on each other’s energy infrastructure despite Trump’s push for an “energy ceasefire” as he moves ahead with plans to import Russian diesel. And elsewhere in the Middle East, Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen have been launching attacks on Saudi energy sites and in September seized territory along a key trade route off the Red Sea.
Fishermen and farmers can submit information about their increased fuel costs to HarvestFuel@usda.gov to help inform payment rates under the program, according to the USDA.

title: Obituary: Mrs. Leon A. Huard (Glenda Lou Rowell)
text:
TYLER, Texas – Mrs. Leon A. Huard (Glenda Lou Rowell), 88, died Oct. 15, 2026, at Tyler, Texas.
She was born on Dec. 28, 1937, at the home where she grew up, 284 Madison Ave, Skowhegan, Maine. She was the only child of Howard and Helen (Hafey) Rowell. Both parents were deceased in 1973 and 1989, respectively.
Mrs. Huard graduated Cum Laude from Skowhegan High School, class of 1955, where she was active in all music activities. She played the violin and clarinet in the orchestra and band and sang soprano in the chorus. She was selected to participate in the Kennebec Valley and Allstate orchestras, playing the violin. At graduation she received the Dora T. Nye Music Award.
In 1954, Glenda Lou was a delegate to Dirigo Girl’s State at Colby College. She received musical honors for having written the words to a song about Girl’s State.
For many years Mrs. Huard was a Sunday School teacher and choir member at Bethany Baptist Church in Skowhegan. She was a born-again Christian, and was baptized at Bethany Baptist Church, Easter Sunday evening, 1955.
Glenda Lou was pianist and youth leader for the BYF at the church, and treasurer for the North Kennebec Valley Baptist Youth Fellowship. She was a frequent pianist at the Fairfield Nazarene Church before moving to Texas in 1980.
Mrs. Huard attended Bob Jones University in Greenville, SC. She returned to graduate in 1959 from Farmington State Teachers College with a B.S. degree in Elementary-Jr. High Education.
For many years Mrs. Huard taught in the elementary schools in Central Maine in Augusta and Orono. She took a position as Title 1 Reading and Math Coordinator in S.A.D. #13, Bingham.
In June 1980, Glenda moved to Houston, Texas, where she continued her studies and became a diagnostician and mentor in reading in several Texas schools. She taught in Houston, Pearland, Ft. Worth, and experienced teaching on the Mexican border.
Her last teaching position was at a private school in 2007-2008 at Nassau Bay, adjacent to NASA.
Mrs. Huard maintained memberships in NEA (National Education Association), TSTA (Texas State Teachers Association), Maine Teachers Association, IRA (International Reading Association).
Mrs. Huard is survived by her long-time friend from childhood, her husband, Leon Huard. She has four surviving children from her first marriage to John R. Hamlin. John Howard Hamlin (Kathy) of Palmyra, Maine, Bethany Anne Carver (Dana) of Patten Maine, Rebecca Lynn Swearingen (Jim) of Tyler, Texas, David Rowell Hamlin (Kristen) of Lewiston, Maine. She is also survived by a cousin, Farrilyn Chase of Kingsfield, Maine.
Mrs. Huard has been blessed with several grandchildren as well as great-grandchildren.
Visitation will be from 12 to 1 p.m. at Autry Funeral Home in Jacksonville, Texas. Burial will be following visitation at Mt. Comfort Cemetery in Maydelle, Texas with Pastor Paul Smith officiating.
Pallbearers will be John Hamlin, Jim Swearingen, Douglas Mullins, Jimmy Mullins, Harley Swearingen, and Travis Posey.
Honorary pallbearers will be David Hamlin, Matthew Williamson, John Luke Swearingen, Jonathan Sherrill, Brett Foreman, Scott Rogers, Eli Mullins, Ryan Williamson, Brittan McCloy, Dylan Mullins, Cooper Williamson, Bill Cook, and Lance Cook.

title: NBA champion Knicks celebrate 2 titles on a banner night in Madison Square Garden
text:
NBA champion Knicks celebrate 2 titles on a banner night in Madison Square Garden
The NBA championship banner kept rising high above everyone on the court, just like OG Anunoby did last time the New York Knicks played a meaningful game at Madison Square Garden.
And just like that night four months ago, it felt as if fans would never stop cheering.
The Knicks celebrated their championship Tuesday with a banner night — two of them — before hosting the Philadelphia 76ers in their season opener.
Wearing white uniforms with gold trim for the occasion, the Knicks received their NBA championship rings from Hall of Famer Walt Frazier and then watched as the blue banner reading "2025-26 World Champions" rose to the rafters.
Outside of their preseason exhibition games, it was the first time the Knicks played at home since Game 4 of the NBA Finals, when Anunoby's tip-in with 1.2 seconds remaining capped off a record-setting comeback from a 29-point deficit. The highlight of the play during a montage that played on the overhead videoboard set off some of the loudest roars of the night.
Jalen Brunson began his remarks to fans Tuesday by referencing that game, thanking them for not leaving the arena early.
The Knicks finished off the San Antonio Spurs in the next game, setting off "Knicks in 5! Knicks in 5!" chants around New York that resumed Tuesday night.
Brunson told fans that the Knicks were seeking to turn the page after the team's first championship since 1973.
"But one thing I would like to say," he added. "The joy that this city had this summer, we would love to replicate that again."
Before raising the title banner, the NBA champions hung one at Madison Square Garden to celebrate the NBA Cup title they won last season.
The Knicks broke with tradition last December when they became the first team to win the in-season tournament and then not commemorate it with a banner. They said at the time they were looking ahead to bigger things.
They ended up getting the biggest thing possible in the rematch with the Spurs. The Knicks also defeated San Antonio in the NBA Cup final.
The NBA Cup banner went up sometime after the Sixers held their morning shootaround at the arena.
"I haven't seen it, but I think it's just a recognition of what our journey was like last year, you know?" coach Mike Brown said. "There were a lot of, obviously, ups and downs throughout the course of the year, and our guys rallied and figured out a way to win the NBA Cup, and then you go ahead and win the regular season final, or excuse me, the end of season final, and it's just a recognition to not just to our guys, but to the fans out there."
The two banners were the first hung at Madison Square Garden by the Knicks since they won the Atlantic Division title in 2012-13.

title: True Friends Hall restoration aims to save Louisiana music landmark
text:
DONALDSONVILLE, La. (Aging Untold)— A historic hall that once provided refuge for Black families and performers during segregation is getting new life through a major restoration project.
True Friends Hall, built in the late 1800s in Donaldsonville, served as a cornerstone of the local Black community for decades. The benevolent society that operated the hall helped families in need and provided a gathering place during an era when Black Americans faced widespread discrimination.
“These organizations supported families. If you had a baby, the house burned down, they would come to the aid. These are men who were carpenters, brickmasons,” Darryl Hambrick, founder of the River Road African American Museum, said.
Musical heritage and the Chitlin’ Circuit
During segregation, True Friends Hall was part of the Chitlin’ Circuit, a network of performance venues across the United States for Black musicians, comedians and other entertainers. The circuit helped shape American music by creating new genres such as blues, jazz and rock and roll, producing artists such as Aretha Franklin, B.B. King and Little Richard.
The hall welcomed major performers including New Orleans legends Fats Domino and Irma Thomas, as well as megastars like James Brown. Because African Americans were not allowed at certain venues, True Friends Hall served as a welcoming refuge for Black performers.
“Making their way into New Orleans, you couldn’t stay in hotels, restaurants. Here at True Friends, you got a meal, you got a place to stay, and you had a great time,” Hambrick said.
Community gathering place
Beyond music, True Friends Hall was where Black families and friends could gather and celebrate.
“This was the pulse of the community. You could come here and get help, you could come here and have a great time,” Hambrick said.
Restoration plans
The hall closed in the 1980s and deteriorated over the years. After receiving $1.3 million from the state of Louisiana, Hambrick and the River Road African American Museum are working on a major restoration project.
Plans call for a performance stage, offices and space for a music academy.
The project needs additional funding beyond the state allocation.
Hambrick expects the restoration timeline to be much shorter than the 26 years it took to establish the museum, which involved moving and restoring a Rosenwald school.
“I hope it doesn’t take 26 years to do this building because I don’t have 26 years,” he said.
True Friends Hall is believed to be the largest and oldest existing benevolent hall still standing in Louisiana.

title: China select board reviews recommendations from CESAC
text:
China select board members spent most of their Oct. 19 meeting reviewing recommendations from the China Emergency Services Assessment Committee (CESAC), with consultant Paul Froman and more than half the committee members present.
Before and after that discussion, they approved paying almost $1.7 million in bills (the Kennebec County tax was $861,230, and public works expenditures included paving and part of the cost of the new town truck); postponed action on one expenditure request; and approved a second.
As discussed at their Oct. 5 meeting (see the Oct. 15 issue of The Town Line, p. 2) board members had a price from LaRochelle Consulting, of Augusta, to assist in preparing a revised Tax Increment Financing (TIF) plan. Raegan LaRochelle asked for $15,500, planning to take about nine weeks for the work.
Town Manager Rebecca Hapgood said she had sent LaRochelle several questions. Board members postponed action for more information.
The second proposed expenditure was from contractor and select board member Blane Casey, to replace the handicapped access ramp at the portable building behind the town office. He asked for $16,294 to provide and install a second-hand aluminum ramp, which meets requirements of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).
Board members approved the ramp on a 4-0 vote. Casey removed himself physically from the board during discussion and voting, answering questions from the audience.
Hapgood asked if the new ramp would be installed by Nov. 3, election day, a little over two weeks away. Amid laughter, Casey replied, “Possibly.”
Froman presented the seven recommendations agreed upon by CESAC members, by consensus (see the Oct. 1 issue of The Town Line, p. 3). Select board members thanked committee members for their service.
They did not object to the recommendation that CESAC become a permanent town committee. Present members’ terms run to June 30, 2027, Hapgood said.
One CESAC recommendation is that the three volunteer fire departments remain separate entities; another is that China Rescue become a town department. Much of the discussion was over complications of intermingling town financing and private organizations, and various ways to simplify issues like insurance and liability.
Select board members agreed by consensus to ask Froman to continue as a consultant, developing a proposal for moving toward a town rescue unit.
Preparations for the Nov. 3 election were also on the select board agenda; board members approved election officials. China’s polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., Tuesday, Nov. 3, in the portable building. Early voting ends Thursday, Oct. 29.
The town office will be closed election day, because staff will be working next door. The next holiday closing is Wednesday, Nov. 11, for Veterans Day; all town departments will be closed.
Select board members have three regular November meetings, at 6 p.m. Monday, Nov. 2; Monday, Nov. 16; and Monday, Nov. 30.

title: How do previous Trump voters feel about Republicans heading into the midterm elections?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How do previous Trump voters feel about Republicans heading into the midterm elections?
Voters in Virginia Beach, a key midterm district, express concerns about inflation, foreign conflicts and local representation, with some reflecting on President Donald Trump’s impact.
How do previous Trump voters feel about Republicans heading into the midterm elections?
Voters in Virginia Beach, a key midterm district, express concerns about inflation, foreign conflicts and local representation, with some reflecting on President Donald Trump’s impact.
Some voters in Virginia Beach, a pivotal district in the upcoming midterms, say President Donald Trump’s influence may play a role in their decisions at the polls.
Southeastern Virginia, with a significant military presence and a mix of rural and coastal communities, is home to one of the most competitive districts. In 2024, Trump won this district by a razor-thin margin. The Virginia Beach area, part of the state's 2nd Congressional District, is represented by a Republican.
The University of Virginia's Center for Politics predicts it's leaning Democratic this year.
For Thea, a retired teacher in Virginia who supported Trump in the past, affordability is a pressing issue.
"I spent $50 a week on groceries, and that doesn't get much," Thea said. "Rent is going up. Inflation's going up. ... You can't even buy a pack of underwear for $2.50."
A September Associated Press poll finds that 69% of people believe Trump's handling of the cost of living is worse than expected, including 52% of Republicans.
Last month, at the RNC's midterm convention in Dallas, Trump made a plea to voters to help Republicans regain control of both chambers.
"You've got to do this for me. You've got to pretend I'm on the ticket. I'm on the ticket," Trump said.
Despite his plea, Director of UVA's Center for Politics Larry Sabato said this could hurt the GOP's chances.
"A good deal of the Democratic vote is being generated by opposition to President Trump and opposition to his policies, especially high gas prices, high diesel prices," Sabato said.
A new NPR poll found that 45% of voters say their choice for Congress will be a vote against the president, compared to 24% who call it mostly a vote for Trump.
Another issue potentially swaying voters is the war in Iran.
"I did support him, actually, I did, but, you know, it's kind of looking like, did I make a mistake?" said Anthony Brown, a Virginia voter. "Depending how the war goes ... and just the little answers that he does, you know what I mean, that might affect November."
Other GOP voters are looking to stick with their party.
"I'll vote individually in the midterms because he's not on the ballot for sure, but I am a Republican and will probably go that way," Earl, a Virginia Beach voter, said.
Experts, like political analyst Todd Belt, say these hesitations are worrying some Republicans.
"Donald Trump's popularity is still going down as public approval numbers are really cratering, and that's a real problem for him and his party," Belt said. "Political science shows that it's because the president himself isn't doing well, presidential popularity declines over time during a president's term, and because of that, it pulls down his party."
Not all voters, however, are focused on Trump’s influence.
"I'm more concerned about our local electives. They're the ones who are going to make, you know, the changes for us," said Juan Jorge, a small business owner in Virginia.
Some are prioritizing candidates over party loyalty.
"Typically, I am Republican, but I'm not a die-hard, have-to-vote-Republican," said Rhonda Nichols, a voter from Kentucky.
Her husband, Stuart Nichols, shared a similar perspective.
"It really just comes down to the candidates and stuff and who appeals to us the most, so I don't have a problem voting either side," he said.
Keep watching for the latest from the Washington News Bureau:

title: UMaine shares plan to bring budget deficit down to $3M
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The University of Maine on Wednesday shared a pathway to bring next year’s budget deficit down to roughly $3 million, taking the step about a month after it announced plans to cut the original $19 million gap in half.
The university announced in September a plan to cut about $10 million off its shortfall, including layoffs to faculty and staff, consolidating some courses and decreasing instructional budgets.
A letter shared Wednesday, signed by UMaine administrators, comes with a plan to make up for another $6 million, which would reduce the shortfall to about $3 million.
The letter says the university plans to cut spending and increase revenue through non-academic means. Among other cuts, it states that “workforce reductions will unfortunately be necessary to more closely align the university’s expenses with revenue on an ongoing and permanent basis.”
The plan also includes relying less on external vendors, utilizing reserve funds, and centralizing some functions, such as research centers and institutes.
It also calls for the elimination of vacant positions from athletics, student life and the president’s office. The plan includes an expected $1 million increase in base revenue beginning in fiscal year 2028.
“Assuming these targets are met, the remaining $3M gap will present a challenge and closing this will be the Cabinet’s main focus over the coming weeks,” the letter states.
Last month, university administrators said UMaine’s operating costs have risen faster than state funding or tuition revenue and that federal changes have impacted research funding and financial aid.
The university will present its budget proposal for the next fiscal year to the board of trustees in January.

title: Driver is fatally shot while crossing the George Washington Bridge
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A 46-year-old man was shot and killed while driving across the George Washington Bridge near the end of the evening rush, snarling traffic for hours on the busy span that connects New York City and New Jersey.
Authorities said that while responding to calls about the shooting on the New Jersey-bound side of the bridge’s upper level just after 7 p.m. Tuesday, they found the man unconscious with a gunshot wound in the driver’s seat of a vehicle.
The man, identified as Koran Irvine of Valley Cottage, New York, was later pronounced dead at a nearby hospital. No arrests have been made, and authorities haven’t given a possible motive for the shooting.
The victim worked for Con Edison, the utility said in a statement, calling the shooting a “senseless act of violence.”
“Our deepest condolences go out to his family, friends, colleagues, and everyone who knew and loved him,” the company said.
Closed lanes reopened about five hours after the shooting, said the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which operates the bridge.
Opened to traffic in 1931, the iconic, double-decked bridge spans high over the Hudson River, carrying around 100 million vehicles between New Jersey and Manhattan each year, according to the Port Authority, which calls it the world’s busiest. The bridge and its entrances are teeming with cameras.
Its entrances can be difficult to navigate, as drivers often veer across packed lanes, causing heavy traffic even under normal circumstances.

title: Bonny Eagle-Thornton game highlights this week’s football storylines
text:
The two best high school football teams in Maine go head-to-head this week with identical 7-0 records.
That’s right, it’s time for the annual regular-season showdown that so often gives fans a preview of the Class A South final.
Thornton Academy hosts Bonny Eagle at 1 p.m. Saturday at Hill Stadium in Saco. Both teams have been dominant. Both have star players producing at high levels.
The big question is: Can Bonny Eagle get its first win against Thornton since the Class A championship game in 2019? Thornton has won six straight in the series, including twice last season when the Connor Ayoob-powered Golden Trojans won the regular-season game in Standish and then the regional final in Saco, wearing down the Scots in the second half in both games.
Thornton’s unparalleled depth is again an advantage, but this year’s Bonny Eagle team seems to be built just a bit differently. Also, first-year starting quarterback Lucas Klehn is playing at such a high level that he has emerged as the front-runner for player of the year honors.
Playing behind a big offensive line, Klehn has rushed for 870 yards and 23 touchdowns on 110 carries while completing 68% of his passes (46 of 67, 789 yards), with seven TD passes and zero interceptions. He has real playmakers to help him out in running backs Ben Noe (58 carries, 466 yards) and Ben Havu (31 carries, 291 yards) and receiver Drew Gervais (25 receptions, 428 yards, 3 TDs). Havu is Bonny Eagle’s top tackler, and Klehn is a hard hitter from the secondary.
For Thornton, the big change this season is a dynamic passing game. Second-year starter Noah Fullerton isn’t throwing a lot, but he’s completing 70% of his attempts (42 of 60, 772 yards), with 16 touchdowns and three interceptions. Logan LeBlanc (18 receptions, 454 yards) is the big-play target, with nine touchdown catches. In recent weeks, Brennan Tabor (69 carries, 634 yards, 13 TDs) has emerged as the top rusher, with help from Josiah Blain (57 carries, 371 yards). Tabor and Blain are the defensive leaders at inside linebacker, with 42 and 43 solo tackles, respectively.
JUST HOW GOOD IS LEAVITT?
That question was posed to Hornets coach Mike Hathaway when he was watching host Greely (6-1) beat Hermon (6-1) last week. Those are the two teams closest to Leavitt (7-0) in the Class C standings. Leavitt has beaten Greely and is at Hermon on Friday.
Hathaway said his squad isn’t at the level of the historic 2023 team that went 11-0 and beat Class A contender Oxford Hills, eventual Class A champion Thornton (on the road), and Class B runner-up Lawrence.
But he did put this year’s squad in the very good category, citing the high number of returners and a very deep and talented skill group as key strengths. The defense has also been quite good, allowing only 39 points.
BIDDEFORD IS BACK
Class A and Class C teams have one more game after this week before the playoffs. For the rest of Maine’s teams, this weekend will determine playoff seeding.
Biddeford is trying to follow up on the season’s biggest upset to date, a 37-14 win at previously unbeaten Marshwood in which the Tigers recovered from a 14-0 deficit.
Biddeford (5-2) can secure a bye to the regional semifinals if it beats Cheverus (2-5) on Friday at Waterhouse Field. That result would also end the Stags’ season.
“Our team is maturing, and as they’re maturing, they’re understanding the game better and getting better,” said Steve Allosso, now in his fifth season as Biddeford’s head coach.
Estevao Lembissa, a junior slot back who lines up all over the field, has emerged as a big-time playmaker. He had a 71-yard touchdown reception and a 49-yard rushing TD in the second half against Marshwood.
“He’s fast. He’s quick. He’s tough. And he has super character,” Allosso said. “One of the best I’ve ever coached, and this team is overflowing with character.”
Quarterback Ernest Dore and left guard Caiden Howe are top seniors. Juniors Stanley Richerson (RB/DE) and Alex Gosselin (WR/OLB) give the offense added options. Junior linebacker Marcus Perkins is becoming a force.
Despite their record, the much-improved Tigers have struggled to put together consecutive strong efforts, something Allosso said is a point of emphasis this week. The Marshwood win followed a 37-6 loss at Skowhegan.
KENNEBUNK AT MARSHWOOD
Kennebunk vs. Marshwood is Class B South’s version of Bonny Eagle-Thornton. Both teams are 6-1 and tied for first place in the Crabtree standings. The winner gets the No. 1 playoff seed. The loser would slip to No. 3 and miss out on a first-round bye if Biddeford wins.
Marshwood is dinged up. Fullback Greg Castoras was hurt late in the Biddeford game and is “day-to-day,” said Marshwood coach Andrew Elwell. The Hawks have been without their top halfback, Noah Goodwin, for the past two games. Goodwin is questionable for Friday’s game.

title: Feeding tubes aren’t a magic fix — what families need to know
text:
(Aging Untold) — Eating is about more than nutrition — it’s connection, routine, and dignity. When someone loses the ability to eat normally, families can be thrust into difficult decisions about feeding tubes, comfort and what comes next.
“It’s a bridge, not a magical answer”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, says the first thing families need to understand is what a feeding tube is actually for.
“The feeding tube is really just a bridge. It’s a bridge to give nutrients, medication, fluids when a person temporarily cannot feed themselves,” Rogers said. “I would look at it as a temporary thing depending on what their condition is.”
She explained that patients end up needing a feeding tube for many different reasons.
“Some people have had a stroke. They have difficulty swallowing. Sometimes they have neurological disorders or things like that, or head and neck cancers,” Rogers said.
Ask about the goal before you ask about the tube
Rogers said the real decision isn’t just whether to place a feeding tube — it’s understanding what the family is hoping it will accomplish.
“I think the family needs to understand what are their expectations from this, the route that you’re feeding, and what is the goal,” Rogers said. “Is this temporary ‘til somebody gets healthy, or do they have a disease that’s progressing and they’re not going to get back to a baseline level?”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck was direct about the limits of what a feeding tube can do.
“You need to understand, this is a medical option, not a magical answer,” Cradduck said. “It’s not going to cause you to learn how to swallow again. It’s not going to change the damage that cancer may have done to your throat.”
What caregivers need to watch for
Cradduck also laid out practical warnings for families caring for a loved one with a feeding tube at home.
“There are things that you have to look for. That insertion site can get infected very easy,” Cradduck said. “And if that tube pops out — and I’ve seen this happen even with caregivers — it’s got to be put back in, and you’d be shocked at how quickly that’ll heal and the tissue will cover.”
Her advice: Don’t wait.
“That becomes an emergent — we’ve got to get that back in. Don’t wait and see, or wait until somebody gets home, or wait until the next day, because then you’re having to have a procedure again,” Cradduck said.
A personal story changed one expert’s view
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, shared how watching her own family changed her perspective on feeding tubes.
“I had my whole view of feeding tubes change, watching my father-in-law. He had a feeding tube for seven years. My mother-in-law cooked three meals a day, pureed the food and fed him,” O’Rourke said. “They went on cruises. They danced. He became a special cook. We went out to fabulous restaurants. You forgot he had a feeding tube.”
O’Rourke said her earlier, more negative view came from her professional background.
She said having worked in an industry where people needed to gain weight, they would put feeding tubes in, and then the families wouldn’t know enough to have the conversation to take them out.
“So I saw a lot of people bedridden,” O’Rourke said. “It seemed to perpetuate a vegetative state rather than a living state.”
Rogers compared that misconception to how many people initially react to the word “hospice.”
“It’s the same impression people have when they hear hospice — they see it in a negative state, but not all the things that it encompasses. The same thing would be the feeding tube, because it can be just that bridge and be temporary,” Rogers said.
Ambrose said families should start the conversation early — and keep it open.
“It’s an important conversation to start talking about, and have a plan,” Ambrose said. “And by the way, you have the prerogative to always change your mind. It’s a good thing to be familiar with and kind of know what you think.”
Key takeaways
- A feeding tube can be a bridge to healing, not a magical cure.
- Know the goal before you decide. Families should clarify whether the tube is meant to support recovery to a baseline or to manage a progressing illness.
- Watch the insertion site closely. Infections can develop quickly, and a dislodged tube needs to be reinserted right away — don’t wait.
- A feeding tube doesn’t mean life stops. As O’Rourke’s family experience shows, life with a feeding tube can still include shared meals, travel and normal routines.
- Talk about it before you need to. Discuss expectations and a removal plan before insertion, and remember you can always revisit the decision.

title: He built an M&M museum and keeps adding to the collection
text:
WAGGONER, Ill. (InvestigateTV) - It may not look very big on the outside, but once you step inside Beal’s M&M Museum in Waggoner you’ll be treated to different flavors of iconic memorabilia.
The museum houses more than 5,000 M&M items displayed from wall to wall and floor to ceiling.
Steve and Patricia Beale started the collection with California Raisins. When Steve Beale could not find them anymore, he switched to M&Ms.
The collection was kept in a bedroom in their house. When they could not open the door anymore, they decided to build a space to display it.
The couple built a 20-by-30-foot shed and kept adding to the collection. None of the items are for sale.
“Once you start selling, then you’re not a collector,” Steve told us, “you’re in it for the money.”
The museum is free to visit. Steve Beale said he likes to share what he has and what he knows.
The museum has had visitors from around the world. The Beales give visitors a fun-size bag of M&Ms, and the museum has become a stop on historic Route 66.
Steve Beale said his favorite kind of M&Ms is peanut. Patricia Beale said her favorite is peanut butter.

title: ‘Clayface’ Review: DC’s Villain With a Heart of Schmutz
text:
‘Clayface’ Review: An Antihero With a Heart of Schmutz
In all ways, Clayface is a shapeshifter. At least eight different men and women have used that monicker in the pages of DC Comics; every decade or two a new person decides “Hey! I wanna be Clayface now!” and they annoy Batman for a couple of issues with a cosmically ironic ability to morph their bodies and look like other people — at the cost of their souls.
In 2026, DC Studios called upon Clayface to change shapes yet again: Into the antihero of the company’s first out-and-out horror movie. Their Clayface is a surprisingly graphic creature feature, one that owes as much of its tone and style to classic Universal monster movies as to the comics where the character first originated.
The film’s Clayface — who’s technically smooshed together from multiple versions of the character from comics and cartoons — is an up-and-coming actor named Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries). Matt’s got it all; a burgeoning Hollywood career, his first Oscar nomination, and best of all, a truly magnificent face. With his chiseled cheekbones, sharp jaw, and piercing blue eyes, the dude looks like a star.
READ MORE: Every DC Comics Movie, Ranked From Worst to Best
Or he did look like a star until he pissed off Gotham City mobster Markos Szabo (David Dencik), who retaliates by slashing the actor’s face into a million pieces — slowly and graphically on camera. The unsuccessful reconstructive surgeries that follow are equally gnarly. (Who knew noses looked like that on the inside? I sure didn’t!) And generally Clayface is way gnarlier and nastier than you anticipate from a film about a mid-tier Batman villain. It will almost certainly satisfy gorehounds looking for explicit thrills at the multiplex this Halloween season.
Matt tries to sue Szabo, but the mob controls the Gotham City legal system. (Where’s a costumed vigilante who turns himself into a bat to make his enemies share his dread when you need him?) With his looks, finances, and prospects all destroyed, a desperate Matt turns to a daring scientist, Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), who has invented a “nanocell” powered by artificial intelligence that can regenerate dead human tissues. Surely this unapproved therapy powered by unchecked AI will work exactly as planned!
Matt wants his life back and begs Caitlyn to become her first human test case. Moved by Matt’s story (or possibly swayed by his impressive acting skills) she eventually acquiesces. The initial nanocell infusions look promising, until some unforeseen side effects begin to crop up. (“Side effects,” Matt’s face melting off his skull like he’s in a Salvador Dali painting, same difference.) Frustrated by the pace of his recovery, and enraged that Szabo and his cronies destroyed his life with zero consequences, Matt takes matters into his own hands and injects himself with all of Caitlyn’s nanocells. This, as you might suspect, turns him into a bit of a, well, let’s call him a bit of a Clayface.
Like many of cinema history’s best monsters, Matt Hagen is a pitiful but terrifying creature, one driven by a fatal flaw and cursed with incredible powers that warp his mind and transform him into a gruesome beast. Visually, Clayface pulls very few punches. Director James Watkins does an admirably grotesque job of depicting Matt’s gloppy descent into DC supervillaindom.
When Matt’s eyelids begin to fuse shut on a cross-country flight, for example, Watkins and cinematographer Rob Hardy get right up in Rhys Harries’ handsome mug as he tries to tear apart the fleshy strands covering his eyes with his bare hands. Then they creep even closer when he begins snipping away at his (clay)face with a pair of grooming scissors. The gags only get more repulsive from there. (Complimentary.)
Rhys Harries very much looks the part of a young Hollywood hunk, and he throws himself into Matt’s disgusting transformations. But for reasons I can’t quite understand (maybe an effort to make Matt a little more sympathetic?) Clayface’s screenplay by Mike Flanagan and Hossein Amini gives the character a backstory as a downtrodden street kid from the wrong side of the tracks in Gotham City, whose incredible gift for chameleonic performances extends to his construction of his entire movie-star persona.
That choice to make Matt this brooding blue-collar palooka doesn’t really match Rhys Harries’ physicality or his temperament, and every time the movie asks us to buy this boyish heartthrob as an uncouth galoot it stretches credulity further than the skin on Matt’s face when he gets agitated. (Max Minghella is far more convincing as Caitlyn’s supportive boyfriend, the only honest cop in the Gotham City Police Department.)
I can’t say I got particularly caught up in Matt Hagen’s fall from grace, or the muddy characterization of his subsequent quest for stretchy-skinned revenge. Still, I did enjoy spending time in the seedy, sleazy world of Gotham City, and in basking in Watkins and Flanagan’s dryly sadistic vibes.
Let’s not mince words: Clayface is a pretty gross dude. He’s a walking pile of muck. If you’re gonna make a movie about him, it better make audiences squirm. As a tragic character study of a broken man, Clayface never really digs below the surface. As an amusingly icky horror movie, it actually does get under your skin.
Additional Thoughts:
-Strange but true: The new DC Universe does not have a Batman, but it does have a Clayface. Weird!
RATING: 6/10

title: Maine Veterans’ Homes’ Baker receives National Leader of the Year Award
text:
Donna Baker, director of quality, risk and compliance at Maine Veterans’ Homes, received the 2026 American Health Care Association Leader of the Year Award at the AHCA/NCAL Convention & Expo in Boston.
Presented to one individual nationwide each year, the award recognizes outstanding leadership in long-term care. It is part of the American Health Care Association and National Center for Assisted Living’s Provider Achieving Care Excellence Awards Program.
A registered nurse with more than 33 years of experience, Baker has devoted more than 20 years to Maine Veterans’ Homes. She provides leadership in quality improvement, risk management and regulatory compliance across the organization’s six homes, helping teams strengthen care while protecting residents’ dignity, safety and quality of life.
“Donna’s influence touches each of our six Homes,” Brad Klawitter, CEO of Maine Veterans’ Homes, said. “She helps our teams navigate difficult challenges while prioritizing the needs of our Veterans and their families. She also takes time to listen, teach and support the people around her. We are proud to see her dedication and expertise recognized on a national stage.”
Baker’s leadership has supported initiatives to prevent falls and pressure injuries, reduce avoidable hospitalizations and decrease the use of psychotropic medications when appropriate. She brings staff from nursing, therapy, dietary, social services and other departments together to improve care, helping employees understand both the practices being introduced and why they matter to residents.
Her work has also contributed to three MVH Homes earning the AHCA/NCAL Gold Quality Award, which recognizes sustained excellence in quality and organizational performance.
“It is an honor to receive this award, and I’m grateful to work with people who are exceptional at what they do and so driven by our mission,” Baker said. “Improving care takes everyone, and I see that commitment in our homes every day.”
Baker is a familiar presence throughout the homes. Alongside her clinical and regulatory responsibilities, she attends resident celebrations, speaks with families, recognizes employee achievements and mentors nursing leaders. Her award nomination highlighted her approachability and her commitment to ensuring residents feel known and staff feel supported.
Baker began her MVH career in 2006 at the Augusta home, serving as staff development coordinator and then director of nursing before moving into a systemwide leadership role in 2012. She holds certifications in Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement and healthcare compliance.

title: Oven fire damages popular Maine donut bakery

text:
Fire damages popular Maine donut bakery
Fire damages popular Maine donut bakery
A fire that started in an oven damaged the popular LaBree's Bakery in Old Town on Tuesday evening.
The Old Town Fire Department says the fire was reported at about 4:50 p.m. after employees tried to put the fire out themselves.
Officials say the fire started during normal production operations.
Firefighters had the fire under control within about five minutes of arriving at the scene and contained the flames to an oven, but there was smoke throughout the building.
As of Wednesday morning, the extent of the damage and impacts on operations at the bakery were not clear.
It took about two hours to clear all the smoke from the building.
No one was hurt.
LaBree's apple cider donuts are especially popular at this time of year, adding to the company's normal menu of eight other flavors. The bakery was founded in 1948 and moved to its current location on Gilman Falls Avenue in 1978 as the business continued to grow.

title: Troy Jackson’s partner responds to Republican attack ads
text:
Troy Jackson’s longtime romantic partner is criticizing Republican efforts to exploit their relationship and family in the closing days of Maine’s hotly contested U.S. Senate race.
Lana Pelletier, Jackson’s partner for 40 years and his second cousin, wrote in an op-ed published Wednesday in the Bangor Daily News that national Republicans and Jackson’s opponent, Republican Sen. Susan Collins, have crossed a line by focusing on their personal lives.
“Our children have been dragged into this campaign. Our relationship has been mocked. Our family has been talked about as though there is something shameful about who we are or where we come from,” Pelletier wrote. “There isn’t.”
She added, “I deeply resent watching Collins and her allies treat our lives as something beneath them — especially when serious issues involving women are manipulated into political weapons by people who show so little care for the women involved.”
The final stretch of Maine’s Senate campaign has gotten nasty, with national Republicans mounting an all-out attack on Jackson and his family.
On Tuesday, the SLF PAC, a super PAC tied to Republican Senate leader John Thune, R-S.D., began airing a radio ad about Jackson’s family. It’s a country song whose chorus includes the refrain, “If he’ll screw his own family, he’ll screw yours, too.”
The brass-knuckle tactics highlight the lengths to which powerful D.C. figures will go to win Maine’s Senate seat, which could determine control of the upper chamber during President Donald Trump’s final two years in office.
Since Jackson became the Democratic nominee on July 25, roughly three-quarters of the $101.8 million in ad spending has backed negative ads, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. Republican-aligned groups have spent about $47 million attacking Jackson, while Democratic-aligned groups have spent some $31 million attacking Collins.
Collins has asked the PAC to take down the ad about Jackson’s relationship to his partner. During a campaign stop Wednesday at Simones’ Hot Dog Stand in Lewiston, Collins said she had “nothing to do with” the spot and reiterated her desire for it to be removed from the airwaves.
But it wasn’t the only one that attacked Jackson’s family.
One TV commercial from SLF PAC, which is largely funded by out-of-state billionaires, said Jackson “keeps it in the family,” while another claimed that taxpayer money was used for “a sleazy deal with Jackson’s cousins, who are also his in-laws.” Yet another from an SLF-affiliated group, The Maine Standard, calls him “a creep.”
Republicans have also attacked Jackson’s son Chace, who was a state lobbyist during his father’s final term as state Senate president.
Collins has not remained above the fray. She brought up Jackson’s son’s lobbying during their first televised debate, accusing Jackson of flip-flopping on issues tied to his son’s lobbying efforts.
And in a September video interview with Politico, she coyly noted Jackson’s relationship with Pelletier.
“Well, I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin,” Collins said. “I don’t know whether people know that or not. … It’s not something I’m going to be emphasizing.”
Jackson, meanwhile, has accused Collins of personal corruption. At a debate earlier this month, he implied that she supported Trump’s war in Iran because it would benefit her family’s stock portfolio. Collins demanded that Jackson apologize for the remark. (Collins initially supported Trump’s right to conduct war under the War Powers Act, but voted repeatedly in favor of ending the conflict once the 60-day deadline for congressional approval had passed.)
At her campaign stop Wednesday, Collins noted that she too has been the victim of personal attacks by Jackson and his Democratic allies, who have tied her to disgraced financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein in ads.
Collins voted to table a provision calling for the release of the so-called Epstein files in a defense spending bill, but supported adding such a provision to an appropriations bill. She also joined a unanimous Senate vote in support of the Epstein Files Transparency Act.
An ad by Win Senate, a super PAC linked with Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., accused Collins of voting to cover up the Epstein files. It also claimed Collins received $3 million from a former Epstein business partner — a claim rated false by PolitiFact.
“This campaign has been unique in Maine’s history in the number of personal attacks,” Collins said. “It’s interesting because in comparing with my colleagues who are in tough races across the country, every single one of them has had an ad run against them trying to link us to Jeffrey Epstein. That is so absurd.”
Pelletier said in her op-ed that she expects people to challenge Jackson on his views and his record, “but there should be a line.”
“Collins has been quick to demand respect and decency for herself,” she wrote. “My family deserved the same.”
Jackson’s partner wasn’t the only one pushing back against Republican attacks Wednesday.
His former colleagues from the Maine Legislature gathered at the Maine Women’s Lobby in Augusta to speak out against recent attack ads, at least one of which features some of their faces.
Rebecca Millett, a former state lawmaker from Cape Elizabeth, appears in the “creep” ad crafted by the SLF PAC-affiliated The Maine Standard.
The spot highlights media reports that Jackson would lose his temper as Senate president, including one instance when he allegedly threw a water bottle.
Millett said the spot “reeks of desperation.”
“They put a black bar across my eyes, and the eyes of many other people here today, to suggest that we were somehow victims or villains,” she said, adding that she believes Jackson was a respectful and thoughtful leader and colleague.
The Maine Women’s Lobby also made a formal endorsement of Jackson at the event, a practice Destie Hohman Sprague, its executive director, said the organization usually doesn’t do.
When asked about Jackson’s alleged temper toward female colleagues while leading the state Senate, former Maine Sen. Cathy Breen said his behavior was not gendered in any way.
“When you’re in the thick of it, and the budget is coming down to the final hours, all of us are emotional. All of us are stressed out,” Breen said. “So, yeah, has Troy lost his temper now and then? Sure. So have I. I don’t hold that against him.”
Staff Writer Joe Charpentier contributed to this story.

title: Pentagon grants DHS permission to test heat ray weapon for potential use at border
text:
Pentagon grants DHS permission to test heat ray weapon for potential use at border
The Pentagon has given the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a military-grade heat ray and develop tactics to potentially use it in operations at the southern U.S. border, according to a memo signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month and obtained by CNN.
The heat ray, officially known as the Active Denial System, is a nonlethal weapon that shoots an invisible beam of electromagnetic waves that can reach a little more than half a mile away, according to the U.S. military.
The energy beam causes a burning sensation when it comes into contact with the human skin — which Pentagon officials have previously compared to feeling a blast of heat when opening a hot oven. Military officials have said the resulting “tingling effect” lasts between 10 and 15 minutes but also generates “an instinctive and irresistible urge to run from the effect.”
Deploying the heat ray at the U.S. border would be an unprecedented step, even for the Trump administration, which has made border security and clamping down on immigration a top priority.
The DHS request did not specify where or how the weapon would be tested and how it might eventually be used, but over the years, there have been internal discussions about potentially using it for crowd dispersal along the U.S.-Mexico border, according to current and former Customs and Border Protection officials.
U.S. officials had also considered deploying the system during moments of domestic unrest, including at the end of President Donald Trump’s first term when protests erupted over the murder of George Floyd, according to a former U.S. official familiar with those discussions.
The memo authorizes the “temporary loan” of one ADS system for seven months, starting in September, and states that it “shall not be operated by DoW (Department of War) personnel,” appearing to absolve the Pentagon of any responsibility for how the directed-energy system may ultimately be deployed.
It also states that DHS is solely responsible for “system employment, use and development of tactics, techniques and procedures.” At the end of the seven-month loan period, DHS can submit an additional request for further use of the Pentagon system in border operations based on need, a defense official told CNN.
“CBP is continually evaluating new technologies, especially those that enhance operational effectiveness and strengthen mission capabilities,” a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in a statement to CNN.
The Pentagon referred CNN to DHS when asked for comment.
The U.S. military briefly deployed the system to Afghanistan nearly two decades ago but ultimately declined to use it during active combat operations. The U.S. military also considered using the system for crowd control purposes at U.S. facilities abroad where terrorist detainees were being held at the time but ultimately declined to employ it for that purpose as well, according to a source familiar with those previous internal considerations.
Customs and Border Protection officials have previously entertained the idea of using the system in areas where there’s a high concentration of illegal crossings. Border officials have occasionally discussed potentially using the system as a crowd dispersal tool, but it has never been deployed.
Concerns over effectiveness and legality
Officials ran into hurdles over legalities, use of force, effectiveness, and potential issues over sovereignty, particularly if the system was deployed on people in Mexico who had not yet crossed into the U.S. Chief among those concerns, however, was whether people could be harmed, either directly or indirectly, by the weapon.
“Even if they’re chasing people back to the river, you don’t want them to go in and drown,” a former CBP official told CNN. “For the cost, for the training and for the policies you’re going to create, is the juice worth the squeeze?”
El Centro sector, which covers around 70 miles along the U.S.-Mexico border, evaluated the system several years ago, when Rodney Scott, who now serves as CBP commissioner, helmed that sector, according to a CBP official.
At the time, officials were discussing whether the system might help agents with an influx of illegal crossings along the nearby river by discouraging people from trying to cross in that area or pushing them to get out of the water.
One of the considerations at the time was whether the system might result in more rescues if people were incapacitated by the technology, the official said, though it’s unclear why it wasn’t deployed.
In 2018, prior to midterms, CBP officials also weighed using it against migrants, but then-Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen shot it down.
“The issue was treating immigrants and citizens like enemy combatants,” a former DHS official familiar with previous discussions about using the weapon against migrants told CNN. “Thematically, inhumane treatments typically get rejected.”
Some Border Patrol agents have more recently cast doubt over whether they need the tool at all amid low border crossings and an increase in personnel, according to another former CBP official.

title: Hail the size of golf balls pummel parts of Arizona as rare storm moves through the West
text:
PHOENIX (AP) — Hail the size of golf balls and damaging wind gusts pounded northern and central Arizona in a rare storm blowing through, bringing with it tornado risks and possible flash floods.
The National Weather Service issued multiple warnings as severe thunderstorms moved through the state overnight Tuesday and into Wednesday, encouraging people to seek shelter and stay away from windows as damaging 2-to-3-inch hail struck the area. Hail pummeled people’s roofs, shattered windows and dented cars.
Tornado watches were issued for multiple areas — the first the state has seen since Oct. 6, 2010.
Warm, moist air moving north fuels storms coming off the California coast. Changing winds can make them spin, creating the conditions for tornadoes, said Ryan Bernhart, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Flagstaff.
“This is very unusual for this area at this time of the year,” Bernhart said.
Strong winds toppled trees in Flagstaff and Mesa, with some landing on walls and carports. A few dozen ponderosa pines over 30 feet tall fell down in the Coconino National Forest, northwest of Flagstaff.
“These are not small trees that are down,” Bernhart said. “These are pretty strong trees that had been knocked down.”
The greatest threat to the Phoenix metro area is heavy rainfall and flash flooding tonight and Thursday morning, said Mark O’Malley, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service office in Phoenix.
___
Jessica Hill reported from Las Vegas.

title: Sunshine & Pleasant Today... More Clouds & Breezy Thursday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Strong high pressure will provide us with lots of sun again today. Coastal areas will see some high clouds mixed in at times associated with low pressure spinning well to our south. Temperatures will be seasonable today with afternoon highs averaging in the mid-50s. Low pressure to our south will drift a bit northward tonight... pushing some more high clouds into the state as the night progresses. Skies will be clear to partly cloudy across the north and partly to mostly cloudy elsewhere with the bulk of the clouds being over coastal locales. Temperatures tonight will drop to the 30s for most spots... some upper 20s possible across the north.
Low pressure to our south will continue to move a bit further northward on Thursday... keeping high clouds across much of the state throughout the day. Expect partly to mostly cloudy Thursday with the bulk of clouds closer to the coast and brighter conditions inland and across the north. As the low approaches... the pressure gradient will tighten up a bit... resulting in a gusty north/northwest wind up to 25-30 MPH at times from late Thursday morning through the afternoon. Temperatures on Thursday will again be in the mid-50s on average. The ocean storm will pull away from New England on Friday... taking the high clouds with it and leading to a brighter day with mostly sunny skies expected. Strong high pressure building in from the west on Friday combined with the storm departing to our east will keep the pressure gradient tight so plan on another breezy day Friday with a northerly wind gusting to 25-30 MPH at times.
High pressure will bring us a gorgeous weekend with lots of sunshine both Saturday and Sunday. The high will build to our south through the weekend... which will allow warmer air to return as the weekend progresses. Temperatures will top off in the 50s on Saturday then mid-50s to low 60s for highs on Sunday. This fantastic fall weather continues into next week too. There may be a few showers Monday night with the passage of a cold front otherwise those chances look pretty minimal and the frontal passage may very well come through dry. The next best chance for some precipitation will be later in the week with some showers possible Friday.
Rest of Today: Mostly sunny. Highs in the mid-50s. Northeast wind 5-10 MPH.
Tonight: Clear to partly cloudy north... partly to mostly cloudy closer to the coast. Lows mainly in the 30s. Light and variable wind.
Thursday: Partly to mostly cloudy and breezy. Highs in the 50s. North/northwest wind 10-15 MPH with gusts to 25-30 MPH possible.
Friday: Mostly sunny and breezy. Highs in the mid-40s to low 50s.
Saturday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s.
Sunday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the mid-50s to low 60s.

title: Maine’s Youth Deer Hunting Days to be held this week
text:
Licensed junior hunters are allowed to harvest a deer on Friday or Saturday, an opportunity to try their luck before the firearms season opens for adults.
For 20-plus years, the state offered a single Youth Deer Hunting Day. In 2023, Maine expanded that program to two days. Any child under 16 years old can get a junior license and must be accompanied on Youth Deer Hunting Days by an adult who meets certain licensing or safety criteria.
Archery season for deer is already underway and will end in most parts of the state on Oct. 30. Firearms season for deer starts for adult residents on Oct. 31 and nonresidents on Nov. 2. The last day for residents and nonresidents is Nov. 28.
Muzzleloader season for deer starts Nov. 30 and ends Dec. 5 in most parts of the state. The season extends in December only in certain districts.
In 2025, the total number of deer harvested was 55,876 — many more than other types of large game, according to data on the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife website.
For more information about Youth Deer Hunting Days, as well as general regulations, such as season dates and bag limits, visit the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife website.

title: Here are the most popular baby names of 2026, according to BabyCenter
text:
(Gray News) - BabyCenter has released its list of the most popular baby names of 2026.
Olivia and Noah remain the top names for girls and boys, according to the list. The top five boy names have stayed the same for the third year in a row.
Top boy names
Liam and Oliver rank second and third on the list. Elijah and Mateo round out the top five boy names.
Lucas rose one spot to No. 6. Elias jumped eight spots to join the top 10 for the first time at No. 7. Levi fell two spots to No. 8, and Ezra fell one spot to No. 9. Leo rose one spot to rejoin the top 10 at No. 10. Asher, at No. 11, and Luca, at No. 12, fell out of the top 10.
Top girl names

title: 5 candidates vying for 3 Old Town City Council seats
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Five candidates, in which two are incumbents, are running for three seats on the Old Town City Council.
The candidates — Robin Cacace, John Dieffenbacher-Krall, Linda McLeod, Scott Wilcox and Katrina Wynn — bring various experience on the City Council, in the city’s school, environmental efforts and city administration. Electees will serve a three-year term.
Councilor David Wight, who was first elected in 2020, is not seeking re-election.
Electees will join an Old Town City Council that recently voted in favor of city staff cuts as it navigates rising costs and a drop in tax revenue after Nine Dragons Paper closed in 2023.
The candidates appear in alphabetical order.
Robin Cacace
Cacace, a retired teacher and coach of the Leonard Middle School boys soccer team, decided to run for council to give back to her community, she said. Cacace isn’t running on a single issue or with plans to implement a specific policy, but said that she wants to learn how council works and then see how she can act on changes the community wants.
“I don’t want to go in with the idea of: I’m going to go in there and make waves,” Cacace said. “I just want to go in and try to support what’s going to make our community better, and that’ll take a learning curve.”
Although she hasn’t previously run for council, Cacace said she was involved in a community project to keep a nuclear waste facility out of Edinburg in the ’90s and multiple community projects in Old Town.
While she doesn’t have specific ideas of how to solve issues facing Old Town, including rising taxes, she said they should be worked through with input from community members.
The Juniper Ridge Landfill, and its proposed expansion, are a space for community input, she said. Cacace said she’s against its expansion and worried about the environmental impacts it already had and any possible future contamination.
John Dieffenbacher-Krall
Dieffenbacher-Krall, an environmental activist and previous executive director of Wabanaki Alliance, is running for council for the first time to give residents another option at the ballot box, he said.
Serving on the boards of non-profit organizations, churches and various committees has given him the experience he needs to be on council, he said. His background as a writer and editor for the Maine Sportsman and at the University of Maine will also help him share council’s work, he said.
Using his experience, he said he’d push for Old Town to become a zero-waste community. In response to the Juniper Ridge Landfill possibly expanding, which he calls an “abomination,” Old Town needs to enter a better host agreement with the landfill and do its part in reducing waste, he said.
“We need to go from a throwaway society to a zero waste society, and one of my priorities is to make Old Town a leader of that,” Dieffenbacher-Krall said.
Dieffenbacher-Krall’s other priorities include protecting city services from cuts, increasing recreation for residents and spurring economic growth.
Old Town isn’t “past hard budget times,” but emergency services need to be funded and staffed, he said. As a councilor, Dieffenbacher-Krall said he would look for efficient ways for the city to keep its services while keeping taxes affordable.
Linda McLeod
McLeod, who has served as a councilor since 2017, was previously a teacher and principal at Indian Island School and later the Maine Indian Education superintendent. She is currently the longest serving councilor on the Old Town City Council.
McLeod did not respond to requests for comment about why she is running for re-election or what her priorities are. When she ran for re-election in 2023, she said one of her top priorities was to attract new business to the city.
Scott Wilcox
Wilcox is the chief executive officer of the Old Town-Orono YMCA and was previously the Old Town public safety director. He stepped down from the position in 2023 after 26 years as a police officer.
Old Town is going through “some difficult times” that Wilcox said he thought he could help with, prompting him to run. Rising property taxes and stagnant growth for both businesses and family housing are the city’s largest issues, he said.
ND Paper’s closure in 2023 changed the town’s taxes and budgeting, but the city should still be making an effort to find a business to replace the mill, or use that space, Wilcox said.
“I think maybe it’s time that we re-identify ourselves not as a mill community any longer, but try to find something else to go there or work with [ND Paper] to do something different,” he said.
As a councilor, Wilcox said he would talk with the mill owners, electrical businesses that previously showed interest in the site, and with University of Maine to see what collaboration could be done to attract new business to the city. Opening up conversations with businesses that have decided not to come to Old Town could also show how the city could grow, he said.
With businesses not bringing in additional taxes to the city, Wilcox said he would want to review city services for any overlaps and decide what is needed or what is “nice to have.” Conversations with community members, and a possible committee, would be needed to see what residents want the city to provide, he said.
When asked about the Juniper Ridge Landfill and its possible expansion, Wilcox said Casella Waste Management have been good community partners but the city should better understand what the state’s end goal for the landfill is.
Katrina Wynn
Wynn, who was elected to half a term in 2025, is running for re-election because she wants to be able to represent a demographic that isn’t always present at meetings or in decisions — parents with kids in the school system.
In her last 16 months on the City Council, Wynn said she’s learned more about how the council works but didn’t have time to bring forward priorities she wants to see in front of the council. Her largest concern is Old Town’s affordability.
“I think the biggest issue is we’re a mill town without a mill. We have services built on mill money and no mill,” Wynn said.
Residents have told Wynn that they don’t want city services to be cut but also don’t want to pay more in taxes. Wynn said “it’s fairly impossible to do both,” and she’s prioritizing services while still trying to keep tax increases minimal.
There are ways to create a higher quality of life for residents without a spike in the budget, Wynn said. More accessible crosswalks, removing library late fees and creating additional access to recreation and the environment are relatively small changes but could all make residents’ lives easier, she said.
Correction: An earlier version of this story misidentified the municipality where Robin Cacace was involved in a community project to keep out nuclear waste.

title: Woman seeks full $16M payment from New Hampshire DHHS after sexual assault verdict
text:
Woman files appeal seeking full $16 million payment from New Hampshire DHHS after sexual assault verdict
The woman who was awarded $16 million by a jury over sexual abuse she suffered as a teenager has filed an appeal with the New Hampshire Supreme Court.
Kristy Gesse is appealing on the basis that the majority of what she is owed is being withheld due to the deaths and closure of the parties liable.
The New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) filed a cross-appeal, basing its argument on the statute of limitations of Gesse's claims, according to WMTW sister station WMUR.
In June, a jury ruled in favor of Kristy Gesse as part of a lawsuit she filed regarding the abuse she endured during her time at Saddleback Mountain Retreat group home while in the legal custody of DHHS in the early 1990s.
Gesse's lawsuit claimed the state did not protect her from sexual abuse.
Jurors found that DHHS was negligent and its conduct was a substantial factor in causing Gesse harm.
The jury ruled that DHHS was responsible for 25% of the damages and the other 75% went to Saddleback and its two owners, Peter and Beverly Tsetsilas.
But Saddleback has since closed and the owners are dead, meaning Gesse is not receiving more than $12 million.
Gesse now wants DHHS to pay the entire $16 million she was awarded by the jury.
DHHS has filed its own appeal over the 25% it was ordered to give Gesse in the original verdict.
In the original verdict, the jury rejected the state’s argument that the case was filed too late.

title: Trump administration is releasing Northeast heating oil reserves as Maine prices soar
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Northeast heating oil reserves will be tapped for just the second time in history.
The federal government’s move comes after U.S. Sens. Angus King and Susan Collins in September called for reserves to be released as energy prices climb during President Donald Trump’s ongoing war in Iran.
Last week, the average price for a gallon of heating oil stood at $5.97 in Maine, down slightly from last month’s record high of $6.02 but still 80% higher than the same time last year.
That means it will cost Mainers an additional $731.50 to fill a standard 275-gallon tank.
In eastern and Down East Maine, prices range from a low of $5.50 to a high of $6.30.
Collins said Wednesday that she was glad the Trump administration acted on the request, saying the U.S. Department of Energy believes the release of approximately 315,000 barrels, or 13.2 million gallons, will “put downward pressure on home heating oil costs and make a real difference for Maine homeowners as they prepare for winter.”
The release, just the second made since the stockpile was created 26 years ago, amounts to a third of the Northeast reserves, some of which are kept in South Portland. The stockpile was last tapped in 2012 after Hurricane Sandy.
Gov. Janet Mills welcomed the news, saying she hopes that it provides Mainers “meaningful financial relief.”
“I also want to be clear: while we are hopeful this decision will ease prices for Maine people in the near-term, it will not solve the long-term problem driving up costs — the President’s war — and Maine people deserve long-term solutions that bring down costs, not just temporary relief from a crisis of the President’s own making,” she said in a statement.
Earlier this month, the Trump administration released about $37 million in low-income heating assistance for Maine. An additional $1.4 million was awarded to the state’s four federally recognized tribes.
About half of Maine households (more than 300,000) rely on heating oil to stay warm during the winter, and consumption can average 2 to 7 gallons a day, depending on how cold it is outside. This release would amount to approximately nine days of consumption at a rate of five gallons a day.
Trump’s ongoing war against Iran effectively halted fuel shipments out of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s natural gas and oil passes. The ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine also has strained global fuel supplies as both sides trade blows on each other’s energy infrastructure despite Trump’s push for an “energy ceasefire” as he moves ahead with plans to import Russian diesel.
“Maine has been hit especially hard by the run up in fuel prices since the beginning of the Iran War and the most obvious example is home heating oil,” King said in a statement. “Maine is one of the most dependent states in the country on home heating oil and the cost is absolutely through the roof. This release of stored oil in New England will hopefully be some help. While this is good news, we also want to keep pressuring the Administration to bring those prices down before winter really sets in.”
These reserves will be available on an exchange where companies can bid for a share of the barrels.

title: ‘We’re lucky to be alive’: Women recount slamming head-on into water buffalo at 52 mph
text:
STOCKHOLM, N.Y. (WWNY/Gray News) - Two New York women say they are lucky to be alive after they crashed head-on into a water buffalo on their way home from a church event.
Kristen Rozelle, 50, was driving Lindsey Baker, 27, home from a church event around 7 p.m. Saturday when their Jeep collided head-on with a water buffalo in the town of Stockholm.
“If you look at my Jeep, we’re lucky to be alive. Literally, if I did not have a Jeep Limited, I’d be dead,” Rozelle said.
Rozelle said she was traveling 52 mph before hitting the water buffalo that weighed about 2,300 pounds, according to a state trooper. She said it felt like hitting a freight train.
“All of a sudden, I just see black. I didn’t see anything at all. And then, boom,” she said. “We didn’t know it was even there.”
“I’m like, ‘What did we hit?’” Baker said.
Good Samaritans helped after the crash
Rozelle said she passed out briefly after the crash. When she came to, smoke from the deployed airbags made her think the Jeep was on fire. The airbags blocked the door handles, making it difficult to get out.
Baker said she saw the airbags and smoke and heard Rozelle yelling to get out of the Jeep.
“I turned to see, and then, she’s panicking. She can’t get out, so I checked to see if she was still buckled. She wasn’t,” Baker said.
Baker said she got out of the Jeep.
“I ran into the road to get help, to wave the car down,” she said. “Thankfully, there were some people who came, and I directed them to where we were.”
Those good Samaritans helped the two women until first responders arrived and took them to the hospital.
“The people were so wonderful and beautiful to help us,” Rozelle said. “That’s the real story here is just that humanness. When we needed it the most, they were there.”
Rozelle said she sustained sprains and bruises throughout her body, along with cuts on her leg and hand, while Baker said she had bruises on her legs and chest.
“We didn’t walk out of this with nothing,” Rozelle said. “We’re struggling each in our own way.”
A water buffalo?
An eyewitness told Rozelle he saw the water buffalo run across a field and jump the guardrail toward her Jeep. The animal died in the crash.
Rozelle said seeing photos of her crumpled Jeep reinforced just how serious this incident was.
“I knew I was lucky. But when I saw the Jeep, I realized how much more. God’s arms were around me. There’s no other way to express that,” she said. “My Jeep is this huge vehicle, and it was crumpled to nothing in a moment’s notice.”
Baker said she was stunned after learning what they had hit.
“I was in disbelief,” she said. “It had horns. It was black, and that’s all I could see from when the ambulance turned to head to the hospital.”
Rozelle said she wants the focus to remain on the women’s survival, rather than the animal involved.
“I want people to see the Jeep and not the bull anymore,” Rozelle said. “Our lives are worth something... We’re alive. And that’s a miracle. Absolute miracle.”
State police said the owner of the water buffalo, who lives near the crash site, spoke with a trooper at the scene.
Rozelle said she has heard nothing from the owner.
“The only thing that I know is that nobody’s reached out to us,” she said. “And they knew that we almost died... On a human component of it, that’s just a really hard thing.”
Water buffalo, originating from parts of Asia, can weigh more than a ton and stand 6 feet tall.
