title: Give your pumpkin an afterlife at a Maine farm or your compost bin
text:
Food scraps make up about a quarter of what goes into U.S. municipal landfills, producing 58% of the methane gas escaping from them.
Whatever pumpkin ends up on your porch this month is going to get eaten. The only question is by whom: your family, a farmer’s pigs, the worms and microbes in a compost pile, or the oxygen-starved bacteria buried in a landfill. Only that last group turns a pumpkin into tons of methane.
Perhaps you sealed last year’s jack-o’-lantern’s fate by sliding it into a trash bag. You can have a plan for this year’s gourd before it even leaves the farm stand.
What do you plan to do with your jack-o-‘lanterns this year?
This suggested action step is on the food pathway, which covers how we meet one of our most basic needs: sustainable eating, growing, and food system practices, from the field to the table to the compost bin. A pumpkin is a seasonal reminder to practice the whole loop: Buy food you intend to use, eat what you can, and return the rest to the soil.
WHY YOUR PORCH PUMPKIN MATTERS TO OUR PLANET
In 2022, for example, U.S. farms harvested about 2 billion pounds of pumpkins destined to be sold whole, mostly for decoration. Environmental scientist Robert Czubaszek of Bialystok University of Technology estimates that if those pumpkins ended up in landfills, they would release pollution comparable to the yearly emissions of more than 45,000 cars.
Pumpkins heading to the landfill are part of a much larger pattern. The Environmental Protection Agency estimates that food makes up about 24% of the trash in municipal landfills, but because food is completely biodegradable, it produces about 58% of the methane those landfills release to the air. Composted pumpkins, unlike landfilled pumpkins, break down with oxygen and release very little methane. The same pumpkin travels a different pollution path depending on whether it gets buried under a landfill cap.
MAKE A PLAN FOR A PUMPKIN
Start at the farm stand. If you want a pumpkin you can eat, look for a pie pumpkin. These are usually smaller than jack-o’-lantern types, with sweeter, denser, less watery flesh. But large jack-o’-lantern varieties are edible too and cook up with fairly good results.
Then think twice about the knife. Cornell horticulturist Steve Reiners says a healthy, uncarved pumpkin can last eight to 12 weeks, while a carved jack-o’-lantern typically lasts only 10 days. So, an uncarved pumpkin on your steps today can be soup in November. Put a scarf or other decorations on it but leave your pumpkin whole if you’d like to eat it later. Extension educators advise against cooking a pumpkin after you’ve carved and displayed it. Just as your skin protects you from infections and disease, a pumpkin’s unbroken skin does, too.
Give every Halloween pumpkin you buy a sustainable destination for Nov. 1:
• Your kitchen. Roast the flesh for soup, curry, or pie, and roast the seeds for a snack.
• A compost pile. Chop it up so it breaks down faster — and pull out the seeds unless you want a pumpkin patch next summer.
• A farm. The nonprofit Pumpkins for Pigs connects donors with farms and sanctuaries across the United States and Canada through a searchable map. Make sure you skip bleach “preservative” sprays, which make pumpkins unsafe for animals.
• A community collection. Many towns run post-Halloween pumpkin smashes or compost drop-offs. Remove candles, wax, paint, glitter, and stickers first, since decorated pumpkins can’t be composted.
BRING SOMEONE ALONG WITH YOU
Some of the most valuable steps on this pathway can be shared, with family, friends, or neighbors.
Tell your sister you’re starting to cook a pumpkin instead of tossing it. Chat with friends at the Halloween potluck and mention how you’re giving your pumpkin or jack-‘o-lantern its afterlife. Ask your neighbors whether anyone wants to share a run to the farm that takes pumpkins.
YOUR 1 STEP THIS WEEK
Before October ends, decide where every pumpkin in your home will go on Nov. 1, and make that plan easy to follow: Buy an edible variety, carve only as necessary, and cook the remaining pumpkins. Look up your nearest compost drop-off or Pumpkins for Pigs farm now, before the porch fills up. Then, wherever you are on the food pathway, take one more step: Blend pumpkin into one familiar recipe, cook one squash-and-bean dinner, or invite one friend or family member to try either with you.
A pumpkin is a small thing, but it gives you a simple way to practice what the food pathway asks of all of us: Buy food on purpose, eat what you can, and send the rest back to the soil instead of the landfill.
Sustainable Practice empowers you to protect our planet in practical ways. Share this article with whoever buys the pumpkins in your house so this year’s jack-o’-lantern gets a second act instead of ending up in a trash bag.
Fred Horch and Peggy Siegle are principals of Sustainable Practice. You can pick up their new 2026 edition of “Your Earth Share: Seven Pathways to Sustainable Living” or any of their other publications at SustainablePractice.Life. Join their community of sustainable practitioners at that address for both benefits and books.

title: Obituary: Dalmon Ray Perry
text:
PHIPPSBURG – Dalmon Ray Perry, 78, of Phippsburg, passed away at home on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. He was born in Saco on July 29, 1948, the son of Arthur and Olive Perry. He grew up in Bath, graduating from Morse High School class of 1966. While attending Morse, he participated in basketball and track and held the school record for high jump several years after graduation. Illness prevented him from continuing his education at USM and led to his joining the Airforce. He was selected to attend language school in California, learning Chinese. Unfortunately, a motorcycle accident prevented him from continuing. His tour of duty included Labrador and Vietnam with him being honorably discharged in 1972 as a sergeant.
After his service, he drove for several construction companies, the USM women’s basketball team and the Harpswell school bus. He enjoyed being outside and meeting people. He also relished his time at the gym which helped him win many bodybuilding competitions. For 18 years he worked as a supervisor in the post office at the So. Portland distribution center. Dal loved golf and worked mowing the greens at both The Bath Country Club and the Mere Creek golf course. Not liking cold weather, he spent his winters golfing with his girlfriend in California. Loving the world of motorcycling (and it had to be a “Harley”), he belonged to two clubs – one in Maine and one in Palm Desert, Calif. “Aging” brought him into the world of books. He was a veracious reader, reading many books during the month. He also “enjoyed” his times with his girlfriend as he tried to win at Yahtzee and Phase 10.
Dalmon was predeceased by his parents and is survived by his son Ian (Samantha) of Phoenix, Ariz., his sister Linda, his girlfriend Linda, many cousins, and Oreo and Jake (two Boston Terriers he loved and helped raise).
A Mass of Christian burial will be held at St. Mary’s Church of All Saints Parrish, 144 Lincoln St in Bath on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026, at 11 a.m. Visiting hours will be held at Desmond Funeral Home in Bath on Thursday Oct. 22, 2026, from 4–6 p.m. Burial with military honors will be at Oak Grove Cemetery (middle school entrance) in Bath following mass. Please join the family back at the church after burial for fellowship, refreshments and memories.
To express your thoughts and condolences with the family, please visit http://www.desmondfuneralhomes .com
In lieu of flowers, please consider making a donation to your local Humane Society in Dalmon’s name.
He loved animals.

title: October 23rd Trunk Or Treat At Mid Mall Benefits Sarah's House In Holden
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Don't get me wrong, there are lots of awesome things about a local Trunk-or-treat; the fun decorations, the candy, the safe and enclosed space kids can venture about in as they show off their outfits and collect their treats.
Read More: Free Halloween Activities Coming To Glenburn This Fall
But when you incorporate all of that goodness with helping a good cause, that's a real 'level up' as the kids say.
For the third year in a row, you'll be able to level up your trunk-or-treat game at the Mid Mall Trunk-or-Treat in Bangor.
On Friday October 23rd, you can dress up with your kiddos and visit the dozens of local businesses and individuals who have sponsored a trunk and get goodies in the process.
The event will take place in Mid Mall area off the Bangor Mall Blvd, and promises plenty of candy, food trucks, decorated trunks, music and entertainment.
It's a free event appropriate for all ages. Over 24 local businesses have worked together to make the event come to life and keep the event free.
Benjamin Smith, Director of HR & Marketing for FYZICAL Therapy & Balance Centers and event organizer, says they expect about a thousand folks to make their way through the parking lot this year.
That's not only great exposure for the local businesses, but also a fair amount publicity for this year's charity benefactors, Sarah's House in Holden, Maine.
Read More: Trick-or-Treating in Bangor, Maine: Maple Street Is a Must-Visit
"What started as an opportunity for neighboring businesses to come together and do something fun for local families has really grown into something special. One of my favorite things about this event is seeing businesses that might otherwise never cross paths come together for a common purpose. Everyone puts their own creative spin on their trunk, the kids have an absolute blast, and we get to create a fun, safe,
and memorable evening for families in our community. We're expecting our biggest turnout yet, and I couldn't be more excited!"
Smith says not only will people from Sarah's House will be on hand collecting things from their wishlist, if people with to donate, but there's also another way to help the organization, too.
"We're also proud to feature Sarah's House as this year's nonprofit beneficiary. Sarah's House provides a home away from home for individuals traveling to the Bangor area for cancer treatment. Representatives will be on-site collecting much-needed wish list items, and Darling's Ice Cream Truck for a Cause will be helping raise funds for the organization."
Read More: Why Halloween And Daylight Saving Time Overlap In Maine
The 3rd Annual Mid Mall Trunk-Or-Treat will run from 5 PM to 7 PM. Families are encouraged to dress up and bring a treat bag to collect all the candy.

title: OBITUARIES for Thursday, October 22, 2026
text:
SIDNEY H. GELLER
WATERVILLE – Sidney Herbert Geller, 89, of Waterville, passed away peacefully in his sleep on Thursday, October 15, 2026. “Sid” was born in Portland on April 5, 1937, to Mary (nee Blumenthal) and Harry Geller.
A proud Mainer, he was born and raised in Portland and spent his adult life living in Waterville. Upon retirement, he enjoyed winters in Boca Raton, Florida, and summers at “the camp” on East Pond, in Oakland.
He graduated from Deering High School, attended Northeastern University, and earned his bachelor’s degree from Drake University. He later attended Boston University School of Law before earning his law degree from the University of Maine School of Law. True to his sense of humor, he always joked that he was never at the top of his class.
After passing the Maine Bar Exam, Sid moved to Waterville to pursue his career in law. He practiced law in Waterville for 63 years. Throughout his life, he remained deeply committed to giving back to his community. He was very philanthropic and particularly devoted to supporting his synagogue, Beth Israel, in Waterville, and The Cedars, in Portland.
Sid leaves behind a legacy of family, community, loyalty, and laughter.
Sidney was predeceased by his parents; his brother, Arnold; and many aunts and uncles.
He is survived by his wife of 61 years, Elizabeth “Liz” Geller; his three sons, David, his wife Jenny, of Waterville, Michael, his partner Clinton O’Dell, of Rumford, Rhode Island, and Stephen Geller, of Cape Cod, Massachusetts; and his three grandchildren, Chloe Geller and her partner David Barre, of York, and Ian and Ava Geller, both of Waterville; his sisters-in-law Susan Goldberg and Barbara McPherson; along with many nieces, nephews, and cousins.
A funeral was held at the Levey Chapel, in Portland, on Sunday, October 18, 2026.
Memorial service, followed by a reception and shiva, was held on Thursday, October 22, 2026, at Beth Israel Congregation, 291 Main St., Waterville.
In lieu of flowers, contributions can be made to Beth Israel Synagogue, P.O. Box 1882, Waterville, ME 04903-1882, or The Cedars, 630 Ocean Ave., Portland, ME 04103.
STEPHEN THIBODEAU
FAIRFIELD – Stephen “Steve” Thibodeau, 69, passed away on Saturday, October 3, 2026. He was born on August 16, 1957, to Maurice and Methyl (Haslam) Thibodeau.
Steve spent much of his life working with automotive parts and small engines. Known to many as “the parts guy,” he was the owner of DAC Distributors, in Clinton. He took great pride in his work and was known for his incredible knowledge of the industry. His lifelong passion for cars and racing brought him tremendous enjoyment.
Above all, Steve will be remembered for his hard work, generous heart, and kind spirit. Those who knew him often described him as “the nicest guy in the world” and someone who “would give the shirt off his back to anyone.” He treasured his family and the relationships he built throughout his life.
Steve was predeceased by his wife, Lucille “Lucy” Thibodeau; his parents, Maurice and Methyl; his brothers Larry, Mike, and Kevin, and his sister, Brenda.
He is survived by his daughter, Janneen King, and her husband, James; his grandchildren, Kennedy, James, Makayla, Hunter and Takashi; his brother, Rick; his stepdaughters Kami Maheu and Kathy Alley; and many cherished nieces and nephews.
He shared a very special bond with his granddaughter, Savanna Fasulo, who was his sidekick until the very end. She was his devoted caretaker and protector, and their connection was a treasured part of his life.
A celebration of life will be held on Sunday, October 25, 2026, at 1 p.m., at O’Brien’s, in Waterville, to honor Steve and celebrate the life he lived.
DONALD W. RENY
WINSLOW – Donald William Reny, 89, passed away on Friday, October 2, 2026. Don was born on October 31, 1936, in North Vassalboro, the son of Arthur and Dorothy (Lizotte) Reny and the third of eight children.
He graduated from Winslow High School in 1955 and proudly served four years in the United States Air Force, stationed at Loring Air Force Base, in Limestone.
On November 23, 1957, Don married Lorraine Duguay, beginning a life together that would span nearly 69 years. They were blessed with three children: Stephen, Margaret “Peggy,” and Kelly. In 1967, the family moved from Winslow to Yarmouth, where Don built a successful career as a building contractor for more than 30 years.
Following his retirement, Don devoted much of his time to helping others. While spending winters in Kissimmee, Florida, he volunteered for many years at Give Kids the World. Back home in Maine, he volunteered at Notre Dame’s soup kitchen and the Muskie Center, in Waterville. Cooking and preparing meals for those in need brought him tremendous joy and reflected his generous spirit.
Don had many interests throughout his life, including woodworking, hunting, fishing, boating, and reading, but few things brought him more enjoyment than a good game of cribbage. He loved organizing cribbage tournaments and sharing a game with family and friends.
Above all, Don cherished time spent with the people he loved. Whether enjoying a quiet one-on-one visit, gathering with a small group of friends, or hosting a crowd at the family’s summer lake house, Don was happiest when surrounded by others. He was well known for his lobster bakes, pig roasts, and famous “bean hole beans,” which became treasured traditions for family and friends.
Don will also be remembered for his wonderful sense of humor. He loved telling jokes, playing pranks, and finding ways to make those around him smile and laugh. Bringing joy to others was truly one of his greatest gifts.
Don was predeceased by his parents, Arthur and Dorothy Reny; his brother, Robert; his sisters, Pauline Daniels, Lillian Richards, Mary Thorne, and Arlene Mayhugh; and his daughter, Peggy.
He is survived by his wife, Lorraine Reny, of Winslow; his son, Stephen Reny and his wife, Kathleen Kerr, of Yarmouth; and his daughter, Kelly Williams and her husband, Rod Williams, of Yarmouth; his grandchildren, Sam Reny and her husband, Joshua McDougall, of North Yarmouth, Alison Thomas and her husband, Luke Thomas, of Thompson’s Station, Tennessee, Patrick Vigue and his wife, Afton Vigue, of Gardiner, Delia Williams and her fiancé, Mark Matheson, of Franklin, North Carolina, and Madeline Kerr of Yarmouth; his great-grandchildren, Ben, Sunny, Gus, and Levi of Thompson’s Station, Tennessee, and Ambrose and Sawyer McDougall, of North Yarmouth; his brother, Peter Reny, of North Vassalboro; and his sister, Priscilla Perry, of Holden.
A funeral Mass will be celebrated on Saturday, November 14, 2026, at 11 a.m., at St. John the Baptist Church, in Winslow, followed by a Celebration of Life at the Waterville Elks Lodge. A private interment will take place at the Maine Veteran’s Memorial Cemetery at a later date.
In lieu of flowers, the family invites those wishing to honor Don’s memory to consider making a donation to Spectrum Generations at http://www.spectrumgenerations.org.
STANTON M. WHITAKER
AUGUSTA – Stanton M. Whitaker, 93, passed away on Saturday, October 10, 2026, at his home in Augusta, where he has lived since 1965. Stanton was born on March 23, 1933, in Belfast, the son of C. Maynard and Christabelle Fuller Whitaker.
He grew up on the family farm in Windsor and graduated from Cony High School, in Augustta, in 1951.
Before beginning his career with Central Maine Power Company in 1953, he worked on the farm and drove logging and gravel trucks. Stanton worked for Central Maine Power for 38 years before retiring in 1991, and he returned temporarily to help during the ice storm of 1998.
On June 18, 1955, Stanton married his wife, Donna M. Cooper. They shared 58 years together until her passing in 2014.
Stanton enjoyed working with his hands and was always willing to lend his skills to friends and family through construction projects, mowing, and other acts of service. He generously gave of his time to help at Christian Life Fellowship Church, in Chelsea, and the Washington Advent Christian Campground, where he was a member and regular attendee. He also was a member of the Eastern Star, and the Capital Area Wheels chapter of Good Sam as he loved spending time camping with friends and family.
Stanton was predeceased by his wife, Donna; his brother, Jerry Whitaker; his sister, Priscilla Clark; his toddler grandson, Tyler Allen; and his baby great-granddaughter, Brooke Whitaker.
He is survived by his son, David Whitaker, and his wife, Jennifer, of Presque Isle; and his two daughters, Diane Smith, and her husband, Scott, of Hudson, New Hampshire, and Pamela Allen, and her husband, Curt, of Hallowell; 10 grandchildren: Greg Whitaker and his wife, Erica, of Mapleton, Joel Whitaker and his wife, Elizabeth, of Presque Isle, Aaron Whitaker and his wife, Chelsea, of Mapleton, Timothy Smith and his wife Marie, of Hudson, New Hampshire, Rebecca Johansen and her husband, Austin, of Tyngsboro, Massachusetts, Michael Smith and his wife, Alicia, of Hudson, New Hampshire, Chad Allen and his wife, Clarissa, of Bedford, New Hampshire, Laura Brooks and her husband, Joshua, of Waterville, Emily Allen and Katie Allen, both of Winthrop; 14 great-grandchildren.
A celebration of Stanton’s life was held on Thursday, October 15, 2026, at Hope Baptist Church, on Route 202, in Manchester. His burial will take place at Resthaven Cemetery, in Windsor, at a later date.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Washington AC Camp, in care of Pam Allen, 2 Deer Ln., Hallowell, ME 04347.
CARL W. BUTLER
PALERMO – Carl W. Butler, 93, passed away, in Rockland, on Wednesday, October 14, 2026. Born July 31, 1933 at his family’s farm on the West Meadow Road, in Rockland, he was the son of William W. and Beatrice Butler.
He was raised on the farm along with three siblings and graduated from Rockland High School in 1951. He then attended Gorham State Teacher’s College and graduated in 1955 with a Bachelor of Science degree in Industrial Arts.
Carl met Barbara A. Stevens from Portland, the love of his life, while attending college. They married on April 30, 1954, and were married for 66 years until her passing in 2020. Together they raised four children.
Carl began his working career as a High School Industrial Arts teacher in Kezar Falls, from 1955-1957 and then Howland, from 1957-1969.
He was an avid sportsman and loved hunting, fishing and trapping with friends and family members. He trained many beagles over the years that he enjoyed rabbit hunting with, especially his dog Scout. He owned several camps over his lifetime and spent many happy days enjoying life at the lake with family and fishing on Moosehead Lake.
Carl moved his family to the Detroit area of Michigan in 1967 for one year while he attended an Experienced Teacher Fellowship Program at Wayne State University where he studied pneumatics and hydraulics. One qualified person from each state was chosen to attend the program, Carl was chosen from Maine and earned his Master’s degree in 1968. Upon his return, he moved his family to Palermo, and began his career in the Maine Department of Education where he served as Industrial Arts Consultant, Director of Program Services and Finance for Secondary Vocational Education under Bill Cassidy until 1991.
Carl had a passion for cars beginning with his first car, a 1930s vintage Essex Terraplane. Over the years the family never knew what he might bring home for a vehicle, anything from a 1960s vintage Thunderbird to a ’67 Cadillac Coupe DeVille and everything in between! He loved working on cars and fixing them, and would often drive the car for a while before selling it. That passion turned into a business for him upon retiring and he opened CB Auto Sales; a used car dealership operated from his home in Palermo for more than 20 years. He retired from that business when he turned 80.
He and Barbara loved to travel when they could get a chance and went to Bermuda, Hawaii, California and Canada, often with family members or to visit family. In Barbara’s declining years he was faithfully by her side caring for her until her passing at age 86.
Carl was a loved and respected member of the community in Palermo. He often quietly helped those he saw in need more than anyone will probably ever know. He was a wonderful husband, father, grandfather, great grandfather, son, brother and friend to so many, extending to his family of in-laws, nieces and nephews and will be greatly missed.
Carl was predeceased by his parents; his wife Barbara; his brother William A. Butler, formerly of Camden; his sister Doris Stanely and her husband who was his good friend and business partner Gordon Stanely, both formerly of Glen Cove; and a grandson Christopher Costa, formerly of Liberty.
He is survived by his sister Maxine Philbrook, of Thomaston; his and Barbara’s four children, William ‘Bill’ Butler, II and his wife Linda, of Jefferson, Deborah Costa, of Liberty, Cynthia Spearin and her husband Stephen, of Appleton, Kimberly Brown and her husband Blake, of Palermo; his grandchildren; Kathleen Posey and her husband Justin, Daniel Boothby, Victoria Butler, Joseph Costa and his wife Julie, Anthony Costa and his wife Shannon, Allison Costa, Stephen Spearin and his wife Kimberly, Samuel Spearin, Alex Spearin and his wife Grace and Jeremy Brown; as well as 12 great-grandchildren.
Family and friends are invited to visit from 5 – 7 p.m., Wednesday, October 28, 2026, at Burpee, Carpenter & Hutchins Funeral Home, 110 Limerock Street, Rockland. A funeral service will be held at 11 a.m., Thursday, October 29, 2026, at Palermo Christian Church, 322 Branch Mills Road, Palermo.
While flowers are gratefully accepted, those who wish may make donations in memory of Carl and Barbara to the American Cancer Society, P.O. Box 6704, Hagerstown, MD 21741, or online at donate.cancer.org
To share a memory or condolence with the Butler family, please visit their Remembrance Page at www.bchfh.com.
JOHN E. GETCHELL
VASSALBORO – John E. Getchell, 69, passed away on Tuesday, September 8, 2026. He was born on April 1, 1957, in Waterville, to Frank A. and Eleanor S. Getchell.
His greatest joy was growing vegetables for his farm stand. Each summer, many customers looked forward to visiting and enjoying his produce.
He is survived by his companion, Kathy Brown; his brother, Frank, and Frank’s wife, Judy; his niece, Shannon Boyle; and his nephew, Sean Getchell.
A graveside service will be held at 11 a.m., on Saturday, October 24, 2026, at Village Cemetery, in North Vassalboro.
Others Departed
SHEILA DAVIS
WATERVILLE – Sheila Davis, 86 passed away peacefully on Sunday, September 27, 2026. Sheila was born in Waterville on July 5, 1940.
A memorial service will be held on Saturday, November 14, 2026, at the United Methodist Church, 37 Skowhegan Rd., Fairfield, at 12:30 p.m., followed by a gathering in the lower level from 1 – 3 p.m.
A comprehensive obituary detailing Sheila’s life story can be found by visiting Veilleux-Redington-Lawry Brothers website.
In lieu of flowers, the family request donations be made to the Alzheimer’s Association.
ERIC P. POULIN
WATERVILLE – Eric Paul Poulin, 67, of Waterville, passed away Sunday October 4, 2026, following an extended period of poor health. Eric was born on November 15, 1958, at Sisters’ Hospital, in Waterville. He was the son of David J. Poulin (Fairfield/Warren), and Virginia T. Poulin (Waterville).
Eric was a happy sweet little boy, and he carried his kind and tender heart throughout his life. As a boy, he would share anything he had, and he never took the last cookie, he’d always ask if someone else wanted it. He spent some of his early childhood in California where his family lived for several years. The family returned to Maine in the early 1970s and Eric completed his primary education in Waterville. He was especially bright, and loved to read. He graduated from Waterville High school and then went on to trade school. He attended Job Corps, at Husson College, in Bangor, and graduated with a degree in Machine Tooling. After graduating from Job Corps Eric worked as a machinist at Fisher Plow, in Rockland, for several years before returning to live and work in Waterville.
Eric worked a variety of jobs, and eventually became employed at Harris Bakery, in Waterville. He would work at Harris for several years up until they closed. It was at Harris that Eric met his “sweetie,” Linda Fairburn. They fell in love, and shared the next 30-plus years together. After Harris closed, Eric began working for McDonald’s as part of their maintenance crew. The favorite part of his time at McD’s was taking his morning break and having breakfast with some of the weekday morning regulars. Eric loved to tell stories, and hear stories from others. He retired from McDonald’s after having a heart attack in 2016.
He especially loved quick wit and sarcasm, and he took every chance he had to make a wise-crack. He would strike up friendly conversation with anyone. He was a big, loud guy with a tender heart. He was hard to stay in touch with because he wasn’t good at reaching out and even worse at calling back.
Eric was an avid reader until his vision made it difficult. He loved Science Fiction/Dystopian Literature; Douglas Adams, Isaac Asimov, Ray Bradbury. He loved Star Trek, Star Wars, he loved comics – DC not Marvel. He loved Bugs Bunny, the Beatles, the Green Bay Packers and George Carlin. He was a dreamer, with a big imagination.
Eric had the special quality of being able to connect with any animal he met. He loved animals, and enjoyed watching many of the amazing animal videos on YouTube.
He was a loving son, and called his mother every day. He was a kind big brother. He was loved and will be deeply missed.
Eric was predeceased by both of his parents.
He is survived by fiancée Linda Fairburn, of Waterville; his sister Lauren (Poulin) Ross and brother-in-law Rick Ross, also of Waterville.
The family plans a spring 2027 interment and will notify friends and family once plans are finalized.
DARYL DUMENY
NORRIDGEWOCK – Daryl Dumeny of Norridgewock passed suddenly on Monday, October 5, 2026. He was born in Skowhegan to Thomas and Aurilla (Hall) Dumeny.
He was raised in Norridgewock, and graduated Skowhegan Area High School. Daryl also spent several years in the Kansas City area. He returned to Maine and last lived in Norridgewock. Throughout the years, he was employed by various companies as a laborer. Daryl was a huge fan of the Kansas City Chiefs and New England Patriots, enjoyed fishing when he could and the company of family and friends.
Daryl is survived by his sister Chris Moen and her husband Don; sister-in-law Michelle Paquet; sisters Linda Haines, Betty Meader, Alison Haines and her husband Mike; brother Greg Paquet; sisters Mary Houle and Darcy Fortin; brother Terry Dumeny; sister Penny Pease; as well as numerous nephews and nieces.
Daryl was predeceased by his father Thomas Dumeny, Sr., mother Aurilla (Hall) Dumeny; brother Joseph Paquet Jr.; brother Thomas Dumeny Jr., and sister Luralee Wilbur.
Funeral services will be held on Saturday, October 24, 2026, at 1 p.m., at Sunset View Cemetery, Norridgewock.
PEGGY L. YORK WEYMOUTH
CLINTON – Peggy Lou York Weymouth, 84, passed away on Saturday, October 10, 2026. Peggy was born on January 1, 1942, in Skowhegan, to Dwight and Kathleen (Wilcox) York. From an early age, Peggy’s warmth and kindness touched everyone she met, leaving a legacy of love and compassion.
Peggy’s journey began in Clinton, where she attended school. She excelled both academically and athletically, participating in basketball, softball and the drama club. Her dedication and talent led her to graduate as valedictorian, after which she pursued higher education at Barrington College, in Rhode Island, earning a teaching degree.
In a love story for the ages, Peggy married her high school sweetheart, Timothy Weymouth, on July 25. 1964. Together they built a life filled with love and laughter raising two sons, Joel and Dennis. Peggy’s nurturing spirit extended beyond her immediate family, as she dedicated her career to educating and inspiring young minds. She returned to Clinton and taught throughout the state before finding her longterm home at Clinton Christian School, where she remained until her retirement.
Peggy’s faith was an integral part of her life. A devout Christian, she was a lifelong member of the Clinton Baptist Church. She shared her musical talents with the congregation singing solos and duets with her father, Dwight and serving on the music committee. Her dedication to the church community was evident in her involvement in the children’s vacation Bible school, where she brought joy and wisdom to many young lives with the Sunday School Charlie Stories.
Beyond her professional and spiritual pursuits, Peggy was an avid seamstress who found joy in creating beautiful pieces through crochet and knitting. Her talents were recognized at local fairs where she often brought home blue ribbons. She cherished her time with her sewing friends and delighted in knitting slippers for those she loved. Peggy’s culinary skills were equally celebrated with her baked goods becoming a staple of family gatherings and holiday celebrations.
Peggy’s love for classic cars was shared with her husband, Tim. Together they would often be seen driving their cherished 1961 Chevy Impala convertible to local Dairy Queens or participating in Lion’s Club parades.
Peggy was predeceased by her parents, Dwight and Kathleen York; in-laws, Lindell and Jerry Weymouth; and brother in-law, Stephen Weymouth.
She is survived by her husband of 62 years, Timothy Weymouth; brother-in-law and wife Terry and Candy Weymouth and Judy Weymouth-Davis; children, Joel Weymouth and wife Mary Jane, Dennis Weymouth and wife Tracy; grandchildren, Nicholas Weymouth and wife Sydney, Aaron Weymouth and wife Brooke, Andrew Weymouth and wife Zaria , Curtis Weymouth and wife Morgan, Jada Boggs, Nicole Savasuk, Zachary Savasuk and Frannie Higgins; and great-grandchildren, Natalie, Bellamie, Olivia, Lauren, Mason, Madelynn, Addison, and Isla; nieces and nephews Megan, Evan, Tyler, and Caroline and their spouses and children.
A service to celebrate Peggy’s life was held on October 19, 2026,at the Clinton Baptist Church, 10 Spring Street, Clinton, Maine 04927.
In lieu of flowers, the family kindly requests that donations be made to the Clinton Baptist Church Missions Program in Peggy’s memory.
WINSTON S. HIGGINS
BENTON – Winston Sidney Higgins, born February 2, 1942, to Clarence and Laura (Rowe) Higgins of Benton, Maine, passed away on Monday, October 12, 2026.
Winston grew up in Albion where he attended McDonald School. He shared a special bond with his identical twin brother Clifton, a connection that was such a meaningful part of his life along with seven other siblings, Ronald, Clyde, Clayton, Wayne, Freeman, Mike and Jeff.
Winston spent most of his career as a dairy farmer in Albion. Some of his proudest moments were spent with his children, especially his grandchildren, allowing them a wonderful playground of curiosity and the love of animals. Winston was also employed by Lee Brothers, of Albion, and was well respected. After many decades of farming Winston decided to retire, but not for long. He joined Nitram and maintained the winter plowing for the town of Albion, always stopping along the way to chat to a friend or two. He also served the town of Albion as Road Commissioner. And did he stop there? No, Winston went full-time at Johnny’s Selected Seeds where he worked in the warehouse alongside his daughter Sarah.
He had love for all children and was known as Papa to all, including any little friends that crossed his path. He took this role in his life very serious.
Winston is survived by the love of his life Rebecca (Creasey) Higgins of 64 years of marriage, Mark and Judy Higgins, of Sidney, Sarah (Higgins) and Mark Squire, of Albion, Danny Higgins ad Sean Weber, of Orrington, Laurie (Higgins) and Joseph Ball, of Albion, two brothers, Ronald and Linda Higgins, of Portland ,and Jeff Higgins, of Oakland; grandchildren, Nicholas Higgins (Passed), Jake Higgins and Kori Ellis, Lyndsey Weiss and Mike Chasteen, Ashley Ball and Micah Orenstein, Robert Weiss and Kendall Valesquez, Jesse Ball and Chelsea Whitmore, Lucas and Katy Higgins, Emily Higgins, Nicholas Weber, and Jeb Higgins; great-grandchildren, Deven Young, Bella Chasteen, Natalie Weiss-Maheu, Avery Ball, Jonah Orenstein, McKenzie Ball, Easton Higgins, Marley Weiss, Juniper Orenstein, Aubrey Weiss, and Peter Higgins.
Services will be held at the Albion Christian Church on Saturday, October 24, 2026, at 1 p.m.
In lieu of flowers or donation, please send to the Albion Christian Church Outreach Programs, Attn: Julie McKenzie.

title: The Latest: Supreme Court rebuffs Trump restrictions on medical care for trans inmates
text:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to allow the Trump administration to immediately enforce new medical restrictions for transgender people in prison. An executive order by President Donald Trump had called on the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care policies so that federal funds aren’t spent “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.” The new policy, blocked earlier by a lower court, would halt surgeries, taper off hormones and end social accommodations like makeup and wigs.
Meanwhile, Trump plans to visit South Carolina on Wednesday to boost U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, whose stumbles in her first campaign since replacing her late brother have Democratic voters hopeful — but not necessarily optimistic — that their candidate can break Republicans’ grip on the state.
Here’s the latest:
Vance says he will never endorse a foreign candidate again
The vice president was asked by a reporter to explain his comments in a recent interview that he wouldn’t endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection by claiming, “I endorse American candidates,” even though he endorsed Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban in the spring and even campaigned for him in Hungary.
Vance said he has endorsed only one foreign candidate for election and it “didn’t go particularly well,” as Orban lost the election.
But Vance went on and said that was in April and now, “We’re in the middle of an American election cycle where I’m very focused on candidates getting elected in the United States of America.”
He said he wasn’t attacking Netanyahu by not endorsing him but said, “I’m not endorsing any more foreign candidates now or in the future.”
Vance defends Witkoff calling Putin ‘a humanitarian’
Despite backlash from some of their fellow Republicans for Trump’s envoy calling the Russian President Vladimir Putin a “humanitarian,” Vance said, “I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.”
Witkoff made the comments as he thanked Putin for releasing an American who had been jailed for more than four years.
The vice president called Witkoff “a diplomat” and said he was in Russia to get a job done.
“I care much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family. We should all be celebrating that, not be complaining about what Steve Wikoff said in order to get it done.”
Vance says he’s ‘disgusted’ by GOP pushback to Acton ad, calls politics ‘a tough business’
Vice President JD Vance said it was “not really my concern” whether the ad was appropriate and said he’s focused on supporting Republican candidates in midterm races.
“I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” Vance said in his first public comments on the ad.
He added: “Politics is a tough business. And my message to my fellow elected Republicans is: If you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days.”
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s team took credit for the ad featuring the estranged mother of featuring of Amy Acton in the Ohio governor’s race.
Collins says ad attacking Jackson’s family should be taken down
Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins on Wednesday said a new ad calling her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson a “freak” and a “creep” because “he has two kids with his cousin” should be taken down.
The ad, which has attracted attention this week, is from the Senate Leadership Fund, which is backing Collins as she seeks reelection. Democrats are hoping Jackson will win the seat in their pursuit to take back control of the Senate.
Collins distanced herself from the ad on Wednesday, saying that the ad “should be taken down” and she “had nothing to do with that ad.”
In a Politico story earlier this year, Collins referenced Jackson having a relationship with his second cousin. Jackson’s longtime partner, Lana Pelletier, released an op-ed Wednesday criticizing Collins and her supporters’ attacks on her family, saying she never thought they “would stoop this low.”
Supreme Court rebuffs Trump administration restrictions on medical care for transgender inmates
The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to allow the Trump administration to immediately enforce new medical restrictions for transgender people in prison.
The decision leaves in place a lower-court block on the policy. It was adopted after an executive order from President Trump, who’s taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term.
Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas would have allowed the policy to be enforced.
The Supreme Court has previously allowed other policies for transgender people to move ahead for now, including restrictions on military service and passport sex markers.
Trump’s order called on the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care policies so federal funds aren’t spent “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.”
The new policy would halt surgeries, taper off hormones and end social accommodations like makeup and wigs. Prisons would continue to offer mental health services.
Rubio pushes back on criticism of Trump administration’s support for Ukraine in war with Russia
Rubio said Ukraine would no longer exist if it wasn’t for U.S. support.
Rubio’s comments to reporters in Mumbai, India, came as the administration has been taken to task for curtailing intelligence sharing and the supply of weaponry for Ukraine. He said the administration would no longer take such criticism without a response.
“We’re no longer going to be defensive about this topic. If it were not for the assistance of the United States, including under the Trump administration, there would be no Ukraine right now,” Rubio said. “Ukraine as a sovereign state would not exist.”
Rubio insists Ukraine’s issues with Starlink and Starshield had nothing to do with Trump
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insisting that President Trump and the U.S. government more broadly had nothing to do with interruptions to Ukraine’s access to crucial satellite data that Ukrainian officials say have compromised their ability to counter Russian attacks.
Speaking to reporters in India on Wednesday, Rubio said for the third time in four days that any throttling of network access to Ukraine was not directed or ordered by Trump or anyone else in his administration. He suggested, though, that the owner of the system, Elon Musk, may have been involved.
“What I can tell you with certainty is the president of the United States nor anyone in our system ever requested that any changes to that system be made, and that’s what we said repeatedly,” Rubio said. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk. That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”
Brother of former President George W. Bush endorses Democrat James Talarico in Texas US Senate race
That’s Neil Bush, the brother of one Republican president and the son of another, who authored a long Facebook post Tuesday night saying he voted early, and for Talarico over Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
Bush said his decision was two-pronged. Paxton’s past, particularly his spearheading of a failed lawsuit to challenge the 2020 election results, “was an affront to our democratic institutions,” Bush wrote. Those who have “enabled” Trump, he continued, “have done enormous damage to the Republican Party.”
Turning to Talarico, Bush noted that he’d never met the candidate, but that he’s been “enormously impressed” and has seen “integrity, civility, humility” and an openness to listen to those who disagree with him.
“I have been a Republican for most of my life, and I still believe deeply in many traditional Republican principles,” Bush wrote, “but character matters more than party affiliation.”
Lawmakers respond to Trump special envoy’s praise of Putin as a ‘humanitarian’
Some Republican lawmakers are reacting with dismay in response to Trump special envoy Steve Witkoff’s praise of Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian.”
“No. Putin is stone cold killer,” said Republican Sen. John Cornyn in a social media post on X.
“Another embarrassment,” said Republican Rep. Don Bacon, including a clip of Witkoff’s remarks, in his post.
“What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say,” said Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina. “You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a ‘humanitarian.’”
Witkoff’s description came as he thanked Putin for releasing an American who had been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.
Sen. Susan Collins makes campaign appearance with former Democratic Sen. Manchin
Collins made the campaign stop at a hot dog restaurant in Maine on Wednesday morning with former Sen. Joe Manchin as she tries to win reelection to her seat.
Collins, a five-term Republican senator, is in a tough reelection fight with Democrat Troy Jackson. Manchin touted her as a longtime moderate voice during a brief appearance after the morning campaign event.
Manchin, a longtime Democrat who became an independent shortly before retiring from the Senate, called Collins “the soul of the Senate.”
The two are also scheduled to appear at a New Balance sneaker facility in Maine later Wednesday.
In struggling LA, Mayor Karen Bass fights for 2nd term against democratic socialist-backed Raman
To voter Roy Lyons, Los Angeles has been losing luster for years. A homeless crisis endures despite billions of dollars of spending. City Hall’s budget keeps swelling — as do the taxes needed to support it.
As the retired insurance broker from the Sherman Oaks neighborhood ponders his pick in the upcoming mayoral election, he’s leaning toward the unpopular incumbent, Mayor Karen Bass, over her fellow progressive Democrat Nithya Raman, a little-known city council member who’s backed by the Democratic Socialists of America. She endorsed Bass before changing her mind and entering the race.
Neither choice gives him confidence about the future.
“Is this the best we can do?” asked Lyons, a Democrat, who attended a recent candidate forum. “I don’t think either one shines.”
If Bass wins the Nov. 3 election, it will be because she was able to persuade voters like Lyons to give her a second chance after a rough first term that included the deadly Palisades Fire, which ignited when she was out of the country and caught the fire department unprepared.
Putin agrees to resume trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US next month
Russian President Vladimir Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters after a meeting between Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff that the Russian leader has agreed “in principle” to resume the trilateral talks after Nov. 10.
Witkoff held talks with Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as Trump pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Justice Department watchdog declines to investigate handling of Reflecting Pool case, lawyers say
The Justice Department’s inspector general has declined to investigate the handling of the criminal case against a former Olympian cleared of accusations that he intentionally damaged the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, according to a letter Wednesday from the man’s lawyers.
The internal watchdog told David Hearn’s lawyers the allegations of professional misconduct they made fall outside its jurisdiction and are instead within the purview of the department’s Office of Professional Responsibility, according to the letter, which urges Inspector General Don R. Berthiaume to reconsider the decision.
“Given the substantial public attention devoted to this matter, and the significant questions raised concerning the conduct of federal officials, declining independent review would risk undermining public confidence in the Department’s ability to police its own conduct. Such a result would be inconsistent with the purposes for which Congress established the OIG and would be a betrayal of its mission,” the letter says.
Trump to host White House roundtable discussion on cybercrime
The White House says the administration is using every tool available to stop foreign-based organized criminal organizations that exploit Americans online.
According to data supplied by the White House, federal authorities have seized more than 500 fraudulent cryptocurrency investment websites.
They’ve also interrupted millions of social media, email and internet accounts used by foreign criminal organizations to hunt victims in America, and have identified and warned nearly 9,000 people while they were in the process of being victimized, preventing an estimated $562 million in losses.
Trump brings a last-minute rally boost to Darline Graham in South Carolina’s US Senate race
President Trump will visit South Carolina on Wednesday to boost Sen. Darline Graham, whose stumbles in her first campaign since replacing her late brother have Democratic voters hopeful — but not necessarily optimistic — their candidate can break Republicans’ grip on the state.
Although South Carolina isn’t typically a midterm battleground, Trump has been deeply invested in Graham. He supported her appointment to replace Lindsey Graham after his death in July, and he backed her in a special primary when she faced several more experienced Republican opponents.
Now the party wants to make sure Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee and a pediatrician, doesn’t pull off an upset victory. More than $34 million has flowed into the race, and Republicans have hammered Andrews as a “radical liberal” and accused her of supporting surgeries for transgender minors, which she denies.
Russia frees American Stephen Hubbard after over 4 years in prison, during a visit by US envoy
Russia on Wednesday freed an American who’d been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, in a deal completed during a visit by a top U.S. envoy and at a time when President Trump has taken a series of actions meant to benefit Moscow.
Trump said in a Truth Social post that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin during a phone call last week to free Stephen Hubbard, and that, unlike previous releases, his had not required the U.S. to give up anyone in return.
“Welcome home, Stephen, it’s great to have you back,” Trump said.
Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher from Michigan, was on his way home following a visit to St. Petersburg by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who also held talks with Putin about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as Trump pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he wants a ceasefire and permanent peace talks
The Ukrainian president told Fox News on Wednesday that he would agree to a ceasefire with Russia, freezing control of land as it currently stands more than four years since Russia invaded Ukraine, provided the U.S. provides security guarantees as a permanent peace deal is negotiated.
“Freeze and talks and security guarantees,” Zelenskyy said.
Still, Zelenskyy said during the interview that Ukraine does not want to yield any land permanently.
“They are not winning on the battlefield,” he said of Putin’s forces. That’s why Putin is trying to “push us from our land” at the negotiating table, Zelenskyy said. “It’s not fair.”
Ramaswamy takes responsibility for ad with Amy Acton’s mother and will spend millions to promote it
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy ’s team confirmed late Tuesday that it produced a controversial advertisement featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, and the campaign said it will spend $4 million to promote it despite facing bipartisan rebuke for dredging up the painful childhood of his Democratic opponent in Ohio’s governor’s race.
The decision exacerbates a deeply personal element in one of the country’s most closely watched and expensive campaigns for state office. Questions about the video will likely shadow Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire who previously ran for president but has never before held public office, in the final two weeks of the contest. Democrats said he was growing desperate at a moment when more than 676,000 people have already cast ballots in Ohio.
The advertisement features Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her “a liar” and insinuating she has mental health issues. Acton, Ohio’s former public health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather was indicted for raping Acton.
Acton spent Tuesday condemning Ramaswamy for the ad even before his campaign confirmed its provenance.
Trump and Vance announce $25M whistleblower program to encourage public to report alleged fraud
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday announced a $25 million program to encourage the public to blow the whistle on suspected fraud in the U.S. government as they ramp up efforts to end the abuse of federal programs and dollars.
The White House said that under the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, anyone who submits a tip that leads to a fraud conviction or a significant federal enforcement action is eligible to receive up to $30,000, and that the Justice Department will administer the program.
During the announcement, Trump said payments will amount to a 1% commission on the amount of fraud the tip helps uncover. Trump also said he will decide who gets reward money in cases where more than one person claims to have provided the tip.
“I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions,” Trump said in the Oval Office with Vance and other administration officials standing behind him. “It’ll be a binding arbitration.”

title: Interviews scheduled for new Vassalboro town manager
text:
After two hours of executive session discussion Oct. 14, Vassalboro select board members met for another hour in open session.
One executive session was for a discussion with the town attorney. The other was a discussion about hiring a new town manager.
The latter apparently went well, because afterward interim Town Manager Michael Roy reported that interviews with four candidates have been scheduled for Nov. 4 and Nov. 5.
Two candidates for the position of finance director were scheduled to be interviewed the week of Oct. 19. Select board members created an interview committee for this office consisting of Roy, board member Candy Clark, former bookkeeper Dawn Haywood and resident John Melrose.
All interviews will be in executive session, closed to the public, Roy said.
Haywood, though officially retired, continues to assist with town finances, Roy and board chairman Chris French said appreciatively. Office staff also have an assistant from a nearby town one day a week.
Board members voted at the Oct. 14 meeting to hire Pro Tree Service, of Vassalboro, to remove five selected trees in Union Cemetery and three in Oak Grove Cemetery, for $11,400.
French waived the procurement policy, which requires at least three bids, because only two companies bid. Pro Tree’s bid was $900 higher, but the company is local and is recommended by cemetery committee members, Roy said.
The vote was 4 to 1, with Dan Bradstreet opposed.
French listed items for future consideration:
— Requests for a review of the speed limit on Hannaford Hill Road and for consideration of a four-way stop at the intersection of Cross, Cross Hill, Hannaford Hill and Stone roads.
— Plans to replace the computer system at the transfer station – “It’s time for a change,” Roy agreed – and a check to see if the camera system is adequate.
— Consideration of infrastructure repairs, with reference to the fund voters approved at the June town meeting. The fund, to be built up to $200,000 in annual increments when there is money left over at the end of a fiscal year, is for “unscheduled repairs” to town-owned buildings.
Board member Michael Phelps added problems with trespassing and vandalism at the recreation fields, and the bigger issue of “how recreation has been functioning under the town umbrella.”
French said Vassalboro is still waiting to hear whether the town will receive a federal grant for replacing the Mill Hill Road culverts. Notice of the awards was postponed from August to October, he said.
The $200,000 grant previously awarded for part of the cost has expired, French said, while town officials focused on their hope for a larger award.
Roy reported to board members on things he has been dealing with as he familiarizes himself with ongoing issues and tries to help decide future town office staffing.
The next regular Vassalboro select board meeting is scheduled for 6:30 p.m. Wednesday, Oct. 28, in the town office meeting room.

title: Aroostook communities win fight to keep trash services
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Two southern Aroostook communities will keep their trash disposal arrangement with a nearby town after County leaders reversed a decision to terminate the agreement.
Aroostook County Commissioners voted Wednesday to restore the contract Benedicta and Silver Ridge townships have with Sherman, which provides them a site to dispose of solid waste.
The move restores a yearslong interlocal agreement and comes after the communities garnered more than 150 signatures on a petition to have their say in the decision. Residents cited concerns about costs, additional travel and difficulties for residents with limited transportation, according to County Administrator Justin Tibbetts.
“Many residents of these communities are elderly, and some members of the communities are Amish,” Tibbetts said in a memo to commissioners. “Residents expressed that requiring these individuals and families to travel farther and incur additional costs to dispose of household waste would create an undue burden.”
Benedicta, with a population of 227, and Silver Ridge, a community of 110, fall under the Aroostook County government umbrella as unincorporated townships.
Commissioners in August voted to terminate the agreement with Sherman, which would charge $71,000 for a year of service starting in November, and accept a lower-cost option with Northern Katahdin Valley Waste of Dyer Brook. The change was expected to save $60,000, according to commission minutes.
But residents pushed back and wanted to be involved in the discussion, Tibbetts’ memo stated. So he and Commissioner William Dobbins went to a Sherman Town meeting in September, at which Benedicta and Silver Ridge residents discussed the hardships of moving disposal services to Dyer Brook.
County leaders and Sherman officials renegotiated and Sherman shaved $10,000 from the cost. Tibbetts presented the revised contract Wednesday.
Commissioners Paul Underwood and Daniel Deveau noted concerns with the contract. Deveau urged officials to keep working to find less costly arrangements with other communities in the future.
“We cannot continue [with] what Sherman is doing, at these rates,” Deveau said. “To hold us hostage is not acceptable.”
Commissioners nonetheless voted to ratify the contract at a combined cost of $61,706, or $41,561 for Benedicta and $20,145 for Silver Ridge. The service will go from Nov. 17 this year to Dec. 31, 2027.
The new arrangement balances cost concerns and residents’ needs, according to Tibbetts’ memo.
“The revised agreement provides an opportunity to maintain an important and accessible service for the Benedicta and Silver Ridge communities while addressing the Commissioners’ original concern that the proposed 25% increase was not financially responsible,” he said.
Other business included appointing William O’Connell and Jacquelyn Clossey to two vacancies on the Aroostook Opioid Task Force and establishing electricity for Sinclair’s new fire station so construction can continue.

title: Madison schoolteacher receives $7,000 national award for innovative program
text:
MADISON, Maine (WABI) - A teacher in Madison is being nationally recognized as an educational champion for her community contributions.
Julie Wallace, a teacher at Main Street Middle School, was surprised with a $7,000 check presented by Voya Financial.
The national Unsung Heroes program awards $2,000 to select educators every year for their innovative teaching programs.
Out of this year’s 50 finalists, Wallace placed third overall, receiving an additional $5,000.
Wallace is behind the school’s “Aquaponic’s Workforce” program, which teaches students real-world food production skills.
“It’s still not really sinking in yet, but it’s exciting. This is how I would love to see school for everybody,” said Wallace, “The kids, you know, when they leave here, they can comfortably create their own system in their basement someday and grow their own food.”
“Her kids that are now in high school keep coming back and have the opportunity to continue to stay involved, beyond the middle school, which is fantastic,” said Doug Peters, Regional Vice President at Voya Financial.
Wallace says the Aquaponics Workforce program has also helped to provide lettuce to three surrounding communities.

title: Central Maine Growth Council new hire will support 'continuous growth'
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Central Maine Growth Council hired a finance expert to oversee grants and operations.
Leslie Wilson steps into a newly created position that will support “continuous growth,” the Waterville-based public-private economic development organization said in a news release this week.
That will include the expansion of the Dirigo Labs startup programs, as well as “broadening strategic projects across the region and state.” She will directly assist on projects of significant economic and community impact, with a focus on supporting projects that benefit municipal governments, empower the private sector and facilitate resources for startups and entrepreneurs.
“Big ideas get the headlines, but it’s the disciplined execution that turns them into new jobs, stronger downtowns and thriving startups,” said Garvan Donegan, president and CEO of Central Maine Growth Council.
“With the expansion of Dirigo Labs and major infrastructure and development projects ahead, Leslie’s background in financial management, grants and nonprofit systems will be invaluable. She will be instrumental in supporting key initiatives that benefit the local community, businesses, and Maine’s vibrant ecosystem of startups and entrepreneurs.”
Wilson has held key financial leadership roles, including serving as finance director for the Alfond Youth & Community Center. She earned an accounting degree from Thomas College in Waterville.
“It is an honor to join the dynamic team at CMGC,” said Wilson. “As a lifelong resident of central Maine, I have witnessed the revitalization of the region in a new and exciting direction, and I am excited for this opportunity to contribute to the effort.”

title: Russia and Ukraine agree to resume peace talks as American freed after four years
text:
Russia and Ukraine agree to resume peace talks as American freed after four years
Russia and Ukraine have agreed to resume U.S.-brokered peace negotiations following a meeting between Putin and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff, whose visit also secured the release of an American held in Russia for more than four years.
Russia and Ukraine agree to resume peace talks as American freed after four years
Russia and Ukraine have agreed to resume U.S.-brokered peace negotiations following a meeting between Putin and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff, whose visit also secured the release of an American held in Russia for more than four years.
Russia and Ukraine have agreed to resume U.S.-brokered peace talks as an American held in Russian custody for more than four years has been freed during a visit by President Donald Trump's special envoy, Steve Witkoff.
The developments follow Witkoff's meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who agreed in principle to restart negotiations. No date has been finalized, and Moscow has offered no publicly identified concessions on its territorial demands.
Stephen Hubbard, a retired Michigan teacher, was captured in Ukraine in April 2022 and accused by Russia of fighting for Ukraine, an allegation his lawyers dispute. His release occurred during Witkoff's visit, when the U.S. envoy expressed gratitude to Putin for freeing Hubbard.
"You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that," Witkoff said.
The comment drew criticism from some Republicans on Capitol Hill, including Sen. Thom Tillis, who called the remark "embarrassing and outrageous." Vice President JD Vance defended Witkoff's approach.
"I care much less about what Steve said and about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family. We should all be celebrating that, not be complaining about what Steve Witkoff said in order to get it done," Vance said.
Witkoff's broader mission during the visit focused on ending the war in Ukraine. A U.S. official said discussions with Russia included postwar security arrangements and an economic plan for Ukraine.
One of the biggest obstacles remains Russia's demand for Ukraine to give up territory, something Ukraine has refused to do. The next round of three-way negotiations could begin in November, but no date has been finalized.
A U.S. official described the discussions as constructive but did not identify any new concessions from Russia.
The test now is whether Putin is willing to abandon any of his demands or whether another round of negotiations will end without a breakthrough.
Separately, questions have arisen about restrictions on satellite services used by Ukraine's military.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, disrupting Ukrainian drone attacks and air defenses.
The restrictions limited how fast Ukrainian drones could travel while staying connected, affecting attacks on Russian targets and drones used to intercept incoming strikes.
The Journal reported that Musk discussed the decision with Trump, though accounts differ on whether the discussions occurred before or after the restrictions.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration did not request the slowdown and that he was not aware of the administration having advance knowledge of the decision.

title: UN projections say world is losing ground in fight to curb climate change, faulting US a bit
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says.
If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to Wednesday’s update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That’s about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year’s projections by the same science team.
“This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions,” the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas.
“In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation,” the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased like most European nations — added 189 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 70% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report.
The United States is going “hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it,” said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics that measures countries’ climate fighting plans. He wasn’t part of the U.N. report but like several other outside scientists said it was scientifically sound.
Shooting far past Paris climate goal
The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year’s projection.
Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact. The world is now at about 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees.
The world is falling “dangerously short” of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, “but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink.”
Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — “is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen.
“The report’s message is clear,” said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts. She wasn’t part of this study. “We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all.”
An added tenth of a degree of danger
Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century.
“This report shows that America’s retreat isn’t just a political embarrassment. It has real consequences for the planet and for millions of people around the world,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate organization. “An extra tenth of a degree might sound insignificant, but in climate terms it is enormous. It means more dangerous heat waves, more destructive floods, more failed harvests and more lives lost. For vulnerable communities in Africa, already living on the front lines of the climate crisis, every fraction of a degree matters. These are not abstract numbers. They are human lives.”
Hare said that extra one-tenth of a degree pushes an additional 140 million people “into dangerously hot conditions” and increases the odds of the collapse of the Amazon rain forest or ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. It also would cost the world and shave about $1.2 trillion from the global economy, said University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann.
And the U.S. effect is probably even bigger than what the United Nations calculates because if the world’s largest historical climate polluter doesn’t do much to fight global warming other nations ease off in their efforts too, said Johan Rockstrom, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany.
“The rest of the world is exhausted when it comes to counting the damage that the U.S. is willingly doing to allies, multilateral structures, economic cooperation, disaster relief,” Australian climate scientist Malte Meinshausen said. “The rest of the world should probably continue to focus even less on the U.S.”

title: MDI Football trounces Houlton 58-6
text:
BAR HARBOR — The Mount Desert Island High School football team looks to be heating up at the right time of the season, turning in a dominant performance against Houlton at home on Saturday with a 58-6 win over the Shiretowners. The Trojans have won their last two games in a row, and three of their last four, which includes a 50-20 win over rival Ellsworth.
The season did not start this way for MDI, with the Trojans dropping consecutive games against Old Town and Bucksport in the month of September and dropping their first game in October 60-0 against Yarmouth. Since that game, however, the team has looked unstoppable, outscoring Ellsworth and Houlton by a combined score of 108-26 behind a dominant ground attack.

title: Eighth-Grader's Double-OT Winner Highlights Madawaska Soccer Sweep
text:
The County Scoreboard: Eighth-Grader Delivers Double-OT Winner as Madawaska Sweeps Washburn
An eighth-grader provided the biggest moment of Tuesday's County soccer action, helping Madawaska pull out a double-overtime victory over Washburn as the regular season reaches its final day.
Dani Pelletier scored just 57 seconds into the second overtime to give the Lady Owls a 1-0 victory over the Beavers.
Madawaska's boys also picked up a win, defeating Washburn 6-1 behind a pair of goals from Josh Querze.
The two victories came with the regular season winding down and teams preparing for the start of tournament soccer later this week.
Girls Soccer: Pelletier's Double-OT Goal Lifts Madawaska Past Washburn
Madawaska and Washburn needed more than regulation and one overtime period to settle Tuesday's girls soccer matchup.
The two teams remained scoreless through regulation and the first overtime before eighth-grader Dani Pelletier delivered the game-winner just 57 seconds into the second overtime.
The goal gave Madawaska a 1-0 victory in one of the closest games of the final week of the regular season.
For Pelletier, it was a big moment at an important point in the season, providing the Lady Owls with a victory just before the postseason begins.
Boys Soccer: Querze Scores Twice in Madawaska Victory
Madawaska's boys completed the sweep of Washburn with a 6-1 victory.
Josh Querze led the Owls with two goals, while Aiden Gagnon, Oliver Pelkey, Bradley Kennedy and Ashton Guerrette each added one.
Owen Rackliffe scored Washburn's lone goal.
The Owls spread their scoring among five players in another strong offensive showing as the regular season draws to a close.
Soccer Playoffs Are Almost Here
Wednesday, October 21, marks the final countable day of the regular season, and the focus is quickly shifting toward tournament soccer.
For teams across Aroostook County, the next few days will bring the final standings, playoff seedings and tournament matchups.
The first regional preliminary games in eight-player soccer are scheduled for Friday, October 23, with preliminary games in the other classifications following Saturday, October 24.
Regional quarterfinals are scheduled for October 27 and 28.
There are plenty of County teams with reasons to be excited about the postseason.
Presque Isle's girls are looking toward a high seed in Class B North after an impressive regular season, while teams such as Caribou, Fort Kent, Houlton, Central Aroostook, Katahdin, Wisdom, Van Buren, Madawaska and several other County programs will be watching closely as their tournament positions are finalized.
Some teams will have an opportunity to host playoff games, while others will be preparing for road trips with their seasons on the line.
We'll have a closer look at the final standings, County tournament matchups and the games worth watching once the brackets are set.

title: Trump announces $8B plan to provide relief for farmers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH/Gray News) - President Donald Trump announced a new $8 billion program intended to provide temporary relief to farmers heavily impacted by rising fuel and production costs.
Trump made the announcement while speaking in Park City, Kansas, Monday. He was appearing at a rally in support of Sen. Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent who’s in a tight race with Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton.
During his speech, Trump said the program, called the Harvest Fuel Relief program, is “in support to offset diesel costs during this harvest season.” In a news release, the U.S. Department of Agriculture said it will make $8 billion available for one-time payments to farmers.
“This $8 billion investment will help bring certainty to our farmers during this harvest so they can continue to feed our nation,” U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brook Rollins said in the department’s news release.
It would be the second such relief package for farmers in 11 months after a $12 billion aid package was announced last December.
Kansas farmers said it was a mix of welcome news, but frustrations remain and expectations are measured.
While the president said that the $8 billion relief package is coming, Matt Splitter, a Rice County farmer, said he’s more concerned with fair markets and trade policy.
“When an administration does some retaliatory actions to places or other countries where we do source a lot of our inputs, you know, fertilizer being one of them, then it does put some, for agriculturalists, for farmers, it puts some unfair tariffs on the products that we rely on to raise a crop,” Splitter said.
Splitter said the timing of another relief package for farmers fits, as fall harvest and planting is well underway.
“This is our peak season. This is where a lot of our diesel is burned in our machines,” Splitter said.
The timing of the announcement is also not lost when it comes to the midterm election, which is two weeks away.
The relief program for farmers is among the latest financial promises from President Trump. Last month, he pledged to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and the Senate in the midterm elections.
The president repeated the promise during Monday’s speech in Park City.
President Trump also pushed for year-round E15, which is a big desire for corn farmers.
“With Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E-15 permanent. But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it. That’s it. I’m only doing it for him,” Trump said on Monday.
Splitter said his farm is just six miles from an ethanol plant and doesn’t believe the issue should be dependent on who wins the Kansas Senate race.
“The people are voting for who they want, whether it be Marshall or Hamilton, whoever it may be. But then the administration would be retaliatory to what the people have voted for. So I just, I’m not a big fan of that kind of retaliatory actions,” Splitter said.
The Kansas Corn Growers Association said it appreciates the Trump administration’s efforts to address the challenges facing Kansas farmers.
It added that the Harvest Fuel Relief program will help ease the burden, which it says includes signing year-round E15 into law.
