title: Reelect Jackie Sartoris as Cumberland County DA
text:
I met Jackie Sartoris in 2018 at an Augusta rally opposing Brett Kavanaugh’s Supreme Court confirmation. Then a prosecutor working in treatment courts, Jackie showed qualities I still admire: honesty, compassion and a belief that justice should serve people.
As Cumberland County’s district attorney, Jackie has turned those values into action. She secured $2.5 million to address the county’s sexual assault kit backlog. An inventory identified 620 untested kits dating back decades; more than 500 connected to police reports will now be tested.
Her office also partnered with public health officials and police in an effort that housed more than 400 people. She has stood firmly with immigrant communities and pledged accountability when federal agents violate the law.
I value Jackie’s willingness to have difficult conversations about public safety, justice and immigration. We need her principled leadership. Please join me in reelecting Jackie Sartoris for another term on Nov. 3.
Marpheen Chann
Candidate for Cumberland County Commission
Portland

title: Obituary: Glenna Jean Goulet
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND – Glenna Jean (Gauvin) Goulet, “The Dessert Lady”, passed away Oct. 17, 2026, after a courageous battle with cancer. She was born July 15, 1950, in Rochester, N.H., the daughter of Leo and Aline Gauvin of Somersworth, N.H.
Glenna graduated from Somersworth High School in 1968 and began work as a secretary at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, and moved to Maine in 1970 after marrying her high school sweetheart, Richard Leo Goulet. She was as a legal secretary before starting a family, after which she operated a cake decorating business in her home for eight years, an Avon representative for over 25 years, achieving President’s Club, and ran a crafts business, Calico Creations, for over 20 years.
Glenna was very loving and generous with her time. She became known as “The Dessert Lady” for all the church suppers at St. John the Evangelist Church, where she was a Eucharistic Minister, and St. Maximilian Kolbe Church for 29 years. She knitted hats, mittens and scarves for the homeless shelter in Portland, South Portland schools, and Social Services. She made baby Afghans for a Portland agency that helped single mothers, crocheted full-sized American Flag Afghans, which were raffled with all proceeds going to various worthy causes, and donated lap Afghans to Togus Veteran’s Hospital. She often cooked holiday desserts for the Preble St. soup kitchen, and holiday dinners for the elderly who lived alone.
Glenna’s priority in life was family. She loved and was proud of her family, witnessed by spending 21 years writing a book, “Our Family”, for her sons and later started another one titled “Call Me Crazy”. She enjoyed writing humorous children’s books based on true stories about animals, and did all the illustrations herself.
Glenna enjoyed reading, writing, scrapbooking, craft works, doing crossword puzzles, playing Scrabble, and loved to cook and bake for family, friends, neighbors, her church and the soup kitchen. She and husband, Dick, enjoyed spending time in the White Mountains of New Hampshire and going for walks along the beaches of Maine. They traveled to Alaska and Hawaii and to many of the great national parks, but their favorite vacation spot was Branson, Missouri.
Glenna is survived by her husband Dick, her three sons, Brian and his wife Tara of Portland, David of Indiana, and Christopher of Portland; one brother Leonard Gauvin and his wife Marcie of Goffstown, N.H., and several nieces and nephews.
Visiting Hours will be held from 6-8 p.m., on Friday, October 23, at the Conroy-Tully Walker Funeral Home of South Portland, 1024 Broadway, South Portland. A Mass of Christian Burial will be held at 11 a.m., on Saturday, October 24, at St. Maximilian Kolbe Church, 150 Black Point Road, Scarborough with a reception to follow.
To view Glenna’s Memorial Page or to share an online condolence, please visit http://www.ConroyTullyWalker.com.
In lieu of flowers, please consider a donation in Glenna’s name to the South Portland Food Cupboard.

title: Bobby Charles continues to allege wrongdoing by Hannah Pingree
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bobby Charles continues to allege wrongdoing by Hannah Pingree
Despite fact-checking by multiple media outlets, including Maine's Total Coverage, Republican gubernatorial candidate unveiled a six-part exhibit doubling down on claims that his Democratic opponent is involved in corruption.
Bobby Charles continues to allege wrongdoing by Hannah Pingree
Despite fact-checking by multiple media outlets, including Maine's Total Coverage, Republican gubernatorial candidate unveiled a six-part exhibit doubling down on claims that his Democratic opponent is involved in corruption.
On Tuesday in Bangor, the Charles Campaign unveiled six exhibits of what it calls corruption by Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree, including a claim we've already fact-checked.
"She was in the position of authorizing $840,000 to go in a forgivable loan," he said.
Charles is referring to a grant that was awarded to the nonprofit North Haven Sustainable Housing by MaineHousing.
The purpose of the grant, as stipulated by MaineHousing, was to build affordable housing in island communities.
15 island communities, including North Haven, are eligible.
Pingree was the president of North Haven Sustainable Housing and also the director of the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future at the time the grant was awarded.
MaineHousing is not part of that office and Pingree has never worked for MaineHousing.
State law allows a member of the governor's cabinet to also serve as president of a nonprofit, assuming they follow the state's conflict of interest laws and they do not financially benefit from it.
Federal tax documents for North Haven Sustainable Housing show the only paid employee of the nonprofit was the executive director in 2022.
That same document discloses the executive director, Sam Hallowell, is the domestic partner of Pingree's sister.
Pingree's father, Charlie Pingree, is also on the board.
Another grant issued in 2022 was given to the Island Institute. It was $37,458 as part of the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future's Community Resilience Partnership.
Charles claims that the Island Institute used that grant money for Pingree's husband, Jason Mann, to create short films.
Sue McKechnie, chief marketing officer with the Island Institute issued a statement at the time of Charles' first accusations.
"That allegation is false. No federal or state dollars were used by Island Institute for this film series, and we acknowledge the private funders at the end of the film. The Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future grants cited by the Charles campaign were restricted for work with Chebeague, Long Island and Monhegan, to enroll those communities in the Community Resilience Partnership," she said.
"It is still a matter of extraordinary bad judgment," Charles said.
In a statement from Pingree's campaign a spokesperson said, "this is a desperate stunt built on baseless allegations that the media, state government and Hannah Pingree have already knocked down. It’s also straight out of the Trump playbook: invent smears about your opponent so no one asks about your own record. Bobby Charles is a career lobbyist whose campaign took more than $50,000 over the legal limit, who is under Ethics Commission scrutiny, and who made voters wait months for his financial disclosure. He can’t run on his record, so he’s running from it.”
The six-part exhibit includes a 6 and a half minute documentary, allegations that work by the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future on climate raised electricity rates for Mainers and a jar of money along with claims that Pingree is receiving donations from Augusta lobbyists and Charles is not.
As Charles continues to make accusations about Pingree's family, Maine's Total Coverage asked about his wife, Marina, and the lobbying and consulting firm they run together.
"This is a false narrative that I want to say bluntly, 1% of what I ever did had to do with talking to the government," Charles said. "I'm just trying to say a lot of in the debates, that's the way they introduce me. It's a false bogey."
Charles continued to claim he's not a lobbyist but did not answer the question, so we asked again.
"It's not a Washington firm. We file and we pay taxes here, and she runs it, yes," he said.
The Charles Group is a private entity, so its tax forms are not available online. According to a federal form required for lobbying activities, in 2021 the company's address was in Washington, D.C. In 2025, the filing address was Bowdoinham, Maine.

title: 9-year-old boy attacked by stranger while waiting for school bus, police say
text:
HENRICO, Va. (WWBT/Gray News) - A Virginia woman is facing charges after she allegedly punched a 9-year-old boy in the face at his school bus stop.
Henrico Police say 47-year-old Marie Tulette Marsh approached Ratcliffe Elementary School students waiting at their bus stop around 7:30 a.m. Friday. She then allegedly attacked a 9-year-old boy she didn’t know as the bus was pulling up.
A nearby resident, who didn’t want to go on camera, said he ran outside after he heard the victim scream for help. He said he saw a woman punching the boy in the face. The man said he rescued the boy, brought him to his front porch and called 911.
Police arrested Marsh, who is now facing an assault and battery charge. Investigators say the victim suffered injuries to his face but is expected to recover.
Earl Thomas, who lives nearby, is still in shock to hear about what happened in his neighborhood.
“I was devastated,” he said. “My nieces and nephews grew up in this area, and they stayed at this bus stop. So, actually, it was devastating to know that anything like that would even happen in this area and at a bus stop.”
Ratcliffe Elementary Principal Joy Reed said this was an isolated incident. She said counselors are helping support the students who ride that bus, and she plans to visit the bus stop throughout the week to reassure students about their safety and monitor the situation.
For Thomas, the circumstances are making him more aware of his surroundings.
“I’m looking around more obvious to what’s going on at the bus stop,” he said. “It’s definitely bringing awareness. You can’t be too comfortable now.”
Online court records show Marsh is set to have a hearing on Dec. 14.

title: Josephine has formed, but it's still no threat to Maine
text:
Josephine has formed, but storm is still no threat to Maine
A storm that has been swirling off the east coast this week has taken on subtropical characteristics and been given a name by the National Hurricane Center. Subtropical storm Josephine will pass by Wednesday night into Thursday, bringing more clouds to Maine and gusty winds.
The hybrid storm is finally on the move, pushing north Wednesday night, bringing rain to Cape Cod while Maine misses out on the moisture. Clouds stream in Wednesday night into Thursday morning before pulling away Thursday afternoon.
Northerly winds pick up on Thursday as the storm starts to pull away. Gusts of 25 to 35 mph are likely, and it will stay blustery Thursday night and into Friday.
The dry stretch continues through the weekend and into next week. Lighter winds, plentiful sunshine, and seasonable temperatures will make for a nice fall weekend.

title: Feeding tubes aren’t a magic fix — what families need to know
text:
(Aging Untold) — Eating is about more than nutrition — it’s connection, routine, and dignity. When someone loses the ability to eat normally, families can be thrust into difficult decisions about feeding tubes, comfort and what comes next.
“It’s a bridge, not a magical answer”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, says the first thing families need to understand is what a feeding tube is actually for.
“The feeding tube is really just a bridge. It’s a bridge to give nutrients, medication, fluids when a person temporarily cannot feed themselves,” Rogers said. “I would look at it as a temporary thing depending on what their condition is.”
She explained that patients end up needing a feeding tube for many different reasons.
“Some people have had a stroke. They have difficulty swallowing. Sometimes they have neurological disorders or things like that, or head and neck cancers,” Rogers said.
Ask about the goal before you ask about the tube
Rogers said the real decision isn’t just whether to place a feeding tube — it’s understanding what the family is hoping it will accomplish.
“I think the family needs to understand what are their expectations from this, the route that you’re feeding, and what is the goal,” Rogers said. “Is this temporary ‘til somebody gets healthy, or do they have a disease that’s progressing and they’re not going to get back to a baseline level?”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck was direct about the limits of what a feeding tube can do.
“You need to understand, this is a medical option, not a magical answer,” Cradduck said. “It’s not going to cause you to learn how to swallow again. It’s not going to change the damage that cancer may have done to your throat.”
What caregivers need to watch for
Cradduck also laid out practical warnings for families caring for a loved one with a feeding tube at home.
“There are things that you have to look for. That insertion site can get infected very easy,” Cradduck said. “And if that tube pops out — and I’ve seen this happen even with caregivers — it’s got to be put back in, and you’d be shocked at how quickly that’ll heal and the tissue will cover.”
Her advice: Don’t wait.
“That becomes an emergent — we’ve got to get that back in. Don’t wait and see, or wait until somebody gets home, or wait until the next day, because then you’re having to have a procedure again,” Cradduck said.
A personal story changed one expert’s view
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, shared how watching her own family changed her perspective on feeding tubes.
“I had my whole view of feeding tubes change, watching my father-in-law. He had a feeding tube for seven years. My mother-in-law cooked three meals a day, pureed the food and fed him,” O’Rourke said. “They went on cruises. They danced. He became a special cook. We went out to fabulous restaurants. You forgot he had a feeding tube.”
O’Rourke said her earlier, more negative view came from her professional background.
She said having worked in an industry where people needed to gain weight, they would put feeding tubes in, and then the families wouldn’t know enough to have the conversation to take them out.
“So I saw a lot of people bedridden,” O’Rourke said. “It seemed to perpetuate a vegetative state rather than a living state.”
Rogers compared that misconception to how many people initially react to the word “hospice.”
“It’s the same impression people have when they hear hospice — they see it in a negative state, but not all the things that it encompasses. The same thing would be the feeding tube, because it can be just that bridge and be temporary,” Rogers said.
Ambrose said families should start the conversation early — and keep it open.
“It’s an important conversation to start talking about, and have a plan,” Ambrose said. “And by the way, you have the prerogative to always change your mind. It’s a good thing to be familiar with and kind of know what you think.”
Key takeaways
- A feeding tube can be a bridge to healing, not a magical cure.
- Know the goal before you decide. Families should clarify whether the tube is meant to support recovery to a baseline or to manage a progressing illness.
- Watch the insertion site closely. Infections can develop quickly, and a dislodged tube needs to be reinserted right away — don’t wait.
- A feeding tube doesn’t mean life stops. As O’Rourke’s family experience shows, life with a feeding tube can still include shared meals, travel and normal routines.
- Talk about it before you need to. Discuss expectations and a removal plan before insertion, and remember you can always revisit the decision.

title: Man who eluded police in Rumford arrested in southern Maine
text:
A man who prompted police to issue a shelter-in-place order and surround a Rumford apartment last week only to find no one home, has been arrested in Westbrook.
Rumford and Maine State Police held the empty standoff on Oct. 14 after the department got information about suspected drug trafficking in an apartment on Waldo Street, along with complaints that people associated with the apartment had been periodically shooting guns in the neighborhood.
At the time, they announced the suspect as Blake Lachance, 21, of Lewiston, and alluded to additional suspects. Law enforcement subsequently brought in the Maine Violent Offender Task Force, which is led by the U.S. Marshals Service.
On Wednesday, the Marshals Service announced that Lachance had been arrested Tuesday, at a residence in Westbrook. Police had previously obtained a warrant for Lachance’s arrest on multiple felony state charges, including aggravated assault, aggravated reckless conduct and criminal mischief.
The Marshals Service said Lachance tried to flee but was apprehended without incident.
Multiple other state, local and federal law enforcement agencies were involved in the search and arrest, including the Homeland Security Task Force, Lewiston Police Department, Westbrook Police Department, Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office, and Southern Maine Regional SWAT team, which is led by the South Portland Police Department, according to the Marshals Service.
Lachance is awaiting his initial appearance on the state charges, according to the service.

title: Macron calls claims by Trump and others blaming Muslim migrants for French riots ‘stupid’
text:
PARIS (AP) — French President Emmanuel Macron said Wednesday that foreign leaders — including those “on the other side of the Atlantic” — were seeking to exploit France’s tense social climate for political gain following a weekend of street violence and looting.
Protests over soaring living costs have led to widespread rioting and looting that have drawn worldwide attention and shocked many French citizens. U.S. President Donald Trump has used the violence to rally his political supporters, making unsubstantiated claims that Muslim migrants are responsible for the unrest, and urging Macron to “close your borders and take control before it is too late!”
Macron responded by saying there “has been foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath” of the looting in Paris and other French cities last weekend. “And that has led to comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders,” he said.
Asked by a reporter if he was referring to Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.” He added that there have been “AI-generated images depicting scenes that never actually happened in France. We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false.”
Macron did not specify which AI-generated images he was referring to, nor how he knew the content was false.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said his office can provide the countries concerned with the necessary clarification, “to help them avoid spreading or amplifying false information and making baseless claims on social media.”
Macron and Trump once enjoyed a good relationship but Trump regularly mocks the French president in his public speeches.
“The fact is, all the people who are speaking ill of our country right now are people who don’t love our country,” Macron said. “So those people really bother me.”
“When I see leaders who are in the middle of election campaigns, whether in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic — who sometimes naively repeat AI-generated content or spread narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote about what happened in France — they’re using our country for their own political campaigns,” said Macron. “And we don’t need that.”
Macron secures diesel supplies
Macron was speaking in Qatar at the end of a tour of key energy suppliers in Gulf Arab states, where he secured an additional 100,000 metric tons of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates, with a further 100,000 tons to be confirmed in Bahrain.
Macron’s office said he traveled to the Middle East to find solutions to the energy crisis and rising energy prices, and to secure supplies of oil, gas, diesel and jet fuel.
The Élysée said nearly 295,000 additional tons of diesel per month could be secured, including supplies from Saudi Arabia — equivalent to more than 10% of France’s monthly diesel consumption. Macron later traveled to Saudi Arabia to meet Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman “to continue efforts to secure and diversify oil and gas supplies,” according to his office.
Earlier this month, the Group of Seven wealthy democracies agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products, beginning with substantial quantities of diesel after the fuel’s price hit a record high in the United States.
“I would remind you that France initiated the G7 meeting that led to the release of strategic reserves, which, through implementation at the national level, will help bring down prices starting in early November,” Macron said.
New protests planned in France on Thursday and Saturday
Petrol, energy and food prices have surged in recent months, and it remains to be seen whether Macron’s announcement will ease protesters’ anger. He said the additional diesel supplies addressed “some of the anxieties.”
“I also hear the concerns of our high school and university students. Those concerns stem from other factors, but in any case, I think things are moving in the right direction,” he added.
High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools, dilapidated facilities and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighborhoods. Some also say school days, which often run from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., are exhausting and the university admissions system is complex and unfair.
France has had two consecutive quiet nights since the weekend’s unrest. Curfews have been imposed in parts of several major cities, including small areas of Paris.
Further protests are planned for Thursday and Saturday following calls from student unions and groups within the “yellow vest” movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019.
Paris police said Wednesday they would ban Thursday’s planned protest in the French capital, citing concerns for public safety and the protection of property.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who met union representatives on Wednesday, said a “massive” security operation was planned for Saturday to prevent a repeat of the violence by small groups of rioters that had exposed shortcomings in security measures.
“We are using the legal means at our disposal to prevent further incidents of this kind,” Macron said. “Those who intend to cause disturbances in city centers next Saturday will be prevented from doing so. Tomorrow, we will also have a very detailed update on the implementation of these measures, including anticipation, intelligence gathering and security, not just for Saturday, but also for the coming weeks.”

title: Obituary: Sister Arline Gaudette
text:
BIDDEFORD – Sister Arline Gaudette, also known as Sister St. Joseph of Providence, died Oct. 16, 2026, at the age of 99 at the Good Shepherd Convent in Biddeford. Arline was born August 23, 1927, in Lawrence, Mass., to Genevieve Doiron and Peter Gaudette. She was the youngest of seven children. Arline received her education in the public schools of the Lawrence, Mass., area.
In August 1946 she joined the Congregation of the Servants of the Immaculate Heart of Mary (also known as the Good Shepherd Sisters of Quebec) in Biddeford. She had a long career as a teacher in Lawrence and Methuen, Mass., as well as in Old Town. For many years she also was a “housemother” at St. Ann’s Orphanage caring for the children and teaching them such skills as woodworking. Sister Arline’s love of God has always been expressed through her love of music which she shared through the children’s choir in her parish.
When she “retired” in Biddeford, she sewed for the sisters and spent time creating amazing quilts, runners, and handbags. Sister Arline is remembered for being kind, energetic and attentive to other’s needs; she made friends wherever she lived and worked.
Sister Arline will be missed by her religious community, her nieces, nephews, and her many friends. She was ready to meet her Maker and eager for Him to welcome her home.
The Mass of Christian Burial will be celebrated at Most Holy Trinity Church in Saco on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026, at 11 a.m.
Visitation will be held from 10 to 10:45 a.m., in the church. The burial will be at St. Joseph Cemetery, Biddeford.

title: Council approves MOU's for YMCA, Downeast Transportation funding
text:
BAR HARBOR — As part of the changes made to the process for providing funding to outside organizations during last year’s budget cycle, the town announced that it would be entering into a Memorandum of Understanding with three organizations that receive an outsized share of municipal dollars annually compared to other community organizations: the Jesup Library, Downeast Transportation, and the Mount Desert Island YMCA. Now, on the eve of discussions involving the latest budget cycle, two of those MOUs have been approved following a vote by the town council at its regular meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 20, dealing with funding for Downeast Transportation and the MDI Y.
But questions remain regarding some of the responsibilities attached to the funding provided by the town, namely the safe transportation of students from Conners Emerson to after-school programming hosted throughout the school year by the Y. Members of the town’s Superintending School Committee have been advocating for a return of a YMCA bus service that they claim was a requirement built into previous funding arrangements between the Y and the town that had not been fulfilled for some time.

title: Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik has not endorsed Susan Collins
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Gail Dana, an elder tribal citizen, lives in the Passamaquoddy community at Sipayik. A published author, she actively advocates for truth telling, a healthy tribal community and effective and responsible governance.
One should never celebrate too soon, certainly not before the votes have been counted. The Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik has not, in fact, endorsed Sen. Susan Collins, as reported recently by the BDN. The tribal community and the tribal governing body determines the chief’s role and authority through tribal law. The chief of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik is not authorized to endorse political candidates on our behalf.
Here I offer tribal citizens and the citizens of the State of Maine a tribal perspective shaped by deep knowledge of the legacy and impact of tribal, state and federal governance systems on tribal communities. We understand that elected officials are chosen to first serve the interests of the collective. They are expected, not as individuals, but as a governing body to deliberate carefully and to act in the tribe’s best interests. The governing body enacts tribal law and we expect them to abide by it.
Since the 1980 settlement act, the limits of tribal authority have been specifically circumscribed by federal and state law. The Passamaquoddy Tribe was recognized as represented at that time by the Joint Tribal Council (JTC) of the Passamaquoddy Tribe with separate councils at Pleasant Point/Sipayik and Indian Township/Mdocmeegook. Certain authorities continue to be retained by the Joint Tribal Council, while each community, as a political subdivision, is administered by its own chief and council.
In general, tribal governments function as municipalities under state law, except that “internal tribal matters including … tribal organization, tribal government and tribal elections … [are] not subject to the jurisdiction of the State.” In 1990, the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sibyig officially adopted a body of law approved by referendum, now known as the Sipayik Constitution, that circumscribes the role and powers of the chief at Sipayik.
Tribal law requires the chief of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik to chair meetings of the governing body, to implement its policy decisions and retain primary administrative responsibility for tribal government operations. The chief must act in accordance with policy decisions made in tribal council meetings, open to all tribal citizens. As in any responsible, accountable government, the chief’s power and authority are limited. The chief carries out the will of the people in consultation with the tribal council.
We all deserve governments that honor and respect the dignity of every single person. Our tribal traditions and the instructions in our language direct us to each be fully responsible for the decisions we make. We place a high value on each person’s right to choose. We vote to register our support for the candidate that aligns with our most closely held values. Each individual tribal citizen who votes in state or federal elections has the right and responsibility to choose their best candidate.
We do not share that responsibility with tribal government. The right to vote and to make your choices known in state and federal elections arises solely from the recognition of individual U.S. citizenship, completely independent from any tribal citizenship or affiliation.
State and federal elected officials often publicly endorse and sometimes campaign for candidates for positions in those governments. The tribal chief has no standing in those systems. The tribal chief’s role as spokesperson for the tribe, circumscribed by the authority granted to the chief by the people and the tribal council, does not include endorsement of any candidate for office on behalf of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sibyig. Absent direction by the tribal community or its governing body, the chief does not have the authority to speak for the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik.
Neither tribal citizens collectively nor the elected tribal government at Sipayik has taken a position on any candidate currently running for state or federal office. We each alone must make the decision to give our vote to the one who believes in us and we in them.

title: Putin agrees to resume trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US next month
text:
Putin agrees to resume trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US next month
President Vladimir Putin agreed Wednesday to resume trilateral negotiations with Washington and Kyiv on ending the war in Ukraine, a Kremlin official said.
Related video: Imprisoned US man freed by Russia after Witkoff visit
Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters after a meeting between Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff that the Russian leader has agreed “in principle” to resume the trilateral talks after Nov. 10.
THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below.
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as U.S. President Donald Trump pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Witkoff said in televised remarks at the start of the meeting that he hoped to discuss the resumption of the trilateral talks involving the U.S., Russia and Ukraine that would allow the technical teams to discuss the next steps toward a peace settlement.
Putin thanked Trump and Witkoff for their efforts to end the war.
The talks lasted about three hours, the Kremlin said. None of the participants made any immediate comment afterward.
The visit came a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and some European leaders in Norway's capital, Oslo.
Witkoff’s meetings suggested leaders are keen to bring new momentum to U.S.-led peace efforts, more than 4½ years after Russia’s army launched an all-out invasion. Efforts by the Trump administration since early last year to end the war have made no significant progress, and there was no suggestion of an imminent breakthrough.
Russia and Ukraine are still far apart in their terms for a settlement, as their armies remain locked on the battlefield and they pummel each other with daily long-range strikes.
However, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said late Tuesday that the Oslo meeting, which he attended, “made genuine progress.”
Zelenskyy said that freezing the conflict in Ukraine was the “minimum” required from Russia to bring about an end to the war.
“Right now, we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war,” Zelenskyy said in an interview broadcast Wednesday on Fox News.
Witkoff sees ‘some degree of momentum’ in peace efforts
Witkoff and Putin met at St. Petersburg’s Constantine Palace, with Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Putin’s foreign affairs adviser, Yuri Ushakov, also at the table. Witkoff said Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, was due to join the discussion via a video link.
Before the talks, Witkoff said that he would inform Putin about Tuesday’s meeting in Oslo, which he described as “productive,” adding that “there is some degree of momentum.”
He thanked Putin for lifting Russia’s ban on diesel exports, which angered some U.S. lawmakers, adding that it would help reduce prices for U.S. farmers and truckers.
Putin said that he was ready to consider prospects for the restoration of U.S.-Russia economic ties, adding that he's also prepared to discuss the U.S.-led conflict with Iran. Moscow is ready to use its special relationship with Tehran to help bring peace, he said.
Russia on Wednesday released a retired American teacher who had been imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, Witkoff said, in what appeared to be a goodwill gesture by the Kremlin after Trump asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard.
Putin was also due to meet Wednesday with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, who was in St. Petersburg meeting with other Russian top officials, the Kremlin said.
Russia has cultivated its ties with China, and the two countries last month vetoed a U.S. proposal for U.N. experts to keep monitoring sanctions on Iran.
Norway's prime minister sees a possible ‘new phase’ in talks
Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations after his trip to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.
“I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy,” Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday.
Zelenskyy was still in Oslo on Wednesday, where he visited Norway's parliament and met with lawmakers.
Witkoff appeared to be making another attempt at overcoming hurdles that have kept a deal out of reach.
Zelenskyy said Tuesday that on the agenda were future security guarantees for Ukraine, the fate of occupied territories, postwar reconstruction and the possibility of a ceasefire.
Trump said Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a ceasefire in attacks on energy infrastructure. But Russia has kept hammering Ukraine’s power grid and Kyiv has hit Russian oil refineries.
Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war.
Trump presses Zelenskyy to compromise
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Tuesday that Moscow is willing to listen to new U.S. proposals about Ukraine, but he doesn’t expect any “miracle” from Washington.
At the White House on Tuesday, Trump increased the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two leaders have soured again.
“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”
If that doesn’t happen, “I think it’s going to be a very bad thing,” Trump said.
Amid fears that Washington was turning its back on Ukraine, Zelenskyy said Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles, after recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice from allies.
The change happened after Zelenskyy spoke with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Russian attacks kill 5 people and wound 25 others, Ukraine says
Overnight Russian attacks in Kyiv left three people dead and 12 wounded, while 10 residential buildings were damaged, the city’s military administration said.
Energy facilities were targeted in Kyiv and three other cities in Russian attacks early Wednesday, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. Outside the eastern city of Kharkiv, two people died and 11 others were wounded when drones exploded in a residential area, he said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said that overnight its forces struck a warehouse, an electrical substation and a bulk carrier at sea that was headed to the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
The Russian Defense Ministry reported Wednesday that its air defenses intercepted 373 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula and the Black Sea.

title: Man sentenced to 30 years for role in smuggling tragedy that killed 53 people in Texas
text:
(AP) - A federal judge on Tuesday sentenced a Guatemalan man extradited to the U.S. over his role in a 2022 human smuggling attempt that ended in the deaths of 53 migrants who had been transported in a sweltering tractor-trailer in Texas.
U.S. and Guatemalan prosecutors called Rigoberto Ramon Miranda Orozco’s sentencing another step toward justice in one of the deadliest smuggling attempts along the U.S.-Mexico border. Miranda Orozco, 50, was sentenced to 30 years in prison after admitting to arranging travel and accommodations for two people who died and another who was seriously injured.
Nearly 20 people in the U.S. and Guatemala have been convicted since the discovery of the abandoned trailer full of bodies horrified communities accustomed to seeing their young people leave, trying to flee poverty or violence in Central America and Mexico.
“It was clear that they suffered tremendously in their last few hours on this earth,” U.S. Attorney Justin Simmons told reporters at a news conference following the sentencing.
People tried to ‘claw their way out’ of a trailer with no air conditioning
The trailer’s air conditioning malfunctioned and would not blow cool air to the people trapped inside during the sweltering, three-hour ride in June 2022 from the border city of Laredo to San Antonio, authorities said. Prosecutors have said migrants paid up to $15,000 each to be taken across the U.S. border.
When the abandoned trailer was opened on a remote San Antonio back road, 48 migrants were dead. Another 16 were taken to hospitals, where five more died.
Simmons said investigators found clothing passengers had shed to cool off and claw marks on the trailer’s walls.
“They were literally trying to claw their way out,” he said.
Twenty-one of those who died were from Guatemala, Simmons said.
Miranda Orozco’s attorney, Alfonso Cabanas Jr., called the sentence “very tough.” He said his client was in Guatemala at the time and had no control over the type of transportation the migrants would take to San Antonio nor did he know the air conditioning was malfunctioning.
Cabanas said he doesn’t think harsh punishments will “make a dent” in such operations.
“What we do need is comprehensive immigration reform,” Cabanas said.
Other defendants still await sentencing
U.S. District Judge Orlando Garcia sentenced Miranda Orozco, who was arrested in Guatemala in 2024 and extradited to the U.S. the following year.
He pleaded guilty in July to conspiracy to bring a migrant into the U.S. resulting in death, aiding and abetting bringing a migrant into the U.S. resulting in death, as well as aiding and abetting bringing a migrant into the U.S. resulting in serious bodily injury, prosecutors said.
Simmons said prosecutors in Guatemala were integral in securing convictions for Miranda Orozco and others. Simmons was joined by Guatemalan Attorney General Gabriel García Luna, who reflected on the suffering the migrants inside the tractor-trailer endured.
“They paid for a promise, and those who cashed in on that promise abandoned them to their fate,” García Luna said.
Last year, Felipe Orduna-Torres, described by prosecutors as the leader of the smuggling operations inside the U.S., was sentenced to life in prison in the U.S. Armando Gonzales-Ortega, his top assistant, was sentenced to 83 years.
Sentencing dates have been set for more people, including the truck’s driver.
The tragedy is the deadliest among those that have claimed thousands of lives in recent decades as people attempt to cross the U.S. border from Mexico. Ten migrants died in 2017 after they were trapped inside a truck parked at a Walmart in San Antonio.
In 2003, the bodies of 19 migrants were found in a sweltering truck southeast of San Antonio.
___ This story has been updated to correct the name and age of the man sentenced Tuesday. He is Rigoberto Ramon Miranda Orozco, not Rigoberto Román Miranda-Orozco. And he is 50, not 39.
___
Associated Press writer Laura Turbay contributed to this story.

title: Here’s why Alabama’s governor commuted the death sentence of a man convicted of killing a sheriff’s deputy
text:
MONTGOMERY, Ala. (WSFA/Gray News) - Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey commuted the death sentence of a man convicted of killing a sheriff’s deputy.
Toforest Johnson’s sentence was commuted to life in prison with no chance of parole.
“We are grateful to Governor Ivey for diligently reviewing Toforest’s case and taking action to spare an innocent man from execution,” said Ty Alper, one of Johnson’s attorneys. “This significant milestone was made possible by Alabamians from all sectors of society united in their belief that Toforest does not belong on death row. That list now includes Governor Ivey.”
Johnson was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1995 capital murder of Jefferson County Deputy Sheriff William Hardy.
Johnson was sentenced in 1998 and has spent more than half of his life on death row. He is currently housed at Holman Prison in Atmore, Alabama.
In a statement, Ivey raised concerns about the amount of evidence against Johnson, questioning whether it was sufficient to carry out his sentence. However, she did not say she thought Johnson was innocent.
Johnson’s attorney said his client is innocent.
“Now it is up to the courts to overturn his conviction and grant him a new trial. We will keep fighting until he is home with his family,” he said.
In 2024, Jefferson County District Attorney Danny Carr pushed for a new trial. In 2025, former Alabama Attorney General Bill Baxley, along with a group of former Alabama state and federal prosecutors, asked a judge to grant Johnson a new trial.
There are currently 154 people on Alabama’s death row. Johnson was still listed on the Alabama Department of Corrections’ website as on death row at the time of Ivey’s announcement.

title: Family of 5-year-old killed in school shooting asks the world to draw for him
text:
Family of 5-year-old killed in school shooting asks the world to draw for him
Rhoam Summer, the 5-year-old who was among the four victims fatally shot at an Oregon elementary school, is the youngest person ever killed in a deliberate mass attack at a US school, according to his family’s attorney and experts who track school shootings.
The littlest victim, his two classmates and a teacher were gunned down by a former student Thursday in a classroom dedicated to children with special needs at Silver Rail Elementary School in the central Oregon city of Bend.
It was 36th shooting in the United States this year on K-12 school grounds, according to analysis of multiple databases, including the Gun Violence Archive.
Related video above | Safety experts weigh in on additional measure schools could take to prevent or delay a shooter from gaining entry
“Sadly, and maybe callously, I’m not optimistic there are going to be any meaningful changes,” David Riedman, an Idaho State University assistant professor and data scientist who founded the K-12 Shooting Database, said of gun violence in US schools.
Rhoam is the youngest victim in 176 planned, gun-related attacks at schools since 1966 – in which 762 people were killed or wounded, including the four deaths at Silver Rail, according to Riedman’s research. Teacher Megan Lambert was killed along with Rhoam and two others, aged 8 and 11, police said. Reidman’s database includes incidents in which in a gun is fired, brandished or in which a bullet strikes K-12 school property.
School shootings in the U.S. have declined for the past two years and the same is expected this year, according to Riedman’s research. In 2025, his data showed 235 school shootings compared to a peak of 352 in 2023.
Mass shootings at elementary schools are rare, experts say.
“It’s rarer than high schools because the children are younger, and most school shooters are between 13 and 17. So they’re usually either middle school or high school students, but there are a fair number at elementary schools, too. It’s about half are at high schools, and then about a quarter at elementary, and a quarter are at middle schools,” Riedman said.
A group of attorneys retained by Rhoam’s parents, in a statement, said the boy is the youngest person ever killed in a US school shooting.
“No child should have to experience or worry about violence in their school or parent fear for the safety of their kid in school,” one of the attorneys, Tim Williams, said Tuesday.
“You would expect it more to happen at a high school as opposed to a grade school. It’s just these poor parents that have really no inkling of caution because your kid’s entering kindergarten. You’re not going to think your school’s going to get shot up if your kid’s in kindergarten. I don’t even have words for it,” Williams added.
In a statement, Rhoam’s parents, Kelik and Lillian Summer, recalled his kindness.
“Anytime there were guests in our home, he would pull out cups to get everyone drinks or make sure everyone had a snack or make sure everyone had a stuffy to cuddle,” the parents said. “He wanted to share everything he had. His heart knew no limits and it grew with him every single day. We were so proud of who he was and who he was growing to be.”
His parents asked people to draw in his honor.
“Rhoam was not a child art prodigy, but he had the purest heart and he put love into every scribble, splash or paint, or smashed leaf he tried to shape,” they said.
Last Thursday, a 16-year-old shooter forced his way into the Oregon school by firing into the glass panes of an external set of doors, according to police. He was identified as Griffin J. John II, a former special needs student at the school, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.
A teacher, who was not injured, threw her cellphone at the shooter, tackled him and tried to get the gun, the police chief said. Kaylub Giamanco, whose children attend the school, followed the suspect and shot him to death.
Becky Drury, a 54-year-old inclusion educational assistant from Bend, and Saylor Graham, 7, were injured in the shooting.
The two deadliest elementary school shootings in the US involved victims between the ages of six and 11. At the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting in Newtown, Connecticut, a former student on December 14, 2012, killed six adults and 20 children, who were 6 and 7 years old. In 2022, the 19 children killed at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, were between 9 and 11 years old.
“With Sandy Hook, it didn’t make a difference, much of a difference really,” James Alan Fox, a professor at Northeastern University who, with USA Today and The Associated Press, helped create the Mass Killing Database, said of stemming gun violence in schools.
“We had lots of young children killed in Uvalde. It didn’t make a difference. The fact this boy is the youngest, I guess you could say it will have an effect, but really no difference in substance in terms of five versus six, versus seven versus eight. And for the families, it doesn’t matter, obviously.”

title: Legislative response to AI is already overdue
text:
Jake Plante is a resident of Brunswick and author of the book “Uncle Sam and Mother Earth: Reflections on the Environmental Movement and the Role of Governance.”
Although I really can’t fathom how AI could destroy human civilization in a matter of years, the dire warnings from AI developers are enough to get me to sit up and pay attention.
But there’s something Silicon Valley isn’t saying. It’s something that offers a ray of hope for our collective management of AI risk.
As best as I can tell, the AI threat to humanity centers around its ability to percolate through and take over the internet. The internet is AI’s breathable atmosphere.
So wouldn’t it make sense to reexamine our reliance on the internet?
Much of our critical infrastructure, including financial services, energy management, government records and communication systems, is now inextricably woven to the internet. And it just keeps on progressing in this direction. Banks, stores, medical services and the business world at large are constantly pushing us to conduct our transactions online.
Relying on the internet as our economic backbone is great — until it isn’t. The internet offers major efficiencies but the downside is that it leaves us vulnerable. I’m reminded of this every year when I receive a written letter apologizing for the seizure of my personal data by hackers.
A similar trade-off exists with the electric grid. Power interruptions are happening more frequently due to rough storms. The result is a growing lack of user confidence in reliable service and the considerable cost to families if they lose heat or have to replace spoiled foods. The answer for many has been to acquire back-up generators.
Having back-up systems to the internet is one option to protect us against an internet takeover or collapse. This would require government and businesses to create redundant local networks with independent servers, which would kick in when the internet goes down. These back-ups would maintain vital services and help thwart worst-case scenarios involving diabolical takeovers by AI.
Another option is to unplug from the internet altogether. This seems extreme given the times we live in but that approach has security benefits, as demonstrated in the way we uphold our democracy. Our voting machines and tabulations are separated from the internet and the system is backed up by paper ballots in virtually every state. Likewise, our nuclear weapon systems are isolated from the public internet.
Imagine if internet connectivity was a business option and not an accepted fact. It’s something to think about at all levels, including individual transactions. Would it be too retro to incentivize renewed use of cash and checks?
Disentangling our nation’s vital services from internet failures provides some peace of
mind. Certainly, it wouldn’t be the whole answer. AI might attack us with drones, robots and viruses so they say. To meet the challenges, in addition to reducing our dependency on the internet, the time has come to legislate guardrails on AI development.
Humans don’t heed warnings very well unless something collapses in a visible way and people get hurt. Our lackadaisical mindset hurts our response to problems like climate change. It permeates the financial sector with risky acceptance of cryptocurrency.
We’re slow to react in many other ways, including the new existential threat from AI. We’ve let the genie out of the bottle and now we have to figure out what to do.
It’s hard to slow technological wheels from turning. The AI race is being fueled by the inertia of greed and competition, including fears about China winning the race. It’s hard to urge caution when it comes to human exploration. In the 19th century, the British military crushed the Luddite rebellion over textile workers’ resistance to job-changing automation. The Luddites, who wanted fair labor practices, have been wrongly characterized as anti-technology ever since.
Today, our equivalent of the Luddite rebellion isn’t destroying AI models or the internet, it’s having the foresight and courage to manage them safely and wisely.

title: ‘We’re lucky to be alive’: Women recount slamming head-on into water buffalo at 52 mph
text:
STOCKHOLM, N.Y. (WWNY/Gray News) - Two New York women say they are lucky to be alive after they crashed head-on into a water buffalo on their way home from a church event.
Kristen Rozelle, 50, was driving Lindsey Baker, 27, home from a church event around 7 p.m. Saturday when their Jeep collided head-on with a water buffalo in the town of Stockholm.
“If you look at my Jeep, we’re lucky to be alive. Literally, if I did not have a Jeep Limited, I’d be dead,” Rozelle said.
Rozelle said she was traveling 52 mph before hitting the water buffalo that weighed about 2,300 pounds, according to a state trooper. She said it felt like hitting a freight train.
“All of a sudden, I just see black. I didn’t see anything at all. And then, boom,” she said. “We didn’t know it was even there.”
“I’m like, ‘What did we hit?’” Baker said.
Good Samaritans helped after the crash
Rozelle said she passed out briefly after the crash. When she came to, smoke from the deployed airbags made her think the Jeep was on fire. The airbags blocked the door handles, making it difficult to get out.
Baker said she saw the airbags and smoke and heard Rozelle yelling to get out of the Jeep.
“I turned to see, and then, she’s panicking. She can’t get out, so I checked to see if she was still buckled. She wasn’t,” Baker said.
Baker said she got out of the Jeep.
“I ran into the road to get help, to wave the car down,” she said. “Thankfully, there were some people who came, and I directed them to where we were.”
Those good Samaritans helped the two women until first responders arrived and took them to the hospital.
“The people were so wonderful and beautiful to help us,” Rozelle said. “That’s the real story here is just that humanness. When we needed it the most, they were there.”
Rozelle said she sustained sprains and bruises throughout her body, along with cuts on her leg and hand, while Baker said she had bruises on her legs and chest.
“We didn’t walk out of this with nothing,” Rozelle said. “We’re struggling each in our own way.”
A water buffalo?
An eyewitness told Rozelle he saw the water buffalo run across a field and jump the guardrail toward her Jeep. The animal died in the crash.
Rozelle said seeing photos of her crumpled Jeep reinforced just how serious this incident was.
“I knew I was lucky. But when I saw the Jeep, I realized how much more. God’s arms were around me. There’s no other way to express that,” she said. “My Jeep is this huge vehicle, and it was crumpled to nothing in a moment’s notice.”
Baker said she was stunned after learning what they had hit.
“I was in disbelief,” she said. “It had horns. It was black, and that’s all I could see from when the ambulance turned to head to the hospital.”
Rozelle said she wants the focus to remain on the women’s survival, rather than the animal involved.
“I want people to see the Jeep and not the bull anymore,” Rozelle said. “Our lives are worth something... We’re alive. And that’s a miracle. Absolute miracle.”
State police said the owner of the water buffalo, who lives near the crash site, spoke with a trooper at the scene.
Rozelle said she has heard nothing from the owner.
“The only thing that I know is that nobody’s reached out to us,” she said. “And they knew that we almost died... On a human component of it, that’s just a really hard thing.”
Water buffalo, originating from parts of Asia, can weigh more than a ton and stand 6 feet tall.

title: Booking a flight by phone? One airline will now charge you extra for that
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(CNN) - Air Canada has started charging a fee for reservations booked with a live person, $30 per ticket.
The fee applies per ticket, so a pair of seats booked over the phone costs $60.
The fee is non-refundable, even if the ticket is canceled.
Why Air Canada made the change
Air Canada made the change because it wants customers to use its website or app to book flights.
Who is exempt from Air Canada’s phone booking fee?
There are a few exceptions.
Passengers who need special care, like wheelchair assistance, will not be charged.

FDA issues highest-risk warning for cheese recall after more than a dozen sickened
text:
(Gray News) - The FDA issued its highest-risk warning for a California-based company amid concerns over a multistate cheese E. coli outbreak.
The Class I classification applied to all affected Graziers raw milk cheese products manufactured by California-based Sierra Nevada Cheese Company, including Monterey Jack, jalapeño jack, medium cheddar and sharp cheddar varieties, according to a press release.
The affected products were distributed in Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, Texas, Washington and Wisconsin.
Investigators said 13 people in nine states became sick. More than half of those infected were children age 5 and younger.
The company announced the initital recall on Sept. 28.
The company is telling consumers not to eat any of the recalled cheeses. People should either throw the cheeses out or return them to the store where they were purchased for a refund.

title: UMaine outlines non-academic cuts to address budget shortfall
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MAINE (WABI) - The University of Maine and University of Maine at Machias have announced planned non-academic cuts to help close a projected $19 million budget shortfall for Fiscal Year 2028.
In a previous letter, University President Joan Ferrini-Mundy announced $10 million would be cut from academic affairs, which makes up roughly half of the budget.
In a letter posted to the university’s website Wednesday, leaders outlined the non-academic changes, though they say they are limited in adjustments due to existing collective bargaining agreements.
University leaders say they hope the changes will account for about $6 million of the $9 million non-academic shortfall, adding that plans to close the remaining $3 million gap will be their main focus in the coming weeks.
Strategies include changing the length of annually appointed contract staff, cutting back on overtime, eliminating vacant positions, consolidating units, seeking outside funding through sponsorships and licensing opportunities, added facility fees for those outside of the university, fee increases, and the sale of property and other assets.
The adjustments will impact multiple departments including athletics, student life, research, strategic partnerships, resources, innovation and engagement, Finance and Administration & Facilities Management, and the President’s Office, which includes Cultural Affairs and Marketing and Communications.
The university says it also hopes to increase revenue by hosting more events and conferences on campus while planning around numerous variables, including projected enrollment as well as state and federal funding.

title: Registered nurses at Houlton hospital want CEO fired
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Registered nurses at Houlton Regional Hospital on Wednesday called on the board of trustees to terminate the hospital’s top leader immediately in a petition of no confidence, according to the nurses union.
The 55 Houlton registered nurses, members of the Maine State Nurses Association/National Nurses Organizing Committee, said Wednesday that CEO Jeff Zewe has caused “significant damage to the hospital and community” in his 16-month tenure.
In response, the Board of Trustees said they stand “fully and unanimously” behind CEO Zewe.
“We have complete confidence in his leadership, the direction he has set for Houlton Regional Hospital and his vision for its long-term future,” Board of Trustees Chairwoman Lynette McLaughlin said. “Under his guidance, we are building an organization that will serve our community with excellence for generations to come.”
Wednesday’s action comes on the heels of a letter of no confidence sent to Zewe earlier this month by registered nurses at Northern Maine Medical Center in Fort Kent, which he also leads. The northern Maine nurses issued the letter after half of the emergency department nurses resigned citing a toxic environment created by Zewe.
The nurses bargaining unit and hospital executives have been battling over safety and staffing concerns at both the Fort Kent facility and Houlton Regional Hospital. As contract negotiations appeared to drag on, especially related to emergency department staffing and patient safety concerns, several nurses expressed frustrations with leadership during multiple strikes and other public actions.
The Houlton nurses called a four-day strike in May, the second strike in six months, and still don’t have a contract.
Northern Maine Medical Center registered nurse Ami Maxwell said earlier this month that six emergency department nurses resigned and more were looking for new jobs. The nurses did not want to leave, but chose to look for new positions because it is an “awful toxic” work environment, Maxwell said.
Each hospital has 25 acute care beds and is classified as critical access, meaning it can claim some higher federal reimbursement rates. Combined, the two facilities serve almost half of Aroostook County’s 70,000 people, according to hospital officials.
In June 2025, Zewe, who had led the Fort Kent hospital since 2022, took on the Houlton hospital leadership in a management agreement intended to increase patient access, enhance quality outcomes and improve the long-term financial stability of both hospitals, with a more “formal affiliation” as its goal, hospital officials said at the time.
Zewe took the Houlton hospital reins a month after its labor, delivery, recovery and postpartum department closed on May 2, 2025.
The hospital’s medical executive committee felt compelled to respond to allegations recently published in the press, Dr. Soloman Olabiyi said Wednesday.
“The allegations presented in recent press coverage do not reflect our firsthand experience,” he said. “As physicians directly involved in delivering care, our assessment is grounded in our daily work and observations.”
Olabiyi said the committee unanimously supports the positive changes made under Zewe, including improvements in the quality of care, recruitment of highly qualified staff, and a patient-centered approach that has strengthened patient safety and care for the community.
Yet Zewe’s tenure in Maine mirrors similar concern from unionized nurses at hospitals he previously led in New York and Pennsylvania.
The New York State Nurses Association reported 753 formal protests of assignment — written documents notifying the employer that a nursing assignment is unsafe — signed by 2,820 nurses from 2019 to 2020 at Olean General Hospital. Zewe held executive leadership roles at the hospital from 2015 to 2021.
He was appointed chief operating officer in 2015 and chief executive officer in 2020. By June 2021, Olean nurses were publicly describing severe staffing pressures, according to multiple news accounts and New York State Nurses Association statements. He resigned in 2021, although no reason was given for his departure, according to a hospital statement.
Zewe did not comment about his previous employment when the Bangor Daily News asked him on Wednesday.
Since he has been in Maine, multiple complaints have been filed with the state Labor Relations Board by union members, claiming retaliatory actions by hospital leadership. The BDN has filed Freedom of Access Act requests with the labor board to access details of five open cases and is awaiting a response.
Houlton registered nurses said Wednesday they must take action “while there is still time to preserve and protect our community hospital.”
The nurses told the board of trustees in a written statement that they have no confidence in Zewe’s leadership for the following reasons: Failure to retain staff and local expertise; diminishing security capacity; failure to staff appropriately; failure to reach a fair contract; reliance on outside consultants; and creating an unhealthy culture.
Chief Operating Officer Gina Brown disagreed and said that retaining employees has been a top priority since Zewe became CEO.
“I can say with confidence that we are in a better place today under Jeff’s leadership,” Brown said. “We are on the right track to continue delivering quality care to the patients and families of our community.”
The bargaining committee, which includes registered nurses Tori Quint, operating room; Mary Howland, acute care department; Erin Mitchell, emergency department; Cassidy Hardy, acute care; Brooke Howland, acute care; Christina Schimdt, operating room; and Kelli Lawlor, operating room, sent a letter of no confidence in Zewe to the board of trustees in July and invited the board to a meeting to hear their concerns.
“They didn’t show up. All we’ve heard is silence,” several members of the bargaining committee said in a Wednesday statement. “We are greatly saddened that the Houlton Regional Hospital Board of Trustees didn’t keep its word to listen to employees.”

title: 7-year-old girl’s body exhumed months after death from alleged abuse
text:
SUFFOLK COUNTY, N.Y. (WABC) — The body of a 7-year-old New York girl has been exhumed months after her death, according to her mother’s attorney.
Prosecutors said Jor’Dynn Duncan suffered months of abuse before dying from an untreated infection.
Attorney Heather Palmore said her client, Portia Duncan, gave authorization to the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office for Jor’Dynn’s body to be exhumed.
“We don’t know why they asked for the exhumation of Jor’Dynn’s body,” Palmore said. “What I will say is, in my experience as a former prosecutor, there may be things or evidence that they’re looking to corroborate or uncover.”
Mother described as devastated
Palmore said the 7-year-old’s mother is emotional over the exhumation but understands it is a necessary part of getting to the truth and getting justice for Jor’Dynn.
“She’s devastated,” Palmore said. “It is a nightmare for her. It’s a nightmare for her family and those who love Jor’Dynn.”
Details of the case
According to prosecutors, the girl endured months of alleged systematic cruelty and sadistic abuse, much of which was recorded on a cellphone, before dying from a massive untreated infection from her injuries.
The 7-year-old had about 90 injuries on her body at the time of her death, according to the Suffolk County Medical Examiner’s Office.
Jor’Dynn’s legal guardian, Emily Kelly, her mother, Barbara Renner, and Kelly’s daughter, Elyssa Seymore, are all facing charges in connection with the child’s death and previously pleaded not guilty.
“Any reasonable person would have been able to conclude that something was wrong here,” Palmore said.
The second grader was taken out of her mother’s custody after an alleged failed drug test.
Notice of claim filed
In July, Portia Duncan’s attorneys filed a notice of claim alleging the county, Bayport-Blue Point School District and others were negligent in monitoring her health and safety and failed to intervene.
Palmore said they will be filing a lawsuit shortly.
“It’ll be very clear that the institutions that were set in place and that we rely on to take care of children when their parents can’t, that they failed her,” Palmore said.
The Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office declined to comment. The three women charged in the case are awaiting trial.

Vance says he’s ‘disgusted’ by GOP pushback to Ramaswamy ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Vice President JD Vance said during a campaign visit to Ohio on Wednesday that he is “disgusted” by the Republican pushback against an ad by Vivek Ramaswamy that features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent in the governor’s race, Dr. Amy Acton, and raises questions about her traumatic childhood.
“Politics is a tough business,” Vance said to reporters.
In Cincinnati, the vice president said it was “not really my concern” whether the controversial 60-second spot was appropriate, and said he was focused on supporting Republican candidates in their midterm races.
“I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” Vance said in his first public comments on the ad, which has roiled one of the most contentious and expensive governor’s races in the country.
The advertisement features Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her “a liar” and insinuating she has mental health issues. It was criticized by both Democrats and Republicans when it exploded into public view Tuesday, just two weeks before Election Day.
Ramaswamy, a billionaire tech entrepreneur and 2024 Republican presidential candidate, claimed credit for the ad and said he will spend $4 million to promote it despite the backlash from some members of his own party. He didn’t address it in remarks before Vance spoke at a rally outside Cincinnati.
Acton, Ohio’s former health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child.
Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather was indicted for raping Acton. Police and court records show Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton’s biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978.
Her campaign on Tuesday posted a video of her brother who supported her backstory about living in a tent and being abused.
In his remarks to reporters ahead of the rally, Vance said Acton, “lies about every single one of her positions.”

title: Vance says GOP shouldn’t complain about Ramaswamy ad with Amy Acton’s estranged mother
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Vice President JD Vance defended an ad Wednesday by Vivek Ramaswamy that features the estranged mother of Dr. Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent for Ohio governor, and spotlights the abuse she experienced as a child, even as the Republican in a tight race to retain Vance’s former seat in the Senate distanced himself from the ad.
During a campaign visit to Ohio, Vance told reporters he was “disgusted” by fellow Republicans who were pushing back against the ad, then later drew cheers at a political rally when he defended Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and 2024 presidential candidate.
Vance said he has watched Democrats “throw every dirty trick in the political book at Vivek,” who he considers a close personal friend -- including calling him a ‘murderer’ — while “the whole time Vivek has stood tall and talked about what he wants to accomplish.”
“And now the media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because, guess what, Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out as it is and calls Amy Acton a liar,” he said.
During the same rally, U.S. Sen. Jon Husted shared the stage with Vance and Ramaswamy, but steered clear of discussing the ad, in which Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, calls her daughter “a liar” and insinuates that she has mental health issues. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather was indicted for raping Acton, and the candidate has not seen her since 1978.
“I would not have run that ad,” Husted said in a statement to The Associated Press. A day earlier, his Democratic opponent, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, called the spot “disgusting” and said everybody — including Husted — should denounce it.
President Donald Trump also weighed in Wednesday, telling reporters he knew nothing about the ad but had heard that “the mother went very rogue on the daughter.”
“It’s a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much, but I don’t think that has anything to do with Vivek,” the president said.
‘Let’s heal,’ Acton implores voters
Acton, Ohio’s former state health director, spent the day traveling to a previously scheduled campaign appearance in rural Wyandot County, in the northwestern part of the state. Her campaign also released a new positive ad, which — somewhat ironically — featured her appealing to voters to “find more breathing room, and let’s heal what has divided us.” She has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child.
In Cincinnati, the vice president said “politics is a tough business” and that the contents of Ramaswamy’s ad were “not really my concern.” He said he was focused on supporting Republican candidates in the midterm elections.
“I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” Vance said in his first public comments on the ad, which has roiled one of the most contentious and expensive governor’s races in the country.
Some Republicans denounce ad, Ramaswamy. Haley calls him ‘a bad guy’
The video was criticized by both Democrats and Republicans when it exploded into public view Tuesday, just two weeks before Election Day.
Nikki Haley, who sparred with Ramaswamy during the 2024 Republican presidential primary over the personal nature of his attacks, called him “a bad guy” in a social media post Tuesday. “It’s a shame he continues to get away with it,” she wrote. Meghan McCain called it “dastardly” and Dan Hauser, a long-time aide to Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, said he deleted his post sharing the video once he realized “the very serious accusations that caused their issues.”
The Ramaswamy campaign’s initial statement on the ad did not claim responsibility for its production, but the candidate eventually did so when he spoke to reporters at an evening campaign event. His campaign will spend $4 million to air it on TV and online in the closing weeks of the race, despite the backlash. He didn’t address the ad in remarks at the rally where Vance spoke outside Cincinnati.
Police and court records show Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton’s biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur, who has since died, failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive.
Acton said she has not seen her mother since she appeared in a courtroom in the late 1970s. Her campaign on Tuesday posted a video of her brother who supported her backstory about living in a tent and being abused.
Vance told reporters before the rally that Acton “lies about every single one of her positions.”
Acton’s campaign declined to respond to Vance’s comments, saying that her painful backstory was not the centerpiece of her run for governor.
Voter: ‘I don’t think it’s right’
Michael Wedding, 20, came to Vance’s rally Wednesday — but not to support Ohio’s Republican ticket. He said he would be parting with his large Republican family and vote for Acton for governor, adding that he attended the rally in large part to see Ramaswamy in person.
He said he had seen the ad and found it “very, very gross.”
“She was sexually abused as a child,” he said of Acton, ”and I thought it was kind of scummy that they would use that in an advertisement. I don’t think it’s right to use her sexual abuse as a kid, or give any sort of platform to that.”
___
Binkley reported from Washington. Associated Press video journalist Patrick Aftoora-Orsagos contributed to this story from Sharonville, Ohio.

title: Gunman opens fire into family’s car on Florida interstate, injuring 2 children
text:
MACCLENNY, Fla. (WCJB/Gray News) - Authorities in Florida are searching for a gunman who opened fire on a mother and her two children as they drove on Interstate 10.
Baker County sheriff’s deputies said the family left Macclenny and entered the interstate headed east toward Jacksonville around 11 p.m. Sunday, when someone in another vehicle shot at them.
A 6-year-old child was shot in the arm, and an 11-year-old was hurt by bullet fragments. Both children were treated for their injuries and are recovering.
Deputies say the family may have been followed from their Macclenny home onto the interstate.
Detectives have not publicly identified any suspects and ask anyone who may have information to call 904-259-9218 or report anonymously to First Coast Crime Stoppers at 866-845-8477.
