title: Video shows moments leading up to deadly police shooting at Walmart that killed 1-year-old child
text:
SENATOBIA, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - Video has been obtained showing the moments leading up to a shooting involving Senatobia police that killed a 1-year-old child in June.
Darkhorse Press released the video days after Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s office determined the officers’ actions that day were justified.
The footage included five videos: three body-camera videos from Senatobia officers and two surveillance videos from Walmart.
On June 14, Senatobia police responded to an alleged shoplifting involving diapers at an area Walmart involving two women.
One-year-old Kohen Wiley was inside a car with his mother, who was holding him, and his great-aunt, who was driving when the shooting occurred.
One of the released videos from that day shows the store’s security guard talking to the child’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, and his great-aunt.
Moments later, video showed the child, identified as Kohen Wiley, being held by his mother while they were running to the car.
Kohen’s mother gets in the passenger seat of the vehicle with him, while the other woman jumps into the driver’s seat.
Another video showed law enforcement officers in the store’s loss prevention office being interrupted by a store employee saying, “Two women are running.”
Moments later, video showed law enforcement officers running after Vellesiya Wiley and the other woman as both got into the car.
Officers were then seen in front of the car as the driver backed out of the parking spot, telling the driver to stop with guns drawn.
However, the driver appears to then drive toward officers, hitting one and crossing into the next parking lot aisle, striking a parked vehicle, prompting police to shoot.
It was unclear from the videos provided which officers fired their weapons. One-year-old Kohen Wiley did not survive the shooting.
Body-camera video from the officer who was hit by the vehicle was not part of the videos released.
In the final body-camera video that was released, officers were outside of an emergency medical center, where one can be heard saying, “I didn’t even see a f—ing baby in her lap.”
“Nobody knew the baby was there,” another officer said. “All I saw was two females in the car.”
The footage appears to contradict parts of Vellesiya Wiley’s previous account.
In a June 17 video statement released through attorneys Ben Crump and Van Turner, Vellesiya Wiley said she continued walking “because it had nothing to do with me” after officers stopped her friend, and said her friend drove toward the other side of the lot, away from officers.
Vellesiya Wiley also previously said she had lifted Kohen up “trying to show them that he was in the car” after seeing officers draw their guns.
According to the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, it has assigned five agents to the case, with investigators reviewing witness statements, body- and dash-camera video and Walmart surveillance video.
The officer who fired was placed on administrative leave, which city leaders said was standard practice after deadly police shootings.
In July, Kohen Wiley’s cause of death was ruled a homicide, according to an independent autopsy report requested by the family.
Van Turner, along with civil rights attorney Ben Crump, is representing the Wiley family. They have renewed calls for MBI and Walmart to release all surveillance video from the incident.
WMC has reached out to the Mississippi Department of Public Safety about the released videos through Darkhorse Press and whether there were plans to release the videos independently.
DPS said it still plans to sit down with the Wiley family this week and then release it.
Family attorneys were aware of the video and plan to meet with the family Thursday to review the video themselves.

title: Are Maine’s votes for sale?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Millions of dollars have been pouring into Maine lately, and not because outsiders think we Mainers are swell folks. No.
They could have sent large checks to the state treasurer for that. Instead, that money has been sent for specialists to pummel us with skewed political assertions. But a lie repeated is still a lie. Repetition does not make something true.
PAC dollars are an investment in Sen. Collins’ votes because that’s where the donors’ gravy is. The only hope they have to get Collins’ votes is to buy ours. Is our vote for sale?
Thankfully, Sen. Collins does have some successes to show. However, increasingly her votes have sent a lot more money elsewhere, including the president’s whims. Really, 30 years of influence buys us road salt, cement and concrete?
Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me six times, shame on me.
M-A Barker
Scarborough

title: ‘I thought I lost my baby’: Mother speaks out after toddler found alive in morgue
text:
GILBERT, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - New details are emerging in the case of an 18-month-old boy who was pronounced dead at an Arizona hospital, only to be found alive in the morgue hours later.
Vincent Fiordilino, 18 months, was taken to Mercy Gilbert Medical Center on Feb. 8 after nearly drowning in a swimming pool. He was pronounced dead — but five hours later, he was found alive in the hospital morgue.
Now, nearly eight months after the incident, Vincent’s mother, Alexus Fiordilino, is speaking publicly for the first time. She said she still relives that day.
“I didn’t even think stuff like that happened. I thought I lost my baby, and he was back,” she said. “There isn’t a day I don’t think about that day.”
The incident began when the family found Vincent floating face down in a pool at a Super Bowl party. Police arrived and performed CPR before paramedics took the toddler to Mercy Gilbert.
Fiordilino said she begged first responders to save her son.
“I remember just begging the police officers and the fire department to just save him,” she said. “I’m saying goodbye. And I’m begging him. I’m just begging Vincent to come back.”
Hours later, she got the call that he was alive.
“I remember feeling really grateful. And I remember just wanting to rush to him. I needed to get back to him. I felt so bad that he was alone,” she said.
Attorney questions canceled test, delayed labs
The family’s attorney says new documents reveal a potential lapse in care, stating the doctor ordered then canceled a test that would have shown how much oxygen was in Vincent’s blood.
The toddler arrived at the hospital around 6:04 p.m. on Feb. 8. At 6:08 p.m., a doctor ordered an arterial blood gas test to check oxygen in the blood. That test was canceled, according to documents shared by the family’s attorney. At 6:11 p.m., labs were collected. At 6:20 p.m. — nine minutes later — Vincent was pronounced dead.
Body camera footage shows officers asking at 6:13 p.m., “Do we have results on the gas yet?” Staff responded they did not. Those results did not come in until 6:38 p.m., 18 minutes after the toddler was declared dead.
The documents also show the doctor did not sign his report until the day after Vincent was found alive.
“I think that man failed to do his job properly... He failed my son in every step of the way,” Fiordilino said.
Gilbert Police are asking the Arizona Attorney General’s Office to review the case for possible felony child abuse charges against the doctor. The family’s attorney said they will be filing a complaint against the hospital and doctor next week.
Fiordilino said she believes if doctors had waited for the lab results, Vincent would be in a very different place. The toddler has significant medical issues that will require lifelong care, the family’s attorney said.
“We trusted the professionals that took an oath, made a promise, that they would do everything they could. And they looked at my son for whatever reason and decided he wasn’t worth it,” she said.
The attorney general’s office said it has not decided whether to review the case at this time.

title: Maine’s Youth Deer Hunting Days to be held this week
text:
Licensed junior hunters are allowed to harvest a deer on Friday or Saturday, an opportunity to try their luck before the firearms season opens for adults.
For 20-plus years, the state offered a single Youth Deer Hunting Day. In 2023, Maine expanded that program to two days. Any child under 16 years old can get a junior license and must be accompanied on Youth Deer Hunting Days by an adult who meets certain licensing or safety criteria.
Archery season for deer is already underway and will end in most parts of the state on Oct. 30. Firearms season for deer starts for adult residents on Oct. 31 and nonresidents on Nov. 2. The last day for residents and nonresidents is Nov. 28.
Muzzleloader season for deer starts Nov. 30 and ends Dec. 5 in most parts of the state. The season extends in December only in certain districts.
In 2025, the total number of deer harvested was 55,876 — many more than other types of large game, according to data on the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife website.
For more information about Youth Deer Hunting Days, as well as general regulations, such as season dates and bag limits, visit the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife website.

title: Man accused of throwing knives at police during standoff in Waterville
text:
Man accused of throwing knives at police during standoff in Waterville, Maine
A man from Waterville is facing a list of charges after police say he threw knives at them during an hours-long standoff on Tuesday night.
Police say they first went to a home on Autumn Street in Waterville at about 6 p.m. to look for John Whitney, 41, who was wanted on terrorizing charges alleging he made several online threats over the previous day.
Police say Whitney refused to open the door to his apartment and threatened to shoot and kill officers several times.
Police set up a perimeter and called in crisis negotiators.
After a few hours, police say Whitney started throwing knives at officers around the perimeter, while still remaining inside his apartment.
At about midnight, the Maine State Police tactical team was able to arrest Whitney.
He was taken to MaineGeneral Medical Center, Thayer campus, to be treated for minor injuries and then taken to the Kennebec County Jail.
Whitney is charged with aggravated reckless conduct, criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon, terrorizing, refusing to submit to arrest or detention, and creating a police standoff.
He is scheduled to be in court in late December.

title: Chemical tank explodes in Ohio, forcing evacuations and prompting fears of another blast
text:
Chemical tank leak in Ohio forces evacuations as city allows plume to vent
A ruptured chemical tank billowed a white plume into the air for hours Wednesday, forcing hundreds of residents out of their homes due to the potentially toxic leak and the possibility of an explosion.
More than 50,000 people in Toledo, Ohio, were advised to stay indoors as a precaution.
City leaders were allowing the chemical to vent instead of trying to stop the leak, saying that would be more dangerous. Videos show a plume still swirling from the tank early Wednesday afternoon, more than 14 hours after the tank began leaking Tuesday night in an industrial area.
Some residents felt irritation in their eyes and throats and sought treatment, and city officials said one sheriff's deputy who responded to the blast later drove himself to a hospital because he felt unwell.
Mark White Jr., who lives within the affected area, was sleeping with his windows open and woke to what he described as a burning plastic smell. He decided to evacuate to a shelter at an elementary school because he has asthma.
"I don't know what this chemical can do to my lungs, long term or anything," White said.
Video below: Dense fog takes over Toledo neighborhood after release of chemical nearby
MC Tank Transport said the tank contained glycidyl methacrylate, which it described as "an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better."
The Ohio Environmental Protection Agency said without elaborating that the leak happened because of an error while the material was being transferred.
Mayor says the chemical leak has slowed
Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz said Wednesday afternoon there was no reason to panic and that the city was working with state and federal environmental officials.
He said they decided to allow the tank to continue releasing the chemical because there was little threat to the public and that it would be more dangerous to ask first responders to go near the chemical trucking company's facility where more tanks were stored.
"There's no question the situation is improving," said Kapszukiewicz, who added that drones monitoring the leaking tank show its temperature is dropping and that the plume is diminishing.
Still, it could take hours before the tank is safe to approach, he said.
Nearly 1,000 residents were told to evacuate overnight within a 1-mile (1.6-kilometer) radius of the leak.
A shelter-in-place order for more than 50,000 people covering a 3-mile (4.8-kilometer) radius included neighborhoods along the Lake Erie shoreline and stretched just across the state line into Michigan. Schools across the city were closed Wednesday, and automaker Stellantis shut down production at its nearby Jeep assembly plant.
Residents worry about chemical's risks
Health officials said the symptoms reported so far were primarily eye and throat irritation. Testing was ongoing to determine the chemical's concentration in the air and whether it posed additional health risks.
ProMedica, which operates hospitals and urgent care centers in the Toledo area, said it evaluated about 30 people who reported symptoms that might have been related to the leak. Most were treated and released, the health care provider said.
Residents well beyond the shelter-in-place zone described smelling paint or burning chemicals. City officials tried to assure them that the odors did not indicate there was anything harmful in the air.
Kristine Kowalinski, who lives just outside the affected area, said she was staying inside because she's sensitive even to smoke from wood burning. She said she's worried about what's in the air and on the ground.
"My main concern is how did that affect everything overnight when it was raining down on cars, houses, my garden," she said.
Kapszukiewicz said the chemical is liquid inside the tank but becomes a gas when released. Officials began worrying early on that the tank, which can hold 5,500 gallons of the chemical, could explode, he said.
Chemical can irritate eyes and cause headaches
People who come into contact with glycidyl methacrylate may feel as if their eyes, nose, mouth and skin are burning, the city fire department said. Overexposure can cause headaches, dizziness, tiredness, nausea and vomiting.
"It's really toxic if you touch it, if you ingest it," said Karim Baroudi, director of the Toledo-Lucas County Health Department. "Now we're trying to kind of determine how much of a toxicity is in the air that the people are breathing so we can give better guidance."
Baroudi advised residents to close their windows and that those who "feel irritation in the eyes, heavily breathing, just take a shower for now." The fire department said those who experience symptoms should contact a medical professional.
Emergency and hazardous material crews were not approaching the tank because of the risk of an explosion, Kapszukiewicz said.
Arkansas-based MC Tank Transport said in a statement the company is working with the fire department and other emergency authorities. Company representatives were on their way to Toledo, Kapszukiewicz said.
"Our immediate and overriding concern is the safety of area residents, emergency responders and our employees," the company said.
___
McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire. Associated Press journalists Beatrice Dupuy in New York and Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

title: How a photo of a person’s face could help predict whether they’ll survive cancer treatment
text:
How a photo of a person’s face could help predict whether they’ll survive cancer treatment
A simple selfie could hold surprising clues to your overall health and longevity, especially among people with cancer.
Researchers at Mass General Brigham in Boston have developed artificial intelligence models that they say can predict a cancer patient’s biological age and chances of survival using nothing more than a single photograph of their face.
Related video above | What to know about lung cancer and when to get screened
The research, published Monday in the journal The Lancet Digital Health, suggests that facial analysis could become an additional tool for doctors to consider when evaluating a patient’s chances of survival and when deciding which treatment approaches may work best for their cancer patients.
“I was pretty surprised to find out that we could pick up signs of mortality risk from just a facial photograph,” said study author Dr. Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist at Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute and a faculty member in the Artificial Intelligence in Medicine program at Mass General Brigham.
The AI models – trained on more than 40 million facial images – specifically assess different aspects of the face to gauge a cancer patient’s overall health and biological age.
Unlike chronological age, which measures the number of years a person has lived, biological age reflects how well the body has aged at the cellular and physical level.
“The age estimation algorithm is looking at the area around the temples, the area on the forehead, above the eyes and then what we call the nasolabial fold, the line that connects the nose down to the corner of your mouth,” Mak said of what parts of the face the AI models consider when assessing biological age.
“In contrast, the mortality risk prediction algorithm is looking at a totally different part of the face,” Mak said. “It’s looking at the bridge of the nose and the area under the eyes.”
Eerily, the same regions of the face that the AI model assesses to predict biological age and survival are the same parts that Greek physician and philosopher Hippocrates referenced in the Book of Prognostics, written around 400 B.C., when he described “the nose sharp, the eyes sunken, the temples fallen in” as signs of muscle wasting and mortality risk.
“To think that our algorithms might be replicating that wisdom of Hippocrates from millennia ago was mind-blowing to us,” Mak said.
The AI algorithms had no awareness of Hippocrates’ ancient texts, because “our algorithms are trained purely on face photographs and then whether somebody died or not, or their age,” Mak said.
“It does not factor in the text, knowledge or wisdom that’s aggregated on the internet,” he added. “So hearing Hippocrates echo over millennia in our algorithms was very eerie.”
Mak and his colleagues originally built a robust AI model called the Foundation Artificial Intelligence for Health Recognition-Face (FAHR-Face) that was trained on more than 40 million facial images spanning diverse ages and ethnic backgrounds.
The model was then fine-tuned and used as a foundation to build two other models that could perform specific tasks: The FAHR-FaceAge model estimates the biological age of someone based on a single photo, and the FAHR-FaceSurvival model predicts a cancer patient’s chances of survival by combining facial features with other clinical information.
With the FAHR-FaceSurvival model, the researchers found that among 122 cancer patients who were indicated by the model to have a high risk of death, more than half – 52.5% – died within 90 days of the assessment, as predicted. In comparison, only about 2% of the 975 patients in the lowest-risk FAHR-FaceSurvival group died within 90 days.
When evaluating the FAHR-FaceAge model, the researchers found that 21% of the 1,060 patients whose biological age was more than 20 years above their chronological age died within 90 days. In comparison, about 6% of the 4,195 patients with biological ages at least 10 years younger than their chronological age died within 90 days.
The researchers found that cosmetic changes to the face – such as surgery, injectables like Botox or makeup – did not affect the AI models’ performance.
‘A promising proof of concept’
The study authors emphasize that their AI models are not intended to replace physicians or existing clinical evaluations. Instead, they describe the technology as an emerging tool that could someday help inform a doctor’s assessment of a patient’s health or their decision-making around treatment options.
“If we can pick up accelerated aging or higher mortality scores early, we might be able to screen for those or identify patients who may benefit from further testing for serious conditions earlier,” Mak said.
And while the new study was conducted only among cancer patients, Mak said more research could reveal whether similar findings may emerge among otherwise healthy people who may be interested in their longevity.
The study’s use of AI technology is fascinating but still needs to be evaluated clinically, said Dr. Wilbur Lam, research chair and professor of pediatrics and biomedical engineering at Emory University.
“This is an extremely compelling study that stems from a large data set and its associations between facial images and biological age as well as cancer survival risk appear to be robust. Its true clinical utility, however, will need to be demonstrated prospectively,” Lam, who was not involved in the study, said in an email.
“Moreover, as the authors themselves allude to, whether this tool can be accurately used for specific subpopulations remains a question,” he said. “For example, how strong the effects are for people with specific facial features, skin color, age groups will also need to be prospectively tested in order for the technology to be clinically implemented.”
The study provides “convincing evidence” of a statistical link between facial appearance and survival in cancer patients receiving radiotherapy, Miroslaw Bober, professor of video processing and machine intelligence at the University of Surrey, said in a statement distributed by the UK-based Science Media Centre.
But “predicting an outcome is not the same as explaining it. Despite the references to ‘biological age’, the AI estimates age from facial appearance rather than directly measuring any underlying biological ageing process,” said Bober, who was not involved in the study.
“The authors link the facial regions the AI relies on to the ‘look of dying’ described by doctors. However, the study did not test whether the AI recognises anything a doctor would not,” Bober said.
“It has not shown that these predictions add clinically useful information beyond doctors’ assessments of a patient’s general health and fitness, which were not measured in the study,” he said. “This is a promising proof of concept, but it is not ready for clinical use. The tool still needs testing against doctors’ own judgement and across different hospitals and patient groups.”
